facts.why: Finding facts for a test, following a procedure, understanding an argument, or learning vocabulary call for different marks, organizers and prompts.

facts.ask: on what device or paper will learners read it, and will anyone be there to explain it?
facts.fact: Who reads the aid, where, and on what
facts.why: A printed sheet in class, a page on a phone, a guide shared with remote learners, a patient handout read alone at home, and a guide translated for second-language readers each need a different format.

facts.ask: what will learners be asked to do at the end, and which part (knowing, applying, speaking, writing) counts most?
facts.fact: Which components the target has, and which the brief will judge
facts.why: A unit judged only on content knowledge needs less of the application-serving method than one judged on applying it.

facts.ask: what has each method been shown to improve, for learners like these, and is either already strongly supported on the outcome that matters?
facts.fact: What evidence each competing method has, and for which component
facts.why: A method with strong evidence for the whole target is kept whole; one whose evidence is for one component is given that component.

facts.ask: who will lead each method, how many minutes a week does each get, and can someone see the learners' work in both?
facts.fact: Who will run each half, and with how much time
facts.why: In the one trial, a method whose live facilitation lapsed lost its knowledge outcome.

principles/harmonize-opposites-in-educat.title: Harmonize opposites: strike a balance between competing educational ideas rather than embracing one method wholesale

facts.ask: does the learner speak, read and write the heritage language, at what level, and when did schooling in it stop?
facts.fact: How far the learner's heritage language is developed, and in which skills
facts.why: A newcomer who reads and writes the heritage language at grade level can transfer that literacy; a child who understands but no longer speaks it, or who has had interrupted schooling, needs it developed before it can carry much.

facts.ask: who in the setting (teachers, aides, peers, families) speaks the learner's language, and how much time could go to it each week?
facts.fact: What the setting can staff and allocate
facts.why: A dual language programme needs bilingual teachers and enough learners sharing one language; a class with one teacher and ten home languages can still assess in both, advise families, use bilingual texts and keep support after transition.

facts.ask: is this about how to teach, how to assess, whom to refer, or when to end support?
facts.fact: What the decision is for
facts.why: Placement, referral for a suspected disorder, exit from support and day-to-day teaching each need a different move, and the evidence differs for each.

principles/heritage-language-maintenance.title: Preserve Heritage Language While Acquiring an Additional Language

facts.ask: before instruction, can they sketch how the main ideas relate, or carry out a simple complete version of the task, and place one detail?
facts.fact: Whether learners already hold an organisation for this content or task
facts.why: Without one they need the whole and the closing placements; with one they need a quick check and the part they lack, and an overview costs time.

facts.ask: will they explain, solve and transfer, or recall specific facts, and in what form will they be assessed?
facts.fact: What they will be asked to do
facts.why: A whole organised around general ideas helped tasks that drew on those ideas and showed no detected benefit on tasks resting on single details.

facts.ask: can one of the top-level ideas be understood without the others?
facts.fact: How much the ideas interact, against the learner's prior knowledge
facts.why: If the whole only makes sense once several new ideas are held together, a novice may not be able to follow it first.

facts.ask: is anyone here directly affected by the issues we will discuss, and can they choose how much of that to share?
facts.fact: Who in the group the social issue touches, and how safe it is to say so
facts.why: A discussion that is identity work for some learners is an academic exercise for others, and what it does may differ between them.

facts.ask: what must learners be able to do at the end, who decides that, and did they choose to come?
facts.fact: What the course is for, and whether it is the learners' choice to be there
facts.why: A voluntary community course can make social questioning its goal; a mandatory workplace or credentialing course has a set target and learners whose employer or assessor holds power over them.

facts.ask: how many sessions, how long each, and how many learners per facilitator?
facts.fact: How much time and facilitation there is
facts.why: Hearing and answering each view takes facilitator time; the evidence here comes from units lasting months.

principles/humanistic-radical-adult-educ.title: Adopt humanistic and radical approaches so adult learners develop as individuals and can question social injustice

facts.ask: in the moments that go wrong, who is there, and how much time and capacity do they have?
facts.fact: Which adult is present when the young person needs to regulate, and whether that adult is available and able
facts.why: A teacher can cue a skill in class, a carer at home, a supervisor at work; an adult under heavy stress may need support for their own regulation before they can co-regulate.

facts.ask: how old are the learners, and have they agreed to the adults being involved?
facts.fact: The young person's age and wishes
facts.why: At 14 the adults around them shape most settings; at 22 the young person chooses whom to involve, and an adult cueing them uninvited can read as control.

facts.ask: what would the young person and the adults see differently, where, and by when?
facts.fact: What counts as success, and in which setting
facts.why: Fewer incidents at school, coping at work, a self-reported skill and achievement are separate outcomes; the adult component should sit in the setting where the target outcome happens.

principles/include-caregivers-as-self-re.title: Include parents, teachers, or mentors in any self-regulation intervention and support their own skills and coaching capacity

facts.ask: when do learners do the work, on what device, and who could they ask at that moment?
facts.fact: When and where learners get stuck, and how they can reach anyone then
facts.why: A learner stuck on a weekday evening in an asynchronous course needs a different route from a pupil stuck in a lesson with the teacher in the room.

facts.ask: how many learners, how many staff hours a week for questions, and when are the deadlines?
facts.fact: How many learners per instructor hour, and how demand peaks
facts.why: Promises that work for 15 learners fail for 300, and demand piles up before deadlines.

facts.ask: who has dropped out or gone quiet in past runs, and why?
facts.fact: Who is least likely to ask
facts.why: Learners who most need help are often the ones who do not use optional routes (low confidence, first in family at university, working full-time, different language or culture of schooling).

facts.ask: who reads an entry, how soon, and what changes because of it?
facts.fact: Will anyone use the entries, and when?
facts.why: A journal that feeds the next class, a feedback reply or the next attempt has evidence behind it; one that is filed and never read had none in the one trial that tested it.

facts.ask: what should a learner be able to do or understand at the end that they could not before, and how will that be checked?
facts.fact: What is the journal for?
facts.why: Understanding course content, planning and self-regulation, professional reflection on practice, language practice with a teacher, and emotional processing are different aims with different evidence and different prompts.

facts.ask: who sees each entry, and does anything about it count towards a mark?
facts.fact: Who reads it, and is it graded?
facts.why: Private, ungraded entries were more analytic than public ones in one course; graded or shared entries invite performance.

facts.ask: name three things learners must do with this topic afterwards, unaided, and when.
facts.fact: What the learner will have to do with the knowledge
facts.why: The organization should be built for those tasks; one built for another task can help nothing or help the wrong task.

facts.fact: How the learner holds the topic now
facts.why: A learner with isolated facts needs a given organization; one with an organization of their own may need it challenged or extended, not replaced; one who cannot yet use any organization may not benefit. If unstated, ask the learner to sort ten items from the topic into groups and say why, before teaching.

facts.ask: do the tasks need learners to connect items, or only to recall each one?
facts.fact: Whether the content has relational structure at all
facts.why: Causes, hierarchies, principles and developments have it; a list of independent items does not, and imposing one adds work without benefit.

facts.ask: on one play-through without help, how much of the scene can the learner retell, and how many words in a sample paragraph are unknown to them?
facts.fact: How far above the learner the material sits
facts.why: Helps carry most when the learner can follow the gist but not every word; a learner who follows nothing needs easier material, and one who follows everything needs no helps.

facts.ask: in a trial scene, which helps did learners open, how often, and before or after trying?
facts.fact: Whether learners will use the help, and when
facts.why: On-demand help works only if it is taken, at the point of difficulty, and not as a way round the task.

facts.ask: will the learner be checked on vocabulary, on following the scene, or on taking part in a conversation like it, and with or without helps?
facts.fact: What counts as success: the words, the whole, or the exchange
facts.why: Glosses help the words looked up more reliably than comprehension of the whole text.

principles/learner-control-information-f.title: Keep the learner in control of the information flow with on-demand tools and supports

facts.ask: on this term's class tasks, with which supports, what can the student do now, and what can they not?
facts.fact: What this student needs that the supported general class cannot yet give
facts.why: Access only (a wheelchair-accessible room, captioning, a reader), adapted curriculum on the same unit, or intensive instruction on a skill far below grade lead to different mixes.

facts.ask: what instruction happens in the separate time, how is progress checked, and which class does the student miss to get it?
facts.fact: What the separate setting would deliver, and what it would displace

facts.ask: who is on the team, does the student take part, and when is the next data check?
facts.fact: Who decides, and how soon the decision is reviewed

facts.ask: which employers have said they will interview, hire or take apprentices from this program, when is their intake, and which credential do they ask for?
facts.fact: Is there an employer who hires at this entry point, on this credential, near the learners?
facts.why: Without one, the link is a hope.

facts.ask: is the learner working now, what do they need to earn and by when, and what kind of work do they want?
facts.fact: What the learner wants from the program, and how soon
facts.why: Someone needing income this month, someone already employed seeking promotion, and a school leaver exploring work need different first steps; and learners chasing pay alone may leave for any better job.

facts.ask: how many hours a week can learners give, at what times, and for how many weeks?
facts.fact: How much time the learners have, and when
facts.why: Working adults and carers leave over time more than over content.

principles/link-programs-to-workforce-en.title: Link program elements to workforce entry points and employer-recognized credentials so learners see an immediate economic payoff

facts.ask: have they used the innovation yet, and when they think about it, what are they concerned about?
facts.fact: Where each person stands now, in concerns and in use
facts.why: A group of nonusers with high informational and personal concerns needs different support from experienced users whose concerns are about student effects.

facts.ask: who will be in touch with each person once they start using it, how often, and for how long?
facts.fact: How much facilitator contact there is after launch
facts.why: The guidance depends on continued, adaptable contact; a one-day event with nothing after it cannot be matched to anyone over time.

facts.ask: can they choose, and will what they say about their concerns, or their use, be seen by anyone who evaluates them?
facts.fact: Whether taking up the innovation is voluntary, and what is at stake for the person
facts.why: Mandated change linked to evaluation is likely, though untested here, to raise personal concerns and make honest reports of concerns less likely.

principles/match-interventions-to-stages.title: Match the form and content of staff development interventions to clients' assessed Stages of Concern

facts.ask: when must the learner do this unaided, in what form, and with what aids?
facts.fact: The horizon and what counts at it
facts.why: A quiz tomorrow, an exam in six weeks and use at work next year need different spacing, different checks and different evidence.

facts.ask: after today, when will the learner next meet this material, and who decides?
facts.fact: How many later encounters the design controls
facts.why: A course with weekly sessions can schedule returns; a one-off workshop or a self-paced app with irregular use cannot, and the returns must be handed to the learner or the software.

facts.fact: What the learner can already do with this material
facts.why: A learner who cannot yet recall or use it needs first learning and short-gap returns; one who already can needs only occasional spaced checks, and extra review is time taken from something else. If unstated, ask for one unaided item now, and another a few days later.

facts.ask: what should be different in the five minutes after the routine, and what over a term?
facts.fact: What the routine is for
facts.why: Settling before a lesson, getting through an assessment, de-escalating after conflict and teaching regulation as a skill are different designs with different doses, and only the last has (review-level) evidence of its own.

facts.ask: are there learners for whom closing their eyes or attending to their body is likely to be distressing, and is there an adult who would notice?
facts.fact: Who the learners are, and what they bring
facts.why: Age, prior experience of mindfulness, and especially stress or trauma history change which practices are safe and how much choice to give.

facts.ask: who will lead it, how confident are they, and how many minutes does the session have?
facts.fact: Who leads it, and how much time they have
facts.why: A trained, willing facilitator with a stable group can run a daily routine; a teacher with one minute and no buy-in, a volunteer, or software cannot do the same thing.

facts.ask: is there a single correct response (or a tolerance) for each item, or must the learner explain or apply an idea to new cases?
facts.fact: What kind of target it is
facts.why: A precise response or an arbitrary pairing suits error minimization; a concept or rule the learner must understand may be better served by an attempt that fails first.

facts.ask: before any teaching, how many of ten items (or how many of ten attempts within the final tolerance) does the learner get right unaided?
facts.fact: The learner's starting response on these items

facts.ask: when must the learner produce the response, with what aids, and how will that be checked?
facts.fact: The horizon and the test conditions
facts.why: Error-free practice with full cues can look good at the end of a session and fade by the next week.

principles/minimize-errors-for-precision.title: Teach response precision and new associations with minimal errors, using mediators and stimulus fading

facts.ask: have these learners had comments from this teacher or tool before, and could they say what each mark means?
facts.fact: Whether the learner already knows the feedback routine and its terms
facts.why: A learner who has never seen your symbols, abbreviations or grammar terms cannot act on them, however accurate they are.

facts.ask: on the last piece of work, did this learner act on most comments, a few, or none, and why?
facts.fact: The learner's writing level and confidence
facts.why: Detailed, comprehensive feedback is reported to overwhelm some students and to suit advanced writers best; a learner who is still developing needs fewer, ordered priorities.

facts.ask: who else comments on this draft, through what channel, and does anyone pull it together?
facts.fact: How many sources of feedback reach the learner at once, and in what form
facts.why: Teacher comments, peer comments and a tool's output on the same draft can disagree or simply pile up.

principles/minimize-student-frustration-.title: Minimize student frustration by making feedback clear, legible, focused, and transparent

facts.ask: what will the learner have to do with these items, and is there a reason behind the order or grouping they could learn instead?
facts.fact: Whether the content is arbitrary for this learner, and what must be done with it
facts.why: A list of names, a foreign word or a fixed order fits a mnemonic; an idea whose parts follow from each other does not, and a goal of reasoning or transfer needs teaching beyond recall.

facts.ask: can the learner recall these items now, and do they know the words the cue uses?
facts.fact: The learner's prior knowledge, ability and language
facts.why: The strongest evidence is for students with mild disabilities and low-ability learners; advanced learners may gain little, and a cue built from words the learner does not know helps no one.

facts.ask: how many minutes are there for these items, now and across later sessions?
facts.fact: How much time there is, and what else could use it
facts.why: Building a mnemonic costs time that retrieval practice could use, and the comparative claims favour retrieval.

facts.ask: can they produce one example of this performance now, unaided, and say why they made its main choices?
facts.fact: What the learner can already do on this task
facts.why: A learner who cannot begin needs a full, slowed, narrated model first; one who succeeds unaided needs at most a brief model of the new decision, and a full model may be redundant.

facts.ask: where do novices' attempts go wrong, and can that choice be seen in the finished work?
facts.fact: Which decisions the finished product hides
facts.why: If the product shows every step (a solved equation), an annotated product may do; if the decisions are invisible (why a writer cut a paragraph, why a nurse checked a line first, how a mentor defused a classroom incident), they have to be narrated or they are not modelled.

facts.ask: is the problem that learners cannot do it, or that they do not try?
facts.fact: What the model is for: the performance, or the learner's belief they can do it
facts.why: Accurate performance calls for an expert's clear, narrated model; confidence and persistence may call for a model the learner sees as similar to themselves, who struggles and recovers.

facts.ask: what does the learner do when the task starts, and what do they say when asked why they stopped or why they did it at all?
facts.fact: Which component is low for these learners
facts.why: The same withdrawal can come from doubt about success, no reason to care, resentment of control, or not belonging, and each calls for a different move.

facts.ask: can the learner leave, and what happens if they do?
facts.fact: Whether taking part is voluntary
facts.why: In a required course, motivation shows in effort and quality; in a voluntary one (an open online course, an optional programme, adult learning in spare time) it shows first as dropout, and anything that discourages early can cost the learner entirely.

facts.ask: how often does anyone look at each learner's work or attendance, and for how long?
facts.fact: Who can see a learner's effort and respond, and how often
facts.why: A tutor with one learner can diagnose and adjust each session; a teacher with thirty, a volunteer with ten minutes, or an unattended platform cannot.

facts.ask: if a learner showed this capability by speaking, drawing or doing instead of writing, would you accept it as the same capability?
facts.fact: Which response modes belong to the goal
facts.why: If the goal includes writing, speaking or performing in a particular way, that mode stays fixed and only other demands vary; if it does not, the format is free to change.

facts.ask: what decision will this result change, for whom, and can it be reversed?
facts.fact: What the result will decide, and how much rides on it
facts.why: A check that steers tomorrow's lesson needs one quick method and a second only where it misleads; a grade, placement or certification near a cut needs at least two methods and calibrated markers.

facts.ask: who will look at the second piece of evidence, for how many learners, and how many minutes each?
facts.fact: Who can collect and read a second kind of evidence, and how much time they have
facts.why: An oral check costs teacher time per learner; peer and self-assessment cost learner time and training; a portfolio costs marking time.

facts.ask: give a 5-minute segment and look at the notes. Do they hold the main points, in whose words, and is anything wrong?
facts.fact: The learner's current notes on material like this
facts.why: A learner who transcribes, or captures little, needs an outline, modelling and pauses; a learner whose notes already catch the main points needs only a purpose and a review routine.

facts.ask: can learners stop or replay the input, and how fast and dense is it?
facts.fact: Pace, mode and control of the stream
facts.why: Live speech the learner cannot pause, a video they can pause, and a text they can reread need different supports.

facts.ask: what will the learner do with these notes, how long after, and will they have them in hand?
facts.fact: What the notes will be used for, and when
facts.why: A recall test next week, a discussion tomorrow, a procedure on the job, and an essay combining several sources call for different notes and a different review.

facts.ask: after watching ten minutes of this work, can the learner name what the performer attended to and why, in terms a practitioner would accept?
facts.fact: How much of the practice the learner can already see
facts.why: A newcomer needs a narrow written focus, short or recorded segments and a full debrief; someone already partly competent can choose their own focus, watch whole live performances and compare with their own practice.

facts.ask: who will talk with the observer about what they saw, for how long, and how soon after?
facts.fact: Who can explain the performance, and when
facts.why: If the performer or a mentor can talk with the observer before and after, the debrief carries the interpretation; if not (a busy shift, a stranger's lesson, a recording), the record and a written key have to.

facts.ask: when will the learner next do this work themselves, and with what support?
facts.fact: What the learner will do next
facts.why: Observation that leads into the learner's own attempt can be judged by that attempt; observation for orientation, career exploration or confidence is judged differently and should not be loaded with a performance check.

facts.ask: how many minutes per fortnight are set aside for instructional work, inside the timetable, and is there a coach whose time is protected from other duties?
facts.fact: How much protected time exists for ongoing work, and whose time it is
facts.why: A study team or peer-coaching cycle that competes with meetings about attendance and test preparation rarely survives.

facts.ask: will anything seen in a peer observation or team meeting reach a teacher's appraisal?
facts.fact: Whether the ongoing work is tied to evaluation
facts.why: Voluntary, non-evaluative participation goes with more reported change; observation that feeds appraisal changes what teachers show.

facts.ask: what will an observer see in a lesson when the practice is in place, and which student measure, if any, is expected to move, and when?
facts.fact: What the target is: observed practice, or student achievement, on what horizon
facts.why: The pooled effect on practice is much larger than on achievement, and the link between them is weak across studies.

principles/ongoing-study-teams-peer-coac.title: Teacher professional development should include ongoing activities like study teams and peer coaching rather than only occasional large-group sessions

facts.ask: shown one correct example, can they say why it is correct, and do they misclassify a near miss?
facts.fact: Whether learners can already recognise or follow a correct case
facts.why: Pairs sharpen a boundary the learner partly holds; they can confuse a learner with no anchor.

facts.ask: what is the commonest wrong answer or wrong classification, and are the cases pictures, symbols or sentences?
facts.fact: What the non-example is: an incorrect solution or a near-miss instance of a category, and in what material
facts.why: The tested evidence is for incorrect solutions in mathematics; for categories, the evidence is borrowed and depends on whether instances are visual, symbolic or verbal.

facts.ask: on what task, with what aids, and when will the learner show they have the boundary?
facts.fact: Which outcome counts
facts.why: Classifying new cases, explaining the deciding feature, and using the right procedure need different checks; comparison has raised procedural knowledge without raising conceptual knowledge.

facts.ask: can each teacher do the one function the lesson needs now, unaided, and have they used it with a class?
facts.fact: What teachers can already do with the tool
facts.why: A teacher who cannot log in or run the basic function needs the short technical walkthrough first; one who operates it fluently but uses it only to display slides needs subject examples and lesson planning, not more training on features.

facts.ask: how many hours of release time are there across the term, and who can check in with a teacher before and after the first lesson with the tool?
facts.fact: Time between sessions and who supports the first lesson
facts.why: The evidence here points at time and tailored support as the conditions for use.

facts.ask: what should a visitor see in a lesson a term from now, and what student work would show the tool did its job?
facts.fact: What counts as success
facts.why: Frequency of use, teachers' confidence, observed use for a learning goal, and student outcomes are different targets.

principles/pd-integration-not-just-techn.title: Professional development should guide teachers on integrating digital content and tools, not just offer technical know-how

facts.ask: have the learners studied this material, and can each answer one question on it alone?
facts.fact: Whether the explainer knows enough to explain correctly
facts.why: A learner meeting material for the first time can pass on errors; one who has studied it gains from explaining.

facts.ask: during peer work, who will hear an explanation, and what happens when it is wrong?
facts.fact: Who can hear the exchange and correct it, and how often
facts.why: The tutoring and scaffolding evidence leans on trained tutors, scripts and monitoring; with one teacher and thirty learners, or no teacher, the structure has to be in the role cards and the check items.

facts.ask: what will each learner do unaided after the peer work, with what aids, and how long after?
facts.fact: What each learner must be able to do alone, and when
facts.why: A pair can produce a correct answer neither learner could give alone.

facts.ask: on a short diagnostic, how far apart are the learners, and do any need a different way of taking part?
facts.fact: What the learners differ in, on this task
facts.why: Differences in prior knowledge call for tailored support and pace; differences in interest for tailored contexts and choice; differences in access for tailored means.

facts.ask: who sees each learner's work, and how often?
facts.fact: Who or what will do the tailoring, and how often they can look
facts.why: Software can tailor every item; a teacher with thirty learners can tailor sections and groups weekly; a volunteer who checks in briefly can tailor one thing.

facts.ask: what must every learner be able to do at the end, and how will it be checked?
facts.fact: Which outcome counts, and whether it is common
facts.why: Engagement, achievement on an aligned test, time saved and a learner's own goal move separately, and a personalized path is only comparable if the final criterion is shared.

facts.fact: What the learner can already do with print
facts.why: A child who knows no letter sounds, an eight-year-old who decodes single syllables but stalls on longer words, and an adult who reads familiar words but cannot attempt new ones need different starting points and different amounts of phonics. If the brief omits it, ask: can the learner say the sounds of the letters, blend three spoken sounds into a word, and read a short invented word?

facts.ask: how old are the learners, how long have they been taught to read, and has a reading difficulty been identified?
facts.fact: The learner's age and the reason they are behind
facts.why: Effects are largest in kindergarten and first grade and smaller, mainly on decoding, for older readers with difficulties; a diagnosed reading disability changes the dose and the expected gain.

facts.ask: what must the learner be able to read or write, and how will it be checked?
facts.fact: Which outcome counts
facts.why: Decoding unfamiliar words, reading taught words, spelling, reading fluently and understanding text respond differently; phonics predicts the first most strongly.

facts.ask: during a long seated segment, when do learners start to drift, and how many are off task by then?
facts.fact: What the learners do in the seated stretch now
facts.why: Movement is expected to help a group that drifts off task; for a group already on task the reviews give little to gain, and in one school study the least on-task students gained most.

facts.ask: what should be different after the break, how would you see it, and when?
facts.fact: What the outcome is
facts.why: On-task behavior soon after a bout is what the reviews support; test-measured attention, achievement and retention are not.

facts.ask: how much space is there, are all learners able to stand and move, and is anyone joining remotely?
facts.fact: Who can move, where, and how
facts.why: Age, mobility, health, space, dress and mode (in the room, remote, on a phone) decide which moves are possible and safe.

facts.ask: at the point it goes wrong, can the learner say what to do next?
facts.fact: What goes wrong at the hard moment
facts.why: A learner who does not know the next step needs an instructional cue (or the step taught); one who knows it but stops or freezes needs a motivational or reframing cue; one already fluent needs little or none.

facts.ask: is this a new skill with steps to remember, a familiar task done under pressure, or a long effortful task?
facts.fact: The kind of task and how practised it is
facts.why: The direct evidence is on motor and sport tasks, and stronger on novel and fine-motor ones; academic tasks are a transfer.

facts.ask: how many sessions, and minutes in each, can go to modeling and rehearsing, and will anyone prompt the cue at the hard moment?
facts.fact: How much time and support there is to teach and rehearse the cues
facts.why: Trained self-talk did better than untrained.

facts.ask: after reading, what must the learner be able to say or do, and about which parts of the text?
facts.fact: What the later check will ask about
facts.why: If it tests the whole text, factual pre-questions on part of it may cost the rest; if it tests a few central ideas, pre-questions on those are the best-evidenced case.

facts.ask: does this text answer each question, and when will learners compare their guesses with it?
facts.fact: Whether the text resolves the questions, and whether someone checks the attempts against it
facts.why: The benefit on record depends on the answer arriving after the attempt.

facts.ask: who are the readers, how confident are they, is anything scored, and can they leave (an optional course, a self-paced module)?
facts.fact: How the learner will take being wrong
facts.why: Most pre-question attempts fail; a learner who reads that as proof of inability may stop.

facts.ask: which part of the material answers each question, and how soon after the attempt does the learner meet it?
facts.fact: Will the study that follows answer the questions, and when?

facts.ask: will the assessment ask about the same ideas the pretest can ask about, or about everything in the material?
facts.fact: What does the end assessment cover?

facts.ask: is the course optional or self-paced, is anything scored, and how confident are these learners?
facts.fact: Can learners leave, and how will they take failing?

facts.ask: can they do one item of this kind now, unaided, and name the first step?
facts.fact: The learner's starting response on this procedure
facts.why: A learner who cannot begin needs the model, parts and supported attempts; one who completes a representative item unaided needs little more than mixed and spaced practice, and extra guidance can become redundant.

facts.ask: does the procedure always run the same way, and where must the performer choose?
facts.fact: What kind of procedure it is
facts.why: A fixed sequence that must run the same way every time (a dosage calculation, a lab protocol, a safety check) needs accuracy then speed; a procedure full of decisions (choosing a method, debugging, diagnosing) needs the decisions practised and the conditions of use taught. A procedure whose steps interact heavily may need parts first.

facts.ask: what must the learner do, unaided, with what aids, how fast, and when?
facts.fact: When and how it must work
facts.why: Accurate on today's worksheet, fast enough in a real job, still accurate in a month, or adapted to a case not seen before each need different practice and a different check.

facts.fact: How the writer currently plans and revises
facts.why: A writer who already plans and makes global revisions needs a lighter cycle and their own choice of focus; one who writes once and corrects spelling needs explicit strategy teaching, not only more drafts. If unstated, ask for one draft and its revision, written under ordinary conditions, and look at what changed between them.

facts.ask: who will read each draft before the final version, how long after it is written, and how many drafts per writer per week can they read?
facts.fact: Who can read drafts, and how often
facts.why: Teacher response is the scarce resource; peer and self-review stretch it only with criteria and practice.

facts.ask: what must the writer produce unaided, for whom, under what conditions, and when?
facts.fact: The text, reader and horizon that count
facts.why: A timed exam essay, a report for a real client and a portfolio piece need different cycles.

facts.ask: how did schooling go for these learners, and what do they expect of an instructor?
facts.fact: What the learners bring to the relationship
facts.why: Adults who have been failed, judged or mistreated by schools or other institutions, or who belong to groups that report fewer caring adults at school, need slower, more private early steps and more consistency; experienced professionals may want a peer relationship and little personal disclosure.

facts.ask: how many learners, how many sessions, and how many instructor hours outside sessions?
facts.fact: How much contact time the instructor has with each learner
facts.why: A cohort of 15 over a term allows one-to-ones and names by the second week; 200 learners or a single workshop does not.

facts.ask: what should learners be doing by the middle of the course that they would not do with a stranger?
facts.fact: What the relationship is for in this course
facts.why: Raising needs and staying enrolled, taking part in discussion, being open to opposing arguments, or accepting critical feedback on work need different first moves.

principles/productive-instructor-learner.title: Build productive instructor-learner relationships so adults feel connected and take an active role in learning

facts.ask: what can a learner do with this tool that gets the task done without learning the target, and does the assessment catch it?
facts.fact: What the shortcut is and what it would cost
facts.why: An assistant that can produce the full answer threatens unaided performance; free movement through a simulation may cost nothing.

facts.ask: will learners be assessed with or without the tool, and when?
facts.fact: Whether the outcome is measured with the tool removed
facts.why: The constraint evidence is about unaided exams; assisted practice scores rose most where learning did not follow.

facts.ask: can the tool's behaviour be changed, by whom, and can learners get round it?
facts.fact: Who controls the tool
facts.why: A designer who builds the tool can block a shortcut; a teacher handed a commercial assistant can only configure it or set the task around it; a learner with their own device controls it themselves.

principles/productive-usage-guaranteed-b.title: Design tools so productive usage is guaranteed by affordances and constraints rather than instructions

facts.ask: will the writer produce another version of this text, and when?
facts.fact: Whether the writer will revise this draft
facts.why: Comments on a draft that will be revised can be acted on; comments on a final text are read, if at all, as a justification of the grade.

facts.ask: how has this writer responded to critique before, and do they trust the person giving it?
facts.fact: How the writer is likely to read critique
facts.why: A confident writer may need few strength comments; a writer with low confidence, a second-language writer, or one with reason to doubt the teacher's intent may stop reading at the first criticism.

facts.ask: who will respond to each draft, and how long do they have?
facts.fact: Who writes the comments, and with how much time
facts.why: A teacher with ten minutes per draft, a peer, and an AI tool produce different balances of praise and critique.

principles/provide-positive-comments-on-.title: Provide positive comments alongside constructive criticism when responding to student writing

facts.ask: in this segment, is the learner working alone on text, problems or a draft, or talking with others?
facts.fact: Whether the task is focus work or talk work
facts.why: Reading, writing, planning and test preparation call for a protected block; discussion, oral practice and collaborative work call for talk, and silence would remove what they need.

facts.ask: where will learners do this work, who else is there, and on what device?
facts.fact: Who controls the space and the devices
facts.why: In a classroom the teacher can arrange the room and set a device rule; at home, at work, online or on a phone, only the learner can.

facts.ask: how long can these learners now stay on a task like this before drifting, and what usually interrupts them?
facts.fact: How much distraction costs this learner
facts.why: Learners with low working-memory capacity, weak attentional inhibition, attention difficulties, or high stress and fatigue are expected to lose more to competing input.

facts.ask: have they seen a strong and a weak example of this task and said which is which?
facts.fact: Can the learner judge this kind of work?
facts.why: A learner who cannot tell good work from weak work will reflect fluently and wrongly; the design must then supply a criterion, an exemplar or feedback first.

facts.ask: when will they next do something like this, and will anyone see whether they changed it?
facts.fact: Is there a next attempt?
facts.why: Reflection is expected to pay off through a changed next move; with no comparable task to follow, the expected benefit is unsupported.

facts.ask: what would the learner do differently, observably, if the reflection worked?
facts.fact: What is the outcome that counts?
facts.why: Better reflections, better course exams and better practice are separate outcomes, and the evidence here is strongest for the first two.

facts.ask: during the lesson, how will the teacher see each learner's reasoning, and how soon?
facts.fact: Can every learner's thinking be seen during the lesson, and by whom?
facts.why: Most evidence for contingent response is one-to-one; with one teacher and thirty learners, or no teacher, elicitation must reach everyone at once and the response must target the commonest idea.

facts.ask: what ideas do learners usually bring to this task, and does the curriculum say which misconception each activity targets?
facts.fact: Does the teacher have a model of likely ideas for this content?
facts.why: Without one, responses become generic.

facts.ask: what must be covered by when, and what may be moved?
facts.fact: How much freedom to depart from the plan, and how much time?
facts.why: A scripted pacing guide, a fixed short session or a shared exam date limits the moves to small ones inside the sequence.

facts.ask: given a short task for a stated reader, does the learner change anything for that reader, and can they answer one objection?
facts.fact: What the learner does now, on this kind of task
facts.why: A learner who writes with no reader in view needs one move modelled and a process goal; one who already adapts to readers needs harder audiences and outcome goals, and scripted routines may get in the way.

facts.ask: who will actually read or hear the final version, and will they reply or act on it?
facts.fact: Who the audience is, and whether it is real
facts.why: A real reader who will respond changes what learners write; a token one may not.

facts.ask: what must the learner produce, for whom, judged on what, and when?
facts.fact: The kind of goal
facts.why: Argument quality in a subject, persuasive or professional writing, public speaking, and everyday interpersonal communication call for different tasks, criteria and situations.

facts.ask: which learners might read a poor result here as confirming something about who they are, and what tells you so (past results, who drops out, what learners say)?
facts.fact: Whether, and for whom, the evaluation is a threat
facts.why: The tested effect appeared only for students in a group stereotyped in the domain, and not reliably even there.

facts.ask: when is the first graded test, the first critical feedback, the gateway assessment, and how far apart are they?
facts.fact: When the threatening moments are
facts.why: The exercise is placed before them.

facts.ask: will anyone read, grade, store or code what learners write, and do the learners know?
facts.fact: Who will see the writing
facts.why: The mechanism assumes the writing is private and unjudged.

facts.ask: can they do two or three items of the target kind now, and can they say what they will do next week and how they will know it worked?
facts.fact: What the learner can already do with this content, and how well they plan
facts.why: A `novice` on the content needs instruction and a narrow hand-over (pace, product); a learner who succeeds on the baseline and writes a workable plan can take over resources and sequence sooner.

facts.ask: who looks at a learner's log or checkpoint, how long after it is submitted, and what can they do about a learner who is drifting?
facts.fact: Who will read the learner's plans and self-assessments, and how often
facts.why: The hand-over is safe only if someone or something checks the learner's judgement against the criteria.

facts.ask: which choices are the learner's, which are fixed, and what must the learner be able to do, alone, at the end?
facts.fact: Which decisions the brief wants the learner to own, and what counts as success
facts.why: Ownership of the topic, of pace, of strategy or of evaluation are different hand-overs, and a course judged on completion, on achievement or on later independence needs different checks.

facts.ask: when this learner says they understand, how often are they right? Try two items and compare.
facts.fact: What the learner knows about this task
facts.why: A `novice` cannot judge their own work well and is often overconfident; an `advanced` learner may monitor well enough without a checklist.

facts.ask: what exactly should the learner notice, and what would they compare it with?
facts.fact: What is monitored, and against what
facts.why: Comprehension, the steps of a procedure, a draft against a rubric and on-task behaviour are different checks with different evidence.

facts.ask: will a teacher, a peer, an answer key or software ever compare the learner's record with the work, and when?
facts.fact: Who can check the learner's judgement, and how often
facts.why: Without an outside comparison, a learner's record cannot be corrected.

facts.ask: can the learner do one item from the first stage and one from a middle stage now, unaided?
facts.fact: What the learner can already do on this target
facts.why: A learner who already performs the early steps needs a shorter path and fewer protective orders; one who cannot start needs the prerequisites first.

facts.ask: at the end, what must the learner do, on what kind of item, and when (end of session, a week later, on the job)?
facts.fact: The kind of goal and the test that will count
facts.why: Fluent procedure, conceptual understanding and transfer, and discrimination between confusable categories each favour a different order.

facts.ask: can any part be understood or done without the others?
facts.fact: How tightly the parts depend on each other
facts.why: A chain where step 3 is meaningless without step 2 forces an order; a set of loosely related topics leaves the order open and makes the transitions matter more.

facts.ask: what will the learner do in the real setting, with what hands-on component, and which decisions and cues must the simulation keep?
facts.fact: What the learner must do in the real setting, and whether the simulation represents it
facts.why: Decisions and communication travel well to a screen; tactile skill does not.

facts.ask: can they name the parts of the system, and can they carry out one run of the simplest scenario now?
facts.fact: The learner's starting point on this task
facts.why: A novice needs a primer, simplified runs and guidance during the run; a learner who already performs the task needs varied, harder scenarios and less prompting.

facts.ask: who will see each run, who leads the debrief, and how many minutes are there for both?
facts.fact: Who can guide and debrief, and for how long
facts.why: Most of the support evidence comes from a facilitator or tutor responding to one learner.

facts.ask: can each learner do, alone, one small task using each skill the deliverable needs?
facts.fact: Whether learners can already do the parts
facts.why: A sprint integrates and applies skills under a deadline; it does not teach them from scratch, and novices fall behind fastest.

facts.ask: who will look at each team's work before the end, how often, and for how many minutes per team?
facts.fact: Who reviews the work partway through, and how much of their time there is
facts.why: The cycle depends on a checkpoint that changes the next block of work.

facts.ask: what must learners be able to do afterwards, unaided, and does the product have a real user or audience?
facts.fact: What the sprint is for: the learning, the product, or both
facts.why: A deliverable someone will actually use pulls attention to finishing; learning needs the debrief and the criteria to stay visible.

facts.ask: how will the grade or recognition be computed, and how will you know what each member can do alone?
facts.fact: What, exactly, each member's success depends on, and how it is checked
facts.why: A shared grade on one product, a team score built from individual quizzes, and a role that others need are three different structures with different failure modes.

facts.ask: can each member, alone, do or explain a first part of this task now?
facts.fact: Whether members can contribute
facts.why: Dependence on a member who does not yet know enough produces copying or resentment, not explanation.

facts.ask: will the group meet live, for how many sessions, and over how long?
facts.fact: Setting and duration
facts.why: The achievement evidence comes from face-to-face school and undergraduate classes over several weeks; the one online experiment found no achievement effect of interdependence type.

facts.ask: will learners ever see or hear each other live, and on what devices?
facts.fact: The medium, and how much of it is live
facts.why: In a room, people already see each other; in an asynchronous text course, nothing about them is visible unless the design invites it.

facts.ask: how many learners, in what groups, for how many weeks?
facts.fact: How long the group stays together, and how big it is
facts.why: Trust between peers needs repeated contact with the same people; a one-off workshop or a 2,000-learner course cannot rely on it.

facts.ask: what do learners already share with each other, and is anything off limits?
facts.fact: What learners are willing to show, and to whom
facts.why: Norms about self-disclosure, emotional expression and talking to a teacher differ by culture, age, profession and past experience of school, and some learners have reasons to keep their lives private.

facts.ask: what does the score decide, for whom, and which of the test, the sitting and the decision rule can you change?
facts.fact: What the score decides, and whether you control the test
facts.why: A user of an external test (an admissions office, a gifted programme) can change how the score is combined and where the cut sits, not the items; an item writer or test owner can change the items and the sitting; a teacher preparing learners can change only the preparation.

facts.ask: which groups are in the population (sex, race or ethnicity, home language, social class, disability), and roughly how many test-takers in each per cycle?
facts.fact: Which groups the decision must be fair to, and how many learners are in each
facts.why: Prediction checks and DIF statistics need sizeable groups; small groups leave you with content review and second evidence.

facts.ask: what later outcome is the score supposed to predict, and is it recorded for each group?
facts.fact: Whether a later outcome is available to check the score against
facts.why: Differential prediction can only be checked when the criterion (grades, completion, job performance) is recorded for the people the score selected.

facts.ask: what has this learner been seen to do well on a task, by whom, and what labels or records will the teacher meet first?
facts.fact: What the learner has actually been seen to do, and who has been describing them
facts.why: A learner with a record of deficit labels, referrals or failure needs strengths collected from new evidence, not read from the file; one already well regarded needs little framing and mainly harder tasks.

facts.ask: on this course's targets, where is the learner now, and what accommodation or explicit teaching is already planned?
facts.fact: What the learner cannot yet do, and what support that needs
facts.why: The approach adds strengths to an accurate account of barriers; it does not decide whether support is needed.

facts.ask: who will look at each learner's work, how often, and through what channel will feedback reach them?
facts.fact: Who sees the learner's work, and how often
facts.why: Naming specific performances needs someone who sees them: a teacher with five learners can hold a conference each fortnight; one with two hundred, or none, cannot.

facts.ask: what happens to a learner who passes, and to one who fails, and can it be undone?
facts.fact: What decision rides on the result, and for whom
facts.why: A unit grade a teacher can revisit, a course grade on a transcript, and a licence or progression decision call for different breadth, scorer checks and reassessment routes.

facts.ask: what would a learner who has reached the outcome be able to do that one who has not cannot, and with what aids?
facts.fact: What the outcome asks the learner to do
facts.why: Recalling facts, applying a procedure to a new case, analysing, and carrying out a whole performance need different tasks, and a test of one does not report another.

facts.ask: what low-stakes practice of this kind and this format did learners have, and how recently?
facts.fact: What the learners have met before the end-point
facts.why: Learners who have practised retrieval and higher-level questions during the course, and seen the format, are judged on the capability; learners meeting the format or the level for the first time are partly judged on that.

facts.ask: how old are the children, what do they say now (single words, short phrases, stories), and has anyone flagged a delay or hearing loss?
facts.fact: The child's age and current language
facts.why: An infant who points but does not yet speak, a two-year-old with a few hundred words, a four-year-old who tells stories, and a child with a diagnosed language delay need different prompts, group sizes and adult support, and the tested effect shrinks at four to five and for children at risk.

facts.ask: who spends time talking with these children, how many children per adult, and can anyone watch them do it once and give feedback?
facts.fact: Who will carry out the interaction, and whether they can be coached
facts.why: Parents at home, an early-years teacher with a full room, a home visitor, or volunteers each need different training and a different amount of the routine.

facts.ask: what should the children be able to say or do differently, how will anyone know, and when?
facts.fact: Which language outcome counts
facts.why: Expressive vocabulary and the child's own talk are where the tested gain lies; receptive vocabulary, phonological awareness, letter knowledge and later reading need other or additional teaching.

facts.fact: What the student does now on this unit's own work
facts.why: A student who does the end-of-unit task before teaching needs compacting and replacement work; one who learns faster but does not yet do it needs faster pacing within the unit, not removal from it. If a brief omits it, ask: what does the student do, unaided, on this unit's end-of-unit task before it is taught?

facts.fact: Whether the subject is cumulative and whether harder work is available
facts.why: Acceleration needs a next unit, a next course or adaptive material to move into; enrichment needs a task the teacher or a mentor can follow. If omitted, ask: what comes after this unit, and who can read and judge the student's harder work?

facts.fact: How the student came to be identified, and who else shows the same response
facts.why: Provision tied to a label and a test cut-off can miss students who show the response. If omitted, ask: how are students chosen for this provision, and could a student who is not labelled take it on the same evidence?

facts.fact: What the student can do now on this task, and with how much help
facts.why: A student who stops at the first step needs smaller steps and a model; one who does most steps with a prompt needs fewer prompts and the real setting. If a brief omits it, ask: what does the student do now when they try this task alone, and where do they stop?

facts.fact: The level of support needed and who provides it
facts.why: Intermittent support for one routine is a classroom teacher's plan; extensive or pervasive support means a specialist, family and aide share the plan. If omitted, ask: who works with the student during the week, for how long, and who can watch their practice?

facts.fact: What the target is for
facts.why: A school examination item, a daily-life routine, participation in class life and a voice in the student's own plan each need different practice and different checks. If omitted, ask: what should the student be able to do unaided, where, and by when, and what does the student want to be able to do?

facts.ask: who will have to do something differently, did they have a say in choosing it, and what else in the system has to change for it to fit?
facts.fact: Who must change what, and who decided
facts.why: An innovation the adopters chose differs from one handed to them. One that changes only the user's own practice differs from one that needs assessment, timetable or roles to change too.

facts.ask: where has it stalled, and what do the people involved say is stopping them?
facts.fact: Which part is blocking now
facts.why: Adopters' concerns, a cause of resistance, a missing condition in the environment, or the innovation's own attributes each call for a different move.

facts.ask: by when must what be visible, and is the target use of the innovation or its effect on learners?
facts.fact: The horizon and the outcome that counts
facts.why: First use, faithful routine use, and effects on learners come at different times.

principles/systemic-understanding-guides.title: Guide change efforts with systemic understanding, focusing interventions on one framework component at a time as needed

facts.ask: what should learners be able to say, write or do afterwards that they cannot now, and how will you see it?
facts.fact: What the talk and writing are for
facts.why: Understanding a text or concept, reasoning, willingness to speak and accurate language are different targets. For information alone, a clear explanation is not expected to do worse.

facts.ask: in which language can they already explain this content, and how did they respond the last time they were asked to speak in front of the class?
facts.fact: The learners' language and confidence
facts.why: A learner working through a second language, or one who fears being wrong in front of others, may say little however much time is given.

facts.ask: how many learners, in what room or channel, and who can respond to what each one says or writes?
facts.fact: Who hears each learner, and how many there are
facts.why: One teacher with thirty learners hears few voices; pairs, writing and roles are how every learner gets a turn.

principles/talking-and-writing-means-to-.title: Treat talking and writing as means to learning through dialogue-based, student-centered instruction

facts.ask: in a sample of the learners' own writing or speech, how often do they use the form, where, and where do they avoid it?
facts.fact: What the learner's use of the form actually looks like
facts.why: Overuse, avoidance and misuse each call for different work, and a learner who does not yet produce the form needs something else.

facts.ask: what L1s are in the group, and what does each use where the L2 uses this form?
facts.fact: The learners' first language, and whether its nearest equivalent covers a different range
facts.why: That decides whether a side-by-side contrast helps, and whether one contrast serves the whole group.

facts.ask: where, and under what time pressure, must the learner use the form, and how will that be checked?
facts.fact: The use that counts
facts.why: Choosing the form in one's own unplanned writing or speech, passing a gap-fill, and understanding it in reading call for different practice.

principles/teach-conceptual-underpinning.title: Teach the conceptual underpinnings of L2 forms rather than only their structural aspects or formulaic units

facts.ask: can these learners begin a representative task now, unaided?
facts.fact: How much the learners already know about this target
facts.why: A novice needs the teacher to explain and model before handing over the work; a learner who can already start needs the teacher as questioner and consultant.

facts.ask: what will learners do, with what aids, at what point, to show they have it?
facts.fact: What the learners must be able to do, and when it is checked
facts.why: Explaining an idea, using a language in conversation, holding a value, and recalling content for an exam call for different shares of teacher presentation.

facts.ask: during the task, how many learners can the teacher reach, how often, and who else (peers, software, a checklist) can respond to a learner's work?
facts.fact: How much of each learner's work the teacher can see and respond to
facts.why: Mediation by questioning is contingent help, and most of that evidence is one-to-one.

principles/teacher-as-mediator-not-conte.title: Educators should act as mediators and facilitators of learning rather than content disseminators

facts.ask: has the teacher spoken to this family before, and about what?
facts.fact: Whether there is already a problem, and who raised it
facts.why: A first contact about a problem reads as a sanction whoever makes it; a relationship that already exists can carry a hard conversation.

facts.ask: in what language and through what channel does this family answer, at what time of day, and how have past contacts with the school gone for them?
facts.fact: The family's language, channel, hours and starting trust in the school
facts.why: A plan built on evening meetings and English email reaches the families who were already reachable.

facts.ask: how many families, how many minutes a week, and does the school expect and support this work?
facts.fact: The teacher's time and the school's backing
facts.why: A secondary teacher with five classes, or a teacher whose school gives no time for family contact, cannot run a weekly message to every family.

principles/teacher-parent-solidarity-ove.title: Strengthen ties between teachers and parents rather than pressing for remote sanctions behind teaching

facts.ask: can the learner do one representative item now, unaided, and explain it?
facts.fact: What the learner can already do on the task without the tool
facts.why: Tool output that helps a learner with little prior knowledge can hinder one who could do it.

facts.ask: what must the learner do without the tool, and how long after?
facts.fact: Whether the outcome that counts is measured with the tool removed, and when
facts.why: If the target is the product made with the tool, the trade-offs on this page matter less; if it is unaided performance or retention, they decide the design.

facts.ask: can the tool be limited, and who reads its output before the learner relies on it?
facts.fact: What the tool will do when asked, and who checks it
facts.why: An assistant that gives full solutions, invents data or writes feedback the learner simply accepts takes the process over; one limited to hints, or checked by a person, does not.

principles/technology-augments-not-suppl.title: Technology should augment, not supplant, learning processes in student-centered environments

facts.ask: what should a learner have done or produced by the end of the chat, and would a spoken or asynchronous exchange do it better?
facts.fact: What the written exchange is for
facts.why: Negotiating meaning in a second language, asking questions during a talk, giving peer response, or reasoning at length each need a different task and mode; chat turns are short, so extended reasoning belongs elsewhere.

facts.ask: who reads the chat while it runs, how many learners post into one stream, and when will someone respond?
facts.fact: Who can watch the chat, and how many threads it carries
facts.why: A dyad or a group of four can run itself with a closed task; thirty people in one live chat need a monitor.

facts.ask: can every learner type short replies in this language at conversation speed, on the device they will use?
facts.fact: Learners' typing, language and access
facts.why: Keyboard speed, proficiency in the language of the chat, device and bandwidth decide who can keep pace.

facts.ask: is this task about understanding the content, or about reading it unaided?
facts.fact: Whether reading the words is part of what is being learned or assessed
facts.why: If it is, speech is withheld for that practice and its check; if it is not, speech is an access route like any other.

facts.ask: when this learner reads this text, where does it break down, and do they understand it when it is read to them?
facts.fact: The learner's barrier
facts.why: Decoding, low vision, fatigue, a second language, attention or limited vocabulary each call for a different set-up, and only some are helped by speech.

facts.ask: will the learner be looking at anything besides the words, and can they pause and replay?
facts.fact: What else is on the screen and who controls pace
facts.why: Plain text, text with a diagram, and system-paced video each change what should be spoken and what shown.

facts.fact: How far the target situation is from the taught one
facts.why: A new surface in the same domain (`near-transfer`) is supported here. A different domain or form (`far-transfer`) is barely moved in the evidence the wiki holds. If the brief does not say, ask: what new situations must the learner handle, and how different are they from the ones in the course?

facts.fact: Whether the original learning is secure
facts.why: A learner who cannot do the taught case unaided has nothing to transfer, and extra varied cases add load. If the brief does not say, ask: can the learner do one taught item now, unaided, and explain why it works?

facts.fact: Whether the target setting supports the use
facts.why: In workplaces, transfer depends on cases, equipment and colleagues in the setting as well as on the course. If the brief does not say, ask: will the learner meet the situations, and have the resources, to use this within weeks of the course?

facts.ask: can learners already produce something, however rough, in this domain, and is the target an idea to understand or a step sequence to follow?
facts.fact: What the learner already knows about this target, and what kind of target it is
facts.why: Clue-led exploration needs learners who can make attempts and talk about them, and a `concept` or `principle` to find; a procedure never seen, a domain-general skill or a set of facts is better told first.

facts.ask: during making, who will see each learner's or group's attempt and talk with them, and for how long?
facts.fact: Who can ask the questions during exploration, and how often
facts.why: The evidence for guiding by questions comes from teachers sitting with small groups and from one-to-one tutoring; with one teacher for many groups, or none, the questions must be prepared in advance or built into the task.

facts.ask: what must the learner be able to do at the end (judge a new case, explain why, produce work), and when?
facts.fact: Whether the principle will be named after the exploration, and what outcome counts
facts.why: Exploring before being told helps conceptual understanding when instruction follows; it does not help procedural fluency.

principles/understanding-cultivated-not-.title: Understanding must be cultivated through exploration, not described or told

facts.ask: what must the learner be able to do at the end, with what aids, and which parts of each activity are only the way in?
facts.fact: Which demands belong to the goal
facts.why: An alternative to a demand that *is* the goal (spelling in a spelling course, reading the drug label as printed) removes the learning, not a barrier.

facts.ask: who has struggled with this unit before, what accommodations are on record, and which languages and devices do learners use?
facts.fact: Who is in the cohort and what stops them
facts.why: Learners with a sensory or motor impairment, learners in a second language, learners with little prior knowledge and learners who have stopped engaging meet different barriers, and the options that help one can burden another.

facts.ask: can learners already do one task of this kind unaided, and have they chosen supports for themselves before?
facts.fact: What the learners can manage choosing
facts.why: Novices pay for every option in attention; experienced learners can choose well and are slowed by supports they no longer need.

facts.ask: who will use this, for which five tasks, and can we reach some of them before launch?
facts.fact: Who the users are, and which tasks they must do with the interface
facts.why: A learner submitting work, a teacher reading a dashboard and a parent reading a report need different tests with different people.

facts.ask: what will they open it on, where, and does anyone use a screen reader, magnification or captions?
facts.fact: The device, connection and access needs the users actually have
facts.why: Phones, shared or school-managed devices, slow connections and assistive technology change what fails.

facts.ask: what must a user be able to do with this screen, and how will we know they did it right, not only that they liked it?
facts.fact: Which outcome decides success
facts.why: Rated usability, completing a task, and learning the content are separate outcomes and can disagree.

facts.ask: what decision will this result change, for whom, and can it be reversed?
facts.fact: What the score will be used for, and how much rides on it
facts.why: A check that steers tomorrow's lesson tolerates a few items and one marker; a grade, placement or certification needs more items, calibrated scoring and caution at the cut.

facts.ask: who are the learners (languages, literacy, background, access needs), and what must they do to show the capability that is not the capability?
facts.fact: Which demands besides the target capability the task makes, and whether they differ across the learners
facts.why: Language, reading load, cultural reference, speed, anxiety and the response mode are the usual ones.

facts.ask: is the response scored by key or by judgement, by how many people, and with what criteria and examples?
facts.fact: Who scores, and how
facts.why: Selected-response items remove rater variation but narrow what can be assessed; performances and constructed responses widen it but depend on the rater.

principles/validity-reliability-and-bias.title: Validity, Reliability, and Bias in Classroom Assessment

facts.ask: after one viewing of a two-minute clip, which moments does the learner pick out, and would an experienced colleague pick the same ones?
facts.fact: How accurately the learner already sees their own performance
facts.why: A novice needs a narrow focus, others' clips first and a coach choosing the moments; a practitioner who already names the right moments needs only the recording, their own focus and a check.

facts.ask: who may watch this clip, where is it kept, and has everyone in it agreed?
facts.fact: Who will see the recording, and who is in it
facts.why: Self-review, review with one trusted coach, and review in a group are different levels of exposure, and other people on screen need consent.

facts.ask: when does the learner next do this task, and can that attempt be recorded too?
facts.fact: What the next performance is, and when
facts.why: Replay changes performance only through the next attempt.

facts.ask: who gives the feedback, who receives it, how long have they worked together, and has the learner had reason to read criticism as a low expectation?
facts.fact: Whether the learner has reason to doubt the giver's intent
facts.why: The framing is aimed at a learner for whom critique is ambiguous: across a racial or ethnic difference, in a domain where their group is stereotyped, early in a course before trust exists, or after a history of low expectations. Where the learner already trusts the giver, it adds little.

facts.ask: what will the comment say, against which criteria, and what can the learner do next with it?
facts.fact: Whether the critique is real and usable
facts.why: The framing is a frame around specific critique the learner can act on. If the feedback is a grade, a mark or general praise, fix that first.

facts.ask: is there a revision or re-attempt, and what else does this learner hear from this giver and this institution?
facts.fact: Whether the learner gets a next attempt and the giver's other conduct agrees
facts.why: An assurance with no revision, or amid grading, discipline or comments that say otherwise, has nothing to stand on.

principles/wise-feedback-across-differen.title: Wise Feedback Across Racial and Ethnic Difference

rows.basis: [Vocabulary instruction improves comprehension](claims/vocabulary-instruction-improves-comprehension.md) [+M]
rows.change: Teach those words explicitly, a few at a time, with examples and non-examples, and test comprehension on texts that use them; expect little gain on standardized reading tests
rows.if: The material depends on a set of disciplinary terms

rows.basis: [Vocabulary instruction improves comprehension](claims/vocabulary-instruction-improves-comprehension.md) [+M]
rows.change: Prioritize explicit teaching of the target words; the gains on custom measures were largest for this group
rows.if: Learners with reading difficulties

rows.basis: [Embedded aids improved reading comprehension](claims/embedded-aids-improve-reading-comprehension.md) [+W]
rows.change: Add embedded aids alongside the original text (a running commentary on key concepts and terms, questions), instead of rewriting it
rows.if: A content text (science, say) must be read as written

rows.basis: [Linguistic simplification can improve math performance](claims/linguistic-simplification-improves-math-performance.md) [+W]
rows.change: Simplify the non-mathematical wording (sentence length, nested clauses, unfamiliar everyday words) and keep the mathematics unchanged
rows.if: English learners or low-SES learners face mathematics word problems

rows.basis: [Unfamiliar contexts and vocabulary distract from the mathematics](claims/unfamiliar-contexts-distract-from-mathematics.md) [+W]
rows.change: Reword them into familiar contexts, or clarify the unfamiliar words before problem solving
rows.if: Word problems use contexts unfamiliar to the learners

rows.basis: [Interactionally modified input aids comprehension but not retention](claims/interactionally-modified-input-aids-comprehension-not-retention.md) [~M]; [Negotiation benefited lower-ability learners](claims/negotiation-benefit-limited-lower-ability-learners.md) [~M]
rows.change: Adjust language in response to what learners show they do not understand, rather than only pre-simplifying; expect a gain in comprehension now, not in retention of the structures
rows.if: Beginning second-language learners, live teaching

rows.basis: [Simplification and glossaries preceded second-cycle gains](claims/simplification-and-glossary-supported-second-cycle-gains.md) [+W]; untested proposal for the return to the original
rows.change: Give a simplified version and a glossary of unfamiliar terms first, then return to the original
rows.if: Learners must read research articles or other authentic texts beyond their level

rows.basis: [Passage cohesion showed no effect on delayed recall](claims/cohesion-no-effect-delayed-recall.md) [-M]
rows.change: Build the learners' knowledge of the topic first; cohesion did not help delayed recall, familiarity with the topic did
rows.if: The plan is to make a passage more cohesive so it will be remembered

rows.basis: [Minimal technical English limits workplace training](claims/minimal-technical-english-limits-training.md) [+W]
rows.change: Teach the technical terms and written forms the job uses, alongside the skill
rows.if: Workplace training for learners with limited technical English

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Give the same items as written and with non-target wording simplified, and compare the scores before deciding
rows.if: Unclear whether a failure comes from the language or the concept

rows.basis: untested proposal; see [Scaffolding and Fading](principles/scaffolding-and-fading.md)
rows.change: Withdraw them on a planned schedule, checking each learner on unsupported authentic items first
rows.if: Supports (glossaries, simplified versions) are in place and the target is the authentic text

rows.basis: [Prior-knowledge activation had little effect on retention](claims/prior-knowledge-activation-little-effect-on-retention.md) [-M]; [Pretesting enhances learning](claims/pretesting-enhances-learning.md) [+M]
rows.change: Do not open with a free brainstorm of what they know; ask a few questions on the coming content instead
rows.if: Learners know little about the topic

rows.basis: [Pretesting enhances memory for tested text](claims/pretesting-enhances-learning.md) [+M]; [Pretesting enhances memory for tested video](claims/pretesting-enhances-memory-tested-video.md) [+M]
rows.change: Put a few pre-questions before the reading or between video segments, and expect the gain mainly on the questioned content
rows.if: The material is expository text or video to be studied

rows.basis: [Effects on untested materials are inconsistent](claims/pretesting-untested-materials-inconsistent.md) [~M]
rows.change: Do not count on pre-questions for it; benefits for untested content were inconsistent across experiments
rows.if: The outcome covers content the pre-questions did not ask about

rows.basis: [Classroom pretesting improves exam performance](claims/classroom-pretesting-exam-gains.md) [+M]
rows.change: Give short ungraded pretests at the start of units on the content the exam will cover
rows.if: A multi-week course with a high-stakes exam

rows.basis: [Pretesting can harm motivation](claims/pretesting-can-harm-motivation.md) [-M]
rows.change: Keep any pretest short and optional, and tell learners it is not graded; pretests reduced persistence in one MOOC
rows.if: A voluntary online course (MOOC) where persistence matters

rows.basis: [Feedback timing moderates pretesting](claims/feedback-timing-moderates-pretesting.md) [~M]
rows.change: Give the correct answer immediately after each pre-question; delayed feedback removed the benefit for paired items
rows.if: The content is vocabulary or paired items

rows.basis: [Misconceptions interfere with new learning](claims/misconceptions-interfere-with-new-learning.md) [~M]; [Refutational text enhances recall](claims/refutational-text-order-enhances-retention.md) [+M]
rows.change: Surface the belief, then confront it directly (state the misbelief, then the fact and why) rather than presenting the correct account alone
rows.if: Learners are likely to hold misconceptions

rows.basis: [Advance organizers improve learning](claims/advance-organizers-improve-learning.md) [+M]
rows.change: Use one, and expect a small effect, larger for higher-ability learners
rows.if: The designer can write an organizer relating the new content to what learners know

rows.basis: [Activation improves learning](claims/activation-improves-learning.md) [~M]
rows.change: Activate what they know about how to read (strategies, monitoring) rather than what they know about the topic
rows.if: Primary-school pupils will read a text for comprehension
