rows.change: Design the segments as well; in one experiment the stop/play buttons were rarely used, and learner control in general showed almost no effect
rows.if: The plan is to give learners stop/play controls instead of designed segments

rows.basis: [Segmentation increases learning time](claims/segmenting-increases-learning-time.md) [~M]
rows.change: Budget extra time for segmented material; segmenting lengthens learning time
rows.if: Session time is tight

rows.basis: [Learner pacing helped on complex material only](claims/learner-paced-beats-system-paced-complex-material.md) [~M]
rows.change: Expect little from segmenting it; spend the effort elsewhere. The gains reported are for complex material
rows.if: The material is simple, with few elements to relate

rows.basis: [High prior knowledge benefited more on retention](claims/prior-knowledge-moderates-segmenting-retention.md) [~M]; [Segmentation's efficiency advantage disappeared at higher prior knowledge](claims/segmentation-benefits-shrink-with-expertise.md) [~M]
rows.change: Keep segments for retention, but offer longer units or a skip option and check with a changed problem; the evidence on prior knowledge points both ways
rows.if: Learners already know the topic well

rows.basis: [Segmented videos reduce hesitations for participants with ADHD](claims/segmentation-reduces-hesitations-adhd-participants.md) [+W]
rows.change: Segment instructional videos; in one study segmented videos cut hesitations sharply for participants with ADHD
rows.if: Learners include people with ADHD or attention difficulties

rows.basis: [Short chunking study outlines beat long ones](claims/short-cso-improves-test-performance.md) [+W]
rows.change: Keep the outline short
rows.if: Learners study from a printed text with a study outline

rows.basis: [Chunking reduces working memory load](claims/chunking-reduces-working-memory-load.md) [+W]
rows.change: Group the items into a few groups that mean something to these learners, rather than one long list
rows.if: Learners must memorise a list (terms, steps, codes)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: After the units, add a task that uses them together, and check that whole performance at a delay
rows.if: The goal is the whole task, not each unit

rows.basis: Movement breaks: [Classroom physical activity increases children's on-task behaviour, with no consistent gain on attention or other cognitive tests](claims/classroom-physical-activity-improves-attention.md) [+M] (primary-school children; on-task behaviour). Displays: [Classroom Design Affects Learning Progress](claims/classroom-design-affects-learning-progress.md) [+M] (English primary schools; observational). Rest untested
rows.change: Three rules shown with pictures; each procedure rehearsed physically, daily for four to six weeks; one transition signal (a song or chime); movement breaks of about five minutes between segments; displays at child eye height, mostly their own work
rows.if: Learners are a young `child` (preschool, early primary)

rows.basis: [Students value knowing class routines](claims/students-report-routines-help-and-rushed-pacing-hurts.md) [+W] (high school students' reports); rest untested
rows.change: Give the reason for each procedure; agree the rules with the class in week 1; align procedures with the other teachers where you can (one attention signal, one way to hand in work); keep pacing room for questions
rows.if: Learners are `adolescent`s who meet many teachers a day

rows.basis: untested proposal; no claim here tests adult groups
rows.change: Replace rules with a short working agreement drafted with the group in the first session; keep procedures for start times, breaks, materials and getting help; arrange the room for the main activity and let adults choose where to sit
rows.if: Learners are `adult`s in a work setting, adult education or training

rows.basis: untested proposal; from the earlier page
rows.change: A portable cart or bag with all materials for each lesson; the same attention signal and start routine in every room; one shelf or corner agreed in each room; arrive before learners where possible, or teach the class to set up
rows.if: The teacher has no room of their own (floating between rooms, specialist subjects, a shared training room)

rows.basis: untested proposal; the universal-management meta-analysis is K–12 classrooms, not lecture halls
rows.change: Rely on procedures and a visible signal rather than walking to learners: one attention signal, short timed tasks with a clear start and end, a help routine that does not need the teacher (a neighbour, a shared question board); use the aisles and the front rows for checking
rows.if: A lecture hall or room with fixed seating, one teacher with a large group

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Make every procedure work in both: one attention signal on screen and aloud, a named way to ask for help in each mode (hand, chat), materials posted online before the lesson, transitions announced with a countdown on screen; check phone-only learners can see the shared screen
rows.if: Mixed modes: some learners online, some in the room, or phone-only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Turn procedures into short written norms shown at the start of each session (chat, mute, cameras, breakout rooms); prepare breakout rooms and links before the session so transitions take seconds; put the "while you wait" task in the chat
rows.if: Online class only (`online-instructor-led`)

rows.basis: [Learning Space Redesign Alone Insufficient](claims/learning-space-redesign-alone-insufficient.md) [~M] (one Australian secondary school, three classes)
rows.change: Change the activities with the room: plan which lessons use which layout and teach how to move furniture between them; do not judge the room by learners' liking it
rows.if: The room has just been redesigned, or flexible furniture was bought

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Do not build a system: arrange seats for the main activity before learners arrive, state three expectations and one attention signal, have every material ready so there is no gap, and use the host's routines where you know them
rows.if: A single session only (a cover lesson, a one-off workshop)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Teach the two procedures that recur most (start of lesson and the attention signal) first, three to four minutes each with one rehearsal; add one procedure per lesson after that
rows.if: A fixed short time budget for setting up (for example ten minutes a lesson for routines in week 1)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Put the procedures, rules and transition signal on one page every adult uses the same way; prepare materials in labelled trays learners can collect themselves
rows.if: Scarce facilitator time (volunteers, a busy shift, one tutor checking in briefly)

rows.basis: untested proposal; teaching routines rather than posting them is the core of [universal classroom management](claims/universal-classroom-management-reduces-problem-behavior.md) [+M] as a programme, not tested as a single change
rows.change: Keep them and their wording; change only what matters here: teach and rehearse them rather than only posting them, keep procedures separate from the few rules, and prepare transitions
rows.if: The brief names its own routines, rules, expectations matrix or rubric

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Show procedures with pictures, gestures and demonstration, not text; rehearse rather than explain; give a non-verbal help signal; never use reading aloud as part of a routine for those who find it hard
rows.if: Learners with low literacy, a language barrier or low confidence

rows.basis: Comfort with structured assignments: [Neurodivergent students' comfort is highest for fully structured assignments](claims/nd-comfort-highest-fully-structured-assignments.md) [~W] (computing students' survey; comfort, not learning). Fading: [Contingent scaffolding](claims/contingent-scaffolding-improves-learning.md) [~M], carried from one-to-one tutoring
rows.change: Give fuller structure on assignments early (criteria, stages, an example outline), warn before every transition, keep a fixed seat if a learner wants one, and fade structure one support at a time
rows.if: Learners with learning difficulties, or neurodivergent learners

rows.basis: [Expertise reversal](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M] (cognitive-load studies, carried to assignment structure they did not test)
rows.change: Give the criteria only; drop the stage list and example outline
rows.if: Learners already `advanced` on the assignment type

rows.basis: [Rushed pacing](claims/students-report-routines-help-and-rushed-pacing-hurts.md) [~W] and [pacing calendars](claims/pacing-calendars-standardized-assessments-impediments.md) [~W] (student and teacher reports); timings untested
rows.change: Keep a five-minute check-and-correct slot each lesson; move fixed coordination tasks (attendance, handing in) into procedures that take under a minute; tell students when and how they can get one-to-one help
rows.if: A tight pacing guide or high-stakes course (Advanced Placement, a licensing exam)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep the performance whole; put procedures around it: equipment set out beforehand, a safety and setup routine rehearsed in advance, a single stop signal everyone obeys at once, and roles for moving on and off
rows.if: A practical, rehearsal or performance for a real audience (a lab, a workshop, a concert) that the brief wants kept whole

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Arrange seats without announcing reasons; keep notes on individual needs with the teacher; let learners ask privately to move
rows.if: Seating or behaviour information is private or sensitive (who sits apart, seating for a learner's needs)

rows.basis: [Strict AI prohibitions can intensify students' moral conflict](claims/strict-ai-prohibition-intensifies-moral-conflict.md) [~W] (one interviewed student)
rows.change: Write the rule as what learners do and disclose (for example, "say how you used AI"), and check that learners can keep it; a ban learners do not keep adds conflict without stopping use
rows.if: The class sets rules on generative AI use or another practice learners do privately

rows.basis: [Clear structure improves learning](claims/clear-structure-improves-learning.md) [+M]; [Signaling improves learning](claims/signaling-improves-learning.md) [+M]
rows.change: Add signals: headings, a short preview, a summary, and cues that point to the critical elements and how they connect
rows.if: Learners meet unfamiliar expository or multimedia material

rows.basis: [Signaling improves learning](claims/signaling-improves-learning.md) [~M]
rows.change: Keep signals light, or let learners turn cues off; added cues helped low-prior-knowledge eighth graders and harmed high-prior-knowledge ones in one field study
rows.if: Learners already know much of the material

rows.basis: [The change on the verbally described object was the most detected](claims/signalled-and-cued-object-change-most-detected.md) [+W]; [Change in the central object was detected at a low rate unless signalled and cued](claims/central-object-change-detection-low-without-cueing.md) [+W]; [Of two equally signalled objects, the arrow-cued one drew attention](claims/cueing-outcompetes-signalling-alone-for-attention.md) [+W]; [Changes were detected more easily on screens with fewer objects](claims/fewer-objects-easier-change-detection.md) [+W]; [Signalling focuses attention and reduces detection elsewhere](claims/signalling-focuses-attention-reduces-change-detection-elsewhere.md) [~W]. All five come from one small eye-tracking study of undergraduates, with descriptive detection counts and no comparison group
rows.change: Signal and visually cue that element (an arrow as well as a highlight), and keep the number of objects on screen low; expect learners to notice less elsewhere
rows.if: A busy screen or animation, with one change or element learners must notice

rows.basis: [Clear structure improves learning](claims/clear-structure-improves-learning.md) [~M]
rows.change: Use organizational signals, and test what is recalled as well as how much; signals may shift which ideas are recalled more than the total
rows.if: The goal is recall of the main ideas from a text

rows.basis: [Graphic organizers support novice comprehension](claims/graphic-organizers-support-novice-comprehension.md) [+M]
rows.change: Have them construct a node-link map of the material, or study a prepared one; constructing gave the larger effect
rows.if: Learners are `novice` and can build or study a concept map

rows.basis: [Advance organizers produce a small average benefit, larger for high-ability learners](claims/advance-organizers-improve-learning.md) [~M]
rows.change: Do not expect the largest benefit for low-ability learners; use it for all, and check its effect
rows.if: The plan is an advance organizer to help weaker learners most

rows.basis: [A hierarchical organization helps only when matched to the task](claims/organization-task-match-determines-benefit.md) [~M]; [Mismatched graphic organizers increase extraneous load](claims/mismatched-graphic-organizers-increase-extraneous-load.md) [~M]
rows.change: Organize the material, or the organizer, around the structure of the task it must serve
rows.if: The task learners will face is organized differently from the content (by procedure rather than by history, say)

rows.basis: [A clear lesson beat an unclear one for a complex concept structure](claims/clear-variable-coordinate-beats-unclear.md) [+M]; [Clarity matters less for simpler structures](claims/clarity-less-relevant-simpler-structures.md) [~M]; [Each clarity move correlated with concept achievement](claims/positive-clarity-moves-correlate-achievement.md) [+W] (correlational, same study)
rows.change: Present it clearly: state what is coming, link each part to the last, focus on the key attributes and give examples; clarity mattered most for the complex structure
rows.if: A lesson teaches concepts with variable, interrelated attributes

rows.basis: [Chunking reduces working memory load](claims/chunking-reduces-working-memory-load.md) [+M]
rows.change: Group the items into a few meaningful chunks and present them chunk by chunk
rows.if: Long working-memory demands: many new items at once

rows.basis: [Definitions, checkpoints and staged pacing improved clarity for novices](claims/checkpoints-and-definitions-improved-clarity.md) [+W]
rows.change: Add brief definitions, staged progression and checkpoints that test understanding before moving on
rows.if: Novices meeting new technical vocabulary in a fast-moving tutorial

rows.basis: [Students responded best to projects organized in a clear sequence with milestones](claims/student-engagement-authenticity-clear-sequence.md) [+W]
rows.change: Lay out a clear sequence with manageable milestones from the start
rows.if: Project-based work over several weeks

rows.basis: untested proposal; no claim in the wiki tests course-level structure
rows.change: Give a module map and weekly checklists, and test navigation separately from learning
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, and the learners' problem is finding what is due

rows.basis: [Minimal guidance is less effective for novices than explicit instruction](claims/minimal-guidance-less-effective-for-novices.md) [~S]
rows.change: Open with one worked example or short explanation; then a single, narrow "why" prompt per step; give a model answer after each attempt; no open discovery task first.
rows.if: Learners are `novice` for this relation

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Drop the opening example and step-by-step prompts; give an unfamiliar case to explain, or two solutions to compare and choose between, and ask for a justification.
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` for this relation

rows.basis: [Self-explanation prompts improve learning from worked examples](claims/self-explanation-improves-conceptual-understanding.md) [+M] (pooled across levels of education, and one study with eighth graders; the adaptations themselves are untested)
rows.change: Keep the "why" prompts but allow spoken answers; use two concrete cases rather than abstract descriptions; one relation per session.
rows.if: Learners are children or young adolescents (`child`, `adolescent`)

rows.basis: [Comparing contrasting cases improves learning](claims/comparing-contrasting-cases-improves-learning.md) [+M] (the transfer experiment was with undergraduates learning negotiation; untested in workplace training)
rows.change: Draw the two cases for comparison from the learners' own work, differing on the one feature that matters, and ask what they share before naming the principle.
rows.if: Learners are adults or professionals (`adult`, `adult-workplace`)

rows.basis: [Comparing contrasting cases improves learning](claims/comparing-contrasting-cases-improves-learning.md) [~M] (one algebra study: procedural and flexibility gains, no added conceptual gain)
rows.change: Compare two solution methods side by side and ask when each is better; expect gains in using and choosing methods, and check conceptual understanding separately.
rows.if: The goal is a `procedure`

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Do not build explanation or comparison tasks around isolated facts; use retrieval with feedback, and keep activation for the relations among the facts.
rows.if: The goal is facts or vocabulary (`verbal-association`)

rows.basis: [Self-explanation prompts improve learning from worked examples](claims/self-explanation-improves-conceptual-understanding.md) [+M] (prompting is tested; the reveal-after-commit step is untested)
rows.change: Put the prompt in the material with a required typed answer before the model explanation is revealed; the learner then compares the two.
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: [Teachers had minimal success designing Constructive and Interactive activities](claims/teachers-struggle-designing-interactive-activities.md) [~M] and [Students learned more in Constructive than Active activities](claims/students-learned-more-constructive-than-active.md) [+M]; [Most prospective teachers see constructivist conceptions as highly valuable but not very applicable](claims/constructivist-valued-but-not-applicable-person-level.md) [~W] (304 Turkish prospective teachers: 76% valued constructivist teaching highly but rated it hard to apply; beliefs, not task design; the one-task-per-lesson step is untested)
rows.change: Before teaching, check each planned task against step 4 (does the output go beyond the material?), with a colleague if possible; expect tasks planned as interactive to come out merely active. For teachers new to this, plan one rewritten task per lesson rather than a whole activating unit.
rows.if: `classroom` with a teacher designing their own tasks

rows.basis: [Students often adopt AI-generated solutions quickly, bypassing effortful meaning-making](claims/ai-answers-bypass-effortful-meaning-making.md) [~W] and [Immediate LLM explanations risk bypassing the generative processes required for durable understanding](claims/genai-offloading-bypasses-desirable-difficulties.md) [~W] (both theoretical arguments); [Error correction supports learning when it requires substantive cognitive work](claims/error-correction-effort-supports-learning.md) [+W] (one pre/post error-correction experiment, reported second-hand, not in naturalistic AI use). The commit-then-compare order is untested.
rows.change: Require the learner's own explanation, prediction or comparison to be committed before any AI output is shown; then have the learner check the AI's answer against their own and correct or justify the differences; set the assistant to ask "why" rather than supply explanations where it can be configured.
rows.if: Learners have a generative AI assistant or answer source to hand

rows.basis: [Purposely teaching for higher order thinking skills enhances critical thinking](claims/hots-teaching-enhances-critical-thinking.md) [+W] and [HOTS-oriented teaching improves critical-thinking dispositions](claims/hots-teaching-improves-ct-dispositions.md) [+W] (one non-randomised high-school science study, no effect size)
rows.change: Make the thinking moves explicit (what counts as evidence, weighing alternatives) and practise them in demanding tasks persistently across the course, not in one unit; assess with a critical-thinking instrument as well as content tests, before, after and some weeks later.
rows.if: The goal is critical thinking or another higher-order skill as an outcome in its own right

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: One relation, one activating task, one probe at the end; leave comparison of methods and justification for later. In a unit (`days-weeks`), sequence example, then prompts, then comparison, then justification, with a delayed probe.
rows.if: One session only (`single-session`)

rows.basis: [Self-explanation prompts improve learning from worked examples](claims/self-explanation-improves-conceptual-understanding.md) [~M] (evidence for classroom and delayed gains much more limited)
rows.change: Add at least one changed-case item to the assessment, and a delayed one if retention matters; do not read an immediate gain as durable.
rows.if: Stakes: the assessment is recall-only or the gain must last

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Accept explanations in the first language, orally, or with a sentence frame, so the task tests the relation rather than the wording.
rows.if: Learners work in a second language of instruction

rows.basis: [Conflict-based instruction improves science conceptual learning](claims/cognitive-disequilibrium-motivates-conceptual-change.md) [+M]
rows.change: Build the unit as predict, confront, resolve: elicit a committed prediction, show the case it gets wrong, then teach the better model explicitly
rows.if: The topic is science with well-known misconceptions (force and motion, heat, natural selection)

rows.basis: [Instruction that confronts misconceptions produces conceptual change more often than exposition](claims/misconceptions-interfere-with-new-learning.md) [+M]; [Refutational text order enhanced recall in one experiment](claims/refutational-text-order-enhances-retention.md) [+W]
rows.change: Use refutation text: state the common misconception, say that it is wrong, and give the scientific account with its reason
rows.if: The material is mainly read (textbook, online text)

rows.basis: [High-confidence errors lead to better retention after correction](claims/high-confidence-errors-improve-retention.md) [+M]
rows.change: Ask for confidence with each answer, and give immediate, clear, non-punitive correction; confident errors are then corrected best
rows.if: Learners answer questions with a stated confidence (quizzes, clickers, polls)

rows.basis: [Peer conflicts worked only for students prepared to reflect](claims/peer-conflicts-conditional-on-reflection.md) [~M]; [Co-construction needed personal sense-making for stable change](claims/personal-construction-required-stable-conceptual-change.md) [~W]
rows.change: Add an individual step: each learner writes what they expected, what happened and how they now explain it; peer conflict changed conceptions only for students who reflected on and rebuilt their own
rows.if: Learners will resolve the conflict in pairs or groups (for example at a simulation)

rows.basis: [High equality and mutuality were not sufficient for conceptual change](claims/high-equality-mutuality-not-sufficient-conceptual-change.md) [~W]
rows.change: Still check each learner's model on an individual probe; equal, mutual engagement did not ensure conceptual change
rows.if: The group looks engaged and contributions look balanced

rows.basis: [Emotion dynamics predict learning in a way that depends on scaffolding](claims/emotion-dynamics-during-problem-solving-predict-learning-outcomes-context-dependently.md) [~M]
rows.change: Add scaffolding to the attempt so that confusion and surprise lead somewhere; unscaffolded attempts produced more confusion, and emotions related to transfer differently by condition
rows.if: Novices meet the problem before any instruction, with no support

rows.basis: [Confusion amplifies the negative effect of incorrect trials](claims/confusion-amplifies-negative-effect-of-incorrect-trials.md) [-W] (exploratory)
rows.change: Lower the difficulty or give support now rather than more contradiction; confusion with repeated errors predicted worse later performance
rows.if: Learners are getting most practice items wrong and say they are confused

rows.basis: [One-step advance regardless of discrepancy size](claims/one-step-advance-regardless-of-discrepancy-size.md) [~W] (one 1975 spatial-reasoning study)
rows.change: Pitch the discrepant task one level above the learner's current level; two levels above produced no more advance, and all advances were one level
rows.if: The target is a developmental reasoning skill and the brief asks how big a challenge to set

rows.basis: [Force-and-motion conceptions were very difficult to change](claims/force-motion-conceptions-difficult-to-change.md) [~W]
rows.change: Plan a delayed probe the old model would answer wrongly, and revisit; in one physics study 7 of 14 students showed no change at post- or delayed test
rows.if: The revised model must hold for months

rows.basis: [Conceptual change strategies in cooperative groups reduced misconceptions](claims/cooperative-conceptual-change-chemistry-misconceptions.md) [~W]
rows.change: Prepare group leaders or assign roles so the discussion stays on the conflicting ideas; poor leadership undermined it
rows.if: Learners will discuss in cooperative groups (for example college chemistry)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Collect predictions privately or anonymously and say that wrong predictions are expected
rows.if: Learners are anxious about being wrong, or the setting is public

rows.basis: [Part-task practice reduces cognitive load for absolute novices during initial skill acquisition.](claims/part-task-practice-reduces-load-for-novices.md) [~M]; population not reported on the claim page
rows.change: Start with one case and part tasks; add the second and third case only after the simple version is completed unaided; prompt the named dimension of comparison.
rows.if: Expertise `novice` in the domain, high element interactivity

rows.basis: [Presenting multiple cases from different perspectives supports transfer in ill-structured domains](claims/cognitive-flexibility-theory-multiple-cases.md) [+M]; tested with first- and second-year undergraduates, untested with professionals
rows.change: Use criss-crossing: revisit each concept in several short cases under different themes across sessions; drop the step-by-step part tasks.
rows.if: Expertise `intermediate` or `advanced`, an ill-structured domain (clinical reasoning, law, policy)

rows.basis: untested proposal; no claim here tests case comparison with children
rows.change: Use two cases at a time, side by side, with the one dimension that differs named by the teacher; no free navigation among cases.
rows.if: Age `child` (under 12)

rows.basis: [Numerical routines individualize through a three-stage sequence of vertical and horizontal bonding](claims/numerical-routines-individualize-through-bonding.md) [+W]: a teaching experiment with four children, no comparison group; it describes a sequence, not an effect
rows.change: Embed the comparison in a purposeful choice ("which pile do you want?"); model one method and ask what its result means for the choice, then show that a second method gives the same answer; expect the child to propose the cross-check unprompted only later, across months.
rows.if: Age `child`, early years (about 2–5), a number `concept` reachable by several methods (estimating, counting, lining up)

rows.basis: [Intermediate mechanics students start the semester more familiar with the integration constants (+C) method than with the limits method, and the +C method remains preferred by at least one student even after instruction modeling the limits method](claims/students-start-semester-more-familiar-with-integration-constants-method-than-limits-method.md) [~W]; [Students using the limits method initially choose unphysical integration limits, failing to consider the functional relationship between limits on either side of the equal sign](claims/students-choose-unphysical-limits-ignoring-functional-relationship-across-equal-sign.md) [+W]: one qualitative study of two student groups in one course; see also the adolescent algebra row below, which found comparison raised method flexibility
rows.change: Show both methods as routes through the same ideas, side by side; give cases where the familiar rule of thumb fails (a non-zero starting value), and ask what each part of the new method stands for; expect the familiar method to persist after one modelled demonstration.
rows.if: Learners fluent in one solution method must take up a second (for example, undergraduate STEM procedures)

rows.basis: [Comparing cases side by side improves learning and transfer by a moderate average amount, though in one algebra study it raised procedural knowledge and flexibility but not conceptual knowledge](claims/comparing-contrasting-cases-improves-learning.md) [~M]; tested with seventh-graders, procedural flexibility rose, conceptual knowledge did not
rows.change: Have learners compare alternative solution methods side by side; expect gains in choosing methods, and add a separate item asking why each method works.
rows.if: Age `adolescent`, goal a mathematics `procedure`

rows.basis: [Presenting multiple cases from different perspectives supports transfer in ill-structured domains](claims/cognitive-flexibility-theory-multiple-cases.md) [~M]: the drill group recalled more facts
rows.change: Do not make criss-crossing the main activity; give facts their own retrieval practice, and use varied cases only for the transfer part of the objective.
rows.if: Goal `verbal-association` (facts, terms), or recall-weighted high-stakes assessment

rows.basis: [Multiple representations improve learning](claims/multiple-representations-improve-learning.md) [~M]; one undergraduate physics field study and a review; benefit depends on representational competence. [Students who got stuck on the desk-scale number line proactively returned to the body-scale number line to validate their answers, achieving perspectival mutuality](claims/returning-to-bnl-perspectival-mutuality.md) [+W]: one middle-school design study, no comparison group
rows.change: Add a second representation (sketch, simulation, an embodied or walk-on model) beside the formula, with tasks that connect them; keep the first available so learners can switch back to check; monitor reported load and representational skill.
rows.if: Goal a STEM `concept` taught through representations

rows.basis: [A flexible hypertext course group averaged 76% on achievement tests against 59% for a direct-design group that studied different software, so the contrast confounds design with content](claims/cft-hypertext-design-higher-achievement-scores.md) [~W]: groups studied different software, so it does not isolate the design; navigation burden is untested, from the theory page
rows.change: Give a guided route through the cases (a theme per pass) rather than free browsing, and build the comparison prompts into the pages.
rows.if: Setting `online-self-paced` or hypertext

rows.basis: [Unstructured LLM use contributes to epistemic narrowing by privileging convergent outputs and dominant viewpoints](claims/unstructured-llm-use-epistemic-narrowing.md) [-W]: a theoretical argument, untested; no claim here tests AI-generated case sets
rows.change: Do not let the assistant supply the cases unprompted; ask learners to request deliberately contrasting cases or viewpoints, name whose view each represents, and compare them as for any other case set.
rows.if: Learners use a generative AI assistant to produce cases, explanations or perspectives

rows.basis: [Comparing cases side by side improves learning and transfer by a moderate average amount, though in one algebra study it raised procedural knowledge and flexibility but not conceptual knowledge](claims/comparing-contrasting-cases-improves-learning.md) [+M]: comparison helped in single experiments, more at immediate tests
rows.change: Use two or three contrasting cases with a similarities prompt and the principle stated after; test on a new case the same day. If the course allows, revisit the cases later under a new theme.
rows.if: Duration `single-session`

rows.basis: [Presenting multiple cases from different perspectives supports transfer in ill-structured domains](claims/cognitive-flexibility-theory-multiple-cases.md) [+M]: the advantage appeared by the fourth session; delayed benefit untested
rows.change: Return to the same concepts in each session through new cases and new themes; schedule a delayed transfer case.
rows.if: Duration `days-weeks` or `term-plus`

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep cases short, give them in accessible language, and present the comparison as a table learners fill in, so reading demand does not swamp comparison.
rows.if: Constraint: cases in a second language, or heavy reading load

rows.basis: [A pretraining primer improved knowledge and transfer](claims/pretraining-improves-transfer.md) [+M]
rows.change: Start with a short primer that names the parts and what they do, then the main lesson
rows.if: A new topic with many unfamiliar parts or terms (equipment, anatomy, a system)

rows.basis: [Isolated parts first helped novices on complex tasks](claims/part-task-practice-reduces-load-for-novices.md) [+M]
rows.change: Teach the interacting parts in isolation first, then combine them in the whole task
rows.if: A complex whole task that novices cannot yet coordinate

rows.basis: [Segmenting and worked examples improved learning, with qualifications](claims/cognitive-load-management.md) [+M]; [Segmenting improves multimedia learning](claims/segmenting-improves-multimedia-learning.md) [+M]; [Weeding extraneous content improved retention and transfer from video, reported second-hand in an essay](claims/weeding-extraneous-content-improves-video-learning.md) [+W]
rows.change: Segment it at conceptual breaks; allow extra time; cut background music, busy backgrounds and other interesting but unneeded material
rows.if: Transient media (video, narrated animation) carry the content

rows.basis: [Picture or animation with voice beat picture with text, 36 adults, 15 minutes of immunology](claims/voice-media-outperform-picture-text-overall.md) [+W]
rows.change: Give the explanation as narration rather than as on-screen text beside the picture
rows.if: A picture or animation has to be explained in words

rows.basis: [Worked examples improve mathematics performance](claims/worked-examples-improve-math-performance.md) [+M]
rows.change: Begin with worked examples before unaided problems
rows.if: Novices learning a structured problem type (mathematics, science procedures)

rows.basis: [Guidance that helps novices can become redundant as expertise grows](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M]
rows.change: Withdraw guidance step by step and check with an unsupported changed problem before removing it entirely
rows.if: Learners are progressing, or are experienced on the task

rows.basis: [Effortful conditions can improve delayed retention](claims/desirable-difficulties-enhance-learning.md) [~M]
rows.change: Once the material is understood, reintroduce effort: spaced practice and retrieval quizzes, even though practice gets harder
rows.if: The outcome is retention at a delay (an exam weeks away)

rows.basis: [Problem-solving before instruction improved conceptual learning](claims/productive-failure-improves-conceptual-learning.md) [~M]
rows.change: Consider a problem-solving attempt before instruction, always followed by the instruction
rows.if: The goal is conceptual understanding, with secondary or older students

rows.basis: [Problem-solving before instruction improved conceptual learning](claims/productive-failure-improves-conceptual-learning.md) [-M]
rows.change: Teach first, then practise; the problem-first advantage reversed for these groups
rows.if: Learners are in grades 2–5, or the skill is domain-general

rows.basis: [Effortful conditions can improve delayed retention](claims/desirable-difficulties-enhance-learning.md) [~M]
rows.change: Present items blocked by category rather than interleaved; interleaving hurt for words
rows.if: The material is word lists or vocabulary

rows.basis: [Foreign-language AI explanations impose a double burden](claims/double-burden-language-of-ai-instruction.md) [~W]
rows.change: Give explanations in the first language or bilingually where possible
rows.if: Instruction is in the learners' second language

rows.basis: [Higher task complexity went with lower written production](claims/task-complexity-negatively-related-child-written-production.md) [-W]; [Task complexity showed no effect on oral production](claims/task-complexity-no-effect-child-oral-production.md) [~W]
rows.change: Keep the task simple while the form is new; written production fell as task complexity rose, though oral production of the same form did not differ
rows.if: Child learners writing a target form in a second language

rows.basis: [Mental effort and study time rose with element interactivity](claims/mental-effort-study-time-indicate-element-interactivity.md) [+M]; [Retention and transfer scores fell as interactivity rose](claims/retention-transfer-scores-decrease-with-element-interactivity.md) [+W]; [CLT design produced higher effective learning scores at retention and transfer](claims/clt-design-effective-learning-retention-transfer.md) [+M]; counting elements is not enough, since problems with the same number of moves can differ sharply in difficulty ([difficulty is not set by element interactivity alone](claims/difficulty-beyond-element-interactivity.md) [~W])
rows.change: Classify the topics for these learners (expert judgement first, then rated effort and study time from the first sessions) and give the high-interactivity ones the most sequencing and support
rows.if: A unit mixes topics of low and high element interactivity (a science unit)

rows.basis: [Revised visuals had no learning effect](claims/revised-visuals-no-learning-effect.md) [~M]; [Revised visuals changed processing of text in opposite directions by prior knowledge](claims/revised-visuals-processing-text-prior-knowledge-interaction.md) [~M]; [and of the mathematics visuals](claims/revised-visuals-processing-math-visuals-interaction.md) [~M]
rows.change: Check the revision on a learning outcome and separately for each prior-knowledge level; do not expect test gains from the revision alone
rows.if: Revising existing materials (adding signals, moving labels next to what they label, cutting decorative visuals) for a class whose prior knowledge varies

rows.basis: [Fast drills disadvantage older learners](claims/rote-drills-disadvantage-older-learners.md) [~W]; [Learning ability does not decline with age in healthy adults](claims/learning-ability-does-not-decline-with-age.md) [+W]; [One digest's account that older adults can learn a language](claims/no-evidence-older-adults-cannot-learn-language.md) [~W]; [An older-beginner class taught this way made gains, with no comparison group](claims/older-beginner-esl-outcome-gains.md) [+W]; set task difficulty per learner rather than one level for all: in laboratory working-memory tasks (not learning tasks), age-group differences in accuracy were much smaller in studies that titrated difficulty to each person ([titration reduced age differences](claims/titration-reduces-age-differences-storage-dual-task.md) [+W]; [titration, not domain overlap, accounted for it](claims/titration-dominates-domain-overlap-combined-metaregression.md) [~W])
rows.change: Slow the pace, introduce one new concept per activity with extra review and wait time, and avoid fast, competitive drills; do not lower expectations of what they can learn
rows.if: Learners are older adults (55+)

rows.basis: [Group learning was more efficient for high-complexity tasks and individual for low, as one review reports an earlier experiment](claims/collective-working-memory-effect-complexity-dependent.md) [+W]; [Collaboration spreads load across working memories for high-load tasks, reported second-hand](claims/collaborative-learning-collective-working-memory-advantage.md) [+W]; [Communication and coordination costs can cancel that benefit (theoretical)](claims/transactive-costs-annul-load-sharing-benefit.md) [+W]; [Experienced groups were more efficient only at high information density](claims/zambrano-2019-efficiency-advantage-only-high-density.md) [~W]; [Low information density lowered effort and raised efficiency during the group learning phase](claims/zambrano-2019-low-density-lower-effort-learning.md) [+W]
rows.change: Use groups for high-complexity tasks and individual work for simple ones; structure the communication and division of work, and prefer groups that have worked together before when the information to share is dense
rows.if: Learners will work in groups on the task

rows.basis: [Web search produced better justifications than an AI chatbot, 91 students](claims/web-search-higher-quality-justifications-than-llm.md) [+M]; [In an exploratory analysis, lower germane load in the chatbot group accounted for that difference](claims/germane-load-mediates-tool-effect-on-justification-quality.md) [+W]
rows.change: Keep the effortful part of the inquiry: ask for justification from several sources, or have learners search and weigh sources themselves, and judge the work on its reasoning, not its ease
rows.if: Learners research a question with a generative AI chatbot rather than a search engine

rows.basis: [Constantly high complexity beat a gradual increase on posttest time and trials two days later, 132 participants](claims/constantly-high-complexity-improves-posttest-performance.md) [~M]
rows.change: Do not assume a gradual ramp of complexity is better; try full complexity from the start with a delayed check, keeping simpler steps for learners who stall
rows.if: A rule-governed skill learners can attempt whole from the start (verb conjugation), tested days later

rows.basis: [Disfluency had no effect while expecting a test improved retention and transfer](claims/disfluency-no-effect-test-expectancy.md) [~W]; [Disfluency helped only learners with high working memory capacity](claims/disfluency-benefits-high-working-memory-only.md) [~W]; [Neither disfluency nor prompted imagination improved performance in two small experiments](claims/gcl-activation-no-task-performance-effect.md) [-W]
rows.change: Do not; reintroduce effort through retrieval, spacing or an announced test instead
rows.if: The plan is to make material harder to perceive (a hard-to-read font) so learners work harder

rows.basis: [Reducing split attention improves learning](claims/cognitive-load-reduction-improves-learning.md) [+S]; [Integrating text and diagrams beats separating them](claims/split-attention-effect-degrades-learning.md) [+M]; [text repeating a diagram's frequencies made no detectable difference](claims/redundant-text-no-effect-posterior-probability-lesson.md) [~M] (198 undergraduates, a print probability lesson; not an equivalence test; see [Redundancy](principles/redundancy.md))
rows.change: Place each label or explanation on or next to the part it describes; present narration at the same time as the animation it explains. Where the text only restates what the diagram already shows, do not expect removing or keeping it to matter much
rows.if: Text and diagrams refer to each other (labelled figures, worked solutions with a diagram)

rows.basis: [Animation or picture with voice beat picture with text](claims/voice-media-outperform-picture-text-overall.md) [+M] (36 adults, a 15-minute immunology lesson, p = .004, no effect size printed)
rows.change: Speak the explanation instead of printing it beside the picture; keep printed words to labels; see [Modality](principles/modality.md)
rows.if: Pictures or an animation are explained by printed words, and the lesson runs at the system's pace

rows.basis: [Reducing extraneous load improved learning, more for complex material](claims/cognitive-overload-degrades-learning.md) [+M]; [Integration helps more for high element interactivity](claims/element-interactivity-moderates-contiguity-effect.md) [+M]
rows.change: Apply the load-reducing design principles first here; their effect was largest for complex material
rows.if: The material is complex, with many interacting elements

rows.basis: [Design principle effects moderated by pacing and complexity](claims/design-principle-effects-moderated-by-pacing-and-complexity.md) [~M]
rows.change: Expect a smaller gain from redesign; reported effects were smaller for simple and for learner-paced media
rows.if: The material is simple, or learners control the pace (a website, a document)

rows.basis: [With images or animation, verbal redundancy does not help](claims/images-animation-eliminate-redundancy-benefit.md) [~M]; [adding written text to narration made no significant difference for middle-school students](claims/redundancy-effect-not-significant-middle-school.md) [~M] (abstract and concrete animation; a quasi-experiment, source without a DOI)
rows.change: Drop the verbatim on-screen text; with images or animation, adding it gave no benefit. Removing text that is already there is a small change, not a rescue
rows.if: Narration plus the same words on screen, alongside pictures or animation

rows.basis: [Spoken–written advantages are larger for L2 and nonfluent readers](claims/reader-fluency-prior-knowledge-moderate-redundancy.md) [+M]
rows.change: Keep spoken and written text together (narration with captions); the benefit was larger for these readers
rows.if: Learners are second-language or less fluent readers, and the material is text without pictures

rows.basis: [Foreign-language AI explanations impose a double burden](claims/double-burden-language-of-ai-instruction.md) [~W]
rows.change: Give explanations in the learners' first language or bilingually where possible
rows.if: The instruction is in a language the learners are still learning

rows.basis: [Differentiated materials beat one adapted version within each proficiency level](claims/within-stratum-differentiated-advantage-reading-comprehension.md) [+M] (one EAP study: d = 0.60 low, 0.16 intermediate, 1.40 high); [lower rated load for low-proficiency readers with differentiated materials](claims/descriptive-process-estimates-support-layers.md) [~M] (descriptive only, measured in the same session as the outcome)
rows.change: Give each proficiency level its own version: glosses and sentence unpacking for the least proficient, different support for the others, checked by a comprehension test per level
rows.if: Second-language readers of different proficiency share one set of reading materials

rows.basis: [Guidance that helps novices can become redundant as expertise grows](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M]; [Split-attention benefit reverses into redundancy for experienced learners](claims/expertise-reversal-split-attention-redundancy-review.md) [~M]
rows.change: Remove explanatory text from diagrams and other guidance that repeats what they know; check with an unsupported task
rows.if: Learners are experienced on this task

rows.basis: [Example-first sequences beat problem-first ones for novices on an immediate test, with lower rated effort](claims/worked-example-problem-sequences.md) [+M]; [Lower-prior-knowledge learners did better with full than completion examples](claims/lower-prior-knowledge-learners-score-higher-with-full-than-completion-worked-examples.md) [+M]
rows.change: Open with a full worked example, not a problem: examples only or example–problem pairs, then problems; use full worked examples rather than completion problems at first
rows.if: Learners are novices on a multi-step procedure

rows.basis: [Contingent support beat fixed or absent support, mostly in one-to-one tutoring](claims/contingent-scaffolding-improves-learning.md) [+M]; [Worked-example guidance becomes less effective as expertise grows](claims/worked-examples-less-effective-with-expertise.md) [~M]
rows.change: Raise support after a failed step and lower it after a success, instead of fixing one level for everyone; fade full examples as independent success holds
rows.if: Support can be adjusted to each learner's last response (one-to-one tutoring, a small group, an adaptive system)

rows.basis: [Isolated parts first helped novices on complex tasks](claims/part-task-practice-reduces-load-for-novices.md) [+M]
rows.change: Teach the interacting parts separately first, then the whole task
rows.if: A complex whole task that novices cannot yet coordinate

rows.basis: One trial in the wiki: [structured training to use generative AI as a collaborative partner raised electromagnetism posttest scores over problem-solving training](claims/genai-scaffolding-training-improves-revision-performance.md) [+M] (sophomore STEM students, d = 0.81) while [total rated load did not differ and intrinsic load was marginally higher](claims/genai-training-comparable-load-marginal-intrinsic-increase.md) [~M] (d = 0.17; d = 0.37, p = .079). Otherwise conceptual arguments: [AI lowers access complexity, not the task's cognitive demand](claims/ai-raises-problem-complexity-ceiling.md) [~W]; [Outsourcing productive struggle to AI risks cognitive debt](claims/cognitive-debt-reactive-ai-approaches-insufficient.md) [~W]; [AI as scaffolding that lowers the threshold for understanding](claims/ai-intelligent-scaffolding-lowers-knowledge-threshold.md) [~W]; [Intrinsic and extraneous load differ by whether interactivity is essential to the task](claims/intrinsic-extraneous-distinction-essential-vs-instructional.md) [~W]
rows.change: Let it remove access barriers (finding, formatting, translating material) but keep the interacting elements the task is meant to teach for the learner to process; teach learners to use it as a partner that questions and checks rather than an answer source; check unaided performance, and do not expect rated load to fall
rows.if: Learners have an AI assistant or tutor

rows.basis: [Low information density lowered rated effort and raised efficiency during group learning](claims/zambrano-2019-low-density-lower-effort-learning.md) [+M] (one 2×2 experiment); [its retention advantage had faded by the delayed test](claims/zambrano-2019-low-density-benefit-shortlived.md) [~M]
rows.change: Keep the amount of information each group must pool and coordinate low at first; prefer groups that have worked together when it is dense; check retention after a delay, not only the next day. Group size and structure are on [Cognitive Load Management](principles/cognitive-load-management.md)
rows.if: Learners work in groups on a shared complex task

rows.basis: [Reducing extraneous load can also remove affordances for germane processes](claims/extraneous-load-reduction-may-remove-germane-affordances.md) [~W] (de Jong's review, citing a hypertext example; an argument, untested in the wiki)
rows.change: Before removing it, ask whether that processing is the target; if it is, keep it and reduce load elsewhere (pre-teach parts, integrate sources), then compare learning, not ratings
rows.if: The redesign would remove work learners are meant to learn from (comparing examples, relating two representations, choosing a path through linked material)

rows.basis: [Design interventions yield small improvements in load measures](claims/design-principles-improve-cognitive-load-management.md) [~M]; [Tree diagrams raised rated load](claims/tree-diagrams-increase-cognitive-load.md) [~M], yet [format made no difference to conceptual or situational knowledge](claims/no-format-effect-conceptual-situational-knowledge.md) [~M] and [adding equations lowered load without better outcomes](claims/adding-equations-to-diagrams-reduced-load-not-outcomes.md) [~M]; [principles before case comparison raised rated germane load and lowered extraneous load by large amounts](claims/input-before-raises-germane-lowers-extraneous-load.md) [~M] while [timing made no difference to knowledge](claims/input-timing-no-effect-knowledge-case-comparison.md) [~M] (student teachers); [drawing support raised rated difficulty](claims/drawing-support-increased-perceived-difficulty.md) [-M]
rows.change: Measure performance and transfer as well; load ratings moved little even where design changes improved learning, and moved without any change in learning in a combinatorics simulation and a case-comparison study; an added support can raise ratings, so a higher rating alone does not show the support failed
rows.if: Success will be judged by learners' effort or load ratings

rows.basis: [Learning Styles Matching Does Not Improve Learning](claims/learning-styles-matching-does-not-improve-learning.md) [-S] (learning styles, not cognitive styles; fifth graders and adults); [No significant interaction between learning mode and learning style on gain scores](claims/no-mode-by-style-interaction-vr-gains.md) [-M] (one VR experiment, Kolb styles)
rows.change: Do not split materials by style. Give everyone the format the content needs; use the time saved for structure and checks on the tasks where learners stall
rows.if: The brief proposes sorting learners by a style inventory and giving each group matched materials

rows.basis: [Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows.](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~S] (cognitive-load studies; does not address styles)
rows.change: Novice: give the structure or worked model to all, regardless of style. Advanced: drop the frame and check the approach on one unaided task; prior knowledge, not style, sets how much guidance to give
rows.if: Learners are `novice` on the task, or `advanced`

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Never tell a child, or their parents, what style they "are". Teach the structure or check as a tool for a kind of task ("for lab reports we use this frame"), with shorter rounds (5 minutes of modelling)
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary age)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Ask how they already tackle this kind of task at work; build the structure or check into their own job aid or form rather than a classroom frame, and let them keep it
rows.if: Learners are `adult` in a work setting (`adult-workplace`)

rows.basis: untested proposal; modifiability argued in [styles socialized and modifiable](claims/styles-socialized-and-modifiable.md) [+W]
rows.change: Model the structure with a worked case, then a printed frame, then a checklist, then a blank page (step 4 of the default design)
rows.if: The task needs part-by-part analysis and some learners see only the whole

rows.basis: untested proposal; [stylistic rigidity](claims/stylistic-cognitive-rigidity-reduces-adoption-of-opposites.md) [~W] (argument, no data)
rows.change: Timed 2–3 minute rounds with judgement deferred, not graded (step 6)
rows.if: The task needs quick spontaneous response and some learners hold back

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use one of the learners' actual wrong answers as a worked contrast: show the answer, then the 1-minute check that would have caught it, then add the stop-and-check step to every problem for three or four sessions
rows.if: The brief reports careless errors on multi-step problems

rows.basis: [Embedded figures and intelligence](claims/embedded-figures-test-sex-difference-intelligence-correlation.md) [~M] (one study in a 1985 review)
rows.change: Treat it as partly an ability and language measure; observe the learner on two or three real tasks before acting, and do not place a learner in a group or track on it
rows.if: A style or embedded-figures score is the only evidence about a learner

rows.basis: [Cultural and linguistic background influences measured learning and cognitive styles](claims/cultural-background-influences-learning-style-measurement.md) [~M] (Native and non-Native samples in Canada and Alaska, reported in a review)
rows.change: Do not use the measure for placement; give instructions non-verbally where possible and judge the approach from task attempts
rows.if: Learners are culturally or linguistically diverse, or the style measure is in their second language

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Present the frame or check as something experts use, not a fix for a weakness; keep the frame's language simpler than the task; let a learner show the structure by sorting cards before writing it
rows.if: Learners have low confidence or low literacy

rows.basis: untested proposal; matching evidence carried ([Learning Styles Matching](claims/learning-styles-matching-does-not-improve-learning.md) [-S])
rows.change: No style quiz at entry. Offer the frame or checklist as an optional download beside every analytic task and a built-in check step on multi-step problems; let the learner hide them once they no longer need them
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Share the frame as a single on-screen checklist everyone uses, not a printed sheet; run timed rounds in a shared document or chat so remote learners contribute in the same round
rows.if: Mixed modes: some learners join remotely while others are in the room, or work on a phone only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Do not diagnose individuals. Build the structure and the check into the task for everyone; spend the brief check-in only on learners who stalled on the last task, looking at one section of their work
rows.if: One teacher with a large group, or scarce facilitator time (volunteers, one tutor checking in briefly)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Give every learner the structure or check the task needs, model it once (5 minutes), and leave it in place; do not try to change a habit or claim it changed
rows.if: A single session only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: 5 minutes modelling the structure on a worked case, 20 minutes on the task with the frame, 5 minutes self-checking against the checklist; one product, revised once
rows.if: A fixed short time budget (for example 30 minutes)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep it as given. Use its categories as descriptions of approaches to tasks, not labels on learners; change only what this page settles: no one restricted to matched tasks, and one supported task per unit in the less-used approach
rows.if: The brief names its own categories, rubric or routine (a school's style framework, its own report template, its own check-in)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: The learner decides who sees any profile or notes on their approach; record observations about tasks, not traits, in shared records
rows.if: A learner's style profile or reflections on how they work are private or sensitive

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Do not split the performance into style-matched parts; keep it whole and put the frame or check inside it. The audience's needs, not the learner's style, set the product's form
rows.if: The goal is a whole-task performance the brief wants kept whole, or a product for a real audience

rows.basis: untested; concern argued in [Schools overwhelmingly reward executive styles](claims/schools-reward-executive-styles.md) [~W]
rows.change: Assess every learner on the same capability and criterion; allow a choice of form only where the objective does not fix it; check the rubric does not reward one way of working the goal does not require
rows.if: Stakes are high (graded assessment, certification)

rows.basis: [Coherence principle](claims/coherence-principle-irrelevant-material-hurts-learning.md) [+S] (13 of 14 experiments in one programme, median d = 0.97); [Seductive details effect](claims/seductive-details-effect.md) [~S] (direction holds, size varies with material and learner)
rows.change: Leave them out of the explanation; if interest is needed, use material that carries the content (a relevant example, an informative picture)
rows.if: The brief asks for engaging extras in an explanation: stock photos, background music, anecdotes, fun facts

rows.basis: [Design principle effects moderated by pacing and complexity](claims/design-principle-effects-moderated-by-pacing-and-complexity.md) [~M] (g = 0.70 complex, 0.20 simple, across principles); [Multimedia principles benefit novices](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M]
rows.change: Apply the audit at full strength, and expect it to matter most here
rows.if: Learners are `novice` on the content, and the explanation has many interacting parts

rows.basis: [Revised visuals raise processing for middle prior knowledge students](claims/revised-visuals-cognitive-load-text-prior-knowledge-interaction.md) [~M]; [Revisions had no effect on test scores](claims/revised-visuals-no-learning-effect.md) [~M]; [Multimedia principles benefit novices](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M]; [Split attention reverses into redundancy for experienced learners](claims/expertise-reversal-split-attention-redundancy-review.md) [~M]
rows.change: Do not expect a gain from stripping further; also cut support they no longer need, and check transfer before and after
rows.if: Learners have middle or high prior knowledge of the content

rows.basis: [Design principle effects moderated by pacing and complexity](claims/design-principle-effects-moderated-by-pacing-and-complexity.md) [~M]; [Seductive details effect](claims/seductive-details-effect.md) [~S] (η² = .04 on easy texts)
rows.change: Give the audit lower priority; a decorative picture on a simple page costs little
rows.if: The material is simple: few parts, a short text

rows.basis: [Seductive details effect](claims/seductive-details-effect.md) [~S] (Lenzner et al., grades 7–8; Garner et al., adults and children); younger children untested
rows.change: Keep decorative pictures out of and away from the instructional pictures; the evidence with 7th and 8th graders found no overall harm but a weaker benefit from the informative picture. For children below that age, treat it as a proposal
rows.if: Learners are children or young adolescents (`primary`, `secondary`)

rows.basis: [Design principle effects moderated by pacing and complexity](claims/design-principle-effects-moderated-by-pacing-and-complexity.md) [~M] (g = 0.41 system-paced, 0.27 learner-paced, across principles)
rows.change: Cut hardest here: learners cannot slow down or skip. No background music, no tangential clips, stories before or after
rows.if: Video, a narrated animation or a live lecture (system-paced)

rows.basis: [Design principle effects moderated by pacing and complexity](claims/design-principle-effects-moderated-by-pacing-and-complexity.md) [~M]; [Hypermedia usability problems](claims/hypermedia-usability-problems-hinder-effectiveness.md) [~M] (distraction and overload in learner-controlled hypermedia)
rows.change: Still cut, but expect a smaller effect; give learners a clear path through essential content so optional extras can be skipped
rows.if: `online-self-paced` pages, learner-paced

rows.basis: [Seductive details effect](claims/seductive-details-effect.md) [~S]; [eBook images covering the text](claims/hero-elementary-ebooks-not-user-friendly-images-covering-text.md) [~W] (teacher reports)
rows.change: Each slide or page: the essential picture and its words. Remove decorative clip-art and images that cover text
rows.if: Slides or print

rows.basis: untested
rows.change: One idea per screen, no decorative headers or background images, so the essential picture can be large enough to read
rows.if: Phone-only, small screen

rows.basis: untested; the claims in the wiki concern text, pictures, video and narration
rows.change: Keep the scene to the objects the task needs, and remove ambient sound and decoration that carry nothing for the task
rows.if: VR or an immersive simulation

rows.basis: [Coherence principle](claims/coherence-principle-irrelevant-material-hurts-learning.md) [+S]; [Revisions made no reliable difference to time](claims/revisions-no-effect-time-with-lesson.md) [~M]
rows.change: Spend the minutes on the essential explanation and the brief's own check. Do not plan on cutting extras to save time: a combined revision made no reliable difference to time with the lesson
rows.if: A single session, or a fixed short time budget

rows.basis: [Design principle effects moderated by pacing and complexity](claims/design-principle-effects-moderated-by-pacing-and-complexity.md) [~M]; placement untested
rows.change: Keep the explanation itself free of digressions; tell the anecdote after the point it illustrates, and only if it is an instance of it
rows.if: One teacher for many learners, a live lecture

rows.basis: [Seductive details effect](claims/seductive-details-effect.md) [~S] (larger cost with lower working memory; language moderated the meta-analysis); [Split attention reverses into redundancy for experienced learners](claims/expertise-reversal-split-attention-redundancy-review.md) [~M] (Yeung et al., as reported in a review: explanatory notes built into a text helped learners with low language competence and hindered more knowledgeable ones, so what to cut depends on the reader's language level); second-language learners as such carried over, untested
rows.change: Every extra sentence costs reading effort: cut text the goal does not need first, and keep an informative picture
rows.if: Learners with low literacy, or studying in a second language

rows.basis: [Seductive details effect](claims/seductive-details-effect.md) [~S] (González et al., Study 2: harm only with low attentional inhibition)
rows.change: Treat removal as essential, not optional; this is where the cost was measured on harder texts
rows.if: Learners with attention difficulties, or low attentional control

rows.basis: untested
rows.change: Mark decorative images as decorative (empty alt text) so a screen reader skips them; give no background music under narration; caption only the essential audio
rows.if: Learners who are blind or partially sighted, or deaf or hard of hearing

rows.basis: untested
rows.change: Keep them as given. Audit the supplied materials only for additions that carry no content and remove those; run the brief's own assessment as given
rows.if: The brief supplies its own materials, routine or rubric

rows.basis: [Hispanic adults valued culturally relevant visual design](claims/culturally-relevant-visual-design-lcs-materials.md) [~W] (preference, not a learning outcome)
rows.change: Keep it where learners value it, and make it carry content where possible (people from the community doing the task being taught); keep it out of the explanatory diagram
rows.if: The brief wants culturally relevant imagery, or learners to see people like themselves

rows.basis: [Personalized problem contexts](claims/personalized-problem-contexts-boost-engagement-grades-4-8.md) [~W] (practice-guide assertion); [Decorative photographs distract from the mathematics](claims/decorative-images-distract-from-math-problems.md) [+W]
rows.change: A context that carries the problem's structure is not a seductive detail; keep it, and remove only the setting details the mathematics does not use
rows.if: The brief wants problems set in learners' own interests or contexts

rows.basis: [Causal knowledge helps novices with cases containing irrelevant findings](claims/biomedical-causal-knowledge-improves-novice-diagnosis-irrelevant-findings.md) [~W] (carried over: a test case with irrelevant findings, not a lesson with seductive details)
rows.change: Do not strip details the real performance has to deal with; deciding what is irrelevant may be the skill. Cut only presentation extras around the task
rows.if: A whole task is kept whole: a realistic case or authentic problem

rows.basis: untested
rows.change: Use only the details the explanation needs; personal detail that carries nothing for the goal is both extraneous and a privacy cost
rows.if: The brief involves private material: learners' own cases, records or stories

rows.basis: [Classroom design affects learning progress](claims/classroom-design-affects-learning-progress.md) [~M] (associational; moderately decorated rooms outperformed bare and heavily decorated ones)
rows.change: Aim for moderate display, not bare walls and not clutter
rows.if: The brief is about the physical classroom: walls and displays

rows.basis: untested for delayed outcomes
rows.change: Apply the audit, and check understanding on the brief's own assessment at the delay that matters, since the recorded effects are mostly on immediate tests
rows.if: High stakes: certification, a safety-critical procedure

rows.basis: [Collaborative learning improves outcomes](claims/collaborative-learning-improves-outcomes.md) [+M]; [Small-group learning improves undergraduate STEM achievement](claims/small-group-learning-improves-stem-achievement.md) [+M]
rows.change: Put small-group work on tasks that need explaining and comparing alongside instruction, rather than instruction alone; expect a programme-level gain, not one for every learner
rows.if: The goal is understanding of concepts or principles, in a school or undergraduate course running several weeks

rows.basis: [Co-construction needs personal construction for stable change](claims/personal-construction-required-stable-conceptual-change.md) [~W]; [Equal, mutual engagement did not ensure change](claims/high-equality-mutuality-not-sufficient-conceptual-change.md) [~W]
rows.change: After the group task, ask each member alone for the explanation, straight away and again later, on changed wording; do not let the group's answer stand for it
rows.if: The target is each member's understanding at a later test

rows.basis: [Collaborative writing improves text quality](claims/collaborative-writing-improves-text-quality.md) [+M]
rows.change: Have learners plan, draft or revise together; then set an individual piece to see whether the gain carries to each writer
rows.if: The goal is a written text

rows.basis: [Aligned problem perceptions predict self-reported, not measured, outcomes](claims/homogeneous-problem-perceptions-predict-regulation-success.md) [~M]
rows.change: Add an individual knowledge check; read the self-report as an observation of the group's process only
rows.if: Success will be judged by learners' satisfaction or their report that the group worked well

rows.basis: [Structuring interdependence did not change achievement online](claims/interdependence-type-no-achievement-effect-asynchronous.md) [~M]; [Students rated collaboration worse online](claims/collaboration-interest-belonging-worse-online.md) [~W]
rows.change: Plan the interaction explicitly (shared task, deadlines for responding to each other); do not expect a role or reward scheme alone to raise achievement
rows.if: The setting is `online-self-paced` or asynchronous online groups

rows.basis: [Effects on critical thinking were largest in groups of 2–3 and fell below ES 0.5 above seven](claims/mixed-courses-and-small-groups-strongest-cps-effects.md) [~M]; [Large groups limited individual participation](claims/large-group-size-limited-participation-confidence.md) [~W]; in discussion forums, [small groups were needed for students to relate deeply to the discussion](claims/forum-collaborative-learning-small-group-sizes.md) [~W]
rows.change: Default to pairs or threes; in groups of four or more, rotate who does each step so every member does every step. Expect the gain to shrink as groups grow
rows.if: Group size is open, or groups of four or more share limited equipment or one hands-on procedure

rows.basis: [Collaborative problem solving improves critical thinking (ES 0.82, 36 studies, I² = 86%)](claims/collaborative-problem-solving-improves-critical-thinking-overall.md) [+M]
rows.change: Set real, open problems that the group must solve together, with an individual critical-thinking measure; expect a programme-level average with wide spread across studies
rows.if: The goal is critical thinking or problem solving

rows.basis: [Scripts targeting coordination, or negotiation with information sharing, gave the largest domain-learning effects; three-way combinations smaller](claims/specific-activity-combinations-domain-learning-moderator.md) [~M]; [Two transactivity scripts each helped, combined they interfered](claims/combined-transactivity-scripts-interfere.md) [~W]; [Teacher orchestration matters as much as script design](claims/teacher-orchestration-over-script-design.md) [~W]; [A script raised partner-evidence integration in a pre-study](claims/prestudy-ddr-perspective-integration.md) [+W] but [not learning gains in the main study](claims/script-no-direct-effect-learning-gains.md) [-W]
rows.change: Script one or two named activities (coordinating the work, or negotiating while sharing information) rather than prompting every collaborative activity at once; plan the teacher's rounds of the groups as part of the script; judge the script by an individual knowledge measure, because a script that visibly changes the talk may leave learning gains unchanged
rows.if: The group works in a computer-supported environment with a collaboration script

rows.basis: [Prolonged early planning facilitated later co-regulation](claims/temporal-phases-prolonged-early-planning-facilitates-later-co-regulation.md) [~W] (two medical-student samples, reported in a discussion article; process outcome only)
rows.change: Give the first session's opening to agreeing shared goals and common ground before the task itself, and keep a short planning step at the start of later sessions
rows.if: Groups will work together over several sessions or weeks

rows.basis: [Mixed-first-language groups gained slightly less online-interaction self-efficacy (η² = .004)](claims/first-language-heterogeneity-reduces-online-interaction-self-efficacy-gains.md) [~W] (associational; a very small difference in self-efficacy, not in learning)
rows.change: Keep the groups mixed but support the interaction (time to respond in writing, an agreed glossary for the task; untested), and check members' confidence in taking part online, not only the product
rows.if: Online groups mix students whose first languages differ

rows.basis: [Visible gaze feedback increased information pooling](claims/gaze-feedback-improves-collaborative-process.md) [+M]; [Real-time shared programming produced joint revision loops absent in individual work](claims/rtc-behavior-patterns-two-way-loops.md) [+M]; [How well partners model each other emerged through the task and depended on awareness tools](claims/partner-model-quality-emerges-through-task.md) [~W]
rows.change: Give each member a view of where the partner is looking or working (shared gaze, live shared editing), and still check each member's learning; these tools are evidenced on the collaboration process, not on what each learner learned
rows.if: Pairs work remotely through screens on a task that needs pooling what each knows

rows.basis: [Extensive reading with peer interaction beat reading without it, no reading, or teacher conferences](claims/er-peer-interaction-greater-achievement-gains.md) [+M]; [Group activities are not a guarantee when students have not read](claims/cl-not-magic-wand-for-er-motivation.md) [~W]
rows.change: Add regular peer sharing about what each has read, and check that members are reading before relying on it
rows.if: The task is independent reading (extensive reading)

rows.basis: [High-performing groups often failed when they did not take up each other's ideas](claims/high-performing-groups-fail-without-collaboration.md) [~M]
rows.change: Do not assume they will collaborate; watch whether each member's proposals are discussed before being accepted or dismissed, and give feedback on that
rows.if: Groups are made of strong or high-attaining students

rows.basis: [Open collaboration with AI, offloading and lower independent thinking](claims/offloading-mediation-lower-independent-hot.md) [-W]; [Teachers report "collaborative hollowing" and mistrust from secret AI use](claims/cll-four-ethical-tensions.md) [-W] (teachers' perceptions, online higher education)
rows.change: Bound how the AI may be used and check each member's independent work without it; open use was associated with offloading and lower later higher-order thinking, and teachers report groups handing in AI-done work with no real collaboration behind it. Ask each member to say what they contributed and how
rows.if: Learners have generative AI tools available during the group work

rows.basis: [Human pairs reported the most collaboration and social presence, above AI-assisted pairs and individuals](claims/human-pairing-highest-collaboration-social-presence.md) [+W] (self-reported perceptions in one quasi-experiment)
rows.change: Keep a human partner where the aim includes collaboration or social presence; if an AI assistant is used, still check each learner's own performance
rows.if: Pair work might be done with an AI assistant instead of a human partner

rows.basis: [Human and AI discourse differ functionally](claims/human-ai-discourse-functional-differences.md) [~M]
rows.change: Leave the reasoning and the reasoned coordination to the learners (for example, the AI asks and the learners justify), and look at who gives reasons in the transcript; in recorded human-AI problem solving the AI supplied most reasoning and agreement while students mostly invited and regulated
rows.if: An AI agent takes part in the group as a partner

rows.basis: [Well-defined tasks support shared creative influence](claims/well-defined-tasks-and-accessible-materials-support-shared-creative-influence.md) [~W]
rows.change: Start with a well-defined subtask and familiar materials, so that influence in the group rests on reasons rather than on who dominates
rows.if: The task is open-ended or ill-defined, with young adolescents

rows.basis: [Concept mapping with a peer beat mapping alone](claims/interactive-beats-constructive-concept-mapping.md) [+W]
rows.change: Have learners build it with a partner rather than alone
rows.if: The task is building a concept map or similar diagram

rows.basis: [Mixed-proficiency dyads negotiate meaning more](claims/mixed-dyads-negotiate-more-than-matched.md) [~W]
rows.change: Pair a stronger with a weaker speaker for tasks meant to produce negotiation of meaning; this is evidence about talk, not about later proficiency
rows.if: Second-language learners of mixed proficiency do speaking tasks in pairs

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep the joint task to one question with an individual answer before and after; do not expect the multi-week effect
rows.if: The brief allows only one short session

rows.basis: [Spoken–written beats spoken-only](claims/spoken-written-beats-spoken-only-not-written-only.md) [+M], carried from postsecondary learners without a recorded hearing loss; room fixes untested
rows.change: Room fixes first (doors shut, machines off, face the group, seat by need); write every new item as it is spoken; repeat questions from the floor
rows.if: Older `adult` learners, some with hearing loss, in a classroom with background noise

rows.basis: untested proposal; from the earlier page
