rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Spend the first 5 to 10 minutes on two or three prerequisite questions answered by everyone at once (cards, a poll); adjust the session's starting example to the answers; claim nothing about later readiness
rows.if: A single session only (a one-off workshop, a short course start)

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Fit the check to the time given (for example 10 minutes: three items and one observed task); drop items that would not change the first week's plan
rows.if: A fixed short time budget for the check

rows.basis: Untested; from wave lessons on keeping a brief's own routine
rows.change: Keep it and run it as given; add only what it lacks for this decision: one item on each prerequisite the first tasks use, and a record of what the teacher side will provide
rows.if: The brief names its own readiness tool, screening or criteria (a district's readiness assessment, a programme's indicators, its own rubric)

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Share results with the family and the teachers who act on them, not more widely; record observations, not labels; let families see and correct what is recorded
rows.if: Readiness records concern young children, families or disabilities (sensitive)

rows.basis: Untested; [Kindergarten test scores … identify students at risk](claims/kindergarten-scores-predict-third-grade-trajectories.md) [+W] supports using scores to flag, not to decide
rows.change: Do not decide from one check; use at least two observations at different times and the families' account; record what adjustment was tried first
rows.if: The stakes are an entry or placement decision (admission, a special-education referral, a retention decision)

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Check readiness by observing the learner in the whole performance with support, and note which parts needed help, rather than splitting it into separate items
rows.if: The goal is a whole performance the brief wants kept whole (taking part in a full school day; a whole lab task in a course)

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Use it as the first item on the prerequisite list and as the contrast in planning: what the setting assumed against what the learners did
rows.if: The brief reports a mismatch learners actually showed (children unable to sit through long seated lessons; students who could not do the algebra in week 1)

rows.basis: [Universal classroom management](claims/universal-classroom-management-reduces-problem-behavior.md) [+M] and [less disruption in all 12 studies](claims/universal-classroom-management-reduces-problem-behavior.md) [+M] (K–12 classrooms, against usual practice); [clear behavior expectations](claims/clear-behavior-expectations-strong-evidence-14-studies.md) [+M] (K–5)
rows.change: Start with steps 1 and 2: re-teach every routine for two weeks, with daily rehearsal, before adding any new consequence; tally disruptions before and after
rows.if: The whole class is disruptive

rows.basis: untested here; see [Functional Behavior Assessment](principles/functional-behavior-assessment.md)
rows.change: Keep the class plan; start an individual assessment of what triggers and keeps up each learner's behavior
rows.if: One or two learners cause most incidents despite the plan

rows.basis: the meta-analysis covers K–12 without an age breakdown; taught expectations are supported for grades K–5 ([clear behavior expectations](claims/clear-behavior-expectations-strong-evidence-14-studies.md) [+M]), not for preschool; the pictures, number of rules and length are untested
rows.change: Fewer rules (three), shown with pictures; routines rehearsed physically and daily for longer (four to six weeks); immediate, frequent praise; redirection by proximity and a quiet prompt, not warnings; no self-recording yet
rows.if: Learners are a young `child` (preschool or early primary)

rows.basis: [Greetings at the door](claims/positive-greetings-at-the-door-improve-engagement.md) [+M] (middle-school classes); [self-monitoring](claims/self-monitoring-improves-on-task-behavior.md) [+M] (grades 4–12, students with or at risk for disabilities); the rest untested
rows.change: Agree the rules with the class in the first week; give reasons for every procedure; greet each learner at the door; correct in private, never in front of peers; add self-recording for learners who want it
rows.if: Learners are `adolescent`s who meet many teachers a day

rows.basis: untested proposal; no claim here tests adult groups
rows.change: Replace rules with a short working agreement drafted with the group in the first session (phones, start times, how to disagree); keep the routines for materials, breaks and getting help; handle problems in a private conversation; drop rewards and the consequence ladder
rows.if: Learners are `adult`s in a work setting, adult education or training

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Make every routine work in both: one attention signal that shows on screen and in the room, a named way to ask for help in each (raised hand, chat, a direct message), greet remote learners by name at the start; keep cameras optional and correct remote learners only by private message
rows.if: Mixed modes: some learners online, some in the room, or phone-only

rows.basis: untested proposal; the greeting claim is from middle-school doorways, carried to an online join it did not test
rows.change: Turn the routines into written norms posted at the top of each session (mute, chat use, breakout rooms, when to use cameras); greet each learner by name as they join; scan the participant list as you would the room
rows.if: Online class only (`online-instructor-led`)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Rely on prevention and routines more than on individual redirection: a visible attention signal, short timed tasks with a clear start and end, a routine for asking for help without the teacher, and peer roles for materials; respond to the group, then to individuals after class
rows.if: One teacher with a large group (a lecture, a large class, no assistant)

rows.basis: [Greetings at the door](claims/positive-greetings-at-the-door-improve-engagement.md) [+M], carried to a single session it did not test; the rest untested
rows.change: Do not build a plan; state three expectations at the start, greet each learner, use the host's existing routines where you know them, redirect with the least intrusive move, and leave a short note on what happened for the regular teacher
rows.if: A single session only (cover teacher, a one-off workshop, a guest)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Fit the routines to the minutes: in a ten-minute budget, two minutes of greeting and start-up, one routine rehearsed for three minutes, and the rest left for the attention signal and transitions; in a single workshop, a two-minute agreement at the start and one attention signal
rows.if: A fixed short time budget (for example ten minutes a lesson for management, or a two-hour workshop)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Cut the plan to one page: three expectations, one attention signal, one help routine and one consequence; give every adult the same page so learners meet the same responses; one named person reviews a weekly tally for five minutes
rows.if: Scarce adult time (volunteers, a busy shift, one tutor checking in briefly)

rows.basis: untested proposal; see [Check In Check Out](strategies/check-incheck-out.md) and [Good Behavior Game](strategies/good-behavior-game.md); rewards: [expected tangible rewards](claims/rewards-undermine-intrinsic-motivation.md) [~M]
rows.change: Keep it and its categories; change only what the evidence says matters: teach and rehearse its expectations rather than only posting them, apply its consequences the same way every time, add a greeting, and write down when any tangible reward in it will be thinned
rows.if: The brief names its own routine or system (a school behavior policy, a schoolwide expectations matrix, a class points chart, check-in/check-out, the Good Behavior Game)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use its wording as the rules; build the routines and the ladder around those categories rather than adding a new set
rows.if: The brief gives its own rules, criteria or rubric for behavior

rows.basis: [Expected tangible rewards](claims/rewards-undermine-intrinsic-motivation.md) [-M] (meta-analyses of mostly laboratory tasks; stronger for children in one)
rows.change: Use specific praise and the activity's own payoff instead; keep tangible rewards for tasks learners find dull, tied to a standard, with a date for thinning them
rows.if: The plan relies on prizes or points for activities learners already enjoy

rows.basis: [Empathic discipline](claims/brief-intervention-empathic-discipline-cuts-suspensions.md) [+M] (middle-school teachers; narrowed a racial suspension disparity in the preregistered replication); norms: [Culturally Responsive Classroom Norms](principles/culturally-responsive-classroom-norms.md); who gets the attention: [two gendered classroom cultures](claims/two-gendered-classroom-cultures.md) [~W] (one Swedish school's field study: disruptive boys drew a disproportionate share of teacher time, which one teacher had not noticed until reading the field-notes)
rows.change: Review who is corrected and excluded, by group, every two weeks; widen the participation and correction norms; read departures as possible differences of convention first; offer staff the empathic-discipline exercise
rows.if: Learners' cultural norms differ from the classroom's, or one group receives most corrections

rows.basis: [Empathic discipline](claims/brief-intervention-empathic-discipline-cuts-suspensions.md) [+M] (overall effect small and marginal; larger for previously suspended students)
rows.change: Show the tally and who is being excluded; agree a short consistent ladder in advance; keep consequences that repair rather than shame
rows.if: Staff or the school want harsher punishment or exclusion

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Do not display individual behavior charts or names publicly; keep tallies at class level on the wall and individual records with the teacher and the learner (and family, where a school requires it); let older learners keep their own self-recording sheet
rows.if: Behavior records are private or sensitive (individual charts, notes on a learner)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Show rules and routines as pictures, gestures and demonstrations, not text; rehearse rather than explain; give a non-verbal help signal; never use reading aloud or public answering as a consequence
rows.if: Learners with low literacy, a language barrier or low confidence

rows.basis: [Self-monitoring](claims/self-monitoring-improves-on-task-behavior.md) [+M] (single-case studies; on-task behavior, not achievement)
rows.change: Add self-recording of on-task behavior at prompted intervals for those who need it, with brief training; keep the class routines the same for everyone
rows.if: Learners with or at risk for disabilities in the class

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep the performance whole; put the routines around it: a safety and equipment routine rehearsed beforehand, a single stop signal everyone obeys at once, roles for each learner, and redirection that does not stop the performance
rows.if: A practical, rehearsal or performance for a real audience (a lab, a workshop, a concert, a public presentation) that the brief wants kept whole

rows.basis: Need: [inexperienced teachers report too few strategies](claims/inexperienced-teachers-insufficient-management-repertoire.md) [~W] (self-report, second-hand); a written plan: [formal discipline plan](claims/formal-discipline-plan-increases-teacher-control-and-competence.md) [+W] (teachers' feelings); [Coaching increases teacher praise](claims/coaching-increases-teacher-praise.md) [+W] (a review of coaching studies; teacher behavior, not student outcomes); student-side effects are mixed: [supervisory coaching](claims/supervisory-coaching-mixed-teacher-student-outcomes.md) [~W]
rows.change: Give the teacher the one-page plan, a short ladder and a coach who observes and gives feedback on praise and redirection in the room
rows.if: A new or inexperienced teacher, or one with few strategies

rows.basis: [Elaborative interrogation benefits increase as learners' prior knowledge increases](claims/elaborative-interrogation-prior-knowledge-moderator.md) [~M] (one study reported in a review: larger gain in the high-knowledge domain)
rows.change: Use why-prompts freely, on denser material, with fewer modelled answers; move early to learner-written questions
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` or `intermediate` on this topic

rows.basis: [Elaborative interrogation produced lower posttest accuracy than reading the lesson twice in a written lesson on posterior probability](claims/elaborative-interrogation-lower-posttest-than-read-twice-posterior-probability.md) [-M] (undergraduates, one written lesson)
rows.change: Explain it or show a worked example first; put prompts on the steps of the example; do not replace a second reading with why-prompts on a lesson met cold
rows.if: Learners are `novice` on a calculation, rule or procedure

rows.basis: [Elaborative interrogation instructions produce better recall and recognition of science facts than reading-for-understanding instructions](claims/elaborative-interrogation-improves-science-fact-learning.md) [+M] (grades 6 and 7)
rows.change: Why-prompts on each fact, answered in writing or aloud; target facts that contradict common beliefs
rows.if: Learners are `adolescent` (lower secondary) reading science or social-studies text

rows.basis: untested proposal; the experiments recorded here are with grade 6 and 7 students and older
rows.change: Ask why-questions aloud in a small group, one statement at a time, accept spoken answers, and give the reason after each answer
rows.if: Learners are `child` (under 12)

rows.basis: [Readers given a perspective or schema recall more text information than readers instructed to carefully read the story](claims/schema-perspective-improves-text-recall.md) [+W] (one story-recall experiment reported second-hand in an essay; not tested with workplace learners); the work-case prompt is an untested proposal
rows.change: Have them connect each statement to a case from their own work ("where have you seen this, and why did it happen?") rather than to textbook examples
rows.if: Learners are `adult-workplace`

rows.basis: [Elaborative interrogation produced greater pretest-to-posttest gains on items about common misbeliefs than reading control in Experiment 2](claims/elaborative-interrogation-improves-misbelief-items-pretest-posttest.md) [+M]
rows.change: Put why-prompts on the statements that contradict the belief, and check confidence as well as accuracy
rows.if: Goal is to correct misconceptions

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page's constraint (no claim here tests elaboration on arbitrary material)
rows.change: Do not use why-prompts; use mnemonics or retrieval practice
rows.if: Goal is arbitrary associations (vocabulary, labels, symbols)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep the task whole; ask "why that step?" at two or three decision points during or after the performance, not as separate paper items
rows.if: Goal is a whole-task performance the brief wants kept whole

rows.basis: untested proposal; carried from the classroom biology study ([Elaborative interrogation improved true/false test performance in an introductory biology course context](claims/elaborative-interrogation-biology-course-context.md) [+M]), which did not test the self-check
rows.change: Embed the prompts in the text with a text box; after each answer, reveal a short reference answer to compare against
rows.if: Setting is `online-self-paced`, no teacher

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use short typed answers (one sentence) in a shared chat or form so remote and in-room answers are seen together; read two or three aloud, from both groups
rows.if: Mixed modes: some learners remote, some in the room, or phone-only

rows.basis: untested proposal; answer quality was poor in [Answers to elaborative interrogation questions were mostly poor in quality, and answer quality correlated positively with posttest scores](claims/elaborative-interrogation-answer-quality-poor-correlates-with-posttest.md) [~M]
rows.change: Everyone writes an answer; the teacher reads a sample of five, models one strong answer to the class, and gives the missing reason for the commonest failure
rows.if: One teacher with a large group

rows.basis: [The quality of elaborative-interrogation answers had little effect on retention; even failed or inadequate why-answers facilitated learning relative to reading](claims/response-quality-little-effect-on-elaborative-interrogation-retention.md) [~M] (science facts; not shown for procedures)
rows.change: For fact learning, skip marking individual answers; give a reference answer for self-checking and use the check-in to model one answer
rows.if: Scarce facilitator time (volunteers, a busy shift, a tutor who checks in briefly)

rows.basis: [Elaborative interrogation increased perceived difficulty and time spent with the lesson](claims/elaborative-interrogation-increases-difficulty-and-time-on-lesson.md) [~M]; minutes are an untested proposal
rows.change: Elaborate only the five to ten statements that matter most; plan about 20 minutes for 10 prompts with one modelled answer; do not claim retention from one session
rows.if: A fixed short time budget, or a single session only

rows.basis: [Concept mapping improves learning over most comparison conditions by a moderate average amount, but not over time-matched retrieval practice](claims/concept-mapping-improves-learning.md) [~M]; [Whether prompting students to construct explanations during retrieval adds benefit beyond initial free recall is mixed across studies](claims/adding-explanation-prompts-to-free-recall-retrieval-has-mixed-effects.md) [~M]
rows.change: Pair elaboration with retrieval: answer the why-prompt, then later recall the statement without the text; prefer retrieval over map-building when time is matched
rows.if: High stakes, with an unaided test of the same content soon

rows.basis: [Elaborative processing of prose enhances later retrievability, accounting for roughly 30% of variance in one-month recall when original learning is controlled](claims/elaborative-processing-enhances-retrieval.md) [+M] (replicated with less able middle-school students); frames are an untested proposal
rows.change: Choose familiar passages; let answers be spoken; give a sentence frame ("This is true because…"); tell them a partial answer still helps
rows.if: Learners with low confidence or low literacy

rows.basis: [Explicitly unfolding higher-order contributions into lower-order concept elements produces deeper conceptual learning opportunities than jumping directly to procedure](claims/unfolding-knowledge-elements-produces-deeper-conceptual-learning-opportunities.md) [+M] (qualitative; learning opportunity, not measured learning)
rows.change: When a student offers a formula, ask them to show the structure it stands for, then reconnect it to the formula
rows.if: Whole-class mathematics discussion

rows.basis: untested proposal (wave lessons)
rows.change: Keep the named routine and its categories; change only what the evidence says matters: attach one why-prompt to specific statements, and add one modelled answer
rows.if: The brief names its own routine, prompt, rubric or categories (its own question stems, a reading log, a check-in)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use the wrong answer as a contrast: put a why-prompt on the correct statement beside the common wrong one
rows.if: The brief reports an error learners actually made

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Learners connect content to their own experience privately; only answers they choose to share are read
rows.if: Private or sensitive material (personal experiences, health, family)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep elaboration in the learner's drafting notes or a debrief, not in the product the audience sees
rows.if: A product or performance for a real audience

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Judge from the answers themselves and from later use; add no quiz
rows.if: The brief asks for no test or quiz

rows.basis: [Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals.](claims/process-goals-outperform-outcome-goals-for-novices.md) [~M] (high-school writing revision); the step-size move is untested
rows.change: Shorten steps, give a worked example first, set process goals; do not add hooks or rewards
rows.if: Learners are `novice` on the task and withdraw after early failure

rows.basis: [Expected tangible rewards reduce later free-choice engagement with a rewarded task, while verbal praise does not](claims/rewards-undermine-intrinsic-motivation.md) [~S] (one meta-analysis reports rewards more detrimental for children than college students); block lengths untested
rows.change: Keep the arrival routine, short work blocks, teacher-held progress chart; avoid tangible rewards for taking part
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary age)

rows.basis: [Positive Greetings At The Door Improve Engagement](claims/positive-greetings-at-the-door-improve-engagement.md) [+M] (middle school); [Self Monitoring Improves On Task Behavior](claims/self-monitoring-improves-on-task-behavior.md) [+M] (students with or at risk for disabilities; carried to others untested)
rows.change: Add the greeting routine at every lesson; for individual learners, cued self-recording of on-task behaviour in work blocks
rows.if: Learners are `adolescent`, with disruptive or off-task behaviour

rows.basis: [Belonging Interventions Improve Outcomes](claims/belonging-interventions-improve-outcomes.md) [+M] (first-year college students; worked only where the institution afforded belonging)
rows.change: Before or at the start of the course, a short exercise in which learners read and write about adversity as common and temporary; check that the setting gives them real opportunities to belong
rows.if: Learners are `adult` or in their first year of college, unsure they belong

rows.basis: [Constructive learning beats active and passive learning](claims/constructive-learning-beats-active-passive.md) [~M] (ordering only partly held in the field)
rows.change: Judge success by an explanation or prediction probe, not by on-task time; make the engaged task one of explaining or predicting
rows.if: Goal is a `concept` or `principle`, measured by `conceptual-understanding`

rows.basis: [Learners invest more effort in tasks they perceive as interesting, personally important, or useful to their future goals.](claims/task-value-increases-motivation-and-engagement.md) [+M] (reviews; utility-value effects reported second-hand)
rows.change: Measure voluntary return or later course choice, not enjoyment ratings at the end of a session; use relevance writing at unit starts
rows.if: The goal is `attitude-motivation` itself (interest in a subject, continued study)

rows.basis: untested; [Intervention engagement (narratives consumed) showed no clear association with outcome changes](claims/story-mine-engagement-outcome-null-association.md) [~W] warns that usage counts need not track outcomes (a mental-health app, not learning)
rows.change: Replace the greeting with a named welcome and first-minute check-in; build a visible progress record and automatic learning checks; track return days, not only clicks
rows.if: Setting is `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: [Interesting but irrelevant details can impair comprehension and transfer, with effects that vary with the material and the learner](claims/seductive-details-effect.md) [-M] (school and university learners; harm larger for low prior knowledge or low attentional inhibition)
rows.change: Keep only additions that show the target idea; place any purely motivating story before or after the core explanation
rows.if: Materials are being "made more engaging" with images, stories, jokes or video

rows.basis: [Gamification has small positive effects on cognitive, motivational and behavioral learning outcomes](claims/gamification-has-small-positive-effects-on-learning-outcomes.md) [~M]; [rewards](claims/rewards-undermine-intrinsic-motivation.md) [~S]
rows.change: Use them only alongside a task that requires thinking with the target; do not give tangible rewards merely for taking part; measure learning separately
rows.if: The plan relies on points, badges, leaderboards or prizes

rows.basis: untested at scale; the greeting claim is from middle-school classrooms ([greetings](claims/positive-greetings-at-the-door-improve-engagement.md) [+M])
rows.change: Make participation visible all at once (everyone writes or shows a response); use spot checks of on-task behaviour across the room; greet at the door even if briefly
rows.if: `classroom` with one teacher and a large group

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use the reason-for-task and a constructive task; do not claim durable engagement; record one learning probe
rows.if: Time is one session, or a one-off workshop

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep relevance and progress supports; do not let engagement indicators stand in for evidence of competence
rows.if: Stakes are high (assessed course, certification)

rows.basis: [Positive teacher–student relationships are associated with greater student engagement and, more weakly, with achievement](claims/teacher-student-relationships-improve-engagement.md) [+M] (correlational; direction not established)
rows.change: Start with the contact routine and warm, high-expectation feedback before adding choice or open tasks
rows.if: Relationship with the group is new or strained

rows.basis: [Elementary students prefer mechanistic explanations](claims/elementary-students-prefer-mechanistic-explanations.md) [+W]: grades 2–6, observed in interviews, no instruction tested
rows.change: Frame questions as "how does it happen?" and have learners compare a mechanistic and a non-mechanistic explanation of a familiar phenomenon, giving a reason; keep content to what they already know, since they reject explanations that conflict with their knowledge. Do not expect web-source evaluation routines to transfer down.
rows.if: `child` learners (primary school)

rows.basis: [Critiquing problematic inquiry cases before virtual-lab inquiry](claims/critique-before-virtual-lab-inquiry-augments-scientific-literacy.md) [+W]: 50 middle-school students, critique against teacher demonstration, no effect size printed
rows.change: Before learners run their own investigation, have them critique one or two problematic inquiry cases (an uncontrolled variable, a conclusion the data do not support) and say how to fix them, rather than only watching the teacher demonstrate a correct procedure.
rows.if: `adolescent` learners, science inquiry (a lab, a simulation or a virtual lab)

rows.basis: [Civic Online Reasoning Instruction Improves Evaluation](claims/civic-online-reasoning-instruction-improves-evaluation.md) [+M]: high-school field study, matched controls
rows.change: Embed six 50-minute lessons on lateral reading in an existing subject (government, history), with teacher preparation; practise on live sites.
rows.if: `adolescent` learners, web or news sources, a school course

rows.basis: [Collaborative critique-and-redesign](claims/collaborative-evidence-critique-shifts-students-toward-procedural-objectivity.md) [+M]: first-year psychology, single group, no control
rows.change: Run small-group critique and redesign of flawed studies in the discipline across the course (three tasks in a 12-week course), and teach credibility of sources separately if it is also a goal.
rows.if: `adult` learners, university, judging research

rows.basis: [Collaborative critique-and-redesign](claims/collaborative-evidence-critique-shifts-students-toward-procedural-objectivity.md) [~M]: no change on the untaught lay-credibility judgments
rows.change: Name the specific judgments it should show up in and teach and assess each; do not assume one transfers to another.
rows.if: Goal is a general disposition ("critical thinking", "scepticism")

rows.basis: [Argumentation Improves Reasoning](claims/argumentation-improves-reasoning.md) [+M]: multi-year study with young adolescents; online-science synthesis
rows.change: Use repeated peer argument on contested questions, followed by individual essays on new topics; plan for many sessions, not one.
rows.if: Goal is writing or arguing a case with evidence

rows.basis: [Checklist-based evaluation](claims/checklist-evaluation-ineffective-online.md) [~M]: one-session checklist and networked framework did not differ; gains modest
rows.change: Teach one move (leave the page and search what others say about the source) rather than a long checklist, and expect modest gains; schedule a follow-up task if at all possible.
rows.if: Only one session (e.g. a library visit)

rows.basis: [Students describe concrete verification behaviors for GenAI explanations](claims/iterative-verification-of-genai-explanations.md) [+W]: ten computing students, interviews and think-aloud, describes what they did and teaches nothing; [Children use a 'trust test' strategy](claims/children-trust-test-chatbot-with-known-answers.md) [~W]: exploratory K-8 study, the strategy reinforced trust after correct answers. No claim in the wiki tests instruction in judging AI output
rows.change: Treat the AI's output as a source to check, not an authority: teach learners to cross-check it against an independent reference they trust (course notes, a worked example, a reference work), to ask follow-up questions that expose inconsistency, and to treat verification as repeated filtering rather than one accept-or-reject decision. Show children explicitly why a chatbot that answers questions they already know is not thereby reliable on questions they do not. Assess on AI answers that contain planted errors.
rows.if: Learners will judge answers from a chatbot or generative AI

rows.basis: [Data construction embeds privilege in data](claims/data-construction-embeds-privilege-in-data.md) [+W]: one theoretical philosophy-of-education article; untested with learners
rows.change: Add to the study-method standard a question about how the data were made: who was counted and who left out, by whom, for what purpose; have learners name what the data could not show.
rows.if: Goal is judging arguments built on data or statistics

rows.basis: Untested proposal; the online-argumentation synthesis does not report teacher presence
rows.change: Provide recorded demonstrations of the expert move, live practice items with model reasoning shown after the learner commits a judgment and a confidence rating, and a delayed check on new items.
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: Untested proposal; one nursing study is single-session and is read in the checklist row
rows.change: Use the claims they will meet at work (health websites, research summaries); teach both source checking and study-method judgments if both occur, and assess each.
rows.if: `workplace-clinical` learners (e.g. nurses judging health information)

rows.basis: Untested proposal; constructed-response and five-week tests appear in the lateral-reading studies
rows.change: Assess with constructed responses on unseen claims, scoring the reason and the verdict, at a delay; a multiple-choice verdict alone can be right for the wrong reason.
rows.if: High-stakes assessment of the skill

rows.basis: Untested proposal; the lateral-reading claim's discussion names the constraint, no study tests it
rows.change: Lateral reading cannot be practised as such; supply a curated packet of outside documents about each source and teach the learner to look for them, or shift the target to judging the reasoning inside the source.
rows.if: No open web access, locked devices, or offline exam

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page
rows.change: Do not open with errors. Teach or show one or two correct worked examples first; add one erroneous example per misconception only once the learner can follow a correct one.
rows.if: `novice`: no correct model of this task yet

rows.basis: [productive failure](claims/productive-failure-improves-conceptual-learning.md) [~M]; [overt correction for young children](claims/overt-error-correction-speeds-young-children-learning.md) [~W] (second-hand, 1962 study)
rows.change: Keep correction overt (show the correct answer and how, not only right/wrong); use constructed peer errors after instruction rather than problem-first failure, which reversed for second to fifth graders.
rows.if: `child` (primary school)

rows.basis: [high-confidence errors](claims/high-confidence-errors-improve-retention.md) [+M]; tested on recall, untested on professional judgement
rows.change: Collect a confidence rating on each answer; review confident errors first and in most depth; low-confidence errors may need re-teaching, not analysis.
rows.if: `adult` or professional, `intermediate`

rows.basis: [corrective feedback after failed retrieval](claims/feedback-enhances-retrieval-practice.md) [+M]; [multiple-choice feedback](claims/feedback-after-multiple-choice-tests-halves-lure-intrusions.md) [+M]
rows.change: Skip erroneous-example analysis. Use retrieval attempts followed by the correct answer after every error; always give feedback on multiple-choice items.
rows.if: goal is `verbal-association` (facts, vocabulary, terms)

rows.basis: [erroneous examples](claims/erroneous-examples-build-conceptual-knowledge.md) [+M] (children, decimals, one session); [productive failure](claims/productive-failure-improves-conceptual-learning.md) [~M] (gain on conceptual, not procedural, outcomes)
rows.change: Build one incorrect/correct pair around the misconception, require a written "why" explanation, and test with changed problems, not only the practised procedure.
rows.if: goal is a `concept` or `principle` with a known misconception

rows.basis: [noticing particular errors in writing](claims/noticing-errors-decreases-errors-preserves-quality.md) [+W] (one study, reported in a review, EFL college writing)
rows.change: Ask learners to look for one or two named error types in their own draft or performance, then revise; do not mark every error at once.
rows.if: goal is a `complex-skill` (writing, a whole clinical or technical task)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Make error analysis routine and ungraded; use peer-anonymous errors; measure willingness to attempt, not only accuracy.
rows.if: goal is an `attitude-motivation` (comfort with error, persistence)

rows.basis: [confusion with prior incorrect trials](claims/confusion-amplifies-negative-effect-of-incorrect-trials.md) [~W] (exploratory); the switch rule is an untested proposal
rows.change: The system must supply the correct solution and the explanation; log error streaks and self-reported confusion, and switch to a worked example after repeated errors on one item type.
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: [erroneous examples](claims/erroneous-examples-build-conceptual-knowledge.md) [+M] (brief session, immediate outcome)
rows.change: Use one comparison set per target misconception with explanation prompts and a short immediate check; do not expect the delayed effect to be shown.
rows.if: `single-session`: one lesson or less

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page
rows.change: Use constructed erroneous examples or simulation rather than live errors; analyse errors privately or in writing; keep error analysis out of graded assessment.
rows.if: high stakes, public setting, or `workplace-clinical` where real errors are unsafe

rows.basis: [Civic Online Reasoning Instruction Improves Evaluation](claims/civic-online-reasoning-instruction-improves-evaluation.md) [+M] (high-school field study with matched controls, and eleventh graders without a control)
rows.change: Embed six or so 50-minute lessons in the subject's own topics, with teacher preparation beforehand; practise on live sites about the unit's questions
rows.if: `adolescent` learners in a school subject (government, history, science)

rows.basis: [Civic Online Reasoning Instruction Improves Evaluation](claims/civic-online-reasoning-instruction-improves-evaluation.md) [+M] (randomised pilot, four sections; five-week posttest)
rows.change: Two or more 75-minute lessons inside a writing or critical-thinking course, with a check on unseen sites several weeks later
rows.if: `adult` learners at university

rows.basis: Untested; the claim's adults are university students. From the earlier page's target learners
rows.change: Start from sources they already use (health, benefits, news, job information); teach the off-page move on those first; keep reading load of practice sites manageable and model searching step by step
rows.if: `adult` learners re-entering study, or adult basic education

rows.basis: Untested; no claim here tests source-evaluation teaching with children
rows.change: Use a curated set of sources and a single question ("who made this, and what do others say about them?") asked with the teacher; do not expect the full routine
rows.if: `child` learners (primary age)

rows.basis: [One-session checklist (CRAAP) instruction did no better than the alternatives it was compared with](claims/checklist-evaluation-ineffective-online.md) [~M] (first-year business and nursing students; one session of either method, modest gains, no difference)
rows.change: Teach one move (leave the page and search the source's name) and one practice round rather than a long checklist; tell the course teacher what to follow up
rows.if: Only one session (a library visit, an orientation)

rows.basis: [One-session checklist (CRAAP) instruction did no better than the alternatives it was compared with](claims/checklist-evaluation-ineffective-online.md) [~M] (learners kept using domain and design cues after training); the re-purposing is untested
rows.change: Keep the checklist questions as prompts for what to look up elsewhere, not as on-page criteria; add practice on polished but unreliable sites where the checklist misleads
rows.if: The existing course teaches a checklist (CRAAP or similar)

rows.basis: [Collaborative critique-and-redesign instruction shifts students from a value-free view of objectivity toward a procedural one](claims/collaborative-evidence-critique-shifts-students-toward-procedural-objectivity.md) [~M] (one psychology course; source-credibility judgments did not change)
rows.change: Teach the standards for judging a study (valid methods, replication) as a separate target, with small-group critique and redesign of flawed studies; assess source credibility separately
rows.if: Goal is judging research studies, not websites

rows.basis: Untested; all studies were taught in classes
rows.change: Short recorded demonstrations of the off-page move; practice items where the learner commits a verdict, a reason and a confidence rating before a model answer and the fact-checker's search are shown; a delayed check on new sites
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: [One-session checklist (CRAAP) instruction did no better than the alternatives it was compared with](claims/checklist-evaluation-ineffective-online.md) [~M] (nursing students, one 110-minute session); the multi-session design is untested in this setting
rows.change: Practise on the health sites and summaries they will meet, including misinformation sites; add judging study methods if they read research
rows.if: `workplace-clinical` learners (e.g. nurses and health information)

rows.basis: Untested; the claim's discussion names this constraint, and no study tests it
rows.change: Supply a packet of outside documents about each source (reviews, a reference entry, a fact-check) and teach learners to look for them; or shift the target to the reasoning inside the source
rows.if: No open web access, locked devices, or an offline exam

rows.basis: [Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows.](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M] (cognitive-load studies, carried to this skill)
rows.change: Skip the modelling; give harder cases (reliable sources that look poor, unreliable ones with good coverage elsewhere) and peer critique of reasons
rows.if: Learners already check sources off the page on the first judgment

rows.basis: Untested; constructed-response tasks were used in the eleventh-grade study
rows.change: Grade on unseen sources with constructed responses, scoring the reason and the verdict separately; a verdict alone can be right for the wrong reason
rows.if: High stakes, or the skill is graded

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Start from clearinghouse summaries and a one-page question card (comparison, how groups formed, outcome, horizon); do not ask them to read primary statistics first
rows.if: Decision-makers are `novice` at reading research (most classroom teachers, school leaders)

rows.basis: Double-blind experimental design can be successfully implemented in CALL-based pedagogical intervention research [+W] (one language-learning software study; carried to other settings)
rows.change: Skip summaries; read primary studies; run local trials with random assignment, through software where possible
rows.if: Decision-makers are `advanced` (teacher-researchers, a district research office)

rows.basis: [First-grade math achievement is significantly higher under Math Expressions and Saxon Math than under Investigations in Number, Data, and Space and Scott Foresman-Addison Wesley Mathematics](claims/math-expressions-saxon-outperform-investigations-sfaw-first-grade.md) [+M] (first graders in 39 schools; one cohort)
rows.change: Choose by the randomised comparisons available; weight them above endorsements
rows.if: Learners are `child` in early grades and the choice is a maths curriculum

rows.basis: [There is not yet much rigorous evidence to guide decision making around instructional and support strategies for adult learners](claims/little-rigorous-evidence-adult-learner-strategies.md) [~W]
rows.change: Expect few rigorous comparisons; adopt as a one-term local trial with a written dropping rule; carry school evidence only with a note that it was not tested on adults
rows.if: Learners are `adult` (adult basic education, literacy, ESOL)

rows.basis: untested proposal; the claims here are about schools and adult education
rows.change: Same steps; define the outcome as performance on the job at a stated delay, not end-of-course satisfaction; pilot with one cohort against the existing course
rows.if: Adults in work settings (training in a company, a health service, a public agency)

rows.basis: [No readily accessible sources of rigorous evidence exist for most ed-tech products](claims/no-rigorous-evidence-ed-tech-products.md) [~W]; [Most surveyed ed tech developers report their products are informed by research, but purchasers struggle to evaluate that research](claims/developers-report-research-informed-products.md) [~W]; [More than 70 percent of the 180 most popular literacy applications referenced no research in their design](claims/literacy-apps-lack-research-reference.md) [~M] (a market scan of children's literacy apps, as recorded here)
rows.change: Ask the vendor for a third-party study and who paid for it; a "research-informed" label is not a comparison; without one, trial it against current practice for a term before buying for all
rows.if: The choice is an ed-tech product or app

rows.basis: [Districts rely more on peer recommendations and pilots than on rigorous evidence when choosing ed-tech products](claims/districts-rely-peer-recommendations-pilots-over-rigorous-evidence.md) [~W] (a survey; describes practice, does not test it)
rows.change: Keep the pilot; give it a comparison class, a pre-set outcome and a dropping rule, so it can come out against the product
rows.if: The district already decides by peer recommendation and informal pilots

rows.basis: [Low-performing CSR elementary schools that adopted models with scientific research bases gained in mathematics achievement after three years](claims/low-performing-elementary-csr-math-gains-research-models.md) [+W]; [No relationship existed between elementary reading achievement gains and selection of a model with a scientific research base](claims/elementary-reading-no-relationship-research-model.md) [-W] (one evaluation, Orland 2010)
rows.change: Prefer a model rated as having a scientific research base; expect a small maths gain over three years, and do not expect the rating to predict reading gains
rows.if: A whole-school reform model is being chosen for a low-performing elementary school

rows.basis: The ST Math evaluation's quasi-experimental design cannot rule out selection bias because treatment grades volunteered to participate [~W]; Not all intervention programs can be evaluated using an RCT, so non-experimental study designs may be needed to build an evidence base [~W]
rows.change: Use a matched comparison, write down how schools or classes chose to take part, and report gains as possibly reflecting the volunteers
rows.if: The programme cannot be randomised (whole-school, opt-in, statutory)

rows.basis: [Matching Instruction To Styles No Effect](claims/learning-styles-matching-does-not-improve-learning.md) [+M]; [Mi Lacks Empirical Theory Testing](claims/mi-lacks-empirical-theory-testing.md) [+M]
rows.change: Do not place, group or match on learning styles or multiple-intelligence profiles; match format to content; require outcome evidence for any classification before using it for placement
rows.if: High stakes: placement, grouping or tracking by learner type

rows.basis: A null study finding can have multiple possible causes and requires interpretation before it informs decisions [~W]
rows.change: Check implementation, number of learners, outcome alignment and horizon before dropping the approach; record which explanation the study can rule out
rows.if: A study found no effect

rows.basis: [Focal math teachers relied primarily on their own observations of student behavior to understand students' feelings about math, supplemented by surveys, with disaggregated data rare](claims/teacher-observation-primary-perception-data-source.md) [~W] (10 middle-school maths teachers; describes practice)
rows.change: Keep their observation; add one brief anonymous student survey and compare the two before changing practice
rows.if: Teachers judge how learners feel or engage mainly from what they notice in class

rows.basis: [A physics-education review reports one study (Ding et al. 2023) in which high-trust students agreed with ChatGPT's answers 100% of the time although those answers were 82% accurate](claims/trust-not-equivalent-to-ai-accuracy.md) [+W] (40 undergraduates in physics, reported in a review)
rows.change: Check a sample of its answers against an authoritative source before relying on it, and teach learners to do the same; do not take agreement for accuracy
rows.if: Learners or teachers use an AI chatbot as a source of answers

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: If the brief sets its own end-of-session assessment, schedule it first (step 11); otherwise do steps 1–5 in 45 minutes on one live decision; end with a decision to trial, not to adopt; schedule the review of the trial
rows.if: A single session only (one meeting or one in-service day)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: 5 minutes writing the claim and what would show it wrong; 10 minutes reading one prepared clearinghouse summary; 5 minutes for one person's case against
rows.if: A fixed short time budget (20 minutes in a staff meeting)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Teachers work from the question card and a shared template; the coach checks only two things per plan: the pre-set outcome and the dropping rule
rows.if: Scarce facilitator time (one coach for many teachers, volunteers, a busy shift)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Run that assessment as given, in full, inside the stated time; schedule it first and plan backwards; add practice of this page's moves before it only if time remains; keep any contradictory-data revision, with learners revising in writing and naming what the data contradicted
rows.if: The brief names its own assessment, rubric or revision task (a certification task, an evidence-review exercise, new contradictory data that learners must respond to)

rows.basis: [Matching Instruction To Styles No Effect](claims/learning-styles-matching-does-not-improve-learning.md) [+M] (a widely reported practice that failed its tests); [Districts rely more on peer recommendations and pilots than on rigorous evidence when choosing ed-tech products](claims/districts-rely-peer-recommendations-pilots-over-rigorous-evidence.md) [~W]
rows.change: Ask who tested it against what, and whether anyone tried to refute it; treat public reporting as an invitation to check, not as the check
rows.if: A practice is presented as proven because it is published, widely reported, popular or endorsed

rows.basis: The RCT is considered the gold standard of research evidence because randomization ensures only the intervention could cause treatment-control outcome differences [+W]; The ST Math evaluation's quasi-experimental design cannot rule out selection bias because treatment grades volunteered to participate [~W]
rows.change: Check how groups were actually formed and what the comparison was before giving it weight; the wording alone does not make the test fair
rows.if: A study is described as "randomised", "controlled" or "research-based"

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep it and its categories; add only what the evidence here bears on: one line stating what result would show the choice wrong, and one comparison or a local trial
rows.if: The brief names its own routine (a district adoption rubric, an ESSA evidence tier check, a PLC or data-inquiry protocol)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Put the study summary and question card in a shared document read before the meeting; take the case against in writing so remote participants contribute equally
rows.if: Mixed modes: some teachers remote, some in the room, or phone-only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: The teacher decides who sees their trial results; share only class-level summaries with the group; never rank teachers by them
rows.if: Teachers' own classroom results or student data are private

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Replace the card with three spoken questions (compared with what? on whom? measured how?); give one plain-language paragraph per study; no statistics
rows.if: Low confidence or literacy with research (paraprofessionals, volunteer tutors, new teachers)

rows.basis: untested proposal; from the earlier page (public, self-correcting knowledge)
rows.change: Report the comparison, how groups were formed, the outcome and its horizon, nulls included, and what would change the decision; keep the limits in the same document as the result
rows.if: The result goes to a real audience (a school board, parents, a funder)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Judge and trial the whole programme against the alternative; do not pick components from it and assume the programme's evidence carries to them
rows.if: The brief wants a whole programme adopted as designed

rows.basis: [In one practitioner's report on her own older-beginner Step One class, with no comparison group, students gained an average of 128 BEST Plus points over 6 months and two former absolute beginners passed the citizenship test](claims/older-beginner-esl-outcome-gains.md) [+M] (one practitioner's class of 11, no comparison group; the network moves are untested)
rows.change: Make the class itself the first network: the same small group every session, veteran learners mentoring new arrivals, classmates helping one another, open praise for gains; go at a measured pace with one new thing at a time; bring outside contacts (a library, a senior centre, a citizenship clinic) in only once the group is stable
rows.if: Learners are older adults, socially isolated, beginning English (older immigrant learners)

rows.basis: [In Year 1, teens left on their own did not automatically connect with structured workshops; adult mentors reaching out socially changed this](claims/youmedia-teens-needed-mentor-outreach-to-connect.md) [+M] (one library learning space, observation and interviews)
rows.change: Have adults reach out socially to each young person, as guides and collaborators, before expecting them to join workshops; do not rely on posters or sign-up sheets
rows.if: Learners are `adolescent`, in a drop-in or out-of-school space

rows.basis: untested proposal; [Participants report career transitions, certifications, networking gains, financial and social gains from tech-centered education and training programs](claims/tech-program-accomplishments-gains.md) [+W] reports networking as a gain, without comparison
rows.change: Tie each contact to the job goal: informational interviews with a rehearsed two-sentence ask, alumni or employer panels followed by one individual introduction each, and a written follow-up within a week
rows.if: Adults in work settings: job seekers, career changers, workers in training

rows.basis: [A facilitated Community of Practice helped isolated state American Indian Education Directors build relationships that broke down silos and combated professional isolation](claims/cop-relationships-combat-aie-director-isolation.md) [+M]; [Interacting repeatedly across convenings built trust that enabled districts to give and receive critiques of one another's plans](claims/repeated-convenings-trust-enables-critique.md) [+M] (both participant report)
rows.change: Convene a small facilitated community of the same people several times a year around problems they bring; keep membership stable so trust can form; let members lead sessions once it is running
rows.if: Learners are professionals isolated in their role (a lone specialist, a rural principal, a state director)

rows.basis: [The student-tutor relationship alone is judged insufficient: peer mixing and virtual communities are needed to counter isolation in online research supervision](claims/virtual-communities-counter-supervision-isolation.md) [+M] (doctoral supervision, consultation study); [SPICE learners report that the virtual Center reduced their rural isolation and made learning enjoyable](claims/spice-learners-report-reduced-isolation.md) [+W] (family literacy, testimonials)
rows.change: Add a peer group of learners in the same situation with set participation norms (one weekly post, one reply) rather than relying on the tutor relationship alone
rows.if: Setting is `online-self-paced` or learners study alone at home

rows.basis: untested proposal; [Geographic distance and insufficient internet bandwidth can derail rural schools' plans for cross-school professional learning communities](claims/rural-distance-and-bandwidth-derail-plans-for-cross-school-plcs.md) [~M] (one rural school's case)
rows.change: Put every learner in the same peer group whatever their mode; run the group's exchange by phone call or text message as well as video; test the connection before relying on a live online meeting
rows.if: Mixed modes: some learners in the room, some remote, some on phones only, or poor bandwidth

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use veteran learners as mentors and brokers; spend staff time on two things only: the first outreach to learners who have not joined, and asking at each check-in "whom did you contact, and what is your next step?"
rows.if: One teacher or coordinator for many learners, or scarce facilitator time (volunteers, a busy shift, one tutor checking in briefly)

rows.basis: untested proposal; [Core to College network interactions were primarily information sharing and making connections between K–12 and higher education](claims/core-to-college-interactions-primarily-information-sharing.md) [~M] (contact without deeper collaboration)
rows.change: Make one introduction per learner to a named person or organisation that fits their goal, exchange contact details on the spot, and set one follow-up step with a date; do not claim a network was built
rows.if: Time is one session only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Spend it as 15 minutes of stable peer-group exchange and 5 minutes on each learner's follow-up step; move outside introductions to the weeks when the budget allows a longer slot
rows.if: A fixed short time budget inside another course (for example 20 minutes a week)

rows.basis: untested proposal; [Successful program completion increased participants' self-confidence, self-esteem, and autonomy, which aided their settlement and integration into Canadian society](claims/program-completion-increased-confidence-autonomy-settlement.md) [+W] (two immigrant women's interviews; about completing a programme, not about networking)
rows.change: Start with one peer in the same situation, not a room of strangers; let learners speak in their first language where a peer shares it; rehearse each ask aloud before it is made; let the learner decide when they are ready for an outside contact
rows.if: Learners have low confidence, low literacy, limited English, or have been through adverse experiences

rows.basis: untested proposal; the folded older-learner page names depression, homesickness, bereavement and loss of independence as realities to work with, not gloss over
rows.change: The learner controls what is shared and with whom: introductions are opt-in, nothing is posted to a group without consent, and there is no public roster of who has which need
rows.if: The material is private or sensitive (immigration status, unemployment, bereavement, health)

rows.basis: [Access to mentors and coaches is inequitably distributed, with high-poverty schools far less likely to have supported principals](claims/mentor-coach-access-inequity-poverty.md) [~M] (principals, survey; carried to learners untested)
rows.change: Broker for the least connected first; keep a monthly list of who has a mentor, a peer partner and an outside contact; do not let open networking events be the only route
rows.if: Some learners start with far fewer ties than others

rows.basis: untested proposal; the three moves rest on the convening, community and outreach claims above
rows.change: Keep it; change only what the evidence here points to: the same people meeting repeatedly, someone reaching out to those who do not join, and a follow-up step after each contact
rows.if: The brief names its own routine (its own mentoring scheme, convening format, check-in or intake form)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use the brief's categories and criteria to record ties and judge progress; do not substitute this page's list
rows.if: The brief gives its own categories of useful connection or its own success criteria

rows.basis: untested proposal; [Social collaboration in authentic assessment is mostly peer- and teacher-based, with few connections to industry or community partners and rare equitable teacher-student collaboration](claims/aa-social-collaboration-limited-community-connection.md) [~M] (a scoping review: such links are rarely designed in)
rows.change: Use the product as the occasion for contact: invite the people the learners need to meet as the audience, and plan one individual conversation with each after the event
rows.if: Learners produce work for a real audience (a presentation to employers, a community project)

rows.basis: [Offering FAST produced no meaningful, enduring effects on family functioning, family-school relationships, academic learning, or social-behavioral outcomes in a 60-school cluster RCT](claims/fast-rct-no-meaningful-enduring-effects.md) [-M] (families of kindergarten pupils; a programme building parents' social support among other aims)
rows.change: Do not promise outcomes from the programme; record ties formed and used, and measure the outcome that matters at a later point
rows.if: Stakes are high: settlement, employment or a family's wellbeing depends on the outcome

rows.basis: [Unassisted discovery produces less learning than explicit instruction, while discovery enhanced with guidance outperforms other instruction](claims/minimal-guidance-less-effective-for-novices.md) [~S]; tested on discovery tasks, school and mixed domains, not on placements
rows.change: Teach or demonstrate the key idea first, with a worked example; narrow the experience to one or two variables; supply the reflection prompts and the vocabulary for naming the concept; check an unaided step before removing support
rows.if: Learners are `novice`s on the target task

rows.basis: untested proposal; the guided-inquiry claim's narrative review argues that the advantage of guidance recedes with prior knowledge, which no recorded study tests here
rows.change: Shorten the preparation, make the experience less structured, and have learners write their own debrief questions; keep the second attempt with feedback
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` or experienced practitioners

rows.basis: [Hands-on learning improves achievement](claims/manipulatives-improve-math-learning.md) [+M] (mathematics, kindergarten to college); [Unassisted discovery produces less learning than explicit instruction, while discovery enhanced with guidance outperforms other instruction](claims/minimal-guidance-less-effective-for-novices.md) [~S] (third and fourth graders)
rows.change: Use short, concrete hands-on tasks and connect each to its symbol or written form in the same session; tell them what to try, not only to explore
rows.if: Learners are `child`ren, or school-age

rows.basis: [Simulation Based Education With Deliberate Practice](claims/simulation-based-education-with-deliberate-practice-improves-clinical-outcomes.md) [+M]; medical education, procedural skills only; boosters untested
rows.change: Replace one-off exposure with simulated practice repeated to a stated mastery standard, immediate feedback after each attempt, rising difficulty, and a debrief; add booster sessions if the skill is not used soon
rows.if: Adult professionals, `workplace-clinical`, a `procedure` or psychomotor skill

rows.basis: [Physical Experience Enhances Science Learning](claims/physical-experience-enhances-science-learning.md) [~M] (undergraduate physics); [Hands-on learning improves achievement](claims/manipulatives-improve-math-learning.md) [+M]
rows.change: Have learners manipulate the system (physical or virtual), predict before acting, and map the result onto the formula or diagram afterwards; if a physical lab is unavailable, a virtual one is a fair substitute
rows.if: The goal is a science or mathematics `concept`

rows.basis: [Service-learning is associated with improvements in self-efficacy and social responsibility](claims/service-learning-improves-civic-and-personal-outcomes.md) [+W]; second-hand and self-reported
rows.change: Use service or community experience with structured reflection, and measure a behaviour or a decision in a new case, not only self-report; treat any benefit as unconfirmed
rows.if: The goal is an attitude or disposition (civic responsibility, empathy, respect for diversity)

rows.basis: [Reflective Practice Improves Outcomes When Structured](claims/reflective-practice-improves-outcomes-when-structured.md) [+M] for specific written prompts (engineering undergraduates, in a classroom course); untested online
rows.change: Replace the live debrief with specific written prompts after each task and a model answer to compare against; let learners retry a changed task with automatic feedback
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, no facilitator present

rows.basis: untested proposal, from the experiential-learning-cycle pattern
rows.change: Run one complete loop (brief experience, prompted debrief, named rule, one retry) rather than a long experience with no debrief; cut loops, not stages
rows.if: One session (`single-session`)

rows.basis: untested proposal, from the pattern; the reflection synthesis reports peer interaction as a moderator but the claim page does not say in which direction
rows.change: Run debriefs in pairs or small groups against a shared written protocol; spend facilitator time on the conceptualization step, where a wrong rule is hardest for peers to catch
rows.if: Large group, one facilitator

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page's constraint that reflection must go beyond narration
rows.change: Assess performance on a new unaided task; do not grade journals for completion; score explanation and performance separately
rows.if: Assessment is high-stakes, or credit attaches to reflection

rows.basis: untested proposal, from the pattern's personalization
rows.change: Offer written or recorded reflection, in the language they choose, before any group debrief; give sentence starters for the prompts
rows.if: Learners reflect in a second language, or are uncomfortable reflecting in public

rows.basis: [Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows.](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M] (cognitive-load studies; gives no crossover point)
rows.change: Skip demonstration of anything they do unaided on the first try; start each session with their own task and teach only the step where they stop
rows.if: Learners already use some routines (can browse, send a message) and want more

rows.basis: Pacing: [Common language teaching methods such as oral drills, memorization, and fast-paced competitive activities disadvantage older learners](claims/rote-drills-disadvantage-older-learners.md) [~M] (a 1987 digest on older language learners, no data; carried to device skills). That they can learn it: [Learning ability does not decline with age in healthy older adults](claims/learning-ability-does-not-decline-with-age.md) [+M] (the same digest, citing studies on ageing). Enlargement and gestures: untested
rows.change: Slow the demonstration; enlarge text and pointer before teaching anything else; allow more run-throughs and no timed or competitive tasks; teach touch gestures or mouse clicks as a routine of their own
rows.if: Learners are older adults, possibly with poorer eyesight, hearing or fine motor control

rows.basis: [The most cited barriers to adult learning are situational, but adults also face internal barriers such as low confidence in their ability to learn](claims/adult-learner-barriers-situational-and-internal.md) [~M] (a report summarising earlier research on adult learning barriers); the moves are untested
rows.change: Say at the start that nothing they press will break the device, and show undo or back; let them practise privately before anyone watches; praise a correctly followed step, not speed; never take over the device
rows.if: Learners have low confidence, fear breaking something, or have been made to feel slow before

rows.basis: untested proposal; from the earlier page's call for plain-language explanation of interface vocabulary
rows.change: Teach by doing before naming; keep step cards to pictures, screenshots and a few words; say interface words aloud and point; choose routines that need little reading first (icons, voice input)
rows.if: Learners have low literacy, or are learning in a second language

rows.basis: untested proposal; the evidence for responsive help is one-to-one ([Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support.](claims/contingent-scaffolding-improves-learning.md) [~M], whose classroom-scale effect is not shown)
rows.change: Teach one routine to all, then have every learner do it at once; at a set point everyone turns their screen or holds up the phone so the teacher can scan; pair a learner who has finished with one who is stuck, with the rule that the stuck learner keeps hands on the device; collect one unaided run-through from each learner before the next routine
rows.if: Setting is a classroom or lab: one teacher, many learners

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Spend the tutor's minutes on the demonstration and on watching the first run-through only; leave the learner with their own step card and one routine to repeat until the next visit; at the next visit, watch one unaided run-through before teaching anything new
rows.if: Scarce facilitator time: volunteers, a busy library shift, a tutor who checks in for ten minutes

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: For remote learners, have them share their screen or point a second camera at the device, and demonstrate on the same kind of device they hold; teach phone-only learners on the phone with touch routines, not on a lab computer; if screens cannot be shared, ask the learner to say aloud what they see after each step
rows.if: Mixed modes: some learners join remotely while others are in the room, or a learner has only a phone

rows.basis: Practice: [In one experiment with 256 undergraduates, computer-based lesson versions that included practice produced significantly higher posttest scores than versions without practice](claims/practice-presence-raises-cbi-posttest-achievement.md) [+M] (undergraduates in a computer-literacy course, computer-based lesson). Segment length: untested
rows.change: Show one routine per short video segment, then a practice task on the learner's own device with a check the learner can see (did the email arrive in the test inbox?); include a practice task after every demonstration, never demonstration only
rows.if: No teacher: a self-paced video or online course

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Plan one routine from the learner's own task: about 5 minutes finding where they stop, 5 minutes demonstration, 20 minutes guided and then unaided run-throughs, 5 minutes writing the step card. Do not add a second routine; record what the learner did unaided at the end and do not claim it will last
rows.if: Time is a single session only (a drop-in clinic, one workshop)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Fit one routine: 3 minutes unaided warm-up on the last routine, 3–5 minutes demonstration, 15 minutes guided and unaided run-throughs, 5 minutes on the step card and what to try at home
rows.if: A fixed short time budget per session (for example 30 minutes)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Teach the routines on the system and accounts they will use at work or in applications, in the order the job uses them; count a routine as learned only when done unaided on a real work item
rows.if: Adults in work settings (staff learning a new system, job seekers)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Practise the routine on a test message or draft first; when the real one is sent, the learner sends it themselves; the tutor checks it only if the learner asks
rows.if: The learner's task produces something for a real audience (an email to a family member, a job application, a form to a benefits office)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: The learner types passwords and personal details themselves, out of the tutor's view; teach on a practice account or a demonstration site first; the learner decides whether anyone sees the real account; teach how to log out and how to recognise a scam message as routines
rows.if: The task involves private or sensitive material (passwords, bank or health accounts)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep it and its order; change only the delivery: demonstrate one item at a time, have the learner do it at once, check unaided success before ticking it off
rows.if: The brief names its own routine, checklist or curriculum (a programme's digital-skills checklist, a library's standard workshop)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use those categories and that assessment as given; if it credits a task completed with help, keep that, and add beside it one unaided run-through of the same task
rows.if: The brief names its own categories or assessment (a skills framework's levels, a checklist the programme reports to a funder)

rows.basis: untested proposal; from the earlier page's caution against abstract training that never transfers
rows.change: Teach the routines inside the task, in its order, and return to the whole task at the end of every session rather than drilling routines separately; the last sessions are the whole task done unaided
rows.if: The brief wants a whole task kept whole (apply for a job online; book a medical appointment)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use it as the first worked contrast: show the wrong step and the right one side by side, say what to look for on the screen that tells them apart, then practise the right one
rows.if: The brief reports an error learners actually made (closing the browser instead of the tab, replying to a scam email)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Teach only the routines the deadline needs, with more run-throughs and a written step card; judge readiness only on an unaided run-through on the real system; arrange a named person to call if something goes wrong
rows.if: Stakes are high (a deadline for a benefits claim, a learner's job depends on it)

rows.basis: [Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows.](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M] (cognitive-load studies, carried to searching)
rows.change: Skip the modelling; give harder questions (unfamiliar field vocabulary, specialist databases, conflicting results) and peer comparison of search logs
rows.if: Learners already pick key terms and revise on their first observed search (`advanced` searchers)

rows.basis: Untested; no claim here tests search teaching with children
rows.change: Use a child-safe engine or a curated set of sites; teach two steps only (pick the key words, try a different word when it does not work) with the teacher at the screen; no operators
rows.if: `child` learners (primary age)

rows.basis: Untested as search teaching; the session counts are of the order used in [Civic Online Reasoning Instruction Improves Evaluation](claims/civic-online-reasoning-instruction-improves-evaluation.md) [+M] (high-school and eleventh-grade fact-checking lessons, carried)
rows.change: Embed four to six sessions in the subject's own inquiry questions, with the planning sheet early and a revision log later
rows.if: `adolescent` learners in a school subject

rows.basis: Untested; from the earlier page's target learners
rows.change: Start from searches they already need (health, benefits, housing, jobs, their children's school); model typing and reading results step by step; let them say terms aloud before typing; keep result pages short and reading load low; praise a revision, not only a find
rows.if: `adult` learners returning to study, or with low confidence or literacy

rows.basis: Untested; carried from the earlier page
rows.change: Practise on the tools and questions of their job (a clinical database, an internal knowledge base, a supplier catalogue); use the field's own vocabulary lists as the source of terms; check with a work question weeks later
rows.if: `adult` learners in a work setting (`workplace-clinical`, office, trades)

rows.basis: [Game-based learning improved pharmacy students' literature searching course scores in one reported study](claims/game-based-learning-improves-literature-searching-scores-pharmacy.md) [+W] (second-hand report; credits were given for task completion, not search quality)
rows.change: Teach the field's database and its subject headings; consider a game or competition format for practice, but score the quality of the search strategy, not only completion
rows.if: A discipline's literature search (health sciences, law, pharmacy)

rows.basis: [Task complexity moderates whether users experience the constructive information search process](claims/task-complexity-moderates-information-search-process.md) [~M] (workers' information seeking; routine tasks were straightforward, carried to learners)
rows.change: Teach the key-term and scanning steps only; do not require a full log
rows.if: The task is a quick look-up, not an open question

rows.basis: [Task complexity moderates whether users experience the constructive information search process](claims/task-complexity-moderates-information-search-process.md) [~M] (complex tasks involved construction and formulation over time, carried)
rows.change: Expect the question to change as learners search; build in a point where they rewrite the question from what they have found, and log both versions
rows.if: The task is an open, complex research question

rows.basis: Untested; carried from the default design
rows.change: Short recorded demonstrations of each step and of a failed search being repaired; practice questions where the learner submits their queries and reasons before a worked model log for the same question is shown; a delayed check in a new tool
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Run the modelled search on a shared screen visible to both groups; have remote and phone users paste their queries into the shared chat or a shared document so the teacher sees all of them; on phones, practise with voice search as well as typing and keep the log to two lines
rows.if: Mixed mode: some learners remote, some in the room, or phone-only

rows.basis: Untested; contingent-support evidence is one-to-one ([Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support.](claims/contingent-scaffolding-improves-learning.md) [~M])
rows.change: Have every learner post their first query for the same question at once (a shared document or poll); discuss the commonest problem with the whole class; read only the logs of learners who found nothing usable
rows.if: One teacher, a large class

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Give a one-page worked log for each practice question; the facilitator checks one thing per learner: whether the last revision had a reason
rows.if: Scarce facilitator time (volunteers, one tutor checking in briefly)

rows.basis: Untested split; the evaluation part draws on [Evaluating Sources](principles/evaluating-sources.md), and one-session information-skills teaching gave only modest gains ([One-session checklist (CRAAP) instruction in source evaluation did no better than the alternative methods it was compared with in two quasi-experiments](claims/checklist-evaluation-ineffective-online.md) [~M], carried from source evaluation)
rows.change: Session 1, card steps 1–3 (question, words, query, reading results): 5 minutes explanation, 10 minutes modelling with think-aloud on one question including a failed search, 20 minutes guided practice on a set question with the card and immediate correction of each learner's first query, 10 minutes independent search on a second question. Session 2, card step 4 and judging what was found: 5 minutes recap from session-1 logs, 10 minutes modelling checking and revising (including leaving a page to see who is behind it), 20 minutes guided practice on the learners' own questions with corrective feedback on revisions and source choices, 10 minutes assessed independent search on a new question, scored with the card. Do not expect retention beyond the sessions
rows.if: Two sessions only (for example two 45-minute lessons)
