rows.basis: Untested; feedback that responds to where the search broke down is carried from [Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support.](claims/contingent-scaffolding-improves-learning.md) [+M] (one-to-one tutoring)
rows.change: Keep the sequence and its order; teach one or two card steps per pass through it rather than replacing it with this page's steps; give the corrective feedback on the query and the revision, not only the source found
rows.if: The brief names its own instruction sequence (explanation, modelling, think-aloud, guided practice, corrective feedback)

rows.basis: Untested; the one-session evidence in [One-session checklist (CRAAP) instruction in source evaluation did no better than the alternative methods it was compared with in two quasi-experiments](claims/checklist-evaluation-ineffective-online.md) [~M] is for source evaluation, where one session of either method gave modest gains
rows.change: Model one search including a failed one and its repair, then one logged practice search on the learners' own assignment question; give the course teacher the planning sheet to reuse
rows.if: A single session only (a library visit, an orientation)

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: 5 minutes modelling the key-term step, 2 minutes on one failed search and its repair, 10 minutes of learner searching on one question with a two-line log, 3 minutes comparing one log with a model
rows.if: A fixed short time budget (for example 20 minutes)

rows.basis: Untested; the reason-giving step is carried from [Prompting learners to self-explain improves understanding and problem solving on immediate tests by a moderate average amount, with little evidence yet on delayed or classroom gains.](claims/self-explanation-improves-conceptual-understanding.md) [+S]
rows.change: Keep it and its categories; add only what the evidence here says matters: modelled examples, a stated reason for each revision, and feedback on the queries
rows.if: The brief names its own search routine (a library's search worksheet, PICO, a database's own guide, a company template)

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Let the learner choose whether anyone sees their log; practise the routine on a neutral question in class and let them apply it privately; teach clearing history on shared devices
rows.if: Learners search on private or sensitive topics (health, immigration, money, identity)

rows.basis: Learners' belief that chatbots search the web: [Undergraduate students' genAI knowledge contains specific confident misconceptions, most prevalently that AI chatbots perform web searches](claims/genai-misconceptions-web-search-item.md) [~M] (one undergraduate sample; describes beliefs, tests no teaching). The comparison activity is untested
rows.change: Show what the chatbot did and did not do (it may not have searched anything); have learners run the same question as a search, compare, and trace any claim to a source they found
rows.if: Learners use a generative AI chatbot in place of search

rows.basis: [AI overviews in an academic search engine showed mixed effects: summaries may reduce mental demand and frustration for some users, with slightly fewer clicks and query reformulations](claims/ai-overviews-mixed-effects-academic-search.md) [~M] (one within-subjects user study; mixed effects, fewer reformulations)
rows.change: Ask learners to open and check at least one source behind the summary before using it; log whether the summary changed what they searched next
rows.if: The search tool shows AI summaries above results

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Keep the product whole; teach searching inside it at the point the learners need sources, and assess the search log alongside the product rather than as separate items
rows.if: The goal is a whole inquiry product for a real audience (a report, a brief, a presentation)

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Let learners list terms in their first language first, then find the second-language and field terms; show that changing the search language changes results
rows.if: Instruction or sources are in the learners' second language

rows.basis: Untested; carried from the earlier page's point that durable principles matter more than one interface
rows.change: Teach on a library database or saved result pages; assess with a planning sheet and a set of printed result lists from which learners choose and justify a revision
rows.if: No open web access, locked devices, or an offline exam

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Grade on a new question in an unfamiliar tool, scoring the terms, revisions and reasons as well as the sources found
rows.if: High stakes, or the skill is graded

rows.basis: untested proposal; the page's earlier constraint ("a conceptual foundation strong enough..."); [Example–problem sequences reduce cognitive load and improve learning outcomes](claims/worked-example-problem-sequences.md) [+M] for starting from a worked example (secondary-school novices, electrical circuits)
rows.change: Teach the computation or concept first; postpone strategy teaching; keep strategies to one, with a full worked example
rows.if: Learners cannot yet do the computation, or lack the concept

rows.basis: [Comparing cases side by side improves learning and transfer by a moderate average amount, though in one algebra study it raised procedural knowledge and flexibility but not conceptual knowledge](claims/comparing-contrasting-cases-improves-learning.md) [+S] (seventh graders in the algebra study); [Fading support promotes the transfer of responsibility from instructor to learner.](claims/fading-support-promotes-transfer-of-responsibility.md) [+S]
rows.change: Skip single-strategy modelling; go straight to comparing their method with an alternative on problems where the alternative is quicker; mixed problems requiring a choice
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` or already fluent in one method

rows.basis: [Productive Failure Improves Conceptual Learning](claims/productive-failure-improves-conceptual-learning.md) [~S]; [PS-I fosters learning only if specific design features (contrasting cases or building instruction on student solutions) are implemented](claims/ps-i-fosters-learning-only-with-contrasting-cases-or-student-solutions.md) [+M]
rows.change: Open with a 10–15 minute problem attempt, then teach the strategy by comparing learners' solutions with it
rows.if: The goal is conceptual understanding or transfer, learners are secondary-school age or older

rows.basis: [Productive Failure Improves Conceptual Learning](claims/productive-failure-improves-conceptual-learning.md) [~S] (no procedural advantage for problem-first; reversed for second to fifth graders)
rows.change: Teach the strategy first, then practise; no problem-first phase
rows.if: The goal is a procedure, or learners are `child` (early primary)

rows.basis: [Alternative-strategy practices are most effective for improving procedural flexibility, with weaker evidence for conceptual and procedural knowledge](claims/alternative-strategies-most-effective-for-procedural-flexibility.md) [+M]; [Comparing cases side by side improves learning and transfer by a moderate average amount, though in one algebra study it raised procedural knowledge and flexibility but not conceptual knowledge](claims/comparing-contrasting-cases-improves-learning.md) [+S]
rows.change: Make side-by-side comparison of two methods the core of each session, with "which is quicker here, and when would you use the other?"
rows.if: The goal is flexibility, choosing the better method

rows.basis: [Polya Method students outscore Dahmus Method students on the equation criterion for verbal problems](claims/polya-method-beats-dahmus-on-equation-criterion.md) [+M]; [Dahmus Method students translated phrases successfully but failed to combine them into a single solution equation](claims/dahmus-students-translate-but-no-single-equation.md) [+W]; the combination is untested (ninth-grade girls, 1972)
rows.change: Teach the whole-problem plan (unknown, relation, one equation, check); keep translation as a step inside it; offer the pure translation or pure planning version to learners who struggle with the combination
rows.if: Algebra word problems; learners translate phrase by phrase but do not form one equation

rows.basis: [Comparing cases side by side improves learning and transfer by a moderate average amount, though in one algebra study it raised procedural knowledge and flexibility but not conceptual knowledge](claims/comparing-contrasting-cases-improves-learning.md) [+S] (compared methods, not errors); [PS-I fosters learning only if specific design features (contrasting cases or building instruction on student solutions) are implemented](claims/ps-i-fosters-learning-only-with-contrasting-cases-or-student-solutions.md) [+M] (instruction built on students' own solutions, in problem-first designs); using an observed error this way is untested
rows.change: First check the concept behind it on one real item; then make the error one of the compared cases: show the erroneous attempt (anonymised) beside a correct method on the same problem, ask where they part and how to check, then have learners redo a similar item with the correct method and a stated reason
rows.if: The brief reports an error the learners have made (a ratio applied to one quantity only, an operation chosen by keyword)

rows.basis: [Fourth-graders perform substantially better on computation tests than on word problems using the same numbers](claims/computation-outperforms-word-problems-same-numbers.md) [+M]; [Three weeks of explicit language-focused strategy instruction produced no significant word-problem gain in this study](claims/explicit-strategy-instruction-no-significant-gain.md) [~M] (one class of fourth graders, no comparison group)
rows.change: Add reading work to each problem: read aloud, retell the story in own words, name the unknown and the relation before any numbers; do not expect a short strategy unit alone to close the gap; measure it
rows.if: Word-problem scores are far below computation scores; learners have low literacy or are learning in a second language

rows.basis: [Algebra ability level differences appear on both criteria with no treatment-by-ability interaction](claims/ability-level-differences-verbal-problem-solving.md) [~M] (a non-significant interaction does not show the strategies suit all levels equally)
rows.change: Teach the same strategy to all, with more worked examples and more guided rounds for lower attainers; do not assign different strategies by ability on this evidence
rows.if: Learners differ widely in ability or prior attainment

rows.basis: untested proposal; the earlier page's source is an adult-education practice guide, not a claim
rows.change: Keep the brief's own sequence, setting and materials (the kitchen, the recipe card, the shift); teach the strategy on the work's own quantities at the point the work needs it; ask which methods they already use and compare one of theirs with the taught method; check with a work task (scale tomorrow's batch), never a classroom test
rows.if: Learners are `adult` in work settings (apprentices, trainees, `adult-workplace`), or in adult basic education

rows.basis: [Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals.](claims/process-goals-outperform-outcome-goals-for-novices.md) [+M] (writing revision, carried to mathematics); the rest untested
rows.change: Show two valid methods early so "more than one way" is visible; mark following the strategy and giving a reason in early sessions, not right answers; let learners answer privately (paper, device) before anything is shared
rows.if: Learners are anxious about mathematics or low in confidence

rows.basis: [Fading support promotes the transfer of responsibility from instructor to learner.](claims/fading-support-promotes-transfer-of-responsibility.md) [+S] (worked-example fading, carried to self-paced mathematics); [Sixth graders scored significantly higher on posttests that included the seven-step problem-solving plan than on unformatted posttests](claims/formatted-problem-solving-plan-posttest-advantage.md) [+M] (a plan printed with the problems)
rows.change: Put the reason beside every worked step; use completion problems that leave the last steps to the learner; check each answer automatically and show the worked solution; give a one-screen plan card the learner can open
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, phone-only, or no teacher present

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Show both methods on one shared screen; everyone, remote or not, posts the method they chose and one reason (chat, poll) before discussion; read out a remote learner's reason first
rows.if: Mixed modes: some learners remote, some in the room

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Put two learner methods side by side on the board; everyone shows a method choice at once (cards, mini-whiteboards); discuss the commonest wrong choice; then go to those who chose by keyword
rows.if: One teacher for a large class

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Spend the check-in on one thing: ask the learner which method they chose on one problem and why; leave answer checking to an answer key
rows.if: Scarce facilitator time (volunteer tutor, short check-ins)

rows.basis: untested proposal; a three-week unit showed no significant gain in one class ([Three weeks of explicit language-focused strategy instruction produced no significant word-problem gain in this study](claims/explicit-strategy-instruction-no-significant-gain.md) [~M])
rows.change: Check the concept on one real item (5 min), model one strategy with its reason (10 min), one side-by-side comparison, using an observed error if there is one (10 min), one unaided item from the work with a stated reason (5 min); do not claim flexibility or retention
rows.if: A single session only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep one strategy or one comparison per session: 5 minutes model, 10 minutes guided choice with reasons, 5 minutes unaided item; spread the arc over more sessions rather than packing it
rows.if: A fixed short time budget per session (for example 20 minutes)

rows.basis: untested proposal; a printed plan raised scores when it appeared on the test ([Sixth graders scored significantly higher on posttests that included the seven-step problem-solving plan than on unformatted posttests](claims/formatted-problem-solving-plan-posttest-advantage.md) [+M])
rows.change: Keep it and its terms; add only the "when does this fit, and why" talk and one comparison with an alternative; judge with the brief's own rubric
rows.if: The brief names its own routine, heuristic, categories or rubric (a school's problem-solving steps, a keyword chart, a seven-step plan)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Add no pre-test, post-test or delayed check; judge progress from what learners do in the work (the method they choose on the next real item and the reason they give)
rows.if: The brief asks for no test, or names no assessment

rows.basis: untested proposal; scores differed with and without the printed plan ([Sixth graders scored significantly higher on posttests that included the seven-step problem-solving plan than on unformatted posttests](claims/formatted-problem-solving-plan-posttest-advantage.md) [~M]) and the equation and solution criteria diverged ([Polya and Dahmus methods do not differ on the problem solution criterion](claims/no-treatment-difference-problem-solution-criterion.md) [~M])
rows.change: Judge readiness only on problems without the plan card; score the equation or plan and the final answer separately
rows.if: Stakes are high, or the assessment is unaided

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep the task whole; teach the strategy at the point in the task where it is needed, then return to the task; do not split it into separate drill items
rows.if: A whole real task the brief wants kept whole (a budget, a pricing decision, a measured plan for a job), or a product for a real audience

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Let learners use their own numbers privately, or offer realistic substitute figures; nobody else sees the numbers, only the method
rows.if: The problems use learners' own private figures (pay, debts, benefits)

rows.basis: [Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows.](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M] (cognitive-load studies; carried; gives no crossover point)
rows.change: Drop the think-aloud and the curated sets; give one open-web synthesis task with a short debrief on their choices
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` online readers, or keep to a goal and join pages on the check task

rows.basis: Discussion on [Reading Strategy Instruction Improves Comprehension](claims/reading-strategy-instruction-improves-comprehension.md) [~S] (strategy instruction does not make up for weak word recognition; print); the adaptations are untested proposals
rows.change: Work on print reading first, or reduce the reading: short pages, text read aloud by a screen reader, two links per page, a picture-based record; praise and record each return to the goal
rows.if: Learners have weak word reading or low literacy, or low confidence as readers

rows.basis: untested for online reading; contingent help with children is carried from one-to-one long-division tutoring ([Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support.](claims/contingent-scaffolding-improves-learning.md) [+M])
rows.change: Curated sites only; one question; two or three links; an adult-made record template with boxes to tick and one line to write; the teacher checks paths one-to-one or in small groups
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary age)

rows.basis: [Reading Strategy Instruction Improves Comprehension](claims/reading-strategy-instruction-improves-comprehension.md) [+S] (meta-analysis of strategy instruction for English L2 learners, print texts; carried to online)
rows.change: Keep the strategy routine and name each move in plain language (the learners' first language allowed for the record); choose pages slightly below their reading level for the first sessions
rows.if: Learners are `adolescent` or `adult` second-language readers

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use the pages they actually read at work (an intranet, a policy portal, a supplier's documentation) and a real work question; the synthesis is the answer they would give a colleague
rows.if: `adult` learners in work settings

rows.basis: [Metacognitive prompts improve learning](claims/metacognitive-prompts-improve-learning.md) [+S] (computer-based environments); [review-notes compliance](claims/review-notes-compliance-predicts-learning-gains.md) [+M] (one study, associational)
rows.change: Build the supports into the course: a goal box that must be filled before links open, a notes panel beside the reading, a prompt at each page change ("does this page answer your question?"), and a "review your notes and revise your summary" step before the answer is submitted
rows.if: Setting is `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: untested proposal; whole-class strategy programmes showed much smaller effects than researcher-led ones ([Reading Strategy Instruction Improves Comprehension](claims/reading-strategy-instruction-improves-comprehension.md) [~S]) and contingent-support evidence is mostly one-to-one ([Contingent scaffolding …](claims/contingent-scaffolding-improves-learning.md) [~M])
rows.change: Projected think-aloud; everyone keeps the page record on paper or in one shared document the teacher can scan; two checkpoints per task where the teacher reads records and gives whole-class feedback on the commonest drift, then visits those who lost the question
rows.if: `classroom` with one teacher and a large group

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Share the think-aloud screen with remote learners and record it for replay; one shared record document all can write in; phone-only learners work in one tab with a lower link budget (two or three) and keep the record on paper or in a single notes app
rows.if: Mixed modes: some learners remote, some in the room, or phone-only

rows.basis: untested proposal; the prompt card stands in for live prompts ([Metacognitive prompts improve learning](claims/metacognitive-prompts-improve-learning.md) [+S], computer-based prompts; carried)
rows.change: Give learners a prompt card with the four moves and a model synthesis to check their own against; the tutor's one check-in reads the record and asks one question ("where did you leave your question?")
rows.if: One teacher or tutor with little time (volunteers, a busy shift, brief check-ins)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: 45 minutes: goal and questions 3, think-aloud 8, guided practice on a curated set of four pages 22, synthesis 6, debrief on one drift 5, and one unaided question 1–2; record what it shows and claim no lasting change
rows.if: Time is one session only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Goal 2 minutes, a 4-minute think-aloud of one move only (choosing links against the goal), practice on three pages 10 minutes, a two-sentence synthesis 4 minutes
rows.if: A fixed short time budget (for example 20 minutes inside another lesson)

rows.basis: untested proposal; the additions rest on [process goals](claims/process-goals-outperform-outcome-goals-for-novices.md) [+M] and [self-explanation](claims/self-explanation-improves-conceptual-understanding.md) [+S], both carried
rows.change: Keep it; add only what the evidence here points to: a goal written before any link opens, one "why this link?" line per page, and a review of notes before answering
rows.if: The brief names its own routine for reading or research (a school's research log, a KWL chart, an inquiry template)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use them as the headings of the running record and the synthesis; do not substitute this page's moves as the criteria; if the rubric rewards tool use or link use, keep it and add one unaided question beside it
rows.if: The brief gives its own categories, criteria or rubric for the product

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: The learner keeps the record and decides who sees it; teach and check the moves on a neutral practice topic, and let the learner apply them privately
rows.if: The reading is private or sensitive (a health condition, personal finances, immigration status)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Do not split it into separate strategy exercises; teach each move inside the task at the point it is needed and check the moves in the record the task already produces
rows.if: The brief wants a whole-task performance kept whole (a research report, a decision brief, a presentation)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: The synthesis becomes the product; the page record and the reasons stay with the learner and the teacher
rows.if: The product goes to a real audience who should see the answer, not the reasoning

rows.basis: [Interesting but irrelevant details can impair comprehension and transfer, with effects that vary with the material and the learner](claims/seductive-details-effect.md) [~S] (instructional materials, not web pages; carried); college students reporting goal setting and environment structuring reported less digital distraction ([SRL strategies associated with lower digital distraction](claims/srl-strategies-associated-lower-digital-distraction.md) [+M], associational survey)
rows.change: Before reading: close other tabs, silence notifications, use a reader view if available; pick practice pages without decorative clutter for early sessions
rows.if: The pages are full of advertising, pop-ups, autoplay video or notifications

rows.basis: [Letting learners pace instruction helped on complex material in one experiment, while learner control in general showed almost no effect across 18 studies](claims/learner-paced-beats-system-paced-complex-material.md) [~S]; [Learner characteristics … moderate hypermedia learning effectiveness](claims/learner-characteristics-moderate-hypermedia-effectiveness.md) [~M] (review)
rows.change: Keep exploration, but add the goal, the link budget and the record; do not count on the freedom itself
rows.if: The brief proposes free exploration of a rich hypermedia site as the method

rows.basis: untested proposal; strategy measures moved more than standardised comprehension in whole-class print programmes ([Reading Strategy Instruction Improves Comprehension](claims/reading-strategy-instruction-improves-comprehension.md) [~S])
rows.change: Judge readiness only on an unaided online task like the target, with the record kept; never on prompted practice or a strategy-use questionnaire
rows.if: High stakes, or the assessment is unaided

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Hand over to the lateral-reading model on [Evaluating Sources](principles/evaluating-sources.md) rather than adding credibility checks here
rows.if: The real difficulty is whether to trust a page

rows.basis: [Vocabulary Instruction Improves Comprehension](claims/vocabulary-instruction-improves-comprehension.md) [+S] (pre-K–12; students with reading difficulties gained most on custom measures); for students with learning disabilities, teach content words as concepts rather than definitions: [The concept model of vocabulary instruction produced larger gains…](claims/concept-model-beats-definition-model-vocabulary-ld.md) [+M] (six middle-school students); doses untested
rows.change: Keep the set small (3–4 words per session), teach orally with pictures and actions, read texts aloud with the words in them; expect taught-word gains, not general reading gains
rows.if: Learners are `child` (pre-K to primary), or are weaker readers

rows.basis: [Glossing yields medium-to-large positive effects on L2 vocabulary learning…](claims/glossing-medium-large-effects-l2-vocabulary.md) [+W] (second-hand report of meta-analyses); [Correct word inference in reading requires knowing roughly 95–98% of surrounding words…](claims/vocabulary-coverage-thresholds-for-inference.md) [~W] (second-hand); [Proficiency moderates gloss effects…](claims/proficiency-moderates-gloss-vocabulary-effects.md) [~M] (one EFL study: benefits at middle proficiency levels only); first-language glosses: [All three L1 gloss conditions significantly improve immediate vocabulary recall…](claims/l1-glosses-improve-immediate-vocabulary-recall.md) [+M] and, from the same study of 135 Taiwanese undergraduates, only the gloss-with-L2-example and in-text gloss forms held on all three recall tests ([Only L1-gloss-L2-ex and L1-in-text-gloss conditions…](claims/gloss-l2-ex-and-in-text-gloss-beat-control-scheffe.md) [~M]), so prefer those to marginal glosses where retention matters
rows.change: Gloss unfamiliar words in the text (first-language or picture glosses), teach the most frequent words first, and do not rely on inference from context until most surrounding words are known
rows.if: Learners are second-language learners, `novice` in the language

rows.basis: untested; carried from school-age evidence on taught words and word parts ([Morphological Instruction Improves Vocabulary](claims/morphological-instruction-improves-vocabulary.md) [~M], school-age children only)
rows.change: Take the words from their real documents and tasks; teach word parts that recur in the field; check use in the job task (a handover, a report, a conversation with a client), not in a quiz
rows.if: Learners are fluent `adult`s or professionals entering a new field (technical or workplace terms)

rows.basis: [Task-essentialness and productive use of new words…](claims/task-essentialness-goal-directed-vocabulary-retention.md) [+W] (second-hand, five learners); otherwise untested
rows.change: Add at least two speaking or writing tasks per word in which the word is needed to complete the task; give a sentence frame at first, then withdraw it
rows.if: The goal is productive use (speaking, writing) rather than reading

rows.basis: [Vocabulary Instruction Improves Comprehension](claims/vocabulary-instruction-improves-comprehension.md) [~S] (d = 0.10 on standardised measures against 0.50 on researcher-built ones)
rows.change: Say plainly that a small taught set will not move a general comprehension score; spend more time on wide supported reading with glosses, and teach words that recur across many texts
rows.if: The goal is reading comprehension in general, not of particular texts

rows.basis: [Supplemental computer-based spaced repetition…](claims/spaced-repetition-supplement-triples-vocabulary-retention.md) [+M] (EFL cadets, alongside classroom teaching, not instead of it)
rows.change: Build each word as a short card (meaning, example, picture, audio) with recall prompts scheduled by the app over two to three weeks; put the words into short readings or audio inside the course; ask for one typed or spoken use per word
rows.if: Setting is `online-self-paced`, phone-only, or no teacher present

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Put the word set, examples and the shared text where both groups see them (shared screen or document); take uses in the chat or a shared document as well as aloud, and pair a remote learner with an in-room one for the speaking task
rows.if: Some learners are remote and some in the room

rows.basis: untested proposal; the review part rests on [Supplemental computer-based spaced repetition…](claims/spaced-repetition-supplement-triples-vocabulary-retention.md) [+M]
rows.change: Teach the set to everyone at once in 10 minutes; let spaced review run on cards or an app; in the check-in, look at one thing only: a written or spoken use of two or three of the week's words
rows.if: One teacher with a large group, or scarce facilitator time (a volunteer, one short check-in a week)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Teach 3 words, not more: 6–8 minutes introducing them, 8–10 minutes reading or doing a task that uses them, 3–4 minutes of use in the learner's own sentence; give a take-away card for later review; do not claim retention
rows.if: A single session only, or a fixed short time budget (for example 20 minutes)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Let learners show they know a word by pointing, sorting pictures or acting before saying or writing it; use pairs before whole-group use; never correct misuse in front of the group
rows.if: Learners have low confidence, low literacy or anxiety about speaking

rows.basis: [Pairing Contextual Encounters…](claims/pairing-contextual-encounters-with-explicit-instruction-produces-stronger-vocabulary-outcomes-than-either-alone.md) [+M]; [Vocabulary Knowledge Grows Incrementally…](claims/vocabulary-knowledge-grows-incrementally-with-repeated-encounters-in-varied-contexts.md) [+M]
rows.change: Keep the routine; change only what the evidence says matters: put each word into a text or task soon after it is entered, bring it back several times across weeks, and ask for one use, not only a definition
rows.if: The brief names its own routine (a word wall, a Frayer-style chart, a vocabulary log, a glossary its course uses)

rows.basis: untested
rows.change: Teach from that list in its own categories; select within it by what the next texts and tasks need, rather than replacing it
rows.if: The brief gives its own word list, categories or rubric (a course list, a standards list, a job's terminology)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: The learner decides what goes in it and who sees it; check use through a separate task, not by reading the journal
rows.if: Learners keep a personal word journal or notebook, or the material is private

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Teach the words the performance needs beforehand and rehearse them in parts of the real task, then let the performance run whole; do not turn it into a vocabulary test
rows.if: The output is a product or performance for a real audience (a presentation, a client conversation, a published text), and the brief wants it kept whole

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Raise the criterion for "known": correct unprompted use in three tasks, plus recognition in the exact form the exam or job uses; keep spaced review until the event
rows.if: Stakes are high (an exam with a set word list, a safety or medication term at work)

rows.basis: [Unassisted discovery produces less learning than explicit instruction, while discovery enhanced with guidance outperforms other instruction](claims/minimal-guidance-less-effective-for-novices.md) [~S]
rows.change: Set the question and fix which variables may change; require a written prediction before each test; keep a prompt sheet throughout; end with the canonical explanation
rows.if: Learners are `novice` on the target relation (e.g. a first encounter with how a variable affects a system)

rows.basis: [The advantage of guidance begins to recede only when learners have sufficiently high prior knowledge to provide internal guidance](claims/guidance-advantage-recedes-with-high-prior-knowledge.md) [~M] (a review's statement; gives no threshold)
rows.change: Let them set their own goal and test plan; drop the prompt sheet; review the plan briefly instead
rows.if: Learners are `advanced`, or already design fair tests unaided

rows.basis: [Supplementing simulation-based inquiry with learner guidance has a modest effect on learning outcomes (d = 0.49) and inquiry skills (d = 0.41), independent of guidance type (review attribution to D'Angelo et al., 2014)](claims/guidance-improves-inquiry-learning-outcomes.md) [~M] reports that age moderates the effect but not how; the specific changes are untested
rows.change: Fewer variables (two or three), shorter rounds (10 minutes), the teacher reading predictions aloud with the group; allow a prediction to be drawn or pointed at rather than written
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary age)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Start from a question they bring from their work; use their own data or model where possible; let them set the goal from session 1, with a facilitator reviewing the test plan
rows.if: Learners are adults in a work setting (e.g. exploring a pricing model, a process simulation or a spreadsheet of their own operation)

rows.basis: [Teachers reported that students needed dedicated time to learn and explore technologies before being expected to gain mathematics understanding from them](claims/students-need-time-learn-technology-first.md) [~W] (teacher reflection, one unit)
rows.change: Add a 10-minute no-stakes familiarisation task before the content question; pair a confident and a less confident user, swapping the controls each round
rows.if: The learner is new to the interface, or has low confidence with computers

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Replace the written log with a picture or screenshot log (before, after, thumbs up or down for the prediction); give the hypothesis template orally and in the home language where possible
rows.if: Learners have low literacy, or work in a second language

rows.basis: untested proposal; guidance evidence is pooled across settings and does not separate a teacher circulating from built-in prompts ([Guidance during inquiry learning produces a medium-to-large improvement in learners' use of inquiry skills during the inquiry](claims/guidance-improves-inquiry-learning-activities.md) [~M])
rows.change: Run rounds in pairs at one device; groups hold up or post their prediction before testing so the teacher can scan for one-change-at-a-time; the teacher circulates to groups whose log is empty
rows.if: `classroom`, one teacher and many learners at screens

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use a browser tool that works on a phone, or have remote learners send predictions to an in-room partner who runs the tool and shares the screen; collect every prediction in one shared place (chat, shared document) before each test
rows.if: Mixed mode: some learners remote, some in the room, or some on phones only

rows.basis: [Supplementing simulation-based inquiry with learner guidance has a modest effect on learning outcomes (d = 0.49) and inquiry skills (d = 0.41), independent of guidance type (review attribution to D'Angelo et al., 2014)](claims/guidance-improves-inquiry-learning-outcomes.md) [+M] (effects did not depend on guidance type, which suggests built-in prompts can serve; untested as such)
rows.change: Build the question, prediction box, prompts and closing unaided question into the tool or worksheet; show the canonical explanation only after the learner has submitted a rule
rows.if: Setting is `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Spend the facilitator's minutes on the prediction before the round and the rule after it, not on watching the round; a printed prompt card covers the middle
rows.if: Scarce facilitator time (a volunteer, a busy shift, a tutor checking in briefly)

rows.basis: untested proposal; immediate gains may not last ([AI-generated and prebuilt simulations produced higher immediate conceptual-assessment scores than physical laboratory work, but the advantage did not persist in later examinations](claims/simulation-advantage-immediate-not-sustained.md) [~M])
rows.change: 5 min tool familiarisation, 5 min question and predictions, 20 min exploration with the log (three to five cycles), 10 min groups state their rule and hear the canonical explanation, 5 min one unaided question, 5 min spare; claim only immediate understanding
rows.if: Single session only, or a fixed short time budget (e.g. 50 minutes)

rows.basis: [AI-generated and prebuilt simulations produced higher immediate conceptual-assessment scores than physical laboratory work, but the advantage did not persist in later examinations](claims/simulation-advantage-immediate-not-sustained.md) [~M]; [The review reports that simulation games support near transfer of knowledge but evidence for long-term or far transfer is less robust](claims/simulation-near-transfer-robust-far-transfer-weak.md) [~M]
rows.change: Add an unaided question at the end of every round and a spaced return to the idea in later weeks; judge readiness only on unaided answers, never on what was achieved with the tool
rows.if: The outcome that counts is a later exam taken without the tool, or high stakes

rows.basis: [Some students found the guided-inquiry worksheet activities insufficiently thought-provoking and the data exchange troublesome](claims/students-criticize-inquiry-worksheets-low-thinking.md) [~W]
rows.change: Keep it; change only what the evidence says matters: add a prediction line before each test if it lacks one, and replace any copy-the-values item with a reasoning item
rows.if: The brief names its own routine (its own worksheet, rubric, lab report template or check-in)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Run it as given; add one unaided question beside it, not instead of it
rows.if: The brief's own assessment rewards what was achieved with the tool

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use those categories in the prediction template and the closing rule; do not substitute this page's
rows.if: The brief uses its own categories or criteria for a good result (a rubric, a list of accepted explanations)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep exploration and the product separate: rounds of trial on drafts, then a final piece in which the learner says which tried options they chose and why; the audience sees the product, the reasoning log stays with the learner and teacher
rows.if: The product is for a real audience (a composition, a design, a model presented to a client or the public)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Explore inside the whole task: each round changes one feature of the whole, never a detached part; log the change against the whole result
rows.if: A whole-task performance the brief wants kept whole (e.g. tuning a whole system, composing a whole piece)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Let the learner choose to use their own data or a provided dataset; the log stays with the learner and is shared only by their choice
rows.if: The material is private or sensitive (learners' own finances, health or workplace data in a model)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Replay it as a compared case: show both runs, ask which variable caused the change, then run the one-change version
rows.if: Learners report an error they actually made (e.g. changing two variables at once and crediting the wrong one)

rows.basis: untested proposal; the guidance evidence is not specific to computer tools ([Guidance during inquiry learning improves post-inquiry learning outcomes (d = 0.50)](claims/guidance-improves-inquiry-learning-outcomes.md) [+M])
rows.change: Run the same guided cycle with physical materials or a paper model; plan fewer, better-chosen tests, and use the prediction log to make each one count
rows.if: No fast tool is available

rows.basis: [Contingent scaffolding](claims/contingent-scaffolding-improves-learning.md) [+M] (children, one-to-one, long division)
rows.change: Run the loop for them: task-level information on every attempt, a matched retry at once, the step re-modelled after two failed cycles
rows.if: Learners are `novice` on the task

rows.basis: [Expertise reversal](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M] (review of guidance studies, carried to feedback; no crossover point given)
rows.change: Shorten external loops: ask for self-evaluation first, give information only on what the self-evaluation missed, and loop on harder or transfer items
rows.if: Learners are `advanced`, or already accurate unaided

rows.basis: Praise: [Praise for intelligence, rather than for effort, after success undermines children's motivation and performance after a later failure](claims/feedback-praise-reduces-learning.md) [-M] (fifth graders). Cycle length: untested
rows.change: Shorter cycles with the adult reading each attempt; praise the strategy or the work, never ability; small groups so attempts can be seen
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary age)

rows.basis: [Peer Feedback Improves Writing](claims/peer-feedback-improves-writing.md) [+M] (higher education, 24 studies; against no feedback); revision interval untested
rows.change: Loop over drafts: draft, structured peer or teacher feedback against criteria, revision within a few days, then a new piece checked for the same targets
rows.if: Goal is a written or made product (`complex-skill`)

rows.basis: [Corrective feedback on L2 errors](claims/corrective-feedback-effect-on-l2-development-is-significant-and-durable.md) [+S] (two meta-analyses; gains held on delayed tests; prompts larger than recasts in the classroom synthesis; the two disagree on whether longer treatments do better, and younger learners benefited more, so the pooled effect fits adults least)
rows.change: Correct errors in the exchange itself, with prompts that ask the learner to reformulate rather than only recasts; keep it up over many sessions
rows.if: Goal is spoken second-language accuracy

rows.basis: [Trained teachers' loop time](claims/training-increases-feedback-corrective-loop-time.md) [+M] (secondary mathematics, time allocation only, no learning outcome); [rubrics and peer feedback](claims/rubrics-improve-peer-feedback-quality.md) [~M] (rubrics changed peer comments, one study found less reflective feedback)
rows.change: Collect every learner's attempt at once (mini-whiteboards, a poll, a short written item), give whole-class information on the commonest error, have everyone do one matched item, then go to those who still fail; use peers with a rubric for drafts; budget class time for the loop
rows.if: `classroom`, one teacher and a large group

rows.basis: Untested proposal; peer reading carried from [peer feedback on writing](claims/peer-feedback-improves-writing.md) [+M], which tested drafts, not practical tasks
rows.change: Run the loop in buddy pairs: one partner watches an attempt against a posted checklist of two or three points, names one thing to change, and the other retries at once; a wall tally records which checklist points were met; the facilitator rechecks a sample (one new unaided attempt from two or three people per shift) and changes the checklist if the same point keeps failing. No paperwork beyond the tally
rows.if: Little facilitator time or equipment: volunteers, busy shifts, no devices

rows.basis: [Intelligent tutoring systems improve achievement over non-individualised instruction](claims/adaptive-learning-improves-outcomes.md) [+S] (intelligent tutoring beat large-group, textbook and other computer instruction, not human tutoring or small groups; gains were smaller on standardized than on locally developed tests)
rows.change: Build automatically checked items with a retry on a new item after each piece of information; route a learner who fails twice to a worked example; keep a delayed recheck in a later session
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: [Feedback quality predicts revision only with teachers](claims/feedback-quality-predicts-revision-only-in-teacher-condition.md) [~M] (one essay study: teacher feedback quality predicted revised-draft quality, AI feedback quality did not); [enacted feedback uptake](claims/enacted-feedback-higher-uptake-than-directed-self-directed.md) [+M] (uptake, not learning)
rows.change: Keep a person in the loop to help learners interpret and apply the AI's comments; have the learner choose and rank which comments to act on before revising, and check the revision against the chosen targets
rows.if: Feedback comes from a generative AI tool

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use one submission channel everyone can reach (a shared form or chat poll), return information in that channel, and give remote learners the same matched retry; for phone-only learners keep items short and one target per message
rows.if: Mixed modes: some learners remote, some in the room, or phone-only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Run at least two complete cycles inside the session and end with one unaided new item; report what that item shows and claim no retention
rows.if: One session only

rows.basis: untested; [Assessment for Learning](principles/assessment-for-learning.md) holds the stakes model ([retakes and revisions](strategies/retakes-and-revisions.md) is a recipe, untested)
rows.change: Keep loop items ungraded and separate from the graded task; judge readiness only on unaided new items; let a revision replace an earlier mark if revision is the point
rows.if: Stakes are high, or the work is graded

rows.basis: untested proposal; person-focused praise is the one thing with evidence against it ([Praise for intelligence, rather than for effort, after success undermines children's motivation and performance after a later failure](claims/feedback-praise-reduces-learning.md) [-M], children)
rows.change: Give information privately, about the task, in short spoken or shown form (a demonstration, a marked example) rather than long written comments; one target per cycle
rows.if: Learners have low confidence or low literacy

rows.basis: untested; in one teacher-education case, probing feedback with required resubmission helped one candidate and not another ([probing feedback](claims/probing-feedback-revise-resubmit-evidence.md) [+W])
rows.change: Loop on real work outputs (a case note, a call, a procedure); a supervisor or peer reads one output per cycle against a stated criterion, and the next output is the re-observation
rows.if: Adults in work settings (`adult-workplace`, `workplace-clinical`)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Run the loops in rehearsal with a critic using the criteria, before the audience; treat the audience's response as information for the next product, not a judgement on this one; do not show the audience the drafts or the critique if it should see only the finished work
rows.if: A product or performance for a real audience

rows.basis: [revise-summary compliance](claims/revise-summary-compliance-predicts-learning-gains.md) [~M] (associational, 28 college students, one tutoring system)
rows.change: Make the use visible: the learner marks what they changed, or answers "what will you do next?" before the next attempt; no new information until the last was used
rows.if: Learners receive feedback but do not use it

rows.basis: [hypercorrection](claims/high-confidence-errors-improve-retention.md) [~S] (mostly recall; carried to misconceptions untested)
rows.change: Ask for confidence before revealing answers; correct confident errors explicitly and bring the item back later
rows.if: Learners answer confidently and wrongly (misconceptions)

rows.basis: For one outcome, immediate and delayed feedback were equally effective ([feedback after multiple-choice tests](claims/feedback-after-multiple-choice-tests-halves-lure-intrusions.md) [+M], reported second-hand); timing is held on [Immediate Feedback](principles/immediate-feedback.md)
rows.change: Keep the loop closed by attaching a task: the learner uses the returned comments on a new item before the next unit, rather than reading and filing them; whether earlier would be better is not settled
rows.if: Information can only come later (marking takes days)

rows.basis: [Direct and metalinguistic feedback with explanations beat control at the immediate posttest; code-only did not](claims/cf-type-explicit-short-term-differences.md) [+M] (low-intermediate Korean EFL learners, written feedback, four sessions); [code-only caught up two weeks later](claims/cf-type-explicit-long-term-benefits.md) [~M], so the gap is in the short term
rows.change: Give the correct form plus a one-line rule; avoid bare codes, underlines or rising-intonation prompts until the form has been taught
rows.if: Learners are `novice` with the form, or low proficiency

rows.basis: [Prompts and explicit correction larger than recasts in classrooms](claims/recasts-supported-but-effectiveness-varies.md) [~M]; workaround row: [advanced learners content with circumlocution risk fixed errors](claims/l1-interference-errors-fossilization-risk.md) [~W] (one learner's diary)
rows.change: Prompt first (repeat the error, give a rule clue, ask again); give the correct form only if the prompt fails. For an advanced learner who gets by with paraphrase, push for the exact form rather than accepting the workaround
rows.if: Learners are `intermediate` or `advanced`, and the form has been taught

rows.basis: [Recasts in task-based lessons with grade-5 EFL learners](claims/recasts-facilitate-child-efl-third-person-s-development.md) [+M] (pretest–posttest, no comparison group); the classroom meta-analysis found younger learners benefited more ([durable effect](claims/corrective-feedback-effect-on-l2-development-is-significant-and-durable.md) [+S])
rows.change: Recast the target form within the task without stopping it; keep explicit rule talk short
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary age) in task-based lessons

rows.basis: untested proposal; adults were the least represented group in the classroom meta-analysis ([durable effect](claims/corrective-feedback-effect-on-l2-development-is-significant-and-durable.md) [~S])
rows.change: Ask which errors matter in their work (a misunderstanding with a client, a written report); treat those first, privately or in writing; leave the rest unless asked
rows.if: Learners are `adult` professionals using the language at work (`adult-workplace`)

rows.basis: [Global versus local errors](claims/global-versus-local-errors-correction.md) [+W] (theoretical); slot length untested
rows.change: Interrupt only for global errors that block meaning; note local errors for a five-minute slot after the activity
rows.if: Goal is fluency or meaning (a discussion, a role-play, a presentation)

rows.basis: [Metalinguistic feedback and recasts improved wh-question performance; clarification requests did not](claims/metalinguistic-recasts-effective-immediate-wh-questions.md) [+M] (Iranian EFL learners, four intact classes, immediate test)
rows.change: Correct every error in that structure as it happens, with a prompt or a metalinguistic clue; ignore errors in other forms during that activity
rows.if: Goal is accuracy on one target structure

rows.basis: [Metalinguistic ahead immediately, not at ten days](claims/metalinguistic-beats-recasts-immediate-not-delayed.md) [~M]; [feedback type and time interact](claims/time-treatment-interaction-corrective-feedback.md) [~M]
rows.change: Do not pick a correction form for its effect straight after treatment; check unprompted use a week or more later before keeping or changing it
rows.if: Horizon is weeks or a term, not the next test

rows.basis: [Self-correction dominates, read as face-saving](claims/self-correction-dominates-negative-feedback-face-saving.md) [~M]; [AI private practice reduces anxiety](claims/ai-reduces-fl-anxiety-private-practice.md) [~M] (review; carried from AI tools to private correction)
rows.change: Wait for self-correction; correct in private or in writing; in front of the group, correct only common errors without names
rows.if: Learner is anxious, new to the group, or low in confidence

rows.basis: untested proposal; teachers' own preference for end-of-class correction ([teachers favour delayed correction](claims/teachers-favor-delayed-ocf-over-immediate.md) [~M]) is a belief, not an outcome
rows.change: During the activity, walk and note errors on a sheet; afterwards, five minutes on the two or three commonest, written up without names, learners correct them in pairs, then the rule
rows.if: One teacher with a large class

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Give in-room and remote learners the same channel: correct in the chat or a shared document privately during the activity, and post the end-of-activity summary as text for everyone, so remote learners do not get only public spoken correction
rows.if: Mixed modes: some learners remote, some in the room, or phone-only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: One target form per check-in: show the learner one of their own errors, give the correct form and the rule in one line, ask for one new sentence using it; record the form on the learner's list
rows.if: Scarce facilitator time (a volunteer tutor, a brief check-in)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Pick one or two forms; correct only those, in a five-minute slot at the end; record what was corrected and do not claim lasting change
rows.if: Single session only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: About 15 minutes of uninterrupted activity with error notes, 5 minutes of correction on two or three errors; nothing else added
rows.if: Fixed short time budget (e.g. a 20-minute speaking slot)

rows.basis: [Code-only behind at the immediate posttest](claims/cf-type-explicit-short-term-differences.md) [~M]; [code-only caught up at two weeks](claims/cf-type-explicit-long-term-benefits.md) [~M]
rows.change: Keep it and run it well; change only what the evidence says matters: for low-proficiency learners, add the correct form or a one-line rule beside a bare code
rows.if: The brief names its own correction routine (an error code, an error log, a feedback form)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use its categories to decide which errors to treat and report; do not substitute global/local or error/mistake labels for them
rows.if: The brief has its own categories or rubric for errors (e.g. a speaking rubric's "accuracy" band)

rows.basis: untested proposal; the error-as-object model is in [Error Analysis](principles/error-analysis.md)
rows.change: Use it as the first worked case in the correction slot: the learners' sentence beside the correct one, the learners say what changed and why
rows.if: The brief reports an error the learners actually made

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: The learner decides whether it is corrected and who sees the correction; offer correction on a chosen extract, privately
rows.if: Private or sensitive material (a journal, personal writing, a learner's story)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Never interrupt the performance; correct during rehearsal, on the two or three forms that would most affect the audience's understanding; give the rest afterwards, privately
rows.if: A performance for a real audience (a presentation, a public reading, a meeting)

rows.basis: Learners' attitudes were most negative toward the version of a computer-based lesson stripped of practice and other events ([lean version most negative](claims/cbi-version-affects-attitudes-lean-most-negative.md) [~M], undergraduates, a computer-literacy lesson, attitudes not learning); carried to language apps
rows.change: Keep practice items and feedback in the lesson rather than cutting them to shorten it; use the correct form with a rule line for novice learners
rows.if: Online self-paced course or app

rows.basis: [Proactive focus on form, fewer repeated errors](claims/proactive-fof-reduces-error-fossilization.md) [~W] (authors' interpretation, one study)
rows.change: Stop correcting it on the spot; plan a short lesson on the form before the next task that needs it
rows.if: An error survives three or four corrections, or many learners share it

rows.basis: [Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows.](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M] (cognitive-load studies, not grouping); [Learning By Teaching Improves Tutor Learning](claims/learning-by-teaching-improves-tutor-learning.md) [+M] (tutors' own gains)
rows.change: Skip the support group for them; form an extension group with a harder or wider task, or place them in mixed groups as explainers with an explaining role, not answer-givers
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` on this task, or most already pass the check

rows.basis: [Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support.](claims/contingent-scaffolding-improves-learning.md) [+M] (fourth and fifth graders, one-to-one); format and timing untested
rows.change: Fewer formats, taught as routines with visual role cards; similar-need groups with the teacher for 10–15 minutes; other groups do practice they can check themselves
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary age)

rows.basis: untested proposal; the earlier page names adults, including those with learning disabilities and multilingual learners
rows.change: Group by the task or job role in hand and by what learners say they need, not by test scores; let adults choose to join a support session; use mixed groups to pool workplace experience
rows.if: Learners are `adult`, including adults in a work setting or adult basic education

rows.basis: [Students segregated into language cliques whenever allowed to choose peer interactions, despite the 50-50 enrollment design](claims/language-clique-segregation-peer-choice.md) [~W] (one dual-language school, observation); the design move is untested
rows.change: Assign mixed-language groups for discussion and projects, with a role that needs each language; use short similar-language groups only for a stated language goal, then dissolve them
rows.if: Multilingual learners, or a dual-language class

rows.basis: untested proposal; from the earlier page (participation alongside peers, strengths shown)
rows.change: Keep them in mixed groups for shared tasks, with a role matched to a strength (reader, builder, timekeeper, presenter of a drawing); give targeted support in short similar-need sessions that others also join; check unaided work orally or by doing where literacy blocks writing
rows.if: Learners with disabilities, low confidence or low literacy

rows.basis: untested proposal; contingent support is shown one-to-one only ([Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support.](claims/contingent-scaffolding-improves-learning.md) [~M])
rows.change: One similar-need group with the teacher per segment while the rest work in mixed groups with roles and self-checkable tasks; rotate which group meets the teacher across the week; whole-class reteach when more than half share a gap
rows.if: One teacher, many learners (30 or more), or a class of about 50

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Spend the minutes on the similar-need group the last check identified, not on circulating; give mixed groups a printed task card with roles, criteria and an answer check; collect one individual item from everyone for the next check
rows.if: Scarce facilitator time: a volunteer, a busy shift, a tutor who checks in for a few minutes

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Do not split groups by location by default: put remote learners in mixed groups with a shared document and one in-room member who reads the work aloud, or make one remote group with its own facilitator; for phone-only learners, use text-based roles and a short checkable item at the end
rows.if: Mixed mode: some learners remote, some in the room; or phone-only

rows.basis: untested here; individualised routing is modelled in [Adaptive Learning](principles/adaptive-learning.md)
rows.change: Replace live regrouping with branching: a short check routes each learner to a support module or an extension; asynchronous discussion groups are assigned by the course for mixing, and change each unit
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, no live teacher

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: No regrouping cycle is possible: run a two-minute opening check, one similar-need group with the teacher for 15 minutes while others work in mixed pairs, and an individual exit item; do not claim regrouping effects
rows.if: One session only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep one grouping format per session: 3–5 minutes check or recap, 10–12 minutes in groups, 3–5 minutes individual check; regroup only between sessions
rows.if: A fixed short time budget (for example 20 minutes a session)

rows.basis: untested proposal; the formative-evidence step rests on [Assessment for learning improves achievement](claims/assessment-for-learning-improves-achievement.md) [+M]
rows.change: Keep that routine and its categories; change only what the evidence here says matters: groups formed from a recent check on the task, membership reviewed at a set interval, an individual check at the end
rows.if: The brief names its own grouping routine, categories, criteria or rubric (its own station rotation, reading levels, competency list or check-in)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Form groups from task evidence only; never display levels or reasons; let the learner choose whether to tell peers why they are in a session; keep the placement log to the teacher
rows.if: Placement data are private or sensitive (diagnoses, test scores, immigration or family circumstances)

rows.basis: untested proposal; individual accountability as in [In school studies, cooperative and peer-learning methods that reward groups on every member's individual learning raised achievement more than methods without such rewards](claims/cooperative-learning-group-rewards-and-individual-accountability.md) [+M]
rows.change: Keep the whole task in one mixed group from start to finish; pull members out briefly into similar-need sessions for a component skill, then return them; assess each member's part and the whole
rows.if: A whole-task performance or product for a real audience (a project, an exhibition, a client report)

rows.basis: criterion rather than rank: [Fish pond effects: above-norm students became more likely to fail algebra when their skills were low relative to classroom peers after sorting](claims/fish-pond-effects-increase-failure-above-norm.md) [~M] (grades in sorted Chicago algebra classes); the rest untested
rows.change: Judge readiness only on individual unaided checks, never on group products, and against fixed criteria rather than a learner's rank in the group; ensure support groups end with the same item types as the assessment
rows.if: High stakes or an unaided final assessment

rows.basis: [Above-norm students in heterogeneous classrooms with supported below-norm classmates gained .4 additional test score points post-policy](claims/above-norm-score-gains-peer-ability-spillover.md) [+M]; [Average test scores are higher when classes are sorted by skill, driven by large learning gains for high-skilled students and slightly lower scores for low-skilled students](claims/sorting-raises-test-scores-via-high-skill-gains.md) [~M] (the trade-off on test scores); [Policy effects on grades and failure rates differed by incoming ability: most below-norm students' grades improved slightly, but the very lowest-ability students' algebra grades declined](claims/double-dose-effects-vary-by-initial-ability.md) [~M]; all one Chicago ninth-grade algebra policy; flexible grouping within sorted classes is untested
rows.change: Prefer a mixed core class plus an added support period or session for those the check identifies, rather than separate classes; where sorting is fixed by policy, run flexible similar-need and mixed groups inside each class, grade against criteria rather than class rank, and watch the lowest class's climate
rows.if: The school sets or streams classes by attainment, or the brief proposes ability classes for the subject

rows.basis: [Learning By Teaching Improves Tutor Learning](claims/learning-by-teaching-improves-tutor-learning.md) [+M]; in mixed algebra classes, stronger students gained more on the test when weaker classmates were getting added support ([In one Chicago study, above-norm students' post-policy algebra test gains were partly explained by higher peer ability and by having classmates who took support algebra](claims/above-norm-score-gains-peer-ability-spillover.md) [+M]), though sorting also raised high attainers' test scores ([Average test scores are higher when classes are sorted by skill, driven by large learning gains for high-skilled students and slightly lower scores for low-skilled students](claims/sorting-raises-test-scores-via-high-skill-gains.md) [~M]); the concern itself is in [Cooperative learning has drawbacks including slow learners depending on fast achievers, so teachers should stress both cooperative and individual work](claims/cooperative-learning-versus-individual-endeavors.md) [~W] (opinion)
rows.change: Use explaining roles and individual checks so contribution is visible; show the tutor-gain evidence; keep some extension groups
rows.if: Teachers or parents resist mixed groups because high achievers "carry" others

rows.basis: untested; [Active learning improves exam performance](claims/active-learning-improves-exam-performance.md) [~S] is a course-level average that does not separate novices; the guidance limit for novices is on [Active Learning](principles/active-learning.md). In one calculus study, prior achievement and the major taken in senior high school both predicted conceptual understanding in both flipped variants, and the peer-teaching advantage did not depend on either ([Prior achievement level affects calculus conceptual understanding, and PTFC outperforms CFC across achievement levels…](claims/prior-achievement-affects-conceptual-understanding.md) [~M]; [Senior high school majors' background affects calculus conceptual understanding and self-efficacy…](claims/majors-background-affects-outcomes.md) [~M]): weaker starters ended lower under either flip, which no unflipped arm tests
rows.change: Keep the first explanation live, or use a worked-example video with a pause-and-try item after each step; flip only the later, more practised topics; give the opening check before any independent application
rows.if: Learners are `novice` on the topic and the material has many interacting parts

rows.basis: [Flipped classroom learning improves academic performance of undergraduate health professional students…](claims/flipped-classroom-improves-academic-performance-hpe.md) [+M] (44 studies, low certainty, I² = 98%); Only a minority of flipped-classroom studies in health professional education are RCTs… [~M]; [Both flipped and AI-enhanced flipped classrooms achieve higher in-class question accuracy than the traditional classroom](claims/flipped-models-higher-question-accuracy.md) [+W] (three pharmacology cohorts, 68 international students, in-class accuracy, no effect size)
rows.change: Flip with the most confidence here, since this is the setting the one direct test covers; still check preparation, keep most live time for application, and record home time, because the pooled studies varied widely and most were not randomised
rows.if: Learners are undergraduates in a health-professions programme (medicine, nursing, pharmacy and the like)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Make pre-class material a short brief or a reading, and use the session for cases, disagreement and their own examples; drop the note-taking guide and the recap
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` on the topic, or professionals updating practice

rows.basis: untested; [Contingent scaffolding…](claims/contingent-scaffolding-improves-learning.md) [~M] (fourth and fifth graders, one-to-one tutoring) supports the circulating teacher, not the flip
rows.change: Do not set pre-class video as homework; run the exposure in class at a station or as a short whole-class video, then move to guided practice with the teacher circulating ("faux-flipped")
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary age)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep pre-class work to 10 minutes or less on a phone, tied to a task they will do in the session; use the session for practice on their own work tasks; do not penalise missed preparation, run a 5-minute catch-up at the start instead
rows.if: Learners are `adult` in a work setting (`workplace-clinical`), preparing between shifts

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Prefer video with captions and a one-page glossary to reading; add one easy item early in the opening check; let learners show understanding by doing before explaining; make the check private
rows.if: Learners have low confidence or low literacy, or study in a second language

rows.basis: untested; the access constraint is from the earlier page
rows.change: Keep each pre-class item under 5 minutes, downloadable and readable on a phone; give the same material as a printed page; schedule in-class time for those who could not access it
rows.if: Learners have unreliable access, or a phone only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Give remote learners the same opening check in the same tool; put remote learners in their own breakout group with a named facilitator rather than mixing one remote learner into a room group; route the teacher's circulation through the breakouts on a fixed timetable
rows.if: Mixed modes: some learners join remotely while others are in the room

rows.basis: untested proposal; see the [Blended Learning pattern](patterns/blended-learning.md) for the online part's self-regulation
rows.change: Run the check as a poll, application in small breakout rooms with shared documents the teacher can see, and the teacher visiting rooms in turn; keep total screen time per session to what was there before
rows.if: The live session is online (`online-instructor-led`)

rows.basis: [Active learning improves exam performance](claims/active-learning-improves-exam-performance.md) [+S] (held across class sizes, largest in small classes); [Peer-teaching flipped classroom students show higher calculus conceptual understanding…](claims/ptfc-beats-cfc-conceptual-understanding.md) [+M] (two intact classes; the procedure is not described on the claim page)
rows.change: Use the opening check as a poll, pairs or small groups for application, and whole-class feedback on the commonest error, then go to groups still stuck; trained peer teachers or assistants can extend the circulation
rows.if: One teacher with a large group (100+)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Put the feedback into the materials: answers and worked solutions after each pre-class question and each in-class item; let the facilitator spend their minutes only on learners who failed the opening check
rows.if: Scarce facilitator time: a volunteer, a busy shift, a tutor who checks in briefly

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Do not flip; give 10 minutes of exposition in the session, then application with feedback and an exit item
rows.if: Only one session, with no time before it

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Fit to it: 15 minutes pre-class (one short video, two questions); in session 5 minutes check, 5 clarification, 40 application, 10 exit and next step; cut topics before cutting application time
rows.if: A fixed short time budget (for example a 60-minute workshop with 15 minutes of preparation)

rows.basis: untested; [Time-on-task is frequently unequal…](claims/time-on-task-unequal-in-active-learning-comparisons.md) [~M] for the time budget
rows.change: Keep it; change only what the evidence speaks to: make its first item a check on the pre-class material, make sure most of the live time is application, and keep total home time within budget
rows.if: The brief names its own routine (its own pre-class quiz, worksheet, readiness test or discussion protocol)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use them for the opening check, the in-class tasks and the exit item; do not substitute this page's items
rows.if: The brief gives its own categories, criteria or rubric

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: The learner controls who sees it; the opening check asks only about the shared content; in class, learners choose what to bring
rows.if: Pre-class work includes private or sensitive material (reflections on practice, personal experience)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep the task whole in the live sessions: pre-class work supplies only the knowledge the task needs, and each session advances the whole task with feedback, rather than splitting it into paper items
rows.if: The course ends in a whole-task performance or a product for a real audience (a presentation, a client case, a performance)

rows.basis: untested; [Active learning improves exam performance](claims/active-learning-improves-exam-performance.md) [+S] (gateway STEM courses, lower failure under active learning)
rows.change: Keep the opening check low stakes; judge readiness only on unaided exit items; record who did the preparation and who did not, and offer the catch-up route before the exam
rows.if: Stakes are high (a licensing exam, a gateway course)

rows.basis: untested; see [Active Learning](principles/active-learning.md) on lecture and information acquisition
rows.change: A flip adds little; give the information directly (in writing, or a short talk) and use any live time for questions
rows.if: The goal is information acquisition alone (a factual update, a policy change)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep that structure: put the pre-class check where the brief puts it and give the application or simulation the session the brief names; change only the pre-class dose, what the opening minutes check, and how peers support each other when facilitator cover is thin
rows.if: The brief fixes its own session structure (two short sessions a week, a retrieval check before class, a simulation in one session)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Make the pre-class material printable or downloadable once on school wifi (one page or a 5–8 minute clip), or do the first exposure in the first 10 minutes of class (an in-class flip); keep both practical application and a structured discussion in the live time, each with its own task
rows.if: Learners have little or no home internet, or lessons are short

rows.basis: [Assessment for learning improves achievement](claims/assessment-for-learning-improves-achievement.md) [+M]
rows.change: Run the elicit–interpret–adjust cycle within or between units, not only at the end of a course, and plan for a small gain
rows.if: School classes (`pre-k-12`), with achievement on unit tests as the goal

rows.basis: [Feedback improves learning, varying with its information](claims/feedback-improves-learning.md) [+M]; [Feedback works best at task and process levels](claims/feedback-most-effective-at-task-and-process-levels.md) [~M]
rows.change: Add information about the task and how to improve it to what goes back to the learner; a verdict or praise alone carries little
rows.if: The check will produce only right/wrong scores or a grade

rows.basis: [Self-assessment accuracy is low without training](claims/self-assessment-accuracy-is-low-without-training.md) [~M]; [Prior knowledge needed for accurate self-assessment](claims/prior-knowledge-needed-for-accurate-self-assessment.md) [~M]
rows.change: Do not treat the self-rating as the evidence; pair it with a short aligned task, and show a worked model of self-assessment before relying on it
rows.if: The responses that count will be learners' ratings of their own understanding, and the learners are new to the domain

rows.basis: [Self-assessment improves self-regulated learning](claims/self-assessment-improves-self-regulated-learning.md) [+M]; [Rubric-referenced self-assessment improved work](claims/rubrics-improve-student-work.md) [~M]
rows.change: Share the criteria or rubric before the attempt and have learners self-assess a draft they can still revise; expect a small effect on strategy use, and watch for added stress
rows.if: Learners should take part in judging their own work

rows.basis: [Peer assessment improves performance](claims/peer-assessment-improves-performance.md) [+M]; [Structured criteria are not shown to improve peer assessment](claims/peer-assessment-structured-criteria-improve-learning.md) [~M]
rows.change: Add peer review so that each learner gets more feedback than the teacher alone can give; a fixed script is optional
rows.if: A large class with one teacher, and written work

rows.basis: [Contingent scaffolding improves learning](claims/contingent-scaffolding-improves-learning.md) [+M]
rows.change: Adjust the help after each response: less after success, more after failure, rather than a fixed level of support
rows.if: One-to-one tutoring or small groups

rows.basis: [Formative assessment implementation barriers](claims/formative-assessment-implementation-barriers.md) [~W]; [OpenSciEd grading expectations constrain formative practice](claims/openscied-formative-assessment-feasibility-challenges.md) [~W]
rows.change: Keep the elicitation ungraded and separate from the grade, so that partial understanding can show
rows.if: The checks will carry marks, or grading rules reward only final scores

rows.basis: [Diagnostic review gave larger writing gains](claims/diagnostic-review-larger-writing-gains.md) [+W]; [High-level feedback should remain human](claims/high-level-feedback-remains-human-responsibility.md) [~W]
rows.change: Use the scoring as a diagnosis that the teacher reviews with the learner before revision, and keep feedback on reasoning and synthesis with a person
rows.if: Software or AI will score drafts (for example, essays)

rows.basis: [Retrieval practice improves retention](claims/retrieval-practice-improves-retention.md) [+M]
rows.change: Make the check a recall attempt and follow it with the correct answer; recheck after a delay
rows.if: The goal is retention over weeks

rows.basis: [Formative-assessment-based learning analytics show positive effects](claims/formative-assessment-la-positive-effects.md) [+W]
