rows.change: Build the checks into the materials with automatic feedback, and give learners a next action for each result
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, with no teacher reading responses

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Offer a private, low-stakes response channel and compare its answers with the public ones before deciding what the silence means
rows.if: Learners stay silent or guess on checks

rows.basis: untested proposal; from the earlier page (creative answers depend partly on knowing the objects)
rows.change: Teach or revisit the content first; keep generation to 5 minutes on concrete objects they know; give two or three example answers of different kinds after the first round, not before
rows.if: Learners are `novice` in the content

rows.basis: [Concrete reward increases children's mean ideational fluency](claims/concrete-reward-increases-mean-ideational-fluency.md) [~M] (fifth graders: reward per idea raised idea counts in the session, so a reward-free design trades some output for interest); process focus for young children is from the earlier maker-assessment page, untested
rows.change: Short rounds (3–5 minutes), oral or drawn ideas collected by the teacher, play-like prompts, no grades on creative work, process and portfolio rather than product
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary age)

rows.basis: [Anonymous real-time sharing mitigates evaluation apprehension](claims/anonymity-mitigates-evaluation-apprehension.md) [+W] (undergraduates, authors' account, carried to work teams untested)
rows.change: Use problems from their own work; run silent individual generation before discussion so seniority does not set the agenda; collect ideas anonymously; converge against the team's own criteria
rows.if: Learners are `adult` professionals, in a workplace setting

rows.basis: [Think first, ChatGPT later group more original on the later unassisted task](claims/regulated-ai-outperforms-independent-originality.md) [+M]; [Free ChatGPT use gains vanish when assistance is removed](claims/chatgpt-free-use-originality-gains-vanish-unassisted.md) [+M] (university students, one experiment); [LLM access boosts individual story creativity while homogenising output across writers](claims/llm-access-homogenises-creative-output.md) [~W] (reported second-hand from one study of writers); [Prototype generation is the only GenAI activity associated with perceived loss of creativity or ownership](claims/prototype-generation-linked-ownership-loss.md) [~W] (design students' survey, self-report; brainstorming with AI was not associated with it); [Overreliance on AWE may lower learners' critical thinking and creativity](claims/awe-overreliance-lowers-critical-thinking-creativity.md) [-W] (a theme in a review, no statistic)
rows.change: Require a first list of the learner's own ideas (or a first draft) before the tool is opened; then use the tool to extend or challenge that list; keep the making of the prototype or product with the learner; where variety across the class is the point, look at the spread of the whole class's ideas, not only each learner's best; judge readiness on a later task done without the tool
rows.if: Generative AI or an automated writing-feedback tool is available, or the setting is `online-self-paced`

rows.basis: [Primary studies report possible benefits of GenAI for children's divergent thinking, narrative creativity and creative self-efficacy, without confirmed efficacy](claims/genai-possible-benefits-children-creative-thinking.md) [~W] (a scoping review of 22 small, heterogeneous studies; none in the wiki separates assisted from unassisted performance in children)
rows.change: As above, and treat any benefit as unestablished: keep the AI step short and after the child's own ideas, and check what the child produces without it
rows.if: Generative AI is used with `child` learners

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Collect every idea through one channel everyone can use (a shared board or poll that works on a phone), with names hidden from peers; read ideas aloud for those on audio
rows.if: Mixed modes: some learners remote, some in the room, some phone-only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Individual silent generation on cards or a poll, then pairs merge lists, then the class sees a sample; the teacher's role in generation is only to keep judgement out and to ask the assumption question to stalled groups
rows.if: One teacher with a large group

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Put the prompt, the time limit, the "no judging yet" rule and the convergence criteria on a card learners run themselves; spend the facilitator's minutes on the convergence step only
rows.if: Facilitator time is scarce (volunteers, a busy shift, one brief check-in)

rows.basis: untested proposal; the program evidence here ran three weeks ([Short-term creativity interventions can be effective](claims/short-term-interventions-change-creativity.md) [+W])
rows.change: 5 minutes content reminder, 6–8 minutes silent generation, 3 minutes sharing, 10 minutes converging on one idea and improving it once; report idea counts and the improved idea, not a gain in "creativity"
rows.if: A single session only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep the proportions: about a third generating, a sixth sharing, the rest converging; cut the number of prompts to one rather than shortening each phase
rows.if: A fixed short time budget (for example 20 minutes inside a lesson)

rows.basis: [Expected tangible rewards reduce later free-choice engagement, while verbal praise does not](claims/rewards-undermine-intrinsic-motivation.md) [~S] (praise did not undermine engagement; carried to creative tasks untested); anonymity: [Anonymous sharing mitigates evaluation apprehension](claims/anonymity-mitigates-evaluation-apprehension.md) [+W]
rows.change: Accept spoken, drawn or acted ideas; collect them anonymously; begin with a prompt about everyday objects where any answer is legitimate; praise the number and variety of ideas, not their cleverness
rows.if: Learners have low confidence or low literacy, or fear being wrong in front of others

rows.basis: [Grading practices can diminish interest and reduce quality of thinking in maker education](claims/grading-harms-maker-education-outcomes.md) [+W] (argument, not a test)
rows.change: Grade the content at its own time; make the creative segment explicitly ungraded, or grade a portfolio of the process with a rubric that scores process, understanding and product separately; never grade single ideas from generation
rows.if: The course is graded throughout, or stakes are high

rows.basis: [Expected tangible rewards reduce later free-choice engagement](claims/rewards-undermine-intrinsic-motivation.md) [~S]; [Reward effects hold across individual creativity tasks](claims/reward-effects-hold-across-individual-tasks.md) [~M] (children, idea counts only)
rows.change: Drop rewards for merely taking part in creative activities learners enjoy; if a reward is kept, tie it to producing ideas and expect a higher count during the session, not lasting interest
rows.if: The plan uses points, badges or prizes for creative work

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep the audience out of the generation phase; bring audience criteria in at convergence; one critique round after a first full draft, then revise once
rows.if: The product is for a real audience (an exhibition, a client, a published piece)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: The learner decides who sees each idea and draft; generation stays in the learner's own space; share only what they choose at convergence
rows.if: The material is private or sensitive (personal stories, a journal)

rows.basis: untested proposal (wave lessons: replacing a brief's own routine lost)
rows.change: Use them at the convergence step as given; do not show them during generation; add only the separation of generation from judgement
rows.if: The brief names its own rubric, criteria or categories (a maker rubric, a design brief's criteria, the learners' own categories)

rows.basis: untested proposal; AI step: [Think first, ChatGPT later](claims/regulated-ai-outperforms-independent-originality.md) [+M]
rows.change: Keep the routine; change only what the evidence speaks to: one protected generation step without comments, and own ideas before AI
rows.if: The brief names its own routine (its brainstorm template, design cycle or check-in)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Do not break it into separate creativity exercises; build the generate-then-judge split into each stage of the whole task (ideas, then choose; prototype, then critique)
rows.if: The brief wants a whole-task performance kept whole (a design project, a performance piece)

rows.basis: [A 50-minute metacognitive strategy instruction produced positive effects on fluency, flexibility and originality](claims/strategy-instruction-improves-divergent-thinking.md) [+M] (Grade 11, two cohorts at one school, against a regular brainstorm lesson; carried to adults and other subjects untested)
rows.change: Teach generating strategies explicitly in one lesson before more open-prompt practice, and have learners check their own lists against the strategies (categories covered, distance from the first idea)
rows.if: Learners already brainstorm often and their ideas have stopped getting more varied, or they are `adolescent` or older and new to creative tasks in this subject

rows.basis: [Unconscious thinkers outperform conscious thinkers and immediate responders in selecting their most creative idea](claims/unconscious-thought-improves-most-creative-idea-selection-exp1.md) [+M] (university students, laboratory, one paper with a replication; carried to classrooms untested)
rows.change: Put an unrelated activity or a break between generating and choosing; do not ask for the choice straight after the list, and do not replace the gap with on-the-spot deliberation
rows.if: Learners must pick their own best idea (a project to develop, an entry to submit)

rows.basis: [Stepwise constructive-conflict guidance reduced new idea generation](claims/stepwise-conflict-guidance-reduces-idea-addition.md) [-M] (novice interaction designers, AI agents, one experiment)
rows.change: Leave room for the learner's own reflection before step-by-step critique, or expect fewer new ideas in the next version
rows.if: Feedback during revision is structured step by step (by a teacher, tool or AI agent)

rows.basis: [AI-mediated feedback in hands-on exhibits](claims/ai-mediated-feedback-in-hands-on-exhibits-improves-learning-and-engagement.md) [~M] (grade-2 children, one museum exhibit on stability; mixed-age families untested)
rows.change: Make the first loop a two-to-five-minute action with no reading; add a responsive predict–show–explain cycle where the outcome can be sensed; put the depth in optional later levels
rows.if: A museum or science-centre exhibit, visited once, families or mixed ages

rows.basis: [Choice-rich infrastructure](claims/choice-rich-infrastructure-supports-productive-deviation-and-learning.md) [~M] (one studio, two sixth graders, an extreme case; shows what is possible, not how often)
rows.change: Protect it from grading; stock a leveled challenge library and shared tools; train facilitators to observe and route help to peers; follow the arc across sessions above
rows.if: A recurring in-school block learners must attend but may spend as they choose

rows.basis: [Moderate agency in game-based learning](claims/moderate-agency-better-learning-outcomes.md) [~W] (second-hand report of one game study: moderate agency beat none and high); [connectivist courses](claims/connectivist-courses-student-agency-problems.md) [~W] (open online courses, second-hand: not all could direct themselves). Both carried to this setting
rows.change: Keep the first action wordless; narrow the choice to two or three challenges at first; offer a worked starter project to copy and change; let a facilitator or peer start alongside
rows.if: Learners are `novice` in the topic, or have low confidence or low literacy

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Point them straight to the open or highest level and to the tools for building their own; invite them to be the peer expert for a challenge
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` or long-standing enthusiasts

rows.basis: [AI-mediated feedback in hands-on exhibits](claims/ai-mediated-feedback-in-hands-on-exhibits-improves-learning-and-engagement.md) [~M] (median grade 2)
rows.change: Use the responsive cycle on contrasting cases before open building; keep explanations as a short menu to choose from, not free writing
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary age)

rows.basis: untested proposal; no claim here tests adults in free-choice settings
rows.change: Start from a problem the learner brings from work or their hobby; offer resources and peers to ask rather than a sequence; agree with the learner what a finished project looks like
rows.if: `adult` learners in work settings or hobby communities

rows.basis: [AI-mediated feedback in hands-on exhibits](claims/ai-mediated-feedback-in-hands-on-exhibits-improves-learning-and-engagement.md) [~M] (explanation posttest and unguided building task, same day)
rows.change: Add feedback on that idea inside the activity (prediction, result, chosen explanation, contrasting cases), then fade to open building; check with one unaided task at the end
rows.if: The goal is understanding a particular idea, not only engagement

rows.basis: [Field trips and middle-school science scores](claims/field-trips-small-positive-science-score-effects.md) [+M] (New York City, six years of school data, small effects); [effects largest for Hispanic and lunch-eligible students](claims/field-trip-effects-largest-hispanic-frpl-students.md) [~M] (same study)
rows.change: Treat a visit as a small addition, not a replacement for science teaching; expect the largest gains for students with least access otherwise; record which students went and how often
rows.if: A school is sending classes on field trips to raise science achievement

rows.basis: [Expected tangible rewards and free-choice engagement](claims/rewards-undermine-intrinsic-motivation.md) [~M] (laboratory experiments; the flat-rate moderator comes from one meta-analysis and is unchecked); [grading in maker education](claims/grading-harms-maker-education-outcomes.md) [+W]
rows.change: Keep any grade off taking part; if credit is needed, give it as a flat amount for participation rather than per piece of output, and give feedback on what the learner made
rows.if: The institution requires grades, credits or points

rows.basis: [Low-income schools and test prep](claims/low-income-schools-test-prep-crowds-out-interest-activities.md) [~W] (a theoretical commentary on US schools)
rows.change: Protect the block explicitly in the timetable and say what it is for; do not justify it by test-score gains it has not been shown to produce
rows.if: The school is under heavy test-preparation pressure

rows.basis: [Well-defined tasks and accessible materials](claims/well-defined-tasks-and-accessible-materials-support-shared-creative-influence.md) [~M] (one group of four, a museum architecture workshop)
rows.change: Give a well-defined goal and materials everyone can handle; watch whether ideas are taken up on merit or overridden socially, and step in when one voice is shut out
rows.if: Groups of adolescents work at one table or exhibit

rows.basis: untested proposal; from the folded STEAM page
rows.change: Make the exhibits answer the learner themselves (step 4); route help to peer experts first; limit the adult to brief check-ins with those stuck for about ten minutes
rows.if: One facilitator for many learners, or scarce facilitator time (volunteers, floor staff on a busy shift)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Put the challenge library and tutorials online and phone-readable; let remote learners share their products to the same repository and ask peer experts in a shared chat; keep the first action possible without special hardware
rows.if: Mixed modes: some learners join remotely or on phones only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: One exhibit or challenge, a guided first loop then open building, and a one-minute look back; record dwell time and what learners could explain; do not claim lasting interest
rows.if: Single session only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Five minutes' welcome and choice, about 30 minutes at one or two chosen exhibits, five minutes' look back, five minutes' slack; do not try to cover the floor
rows.if: A fixed short time budget (for example a 45-minute visit slot)

rows.basis: [Choice-rich infrastructure](claims/choice-rich-infrastructure-supports-productive-deviation-and-learning.md) [~M] (the two students' games were uploaded publicly and downloaded; one case)
rows.change: Provide a public place to share (a repository, a showcase evening) and let learners choose whether to share; record downloads or visitors as a signal, not a grade
rows.if: Learners' products go to a real audience

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: The learner decides who sees it; sharing is opt-in; facilitators do not display work without asking
rows.if: Private or sensitive material (a personal project, family history, identity work)

rows.basis: untested proposal (wave lessons)
rows.change: Keep them; change only what the evidence says matters here: no grade on taking part, a response to each attempt, a look back at the end
rows.if: The brief names its own categories, routine, rubric or criteria (its own check-in, challenge levels, evaluation form)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Do not split it into worksheets or items; check progress by what the learner can show and explain at the project
rows.if: The brief wants a whole project or performance kept whole (a game, a build, a show)

rows.basis: [Universal classroom management](claims/universal-classroom-management-reduces-problem-behavior.md) [~M] (12-study meta-analysis, K–12 classrooms; universal practices without functional information)
rows.change: Do not start individual assessments; put universal management in place first (taught routines, clear expectations, frequent positive contact), then reassess which learners still stand out
rows.if: The whole class is disruptive, not one learner

rows.basis: untested proposal; the only functional-analysis claim here is one 4-year-old in a feeding programme ([escape and attention](claims/inappropriate-behavior-maintained-by-escape-and-attention.md) [+W])
rows.change: Rely on adult observation and family interview, not the child's report; use a picture card or gesture as the replacement response; keep consequences immediate and the reinforcer frequent; check sleep, hunger and illness first
rows.if: Learner is a young `child` (preschool or early primary)

rows.basis: [Self-monitoring of on-task behavior](claims/self-monitoring-improves-on-task-behavior.md) [+M] (single-case studies, grades 4–12, students with or at risk for disabilities; behavior, not achievement)
rows.change: Interview the learner as a main source of trigger information; agree the replacement with them; add self-recording of on-task behavior from week 4 or so
rows.if: Learner is an `adolescent` (about grade 4 and up)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Drop the IEP and parent steps; ask the person directly what makes the session hard (shift fatigue, a task they cannot read, being put on the spot); agree the change with them privately; document only what the organisation's policy requires
rows.if: Learners are `adult`s in a work setting or adult education

rows.basis: untested proposal; from the strategy pages (rare behavior cannot be sampled)
rows.change: Do not wait to observe a pattern; put a safety plan in place and refer to a behavior specialist; record each incident in full
rows.if: The behavior is dangerous, or rare but severe

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use a tally sheet with three columns (time, activity just before, what followed) during the two lessons where the behavior is worst, for one week; test one trigger change in the second week
rows.if: One teacher with a full class, no support staff

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Cut recording to a three-question card after each incident (when, what just before, what the learner got), and replace the two-weekly meeting with a five-minute weekly look at the cards by one named person
rows.if: Scarce adult time (volunteers, a busy shift, one tutor checking in briefly)

rows.basis: [Greetings at the door](claims/positive-greetings-at-the-door-improve-engagement.md) [+M] (middle-school classes, carried to a single session it did not test); the rest untested
rows.change: Do not attempt an assessment; use antecedent defaults: greet each learner by name at the door, give instructions one step at a time, show a way to ask for help or take a short break, and pass a note on what happened to the regular teacher
rows.if: Only one session (a cover teacher, a one-off workshop)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Add connection, camera, noise at home and screen size to the environmental trigger list; record from chat and platform logs as well as observation; give remote learners a private channel (direct message) as the help or break request
rows.if: Mixed modes (some learners remote, some in the room; or phone-only)

rows.basis: untested proposal; the plan is an agreement among teacher, professionals, learner and parents (earlier page), and US guidance holds that changes to an IEP go through the IEP process ([IEP processes protect due process](claims/iep-processes-due-process-protections.md) [+W], asserted guidance, not a finding)
rows.change: Keep the existing plan; record against it; bring proposed changes to the team and the family rather than changing it alone
rows.if: The learner has an IEP or a behavior plan

rows.basis: untested proposal; see [Check In Check Out](strategies/check-incheck-out.md) and [Daily Behavior Report Cards](strategies/daily-behavior-report-cards.md)
rows.change: Keep the routine; add one functional check (does the reward or attention the routine gives match what the behavior was getting?) and change only what the check shows, for example the timing of the check-in to just before the known trigger
rows.if: The brief names its own routine (a point sheet, a daily behavior report card, check-in/check-out, a class reward chart)

rows.basis: [Expected tangible rewards](claims/rewards-undermine-intrinsic-motivation.md) [~M] (two meta-analyses of experiments, mostly laboratory tasks; they disagree on size; stronger for children)
rows.change: Use specific praise and the natural payoff (help, a break, time on a chosen task) instead; if tangible rewards are needed, tie them to meeting a standard and fade them
rows.if: The plan is to reward the learner with prizes for an activity they already enjoy

rows.basis: [Empathic discipline](claims/brief-intervention-empathic-discipline-cuts-suspensions.md) [+M] (middle-school math teachers; suspensions; overall effect small and marginal in the preregistered replication, larger for previously suspended students)
rows.change: Present the record and the hypothesis; agree consistent, pre-planned consequences; offer teachers a short empathic-discipline exercise
rows.if: Staff or the school want harsher consequences or exclusion

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Make the replacement response non-verbal (a card, a gesture, a signal); interview through the family or an interpreter; treat unclear instructions as a likely instructional trigger
rows.if: Learners with low literacy, a language barrier or limited communication

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Hypothesise escape from being seen to fail; offer a rehearsal with one adult first, then a small group, then the audience; allow an alternative format while that builds
rows.if: The behavior occurs when the learner must perform for others (reading aloud, presenting, a public performance)

rows.basis: [Low fidelity](claims/tkss-fidelity-ancova-interaction-problem-behavior.md) [~W] and [teacher fidelity](claims/tkss-fidelity-ancova-interaction-problem-behavior.md) [~M] (one study, 37 students with emotional disturbance in self-contained classrooms, no control group)
rows.change: Coach the adults on the plan in the classroom and check, at each review, whether each step was done as written before judging the plan
rows.if: Staff carrying out the plan have little training

rows.basis: [Worked examples between rounds, puzzle game](claims/worked-examples-improve-problem-solving-strategy-transfer-in-a-puzzle-game.md) [~M]; tested with university students, untested with children
rows.change: Add one or two worked examples or a modelled round before unaided play and again between rounds; keep game controls minimal
rows.if: Learners are `novice` on the target task

rows.basis: [Board-game study](claims/number-board-games-improve-numerical-knowledge.md) [+M]; [guided play](claims/play-based-learning-improves-outcomes.md) [~W] (guided play, not games specifically); in K–8 STEM games beat conventional teaching on average ([STEM meta-analysis](claims/games-stem-moderate-positive-effects-cognition-motivation-behaviour.md) [+M], cognition g = .67)
rows.change: Use a simple game whose board or move *is* the representation (e.g. a numbered linear track); an adult plays alongside naming the numbers or quantities; four sessions of 15–20 min over two weeks
rows.if: Learners are preschool or early-primary `child`ren

rows.basis: [School level](claims/school-level-moderates-game-cognitive-effects.md) [~M] (K–8 STEM: secondary pupils gained less than primary, difference g = −0.67, 12 against 28 studies; why is not established)
rows.change: Expect a smaller gain than with primary pupils; keep the game to the one move that carries the target, pair it with taught content and a debrief (step 6), and check the outside-game task before committing more time
rows.if: Learners are `secondary`-school students

rows.basis: [Supplement, not standalone](claims/simulation-games-as-supplement-not-standalone.md) [+M] and [unlimited access](claims/unlimited-access-enhances-simulation-game-learning.md) [+M] (simulation games in training, pooled); the whole-task argument behind building around one job decision is untested
rows.change: Build the game around one job decision with real consequences in its rules; use it as one part of a training programme, not the whole of it; leave it open for repeated voluntary play; debrief against the real procedure; keep competition optional
rows.if: Learners are `adult` or professionals in a `workplace-clinical` setting

rows.basis: [Active comparison](claims/active-comparison-instruction-reverses-simulation-game-advantage.md) [~M] (simulation games: d = −.19 against active instruction, d = .38 against passive, d = .61 against none)
rows.change: Keep the active teaching; add the game alongside it only for a reason other than a learning gain (access, practice volume, interest), and check the outside-game task
rows.if: The game would replace active non-game teaching of the same content (practice with feedback, discussion, problem solving)

rows.basis: [Kahoot! and outdoor games with migrant children](claims/game-based-practice-outperforms-traditional-l2-vocabulary-instruction.md) [+W] (confounded); [adventure game with supplementary material](claims/adventure-games-supplementary-material-vocabulary.md) [+W] (second-hand); [long-term vocabulary retention](claims/dgbl-long-term-vocabulary-retention.md) [+W] (a meta-analysis known only through a later review, no effect size)
rows.change: A quiz or practice game is a reasonable vehicle; add glosses or supplementary word material inside it, and test recall a week later, not only at the end of play
rows.if: The goal is `verbal-association` (vocabulary, facts)

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page
rows.change: Make the core move the reasoning itself; add a debrief and one non-game transfer task; expect slower gains than for facts
rows.if: The goal is a `concept`, `principle` or `complex-skill`

rows.basis: [DragonBox vs Lynnette](claims/intelligent-tutor-lynnette-outperformed-dragonbox-on-test.md) [~W]; [entertainment value did not moderate learning](claims/entertainment-value-does-not-moderate-simulation-game-learning.md) [~M]; games raised motivation over conventional K–8 STEM teaching on average (g = .51, [STEM meta-analysis](claims/games-stem-moderate-positive-effects-cognition-motivation-behaviour.md) [+M])
rows.change: Measure enjoyment and the capability separately; do not report one as the other; a game can win on the first and lose on the second; do not buy entertainment value expecting more learning
rows.if: The goal is `attitude-motivation` (interest, confidence)

rows.basis: [Player configuration](claims/single-noncompetitive-play-largest-effects.md) [~M] (single competitive play g = −0.06 against non-game conditions); [after controls](claims/single-noncompetitive-play-largest-media-effects.md) [~M]
rows.change: Make individual non-competitive play the default; if competition is wanted, use team scores built from each member's learning ([Gamification](principles/gamification.md), step 5) rather than individual head-to-head play
rows.if: The brief wants competition, a leaderboard or head-to-head play

rows.basis: untested proposal; the tested child gains had an adult present
rows.change: Put the modelling, hints and debrief questions inside the game (a worked example screen between levels, a "why did that work?" prompt after each level); log attempts per level to find where learners stall
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: [Sessions](claims/multiple-sessions-benefit-single-session-null.md) [+M] (single-session games g = 0.08, not different from non-game conditions; total minutes unrelated to effect); the single-session plan itself is an untested proposal
rows.change: Use one short game round, a worked example, a second round and a debrief; do not expect a gain over non-game teaching; if `days-weeks` are available, spread play over several sessions rather than lengthening one
rows.if: Time is a `single-session`

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page
rows.change: Do not grade the in-game score unless its measurement has been designed for that ([Assessment Mechanic](elements/assessment-mechanic.md)); assess on an aligned external task
rows.if: Stakes are high or the game feeds a grade

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page
rows.change: Choose a mechanic with no timing or precision demands beyond the target; offer a paper or board version; read text aloud or reduce it
rows.if: Devices, motor demands, reading load or disability limit access

rows.basis: [Rewards claim](claims/rewards-undermine-intrinsic-motivation.md) [~S] and [overjustification claim](claims/rewards-undermine-intrinsic-motivation.md) [~S] (lab tasks, free-choice time; carried to courses)
rows.change: Do not attach expected points, prizes or badges to doing or finishing it; give informational feedback and a progress view only
rows.if: Learners already find the task interesting, or practise it voluntarily

rows.basis: untested here: the rewards claim's Discussion argues there is little interest to undermine, but no recorded entry tests uninteresting tasks; the [overjustification claim](claims/rewards-undermine-intrinsic-motivation.md) [~S] reports less undermining for well-defined tasks with a clear standard
rows.change: Points for accuracy and improvement are reasonable; set a clear quality standard for earning them; plan the week without points (step 8)
rows.if: The task is a dull, necessary drill (fact fluency, verb forms, keyboard practice)

rows.basis: [Rewards claim](claims/rewards-undermine-intrinsic-motivation.md) [-S] (tangible rewards more detrimental for children than college students, lab); [praise claim](claims/feedback-praise-reduces-learning.md) [~M] (fifth graders)
rows.change: Prefer verbal, informational feedback and effort-focused badges to tangible prizes; avoid prizes for completion; no public individual ranking
rows.if: Learners are `child`ren (under 12)

rows.basis: [Seductive details](claims/seductive-details-effect.md) [~M] (school and university readers, not gamified); [cognitive overload](claims/cognitive-overload-degrades-learning.md) [~M]
rows.change: Strip theme, animation and decoration from the screen while items are worked; celebrate only between levels
rows.if: Learners are `novice`s, or the material is complex

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Let them test out of early levels on the step 4 check; give harder challenge levels rather than more points on easy items
rows.if: Learners are `advanced`, or already accurate

rows.basis: untested proposal; the earlier page's view that adults prefer progress views to badges has no claim behind it
rows.change: Tie levels to job tasks passed at a criterion; no badges for completion or seat time; no public ranking among colleagues; keep the theme sober
rows.if: `adult`s in a `workplace-clinical` setting (compliance, onboarding)

rows.basis: [Mangomon app, 21 Thai undergraduates](claims/mangomon-rpg-gamification-improves-business-vocabulary.md) [+W] (pre-post, no control); [Quizizz](claims/quizizz-gamification-better-memorization.md) [+W] and [mixed-methods study](claims/gamification-raises-motivation-satisfaction.md) [+W] (both known only through one review)
rows.change: A quiz or points layer is a reasonable vehicle; test recall a week after the last session, not only in the app
rows.if: Goal is `verbal-association` (second-language vocabulary, terms)

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page (timed leaderboard formats reward speed and suit fluency more than reasoning)
rows.change: Award points for correct explanations and for solving changed problems, not for speed; avoid timed, speed-ranked quiz rounds
rows.if: Goal is a `concept`, `principle` or `complex-skill`

rows.basis: [Group rewards on individual learning](claims/cooperative-learning-group-rewards-and-individual-accountability.md) [+M] (school studies, four weeks or more, not gamified)
rows.change: Use team scores from individual quizzes (step 5), updated once a week on a class board; the teacher reviews the board, not every point
rows.if: `classroom` with one teacher and a large group

rows.basis: untested proposal; the meta-analysis pooled informal and online settings with school ones
rows.change: The software must give the informational message after each item (step 3) and run the level checks (step 4); if streaks are used, allow a missed day without losing the streak, so one absence does not end practice
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Run all scoring and feedback through one tool every learner reaches the same way; make teams mixed across room and remote; avoid speed-ranked live rounds, which penalise slow connections and small screens
rows.if: Mixed modes: some learners remote, some in the room, or phone-only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Automate points, feedback and level checks; the facilitator spends about five minutes a week on the team or progress board and contacts learners whose practice stopped
rows.if: Scarce facilitator time (volunteers, a busy shift, a tutor who checks in briefly)

rows.basis: untested; no claim here tests a single gamified session
rows.change: Do not build a points economy; at most one team quiz round with feedback after each question and a short debrief; do not claim a motivational effect
rows.if: Time is a `single-session`

rows.basis: untested proposal; the earlier page's warning that leaderboards demotivate low-ranked learners has no claim behind it
rows.change: No public ranking; self-referenced progress only; badges and messages short, with icons and audio; first level designed so everyone succeeds
rows.if: Learners have low confidence or low literacy

rows.basis: untested; noted in the [autonomy claim](claims/autonomy-supports-intrinsic-motivation.md) [~W]'s Discussion with no study recorded
rows.change: Offer two options with a recommended default rather than an open menu
rows.if: Learners are uncomfortable choosing (some high power-distance settings, anxious novices)

rows.basis: [No performance gap by competitive preference](claims/no-competitiveness-difference-kahoot-performance.md) [~W] and [enjoyment stable over eight rounds](claims/kahoot-enjoyment-stable-across-groups-and-time.md) [~W]; in-game scores predicted the first course quiz only for students who liked competition, and no later quiz ([Kahoot–quiz relationship differed by competitiveness only on quiz 1](claims/quiz1-kahoot-moderation-competitiveness.md) [~W]) (one undergraduate course, associational, no non-competitive comparison)
rows.change: Use it for low-stakes review: ungraded, feedback after each question, run across the term rather than once; do not read in-game scores as the capability, and check it with a separate quiz
rows.if: A live competitive quiz round (Kahoot-style) is wanted for review in a course

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page (effects weaker in high-stakes settings, no claim behind it)
rows.change: Keep points formative and separate from the grade; grade on an aligned task outside the game
rows.if: Points or badges feed a grade, or stakes are high

rows.basis: [Rewards claim](claims/rewards-undermine-intrinsic-motivation.md) [~S]; [group rewards on individual learning](claims/cooperative-learning-group-rewards-and-individual-accountability.md) [+M]; the combination is untested
rows.change: Keep it; change only what the evidence says matters: give points for accuracy and improvement rather than attendance or completion, add an informational sentence to each award, and base any team score on each member's learning
rows.if: The brief names its own routine (house points, a class reward chart, an existing app's XP or streaks)

rows.basis: [Process goals for novices](claims/process-goals-outperform-outcome-goals-for-novices.md) [+M]; tested with high-school writers, untested in other domains
rows.change: Novices: process goals naming the strategy steps, split into proximal sub-goals, outcome goals only once the process runs unprompted. Experienced learners: outcome goals with a stated criterion, which they may set or negotiate (learner-set goals are an untested proposal)
rows.if: Learners are `novice` on the task (new procedure, first attempts); or `intermediate`/`advanced`

rows.basis: [Goal setting improves performance](claims/goal-setting-improves-performance.md) [~M] (smaller on complex work tasks, not learning tasks)
rows.change: Expect a smaller effect from goal difficulty; prefer learning or process goals for the components over a hard overall score target; monitor strategy use, not only the score
rows.if: Goal is a `complex-skill` (whole task, many interacting parts)

rows.basis: [Specific, difficult goals](claims/specific-difficult-goals-lead-to-higher-performance.md) [+W]; work-task evidence, untested for learning
rows.change: A specific numeric target with frequent progress checks is reasonable (e.g. "18 of 20 items correct on Friday's check")
rows.if: Goal is facts or a `procedure` with a clear score

rows.basis: untested proposal; the self-monitoring evidence is from students in grades 4–12 with or at risk for disabilities and measures on-task behaviour, see [self-monitoring](claims/self-monitoring-improves-on-task-behavior.md) [~M]
rows.change: Teacher sets the goal with the child, one proximal sub-goal at a time, made visible on a chart; monitor with a simple tally or check-in rather than a written plan
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary age)

rows.basis: [Implementation intentions](claims/implementation-intentions-improve-goal-attainment.md) [+M]; mostly university students and online-course adults
rows.change: Elicit the learner's own goal first and tie the task goal to it; add an if-then plan for the named obstacle (work, family time)
rows.if: `adult` or `adult-workplace` learners

rows.basis: [Implementation intentions](claims/implementation-intentions-improve-goal-attainment.md) [~M] (course completion rose for learners in individualist cultures, not collectivist)
rows.change: Build goal setting and an if-then plan into the first session (a short writing activity); show progress against the goal on every return; do not expect the prompt to help every learner
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use one shared goal template and peer or self check-ins against the criterion; teacher reviews goals only for learners whose progress stalls
rows.if: Large class, one teacher

rows.basis: untested proposal; proximal goals evidence is [second-hand](claims/proximal-goals-feedback-peer-models-build-learning-efficacy.md) [+W]
rows.change: Set one proximal goal for the session and one check at its end; skip multi-week goal sheets
rows.if: Time available is one session

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Do not grade goal attainment itself; grade the learning outcome, keep goals as the learner's own tool, so learners do not set easy goals to secure a mark
rows.if: High-stakes assessment or graded goals

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page; [self-efficacy predicts persistence](claims/self-efficacy-predicts-academic-persistence.md) [~W] is associational and does not test this move
rows.change: Start with a goal the learner judges reachable, show early success, then raise difficulty; give feedback on progress, not on the person
rows.if: Low self-efficacy or a history of failure on the task

rows.basis: [Graphic Organizers Support Novice Comprehension](claims/graphic-organizers-support-novice-comprehension.md) [~M] (in five studies each, low-ability learners gained from maps and high-ability learners did not; underpowered subsets); [Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows.](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M] (a review, not tested on organizers)
rows.change: Drop the provided organizer; ask learners to sketch their own quickly, or use none; spend the time on application
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` on this material, or already explain its structure

rows.basis: [Story Mapping Improves Comprehension](claims/story-mapping-improves-comprehension.md) [+M] (third and fourth graders; 22 and 6 students; no standardized effect size)
rows.change: Use a story map (setting, characters, problem, goal, events, resolution), taught by modelling, leading and then testing; withdraw the map once accuracy holds
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary age) reading stories, including learners with learning disabilities

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page and its sources on adult literacy writing, which no claim records
rows.change: Use a planning organizer matched to the genre (claim–reasons–evidence for argument, a sequence for narrative), modelled, then used before each draft, then dropped once the plan can be made in note form
rows.if: Learners are `adult` literacy learners, and the goal is writing

rows.basis: [The same quizzing or concept-mapping activity produces more learning when done without viewing the material](claims/closed-book-versions-of-quizzes-and-concept-maps-outperform-open-book-versions.md) [+M] (second-hand); [Concept mapping improves learning over most comparison conditions by a moderate average amount, but not over time-matched retrieval practice](claims/concept-mapping-improves-learning.md) [~S] (with time matched, mapping beside the text lost to retrieval practice at one week, undergraduates)
rows.change: After comprehension, have learners build or complete the organizer with the text closed, then check against the text; or replace some mapping time with free recall
rows.if: Goal is `delayed-retention` of the content

rows.basis: [Learner-constructed graphic organizers are not shown to outperform provided ones: the one direct test, with college readers, favoured provided organizers on transfer](claims/learner-constructed-graphic-organizers-outperform-provided.md) [~M] (college readers, three experiments; transfer favoured provided organizers)
rows.change: Give a complete, author-built organizer with the text rather than asking for construction; add explanation prompts on its links
rows.if: Goal is `conceptual-understanding` or transfer from a demanding text, with novice readers

rows.basis: [Adding relevant pictures or graphics to text improves learning from it, with a small pooled effect on reading comprehension, though whether dual coding explains the benefit is disputed](claims/dual-coding-improves-learning.md) [+M] (graphics added to text helped reading comprehension, elementary to adult; carried to organizers, which it did not isolate); the reveal-and-compare step is untested
rows.change: Place the organizer next to the text it summarises (not on a separate page); give partial organizers with a reference version revealed after the learner submits; add one explanation question per organizer
rows.if: Setting is `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: [Teacher-student interactive semantic mapping produced higher EFL reading comprehension posttest scores than teacher-initiated and student-mediated semantic mapping](claims/interactive-semantic-mapping-outperforms-teacher-initiated-and-student-mediated.md) [+M] (EFL university students); [Collaborative concept mapping enhances learning more than individual concept mapping](claims/interactive-beats-constructive-concept-mapping.md) [+W] (second-hand)
rows.change: Have pairs build the organizer together; collect a few, project two that differ, and discuss which fits the content better and why
rows.if: `classroom` with a large group

rows.basis: [Teacher-student interactive semantic mapping produced higher EFL reading comprehension posttest scores than teacher-initiated and student-mediated semantic mapping](claims/interactive-semantic-mapping-outperforms-teacher-initiated-and-student-mediated.md) [+M] (187 Egyptian EFL freshmen, 20 one-hour sessions)
rows.change: Build a semantic map of the text with the class before and during reading, the teacher drawing out students' contributions, over many sessions
rows.if: Learners read in a second language

rows.basis: untested proposal; construction costs time and load ([Placing heavier cognitive demands on learners can be counterproductive in mapping tasks](claims/heavy-cognitive-demands-of-mapping-can-be-counterproductive.md) [~W])
rows.change: Provide one organizer with the material, one completion task and one explanation prompt; do not ask for construction from scratch; record what an unaided check shows and do not claim retention
rows.if: Time is one session only

rows.basis: [A hierarchical organization facilitates tasks only when matched to the task domain](claims/organization-task-match-determines-benefit.md) [~M] (20 high-school physics students); [Recall from bar graphs is more accurate when the recall format matches the studied graph format](claims/mismatched-graphic-organizers-increase-extraneous-load.md) [~M] (bar graphs, university students; carried to organizers)
rows.change: Do not force a template: use a sparse outline, or two organizers for two relations; align the organizer with the relation the assessment asks about
rows.if: The content has no single clear structure, or the assessment asks about a different relation than the organizer shows

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Judge readiness only on tasks done without the organizer; keep the organizer as a study and planning tool, not something that must be reproduced
rows.if: Stakes are high, or the assessment is unaided

rows.basis: untested; mechanism from [Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units.](claims/chunking-reduces-working-memory-load.md) [+M] (memory research, not organizer design)
rows.change: Split it into an overview of about five nodes and one linked view per branch; reveal branches as they are taught
rows.if: A dense organizer already exists (a course map, a 30-node concept map)

rows.basis: [Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows.](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M] (review of cognitive-load studies; gives no crossover point)
rows.change: Drop most guided rounds; give one check item, then independent or whole-task practice with selective feedback
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` on this task, or succeed on the first item unaided

rows.basis: Child: [Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support.](claims/contingent-scaffolding-improves-learning.md) [+M] (fourth and fifth graders, long division, 8 per condition). Adult: untested proposal
rows.change: Child: keep the cue–hint–demonstration ladder with one-to-one or small-group checking, and short rounds. Adult or professional: ask what they already do, and move guided items onto tasks from their own work as soon as the step is stable
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary age), or `adult` / professionals

rows.basis: [In one experiment with 256 undergraduates, computer-based lesson versions that included practice produced significantly higher posttest scores than versions without practice](claims/practice-presence-raises-cbi-posttest-achievement.md) [+M] (undergraduates, one computer-based lesson; horizon not reported)
rows.change: Build practice items with automatic checking and feedback after each item into the lesson; do not cut them to save time; add an unaided check item before the next topic
rows.if: Setting is `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: [Taking initial multiple-choice tests without feedback can lead students to later produce the incorrect lure answers they selected](claims/multiple-choice-lures-can-be-learned-as-false-knowledge.md) [+W] (college students, retrieval testing, reported second-hand; untested for skill practice)
rows.change: Give the correct answer and a short reason after every item, so a chosen wrong option is not kept
rows.if: Practice items are multiple choice

rows.basis: untested proposal; contingent-support evidence is one-to-one and its classroom-scale effect is not shown ([Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support.](claims/contingent-scaffolding-improves-learning.md) [~M])
rows.change: Have every learner show each attempt at once (mini-whiteboards, cards, a quick poll) so the teacher can scan them all; give whole-class feedback on the commonest error, then go to those who still fail. With older learners, pairs can also check each other against a worked answer; with young children, or when one misconception is widespread, the teacher's scan is safer than peer checking. Collect one unaided item from everyone before independent work
rows.if: `classroom` with one teacher and a large group

rows.basis: [Human tutoring has a medium effect over no tutoring, and in one small study students learned as well when tutors only prompted them as when tutors also explained and gave feedback](claims/tutoring-effectiveness-comes-from-scaffolding-and-feedback.md) [~M] (eighth graders, 11 tutor–student pairs: prompting without feedback learned as well)
rows.change: Replace some feedback-giving with prompts that ask the learner to explain or predict the next step; include one changed item in each round
rows.if: Goal is a `concept`, `principle` or transfer, not only a `procedure`

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Plan the session as model, three or four guided items, one unaided check; record what the check shows and do not claim retention
rows.if: Time is one session only

rows.basis: untested proposal; no claim sets a success rate for skill practice (a retrieval-practice moderator, [Retrieval practice effects become more robust as initial retrieval success increases, especially above 75%](claims/retrieval-practice-effects-more-robust-when-initial-retrieval-success-exceeds-75-percent.md) [~M], is about recall)
rows.change: Failing: return to the model or simpler items. Succeeding unaided: shorten or end guided practice. Set the threshold locally and record it
rows.if: Many attempts fail with help, or nearly all succeed without it

rows.basis: untested proposal; from the earlier page ("multiple steps, hidden decision points, or a high likelihood of early error")
rows.change: Plan more guided rounds per step; raise the release criterion (more consecutive unaided successes, on representative tasks); add a stage of unassisted work under supervision before full independence; define what "working alone" means (no supervision, or supervision with a way to escalate)
rows.if: The task has many steps or hidden decision points, or an error on the job is costly (safety, compliance, harm to a client)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Judge readiness only on unaided items, never on assisted success during practice; keep a record of every hint given
rows.if: Stakes are high, or the assessment is unaided

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page (adult literacy and numeracy settings)
rows.change: Keep the language of practice items simpler than the target task; let learners show a step by doing it before explaining it; gloss terms the objective does not include
rows.if: Instruction is in the learners' second language, or learners have low literacy

rows.basis: [Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows.](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M] (cognitive-load review; gives no crossover point); [Signaling Improves Learning](claims/signaling-improves-learning.md) [~S] (in one eighth-grade field study, signals linking text and pictures harmed high-prior-knowledge learners)
rows.change: Give a blank template or headings only, or no aid; drop marks and organizers that repeat what they can already see; keep only glosses for terms they do not know
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` on this material, or already find the essential points unaided

rows.basis: Pictures: [Adding relevant pictures or graphics to text improves learning from it, with a small pooled effect on reading comprehension, though whether dual coding explains the benefit is disputed](claims/dual-coding-improves-learning.md) [+S] (the meta-analysis found the effect regardless of grade level). Blanks and modelling: untested
rows.change: Shorter aid (one side), fewer blanks (three to five per section), pictures beside the words they illustrate, and the teacher models filling the first section aloud
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary age)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Make the aid a job aid in the learners' own categories and order of work, usable at the task, with one step per line and the decision points marked; keep it after training rather than withdrawing it if the task is rare or errors are costly
rows.if: Learners are `adult` in a work setting (procedures, compliance, equipment)

rows.basis: Pictures: [Adding relevant pictures or graphics to text improves learning from it, with a small pooled effect on reading comprehension, though whether dual coding explains the benefit is disputed](claims/dual-coding-improves-learning.md) [+S], carried to low-literacy adults and health information it did not test separately. The rest: untested; from the earlier page's sources (Osborne 2006 on health visuals; Mellar et al. 2004 on adult literacy)
rows.change: Plain wording, one idea per line, a picture or icon beside each key instruction, larger type, and an oral walkthrough of the aid; check understanding by asking the reader to say or show what to do, not by a written test
rows.if: Learners have low literacy or low confidence in reading (adult literacy, health information for patients)

rows.basis: [Earlier meta-analyses, as reported second-hand, find that glosses improve L2 vocabulary learning and that text-and-picture glosses outperform single-mode glosses](claims/glossing-medium-large-effects-l2-vocabulary.md) [+M]; [Proficiency moderates gloss effects: vocabulary benefits appear at Levels 2 and 3 but not Levels 1 and 4](claims/proficiency-moderates-gloss-vocabulary-effects.md) [~M]; [Learners hold positive attitudes toward glosses, but their perceptions of which gloss type works best do not match measured performance](claims/gloss-perceptions-mismatch-performance.md) [~M] (EFL university readers; vocabulary outcome)
rows.change: Add first-language glosses beside new terms, with a picture where the term names something visible; do not assume learners know which gloss helps them
rows.if: Learners read in a second language

rows.basis: [Prompting learners to self-explain improves understanding and problem solving on immediate tests by a moderate average amount, with little evidence yet on delayed or classroom gains.](claims/self-explanation-improves-conceptual-understanding.md) [+S] (immediate tests)
rows.change: Replace some blanks with "why" and "how does this connect" prompts; add one organizer showing the argument's structure
rows.if: Goal is understanding an argument or `concept`, not only locating facts

rows.basis: [Guided Notes Improve Note Accuracy](claims/guided-notes-improve-note-accuracy.md) [+S] (both entries read from abstracts; no effect size)
rows.change: Use a guided-notes handout: the lecture outline with blanks for key terms and points, filled during the lecture; collect or check one section
rows.if: Setting is a lecture or video, `postsecondary` or school

rows.basis: [Students in courses with guided note-taking and other active learning activities reported less difficulty with motivation and engagement after the shift online](claims/guided-note-taking-supported-remote-engagement.md) [+W] (focus groups in 28 STEM courses; self-report). Phone format and mixed mode: untested
rows.change: Give one single-column online guide that reads on a phone: section headings that match the reading, short prompts, fillable blanks or a form; the same file for everyone, so remote and in-room learners work from one version; ask remote learners to submit one completed section
rows.if: Setting is `online-self-paced`, or mixed (some learners remote, some in the room, some on phones)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Give a reference version of the completed aid to compare against after learners finish their own, and spend the teacher's time only on the one or two points most learners missed
rows.if: One teacher with a large group, or scarce facilitator time (volunteers, a busy shift)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: One aid of one side: 2 minutes orientation, 20 minutes reading and filling the aid, 5 minutes on one "why" prompt with a partner, 3 minutes comparing with the reference; no withdrawal plan, and do not claim retention
rows.if: Time is one short session (for example 30 minutes)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep it, and use its categories as the aid's headings; change only what the evidence says matters: mark fewer things, cut decoration, add one "why" prompt
rows.if: The brief names its own routine, template, rubric or categories for the aid (a department note template, a reading-log form, a checklist)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep the aid as a reference beside the whole task rather than splitting the task into worksheet items; the aid lists the steps or criteria, and the learner performs the task as a whole
rows.if: Learners will use the aid in a whole-task performance the brief wants kept whole (a presentation, a procedure on real equipment, a product for a real audience)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: The learner keeps the completed aid and decides who sees it; checks use a separate, non-personal item
rows.if: The aid would hold private or sensitive material (health information, learners' own notes about themselves)

rows.basis: [Highlighting shows low utility for improving learning outcomes](claims/highlighting-low-utility.md) [-M] (learner highlighting, review); [In one experiment, students who generated their own underlining did not score significantly higher on tests than students given experimenter-generated underlining](claims/experimenter-underlining-effective-as-student-underlining.md) [~M] (one nonsignificant difference, not equivalence)
rows.change: Mark only the essential points; if learners do the marking, follow it with a task that makes them use the marks (explain, answer, summarize)
rows.if: A teacher is tempted to highlight much of the text, or to ask learners to highlight as their study activity

rows.basis: [Learner-constructed graphic organizers are not shown to outperform provided ones: the one direct test, with college readers, favoured provided organizers on transfer](claims/learner-constructed-graphic-organizers-outperform-provided.md) [~M]
rows.change: For readers of a textbook passage, start with a provided organizer and ask learners to explain or extend it; move to building their own once the provided form is familiar
rows.if: The brief wants learners to build their own organizer instead of receiving one

rows.basis: [The problem-based group achieved significantly larger content-knowledge gains, while the simulation group made no knowledge gains](claims/problem-based-larger-knowledge-gains.md) [+M] (54 seventh and eighth graders, one 4-week trial); the shift across weeks is untested
rows.change: Weight early sessions toward the knowledge-serving method (about 20 of 45 minutes), shifting to application later; check knowledge before handing over
rows.if: Learners are `novice` on the content (low baseline on both knowledge and application)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Skip most of the knowledge-serving method; give the time to application, with one short knowledge re-check
rows.if: Learners are `advanced`, or already pass the knowledge check

rows.basis: [The participatory simulation group achieved significantly larger application gains than the problem-based group](claims/simulation-larger-application-gains.md) [+M]; [Problem-based learning shows null or negative effects on basic knowledge acquisition but positive effects on conceptual understanding and transfer relative to direct instruction](claims/pbl-null-basic-knowledge-positive-transfer.md) [~M] (a synthesis of meta-analyses; no pooled effect printed)
rows.change: Give the application-serving method (simulation, problems, communicative tasks) the larger share, with scaffolds and a process framework, and keep a short knowledge segment
rows.if: The target is application or `near-transfer`, not only knowledge

rows.basis: [Pairing Contextual Encounters With Explicit Instruction Produces Stronger Vocabulary Outcomes Than Either Alone](claims/pairing-contextual-encounters-with-explicit-instruction-produces-stronger-vocabulary-outcomes-than-either-alone.md) [+M]; [Combining intentional and incidental vocabulary learning produces greater gains and better retention than either mode alone](claims/combined-intentional-incidental-greater-gains.md) [+M] (93 Chinese university students, reported second-hand)
rows.change: Pre-teach a small set of word meanings, then give several encounters with them in reading or listening, rather than either alone
rows.if: The target is vocabulary

rows.basis: [Systematic phonics outperforms unsystematic or no-phonics instruction on children's reading overall…](claims/phonics-instruction-outperforms-whole-word-for-generalization.md) [~S] (contested by one review); [Balance Whole Language And Phonics](claims/balance-whole-language-and-phonics.md) [~W] (an essay); see [Phonics](principles/phonics.md)
rows.change: Keep systematic phonics whole as the decoding strand; add whole-text reading and literature around it, and watch individual pupils for those it does not reach
rows.if: Beginning readers (`child`, early grades)

rows.basis: [Communicative Approach introduced to China in the 1990s was initially not very communicative](claims/clt-china-1990s-initial-weak-adoption.md) [~W] (a historical account); the split is untested
rows.change: Keep form practice for what the exam tests; add short communicative tasks (pair talk of 5–10 minutes) rather than replacing the traditional method
rows.if: A foreign language taught where the exam tests grammar and classes are large

rows.basis: [Mead Rapid Change Obsoletes Knowledge](claims/mead-rapid-change-obsoletes-knowledge.md) [+W] (Mead's argument as reported); untested as a design
rows.change: Pilot the new method alongside current practice on one component; add monthly sessions where colleagues pass on what is new; let adults bring their own cases into the application half
rows.if: `adult` learners in work settings, or teachers adopting a reform

rows.basis: [Mixed Homogeneous Heterogeneous Grouping](claims/mixed-homogeneous-heterogeneous-grouping.md) [+W] (an essay); grouping policy in [Flexible Grouping](principles/flexible-grouping.md)
rows.change: Similar-attainment groups for reading instruction; mixed groups for discussion; re-form both from recent work
rows.if: A mixed reading class, and discussion is part of the goal

rows.basis: [cooperative learning with group rewards on each member's learning](claims/cooperative-learning-group-rewards-and-individual-accountability.md) [+M] (school studies; carried here to the balance between group and individual work)
rows.change: Keep groups, but test each member individually and recognise groups on members' gains; add some individual work each day
rows.if: Group work where stronger learners may carry weaker ones

rows.basis: [Some blended learning interventions improve student outcomes, but whether a positive effect exists varies across interventions and domains of achievement](claims/blended-learning-effects-vary-by-intervention-and-domain.md) [~M]; the mode split is in [Blended Learning](patterns/blended-learning.md); untested here
rows.change: Put the method that needs live interaction (simulation, discussion) where people are together or synchronous; put the knowledge segment in short self-paced items that work on a phone
rows.if: Some learners remote, others in the room, or phone-only

rows.basis: untested proposal; from the earlier page (the simulation's knowledge outcomes suffered when educators disengaged) and [Gateway math students benefit from a balance of social, active learning and independent practice, but faculty constraints limit active learning](claims/balance-active-learning-independent-practice-gateway-math.md) [~M] (faculty and student views, US college maths)
rows.change: Give live time to the method whose outcomes fell when facilitation lapsed; run the other through self-checking items or courseware; keep the weekly component check to 5 minutes
rows.if: One teacher for many learners, or scarce facilitator time (volunteers, one tutor checking in briefly)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: One component per method: about 15 minutes of the knowledge segment, 25 of application, 5 of a two-item check per component; do not claim the balance worked from one session
rows.if: A single session only, or a fixed short time (say 45 minutes)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Open with the more directive method, short segments, and success on a few items before the open-ended method; read task instructions aloud
rows.if: Learners with low confidence or literacy

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep it as given; use its categories as the components; add only the complementary method the evidence says it misses, for one segment
rows.if: The brief names its own routine, rubric or categories (its own check-in, method, criteria)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep the performance whole as the application half; put the knowledge-serving segment before it, not inside it as separate items
rows.if: The brief wants a whole-task performance or product for a real audience kept whole

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Let the learner choose individual or group work for that part, and who sees it
rows.if: Material is private or sensitive (journals, personal stories)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Give that component's method enough time to meet the criterion first; keep the other method, but do not cut the tested component's time to fit it
rows.if: High stakes, or the assessment covers only one component

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page (Ediger excludes it)
rows.change: Leave it out; it is not one side of a balance
rows.if: A proposed method is harmful (physical punishment, humiliation)

rows.basis: [Spanish use at home does not limit English learning](claims/spanish-home-use-does-not-limit-english-learning.md) [+M]; [tested in Spanish, bilinguals scored higher in kindergarten mathematics](claims/bilinguals-better-math-tested-in-spanish.md) [+M] (Spanish–English children; carried to other languages untested)
rows.change: Develop the heritage language orally through stories and play in it; tell the family to keep using it; assess early mathematics and language in both languages before any judgement
rows.if: Young `child` in pre-kindergarten or early care, family speaks another language at home

rows.basis: untested; every claim here studied children or adolescents in school

rows.basis: [Dual language programs improved English literacy](claims/dual-language-programs-improve-literacy-achievement.md) [+M]; [no significant literacy gain for the English learner subsample](claims/dual-language-literacy-null-for-english-learners.md) [~M]; [allocation drifted to English in practice](claims/english-priority-over-spanish-in-practice.md) [~M]
rows.change: Default to it where staffing allows; measure English learners' outcomes separately; log actual minutes per language each term

rows.basis: untested proposal; the earlier page's requirement of "adult and peer models fluent in the heritage language"
rows.change: Pair learners who share a language for first-talk on hard tasks; supply bilingual texts or glossaries per topic; recruit family or community members to read in the heritage language; keep assessment in both languages through an interpreter for decisions
rows.if: `classroom` with one teacher who does not speak the learners' languages, or many languages in one room

rows.basis: Kohnert subclaim of [the heritage-language hub](claims/heritage-language-preservation-supports-english-acquisition.md) [+M] (bilingual preschoolers); [conversational fluency misread as proficiency led to misdiagnosis](claims/conversational-fluency-misleading-proficiency-indicator.md) [+W]
rows.change: Assess in both languages before referral; separate attrition (loss of a language no longer used) from a disorder present in both; if intervention is needed, deliver it in both languages

rows.change: Decide on academic reading and writing in the school language, not conversational fluency; keep lighter support for a year after exit
rows.if: Deciding when to exit a learner from bilingual or language support

rows.basis: [L1 at no cost to L2](claims/l1-maintenance-supports-l2-without-cost.md) [+M]; [treating the mother tongue as inferior impedes movement between home and school language](claims/mead-mother-tongue-status-affects-bilingual-learning.md) [+W] (an argument, no data)
rows.change: Explain the no-cost findings and the value for parent help with school work; respect the family's decision and record it; avoid any school message that the heritage language is inferior

rows.basis: untested proposal

rows.basis: untested proposal

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep the moves that need little time: families advised to keep the heritage language, one bilingual book bag sent home a week, assessment in both languages only for placement and referral decisions

rows.basis: untested proposal

rows.if: A fixed short time budget per lesson (e.g. 30 minutes)

rows.basis: untested; the logging rests on [allocation drift](claims/english-priority-over-spanish-in-practice.md) [~M]

rows.if: The brief names its own routine (its own home-language survey, language allocation, rubric or entry assessment)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Build the bilingual glossary and the assessment in those categories, not new ones
rows.if: The brief gives its own categories or criteria (a workplace's job terms, a programme's proficiency bands)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: The learner and family decide who learns which languages they speak; do not mark learners publicly; ask in private and keep records to those who need them
rows.if: The learner's language background, immigration or refugee status is sensitive or private

rows.basis: untested; the reading of the score rests on [tested in Spanish, bilinguals scored higher](claims/bilinguals-better-math-tested-in-spanish.md) [+M]
rows.change: Keep heritage-language instruction; add explicit practice in the test's language and format in the weeks before; read a low score as a school-language measure, not a measure of what the learner knows
rows.if: High stakes: a placement or accountability test in the school language only

rows.basis: untested proposal; see [Authentic Audiences and Purposes](principles/authentic-audiences-purposes.md)
rows.change: Let learners produce it bilingually or in the audience's language, kept whole; use the heritage-language version for family audiences
rows.if: A product or performance for a real audience (a family evening, a community publication)

rows.basis: [Part-task practice for novices](claims/part-task-practice-reduces-load-for-novices.md) [~M] (one experiment; sample and horizon not reported); [pretraining](claims/pretraining-improves-transfer.md) [+M] (one VR lesson, carried to other content)
rows.change: Keep the first whole to two or three ideas; pre-teach the one or two elements it depends on in a short isolated segment, then present the whole in the same session; make each later part small

rows.basis: [Expertise reversal](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M] (review of cognitive-load studies, carried to overviews; no crossover point)
rows.change: Replace the overview with the opening sketch; start at the first part they cannot explain; spend the time on integrative tasks
rows.if: Learners are `intermediate` or `advanced` for this content

rows.basis: [Ability moderates the benefit](claims/ability-moderates-hierarchical-organization-benefit.md) [~M] (college physics volunteers); [advance organizers](claims/advance-organizers-improve-learning.md) [~M] (older meta-analyses); the confidence part is untested
rows.change: Add a closing placement every session, a check on the top-level ideas before moving down, extra practice per part; praise correct placements privately

rows.basis: untested proposal; the hierarchy studies used college and advanced high-school students
rows.change: Make the whole concrete (a picture, story or physical model of the whole), keep each part to one lesson, and have the teacher lead the placement aloud before learners do it

rows.basis: untested proposal; [whole-task practice and transfer](claims/whole-task-performance-improves-transfer.md) [+W] is an argument, not a study
rows.change: Take the whole from their own work: the complete workflow or a real case they handle; elicit what they already do and start at the part where their account breaks down

rows.basis: [No effect on local tasks](claims/no-organization-effect-on-local-tasks.md) [~M] (non-significant, not equivalence)
rows.change: Do not build a whole-first sequence; group the items plainly and use retrieval practice

rows.basis: untested proposal; [whole-task practice and transfer](claims/whole-task-performance-improves-transfer.md) [+W]

rows.basis: [Learner-built organisation](claims/strong-acquisition-tasks-improve-internalization.md) [+M] (classroom study, untested online); [concept mapping](claims/concept-mapping-improves-learning.md) [~S] for the redraw; the persistent map is untested
rows.change: Keep the map on every screen with today's part highlighted; make the closing placement an arrange-or-label activity the system checks; add a redraw-from-memory item from the middle of the course

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Share the map as one image everyone can see on a small screen (few labels, large type); do the closing placement as a numbered poll or chat answer ("which of the five ideas does this detail belong to?") so remote and in-room answers are seen together

rows.basis: untested proposal

rows.basis: untested proposal

rows.basis: untested proposal

rows.basis: untested proposal; [whole-task practice and transfer](claims/whole-task-performance-improves-transfer.md) [+W]

rows.basis: untested proposal

rows.basis: [One adult educator's first-person reflection reports that facilitated class discussions left her feeling empowered as an individual contributor](claims/facilitated-self-directed-learning-empowers-adults.md) [+W] (one author's reflection on her own adult classes)

rows.basis: [Positioning personal experience as an epistemic resource supports expansion from inward to outward critical orientations](claims/positioning-personal-experience-as-epistemic-resource-supports-critical-orientation-expansion.md) [+M] (12th grade, single site, no comparison)

rows.basis: untested proposal

rows.basis: untested proposal

rows.basis: untested proposal

rows.basis: untested proposal; the recorded studies ran for months
rows.change: One 90-minute session: 10 minutes own experience, 25 minutes one source, 35 minutes discussion with every view answered, 10 minutes private written stance, 10 minutes on whether anyone wants to act and how; claim no change in critical reflection
rows.if: Single session only

rows.basis: [Critical speculative design pedagogy supports critical consciousness and justice-oriented sensemaking in science](claims/critical-speculative-design-supports-critical-consciousness-in-science.md) [~M] (reports the cut as a constraint, not a tested variable)
rows.change: Keep source and written stance (about 8 and 7 minutes) and give discussion the rest; drop the opening experience round after session 2. One study's sessions were cut from 75 to 28 minutes mid-unit by scheduling
rows.if: A fixed short time budget per session (for example 30 minutes)

rows.basis: untested; [Immigration discussion frequency shows no significant association with critical reflection or sociopolitical efficacy](claims/immigration-discussion-null-critical-consciousness.md) [~M] for not relying on discussion frequency alone
rows.change: Keep it; change only what this page's evidence speaks to: one source per discussion and one private written stance
rows.if: The brief names its own routine (its own discussion protocol, check-in, rubric or template)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Assess with them as given; add no test, quiz or survey the brief did not ask for; if the rubric scores a position taken, add beside it a criterion for reasons given
rows.if: The brief gives its own categories, criteria or rubric for the learners' work

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: The learner decides who sees the written stance (no one, the educator, the group); sharing in discussion is invited, never required; the educator does not read entries the brief says are private
rows.if: Material is private or sensitive (learners' own experience of injustice, immigration status, health)
