rows.basis: [Renewable assignments such as student-created quiz questions transcend classroom boundaries and can ameliorate economic injustice](claims/renewable-assignments-economic-justice.md) [+W] (conceptual argument); release and naming are untested
rows.change: Keep the whole product whole: draft it, take one round of group response, revise once, release it; learners choose whether their name appears
rows.if: The goal is a product or performance for a real audience (a campaign, a public letter, a resource others reuse)

rows.basis: untested proposal; the old page reports ecofascism-adjacent ideals occasionally emerging in students' imagined futures
rows.change: Use the answer, anonymised and with consent, as a compared case beside a systemic account or an alternative future, and ask the group what each assumes
rows.if: Learners produce the kind of answer the course hopes to move past (blaming individuals for a systemic problem; a future resting on violence or exclusion)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Grade reasoning from sources, never agreement with the educator or the side taken; a second marker samples stances for steering
rows.if: Stakes are high (graded, credentialed)

rows.basis: [Narrative and storying genres in educational inquiry risk disempowering the very people they claim to empower](claims/narrative-genres-may-disempower-while-claiming-empowerment.md) [~W] (theoretical argument)
rows.change: Present at least two sourced positions per issue, state your own as one of them, and review the steering log (step 8) at mid-term with the group
rows.if: The educator holds a strong position on the issue

rows.basis: [Feedback after multiple-choice tests halves lure intrusions](claims/feedback-after-multiple-choice-tests-halves-lure-intrusions.md) [~M]
rows.change: Always give the correct answer; immediately after each item or at the end of the set both work
rows.if: Multiple-choice practice or quizzes

rows.basis: [Feedback timing moderates pretesting](claims/feedback-timing-moderates-pretesting.md) [~M]
rows.change: Show the correct answer right after each pretest item; delaying it removed the benefit
rows.if: Pretests on paired associates, such as vocabulary pairs

rows.basis: [Feedback timing moderates pretesting](claims/feedback-timing-moderates-pretesting.md) [~M]
rows.change: Feedback can wait until the end of the set or a later session; with trivia facts the benefit held with delays up to 24 hours
rows.if: Pretests on trivia facts or other material richer in meaning than word pairs

rows.basis: [Incidental vocabulary retention and feedback timing](claims/incidental-vocabulary-retention-problems.md) [~W]
rows.change: Consider delayed rather than immediate feedback; the one reported comparison favoured delay
rows.if: Second-language vocabulary learned from reading

rows.basis: [Corrective feedback effect on L2 development is durable](claims/corrective-feedback-effect-on-l2-development-is-significant-and-durable.md) [+M]; [Teachers favour delayed oral correction](claims/teachers-favor-delayed-ocf-over-immediate.md) [~W]
rows.change: Correct errors (it helps, and the benefit lasts to delayed tests); hold correction to the end of the activity or give it privately where public correction would embarrass
rows.if: Oral correction of second-language errors in class

rows.basis: [Explicit feedback stronger immediately, implicit better maintained](claims/cf-facilitates-l2-grammar-explicit-implicit-durability.md) [~W]; [Recast gains held while metalinguistic gains declined](claims/recasts-more-enduring-than-metalinguistic-feedback.md) [~M]
rows.change: Do not choose the correction type on the immediate post-test: explicit correction leads there, implicit correction (recasts) holds up as well or better later
rows.if: The outcome is a delayed second-language test, not the next lesson

rows.basis: [Timely feedback improves homework learning](claims/timely-feedback-improves-homework-learning.md) [+W]
rows.change: Return scored feedback before the next set, so that errors are not practised; automated scoring makes this feasible
rows.if: Homework or practice sets learners complete alone

rows.basis: [Tutoring systems improve outcomes with immediate actionable feedback](claims/its-improve-learning-outcomes-with-actionable-feedback.md) [+W]; [Immediate elaborated feedback improved programming learning](claims/immediate-elaborated-feedback-improves-programming-learning.md) [+W]
rows.change: Give immediate, elaborated feedback that says what to change at each step
rows.if: A tutoring system or programming exercises

rows.basis: [Self-controlled feedback decided after the trial improves retention](claims/self-controlled-kr-decided-after-trial-improves-motor-retention.md) [~M]
rows.change: Let the learner decide after each trial whether to see the result, rather than fixing the schedule
rows.if: A simple motor skill practised in trials

rows.basis: [Participants preferred post-session debriefing](claims/feedback-timing-post-session-debrief-preference.md) [~W]
rows.change: Debrief after the performance instead of interrupting it; interrupt only for errors that would otherwise be repeated or cause harm
rows.if: A whole performance, such as a simulated clinical consultation

rows.basis: [Immediate knowledge of results has no effect on achievement estimates](claims/knowledge-of-results-no-effect-achievement-test-dimensionality.md) [~W]
rows.change: Showing results item by item does not change the scores; decide on it for learning reasons, not measurement ones
rows.if: Computer-administered tests used to measure achievement

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Choose the timing locally and record it; no claim in the wiki compares immediate with delayed feedback on drafts
rows.if: Writing or projects, with feedback on drafts

rows.basis: untested here; from the brief's statement that reward and emotion systems mature before control systems at these ages ([adolescent brain imbalance](claims/adolescent-brain-imbalance-reward-versus-control.md) [+W], the brief's summary of research, `q2`)
rows.change: Put more of the component into the adults (teachers and carers cue in the moment, structure the setting); keep the youth's practice short and frequent; give emotion regulation a large share
rows.if: Learners are `adolescent`, 11–15

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: The young person names the adult (mentor, supervisor, tutor, peer mentor); the adult's role is coaching on request and a regular short review, not monitoring; skip parents unless the learner asks
rows.if: Learners are young `adult` (18–25), at college or work

rows.basis: [Parent-mediated intervention](claims/parent-implemented-intervention-improves-outcomes.md) [+M] (children with autism, ages 1–6 and school age); [parent coaching](claims/parent-coaching-outperforms-information-only.md) [+M] (ages 0–7). Both outside this page's 14–25 range
rows.change: Train the parent to deliver the practice at home, with coaching and rehearsal; expect larger effects where the parent delivers practice than from information
rows.if: Learners are `child` (under 12), or have autism or another developmental condition

rows.basis: [Empathic discipline](claims/brief-intervention-empathic-discipline-cuts-suspensions.md) [+M] (middle-school mathematics teachers; overall effect small and marginal in the preregistered replication, larger for students at high risk)
rows.change: Add a short exercise on the teachers' stance towards discipline (relationships first, the student's perspective) before or alongside the student programme; track exclusions by group of students
rows.if: Setting is a school `classroom` and the problem is conduct, exclusions or suspensions

rows.basis: [SEL and achievement](claims/sel-programs-improve-behavior-and-achievement.md) [~S] (K–12; academic gains significant only with school-staff delivery; negligible in recent randomised trials); [SRL training](claims/self-regulated-learning-improves-achievement.md) [~M] (larger effects with researchers than with regular teachers delivering)
rows.change: Have the regular teacher deliver or cue the skills inside academic lessons; promise only a small achievement effect; measure achievement on an independent test
rows.if: The goal is academic achievement

rows.basis: untested; from the brief's constraint that carers in chronic adversity have fewer resources for their own regulation and for co-regulation. The brief's stress claim ([toxic stress](claims/toxic-stress-disrupts-self-regulation-development.md) [~W], its summary of research) concerns the young person, not the carer
rows.change: Reduce the carers' stressors and support their own regulation before coaching co-regulation; add a mentor or programme facilitator as a second adult; keep adult sessions practical, short and at times they can attend
rows.if: Carers live with chronic adversity, poverty or overwhelming stress

rows.basis: [Co-regulation implementation](claims/co-regulation-implementation-factors-context-experience-strategy-ease.md) [~W] (facilitators' reports, adolescent programmes: welcoming easiest, breathing exercises hardest; class size and session length shaped use)
rows.change: Spend the adult time on the three or four adults who see the most young people (teachers, house staff); teach one move per session; replace weekly coaching with a 10-minute check on one logged incident; start with the welcoming routine, which facilitators found easiest
rows.if: One facilitator for many young people, or scarce facilitator time (volunteers, a busy shift, a brief check-in)

rows.basis: untested; the claim page on parent coaching says its evidence does not test remote coaching
rows.change: Hold the first adult session live (in person or video) so moves can be rehearsed and watched; run weekly coaching by phone or messaging around one logged incident; send the youth's cue cards as images
rows.if: Mixed modes: some adults remote, some in the room, or phone-only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Spend it on the adults, not only the youth: one own-regulation routine and one co-regulation move, rehearsed; leave a cue card both sides share; do not promise lasting change
rows.if: A single session only

rows.basis: untested; coached practice beat written self-directed materials for parents at post-test ([parent coaching](claims/parent-coaching-outperforms-information-only.md) [+M], ages 0–7)
rows.change: Teach by demonstration and role-play, not handouts; one move per session; let adults log by voice note or a tick; praise what they already do well
rows.if: Adults have low literacy or low confidence

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Make the supervisor the co-regulating adult; fit coaching into existing supervision meetings (10–15 minutes); use the workplace's own incident types as role-play scenarios
rows.if: Adults in a work setting (supervisors of apprentices or trainees, `workplace-clinical`)

rows.basis: untested; [parent coaching](claims/parent-coaching-outperforms-information-only.md) [+M] for rehearsal over information
rows.change: Keep it; train the adults to run that routine and add only what the evidence says matters: rehearsal with feedback and one specific prompt to the young person
rows.if: The brief names its own routine (its check-in, its breathing step, its behaviour card)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use them as the skill names the adults cue and the incident log's categories; do not substitute the programme's
rows.if: The brief has its own categories, criteria or behaviour rubric

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: The young person decides what adults see; adults are coached on their own responses, not given the youth's journal or check-in entries; agree in advance what a teacher or parent will be told
rows.if: Private or sensitive material (feelings, family conflict, a young person's disclosures)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Give minutes: 75 minutes for the first session (own regulation and one move, rehearsed), then six 15-minute coaching contacts; drop content, not rehearsal
rows.if: A fixed short time budget (for example 3 hours of adult time in a term)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep the performance whole; the adult rehearses with the young person a pre-performance routine and a debrief afterwards, rather than splitting the skill into exercises
rows.if: The young person is to use the skill in a whole real performance (a match, a placement, a presentation to a real audience, a job interview)

rows.basis: [Training facilitators](claims/srae-co-regulation-training-increases-self-regulation-knowledge.md) [~W] (gains were in self-reported knowledge only); coaching components [~W]
rows.change: Add an observed or recorded outcome (incidents, attendance, a rated observation) and a record of whether coaching happened
rows.if: Evaluation relies on the adults' or youth's self-report

rows.basis: [Unassisted discovery learns less than explicit instruction; guided discovery does better](claims/minimal-guidance-less-effective-for-novices.md) [+M]; [Enhanced discovery beats other instruction (d = 0.30)](claims/enhanced-discovery-beats-other-instruction.md) [+M]; [Part-task practice reduces load for absolute novices](claims/part-task-practice-reduces-load-for-novices.md) [+M] (one experiment outside inquiry)
rows.change: Teach or model the relation and the move before or alongside the investigation; do not leave essential content to be discovered unaided. Where the apparatus or procedure has many interacting parts, let novices practise the parts before the whole investigation
rows.if: Learners are novices on the target relation or on the inquiry move (designing a fair test, reading a graph)

rows.basis: [Guidance becomes less effective as expertise increases](claims/worked-examples-less-effective-with-expertise.md) [~M] (reviews of worked-example research in [cognitive load theory](theories/cognitive-load-theory.md); carried to inquiry, untested there)
rows.change: Lower the guidance: fewer prompts, no full worked solutions, a more open question; check on an unprompted task that the moves really are secure first
rows.if: Learners already know the target relation and can make the inquiry moves unaided

rows.basis: [Guidance improves inquiry learning outcomes](claims/guidance-improves-inquiry-learning-outcomes.md) [+M]; [Guidance improves performance during the inquiry](claims/guidance-improves-inquiry-performance-success.md) [+M]
rows.change: Add guidance (process prompts, structured steps, feedback, teacher-led explanation phases) while keeping the question with the learners; in a 72-study meta-analysis guidance improved post-inquiry learning (d = 0.50) and what learners achieved during the inquiry (d = 0.71)
rows.if: The brief asks for open, student-led inquiry with little teacher input

rows.basis: [Inquiry-based teaching improves science achievement](claims/inquiry-based-teaching-improves-science-achievement.md) [+M]; [Teacher-guided inquiry outperforms student-led](claims/teacher-guided-inquiry-outperforms-student-led.md) [+M]
rows.change: Use guided inquiry with teacher-led phases and a synthesis that ties findings to the canonical idea; expect a medium average gain over the comparison instruction, larger for teacher-led than student-led inquiry
rows.if: The goal is conceptual understanding in school science

rows.basis: [Guidance improves learners' use of inquiry skills](claims/guidance-improves-inquiry-learning-activities.md) [+M]
rows.change: Guide the inquiry moves while learners make them and assess the moves directly, not only the final answer; the form of guidance mattered less than giving some
rows.if: The goal is inquiry skill itself (planning tests, interpreting data)

rows.basis: [Guidance added to simulation inquiry modestly improves outcomes and inquiry skills](claims/guidance-improves-inquiry-learning-outcomes.md) [+M]; [PAIR-C scaffolding: near-transfer gain, no far transfer](claims/pair-c-scaffolding-shows-mixed-evidence-for-emergent-phenomena-instruction.md) [~W]
rows.change: Build the guidance into the environment (prompts, annotations, feedback); expect near transfer, and do not expect far transfer from one unit
rows.if: The inquiry runs in a simulation or online (`online-self-paced`)

rows.basis: [A remote learner working from photographs completed a correct inquiry cycle, but it was disembodied](claims/remote-case-d-full-cycle-disembodied.md) [~W] (one case)
rows.change: Supply the data (photographs, readings, recordings) so learners can still run the full reason-from-evidence cycle, and add a live discussion for the social part that remote work loses
rows.if: The inquiry runs remotely, without hands-on materials

rows.basis: [AI-assisted inquiry produced larger decision-making gains than inquiry-only and traditional instruction](claims/ai-assisted-inquiry-largest-decision-making-gains-climate.md) [+W] (one secondary climate-change study, no effect size recorded)
rows.change: Use it inside the inquiry (to question, give feedback, help weigh evidence) rather than instead of it, and assess the reasoning without the assistant
rows.if: An AI assistant is available during the inquiry

rows.basis: [Scripted personally meaningful inquiry](claims/scripted-personal-inquiry-associated-with-inquiry-knowledge-gains.md) [~W] (one Year 8 class against a control class that differed at pretest)
rows.change: Script the phases in a shared toolkit so each step is visible across settings; expect minor technical friction; do not read a gain in inquiry decisions as established
rows.if: Learners investigate across classroom, home and field with mobile devices

rows.basis: [Spontaneous real-world events deepened student-directed inquiry](claims/spontaneous-authenticity-in-pbl-deepens-student-directed-inquiry.md) [+W] (one third-grade classroom)
rows.change: Leave room, and permission, for the teacher to depart from the script when a real event bears on the driving question
rows.if: Teachers work from a written inquiry curriculum

rows.basis: [Course-based research experience boundary objects](claims/course-based-research-experience-boundary-objects-support-disciplinary-integration-and-authentic-research-networks.md) [+W]; [Mentored inquiry with staged mechanistic sensemaking](claims/mentored-inquiry-supports-transition-from-intuitive-to-formal-equation-reasoning.md) [+W] (both descriptive case studies, no comparison)
rows.change: Organise it around a shared product whose standards learners negotiate (for example, a paper), connect learners to outside researchers, and budget far more time for interpreting results than for producing them
rows.if: The inquiry is an authentic research project (a course-based research experience or a mentored student project)

rows.basis: [Inquiry discussion distributed authority among third-grade English learners](claims/third-space-distributes-authority-among-students.md) [+W] (one session, no published DOI)
rows.change: Let peers build explanations together in discussion, drawing on all their languages, and check each learner's explanation individually
rows.if: Learners are multilingual or still learning the language of instruction

rows.basis: [Age moderates discovery-learning effects](claims/age-moderates-discovery-effects.md) [-M]
rows.change: Keep guidance high; adolescents lost most from unassisted discovery against explicit instruction (d = −0.53, adults −0.26)
rows.if: Learners are adolescents

rows.basis: [Domain moderates the unassisted-discovery deficit](claims/domain-moderates-unassisted-discovery-deficit.md) [-M]
rows.change: Teach explicitly first; the deficit of unassisted discovery was largest in this domain (d = −0.95). Inquiry outside science is otherwise untested in the wiki
rows.if: The content is verbal or social skills rather than science or mathematics

rows.basis: [Problem-first improves conceptual learning when instruction follows](claims/productive-failure-improves-conceptual-learning.md) [~M]; [PS-I effects are negative for 2nd–5th graders](claims/psi-effect-increases-with-grade-level.md) [-M]
rows.change: Follow the investigation with instruction that builds on what learners produced; judge it on conceptual and transfer outcomes, not procedure; teach first for 2nd–5th graders
rows.if: Learners will investigate before being taught (problem-first)

rows.basis: [Worked examples confer the largest advantage over unassisted discovery](claims/worked-examples-largest-advantage-over-unassisted-discovery.md) [+M]; [Worked examples reduce novice search](claims/worked-examples-reduce-novice-search.md) [+M] (algebra, outside inquiry); [Comparing cases improves learning and transfer (d = .50)](claims/comparing-contrasting-cases-improves-learning.md) [+M]
rows.change: Prefer worked examples or feedback; they showed larger advantages over unassisted discovery than direct teaching did. Contrasting cases to compare, with the principle given after the comparison, are another option
rows.if: The question is which support to give learners who would otherwise work unaided

rows.basis: [Dependent measure moderates discovery effects](claims/dependent-measure-moderates-discovery-effects.md) [~M]
rows.change: Judge guided discovery on post-tests and acquisition scores; on reaction-time measures the comparison conditions came out ahead
rows.if: Success will be judged by how fast learners perform the task

rows.basis: [Inquiry benefits low-income schools, yet resource demands impede scaling](claims/inquiry-benefits-low-income-equity-tension.md) [~W]
rows.change: Budget materials and teacher preparation before scaling; inquiry may benefit these learners most but its resource demands can block equitable roll-out
rows.if: The school is low-income or short of equipment and teacher time

rows.basis: [Pairs worked better than triads in one stellar-populations inquiry](claims/pairs-better-than-triads-in-stellar-inquiry.md) [+W] (instructors' report, not a test)
rows.change: Use pairs rather than threes where the task allows, and check each member's understanding individually
rows.if: Learners investigate in small groups

rows.basis: [Creating community and interacting with students online required deliberate, planned effort unlike spontaneous face-to-face co-presence](claims/online-community-requires-conscious-effort.md) [+W] (interviews with web-based high-school teachers; carried to adult courses); the channel choices are untested
rows.change: Make the forum and private message the main routes with a published reply window of one working day; put live slots outside working hours and record them; accept questions as text or a short voice note
rows.if: `online-instructor-led`, asynchronous, `adult` learners working or caring

rows.basis: untested proposal; the queue-ordering finding ([NSF](claims/nsf-strategy-increases-helped-students-busy-normal-queues.md) [~M]) is from a simulated online office-hours queue, not a mixed room
rows.change: Run one help queue for both groups (a shared ticket list or chat), alternate between room and remote in it, repeat each in-room question aloud and post it with the answer, and give remote learners a turn first after each in-room one
rows.if: Mixed mode: some learners in the room, some joining remotely

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use a text channel that works on a phone (messaging, forum app); never require video for help; send replies as short text with one image at most
rows.if: Learners work on phones only, or have poor bandwidth

rows.basis: [NSF](claims/nsf-strategy-increases-helped-students-busy-normal-queues.md) [+M] and [no strategy changes wait or resolved requests](claims/scheduling-strategy-no-effect-resolved-requests-wait-time.md) [~M] (simulation from one CS2 course's office hours; outcome is who gets help, not learning)
rows.change: Route task questions to a public forum with peer answers first and staff confirming; turn repeated questions into a frequently-asked page weekly; in live help, serve learners not yet helped first and cap each conversation; add staff or sessions when waits grow, since ordering does not shorten them
rows.if: One instructor for many learners (a large lecture course or an open online course)

rows.basis: [The NSF advantage over FCFS appears only above an arrival-rate threshold](claims/arrival-rate-threshold-nsf-advantage.md) [~M] (simulation: under a relaxed queue no ordering made a difference); the scheduling of extra slots is untested
rows.change: Add live slots in the two or three days before a deadline, publish a cut-off time for questions, and post a common-errors note the day before; outside peaks, one slot may be enough
rows.if: Deadline or exam surges

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: State before the end how learners can reach you afterwards, for how long and for what (a two-week reply window by email, say), and collect one question from each learner before they leave
rows.if: A single session only (a workshop, a one-off training)

rows.basis: [Positive teacher–student relationships are associated with greater student engagement and, more weakly, with achievement](claims/teacher-student-relationships-improve-engagement.md) [~M] (correlational meta-analyses, preschool to high school; negative relationships mattered more in primary school); the routines are untested
rows.change: Accessibility means routines in the room: the teacher circulates on a set route, learners have a help signal (a card or cup) so they need not call out, and the teacher holds brief informal talks with each pupil over a fortnight
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary age)

rows.basis: [Belonging Interventions Improve Outcomes](claims/belonging-interventions-improve-outcomes.md) [~M] (college entrants; worked only where the setting afforded opportunities to belong); [Minority students visited the tutoring center more often, yet tutored minority and first-generation students had lower average GPAs](claims/minority-students-more-tutoring-visits-lower-gpas.md) [~W] (one college, associational)
rows.change: Invite each one personally to a first short contact; offer a private route and say that asking is expected, not remedial; follow up by name after the first quiet week; do not read high use of help as proof that the help works
rows.if: Learners with low confidence or literacy, first in family, or with bad past experiences of school

rows.basis: [In one participatory budgeting case, Latino immigrant participation lapsed under outreach with interpretation and was sustained only after the activity structure was redesigned](claims/resolving-participation-double-bind-requires-redesigned-activity-structures.md) [~W] (one case of Spanish-speaking volunteers in civic budgeting committees; carried from civic participation to courses)
rows.change: Offer a route in the learners' stronger language (a bilingual assistant, written questions that can be translated, a separate session) rather than only interpreting into the main channel
rows.if: Learners study in a second language, or the instructor and learners do not share a language

rows.basis: [Tutors and trainee researchers most value supportive attitude, mastery of the research field, and accessibility in a research project supervisor](claims/supervisor-desirable-characteristics-survey.md) [+W] (online doctoral supervision; what people value, not an effect); the arrangement is untested
rows.change: Name the person to ask on each shift or project and a back-up; agree an escalation route for urgent questions and a slower one for learning questions; schedule short regular meetings rather than relying on ad hoc asking
rows.if: Adults in work settings (workplace training, clinical placement, supervision)

rows.basis: [Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support.](claims/contingent-scaffolding-improves-learning.md) [+M] (one-to-one tutoring; not a test of access)
rows.change: Schedule contact (a booked slot or a required check of the first attempt) rather than waiting to be asked, and answer with prompts before explanations
rows.if: Learners are `novice` on the course's tasks

rows.basis: untested proposal (the expertise reasoning is on [Ask Experts](principles/ask-experts.md))
rows.change: Make contact on request and use it for critique of their work and for decisions they are unsure of, not explanation; keep the reply window but drop the required first contact
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` (experienced professionals, final-year students)

rows.basis: [Human embodiment in video: perceived social presence benefits learning ratings, but instructor-face inclusion shows no significant learning-performance difference](claims/human-embodiment-video-presence-effects.md) [~W] (second-hand review; learners rated learning higher, performance did not differ)
rows.change: Spend effort on replies and live contact rather than on putting the instructor's face in every video
rows.if: The course is pre-recorded video and the budget goes on production

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Publish what kinds of help are allowed before assessed work (clarifying the task, not checking answers), give every learner the same access to that help, and log it
rows.if: High stakes for the learner (a licensing exam, a grade that decides progression)

rows.basis: [Interleaving shows positive effects for all visual stimulus types, largest for paintings](claims/interleaving-strongest-for-paintings-visual-materials.md) [+M] (g = 0.67 for paintings, 0.35 for naturalistic photographs)
rows.change: Interleave from the first practice set after one or two examples of each; this is where the evidence is strongest
rows.if: The goal is to recognise or classify visual categories (artists' styles, species, skin lesions, rock types)

rows.basis: [Interleaving benefits are small for mathematical tasks](claims/interleaving-limited-for-math-texts-and-words.md) [~M] (g = 0.34 for mathematical tasks); [Interleaving improves discrimination](claims/interleaving-improves-discrimination.md) [+S] (shuffled mathematics practice improved a delayed test); [Interleaved practice produces higher mathematics test scores than blocked practice in a classroom experiment](claims/interleaved-practice-higher-math-test-scores.md) [+M] (126 seventh-graders, graph and slope problems over three months); the benefit held for both problem types at 30 days but was not significant for slope problems at 1 day ([by problem type and delay](claims/interleaving-benefit-by-problem-type-and-delay.md) [~M])
rows.change: Mix types in practice and homework once each has been taught; ask the learner to name the type before solving; expect smaller gains than for visual material in laboratory studies, though the one classroom study found more
rows.if: The goal is choosing the right procedure among mathematics problem types (`procedure`, several types taught)

rows.basis: [Interleaved practice improves delayed posttest performance compared with blocked practice](claims/interleaved-practice-improves-posttest-performance.md) [+W] (one experiment with an Italian conjugation task: fewer trials and less time on a test two days later; accuracy on new forms was not the measure)
rows.change: Treat as choosing among rules: mix the forms in practice once each has been met, rather than blocking as for word lists
rows.if: The kinds are grammatical forms the learner must choose between (verb conjugation classes, tense or case endings)

rows.basis: [Interleaving benefits are absent for expository texts](claims/interleaving-limited-for-math-texts-and-words.md) [-M] (no significant effect)
rows.change: Do not interleave passages to improve learning of the passages; keep each text whole
rows.if: The material is expository text or prose passages

rows.basis: [For word materials the effect favoured blocking](claims/interleaving-limited-for-math-texts-and-words.md) [-M] (g = −0.39)
rows.change: Block by category; interleaving reversed in this material
rows.if: The material is word lists or vocabulary categories

rows.basis: [Between-category similarity raises and within-category similarity lowers the interleaving effect](claims/similarity-and-complexity-moderate-interleaving.md) [~M]; a systematic review reaches the same boundary, with blocking possibly better where members of a kind are diverse ([interleaving is most useful when differences are subtle](claims/interleaving-similarity-boundary-condition.md) [~M])
rows.change: Interleaving has little to work on: keep blocks, or first teach what varies within a kind
rows.if: The kinds are easy to tell apart (low similarity between categories), or each kind varies a lot internally

rows.basis: [Interleaving is especially useful without a clear verbal rule](claims/interleaving-rule-based-learning-boundary.md) [~W] (a review's narrative summary: blocking better in one rule-based study, a definition on screen removed the benefit in another)
rows.change: Blocking may do as well; if mixing, take the definition off the screen during the mixed set and ask the learner to apply it from memory
rows.if: Each kind is defined by a clear verbal rule the learner is given (a definition, a stated criterion)

rows.basis: untested proposal; the blocked-then-mixed order is a design choice the meta-analysis did not test; guidance that helps novices may be redundant later ([expertise reversal](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M])
rows.change: Meet each kind on its own first (two or three items), then mix; do not open with mixed practice of unfamiliar kinds
rows.if: Learners are `novice` on every kind and the kinds have not yet been met

rows.basis: [In the few studies that split by ability, learning techniques helped low-ability and not high-ability students](claims/learning-techniques-benefit-low-ability-not-high-ability-students.md) [~W] (interleaved practice had negative effects in the high-ability group; 6 studies of high-ability students across all techniques)
rows.change: Skip the blocked introduction, but check rather than assume that mixing helps them: give a short mixed check first, and if they already discriminate the kinds, spend the time on harder kinds instead
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` on the kinds, or already strong in the subject

rows.basis: [Interleaving effects are larger in university student samples](claims/interleaving-larger-in-university-student-samples.md) [~M]; [the literature is dominated by laboratory studies of undergraduates](claims/interleaving-literature-lab-undergraduate-dominance.md) [~W]; [at a 1-day delay, interleaved practice gave d = 0.42 in a seventh-grade classroom](claims/interleaved-benefit-one-day-delay-d042.md) [+M]
rows.change: Use interleaving where the condition holds, but do not promise the laboratory effect sizes: they come mostly from university samples, and one review found no high-school study at all. The one school study in the wiki, in seventh-grade mathematics, found a benefit
rows.if: Learners are children or adolescents

rows.basis: [Interleaving improves discrimination](claims/interleaving-improves-discrimination.md) [+S] (worse during practice, better at the delayed test); the meta-analysis found no moderation by retention interval ([null moderators](claims/interleaving-null-moderators-retention-test-presentation.md) [~M]); in the classroom study the benefit was d = 0.42 at 1 day and d = 0.79 at 30 days, though the difference between delays was not significant ([the benefit does not diminish over 30 days](claims/interleaving-benefit-persists-thirty-days.md) [+M]); a review finds the benefit persists at delays of a day to ten days ([not caused by spacing, persists over delay](claims/interleaving-not-spacing-persists-over-delay.md) [+W])
rows.change: Expect mixed practice to look worse; judge on a delayed, mixed check instead, a month later where the course allows
rows.if: The test is immediate, or the design is judged on practice scores

rows.basis: [Interleaving improves discrimination](claims/interleaving-improves-discrimination.md) [+S] (Kornell & Bjork: most learners believed blocking had served them better); [Learners judge blocking more effective even when their test performance favours interleaving](claims/metacognitive-illusion-blocking-interleaving.md) [~M] (about two thirds of 114 undergraduates); the same misjudgement for spacing is on [Spaced Learning](principles/spaced-learning.md)
rows.change: Build the mixing into the materials or the software; do not rely on learners to choose it, since learners in two studies judged blocking more effective
rows.if: Learners choose their own practice order (`online-self-paced`, homework, revision)

rows.basis: [Spacing and interleaving are subadditive](claims/spacing-interleaving-subadditive-interaction.md) [~M] (with spaced presentation interleaving did not beat blocking); [interrupting juxtaposition impairs inductive learning](claims/interrupting-juxtaposition-impairs-inductive-learning.md) [~M]; [within interleaved sequences, a larger lag between same-category items helped](claims/larger-spacing-better-interleaved-induction.md) [+M] (d = 0.75; all three from one paper with undergraduates and online adults)
rows.change: Keep items of different kinds next to each other so they can be compared; spread each kind out by placing items of *other* kinds between its instances, not unrelated material
rows.if: The schedule puts other activities between practice items (a quiz, a video, unrelated questions), or a learning app spreads items across the day

rows.basis: [Spaced and interleaved homework practice improves learning and retention](claims/spaced-interleaved-homework-practice.md) [+W] (a practice brief summarising research, not a new study)
rows.change: Mix earlier problem types into each later set, alongside new ones
rows.if: Homework or review sets in a school course

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Introduce the kinds, then one mixed set and one mixed check at the end; do not claim retention
rows.if: A single session only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Give everyone the same mixed set and the same "name the kind first" step; look at which pairs of kinds are confused across the class and re-teach those pairs
rows.if: One teacher for many learners

rows.basis: untested proposal; the condition (high between-category similarity) is where the evidence predicts the largest benefit
rows.change: Interleave the confusable pairs specifically, and require correct discrimination on a delayed mixed check before sign-off
rows.if: Stakes are high and the kinds are dangerous to confuse (look-alike drugs, similar alarms, similar fault patterns)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep the brief's order for introducing kinds; change only the practice and review sets, which mix earlier types back in
rows.if: The brief names its own unit order or textbook sequence (chapter by chapter, one type per chapter)

rows.basis: [Self Assessment Accuracy Is Low Without Training](claims/self-assessment-accuracy-is-low-without-training.md) [~M] (secondary and university students); [structured reflection](claims/reflective-practice-improves-outcomes-when-structured.md) [+M] (first-year engineering students, school writing-to-learn)
rows.change: Two or three specific prompts per entry with sentence starters; every "I understand" line followed by one check item scored against a key; teacher reply on a rotating sample in the first weeks.
rows.if: `novice` to the content or the practice (first-year students, first placement)

rows.basis: untested proposal; peer interaction is a reported moderator in [reflection interventions](claims/reflective-practice-evidence-mixed-in-professional-education.md) [~M], direction not stated on the claim page
rows.change: One open prompt about a decision or case, a fortnightly review entry, and peer reading in small groups; drop sentence starters.
rows.if: `advanced` learners or practitioners

rows.basis: untested proposal; the writing-to-learn synthesis covered elementary to college but reports no age-specific result except smaller effects in grades 6–8 ([Writing To Learn Improves Understanding](claims/writing-to-learn-improves-understanding.md) [~M])
rows.change: Entries of a sentence or two, or a drawing with a label, at the end of a lesson; one specific question at a time; the teacher reads and replies orally to a few each day.
rows.if: `child` (primary school)

rows.basis: [Dialogue journals meet SLA conditions](claims/dialogue-journals-meet-sla-conditions.md) [+W] (a theoretical argument, no data); from the earlier page's adult ESL source
rows.change: Use a dialogue journal: the learner writes, the teacher answers in a few sentences that model correct forms without marking errors, weekly; let the learner choose topics.
rows.if: Learners are learning a second language (adult ESL, multilingual classroom)

rows.basis: untested proposal; the writing-to-learn claim page's Discussion warns that transcription demands can crowd out the thinking writing is meant to prompt
rows.change: Allow spoken entries (a voice note), drawing, or sentence frames; shorten to one prompt; never correct form in a reflection entry.
rows.if: Low confidence in writing, or low literacy

rows.basis: [training with diary](claims/web-based-srl-training-with-diary-raises-srl-knowledge-and-self-efficacy-not-math.md) [~M] and [diary alone](claims/learning-diary-alone-no-significant-srl-gains-online-math-prep-course.md) [-M] (prospective university students, online mathematics preparation; no mathematics gain either way)
rows.change: Put the prompts in the platform at the end of each module, tied to that module; require a "next step" line; show the learner their last "next step" at the start of the next module; pair the diary with short self-regulation training.
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: One shared prompt posted where everyone sees it; entries submitted the same way for all (a short form or message works on a phone, typed or voice); the next-session summary drawn from all entries, remote and in-room alike.
rows.if: Mixed mode: some learners in the room, some remote, or phone-only

rows.basis: untested proposal; the reason for keeping some use of entries is [diary alone](claims/learning-diary-alone-no-significant-srl-gains-online-math-prep-course.md) [-M]
rows.change: Do not promise individual replies. Read a rotating sample (for example five entries a week), give one whole-group reply on the commonest confusion, and use peer reading in pairs with one question each; keep the learner's own reread of their last next step every time.
rows.if: One teacher for many learners, or scarce facilitator time (volunteers, a busy shift, a mentor who checks in briefly)

rows.basis: untested proposal; the gains above come from term-long programmes ([Writing To Learn Improves Understanding](claims/writing-to-learn-improves-understanding.md) [+M], larger with longer treatment)
rows.change: Do not set up a journal. Use one end-of-session reflection of three prompts (see [Reflection](principles/reflection.md)), ending in one change to try.
rows.if: One session only

rows.basis: [reflection interventions](claims/reflective-practice-evidence-mixed-in-professional-education.md) [+M] (higher education, pooled across reflective activities; not specific to logs or workplaces)
rows.change: A fieldwork log: after each shift or visit, one observed event, what was done and why, what to try next; the mentor reads the "try next" line before the next shift; a monthly review entry discussed with the mentor.
rows.if: Adults in work settings (placements, clinical rotations, apprenticeships, coaching)

rows.basis: [public vs private reflection](claims/public-vs-private-reflection-mixed.md) [~W]; [guided vs free reflection](claims/guided-reflection-yields-more-higher-order-paragraphs-than-free.md) [+W] (one graduate service-learning course)
rows.change: Grade completion, the use of the prompt and whether the planned next step was tried, not candour or prose; offer private entries alongside public ones.
rows.if: Entries are graded, or shared publicly (class blog, portfolio for assessors)

rows.basis: untested proposal; public blog paragraphs were more often descriptive but nearly a third were integrative in one course ([public vs private reflection](claims/public-vs-private-reflection-mixed.md) [~W])
rows.change: Keep a private working journal for analysis, and draw the public piece from it as a separate, revised product; judge the public piece as writing for its reader (see [Process-Based Writing](principles/process-based-writing.md)).
rows.if: The journal is written for a real audience (a published blog, a reflective piece shared with a community partner)

rows.basis: [Expressive Writing Improves Health Outcomes](claims/expressive-writing-improves-health-outcomes.md) [~M] (146 randomized studies, very small average effect on health); [Brief expressive writing before an exam can raise test-anxious students' scores, but across the wider literature its effect on test performance is negligible](claims/expressive-writing-improves-exam-performance.md) [~M] (medium effect for test-anxious ninth graders; negligible across a later meta-analysis)
rows.change: Keep emotional writing private and optional, in a few short sessions, and do not expect learning gains from it; keep content prompts separate. Before a high-stakes exam, a short worry-writing exercise may be offered but should not be relied on.
rows.if: The aim is wellbeing, or processing emotionally charged material

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Shorten the entry to one line ("which items did I miss, and what will I do about them?") and spend the time on retrieval practice with feedback.
rows.if: Goal is `verbal-association` (vocabulary, facts)

rows.basis: [structured reflection](claims/reflective-practice-improves-outcomes-when-structured.md) [+M]; [diary alone](claims/learning-diary-alone-no-significant-srl-gains-online-math-prep-course.md) [-M]
rows.change: Keep it. Change only what the evidence says matters: make at least one prompt specific to the day's content and metacognitive (what is unclear, how do I know), add a "next step" line, and make sure someone or something uses the entries before the next session.
rows.if: The brief names its own journal routine, template or prompt set

rows.basis: untested proposal; specific prompts rest on the [structured reflection claim](claims/reflective-practice-improves-outcomes-when-structured.md) [+M]
rows.change: Make the prompt scaffold map line for line onto those criteria, five short lines at most so it fits a phone screen, with feelings optional and named as such; agree in writing who reads entries and what must never appear (names, identifying details), and let the learner choose which entries anyone reads (for example two or three anonymised entries a fortnight), the rest staying private, instead of rotating teacher replies; use the in-person session to rehearse one learner's chosen next step as a role-play
rows.if: The brief gives its own criteria for a good entry (a rubric or checklist), and entries are written privately on phones

rows.basis: [A hierarchical internal knowledge organization facilitates performance on complex recall and problem-solving tasks more than a single-level organization of the same knowledge](claims/hierarchical-organization-improves-complex-task-performance.md) [+M] (college physics, one report)
rows.change: Give the organization complete at first, with sorting tasks; move to partial frames only after they rebuild the top level from memory
rows.if: Learners are `novice` on this topic, holding unconnected facts

rows.basis: [Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows.](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M] (review of cognitive-load studies; carried to organizations, which it did not test)
rows.change: Skip the given organization; ask them to rebuild it from memory, then reorganize it for a new task or critique where it fails
rows.if: Learners are `advanced`, or already state the organization unaided

rows.basis: [Ability moderates the hierarchical-organization advantage: low-ability subjects showed no significant benefit, while medium-ability subjects did](claims/ability-moderates-hierarchical-organization-benefit.md) [~M] (college physics; the adjustments are untested)
rows.change: Fewer items per sort, top level first and checked alone, more sort-and-rebuild cycles before adding levels; check whether they use the organization at all
rows.if: Learners are low-attaining, or struggled with the topic before

rows.basis: untested for organization design; narrative recall is better when stories follow a familiar story structure ([Narrative memory is superior when content follows stereotypical story grammar structure, and goal information is critical to comprehension](claims/story-grammar-structure-aids-narrative-memory.md) [+W], second-hand review, narratives only)
rows.change: Use story-like or picture-card organizations of two levels, sorted physically; for narrative content, organize around goal, events and outcome
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary age)

rows.basis: [A hierarchical organization facilitates tasks only when matched to the task domain](claims/organization-task-match-determines-benefit.md) [+M] (advanced high-school physics, two weeks)
rows.change: Put the principles at the top and examples and procedures beneath them; test with problems that need two branches at once
rows.if: Goal is solving problems that use several principles (`principle`, `near-transfer`)

rows.basis: [Hierarchical versus single-level organization does not significantly affect performance on local tasks relying only on individual detailed steps](claims/no-organization-effect-on-local-tasks.md) [~M] (null result; equivalence not tested)
rows.change: Do not build a hierarchy for its own sake; practise the items with retrieval and feedback; use organization only where items need connecting
rows.if: Goal is recall of individual facts or carrying out single steps

rows.basis: [Comparing cases side by side improves learning and transfer by a moderate average amount, though in one algebra study it raised procedural knowledge and flexibility but not conceptual knowledge](claims/comparing-contrasting-cases-improves-learning.md) [+S] (tests comparison, not organization as such)
rows.change: Organize as a comparison: place two or three cases side by side and have learners list similarities and differences before the principle is named
rows.if: Goal is telling similar categories or cases apart (`concept`)

rows.basis: untested; the closed-book rebuild rests on [The same quizzing or concept-mapping activity produces more learning when done without viewing the material, as retrieval, than while viewing it](claims/closed-book-versions-of-quizzes-and-concept-maps-outperform-open-book-versions.md) [+M] (second-hand, settings not stated)
rows.change: Use drag-and-drop sorting into the organization with automatic checking, then a closed-book rebuild the learner compares with a reference map; do not drop the rebuild to save time
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep the organization as an indented outline that fits a phone screen, not a wide diagram; remote and in-room learners sort into the same shared document; read the top level aloud for those who cannot see the board
rows.if: Mixed modes: some learners remote, some in the room, or phone-only

rows.basis: untested at class scale; pairs building maps together is reported to beat individuals ([An ICAP theory article reports, second-hand and without describing the design, a study in which concept mapping with a peer enhanced learning more than concept mapping alone](claims/interactive-beats-constructive-concept-mapping.md) [+W], one study reported second-hand)
rows.change: One shared organization on the board; pairs sort printed cards into it; the teacher checks only top-level placement across the room, then everyone rebuilds individually from memory
rows.if: `classroom`, one teacher and a large group

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Show the organization, one sort task, one explained link, one closed-book rebuild at the end; record what the rebuild shows and claim nothing about retention
rows.if: Time is one session only

rows.basis: untested; mapping is slow and its advantage over time-matched retrieval is not shown ([Concept mapping improves learning over most comparison conditions by a moderate average amount, but not over time-matched retrieval practice](claims/concept-mapping-improves-learning.md) [~S])
rows.change: Give a finished organization rather than having learners build maps from scratch, which is slow; use the tutor's minutes only to look at a 3-minute closed-book sketch and ask about one link
rows.if: Facilitator time is scarce (volunteers, a busy shift, a tutor checking in briefly)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use pictures or objects on cards for items, let learners explain links aloud or by pointing, and keep labels to a few words; sort before writing
rows.if: Learners have low confidence or low literacy

rows.basis: untested; the task-match finding is carried from physics students to workplace tasks ([A hierarchical organization facilitates tasks only when matched to the task domain](claims/organization-task-match-determines-benefit.md) [~M])
rows.change: Build the top level from the decisions or tasks of the job (for example, "what to check first, what to escalate"), using the learners' own cases as the items to sort
rows.if: Adults in a work setting

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Have them build their own organization of the topic first, then select from it what this audience needs; the audience sees the explanation, not the working map
rows.if: Learners must produce an explanation, talk or product for a real audience

rows.basis: [Hierarchical versus single-level organization does not significantly affect performance on local tasks relying only on individual detailed steps](claims/no-organization-effect-on-local-tasks.md) [~M]
rows.change: Keep separate retrieval practice on the details; judge readiness on both kinds of item, never on the organization exercise alone
rows.if: Stakes are high, and the exam mixes detail items with integrative ones

rows.basis: untested; the rebuild rests on [The same quizzing or concept-mapping activity produces more learning when done without viewing the material, as retrieval, than while viewing it](claims/closed-book-versions-of-quizzes-and-concept-maps-outperform-open-book-versions.md) [+M]
rows.change: Keep it; change only two things: tie its top level to the tasks learners will face, and add one closed-book rebuild of it per session
rows.if: The brief names its own routine (a note-taking template, a KWL chart, a unit map the school uses)

rows.basis: [Proficiency moderates gloss effects: vocabulary benefits appear at Levels 2 and 3 but not Levels 1 and 4](claims/proficiency-moderates-gloss-vocabulary-effects.md) [~M] (EFL undergraduates; no benefit at the lowest level)
rows.change: Use shorter scenes (under two minutes) or easier material; open the first-language glossary and captions from the first pass; keep step 8 to the gist (who, where, what happened)
rows.if: Learners are `novice` in the language, following little of the scene even with helps

rows.basis: [Proficiency moderates gloss effects: vocabulary benefits appear at Levels 2 and 3 but not Levels 1 and 4](claims/proficiency-moderates-gloss-vocabulary-effects.md) [~M] (no benefit at the highest level)
rows.change: Drop the glossary pass; keep replay and the response points; give helps only for idioms and cultural references
rows.if: Learners are `advanced`, following the scene without help

rows.basis: untested proposal; the pacing experiment with primary pupils ([Letting learners pace instruction helped on complex material in one experiment, while learner control in general showed almost no effect across 18 studies](claims/learner-paced-beats-system-paced-complex-material.md) [~S]) tested a pause control, not content helps
rows.change: Fewer helps (a picture glossary and replay), large on-screen buttons, and an adult or peer nearby to prompt help use; shorter sessions (20–30 minutes)
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary age)

rows.basis: [Earlier meta-analyses, as reported second-hand, find that glosses improve L2 vocabulary learning and that text-and-picture glosses outperform single-mode glosses](claims/glossing-medium-large-effects-l2-vocabulary.md) [+M] (second-hand report of syntheses); [Marginal glosses, dictionary use, and repeated occurrence of unknown words each positively affect incidental vocabulary learning](claims/marginal-glosses-dictionary-recurrence-improve-incidental-learning.md) [+M] (advanced university learners of French)
rows.change: Make the glossary the centre of step 2: text and picture for each word, and recycle the looked-up words in the next scene
rows.if: The goal is vocabulary (`verbal-association`)

rows.basis: [L1 glosses do not significantly improve EFL reading comprehension compared with no glosses](claims/l1-glosses-no-reading-comprehension-gain.md) [~M]; [Captioning second-language videos produces large benefits for comprehension and vocabulary acquisition](claims/captioning-second-language-videos-large-benefits.md) [+M] (captions always on, not requested)
rows.change: Do not expect the glossary to carry it; spend the time on the whole-first pass, captions, and the response points with model answers after each attempt
rows.if: The goal is comprehension of the whole, or taking part in an exchange (`complex-skill`)

rows.basis: [Not requesting any hints in at least one problem is related to greater wheel-spinning, consistent with help avoidance](claims/hint-avoidance-related-greater-wheel-spinning.md) [~M] (maths practice software, correlational; carried to language video)
rows.change: Build steps 5 and 6 into the software: a prompt after a wrong answer with no help opened, and a one-screen guide to when help is worth taking; log help use for the learner to see
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Learners work in headphones on their own device for step 2; the teacher circulates to those who have opened no help, then runs a five-minute whole-class check on the scene's two or three hardest lines
rows.if: `classroom` with one teacher and many learners, one device each

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Put every help inside the player so it works on a phone screen (tap a word for its gloss, a replay-line button); run the response points and the unaided pass the same way for both groups; do not rely on a teacher stopping a projected screen
rows.if: Mixed modes: some learners remote, some in the room, or phone-only

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page's warning against instructor-driven use
rows.change: Give a printed glossary of the scene; let learners in turn call for a replay of a line; the teacher stops only when asked, not to explain
rows.if: One projector, no learner devices

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Run steps 1, 2, 3 and 8 once on one scene (5 + 20 + 10 + 5 minutes); do not claim retention
rows.if: A single session only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: One short scene: whole pass 3 minutes, helps open 10, two response points with model answers 4, unaided replay 3
rows.if: A fixed short time budget (for example 20 minutes)

rows.basis: untested proposal; the earlier page's product example (a businessman arriving in the United States) is this setting
rows.change: Use scenes from the learner's own work; glossary entries for the phrases they will need to say, not only to understand; response points that are the exchanges they will have
rows.if: Adults in work settings (a business trip, a customer desk, a clinical handover)

rows.basis: untested proposal; [Students and teachers respond favorably to embedded aids: approximately 90% of students reported no difficulty understanding or using the aids, and over 75% wanted similar aids throughout the book.](claims/embedded-aids-are-acceptable-to-students-and-teachers.md) [+W] reports acceptability only
rows.change: Spoken glosses and replay before written ones; helps that cannot be seen by others; praise taking help as a sensible move
rows.if: Learners with low confidence or low literacy

rows.basis: [Unrestricted GPT-4 access improved practice performance but harmed later exam performance, and a guardrailed hint-based version mitigated the harm, as reported by the whitepaper citing Bastani et al.](claims/gpt4-access-harms-learning-after-withdrawal.md) [~W] (second-hand, mathematics, not language)
rows.change: Set it to give hints first and the answer only on a second request; keep the unaided pass
rows.if: The help is an AI assistant or any tool that can give the whole answer

rows.basis: [Video-watching sequences involving pausing and rewinding are negatively correlated with math task performance in a flipped precalculus lesson](claims/video-pause-rewind-sequences-negative-performance.md) [~W] (correlational; the authors do not suggest discouraging rewinding)
rows.change: Treat it as a signal of difficulty, not of good use: offer an easier segment or a short explanation, rather than more replay
rows.if: Learners rewind and re-look-up repeatedly without progressing

rows.basis: [Unrestricted GPT-4 access improved practice performance but harmed later exam performance, and a guardrailed hint-based version mitigated the harm, as reported by the whitepaper citing Bastani et al.](claims/gpt4-access-harms-learning-after-withdrawal.md) [~W] (performance with help did not carry to the exam without it)
rows.change: Judge readiness only on the unaided pass; keep the helps for practice
rows.if: Stakes are high, or the test is taken without helps

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Put the prompts of step 5 and the help guide of step 6 in the material; the tutor's few minutes go to the unaided pass and the response points
rows.if: Scarce facilitator time (volunteers, one tutor checking in briefly)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep it; change only what the evidence speaks to (helps on request after an attempt, hints before answers, one unaided check). If its rubric rewards tool use, keep that criterion and add an unaided item beside it
rows.if: The brief names its own routine, glossary, rubric or assessment

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Build the glossary and response points in those categories, not in categories of your own
rows.if: The brief uses its own categories for the vocabulary or tasks (a job's phrase list, a course's topic list)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep help use private to the learner; do not display who looked up what; let the learner choose whether the log is shared
rows.if: Help requests or the material are private or sensitive

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page's "holistic experience"
rows.change: Keep the scene and the exchange whole; put helps beside it rather than splitting it into item drills
rows.if: The brief wants a whole performance kept whole (a full conversation, a full scene)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use it as a response point: the learner hears the line, chooses a reply, then compares with the error and the model
rows.if: The brief reports an error learners actually made (a misheard word, a wrong reply)

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page
rows.change: Full general-class placement; plan physical access, seating, assistive technology and materials in accessible formats before the first day; no separate academic time
rows.if: The disability is physical or sensory only and the curriculum needs no change

rows.basis: [A state funding report's research review, citing earlier studies, states that inclusive preschool special education benefits students with and without disabilities and that effective early education reduces later special education identification](claims/inclusive-preschool-benefits-reduced-identification.md) [+M] (a report's review of cited studies, associational)
rows.change: Default to an inclusive preschool or kindergarten class with an aide or specialist in the room; plan the move to first grade as a move to the general class
rows.if: Learners are `child`, preschool or kindergarten age

rows.basis: untested for the co-planning; scheduling from [Students pulled out of other classes to receive LLI were particularly negatively affected](claims/lli-more-dosage-pullout-negatively-affected.md) [+M] (struggling secondary readers, not specifically students with disabilities)
rows.change: Keep the student in the subject class; the subject teacher and special-education teacher co-plan one modified version of the same unit (same topic, adjusted reading load and product); put any intervention block outside core classes
rows.if: Learners are `adolescent` in secondary school and teachers say curriculum modification is too hard at this level

rows.basis: [Secondary students who received more LLI or were pulled out of other classes were particularly negatively affected, possibly from missing grade-level content](claims/lli-more-dosage-pullout-negatively-affected.md) [~M] (one secondary reading trial; more dose was not better there); [Outcomes of students with disabilities improve when they receive specially designed instruction responsive to assessment data](claims/specially-designed-instruction-responsive-to-assessment-data-improves-outcomes.md) [+W]
rows.change: Add one fixed block of specially designed instruction (30 to 45 minutes a day, proposal) with a measure checked every two weeks and a written exit criterion; do not add more minutes by default when progress is slow, change the instruction first
rows.if: The student needs intensive skill instruction (for example, reads several grades below level)

rows.basis: untested here; see [Functional Behavior Assessment](principles/functional-behavior-assessment.md)
rows.change: Assess what triggers and keeps up the behavior before changing placement; write a behavior plan into the IEP and change it only through the team; a move to a separate setting is a team decision with a dated review
rows.if: The main need is recurring behavior

rows.basis: [Peer Tutoring Improves Achievement](claims/peer-tutoring-improves-achievement.md) [+M] (general school populations; carried to inclusion)
rows.change: Set up structured peer tutoring pairs and assigned group roles for the class; build presentation and response options into materials for everyone; the specialist co-plans for 15 minutes a week (proposal) instead of sitting in
rows.if: `classroom` with one teacher, many learners, no aide

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Spend specialist minutes on co-planning and the two-weekly goal check (about 10 minutes per student, proposal), not on supervising seatwork; give volunteers one scripted support (a reading partner routine) rather than open-ended help
rows.if: Scarce specialist or facilitator time (one special-education teacher across many classes, volunteers, a part-time aide)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep the student in the live class (joins the same lessons by video or audio, a named classmate as partner, captions or a transcript, work in the same format as peers); a separate packet or separate online course counts as time away from the class and needs its reason written down
rows.if: Mixed modes: the student learns from home or hospital, the class is partly online, or the family has only a phone

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Plan the student's role and supports for that event in advance so they take part in the same activity; offer an alternative activity only if the IEP names one
rows.if: Single session only (one event, field trip, one-off workshop)

rows.basis: student part: [Self Directed IEP Increases Student Participation](claims/self-directed-iep-increases-student-participation.md) [+S] (secondary students; meeting participation only); family part untested
rows.change: Prepare the student to present part of the IEP meeting (a one-page strengths-and-goals sheet, rehearsed once); give the family a plain-language summary and an interpreter, and ask them first what they want for the student
rows.if: The student or family has low confidence or low literacy

rows.basis: untested; the earlier page's transition-planning source has no claim page in the wiki
rows.change: Train the person on the real job alongside co-workers, with a job coach whose presence fades on the same two-check rule as step 7; a separate training room is time away with a stated reason
rows.if: Adults in work settings (transition to work, workplace or vocational training)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Give the student a real role in the shared production with the supports it needs (a script with cues, a partner, an adapted part); no separate showing
rows.if: A product or performance for a real audience (a school play, exhibition, concert)

rows.basis: untested; scheduling from [Students pulled out of other classes to receive LLI were particularly negatively affected](claims/lli-more-dosage-pullout-negatively-affected.md) [+M]
rows.change: Keep it and run it as given; change only what the evidence here bears on: a written reason for each block of separate time, scheduling that does not take a core class, and a dated review
rows.if: The brief names its own routine (the district's IEP form, placement checklist, progress-monitoring tool or meeting agenda)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use them; record where the student sits on that continuum now and which move is proposed, with the data that would justify the next move
rows.if: The brief uses its own categories or criteria (the district's continuum of placements, percentage-of-day bands, its own goal rubric)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: The student and family decide what classmates are told; deliver supports that do not single the student out (offer the same options to everyone where possible); share the IEP only with the team
rows.if: Private or sensitive information (diagnosis, IEP contents, family circumstances)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: 5 minutes: the student presents strengths and goals; 10: progress data against last goals; 10: supports and the placement mix, each separate block with its reason; 5: next review date and who checks what
rows.if: A fixed short time budget (a 30-minute IEP meeting)

rows.basis: untested; see [Universal Design for Learning](principles/universal-design-for-learning.md)
rows.change: Keep the student in the whole task with an adapted role or tools, not a separate worksheet on part of it
rows.if: A whole-task performance the brief wants kept whole (a lab, a project, a team game)

rows.basis: [The evidence base on inclusion effects is methodologically weak: no randomised studies and nearly all synthesised studies at serious risk of bias](claims/inclusion-evidence-low-quality-serious-risk-of-bias.md) [~M]
rows.change: Document each support offered and delivered, the data at each check, and the team's reasons; separate the question "what does the evidence on placement show" (no average difference in the one review) from "what does this student need"
rows.if: High stakes or legal dispute (due process, a contested placement)

rows.basis: [Single-district SELPAs had meaningfully lower inclusion rates, with a higher proportion of students with disabilities in general education less than 40 percent of the school day](claims/single-district-selpas-lower-inclusion-restrictive-settings.md) [~M] (descriptive, California SELPAs)
rows.change: Compare the student's proposed placement with what comparable districts or schools do for similar needs, and ask for the case-specific reason
rows.if: The district's structure or habit, not the student, seems to drive placement

rows.basis: [Tacoma's progressive inclusion program pervaded district operations and limited out-of-district placements to two over twenty years](claims/progressive-inclusion-limited-out-of-district-placements.md) [+M] (one district's case; placements, not outcomes)
rows.change: List the in-district alternatives tried and why each fell short; ask whether a program could be built in a regular school
rows.if: An out-of-district or residential placement is proposed

rows.basis: [registered apprenticeship employment](claims/registered-apprenticeship-ninth-quarter-employment-impacts.md) [+M] and [earnings](claims/registered-apprenticeship-ninth-quarter-earnings-impacts.md) [+M] (adults in DOL-funded apprenticeships against community-college and employment-service comparison groups, ninth quarter; compares routes, not this design move); the weeks are an untested proposal
rows.change: Use an earn-and-learn route where one exists: paid from the start, wage raised at each credential; first credential in about six to eight weeks
rows.if: Learners are `adult` jobseekers on low incomes who need work quickly

rows.basis: untested; from the [dual-enrollment pathway strategy](strategies/dual-enrollment-pathway-template.md), which cites no claim. Recent high-school graduates were hired in one pilot, with employers relaxing an under-21 rule ([tcsg](claims/tcsg-manufacturing-microcredentials-led-to-hiring.md) [+W])
rows.change: Lay out the pathway year by year with the college; use dual enrollment so prerequisites and a first entry-level credential are done before leaving school; employer contact as visits and interviews, not paid work, where age rules bar hiring
rows.if: Learners are `adolescent`, in high school

rows.basis: [Most rural learner participants reported micro-credentials yielded increased opportunity for skill development, job promotion, salary increase](claims/rural-microcredential-learners-report-skill-and-employment-gains.md) [+W] (learner self-reports, four rural initiatives); the design moves are untested
rows.change: Use tasks from their own job as the practice; choose credentials that count for promotion with their employer; schedule around shifts
rows.if: Learners are adults already in work (`adult-workplace`), seeking promotion

rows.basis: untested here; the same source's companion principle, [accelerated, contextualized basic-skills instruction with cohort support](principles/link-programs-to-workforce-entry.md), is unconverted. Larger wage gains when the first credential is a short-term certificate are reported second-hand ([stacking](claims/stacking-microcredentials-increases-employment-wages.md) [+W])
rows.change: Teach reading and maths inside the occupational tasks, keep the first credential short and achievable, and keep learners in a cohort
rows.if: Learners have low confidence, low literacy or low basic skills

rows.basis: [interest vs economic motives](claims/interest-alignment-vs-economic-motivations-persistence.md) [~M] and [Finding another job and low apprenticeship pay are the largest barriers to completing the LC101 apprenticeship phase](claims/job-and-pay-largest-apprenticeship-barriers.md) [~M] (one coding-and-apprenticeship program, survey of 524)
rows.change: Expect some to leave for another job: make the program's own wage steps competitive, ask what work they want, and treat leaving for a job in the field as an exit point on the pathway, not a dropout
rows.if: Learners say they are there mainly for pay

rows.basis: [time and difficulty barriers](claims/time-and-difficulty-largest-coursework-barriers.md) [~M] (same coding program); flexibility of time and cost listed as a success factor ([workforce micro-credential success](claims/workforce-micro-credential-success-practices.md) [+W])
rows.change: Short modules, evening or weekend sessions, theory online; count prior experience toward the credential
rows.if: Learners work or care for others; little time

rows.basis: untested; the simulator is described in [tcsg](claims/tcsg-manufacturing-microcredentials-led-to-hiring.md) [+W], not compared
rows.change: Put theory and the pathway map online and phone-readable; keep the hands-on credential tasks on site or with a simulator (the Georgia pilot used a VR forklift simulator); schedule employer interviews by video where travel is the barrier
rows.if: Mixed modes: some learners remote or phone-only, practice must be hands-on

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Concentrate contact at the credential milestones: one check-in per learner at each, plus the final-week employer interviews; let the employer advisory group, not the instructor, keep the skills list current
rows.if: One instructor or coordinator for many learners, or scarce facilitator time (volunteers, one adviser)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Give the pathway map: the job, its intake date, the credential, the wage steps, and one named employer contact; do not claim employment outcomes from it
rows.if: A single session only (an information session, one workshop)

rows.basis: untested; the shape follows the two-month Georgia pilot ([tcsg](claims/tcsg-manufacturing-microcredentials-led-to-hiring.md) [+W])
rows.change: Keep the order and compress it: week 1 map and site visit, weeks 2–6 credential tasks, week 7 credential tests, week 8 employer interviews
rows.if: Fixed short time budget (e.g. eight weeks)

rows.basis: untested; the page's claims concern linking to employer-recognized credentials, not replacing them
rows.change: Keep it and assess against it as written; change only the timing (credential early), the employer contact points and the wage-step display
rows.if: The brief names its own credential, competency framework or employer rubric

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Assess the whole task as the employer would see it, on site; use the credential tests only as checks beside it, not as a substitute
rows.if: The brief wants a whole workplace performance kept whole (a shift, a job, a build)

rows.basis: [Unregistered apprenticeship programs had positive, statistically significant impacts on ninth-quarter employment, ranging from 3.9 to 4.8 percentage points](claims/unregistered-apprenticeship-ninth-quarter-employment-impacts.md) [~M], against 7.8 to 8.8 points for registered ([registered employment](claims/registered-apprenticeship-ninth-quarter-employment-impacts.md) [+M]); separate analyses in one evaluation, not a head-to-head comparison
rows.change: Prefer the registered route where available, and ask employers which credential they recognize
rows.if: Choice between a registered (recognized) and an unregistered apprenticeship

rows.basis: [Community-based work programs for transition-age students with disabilities show mixed effects on employment outcomes](claims/community-based-work-programs-mixed-employment-effects.md) [~M]
rows.change: Do not assume a work placement raises employment; add job coaching and transport support, and record employment outcomes
rows.if: Learners are transition-age students with disabilities

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: The learner decides what an employer sees; share credentials and work samples, not case notes, and only with consent
rows.if: Learners' wages, records or immigration status are sensitive

rows.basis: [E-HLTH barriers](claims/college-specific-barriers-limited-ehlth-certificate-implementation.md) [~M] (Virginia colleges, implementation study)
rows.change: Check demand (job ads, employer commitments) before building; choose a sector with hiring, or a credential that transfers across employers
