rows.if: Weak local labor market for the target job

rows.basis: [Mastery learning improves outcomes](claims/mastery-learning-improves-outcomes.md) [+M]
rows.change: End each unit with a check against a stated criterion; below it, give corrective instruction and a parallel recheck before moving on
rows.if: A course of cumulative units at college, high-school or upper-elementary level

rows.basis: [Effects vary with standard, pacing and test type](claims/mastery-learning-effects-vary-with-standard-pacing-and-test-type.md) [~M]
rows.change: Set a high unit standard rather than a low one; programmes with higher standards had larger effects
rows.if: The criterion has not been set

rows.basis: [Self-paced mastery programmes reduce course completion](claims/self-paced-mastery-programs-reduce-college-course-completion.md) [-M]; [Effects vary with standard, pacing and test type](claims/mastery-learning-effects-vary-with-standard-pacing-and-test-type.md) [~M]
rows.change: Prefer group-based pacing with individual correction; if self-paced, add deadlines or pacing support, because completion falls
rows.if: Learners will work at their own pace

rows.basis: [Effects larger for lower-aptitude students](claims/mastery-learning-effects-larger-for-lower-aptitude-students.md) [+M]
rows.change: Use it; both groups gain, and the spread of scores narrows
rows.if: The class mixes stronger and weaker students

rows.basis: [Effects larger in elementary school](claims/mastery-effects-larger-elementary.md) [~M]
rows.change: Expect a larger effect than in high school or college
rows.if: Elementary students

rows.basis: [Effects smaller in science](claims/mastery-science-smaller-effects.md) [~M]
rows.change: Expect a smaller effect than in mathematics, social studies or language arts
rows.if: A science course

rows.basis: [Effects vary with standard, pacing and test type](claims/mastery-learning-effects-vary-with-standard-pacing-and-test-type.md) [~M]; [Tension between mastery and curricular coverage](claims/adaptive-mastery-versus-coverage-tension-null-result.md) [-W]
rows.change: Expect a much smaller effect than on the course's own tests, and check that gating does not stop learners reaching later tested topics
rows.if: Success will be judged on a state or standardized test

rows.basis: [Trained teachers gave 20% of class time to the corrective loop](claims/training-increases-feedback-corrective-loop-time.md) [~W]; [Mastery learning did not reduce pace or scope](claims/mastery-learning-did-not-slow-pace-or-scope.md) [~W]
rows.change: Budget class time for the correction loop (about a fifth of class time in one study) and decide in advance what happens at the time limit
rows.if: The course must keep to a fixed scope or calendar

rows.basis: [Gains persist at follow-up](claims/mastery-learning-gains-persist-at-follow-up.md) [+M]
rows.change: Recheck earlier units at a delay; gains held at about eight weeks
rows.if: The outcome that matters is retention after the course

rows.basis: [Mixed effects on teacher variables](claims/mastery-mixed-teacher-variable-effects.md) [~M]
rows.change: Prepare teachers for feeling less confident at first, even as results improve
rows.if: Teachers are adopting it for the first time

rows.basis: [concerns shifted from nonuser towards user profiles after a two-week workshop](claims/workshop-shifts-concerns-toward-user-profile.md) [+M] (one science curriculum, elementary teachers, no comparison group)
rows.change: Lead with clear information, visits and examples of the innovation in use, and individual reassurance; hold back detailed logistics and student-outcome data until use begins
rows.if: Most people have not used the innovation yet (`novice` for this innovation)

rows.basis: [concerns moved from lower to higher stages over a year of use](claims/stages-of-concern-developmental-trend.md) [+M] (associational, one curriculum); the matching move is untested
rows.change: Drop introductory sessions; give time to look at student work and effects, to collaborate and to try modifications; keep a short check for leftover management problems
rows.if: People are experienced users (`advanced` in this innovation), or already show impact concerns

rows.basis: [individual profiles diverge from group trends](claims/individual-concern-profiles-vary-widely.md) [+W] (two case profiles)
rows.change: Plan whole-group sessions for the peak, then read individual profiles and arrange separate contact for those who differ
rows.if: A whole staff or department is adopting at once, and the group profile has one clear peak

rows.basis: [follow-up contact related most strongly to adoption success](claims/follow-up-contact-strongest-adoption-success-factor.md) [+M] (NDN evaluation, reported second-hand) for keeping contact at all; the triage is an untested proposal
rows.change: Use the written open-ended question instead of interviews; group people by peak stage and give each group one short contact every two to three weeks; let colleagues at later stages handle early-stage questions; keep the facilitator's own time for those with high personal concerns
rows.if: One facilitator for many staff, or scarce facilitator time (a busy term, a part-time coach)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use the first 10 minutes to collect written concern statements, then spend the session on the commonest peak; give one practical next step for use, and name who will follow up and when; do not claim the session changed use
rows.if: Only a single session is possible

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Collect concern statements by a short online form before the session; hold one-to-one follow-ups by call or video, cameras optional for those with personal concerns; share examples of the innovation in use as short videos
rows.if: Some staff join remotely while others are in the room, or contact is by phone or video only

rows.basis: untested proposal; from the sources' description of personal concerns
rows.change: Keep early contact private and one-to-one; start with what will be expected and what help exists; pair them with a colleague who has been through it; avoid observed demonstrations until they ask
rows.if: People are anxious, have low confidence with the innovation, or have high personal concerns

rows.basis: [unmentored teachers reached impact concerns more often than mentored ones](claims/mentors-may-inhibit-concern-development.md) [~M] (four volunteer groups, 39 teachers, association only); untested as a design rule
rows.change: Have the mentor read the newcomer's concerns rather than assume them; check whether the mentoring is holding the person at task concerns, and widen their contacts if so
rows.if: New teachers with an assigned mentor, or a mentoring scheme is the main support

rows.basis: untested; every claim here is from teachers, carried by analogy
rows.change: Use the same diagnosis and stage-matched support, with the questions worded for their work; record whether the stages read the same way
rows.if: Adults in a non-school workplace adopting a new procedure or system (`adult-workplace`, e.g. clinical or office staff)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep concerns data confidential and separate from evaluation (report group profiles only); say so when collecting it; expect higher personal concerns and plan more individual contact
rows.if: The change is mandated, or reports of use feed into performance evaluation

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep it; add one concerns question ("When you think about it, what are you concerned about?") and one use question ("What are you doing with it now?"), and change only the content of the follow-up by what they show
rows.if: The brief names its own routine for checking in (its own survey, staff meeting slot or coaching log)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use its categories for describing use (in place of the LoU chart) and map them to the stages; do not substitute this page's labels
rows.if: The brief supplies its own categories, rubric or implementation checklist

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: The person decides who sees them; the facilitator works from what the person chooses to share or from anonymous group profiles
rows.if: Concerns or reflections are private (a personal journal, confidential statements to a counsellor)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Split it: about 10 minutes of check-in on concerns, about 80 minutes of stage-grouped work, and short individual follow-ups by message between sessions; give minutes, not topics, to each group
rows.if: A fixed short time budget (for example two hours of PD per month)

rows.basis: [the LoU interview can be rated reliably](claims/lou-interview-interrater-reliability-high.md) [+M] (as a way to read use); untested as an outcome rule
rows.change: Judge progress by observed or reported use at the next level, not by session attendance or concern scores alone; keep support attached to real use with real students
rows.if: The goal is full use of the innovation in real classrooms or work (a whole-task performance), not knowledge of it

rows.basis: [follow-up contact related most strongly to adoption success](claims/follow-up-contact-strongest-adoption-success-factor.md) [+M]
rows.change: Add follow-up contacts across the first term of use and a second concerns reading at about week 8
rows.if: A launch workshop is planned and then nothing

rows.basis: [an innovation foreign to its system tends to be rejected](claims/isolated-innovations-are-rejected-by-the-system-they-enter.md) [~M] (two narrative reviews, one author)
rows.change: Pair person-level matching with changes at the game-plan and policy levels (time, materials, assessment) that make the innovation fit
rows.if: The innovation is a single change foreign to the rest of the school's system

rows.basis: [Chunking reduces working memory load by grouping information into fewer, more meaningful units.](claims/chunking-reduces-working-memory-load.md) [~S] (reviews and lab experiments on immediate memory; carried to recall planning, untested); gap choice in [Spaced Learning](principles/spaced-learning.md)
rows.change: Keep the opening recall close to how it was taught, with answers shown at once; group the material into a few units before recall; plan returns at short gaps first
rows.if: Learners are `novice` on this material

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Drop it from the opening rotation; keep one item in cumulative checks; spend the time on newer material
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` or already recall it on a delayed check

rows.basis: untested; the spacing evidence comes mostly from young adults and is thin for children's long-term retention ([Spaced Practice Improves Retention](claims/spaced-practice-improves-retention.md) [~S])
rows.change: Keep recall items short and low-stakes, read aloud where reading is weak, and space returns across days in class time rather than homework
rows.if: Learners are children (`child`, `adolescent`)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Make the later encounters job tasks that need the material (a case at a team meeting, a checklist step on shift), and check unaided in the form the job uses; agree the horizon with the learner
rows.if: Adults in work settings, learning for use on the job

rows.basis: [Spaced Practice Improves Retention](claims/spaced-practice-improves-retention.md) [~S] (one meta-analysis summarised there: longer lags helped verbal tasks up to a point but reduced effects for skill tasks such as typing and music)
rows.change: Reactivate by doing the procedure, not by recalling a description of it; for motor skills use shorter gaps than for verbal material and check on the whole performance
rows.if: Goal is a `procedure` or motor skill, not facts or vocabulary

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Teach, then put a different 10–15 minute task in between, then an unaided recall; hand over a dated self-test sheet for days 2, 7 and 21; state that retention was not measured
rows.if: Only one session, no follow-up

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Spend 2–3 of the 10 minutes on recall of earlier items before new material; never let the review queue take the whole slot; cap new items so returns fit
rows.if: A fixed short time budget (for example 10 minutes a day)

rows.basis: [Learners Misjudge Spacing Benefits](claims/learners-misjudge-spacing-benefits.md) [+M] (adults, lab and flashcard software: learners prefer massing, so do not leave scheduling to them)
rows.change: Put the returns in the app's queue or a dated reminder, with automatic checking; show a delayed check, not a streak, as the progress signal
rows.if: Online, self-paced, or phone-only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Run the opening recall on a shared form or poll both groups answer at once; send remote learners the same dated self-test sheet as those in the room
rows.if: Some learners remote, some in the room

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use self-marked recall (learners check against an answer card) and look only at the items many missed; spend facilitator time on re-explaining those, not on marking
rows.if: One teacher or tutor for many learners, or scarce facilitator time (volunteers, a busy shift)

rows.basis: [Gains from an intensive period of second-language study persist for weeks without rehearsal.](claims/l2-fluency-gains-persist-weeks-without-practice.md) [~M] (18 undergraduates, one pilot, no control group; carried to other material untested)
rows.change: Give a short unaided check first; resume from it; do not reset progress or repeat the whole unit by default
rows.if: A learner returns after a gap with no practice

rows.basis: untested; learners read ease as learning ([Fluent Illusions Mislead Self Assessment](claims/fluent-illusions-mislead-self-assessment.md) [~M], adult lab studies)
rows.change: Keep recall private and ungraded; use oral or picture-cued items; say that forgetting between sessions is expected and that recall that feels hard is still useful
rows.if: Learners have low confidence or low literacy

rows.basis: [Spaced Practice Improves Retention](claims/spaced-practice-improves-retention.md) [+S] (spacing against massing at equal time); release rule untested
rows.change: Plan backwards from the date: at least three spaced cumulative checks before it, the last a few days out, not the night before; judge readiness only on unaided delayed checks
rows.if: Stakes are high, or the assessment date is fixed

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep it; change only what matters here: that the items are answered unaided before the answer is shown, that they include material from two or more sessions back, and that a delayed check decides when an item retires
rows.if: The brief names its own review routine (its own warm-up, flashcard deck, check-in or weekly quiz)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use them as the units for grouping and as the criteria on the delayed check; do not substitute this page's
rows.if: The brief gives its own categories, criteria or rubric

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Learners keep their own recall answers and mark them themselves; report only whether they want help, never the content
rows.if: The material or the learner's answers are private or sensitive

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Reactivate by doing a smaller whole version of the task at later sessions (a short presentation, a full but brief case), not by splitting it into recall items; keep the final performance whole
rows.if: The goal is a whole-task performance, or a product for a real audience

rows.basis: [The timing of acute exercise relative to learning modulates memory consolidation](claims/acute-exercise-timing-memory.md) [~S] (healthy adults, lab episodic-memory tasks; carried to classrooms untested)
rows.change: Schedule the activity after the learning episode, not during it; an activity some hours after has shown more effect than one straight after in adult lab studies
rows.if: The brief plans physical activity or breaks around learning

rows.basis: untested; the claims are about adolescents, young adults and seventh graders
rows.change: Under one minute; movement-based (breath with arm raises) rather than sitting still; adult-led with the same words each day; a picture cue for the steps
rows.if: Learners are `child` (pre-K or primary)

rows.basis: [A practice brief reviewing self-regulation interventions reports substantial benefits of mindfulness programs for cognitive and emotional regulation, stress and mental health in adolescents and young adults](claims/mindfulness-programs-benefit-adolescent-regulation.md) [+M] (practice brief summarising a review of programmes; no effect size; does not test a single routine)
rows.change: Plan a multi-week programme with practice in real situations and a debrief, not a one-off minute; keep the before-task routine as one part of it
rows.if: Learners are `adolescent` or young `adult`, and the goal is better regulation of stress or emotion

rows.basis: untested proposal; from the earlier page (adult learners balancing competing demands)
rows.change: One minute, framed as a focus reset rather than wellness or meditation; no inward-feeling language; open with the agenda straight after
rows.if: Adults in a work setting (`adult-workplace`), or adult learners arriving tired or fragmented

rows.basis: [Math learning gains did not differ between the Mindful and Cognitive conditions](claims/no-condition-difference-math-learning.md) [-M] (42 seventh graders, algebra tutor, pre-post); [Universal school-based SEL programs improve students' behaviour, with a small and, in recent randomised trials, negligible effect on academic achievement](claims/sel-programs-improve-behavior-and-achievement.md) [~S] (SEL programmes generally, carried to mindfulness)
rows.change: Do not count on the routine for it; keep instruction and practice time whole; if the routine stays, keep it under two minutes and outside the practice block
rows.if: The goal is achievement in the session (a test score, problems solved)

rows.basis: [Students who learned mindfulness-based conflict resolution strategies used them outside school with siblings and friends](claims/mindfulness-conflict-resolution-transfer-out-of-school.md) [+W] (one study reported second-hand, no design details); [Mindfulness practices are linked to positive school climate outcomes including compassion, well-being, and self-regulation](claims/mindfulness-positive-school-climate-outcomes.md) [+W]
rows.change: Teach "pause before reacting" as a named move, rehearse it on likely situations, cue it in real disputes, and ask afterwards where learners used it outside class
rows.if: The goal is handling conflict or provocation (classroom climate, peer disputes)

rows.basis: [The mindfulness interventions did not significantly change anticipatory or executive state-MA relative to cognitive support alone](claims/no-condition-difference-state-ma.md) [~M] (seventh graders, tutor setting); the report of reduced test anxiety in [Mindfulness practices are linked to academic improvements including reduced test anxiety, focus, and reading competence](claims/mindfulness-academic-improvement-links.md) [+W] is second-hand and unsized
rows.change: Offer an optional one-minute pause just before the test; do not promise less anxiety; keep the usual preparation
rows.if: A test or high-stakes assessment is next, or learners report test anxiety

rows.basis: [Mindful-condition students completed fewer problem-solving steps and requested fewer hints per step than Cognitive-condition students](claims/mindful-condition-fewer-steps-hints.md) [~M] (log data, exploratory; error rates did not differ: [no-difference-error-rate-log](claims/no-difference-error-rate-log.md) [~M])
rows.change: Put the pause before the session, not between practice steps; keep it skippable; check that learners still complete the practice set
rows.if: Learning is in software or `online-self-paced` (a tutor, an app)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: One spoken script everyone can follow by audio alone; cameras optional; no on-screen step that needs a large display; remote learners need not show they took part
rows.if: Mixed modes: some learners remote, some in the room, or phone-only

rows.basis: [Implementation of co-regulation strategies was shaped by classroom context, facilitator experience and mindset, and varied in ease across strategies](claims/co-regulation-implementation-factors-context-experience-strategy-ease.md) [~M] (youth programmes, nine sites; facilitators found breath to focus the hardest strategy)
rows.change: Start with the easiest routine (a consistent welcome and one breath cue) and add breath-focused practice only once the facilitator is comfortable; keep one fixed script
rows.if: One adult for a large group, or scarce facilitator time (volunteers, a busy shift, a visiting tutor)

rows.basis: untested proposal; from the earlier page (trauma sensitivity) and the trauma-informed strategy page under Examples
rows.change: Eyes-open, outward-focus options only (feet on the floor, name objects in the room); a stated right to sit out; an adult who knows the learners nearby; no body-scan or silence longer than a minute
rows.if: Learners with trauma histories, high anxiety, or low confidence

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: The learner keeps any reflection private; nothing is written for the teacher or shared aloud unless the learner chooses
rows.if: Private or sensitive material (feelings, family events)

rows.basis: untested proposal; from the earlier page (practices that conflict with beliefs)
rows.change: Describe it as an attention practice in secular language; offer the same minute as quiet task preview instead; no chants, bells or postures required
rows.if: Families or learners object on religious or cultural grounds

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: One routine of one minute or less before the hardest task, minutes counted in the session plan; record how long the group takes to start the task; claim nothing about lasting regulation
rows.if: Time is a single session only, or a fixed short block

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep it and its categories as given; change only what this page adds: placing it right before a named task, making it optional, and ending with one task-facing question
rows.if: The brief names its own routine (a school's mindful moment, its own check-in, its own zones or feelings categories)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: A one-minute grounding just before going on, then the performance kept whole; no reflection on feelings until after it
rows.if: A performance for a real audience follows (presentation, recital, client meeting)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Demonstrate rather than explain; three or four spoken words per step; a picture card for each practice
rows.if: Low literacy, or instruction in a second language

rows.basis: [Productive Failure Improves Conceptual Learning](claims/productive-failure-improves-conceptual-learning.md) [~S] (conceptual and transfer outcomes; reversed for second to fifth graders); [The usefulness of induction and errorful learning varies with the type of terminal task being taught](claims/task-type-moderates-induction-error-usefulness.md) [+W] (conceptual analysis)
rows.change: Do not use this design; let learners attempt problems first and teach from their attempts, or use guided practice with explanation prompts
rows.if: Target is a `concept`, `principle` or transfer to new problems, not a pairing or a tolerance

rows.basis: [Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows.](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M] (cognitive-load studies, carried to association and precision practice untested)
rows.change: Drop the mediators, cues and wide band; give mixed unaided items with correction only on misses
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` on these items, or already accurate on the first unaided round

rows.basis: [Overt correction of errors speeds young children's learning compared with knowledge of correctness alone](claims/overt-error-correction-speeds-young-children-learning.md) [+W] (second-hand; block length is an untested proposal)
rows.change: Keep cues and mediators ready-made; correct every error overtly by showing and saying the right answer and having the child repeat it; short blocks (5–8 minutes)
rows.if: Learners are young children (`child`)

rows.basis: [Overt correction of errors speeds young children's learning compared with knowledge of correctness alone](claims/overt-error-correction-speeds-young-children-learning.md) [~W] (adults did not learn faster with overt correction, reported second-hand)
rows.change: Correction can be brief (the right answer shown); invite them to build their own mediators; spend the time saved on unaided, mixed items
rows.if: Learners are adults (`adult`)

rows.basis: [Mnemonic Instruction Improves Recall For Students With Disabilities](claims/mnemonic-instruction-improves-recall-for-students-with-disabilities.md) [+S] (recall of facts and word meanings; the fading rule is an untested proposal)
rows.change: Teach the mediators explicitly (keyword plus picture, acrostic), present them for the learner rather than asking the learner to invent them, and fade the picture only after two sessions of correct recall
rows.if: Learners have mild learning or intellectual disabilities, or find remembering hard

rows.basis: untested proposal; from the earlier page's concern about motivation loss when criteria tighten abruptly
rows.change: Start with the band so wide that the first attempts succeed, narrow only after visible success, and keep errors private (feedback on the learner's own screen or sheet, not aloud)
rows.if: Learners have low confidence, or have given up after repeated failure

rows.basis: untested proposal (the mnemonic claim's own Discussion notes learners must be able to decode the mnemonic; not tested)
rows.change: Use picture and sound mediators rather than written acrostics; check the learner can read or say the mediator before using it
rows.if: Learners have low literacy, or are learning in a second language

rows.basis: [Initial retrieval conditions that provide less cue support, such as free recall rather than recognition or fewer letter cues, tend to produce better retention despite lower initial success](claims/less-initial-retrieval-support-produces-better-retention.md) [~M]; [A review reports that retrieval practice effects grow more robust as initial retrieval success rises, especially above 75%, and separately that giving more retrieval cues yields smaller effects](claims/retrieval-practice-effects-more-robust-when-initial-retrieval-success-exceeds-75-percent.md) [~M] (both word-learning studies reported in a review chapter; keep most practice successful, not all of it trivially so)
rows.change: Fade cues faster, accept some misses with immediate correction, and re-test unaided at the start of later sessions; do not judge readiness on cued items
rows.if: Goal is retention at a delay (a week or a term away), not performance at the end of the lesson

rows.basis: [High-confidence errors lead to better retention after correction than low-confidence errors.](claims/high-confidence-errors-improve-retention.md) [~M] (a review and one experiment; qualifies "minimize errors" for recall items)
rows.change: Ask for a confidence rating before showing the answer; correct confident errors at once and bring them back sooner. A confident error, corrected, is an occasion to fix the pairing, not only a cost to avoid
rows.if: Learners make errors with high confidence (they are sure of a wrong pairing)

rows.basis: untested proposal; the comparison of wrong with right is modelled on [Error Analysis](principles/error-analysis.md)
rows.change: Use it as a contrast: show the wrong and the right response side by side once, then return to cued, correct practice on that item
rows.if: The brief reports an error learners actually made (a swapped pair, a habitual drift in timing)

rows.basis: [Taking initial multiple-choice tests without feedback can lead students to later produce the incorrect lure answers they selected](claims/multiple-choice-lures-can-be-learned-as-false-knowledge.md) [+W]
rows.change: Show the correct answer after every item, including correct ones answered with low confidence
rows.if: Practice items are multiple choice

rows.basis: [Feedback Enhances Retrieval Practice](claims/feedback-enhances-retrieval-practice.md) [+S] (classroom quizzing and a lab word-pair study, carried to self-paced apps untested)
rows.change: Build the cue fading and correction into the items: each miss shows the right answer and returns the item later in the set; a short unaided check opens each session
rows.if: Setting is `online-self-paced`, or phone-only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Give everyone the same practice items on their own device or sheet, with the answer shown after each one; the teacher watches the shared error counts rather than individual voices
rows.if: Some learners join remotely while others are in the room

rows.basis: untested proposal; correction evidence is from quizzing and lab studies ([Feedback Enhances Retrieval Practice](claims/feedback-enhances-retrieval-practice.md) [+S])
rows.change: Have all learners respond at once (cards, mini-whiteboards, a poll); correct the commonest error for the whole class, then re-present that item; work one-to-one only with those still missing it
rows.if: One teacher with a large class

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Put the cue fading and the answer check into the materials (answer on the back of a card, a self-check gauge, an app); use the facilitator's few minutes for narrowing the precision band and for confident errors
rows.if: Facilitator time is scarce (volunteers, a busy shift, a tutor checking in for a few minutes)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: In 20 minutes: 2 minutes measuring current attempts, 5 minutes introducing 6–8 items with mediators, 10 minutes cued practice with fading and correction, 3 minutes unaided check. Report only the end-of-session result; claim no retention
rows.if: Only one session, of fixed short length

rows.basis: untested proposal for the routine; the correction step rests on [Feedback Enhances Retrieval Practice](claims/feedback-enhances-retrieval-practice.md) [+S]
rows.change: Keep it; change only what the evidence speaks to: correct every miss at once, take cues away rather than adding them, narrow a tolerance gradually
rows.if: The brief names its own routine (its own drill, flashcard set, rubric or tolerance)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use those as the final criterion and the items; set only the starting band and the steps between them
rows.if: The brief gives its own categories, criteria or final tolerance

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep error records with the learner; feedback is shown only to the learner unless they choose to share it
rows.if: Material is private or sensitive (a learner's errors seen by peers, workplace records)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Practise on representative tasks with the real instrument; narrow to the job tolerance before unsupervised work; require the final tolerance on two separate occasions, unaided; never relax the final criterion, only the starting band
rows.if: Adults in a work setting where precision matters for safety (a dose, a torque, a measurement)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Shape precision inside short practice runs of the whole piece, not in isolated drills only; finish each session with one whole run judged against the current band
rows.if: A whole performance for a real audience (a recital, a handwritten letter, a demonstration) that the brief wants kept whole

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Judge readiness only on unaided, uncued responses at the start of a session; record every cue and correction given in practice
rows.if: Stakes are high, or the final check is unaided

rows.basis: [Students need clear guidance so they are not overwhelmed by Ecree's feedback, which may be most useful for advanced writers](claims/students-need-guidance-ecree-feedback-advanced-writers.md) [~W] (one study, grade 8–11 English; the advanced-writer point is the brief's hedge)
rows.change: Fewer comments, aimed at higher-level features; let them choose the feature they want feedback on; a full tool report is acceptable
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` writers, or already act on most comments

rows.basis: [Some students may be overwhelmed by Ecree's feedback about their writing](claims/teachers-found-ecree-useful-but-some-students-overwhelmed.md) [~W] (same study; no proportion reported); the cap of two is an untested proposal
rows.change: Two priorities only, one specific strength stated first, the next-action summary written for them; filter any tool output to the current priorities
rows.if: Learners are developing writers, or have low confidence

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page (language learners unfamiliar with feedback jargon)
rows.change: No grammar jargon or abbreviations; plain full sentences; show the change on one instance ("for example, *goes* not *go* here"); allow an audio comment in place of a long written one
rows.if: Learners are second-language writers, or have low literacy

rows.basis: [Praise for intelligence, rather than for effort, after success undermines children's motivation and performance after a later failure](claims/feedback-praise-reduces-learning.md) [~M] (fifth graders on reasoning problems; carried to written comments)
rows.change: Comment on the work and the strategy, never on the child's ability ("you found two reasons; now add an example to each", not "you're a smart writer"); read comments aloud to them
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary age)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use the workplace's own quality criteria in the comments; tie each priority to its consequence for the reader of the document; keep comments private to the learner and their supervisor
rows.if: Learners are `adult`s in a work setting (reports, case notes, client letters)

rows.basis: untested proposal; the brief's routine stays, as earlier waves found briefs reward
rows.change: Keep them; write each comment in the rubric's own words and point to the criterion; add a key for any code; change only wording, number and legibility
rows.if: The brief names its own rubric, criteria or feedback codes

rows.basis: [Some students struggled to use Ecree's and MI Write's automated feedback](claims/some-students-struggled-automated-feedback-use.md) [~W] (a synthesis of one organisation's studies of two tools)
rows.change: Introduce the tool with a guided walk-through of one report; tell learners which part to read first; for developing writers, select the items that match this draft's priorities
rows.if: Feedback comes from an automated tool

rows.basis: [Discrepancies between lenient learner feedback and more critical automated feedback caused tutors confusion, distrust, and demands for rationale](claims/feedback-source-discrepancies-cause-confusion.md) [~W] (tutors receiving feedback, carried to students)
rows.change: One reconciled summary at the top, saying which source to follow where they disagree, and why
rows.if: Several sources comment on the same draft (teacher, peers, tool)

rows.basis: [The Trainer is expected to make peer comments more specific, criterion-referenced, and evidence-based](claims/trainer-expected-improve-comment-quality.md) [+W] (a theoretical expectation, no test)
rows.change: Before they comment, train them on the comment form (feature, location, what to try) with two model comments; give them the rubric's criteria
rows.if: Peers give the feedback

rows.basis: untested proposal; the clearer format rated higher in [AI multimodal feedback is rated higher than educator feedback on specificity, clarity, simplicity, motivation, satisfaction, and lower mental effort, with comparable correctness, trust, and acceptance](claims/ai-feedback-higher-perceived-quality-value.md) [+M] was multimodal, but its source (AI against educator) is confounded with format
rows.change: Typed comments only; next-action summary first, at most three comments visible without scrolling; offer a short audio or video comment for one complex point
rows.if: `online-self-paced` or phone-only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Give every learner the same typed comments and summary through one channel; hold the two-minute "what will you change first" check in the shared document, not aloud in the room
rows.if: Mixed modes: some learners remote, some in the room

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Two priority comments per draft, chosen from a short list of the commonest problems; one whole-class note on the commonest problem with a worked before-and-after; skip line edits
rows.if: One teacher with many learners, or scarce facilitator time (a volunteer tutor, a short check-in)

rows.basis: untested proposal; minutes are a proposal that adds up to 50
rows.change: 5 minutes reading the summary and comments; 2 minutes writing the first change; 30 minutes revising on that change only; 10 minutes for circled comments and a quick look at one revision; 3 minutes to note the next priority
rows.if: A fixed short time budget (one 50-minute session to return and revise)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: One priority and one strength; the learner revises one paragraph on it in the session, so the comment is used at once
rows.if: A single session only, no later draft

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Comments go only to the learner; no display of examples from their text without consent; comment on the writing, not on the experience it reports
rows.if: The work is private or sensitive (a personal narrative, a reflective journal)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Comment on the whole first (does it do its job for its audience), then at most two features; do not break the product into separately marked parts
rows.if: The learner's whole product is to be kept whole (a performance, a full essay for a real audience)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use that comment as a worked contrast in the walk-through: the cryptic version and the full-sentence version side by side, and what each asks the learner to do
rows.if: The brief reports a comment learners misread (a symbol taken as praise, "?" read as "wrong")

rows.basis: untested proposal; that more than a third of feedback interventions lower performance ([Feedback improves learning by a medium amount on average, but its effect varies widely with the information it carries, and more than a third of feedback interventions reduce performance](claims/feedback-improves-learning.md) [~S]) is the reason to keep attention on the task
rows.change: Return the comments before or apart from the grade; say what the grade rests on in the rubric's terms; keep comments that can still be acted on, and label any that cannot
rows.if: Stakes are high (a graded submission)

rows.basis: [Student perceptions of GenAI feedback functionalities diverged, with some finding them redundant when feedback was perceived as clear](claims/divergent-perceptions-genai-feedback-redundancy.md) [~W] (18 university students, one tool)
rows.change: Do not add layers (dashboards, extra explanations, a second tool) to clear feedback
rows.if: Learners already find the comments clear

rows.basis: [Mnemonic Instruction Improves Recall For Students With Disabilities](claims/mnemonic-instruction-improves-recall-for-students-with-disabilities.md) [+S] (secondary-age youth and students with learning and behaviour problems; recall of facts and word meanings; abstracts only)
rows.change: Use supplied mnemonics (keyword images, letter strategies) taught explicitly, with cued and uncued recall each session; keep the sets small; teacher presents cues orally if decoding is weak
rows.if: Learners have learning disabilities, behaviour difficulties or mild intellectual or developmental disabilities

rows.basis: [In the few studies that split by ability, learning techniques helped low-ability students and not high-ability students](claims/learning-techniques-benefit-low-ability-not-high-ability-students.md) [~M] (19 studies, all ten techniques pooled, not mnemonics alone)
rows.change: Skip the mnemonic for items they can already organise; give retrieval practice and use tasks instead; offer a mnemonic only for a truly arbitrary list
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` or high-achieving on this content

rows.basis: untested proposal; the disabilities claim is for school-age students and does not separate ages
rows.change: Supply the cue, as a picture with the words; one mnemonic per lesson; children unpack it aloud; do not ask young children to invent keyword images
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary age)

rows.basis: untested proposal; the earlier page's note that older adults lean on strategic memory aids is uncited
rows.change: Ask what memory aids they already use; offer a mnemonic for a fixed order or list, and pair it with a job aid they can consult; check use in the real task
rows.if: Learners are `adult`s at work, or older adults (terminology, a safety sequence, a medication list)

rows.basis: [retrieval practice produced more learning than … the keyword mnemonic](claims/retrieval-practice-produces-more-learning-than-concept-mapping-and-imagery-elaboration.md) [-M] (vocabulary experiments reported second-hand); [Summarization, highlighting, the keyword mnemonic…](claims/five-techniques-low-utility.md) [-M]
rows.change: Spend the time on spaced retrieval of word–meaning pairs first; use a keyword image only for a few words that keep failing, and practise recall in both directions
rows.if: Goal is second-language vocabulary

rows.basis: [Learning techniques have much smaller effects on deep learning and far transfer than on surface learning and near transfer](claims/learning-techniques-smaller-effects-on-deep-learning-and-far-transfer.md) [~M] (all ten techniques; only 109 of 1,619 effects measured deep outcomes)
rows.change: Teach the relationship first and test it with a changed case; use a mnemonic only for the labels the reasoning uses
rows.if: Goal is a `concept`, `principle` or transfer, not recall

rows.basis: untested for mnemonics; the scheduling carries [Spaced Practice Improves Retention](claims/spaced-practice-improves-retention.md) [+S]
rows.change: Show the cue with a picture and audio, then a recall card that hides it; schedule recall cards at about one day, one week and a month; ask for one use of the items in a short task
rows.if: Setting is `online-self-paced`, phone-only, or no teacher present

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Put the cue and the item list on a shared screen or document; take recall in the chat or a shared form as well as aloud, so remote learners are checked the same way
rows.if: Some learners are remote and some in the room

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Teach the cue to everyone at once in 5 minutes; let recall run on cards or an app between sessions; in the check-in, ask each learner for the items without the cue and look only at that
rows.if: One teacher with a large group, or scarce facilitator time (a volunteer, a brief check-in)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: One mnemonic: 5 minutes meaning and cue, 3 minutes cued then uncued recall, 5 minutes using the items in a task, 2 minutes to write the cue on a take-away card; do not claim retention
rows.if: A single session only, or a fixed short time budget (for example 15 minutes)

rows.basis: untested proposal; the disabilities claim's Discussion notes very weak decoders may need teacher-presented cues
rows.change: Build cues from spoken words and pictures, not spelled initials; let learners recall by pointing or ordering cards before saying or writing; recall in pairs before the group
rows.if: Learners have low literacy or low confidence

rows.basis: untested proposal; spacing from [Spaced Practice Improves Retention](claims/spaced-practice-improves-retention.md) [+S]
rows.change: Keep it; change only what the evidence says matters: explain what each part stands for, add cued then uncued recall, and bring it back in spaced reviews
rows.if: The brief names its own mnemonic, routine or memory aid (a course acrostic, a unit song, a job's checklist)

rows.basis: untested
rows.change: Build the mnemonic on its categories and order; do not regroup the content to suit a nicer cue
rows.if: The brief gives its own categories, list or rubric

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: The learner keeps their cues private and chooses what to share; check recall of the items, not the cue
rows.if: Learners' cues or memory notes are personal or sensitive (images from their own lives)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use the mnemonic to rehearse the order beforehand, then run the performance whole; do not turn it into recall items
rows.if: The output is a performance or product for a real audience, kept whole (a presentation, a clinical handover, a recital)

rows.basis: untested proposal, from the earlier page's warning that some cues oversimplify procedures
rows.change: Check that the cue cannot be misread into a wrong step; require uncued recall and correct performance of the real sequence; keep a written aid at the point of use
rows.if: Stakes are high, or an error is costly (a safety or medical sequence)

rows.basis: [Spoken narration rather than on-screen text alongside graphics improves learning](claims/modality-effect-narration-over-text.md) [+S] (Ginns d = 0.72; Noetel g = 0.38, 0.20 after bias correction); [pacing](claims/modality-effect-moderated-by-pacing.md) [+M] (d = 0.93 system-paced); strongest when the pace is fast for the learner ([boundary conditions](claims/modality-boundary-conditions-pace-control.md) [~M])
rows.change: Narrate the words; keep only labels or key terms on screen
rows.if: System-paced video, narrated animation or lecture, `novice` learners, words explain the picture

rows.basis: [Pacing moderates the modality effect](claims/modality-effect-moderated-by-pacing.md) [~M] (d = −0.14 self-paced)
rows.change: Keep the words printed, beside the part of the picture they describe; do not convert to narration
rows.if: Learner-paced slides, web pages or an e-book learners scroll through themselves

rows.basis: [The modality effect reverses with expertise](claims/expertise-reversal-modality-effect-review.md) [-M]
rows.change: Give the diagram with little or no accompanying text or narration; make narration optional
rows.if: Learners already know this content well, or have used the device or diagram before (`advanced`)

rows.basis: [Design principle effects were not moderated by prior knowledge across reviews](claims/design-principle-effects-moderated-by-pacing-and-complexity.md) [~M]; the mute option is an untested proposal
rows.change: Narrate by default and let more experienced learners mute it or skip ahead
rows.if: Mixed prior knowledge in one group

rows.basis: [Design principles mattered more in complex media (g = 0.70) than simple (g = 0.20)](claims/design-principle-effects-moderated-by-pacing-and-complexity.md) [+M]
rows.change: Narration is the priority; apply it before lower-value refinements
rows.if: Complex material: a process with many interacting parts (circuits, physiology, machinery)

rows.basis: [same](claims/design-principle-effects-moderated-by-pacing-and-complexity.md) [~M]
rows.change: Either channel is acceptable; choose by access and cost
rows.if: Simple material, few interacting parts

rows.basis: [Modality effects differ by field: science d = 1.20, social science d = −0.13](claims/modality-effect-field-of-study-moderator.md) [~M]
rows.change: Do not expect a benefit from narrating; printed words the learner can reread are as good
rows.if: Content is social science (argument, policy, history) rather than science, engineering or mathematics

rows.basis: [The modality effect held for middle-school students learning electricity, d = .35](claims/modality-effect-holds-middle-school-electricity.md) [+M] (quasi-experiment); [adding written text to narration made no significant difference](claims/redundancy-effect-not-significant-middle-school.md) [~M]
rows.change: Narrate; expect a smaller effect than in the adult lab studies. Adding the written words under the narration is not needed, but did no measurable harm in the same study
rows.if: Middle-school children (`k-12`) learning a science unit from animation

rows.basis: Modality comparison untested; [narration with finger-tracking animation directed bilingual preschoolers' looking to the print being read](claims/enhancing-features-direct-attention-dual-language-e-books.md) [~M] (attention measured, not learning; the effect stopped when the animation ended)
rows.change: Speech is the default for any accompanying explanation; untested as a modality comparison at this age. In an e-book whose aim is exposure to print, pair the narration with highlighting or a tracking pointer on the words being read, which draws children's eyes to the text
rows.if: Younger children, still learning to read

rows.basis: [Mayer: 17 of 17 experiments with college learners, median d = 1.02](claims/modality-principle-mayer-2008.md) [+M]; [animation or picture with voice beat picture with text for 36 adults](claims/voice-media-outperform-picture-text-overall.md) [+M]
rows.change: Narrate system-paced explanations
rows.if: Adults (`postsecondary`, workplace training)

rows.basis: Conflicting: [the modality effect was larger with head-mounted displays (d = 1.34) than computer screens (d = 0.55)](claims/modality-effect-stronger-in-virtual-reality.md) [~M] (a moderator contrast, few studies); in a later VR experiment (61 learners, a unit on HIV) printed text beat narration on [recall](claims/vr-reverse-modality-effect-recall.md) [-M] and [comprehension](claims/vr-reverse-modality-effect-comprehension.md) [-M], with Bayesian tests favouring the reversal ([reverse modality effect in VR](claims/vr-reverse-modality-bayesian-evidence.md) [-M])
rows.change: Do not assume narration wins. Pilot both channels on the brief's own test; if printed text is used, keep it short and anchored to the object it names rather than floating over the scene
rows.if: VR headset or immersive scene

rows.basis: untested
rows.change: Make the narrated version the default but ensure the lesson works with captions on and learner pause control
rows.if: Phone-only, commuting or noisy settings where learners may not listen

rows.basis: untested on this page; see the placement rows of [Multimedia Learning](principles/multimedia-learning.md)
rows.change: Modality does not apply; put each sentence next to the part of the diagram it explains
rows.if: Print only (handout, workbook)

rows.basis: [Redundancy principle: animation plus narration beat animation, narration and on-screen text](claims/redundancy-principle-mayer-2008.md) [+M]; carrying it from computer lessons to a live teacher is untested
rows.change: The teacher's speech is the narration: show the picture with key terms, and do not read out a slide of full sentences
rows.if: Live teacher with slides

rows.basis: [captioning L2 video aided comprehension (g = 0.99)](claims/captioning-second-language-videos-large-benefits.md) [~M]; [spoken–written beat spoken-only only when system-paced](claims/system-paced-moderates-verbal-redundancy.md) [~M]; [no spoken–written benefit once pictures were present](claims/images-animation-eliminate-redundancy-benefit.md) [~M]; where listening itself is a goal, captioned video is reported to improve L2 listening ([bimodal captioned input](claims/bimodal-captioned-input-improves-segmentation.md) [~W], reported second-hand)
rows.change: Keep narration for system-paced lessons with pictures, slow it or segment it, and offer captions; for picture-free audio, written text alongside helps
rows.if: Learners study in a second language

rows.basis: [Spoken–written redundancy is not harmful on average; key terms beat verbatim text](claims/redundancy-hurts-learning.md) [~S]; [Mayer: verbatim on-screen text over narrated animation hurt transfer](claims/redundancy-principle-mayer-2008.md) [-M]; [middle-school null](claims/redundancy-effect-not-significant-middle-school.md) [~M]
rows.change: Keep them, condensed to key terms where the policy allows; narration stays the main channel for the explanation
rows.if: Captions or on-screen text must stay on for everyone (accessibility policy, platform default)

rows.basis: untested; the evidence was gathered with readers
rows.change: Narrate; printed explanation alongside a picture adds a reading load these learners cannot spare
rows.if: Low literacy

rows.basis: untested; the modality evidence assumes the learner hears the words
rows.change: Printed words (captions or text) are required; place them next to what they describe and give learners pause control, which removes most of the pacing cost
rows.if: Deaf or hard-of-hearing learners

rows.basis: untested
rows.change: The picture is not the channel; narration must describe what the picture shows, and the modality comparison does not apply
rows.if: Blind or low-vision learners

rows.basis: [Matching instruction to learning style does not improve learning](claims/learning-styles-matching-does-not-improve-learning.md) [-S]
rows.change: Choose the channel by the material and pacing, not the stated style
rows.if: A learner says they are an "auditory" or "visual" learner

rows.basis: [Letting learners pace helped on complex material, while learner control in general showed almost no effect](claims/learner-paced-beats-system-paced-complex-material.md) [~M]; the check question is an untested proposal
rows.change: Narrated short segments with pause and replay; a short "what happens if" question after each
rows.if: One teacher for many, or `online-self-paced` with no teacher

rows.basis: untested
rows.change: Keep the lesson as long as it is; narrating does not lengthen a system-paced lesson. Do not add a test the brief did not ask for
rows.if: A single session, or a fixed short time budget

rows.basis: untested
rows.change: Keep them as given; change only the channel of the explanatory words, and run the brief's own assessment as given
rows.if: The brief's own materials, routine or rubric

rows.basis: untested
rows.change: Provide a captioned or transcript route so no learner must play audio aloud
rows.if: Private or sensitive material, or learners in shared spaces

rows.basis: untested
rows.change: Narrate within the whole demonstration, segmenting at natural breaks rather than splitting the task
rows.if: A whole task kept whole (a full procedure shown end to end)

rows.basis: [Spoken narration rather than on-screen text improves learning](claims/modality-effect-narration-over-text.md) [+S]
rows.change: Use narration for system-paced explanations but plan for the smaller bias-corrected effect (g = 0.20) and pilot on the real assessment before relying on it
rows.if: High stakes (certification, safety)

rows.basis: [Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows.](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M] (review of cognitive-load studies; no crossover point)
rows.change: Skip the full model: let them attempt first, then compare their work with an expert model and name the differences; model only the one new decision
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` on this task, or succeed on the first item unaided

rows.basis: [Lower-prior-knowledge learners scored higher on an algebra posttest after full-worked than completion-worked examples, while higher-prior-knowledge learners' non-significant advantage ran the other way](claims/lower-prior-knowledge-learners-score-higher-with-full-than-completion-worked-examples.md) [~M] (college algebra, one experiment; carried to live modelling)
rows.change: Keep complete models (every step shown and narrated) for longer before any partial or completion model; slow down and segment further (one decision per pause)
rows.if: Learners have very low prior knowledge of the task

rows.basis: [Modeling training improved imaginative play in disadvantaged kindergartners, with gains in imaginativeness, verbal communication, spontaneity, and attention span persisting two months](claims/modeling-training-improves-imaginative-play.md) [+W] (80 kindergartners, a 1973 report read second-hand; modelling combined with direct teaching)
rows.change: Model by acting out with materials in small groups, over several short sessions (the study used eight), and let children re-enact straight after
rows.if: Learners are young `child`ren, and the target is play, social or motor behaviour

rows.basis: [Prompting learners to self-explain improves understanding and problem solving on immediate tests by a moderate average amount, with little evidence yet on delayed or classroom gains.](claims/self-explanation-improves-conceptual-understanding.md) [+S]; [Erroneous examples improve conceptual understanding by forcing comparison with correct models.](claims/erroneous-examples-build-conceptual-knowledge.md) [+M] (grades 4–5, decimals, tutoring; carried to live modelling)
rows.change: Model on two items that differ on the surface; at each pause ask why, not what; include one error and its repair, and ask learners what gave it away
rows.if: Goal is a `concept` or `principle`, or transfer, not only a `procedure`

rows.basis: [Learners' task-specific self-efficacy beliefs predict whether they initiate, persist through, and recover from difficulty on academic tasks.](claims/self-efficacy-predicts-academic-persistence.md) [+M] (two reviews; names watching similar others as one source of self-efficacy, does not compare model types). [Proximal goals and ability attributional feedback for early learning raise self-efficacy more than distant goals and effort feedback, by a review's report of earlier studies](claims/proximal-goals-feedback-peer-models-build-learning-efficacy.md) [~W]: its title names peer models, but neither of its entries reports them
rows.change: Use a model the learners see as like themselves (a peer, a former student, the teacher showing an early struggle), who makes and recovers from mistakes and says what they did next; pair it with an early task they can succeed at
rows.if: Goal is confidence, persistence or willingness to try (`attitude-motivation`), not only skill

rows.basis: [Mentor modelling and a school-wide behaviour program's strategies transferred to the mentee's classroom management practices](claims/mentor-modelling-strategies-transfer-mentee-behaviour-management.md) [+W] (one preservice teacher, qualitative case); [Vicarious experiences are positively related to agriculture teachers' general teaching efficacy, with observing a first year teacher explaining 11% of variance](claims/vicarious-experiences-positive-teaching-efficacy.md) [+W] (correlational, reported in a review)
rows.change: Model the performance in the real setting (the mentor's own lesson, a supervised shift), then debrief the decisions it involved, then have the novice try the same move with the mentor watching
rows.if: `adult` learners in a work setting (`workplace-clinical`), or teachers in training

rows.basis: [Comparing original texts to model paragraphs prompted noticing that was again focused on lexical features](claims/model-comparison-noticing-lexical.md) [~W] (one EFL learner, case study); [Teacher modeling with worked examples helped EFL students internalize reading comprehension strategies](claims/teacher-modeling-internalizes-reading-strategies.md) [+W] (students' questionnaire comments, one study); otherwise untested
rows.change: Draft live in front of learners, thinking aloud about audience and choices, and revise visibly; show two different good products and name the features they share, so learners do not copy one product's wording
rows.if: Writing, composing or other open tasks with no single right answer

rows.basis: [Students are more attentive to the teacher's model track when they hear their own recording first](claims/student-recording-first-increases-attention-to-model.md) [+W] (language lab, design report; attention, not learning, was observed). For true novices on a new performance, model first (step 2 of the default)
rows.change: Have learners record their own attempt, listen to it, then hear the model, then try again
rows.if: Pronunciation, music or other performances learners can record

rows.basis: untested proposal; the explanation prompt is carried from [Prompting learners to self-explain…](claims/self-explanation-improves-conceptual-understanding.md) [+S]
rows.change: Record short clips, one decision each (about 2–5 minutes), each ending in a predict-or-explain question the learner must answer before the next clip; follow with automatically checked practice items
rows.if: Setting is `online-self-paced`, or video only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Model on a shared screen or document camera rather than a whiteboard; narrate into the microphone; at each pause collect predictions in the chat or a poll from everyone, remote first; record the model and share it after for replay. For phone-only learners, send the recording cut into short clips with the pause questions in text
rows.if: Some learners are remote while others are in the room, or some join by phone only

rows.basis: untested proposal; the explanation step is carried from [Prompting learners to self-explain…](claims/self-explanation-improves-conceptual-understanding.md) [+S], and the large field study under [Constructive learning beats active and passive learning](claims/constructive-learning-beats-active-passive.md) [~M] found only the most interactive activities ahead of passive ones in real classes
rows.change: Give one live model to all; at each pause have every learner show a prediction at once (cards, mini-whiteboards, a poll); then in pairs, one learner narrates the next item while the other checks against the modelled decision list; re-model only for the error most pairs show
rows.if: One teacher with a large group

rows.basis: [Example-based sequences outperform problem-only practice for novices, and fading support is argued to aid transfer](claims/worked-examples-with-practice-improve-transfer.md) [+M] (example-first beat problem-first in one short troubleshooting task, immediate test)
rows.change: Model one item fully with narration, then a partial model the learners finish, then one unaided item; record what the unaided item shows and do not claim retention
rows.if: Time is one session only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Model by doing more than by telling: fewer words, gestures, labelled pictures; name and display only the key terms; let learners show the next move rather than explain it in words
rows.if: Learners have low literacy, or work in a second language

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Model the finished performance once at full speed as the audience would see it; then model it again slowed down with the reasoning narrated, in a rehearsal space the audience never sees; keep the reasoning in a debrief or a separate annotated version
rows.if: The performance is for a real audience, or a product whose audience should not see the reasoning (a client-facing call, a published piece)

rows.basis: untested proposal; the error step is carried from [Erroneous examples improve conceptual understanding by forcing comparison with correct models.](claims/erroneous-examples-build-conceptual-knowledge.md) [+M]
rows.change: Model the whole procedure once at normal speed, then step by step with what to check and why; include the commonest error and how it is caught; require an unaided demonstration under supervision before the learner works alone
rows.if: High stakes or safety (clinical, lab, machinery)

rows.basis: [Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals.](claims/process-goals-outperform-outcome-goals-for-novices.md) [+M] (high-school writing revision); [self-efficacy predicts persistence](claims/self-efficacy-predicts-academic-persistence.md) [+M] (predictive reviews, not a test of the move)
rows.change: Treat expectancy as the low component: an item they can do first, process goals, feedback naming the strategy that worked; hold back rewards and hooks
rows.if: Learners are `novice` on the task and withdraw after early failure

rows.basis: [Expected tangible rewards reduce later free-choice engagement with a rewarded task, while verbal praise does not](claims/rewards-undermine-intrinsic-motivation.md) [~S] (undermining is for tasks already found interesting); choice and challenge untested here
rows.change: Do not add tangible rewards or points for taking part; offer harder goals and choices of topic or product
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` or already interested in the topic

rows.basis: [Rewards](claims/rewards-undermine-intrinsic-motivation.md) [~S] (one meta-analysis found rewards more detrimental for children than college students); [praise for intelligence](claims/feedback-praise-reduces-learning.md) [~M] (fifth graders, nonverbal problems); [parents' process praise to toddlers](claims/process-praise-toddlers-predicts-achievement-via-incremental-frameworks.md) [+M] (53 children, associational, from age one to fourth grade)
rows.change: No tangible rewards for merely taking part; praise the strategy or effort, not the child's cleverness, especially before harder work; the teacher keeps the progress chart; where families are involved, suggest they praise what the child did rather than what the child is
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary age)

rows.basis: [Task value](claims/task-value-increases-motivation-and-engagement.md) [+M] (reviews; the writing exercise reported second-hand); [interesting instruction and engagement](claims/interesting-science-instruction-associated-emotional-engagement.md) [+M] and [grade moderates the link](claims/grade-moderates-interesting-instruction-engagement-link.md) [~M] (one multilevel study of 6,465 science students; steepest in grade 6; associational)
rows.change: Value first: the relevance-writing exercise at each unit start, two or three options of topic within the unit; in a transition year (the first year of middle or secondary school), put effort into making lessons interesting and understandable, because perceived interest goes with emotional engagement most strongly then
rows.if: Learners are `adolescent` and say the subject is pointless

rows.basis: [L2 Learning Experience Beats Ideal L2 Self](claims/l2-learning-experience-beats-ideal-l2-self.md) [+M] (one survey of 511 learners in Japan, intended effort self-reported); [intrinsic motivation and intended effort](claims/sdt-path-strengths-effort.md) [+M] (same learners); associational, so the move is untested
rows.change: Put the effort into the lessons themselves (early success, enjoyable tasks, a teacher and group the learner wants to come back to) before future-self or career-vision exercises; ask what the learner wants to use the language for and build tasks on it
rows.if: Learners are studying a second or foreign language

rows.basis: [Prolonged reading failure leads students to attribute failure to fixed low ability and define reading as a failure situation](claims/reading-failure-fixed-ability-attribution.md) [+W] (an ERIC paper reporting an earlier fifth-grade experiment second-hand); the moves are untested for this group
rows.change: Treat expectancy as the low component and expect them to read success as luck: a private success first, then name the strategy that produced it so the learner can own it; avoid criticism tied to the learner rather than the work
rows.if: Learners have a long history of failure in the subject (struggling readers, learners repeating a course)

rows.basis: untested proposal; [task value](claims/task-value-increases-motivation-and-engagement.md) [+M] carried from school and college reviews to the workplace
rows.change: Ask what each learner wants from it; tie each module to a task from their own job; cut time cost (short modules in work time); give a reason for each required item
rows.if: Adults in work settings, training they did not choose (compliance, onboarding)

rows.basis: [Belonging Interventions Improve Outcomes](claims/belonging-interventions-improve-outcomes.md) [+M] (college entry only; no effect where belonging was not afforded); [smaller decline after a belonging intervention](claims/belonging-intervention-smaller-decline.md) [+M] and [belonging predicts intention to persist](claims/sense-of-belonging-predicts-persistence-intentions.md) [+M] (one first-year college study; intention, not enrolment); for school-age learners, [school belonging carried a group difference in intrinsic motivation](claims/school-belonging-mediation-dominican-intrinsic-motivation.md) [+W] (middle childhood, associational) and [Teacher support is the strongest predictor of school belonging](claims/teacher-support-strongest-predictor-school-belonging.md) [+M] (associational) supports starting with teacher contact
rows.change: A short belonging exercise at entry (adversity is common and passes, written in their own words); check that the setting gives them real ways to take part; keep up personal contact across the year, since belonging tends to fall over a first year even where the exercise works
rows.if: First year of college, a new school, or learners from groups who are often told they do not belong

rows.basis: [Math anxiety has a small-to-moderate negative correlation with math achievement (r = −.28) in a meta-analysis of correlations from 223 studies](claims/math-anxiety-degrades-performance.md) [~M] (correlation r = −.28 across 223 studies; direction not established); [Girls show less confidence and interest in math and science from early adolescence, and a strong math/science self-concept predicts course choice and performance for both genders](claims/girls-confidence-interest-gap-self-concept-predicts-choices.md) [+M] (a practice guide's review of correlational studies; girls in math and science) for treating low confidence as a reason learners avoid the subject; [automatically marked formative checks and exam confidence](claims/automated-marking-higher-exam-confidence.md) [+M] (one A-level sciences study, d = 0.76 on self-reported confidence; reduced mathematics anxiety reported only in qualitative feedback) for the frequent checks; the other moves are untested
rows.change: Private, untimed first attempts; no public answering until the learner has succeeded privately; simpler language in instructions than in the target task; frequent short checks marked at once, so confidence is built on results the learner can see
rows.if: Learners with low confidence, low literacy, or anxiety about the subject (for example mathematics)

rows.basis: [Pre-tests reduced adult learners' persistence in a MOOC, though they improved post-test scores among those who completed it](claims/pretesting-can-harm-motivation.md) [~M] (one randomized MOOC experiment, abstract); [Teachers treat resilience under challenge as a teachable skill that current routines and dashboards do little to support](claims/resilience-teachable-skill-unsupported.md) [~W] (one teacher workshop, qualitative) for the flag; the rest untested
rows.change: Do not open with a test on material not yet taught, or make it optional and say errors are expected; track return days and completion, not clicks; build the four questions into the first activity; flag learners who abandon a problem right after a first failure, so someone or something responds
rows.if: `online-self-paced` and voluntary (an open online course)

rows.basis: [Nearly all students valued learning through effort while feeling drawn toward AI, and split into those who limited use and those whose use conflicted with stated values](claims/value-effort-tension-ai-shortcuts.md) [~W] and [Peer AI use diminished some students' sense of their own effort's value through social comparison, independent of their own AI use](claims/peer-ai-use-social-comparison-devalues-effort.md) [~W] (one interview study of 13 introductory programmers); [Students express fear and apathy about AI's impact on their careers, shifting focus toward outcomes over process and questioning effort investment in learning computer science](claims/career-fear-apathy-outcomes-over-process.md) [~W] (a second interview study in computing); [Easy access to AI-generated answers may reduce learners' motivation to engage deeply with material](claims/ai-over-reliance-reduces-deep-engagement.md) [~W] (a systematic review reporting it second-hand, hedged); [ChatGPT-assisted students reported substantially lower ownership of their submitted code across self-attributed ownership, psychological ownership, and authorship attribution](claims/chatgpt-lower-code-ownership.md) [~M] (one experiment, g = 1.05–1.11; ownership of the product, not this page's ownership component, which is about whose reasons drive the work); [Students rated the LLM-based assignments as useful, challenging, engaging, and enjoyable at both the first and fifth iterations, with no significant change across the semester](claims/positive-affective-responses-llm-assignments.md) [+W] and [self-efficacy for using generative AI rose over the semester](claims/self-efficacy-growth-generative-ai-semester.md) [+W] (one course, no comparison group)
rows.change: Treat value and ownership as at risk: say what the learner's own effort builds that AI output does not; grade and make visible the process (drafts, attempts, explanations), so effort does not look worthless beside peers' AI-assisted grades; ask learners how much of the submitted work they count as their own; where learners fear AI will take the jobs the course leads to, name what the course builds that they will still need, since that fear turns attention to grades over process. Where AI is a designed partner in an assignment, positive ratings and rising confidence with the tool are not evidence of learning: probe the target unaided
rows.if: Generative AI is available for the work (programming, writing, problem sets)

rows.basis: [A personalized ability signal increased the probability of participating in AP classes by 49 percentage points among surveyed students](claims/ability-signal-increases-ap-participation-49-points.md) [+M] (one district's AP enrolment, surveyed students); [Students who received the ability signal enrolled in and passed about one more AP course the following year](claims/ability-signal-one-more-ap-course.md) [+M] (same study: the choice carried into a passed course the next year; persistence beyond that is not recorded)
rows.change: Send each such learner a short personal message that they have the potential to succeed, added to communications they already receive; follow it with early success once they enrol
rows.if: The decision is whether to take on harder or optional work (an advanced course, an elective, the next level) and learners who could succeed are not choosing it

rows.basis: [expectancy](claims/teacher-expectancy-beliefs-shape-motivation-to-use-ai.md) [+W]; [attainment value](claims/teacher-attainment-value-increases-motivation-to-use-ai.md) [+W]; [utility value](claims/teacher-utility-value-increases-motivation-to-use-ai.md) [+W]; [interest value](claims/teacher-intrinsic-interest-value-increases-motivation-to-use-ai.md) [+W]; [cost](claims/teacher-perceived-cost-reduces-motivation-to-use-ai.md) [+W] (one theoretical paper, no data); untested as a design
rows.change: Ask about each component as it applies to the tool: whether they expect to use it well, whether it serves their professional goals and identity, whether it is enjoyable, and what it costs them; cut the cost first (time to learn it inside paid time, resources and support, honest information on reliability)
rows.if: Learners are teachers or staff asked to adopt a new tool or practice (for example AI applications)

rows.basis: [Students in courses with guided note-taking and other active learning activities reported less difficulty with motivation and engagement after the shift online](claims/guided-note-taking-supported-remote-engagement.md) [+W] (focus groups in 28 STEM courses during the 2020 move online, qualitative) for the guided outline; the rest untested
rows.change: Contact remote learners by name in the first minutes of each session; give them the same private first attempt (a message or form) the room gets; give remote learners something to produce during a live lecture (a guided outline handed in for credit); keep choices workable on a phone
rows.if: Mixed modes: some learners remote, some in the room, or phone-only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Spend the scarce minutes on one question about the likely low component, and on the learners whose behaviour dropped; let relevance sentences and progress records be written by learners without the facilitator
rows.if: One teacher with many learners, or scarce facilitator time (volunteers, a busy shift, a tutor checking in briefly)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Give the reason, one first success, and one choice; record the behaviour; do not claim lasting motivation
rows.if: Time is one session only

rows.basis: untested proposal; how audiences work is on [Authentic Audiences and Purposes](principles/authentic-audiences-purposes.md)
rows.change: Let the audience supply the reason; lower the cost of public failure with a private rehearsal and feedback before the audience sees it
rows.if: A product or performance for a real audience

rows.basis: [Rewards](claims/rewards-undermine-intrinsic-motivation.md) [~S]; [math anxiety](claims/math-anxiety-degrades-performance.md) [~M] (correlational); [Students generally attempted fewer items under ego-involving than task-involving feedback, but this gap disappeared among praised students](claims/feedback-manner-main-effect-motivation-gap-closes-with-praise.md) [+M] (one experiment, 146 students; attempts, not learning); [Participants identified assessment redesign approaches for helping all students feel successful, centering relevance, lowered stakes, choice, emotional support, and preparation](claims/assessment-redesign-insights-tlc-convening.md) [+W] (one convening of teachers and students, interviews); untested as a package
rows.change: Present grades as information about what to do next; keep feedback about mastering the task rather than rank against others; do not add prizes; reduce timed public performance for anxious learners; where the assessment can be redesigned, lower the stakes of early attempts and offer a choice of how to show the learning
rows.if: Stakes are high (grades, certification)

rows.basis: [Children with ADHD show higher external regulation, introjected regulation and amotivation, and lower intrinsic motivation and identified regulation, toward learning than TD children](claims/adhd-motivation-profile-sdt-dimensions.md) [~M] and [Increased motivation eliminated ADHD–TD differences on most attention measures but differences persisted in complex multitasking and commission errors](claims/motivation-reduces-but-not-eliminates-adhd-deficits.md) [~M] (one study of 30 children with ADHD and 30 without; motivation raised by reward and competition during laboratory attention tasks; in-task attention, not learning or later engagement)
