rows.change: Expect ownership to be the component to watch (more work under pressure, less from their own reasons); during sustained-attention work, an immediate incentive or game element can help the learner perform at their level; plan its withdrawal and keep building the learner's own reasons, because an expected reward is what lowers later voluntary engagement; keep tasks that demand several things at once short and structured, since motivation did not close that gap
rows.if: Learners with ADHD or other attention difficulties

rows.basis: [Growth-mindset interventions have weak average effects on achievement, including a negligible GPA gain (d = 0.11) for lower-achieving US ninth-graders in one preregistered national trial](claims/growth-mindset-improves-achievement.md) [~S] (ninth-graders; about a tenth of a grade point for lower achievers, weak overall); [peer norms](claims/peer-norms-sustain-mindset-gpa-effects.md) [~M] and [teacher mindset](claims/growth-mindset-interventions-conditional-teacher-context.md) [~M] (US ninth-graders in national trials; the effect appeared only with supportive peers or teachers)
rows.change: Keep it short, pair it with strategy instruction on the actual work, and make sure effort visibly changes results in the course; aim it at lower-achieving learners; expect a small effect; first ask whether the teachers and the peer group will back it (teachers who say ability is fixed, a class culture that avoids hard problems), and if not, work on that first or drop the message
rows.if: The plan relies on a mindset message, a motivational talk or an assembly

rows.basis: untested proposal; [rewards](claims/rewards-undermine-intrinsic-motivation.md) [~S] for the points change
rows.change: Keep it; change only what the evidence says matters: points tied to progress or performance rather than mere participation, the check-in asking about the low component, the survey followed by a probe of learning
rows.if: The brief names its own routine (its own points system, motivation survey, check-in or reward chart)

rows.basis: [Positive motivational assessments of introductory activities correlate weakly with learning outcomes on near-in-time tests but not with distant exam results](claims/motivational-assessments-correlate-weakly-near-tests.md) [~M] (elementary pupils, one study)
rows.change: Measure voluntary return or later course choice, not enjoyment at the end of a session
rows.if: The goal is `attitude-motivation` itself (continued study, voluntary practice)

rows.basis: [Words with pictures against words alone](claims/multimedia-principle-improves-learning.md) [+M] (two lab experiments, immediate test); [words with corresponding graphics beat words alone on transfer](claims/generative-processing-principles-mayer-2008.md) [+M] (Mayer's programme, 11 of 11 comparisons, median d = 1.39). Against: [an instructional image added to biology texts changed neither test scores nor monitoring accuracy](claims/instructional-visuals-no-effect-test-performance-or-test-explain-accuracy.md) [-M] (163 and 48 undergraduates online, d = 0.01 and 0.06), and [graphs did not improve vector-calculus problem solving](claims/no-overall-multimedia-effect-vector-calculus.md) [-M] (36 engineering-physics students, 56% against 52% correct)
rows.change: Add a picture that depicts the process or structure the words describe; keep it to the parts the words name, and say what job it does, since an image added without one may change nothing
rows.if: The lesson explains a process or system, and learners are `novice` on it

rows.basis: [Diagrams helped only when students read the lesson twice, not when they answered questions while reading](claims/diagrams-help-posttest-only-read-twice-condition.md) [~M] (198 undergraduates, posterior probability lesson, no effect size printed)
rows.change: Leave time to study the diagram with the text (a second reading); do not expect the diagram to add on its own while attention goes to the questions
rows.if: Learners will answer questions while reading the illustrated text, or will read it only once

rows.basis: [Animation beat static pictures for identifying motions](claims/animation-beats-static-pictures-for-identifying-motions.md) [+M] (88 pre-service teachers, d = 2.33 and 2.41) and [a single picture beat animation for arrangements](claims/single-picture-beats-animation-for-spatial-arrangements.md) [~M] (d = 1.30); [animation's small overall advantage](claims/animation-small-overall-advantage-over-static-graphics.md) [~M] (61 studies, g = 0.23); [a re-analysis found the advantage only when features of the change were relevant](claims/reanalysis-features-of-change-moderator.md) [~M] (g = 0.34 and 0.65 against 0.04, reported second-hand). See the pattern's row for pacing and commentary
rows.change: Choose by what the learner must identify: an animation for how parts move or change, a single static picture for how they are arranged (not a strip of snapshots); expect a small average advantage for animation, and none when the changes shown are not what is to be learned
rows.if: The choice is between a static picture and an animation

rows.basis: [Sketching and animation gave the best understanding of a geoscience text, a photograph the worst](claims/sketching-animation-best-understanding-photograph-worst.md) [~M] (120 undergraduates, six conditions, ηp² = .19 for condition); [abstract and concrete animations did not differ](claims/abstract-concrete-representation-no-difference.md) [~M] (a middle-school electricity quasi-experiment; not an equivalence test)
rows.change: Prefer a diagram or animation that shows the process, or ask learners to sketch it; how realistic an animation looks mattered less than whether it showed the process
rows.if: The picture on offer is a photograph or a realistic rendering

rows.basis: [Spatially integrating text and diagrams](claims/split-attention-effect-degrades-learning.md) [+M] (meta-analysis, g = 0.63); [Contiguity principles](claims/contiguity-principles-mayer-2008.md) [+M] (Mayer's programme, effect size 1.12)
rows.change: Put each label or sentence next to the part of the picture it refers to, and present narration at the same time as the matching animation
rows.if: Words and the picture they describe are on different parts of the screen or page, or arrive at different times

rows.basis: [Coherence principle](claims/coherence-principle-irrelevant-material-hurts-learning.md) [+M] (13 of 14 experiments, median d = 0.97); [Interesting but irrelevant additions](claims/seductive-details-effect.md) [~M] (harm depends on image type and on learners' prior knowledge); a curriculum revision [replaced a decorative photograph in a math problem with a problem-relevant sketch](claims/decorative-images-distract-from-math-problems.md) [+W] (the developers' view, no data). Qualified by Scherer et al.: [related decorative pictures raised knowledge scores](claims/related-decorative-pictures-improve-knowledge-exp1.md) [~M] (71 teacher-education students, ηp² = .075) and [eighth-graders' monitoring accuracy on knowledge items](claims/related-pictures-improve-metacognitive-monitoring-exp2.md) [~M], but [not transfer in either experiment](claims/related-decorative-pictures-no-transfer-effect.md) [~M]
rows.change: Cut it, and keep only what the explanation needs; replace a decorative photograph with a sketch of what the problem is about. A decorative picture thematically related to the topic need not be cut, but do not count on it for transfer
rows.if: The lesson carries interesting but unneeded material (stories, background music, decorative images, extra facts)

rows.basis: [Redundancy principle](claims/redundancy-principle-mayer-2008.md) [+M] (5 of 5 experiments, median d = 0.72); qualified by [Duplicated words](claims/redundancy-hurts-learning.md) [~S] (with no picture, or for low prior knowledge learners at the system's pace, spoken plus written did not hurt). Where the duplicate is already there, removing it is a small change, not a rescue: [adding written text to narration made no significant difference with abstract or concrete animation](claims/redundancy-effect-not-significant-middle-school.md) [~M] (middle-school classroom quasi-experiment), [redundant text inside a diagram did not affect posttest accuracy](claims/redundant-text-no-effect-posterior-probability-lesson.md) [~M] (198 undergraduates, learner-paced), and [the overall spoken–written effect is small and varies widely](claims/verbal-redundancy-small-overall-effect.md) [~M] (g = 0.15, I² = .82); none of these is an equivalence test
rows.change: Drop the duplicated on-screen text, or keep only key terms
rows.if: An animation or diagram is explained by narration, and on-screen text repeats the narration word for word

rows.basis: [With images or animation, spoken–written was no better than spoken-only](claims/images-animation-eliminate-redundancy-benefit.md) [~M] (g = 0.06, against 0.45 and 0.24 without); [the advantage held for system-paced, not learner-paced, material](claims/system-paced-moderates-verbal-redundancy.md) [~M] (g = 0.34 against 0.12); [larger for unsegmented presentations](claims/segmentation-moderates-verbal-redundancy.md) [~M] (g = 0.53 against 0.15); all moderator analyses in Adesope and Nesbit's meta-analysis. See also the pattern's row for second-language and less fluent readers
rows.change: Give the words both spoken and written (key terms if not the full text); the spoken–written advantage disappears once a picture is added and is larger for unsegmented presentations
rows.if: No picture or animation, the presentation is system-paced, and learners may miss spoken words

rows.basis: [Modality principle](claims/modality-principle-mayer-2008.md) [+M] (17 of 17 experiments, median d = 1.02); [Modality effect](claims/modality-effect-narration-over-text.md) [+W] (Sweller and colleagues' review); [animation or picture with voice beat picture with text](claims/voice-media-outperform-picture-text-overall.md) [+M] (36 adults, 15-minute immunology lesson, p = .004, no effect size printed)
rows.change: Speak them rather than print them, when learners can follow spoken language at that pace
rows.if: Words accompany a diagram or animation, and the words could be spoken

rows.basis: In one middle-school quasi-experiment, [spoken text did not differ reliably from signaled written text](claims/spoken-versus-signaled-written-null.md) [~M] with abstract or concrete animation (not an equivalence test, and not with these learners); the rest is untested, since the modality evidence assumes learners can follow the spoken words
rows.change: Keep printed words, placed next to the picture, signal the key words in them, and give learner control of pace
rows.if: Learners are reading in a second language, are deaf or hard of hearing, or study where they cannot listen

rows.basis: [Segmenting improves retention and transfer](claims/segmenting-improves-multimedia-learning.md) [+M] (56 investigations, small-to-medium effects); [learner-paced segments beat continuous presentation on transfer](claims/segmenting-principle-mayer-2008.md) [+M] (Mayer's programme, 3 of 3 experiments with a "continue" button, median d = 0.98); [Segmentation increases learning time](claims/segmenting-increases-learning-time.md) [~M]; [the effects hold for system-paced segmentation too](claims/segmenting-effects-confirmed-system-paced.md) [+M]
rows.change: Break it into meaningful segments, with a pause or "next" between them; expect learners to take longer
rows.if: The lesson is a long continuous video or narrated animation

rows.basis: [High prior knowledge learners benefited more from segmenting for retention](claims/prior-knowledge-moderates-segmenting-retention.md) [~M] (meta-analysis); this runs against [Segmenting and prior knowledge](claims/segmentation-benefits-shrink-with-expertise.md) [~M] (one experiment: efficiency gain only for lower prior knowledge), so record prior knowledge and outcome type before deciding. In a middle-school electricity quasi-experiment, [prior science level and pretest raised achievement but did not interact with the multimedia configuration](claims/treatment-science-pretest-independent-effects.md) [~M]; a nonsignificant interaction does not show the configurations work equally at every level
rows.change: Segmenting may still help their retention; drop pretraining and extra signals they do not need, and check transfer, not only effort
rows.if: Learners have high prior knowledge of the content

rows.basis: [Pretraining principle](claims/pretraining-principle-mayer-2008.md) [+M] (5 of 5 experiments, median d = 0.85)
rows.change: Before the main lesson, give a short primer naming the key parts and what each does
rows.if: The lesson uses technical parts or terms learners have not met

rows.basis: [Signaling principle](claims/signaling-principle-mayer-2008.md) [+M] (6 of 6 experiments, median d = 0.52); a review reports [the effect extends from animations to video](claims/signaling-improves-retention-transfer-video.md) [+W] (second-hand, no effect sizes); in a middle-school quasi-experiment, [signaling written text helped with abstract animation only](claims/signaling-effect-abstract-only.md) [~M] (d = .35; not significant with concrete animation)
rows.change: Signal them: headings, an outline, highlighting or spoken emphasis on the essential words, and nothing else highlighted
rows.if: The essential points are easy to miss in a busy display or long text

rows.basis: untested proposal for the check; segmenting evidence above
rows.change: Give learners pause and replay control, segment the material, and place a short check after each segment
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: [Multimedia-only stories helped comprehension; stories that also had interactive features did not](claims/multimedia-only-benefits-interactive-features-detrimental.md) [+M] (meta-analysis, g+ = 0.39 against −0.14). The gain was larger in studies of children the authors classed as disadvantaged (g+ = 0.66): a difference reflecting circumstances, not a property of the children or a cause
rows.change: Keep animated illustrations, sound and music that match the story; leave out hotspots, games and other interactive features
rows.if: A digital storybook for young children

rows.basis: [Spoken–written advantages were large for retention and absent for transfer](claims/outcome-constructs-test-formats-moderate-redundancy.md) [~M] (g = 0.53 against 0.01; multiple-choice 0.63 against mixed 0.11); the delayed and real-use cases are untested, since the evidence above is mostly immediate tests
rows.change: Judge the configuration on a transfer item, not a retention or multiple-choice test; do not rely on these effects to carry to a delayed test or real use
rows.if: The test that matters is transfer, or delayed, or use on a real task

rows.basis: Novice: [multiple representations](claims/multiple-representations-improve-learning.md) [~M] (the review ties the benefit to representational competence). Advanced: untested proposal (the claim pages discuss expertise reversal; no entry here tests it for modes)
rows.change: Novice: use words plus one visual type. Teach how to read it first (what the axes, arrows or symbols mean), add one explicit translation prompt per idea, and hold back a second visual type until learners can read the first. Advanced: cut to the most efficient representation, drop duplicating modes, and use translation tasks for checking rather than teaching.
rows.if: Learners are `novice` on this content and unfamiliar with its representations; or `advanced`

rows.basis: [Dual coding](claims/dual-coding-improves-learning.md) [+M]: the meta-analysis effect held across grade levels (elementary to adult); [learning-styles matching](claims/learning-styles-matching-does-not-improve-learning.md) [-M]: no style × modality interaction with 5th graders
rows.change: Pair text with a relevant graphic, picture or flow diagram. Do not sort children by a style inventory.
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary school) readers

rows.basis: [Multiple representations](claims/multiple-representations-improve-learning.md) [+M]: one undergraduate electrodynamics course; untested with children or outside physics
rows.change: Add a dynamic or manipulable representation (simulation) and a learner-made sketch beside the symbolic form. Budget for higher effort while learners work.
rows.if: The goal is a `principle` or `concept` in a mathematical or physical domain (how a quantity behaves)

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page (demonstration and gesture are untested here)
rows.change: Show it (a demonstration or video) with spoken steps, and have learners perform it. Keep a short written step list to consult.
rows.if: The goal is a `procedure` or physical action (`skill-performance`)

rows.basis: [Modality](claims/modality-effect-narration-over-text.md) [~M]: its advantage shrinks when learners control pacing
rows.change: On-screen text beside a static visual is acceptable. Give pause, replay and a text version. Do not convert all text to audio.
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, learner-paced media

rows.basis: [Modality](claims/modality-effect-narration-over-text.md) [~M]; [redundancy](claims/redundancy-principle.md) [~M]
rows.change: Narrate the explanation over the animation. Keep only labels and key terms on screen. Avoid full-sentence duplicate text.
rows.if: Live lecture, broadcast or other system-paced video with animation

rows.basis: [Video with narration and text](claims/video-narration-text-improves-immediate-macs-comprehension.md) [+M]: one randomized study of Chinese-speaking university EFL learners, immediate test only; [redundancy](claims/redundancy-principle.md) [~M] reports reversals for abridged text
rows.change: Keep the text available alongside narration and video rather than removing it as redundant. Monitor comprehension of the words alone.
rows.if: Learners work in a second language (`adult` L2 readers)

rows.basis: [Dual coding](claims/dual-coding-improves-learning.md) [+M]: graphics helped more on open-ended and mixed-format tests than on true/false ones
rows.change: Assess in a format that asks learners to use the representation (explain, predict, sketch), not only true/false recall. Decide in advance whether diagrams may be consulted at the test.
rows.if: Assessment is open-ended or high-stakes

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page ("attention to access"); captions count as accommodation, not redundancy
rows.change: Give every essential meaning a second accessible route: captions and transcripts, text descriptions of visuals, signed or spoken versions. Test the materials on the device learners will use.
rows.if: Deaf, hard-of-hearing or blind learners, or no sound or small screens available

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use one representation pair, not a full set. Build the translation prompts and their model answers into the material, so a learner without a teacher can check a sketch or explanation.
rows.if: One session only, or no teacher present

rows.basis: [Self Assessment Accuracy Is Low Without Training](claims/self-assessment-accuracy-is-low-without-training.md) [~M] (secondary students, one randomised experiment; a higher-education meta-analysis read as an abstract)
rows.change: Teacher-chosen methods; criteria with an example of each level; postpone learner choice of format and self-assessment that counts until learners have practised judging two or three examples
rows.if: Learners are `novice` on the goal and new to judging quality

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page (adults with rich applied experience)
rows.change: Let them propose a method and the evidence it will produce, checked against the criteria before they start; accept work products from their practice
rows.if: Learners are `advanced`, or adults with applied experience

rows.basis: [Preschool children demonstrate behavioral knowledge of classification, one-to-one correspondence, and seriation during everyday free play with everyday materials](claims/free-play-reveals-behavioral-math-knowledge.md) [+W] (one observed play episode, two children); [Assessment tasks built on family-identified funds of knowledge elicited computational thinking from K-2 children in a small design-based study that made no comparison with standard assessment](claims/funds-of-knowledge-tasks-reveal-computational-thinking.md) [+W] (13 K–2 children, design study, no comparison with a standard test); [Post-interviews with props and embodiment revealed understanding of macro–micro particle changes that the multiple-choice post-test did not capture.](claims/step-interview-surfaces-micro-micro-understanding.md) [+W] (early-primary science in a mixed-reality unit; 12 of the children showed in the interview what 2 showed on the two hardest multiple-choice items; descriptive)
rows.change: Observe the goal in play or with objects and pictures, with a short interview ("show me", "why there?"), alongside any written task; record what each child did
rows.if: Learners are young children (`child`, pre-school or early primary)

rows.basis: [For children and adolescents with dyslexia, the silent reading deficit is as large as or larger than the oral reading deficit](claims/dyslexia-silent-reading-deficit-as-large-or-larger.md) [+W] (two Dutch samples, children and adolescents; associational; the silent deficit was somewhat larger in adolescents)
rows.change: Assess the mode of reading the goal names: if the goal is reading silently for understanding (most reading from adolescence on), include a silent-reading measure, not only an oral-fluency one; do not carry an oral score over to silent reading
rows.if: Learners have dyslexia or other reading difficulties, and the goal is reading

rows.basis: [Typical verbal achievement tests may underestimate students' subject-matter knowledge because of a mismatch between the test's symbolic form and students' symbolic encoding](claims/verbal-achievement-tests-may-underestimate-via-symbolic-mismatch.md) [+W] (an argument in a review, not tested)
rows.change: Pair every written method with a spoken, demonstrated or drawn one that does not need the same reading and writing; read instructions aloud; do not read a low written score as low knowledge until the second method agrees
rows.if: Learners have low literacy, are learning in a second language, or have low confidence

rows.basis: [Math anxiety has a small-to-moderate negative correlation with math achievement (r = −.28) in a meta-analysis of correlations from 223 studies](claims/math-anxiety-degrades-performance.md) [~M] (meta-analysis of correlations, r = −.28; does not test a change of format)
rows.change: Add an untimed or low-pressure second method (a conversation, a take-home task, an observed task) before judging; drop time limits unless speed is the goal
rows.if: Learners are anxious about tests, or a timed written test is the only method

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page ("performance plus reflection"); the [Authentic Assessment](patterns/authentic-assessment.md) pattern holds the task design
rows.change: Combine an observed performance or product with the learner's short written or spoken account of the decisions behind it; use one rubric for both
rows.if: The goal is a `complex-skill` or performance (a lab, a clinical task, a design)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: One well-sampled method (many short items) is usually enough; add a second method only to check that a correct answer is not recognition alone
rows.if: The goal is `verbal-association` or a `procedure`

rows.basis: [Static individual assessment misses developing functions; ZPD-based assessment reveals potential competencies](claims/static-assessment-misses-emerging-functions.md) [+W] (a theoretical argument); [Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support.](claims/contingent-scaffolding-improves-learning.md) [~M] (a meta-analysis of 30 dynamic-assessment studies found forms of assisted assessment differ: strategy training above contingent prompting above coaching; it compares forms of help, not assisted with unaided judgement)
rows.change: Give a short third check that removes the demand that differs; for a capability that shows only with help, record what the learner did with one hint, and judge the unaided result
rows.if: A learner's methods disagree (strong in conversation, weak in writing; or the reverse)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep it; add only a second method for the goals the routine samples in one mode, and write the routine's criteria so they apply to both
rows.if: The brief names its own assessment routine (its own rubric, portfolio, check-in or exam)

rows.basis: [Raters differed significantly in severity/leniency in the MFRM analysis](claims/raters-differed-severity-mfrm.md) [~M] (three raters, open-ended items); [In one community-college lab class, six scorers rating six teams with an engineering rubric differed by a mean of 1.2 of 9 points, which the authors read as a sign the rubric may not be reliable](claims/engineering-rubric-low-scoring-reliability.md) [~W] (one class)
rows.change: Rest the decision on at least two methods per goal; calibrate markers on examples in each format and double-mark a sample; give a learner near the cut a third method before deciding; keep untrained peer judgements out of the mark
rows.if: Stakes are high: a grade boundary, pass mark or certification

rows.basis: [Waivers promoted about one-third of third graders and 40% of sixth and eighth graders who failed the 1997 promotional criteria, keeping retention rates well below failure rates](claims/waivers-promoted-failing-students-1997.md) [~W] (Chicago: discretionary routes overrode the test for many learners, with no check of whether they chose better); [Third-grade retention under the Chicago policy produced no sustained academic benefits or substantial negative effects](claims/third-grade-retention-no-sustained-benefit.md) [~M] (what follows the decision; neither study tests a multi-method gate)
rows.change: Do not let one test on one day decide: give a second route to the standard (an alternative test, a portfolio of classwork against the same criteria) and a third check for a learner near the cut; record which route each decision rests on, and plan the support that follows either decision, since the decision itself is not the intervention
rows.if: The result decides grade promotion or retention (a reading or test-score gate)

rows.basis: [Self-determination theory holds that autonomy support raises intrinsic motivation, and a meta-analysis finds expected tangible rewards undermine it](claims/autonomy-supports-intrinsic-motivation.md) [+M] (motivation, not achievement); [Learning Styles Matching Does Not Improve Learning](claims/learning-styles-matching-does-not-improve-learning.md) [-M] (tested for instruction, carried to assessment)
rows.change: Two or three options, one rubric, each option checked for equal demand before release; do not match formats to "learning styles"
rows.if: Learners are offered a choice of format

rows.basis: [Peer assessment improves academic performance by a small average amount relative to no assessment or to teacher assessment](claims/peer-assessment-improves-performance.md) [+M] (meta-analysis of 54 studies; about performance, not the accuracy of peer judgements); the targeting rule is untested
rows.change: Keep one quick common method for everyone; use the second method only for learners near a decision or out of line with their other work; use trained peer review for the second reading of products; a 2-minute oral check per learner at most
rows.if: One teacher for a large group, or scarce marker time (volunteers, a busy shift, a tutor who checks in briefly)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use two methods inside the session (a written item and a 1-minute spoken or drawn one) for the one goal that matters; use the result to steer the next step, not to grade
rows.if: Time is one session only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Choose methods every mode can do (a short spoken or recorded answer, a photo of a drawing or worked page, a poll); give remote and phone learners the same criteria and time; note the mode beside each result and compare across modes before combining
rows.if: Mixed modes: some learners in the room, some remote, some on phones only

rows.basis: untested proposal; from the earlier page (adults with applied experience)
rows.change: Combine observation of the task at work (a checklist) with a short conversation about why each step was done, and a work product; use the workplace's own records where they show the goal
rows.if: Adults in work settings, or the goal is a job task

rows.basis: untested proposal; the audience relationship is owned by [Authentic Audiences and Purposes](principles/authentic-audiences-purposes.md)
rows.change: Judge it against the criteria separately from the audience's response; record the audience's response as its own observation, and add the learner's account of decisions as a second method
rows.if: The work is a product or performance for a real audience

rows.basis: untested proposal; self-assessment limit from [Self Assessment Accuracy Is Low Without Training](claims/self-assessment-accuracy-is-low-without-training.md) [~M]
rows.change: Pair auto-scored items with one short constructed or recorded response per goal, reviewed by a peer with the criteria or sampled by a tutor; have the learner self-assess against the criteria with an example first
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use two methods per decision, not three: the one that shows the performance (an observed task that changes the case, such as a changed order) decides, and the quick one (a quiz) screens; run them as a rotation so the assessor observes while the others work; write an evidence matrix in advance saying what each disagreement leads to (passes quiz, fails task → targeted practice and reassess; the reverse → a short oral check)
rows.if: Little time (one or two sessions) and one assessor

rows.basis: [Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows.](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M] (review of cognitive-load studies; not tested on note-taking aids)
rows.change: Skip guided notes and modelling; state the purpose, keep one recall review; let them choose the format
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` on the content, or already take selective notes

rows.basis: [Guided Notes Improve Note Accuracy](claims/guided-notes-improve-note-accuracy.md) [+M] (meta-analysis reports the benefit "particularly for school-age students", abstract only); timings untested
rows.change: Guided notes with few, well-cued blanks; pauses every 5–8 minutes; teacher models notes on the board for several sessions, not one; review in class
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary) or `adolescent` with little note-taking experience

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Notes are for doing something: a one-page template with "what to do", "when", "who to ask", "one question"; review is applying the note on the next real task, followed by a check with a colleague or supervisor
rows.if: Learners are `adult` in a work setting (training, briefings, meetings)

rows.basis: Pauses and outline: untested here. Quiz: [Retrieval Practice Improves Long Term Retention](claims/retrieval-practice-improves-retention.md) [+S] (carried to reviewing notes)
rows.change: Put the pause points into the video (a prompt screen at each break); give a downloadable outline for the first modules; end each module with a short recall quiz learners answer before reopening their notes
rows.if: Setting is `online-self-paced` video

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Share the outline in a form that works on a phone (a short list of headings with blanks, not a wide table or PDF); say the pause aloud and post it in the chat; ask remote learners to post their one-line restatement in the chat so everyone sees some; send the slides afterwards but not before the session
rows.if: Mixed mode: some learners in the room, some remote, or some on a phone only

rows.basis: [Guided Notes Improve Note Accuracy](claims/guided-notes-improve-note-accuracy.md) [+M] (one quasi-experiment with two intact undergraduate classes); pauses and sampling untested
rows.change: Guided-notes outline for everyone; two or three pauses per hour with a restatement written to a neighbour or a poll; collect a random sample of notes after the first week to check for errors and address the commonest one in the next lecture
rows.if: One teacher with a large lecture group

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Spend the facilitator's minute on one thing: a look at a learner's notes against the key points, naming one missing or wrong point; put the rest in the materials (outline, pause prompts, self-test questions at the end)
rows.if: Scarce facilitator time (volunteer tutors, a busy shift, one brief check-in)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Guided-notes outline, two pauses with a restatement prompt, and a 5-minute recall at the end from covered notes; do not plan the fade; do not claim retention
rows.if: A single session only

rows.basis: untested proposal; the earlier page's "working-memory constraints" learners, and Hughes & Suritsky (1994, Key Sources, no claim page) on university students with and without learning disabilities
rows.change: Fewer and shorter blanks, with word banks or first letters; allow symbols, sketches and first-language words in notes; give the full slides or a transcript after the session so missed content is recoverable; allow audio recording where it is permitted
rows.if: Learners have low literacy, a learning disability, or are working in a second language

rows.basis: [Retrieval Practice Improves Long Term Retention](claims/retrieval-practice-improves-retention.md) [+S] and [self-explanation](claims/self-explanation-improves-conceptual-understanding.md) [+S], both carried to notes; no claim compares note formats
rows.change: Keep it; change only what the evidence points at: add a review in which the learner covers the notes and recalls before checking, and one restatement prompt per section
rows.if: The brief names its own routine or template (Cornell notes, a school-wide organizer, a company note template)

rows.basis: [Laptop note-takers transcribed more verbatim and did worse on conceptual questions than longhand note-takers in one set of experiments, but a direct replication found no consistent difference in test performance](claims/laptop-notes-verbatim-shallower.md) [~M] (replication found no consistent difference)
rows.change: Do not ban on this evidence; instruct paraphrase, keep pauses, and check a sample of notes for verbatim copying; allow devices for learners who write slowly or with difficulty
rows.if: Learners take notes on laptops or tablets, or the brief asks whether to ban them

rows.basis: [Summarization Effective With Training](claims/summarization-improves-learning.md) [~M] (295 adults: summarizing each of five texts gave weaker integrated essays than rereading; carried from summaries to notes)
rows.change: Do not ask for a separate summary of each source; ask for notes organized by the question (a column per claim, with which source says what), then write from those
rows.if: The goal is writing or argument from several sources

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Do not rely on learners' notes as the record: supply a checked reference version after the session, keep the learner's notes for recall practice against it, and correct errors before the assessment
rows.if: Stakes are high (a licensing exam, a safety procedure)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Separate the two: a shared record written to a checklist and checked by a second person, and each learner's own notes kept for their own recall; do not treat reading someone else's notes as a substitute for taking and reviewing one's own
rows.if: Notes will be shared with others (class notes posted for absent peers, meeting minutes for a team)

rows.basis: untested; the [guided-notes claim](claims/guided-notes-improve-note-accuracy.md) [+W] tests teacher-made gapped notes with students, carried here only as "give the structure", not the worksheet form
rows.change: Replace fill-in-the-blank guided notes with a reusable domain grid the learner keeps, built from the categories the brief or the workplace already uses (if none are given, for a handover: facts, actions due, what is uncertain, what to report), with a pre-printed prompt for any item whose omission is dangerous, modelled once with a think-aloud, then used on a real or recorded case; check it by having the learner brief a partner from the grid, not by reading back. In one session of about 75 minutes: 10 minutes modelling the grid on a short clip, 20 minutes filling it on the full case, 10 minutes comparing grids in pairs, 20 minutes briefing a partner from it (with sentence frames such as "The priority is… because…" for learners working in a second language), 10 minutes fixing the grid for reuse
rows.if: Adults whose notes become a job aid (a handover, a shift, a procedure they will use again at work)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Judge the notes by use, not recall: the learner follows their own notes, on their own device, to do the task again while a partner watches (no swapping unfamiliar devices); fix any step the partner cannot follow. Keep any retrieval as optional self-checking, not a quiz
rows.if: The notes are a take-home aid, and the brief asks for an evaluation that does not feel like a test (older adults, community workshops, practical skills)

rows.basis: [Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows.](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M] (cognitive-load studies on instructional formats; carried to observation guidance)
rows.change: Let them set their own focus, observe whole live performances, and compare directly with their own practice; replace the designer's focus sheet with the observed person's question; shorten or drop the corrective part of the debrief
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` or experienced practitioners (in-service teachers, senior staff observing each other)

rows.basis: [Expert teachers interpret complex classroom phenomena more accurately and fluidly than novices and postulants](claims/expert-teachers-interpret-classroom-phenomena-better.md) [~M] (novices struggled to monitor a complex scene); the sequence is untested
rows.change: Start with recorded clips, two focus items at most, a three-column record and a debrief after every clip; do not send them on a long live shadow before session 3
rows.if: Learners are complete newcomers to the practice (first placement, first week in a job)

rows.basis: [In the initial skill acquisition phase, authentic video yielded higher overall observation assignment scores than virtual simulation](claims/av-outperforms-vs-total-observation-score.md) [+M]; [Analytical competence showed a leap-plateau trajectory across sequential authentic-video workshops, improving mainly between Workshops 2 and 3](claims/analysis-leap-plateau-trajectory.md) [+M] (one design-based study, 8 groups, fixed order)
rows.change: Run three or four workshops on authentic classroom video (a simplified simulation first if they are new to observing), each with a group observation assignment covering description, analysis and suggested support, and score it
rows.if: Learners are teacher candidates learning to observe children or classrooms

rows.basis: untested proposal; the debrief is carried from [Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support.](claims/contingent-scaffolding-improves-learning.md) [+M] (one-to-one tutoring of children)
rows.change: Shadow on a real shift in blocks of 1–3 hours, with a pocket focus card of two to four items; a 5-minute check-in before and a 10–15-minute conversation after; follow within the week with the learner doing the same task under supervision
rows.if: `adult` learners in a work setting (`workplace-clinical`, `adult-workplace`): new staff shadowing a colleague

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Set the purpose as finding out what the work involves; give three questions to ask the host (what a typical day holds, what they decide, how they learned it); a short write-up or talk to peers afterwards; do not assess performance
rows.if: School pupils (`adolescent`) job shadowing for career exploration

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Move the explaining into materials: a written focus card and a one-page key of the decisions at stake; the observer brings two questions to a 5-minute conversation; a peer observer compares records with them instead of the mentor where possible
rows.if: Scarce facilitator or performer time (a busy shift, a volunteer host, a mentor who can give five minutes)

rows.basis: untested proposal; the group workshop format follows the teacher-candidate study ([Authentic video outperformed virtual simulation on the higher-order analysis and support dimensions of observation assignments](claims/av-advantage-analysis-support-dimensions.md) [+M])
rows.change: Do not rotate everyone through a live shadow; record one authentic performance, or have the group watch one live performance from the side (a fishbowl), each observer with a different focus item; debrief as a group, observers reporting by focus
rows.if: One expert or teacher for many observers

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Stream the performance with a fixed camera and a microphone near the performer, with consent; an in-room observer types short time-stamped notes into a shared document remote observers can see; in the debrief, take remote observers' records first. Phone-only observers get the recording afterwards, cut into clips with the focus questions in text, and send their record by message
rows.if: Some observers remote while others are in the room, or some join by phone only

rows.basis: untested proposal; the explanation prompt is carried from [Prompting learners to self-explain improves understanding and problem solving on immediate tests by a moderate average amount, with little evidence yet on delayed or classroom gains.](claims/self-explanation-improves-conceptual-understanding.md) [+S]
rows.change: Short authentic clips (5–15 minutes) each with two focus questions the learner must answer before going on, then a written expert account of the clip's decisions to compare with; one replay of the clip after the comparison
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, recordings only, no one to debrief

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: 10 minutes brief and focus card; 25–30 minutes observing one whole short performance (or one clip); 15–20 minutes debrief ending in one thing to try; no more than two focus items
rows.if: A fixed short time budget (for example, 60 minutes in total)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: One focused observation of a whole performance and one debrief; state the outcome as what the observer can now name and explain, not as a change in their own performance
rows.if: One session only

rows.basis: untested proposal; the choice of a similar performer rests on a correlational finding in a review ([Vicarious experiences are positively related to agriculture teachers' general teaching efficacy, with observing a first year teacher explaining 11% of variance](claims/vicarious-experiences-positive-teaching-efficacy.md) [+W])
rows.change: Use a picture or tick-box record instead of written columns; debrief orally; let the observer point to moments on the recording rather than describe them; choose a performer the learner can see as like themselves when confidence is the problem
rows.if: Learners with low confidence, low literacy, or working in a second language

rows.basis: [Vicarious experiences are positively related to agriculture teachers' general teaching efficacy, with observing a first year teacher explaining 11% of variance](claims/vicarious-experiences-positive-teaching-efficacy.md) [+W] (associational, reported in a review; observing did not cause the efficacy)
rows.change: Arrange observation of someone a little ahead of the learner (a first-year colleague, a peer) as well as of an expert; ask the learner afterwards what the performer did when something went wrong
rows.if: Goal is confidence or willingness to take up the work (`attitude-motivation`), not skill

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: The observer is introduced and stays silent; all questions and reasoning are kept for the conversation away from the audience; the record holds no names; the audience can decline an observer
rows.if: The observed work is for a real audience (patients, clients, pupils, customers)

rows.basis: untested proposal; that clinical supervision tied to evaluation has inconclusive research results is a monograph's report ([Research on clinical supervision's effectiveness is inconclusive, partly because practice is diluted and tied to evaluation](claims/clinical-supervision-effectiveness-inconclusive.md) [~W])
rows.change: The observed person controls who sees the recording and the notes, and may end the arrangement; observers' notes are shared with the observed person first and with a supervisor only by agreement; keep observation for development apart from evaluation
rows.if: The material is private or sensitive (a colleague's own lesson video, clinical cases, a learner's reflective record)

rows.basis: the explanation prompt is carried from [Prompting learners to self-explain…](claims/self-explanation-improves-conceptual-understanding.md) [+S]; otherwise untested
rows.change: Keep it; do not substitute the three-column record. Change only what the evidence speaks to: add one prompt asking the observer to explain why, and one debrief that starts from their record
rows.if: The brief names its own observation protocol, form, rubric or categories

rows.basis: [A training-design argument, not tested by any study recorded here, holds that practising whole complex tasks improves transfer of complex skills](claims/whole-task-performance-improves-transfer.md) [+W] (an argument about practice, carried to observation)
rows.change: Observe it whole and debrief it whole; put the focus items on decision points across the whole, not on one segment; do not split it into separate fragments
rows.if: The brief wants a whole performance kept whole (a full lesson, a full client visit, a full shift)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Fix where the observer stands and when they must not speak or touch; brief the stop rules first; observe the procedure once before any hands-on part; require a supervised attempt before working alone
rows.if: High stakes or safety (operating theatre, laboratory, machinery, child protection)

rows.basis: [Peer reflective groups encouraged student teachers to challenge existing theories](claims/peer-reflective-groups-challenge-student-teacher-views.md) [+W] (student teachers; outcome is reported views, not practice); weekly observation untested
rows.change: Put them in a study team with experienced colleagues and a peer reflective group that reads their own lesson notes; pair each with a mentor or coach who models in their class before peer observation starts; observe weekly for the first term
rows.if: Learners are student teachers or teachers in their first years

rows.basis: [Voluntary, non-evaluative participation correlated with improvement](claims/coaching-partnership-voluntary-non-evaluative.md) [+M] (one program's survey, correlations)
rows.change: Let each teacher set their own focus within the shared practice; start with peer coaching rather than a coach; keep group sessions to the one-day launch
rows.if: Learners are experienced teachers who chose to take part

rows.basis: [A literacy-coaching randomised trial found larger classroom-quality and child literacy gains](claims/pd-coaching-expert-support-gains.md) [+M] (early childhood educators, reported in a review; carried to K–3 untested); sequence from the folded literacy-coach page
rows.change: Establish the shared language first in training for teachers and administrators; then a school-based literacy coach trains on evidence-based reading and data use, demonstrates, co-teaches and observes with immediate feedback; study teams look at students' reading data each fortnight
rows.if: Goal is early reading (K–3, foundational skills or the science of reading)

rows.basis: [Colleague collaboration associated with standards-aligned practice](claims/colleague-collaboration-consistently-positive-practices.md) [+M] (survey association); [schools with math-expertise coaches reported greater gains](claims/math-expertise-coaches-associated-greater-gains.md) [+W] (one administrator's report); [31 of 35 reviewed effective-PD studies had a specific content focus, most often job-embedded](claims/pd-content-focus-prevalence.md) [~W] (prevalence among studies a review selected, not a comparison)
rows.change: Make the study team's work collaborative planning and review of lessons in the subject; prefer a coach with expertise in the subject
rows.if: Goal is standards-aligned math or science teaching

rows.basis: [Coaching can be effective face-to-face, at a distance and combined](claims/coaching-effective-all-delivery-modes.md) [~W] (a review: most studies were in person); [no significant in-person versus virtual difference](claims/coaching-no-school-level-or-mode-differences.md) [~M] (too imprecise to rule out moderate differences); in a web-mediated coaching programme for secondary teachers (about 20 hours of in-service over 13 months), [students of participating teachers gained more than controls, the equivalent of moving from the 50th to the 59th percentile](claims/pd-collaboration-prevalence-and-gains.md) [+W] (one trial, reported in a review)
rows.change: Run peer coaching on short filmed segments shared privately with the partner; hold study-team meetings online with the same protocol; keep one in-person session per term if possible
rows.if: Some teachers join remotely, or coaching must be at a distance (phone or video only)

rows.basis: [20 of 24 interviewed teachers said networking with teachers in other schools did most to change their instruction](claims/networking-opportunities-greatest-instructional-influence.md) [+W] and [about 8 in 10 attributed changes in their instruction to the network](claims/teacher-reported-engagement-opportunities-increased.md) [+W] (one network of about 100 hours a year; teachers' own reports); [teacher-level collaboration stayed low where collaborative activities targeted school leaders](claims/teacher-level-collaboration-remained-low-activities-targeted-leaders.md) [-W] (focus groups in one grant programme)
rows.change: Join teachers across schools into a standing network around one shared instructional aim; each teacher tests one change in their own class between meetings and brings back student work; share tasks and materials across schools; make sure network meetings are for teachers, not only for school leaders
rows.if: Teachers are the only one of their subject or grade in the school, or the plan is a network across schools (a networked improvement community, a district subject network)

rows.basis: [Teacher–coach time is a key success factor](claims/coach-teacher-time-key-success-factor.md) [+W]; [effects shrink as programs grow](claims/coaching-scale-up-diminishing-effects.md) [~M] (a descriptive pattern across studies); the peer substitution is untested
rows.change: Let peer coaching carry most observation cycles; the coach trains the peer coaches, leads study-team meetings by rotation, and checks in with each teacher once a month for 15–20 minutes; cap the caseload rather than spread visits thin
rows.if: One coach for many teachers, or facilitator time is scarce (a coach shared across schools, a busy principal)

rows.basis: untested proposal; [daily demands crowd out developmental work](claims/daily-demands-compete-with-developmental-focus.md) [~M] is the reason to keep the item fixed
rows.change: Use it whole for one instructional item: 5 minutes to recall last time's commitments, 25 minutes on one piece of student work or a video clip, 10 minutes to agree one change each, 5 minutes to set the next peer observation
rows.if: A fixed short time budget, such as 45 minutes a fortnight in an existing meeting

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Do not present it as ongoing PD. Use it to form the teams, practise one peer-observation cycle in the room on a video clip, and set the dates of the first two meetings; record that no change in practice can be claimed
rows.if: Only one session is available

rows.basis: untested proposal; the four changes cite the claims in the default design
rows.change: Keep it; change only what the evidence here speaks to: a formally led instructional item, non-evaluative use, protected time, and focus on instruction
rows.if: The brief names its own routine (a PLC protocol, a district observation tool, a coaching cycle)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use it as the look-for list in peer observation and study-team review; do not substitute another
rows.if: The brief gives its own criteria, framework or rubric for teaching

rows.basis: [Partnership framing and non-evaluative support correlated with improvement](claims/coaching-partnership-voluntary-non-evaluative.md) [+M]; [a district coaching culture eased participation](claims/coaching-culture-increases-teacher-participation.md) [+W]; [supervisory coaching shows mixed effects](claims/supervisory-coaching-mixed-teacher-student-outcomes.md) [~M] (16 K–12 studies, 6 meeting all quality indicators)
rows.change: Separate peer observation from appraisal in writing; if that cannot be done, use study teams on student work rather than observation of individual lessons, and measure both teacher and student change
rows.if: Peer coaching or coaching is linked to appraisal, or stakes are high (a school under review)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: The teacher decides who sees a video and which segment; peer debriefs stay between the two teachers; the study team discusses student work, not named teachers
rows.if: Teachers lack confidence, or what is discussed is sensitive (a struggling class, a video of their own lesson)

rows.basis: [A district culture of coaching](claims/coaching-culture-increases-teacher-participation.md) [+W]; [teacher-level collaboration stayed low where activities targeted leaders](claims/teacher-level-collaboration-remained-low-activities-targeted-leaders.md) [-W]; target learners from the folded literacy-coach page
rows.change: Include them in the launch training; make their part protecting team and coaching time and framing coaching as improvement, not inspection; they do not attend peer debriefs; leaders' own meetings do not replace teachers' team time
rows.if: Administrators are among the learners (principals, assistant principals)

rows.basis: [Pooled effect on achievement 0.18 SD](claims/coaching-pooled-achievement-effect-0-18-sd.md) [+M] against [0.49 SD on practice](claims/coaching-pooled-instruction-effect-0-49-sd.md) [+M]; [large practice gains are needed for modest achievement gains](claims/instruction-achievement-weak-link-coaching.md) [~M]
rows.change: Keep observed practice as the first outcome, add an aligned student measure, and expect a smaller student effect than the practice effect
rows.if: The goal claimed is student achievement

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Observe and discuss whole lesson segments (a launch, a discussion) rather than isolated moves, and judge change in the lesson as taught
rows.if: Teaching is to be kept as a whole performance, not split into fragments

rows.basis: [Collaborative planning time was the top support cited by micro-credential earners](claims/collaborative-planning-time-top-micro-credential-support.md) [~W] (a survey of preferences, not outcomes)
rows.change: Give the cohort collaborative planning time as its study-team slot
rows.if: Teachers are earning micro-credentials or working in a cohort

rows.basis: [Monthly coaching helped teachers use and integrate a writing tool with their instruction](claims/monthly-coaching-helped-teachers-integrate-mi-write.md) [+W] (one implementation study, grades 7–8, no comparison); [coached teachers reported greater impact of their technology use on students](claims/coaching-increases-perceived-itu-impact-engagement-learning.md) [+W] (self-report survey against non-coached peers)
rows.change: Make the ongoing work the tool in use in teachers' own lessons: monthly coaching on how it fits their instruction, and a study-team item reviewing one lesson that used it; do not stop at a one-off training on its features. The coaching cycle itself is in the materials-and-tools row of the [Professional Development pattern](patterns/professional-development.md)
rows.if: The goal is integrating a classroom technology tool or platform into teaching

rows.basis: [A six-session biweekly faculty learning community on AI ran in one physics department](claims/physics-faculty-learning-community-ai-workshop-series.md) [+W] (a description of format and attendance, no outcome); [ePortfolio outcomes were stronger at several universities where faculty had extended intensive PD than brief training or none](claims/intensive-professional-development-stronger-epportfolio-outcomes.md) [+W] (a report's summary of other campuses, no statistics); the coaching claims above are from K–12 classrooms
rows.change: Use a department-based learning community in place of a grade-level team: about six meetings across a term, every two weeks, 60–75 minutes, on one shared teaching question; add peer observation of a class, seminar or lab by a colleague from the same department; make the first training extended rather than a brief session
rows.if: Learners are higher-education faculty (a department, a teaching-and-learning centre programme)

rows.basis: [Pilot gains were not consistently sustained when later adopters did not get intensive PD](claims/epdp-pilot-gpa-retention-gains-not-sustained.md) [+W] (one campus, higher education); [coaching effects shrink at scale](claims/coaching-scale-up-diminishing-effects.md) [~M]
rows.change: Give later adopters the launch, the facilitated team meetings and the coached first weeks the pilot group had, rather than a short orientation from the pilot teachers; expect smaller effects as the programme grows and keep observing practice
rows.if: A practice piloted with volunteers is being spread to later adopters

rows.basis: [Example-first sequences](claims/worked-example-problem-sequences.md) [~M] (secondary-school novices, circuits; carried, not a test of non-examples); the novice caution is a precaution on the [erroneous-examples claim](claims/erroneous-examples-build-conceptual-knowledge.md) [~M], not a finding
rows.change: Teach with correct examples only for the first session; add one near-miss pair at the end only if they can explain a correct case; name the deciding feature for them rather than waiting
rows.if: Learners are `novice` and cannot yet recognise a correct case

rows.basis: [Expertise reversal](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~S] (guidance in general, cognitive-load studies; gives no crossover point)
rows.change: Skip anchors and labelled pairs; give only borderline cases, or have them build non-examples for others and defend them
rows.if: Learners are `advanced`, or already discriminate the boundary on a check

rows.basis: [Correct against incorrect examples](claims/erroneous-examples-build-conceptual-knowledge.md) [+M] (grades 4–5, brief tutoring session); the group format is untested
rows.change: One deciding feature per pair, concrete or pictured cases, oral or pointing answers, pairs run with the teacher in a small group
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary age)

rows.basis: [Comparing cases](claims/comparing-contrasting-cases-improves-learning.md) [~S] (seventh-graders comparing algebra methods gained procedural knowledge and flexibility)
rows.change: Pair a correct method with a plausible wrong one, or two correct methods, and ask which works here and why; check method choice on new problems
rows.if: The goal is a `procedure` (choosing or carrying out a method)

rows.basis: [Comparing cases](claims/comparing-contrasting-cases-improves-learning.md) [~S]: in the algebra study comparison did not raise conceptual knowledge, so classification alone may hide it
rows.change: Score the explanation of the deciding feature separately from classification; add the make-your-own non-example task
rows.if: The goal is `conceptual-understanding`, an explanation of why

rows.basis: [Interleaving labelled category examples](claims/interleaving-improves-inductive-learning.md) [~M] (mixing reversed for word-based categories; ages and settings not on the claim page)
rows.change: Show each category's examples together first, then near-miss pairs one feature at a time; mix categories only after that; keep labels visible
rows.if: Instances are verbal (word categories, sentence types, genres) rather than visual or mathematical

rows.basis: [Task-type argument](claims/task-type-moderates-induction-error-usefulness.md) [~W] (a 1966 conceptual analysis, not a test)
rows.change: Do not build non-examples; teach the correct form directly and practise it, so errors are not rehearsed
rows.if: The target is a fact, a simple association or a precise response, not a concept

rows.basis: [PS-I review](claims/ps-i-fosters-learning-only-with-contrasting-cases-or-student-solutions.md) [+M] (benefits only where contrasting cases or instruction built on student solutions were part of the design)
rows.change: Use the pair in the instruction that follows: set learners' own failed attempts or a prepared incorrect solution beside the canonical one
rows.if: The brief wants learners to attempt a problem before instruction

rows.basis: [Teacher modelling with contrasting cases](claims/contrasting-cases-gatekeeper-repositioning.md) [+W] (preparatory students' reflective essays; self-report, no comparison group)
rows.change: Model the check on a credible and a misleading item side by side, thinking aloud; then have learners check a fresh pair and agree a cross-checking routine
rows.if: The concept is source credibility, or checking AI or other generated output

rows.basis: Untested proposal; the tested study was one-to-one tutoring
rows.change: Project one pair; every learner commits an answer at once (cards, mini-whiteboards, a poll), then pairs of learners explain; the teacher names the feature and goes to those who still miss it
rows.if: `classroom`, one teacher and a large group

rows.basis: Untested proposal (see the [contrastive remediation videos strategy](strategies/misconception-aware-contrastive-remediation-videos.md), itself untested here)
rows.change: The system shows the pair, the learner selects or types the deciding feature before feedback; a wrong quiz answer triggers a pair built on that wrong answer; end with mixed unlabelled items
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, no teacher

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Put each pair in one shared image or document with the two cases stacked vertically and labelled A and B, so a phone screen shows both; collect answers in the same channel for everyone
rows.if: Mixed modes: some learners remote, some in the room, or phone-only

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: One concept: one anchor (3 min), two pairs (6 min), five mixed items with feedback (5 min), one-line explanation of the deciding feature (1 min); record what the items show and do not claim retention
rows.if: A single session only, or a fixed short time budget (e.g. 15 minutes)

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Prepare pair cards with the answer and the deciding feature on the back; learners self-check and the facilitator looks only at the explanation line
rows.if: Scarce facilitator time (volunteers, a busy shift, one tutor checking in briefly)

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Keep it; fill its non-example part with near misses on one deciding feature, and use the brief's categories as the labels; change nothing else
rows.if: The brief names its own routine, template or categories (a Frayer model, its own rubric, the job's own fault categories)

rows.basis: Untested proposal; consistent with the tested study, which used plausible incorrect examples
rows.change: Use that error, unchanged, as the non-example in the first pair
rows.if: The brief reports an error learners actually made

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Use pictured or concrete cases, keep labels visible, accept pointing answers; never use an identifiable learner's error as a public non-example
rows.if: Learners have low confidence or low literacy, or are working in a second language

rows.basis: Untested proposal; no claim here tests adults
rows.change: Draw non-examples from real near misses on the job (a rejected claim form, a near-miss incident report), anonymised; check on a fresh case from their work
rows.if: Adults in a work setting

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: The learner decides whether their own error becomes a pair; otherwise build a synthetic pair with the same error
rows.if: Private or sensitive material (learners' own work, patient or client cases)

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Pair two whole performances, one with the flaw, rather than splitting it into items; ask where they differ and why it matters
rows.if: The brief wants a whole performance kept whole (a presentation, a procedure on the job, a piece of writing)

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Take non-examples from published or professional work that misses the mark, not from classmates' drafts
rows.if: A product or performance for a real audience

rows.basis: Untested proposal (the case-comparison benefit was larger on immediate tests, a reason to test late)
rows.change: Test on new, unlabelled cases including near misses, at that delay, not on practice items
rows.if: High stakes, or the assessment is weeks later

rows.basis: [Teacher interviews: subject-specific use cases are the top stated PD need](claims/teacher-interviews-obstacles-and-pd-needs.md) [+M] (stated need, 21 science teachers)
rows.change: Drop the technical walkthrough; spend the whole first session on subject examples and planning one lesson; start the follow-up cycle at once
rows.if: Teachers already operate the tool fluently (`advanced` users) but use it little in teaching

rows.basis: [Single-tool, step-by-step trainings produced uptake where multi-tool trainings did not](claims/district-provided-tools-single-tool-training.md) [~M] (one coach's report)
rows.change: Keep step 2 and make it longer (two short sessions, one function each), with a printed step-by-step card and a buddy; plan the first lesson around one function only
rows.if: Teachers are new to the tool or have low confidence with technology (`novice`)

rows.basis: [Integrated instructional hours correlate more positively with integration ability than stand-alone technology courses](claims/integrated-hours-beat-standalone-tech-courses.md) [+M] (pre-service, association)
rows.change: Put the tool into methods and subject courses, used on lessons students plan for their subject, rather than a stand-alone technology course
rows.if: Learners are pre-service teachers in a preparation program

rows.basis: untested proposal; the claims here are about school teachers
rows.change: Keep the order (goal, one function, examples in their discipline, plan one class session); replace school release time with a scheduled course-design hour; use a colleague in the same discipline as the follow-up
rows.if: Learners are faculty in `postsecondary` teaching or trainers in `adult-workplace` settings

rows.basis: [Teachers cite poor AI output quality and risks to students' cognitive engagement as main obstacles](claims/teacher-interviews-obstacles-and-pd-needs.md) [~M]; the student-side design is owned by the Technology Augments principle
rows.change: Add to step 3 an example of where the tool's output is wrong or does the students' thinking for them, and plan where the student attempts first; take teachers' concerns about output quality as a design input, not resistance
rows.if: The tool is a generative AI assistant

rows.basis: untested proposal; [tailored support helped integration](claims/regular-tailored-support-helped-teachers-integrate-tools.md) [+M] is about support, not its format
rows.change: Keep the first session whole-group; replace one-to-one follow-up with a 10-minute check-in per teacher by message before the first lesson, and a team debrief in the next scheduled meeting; ask teams to share one worked lesson each so examples come from colleagues
rows.if: One coach or technology lead for many teachers, or scarce facilitator time (a volunteer, a busy term, a short check-in only)

rows.basis: untested proposal; [long-term content-specific support is argued to outperform one-shot sessions](claims/fifty-hours-content-specific-pd.md) [~M] (a review citing a survey and an earlier report)
rows.change: Run 60 minutes: 15 on one function, 20 on two subject examples, 25 planning one lesson to teach within two weeks; send one follow-up message offering a check-in. Do not claim sustained use from it
rows.if: Only a single session is possible

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Split it into three 30-minute pieces: one function plus one example; plan a lesson; debrief student work after teaching it. Do not add content to fill time
rows.if: A fixed short time budget (for example, 90 minutes across the term)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Run the walkthrough on each person's own device and account, with the remote group's screen shared; give planning a shared template both groups write in; check that the tool's teacher view works on a phone before assuming it does
rows.if: Mixed modes: some teachers join remotely, some in the room, or some on a phone only

rows.basis: untested proposal; the evidence speaks to PD content and support, not to which framework is used
rows.change: Keep it as the planning template and the debrief criteria; change only what the evidence points at: one function at a time, examples in the teachers' subject, follow-up support
rows.if: The brief names its own routine, framework or rubric (SAMR, TPACK, a district technology standard, its own lesson template or look-for list)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Sort the subject examples and the planned lessons by those categories, and do not substitute another taxonomy
rows.if: The brief uses its own categories for uses of the tool (for example "practice", "feedback", "creation")

rows.basis: untested proposal; the Professional Development pattern's row on low uptake holds the coaching side
rows.change: Separate the follow-up from evaluation; the teacher controls who sees the lesson video and the tool's student records, and chooses what to bring to the team; use anonymized student work in debriefs
rows.if: PD is tied to appraisal, or the debrief would use lesson video or student data that is private

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep the planned lesson whole in step 4 and debrief the whole lesson; do not reduce the PD to practising tool functions in isolation
rows.if: The brief wants a whole lesson taught with the tool, not separate exercises

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use it as a compared case in step 3: the same lesson with the tool as a display and with the tool doing its job, and ask teachers what students do differently in each
rows.if: The brief reports a mistake teachers made (the tool used only to project slides, a quiz tool used with no follow-up on the results)

rows.basis: [Teachers used Ecree less than intended, some lacking time to learn and integrate it](claims/teachers-used-ecree-less-than-intended-lacking-time.md) [~M]
rows.change: Say so in the plan; scope the PD to one function and one lesson per teacher, and expect low use
rows.if: No release time and no follow-up support can be offered

rows.basis: [Peer discussion improves conceptual understanding](claims/peer-discussion-improves-conceptual-understanding.md) [+M]
rows.change: Collect an individual answer first, then discussion of reasoning, a revote, and an individual answer to a new isomorphic question
rows.if: A conceptual question with one defensible answer, in a postsecondary class

rows.basis: [Peer discussion improves conceptual understanding](claims/peer-discussion-improves-conceptual-understanding.md) [+M]
rows.change: Follow the discussion with instructor explanation rather than choosing one; in the recorded comparison the combination helped weak, medium and strong performers more than either alone
rows.if: The class mixes weak and strong performers

rows.basis: [Higher-order clicker questions improve lower-order exam performance](claims/hocs-clickers-improve-locs-exam-performance.md) [+M]
rows.change: Pose higher-order questions for discussion, not only recall; in one course they also raised scores on recall-level exam items
rows.if: The exam includes application or analysis items

rows.basis: [Students perceive both levels as equally helpful](claims/students-perceive-clicker-levels-equally-helpful.md) [~W]
rows.change: Do not choose by ratings; students rated recall and higher-order questions equally helpful although exam results differed
rows.if: Learners' ratings will be used to choose question types

rows.basis: [Clicker participation does not help the lowest quartile](claims/any-clicker-pattern-beats-absence-except-lowest-quartile.md) [~W]; [Homework explanation quality predicts exam performance](claims/homework-explanation-quality-predicts-exam-performance.md) [+W]
rows.change: Add a short take-home written explanation of the discussed question; in one course in-class participation showed no benefit for the lowest quartile, while explanation quality predicted exam success in every quartile
rows.if: The lowest-performing students, or students who miss class, need support

rows.basis: [Correct-correct pattern predicts higher exam performance](claims/correct-correct-clicker-pattern-higher-exam-performance.md) [~W]
rows.change: Do not count the switch as learning; check with a new question answered alone, since only students correct on both votes did better on related exam items
rows.if: Most of the class switches to the right answer on the revote

rows.basis: [Poor group leadership undermined discussion](claims/cooperative-conceptual-change-chemistry-misconceptions.md) [~W]; [Interactive engagement requires constructive turn taking](claims/interactive-requires-constructive-turn-taking.md) [~W]
rows.change: Give roles or a turn rule so every member states a reason and responds to the others; who controls the talk matters more than how much there is
rows.if: Groups are likely to be led by one confident member

rows.basis: [Some discussion approaches improve comprehension](claims/structured-discussion-methods-improve-comprehension.md) [~M]
rows.change: Use a structured discussion approach with modelled discourse moves; more student talk on its own did not produce comprehension gains
rows.if: The aim is comprehension of a text, in a school classroom

rows.basis: [Conflict-based instruction improves conceptual learning, with limits](claims/cognitive-disequilibrium-motivates-conceptual-change.md) [~M]
rows.change: Make sure the disagreement is resolved afterwards; staged contradictions raised learning only for learners who reported being confused
rows.if: The question is built to provoke disagreement

rows.basis: [Group rewards with individual accountability](claims/cooperative-learning-group-rewards-and-individual-accountability.md) [~M]; [Collaborative learning improves outcomes](claims/collaborative-learning-improves-outcomes.md) [+M]
rows.change: Base any group reward on each member's individual learning
rows.if: Discussion will run over many weeks as group work that counts for grades

rows.basis: [Longer wait time goes with higher-level responses](claims/increasing-wait-time-improves-response-quality.md) [+W]
rows.change: Protect a silent pause, or a written answer, before anyone speaks
rows.if: Many learners rarely speak or need time to formulate an answer

rows.basis: [Discussion promotes more active thinking; lecture is no worse for information](claims/discussion-promotes-more-active-thought-than-lecture.md) [~W]
rows.change: Explain directly; reserve discussion for questions where reasoning differs
rows.if: The objective is information transmission rather than revising a misconception

rows.basis: untested proposal; the [self-explanation claim](claims/self-explanation-improves-conceptual-understanding.md) [~S] notes in its discussion that learners without background may reinforce misconceptions
rows.change: Do not ask them to explain unstudied content; study a worked example together first, then explain it to each other step by step; have the teacher check one explanation per pair before swapping
rows.if: Learners are `novice` and are meeting the material for the first time

rows.basis: [Older peers as tutors support gains for older and younger students](claims/tutoring-and-cross-age-peer-tutors-effective.md) [+W] (a narrative policy review, no data printed); [Learning By Teaching Improves Tutor Learning](claims/learning-by-teaching-improves-tutor-learning.md) [+S] for the explainer's side; first-year students in problem-based learning said [selected and trained senior student tutors explained more clearly and in plainer terms than staff tutors](claims/student-tutors-cognitive-congruency-focus-group.md) [+W] (one focus group, perceptions only)
rows.change: Let the more knowledgeable explain to those meeting the material (cross-age or cross-level), with a role card so they question rather than tell; give them harder material to prepare
rows.if: Learners are `advanced`, or some are well ahead

rows.basis: [Peer-assisted learning improves elementary achievement](claims/peer-assisted-learning-improves-achievement.md) [+M] (meta-analysis read as abstract; larger effects for younger, urban, low-income and minority students, and with interdependent rewards, self-referenced evaluation and autonomy); session length is an untested proposal
rows.change: Fixed short scripts (one role card per side), sessions of 15–20 minutes, roles that swap each session, a group reward built from each child's own check
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary age)

rows.basis: untested proposal; the recorded claims are school and university studies
rows.change: Peers explain a procedure or case from their own work to a colleague who must ask how they would handle a variant; the colleague restates; keep the individual check as a short case decision
rows.if: Learners are `adult` professionals in a work setting

rows.basis: [Peer Tutoring and Response Groups positive effects on English language development](claims/peer-tutoring-response-groups-positive-eld-effects.md) [+M] (WWC, three RCTs); limit: [cross-age tutoring showed no significant effect on oral proficiency](claims/cross-level-peer-tutoring-null-oral-proficiency.md) [~M] (42 grade 3–5 students, daily 20-minute sessions over three months)
