rows.change: Use structured response groups and paired tutoring on the language target, with explanation allowed in the first language where the goal is content; check oral proficiency separately, as pairing alone may not move it
rows.if: Learners are English learners, or instruction is in their second language

rows.basis: [Reciprocal Teaching Improves Reading Comprehension](claims/reciprocal-teaching-improves-reading-comprehension.md) [+M] (16 studies; effect much larger on experimenter-made tests than standardised ones)
rows.change: Reciprocal roles on a text: each learner in turn leads predicting, questioning, clarifying and summarising, after the teacher has modelled all four
rows.if: Goal is reading comprehension

rows.basis: [Peer assessment improves performance](claims/peer-assessment-improves-performance.md) [+M] (54 control-group studies, small effect against no assessment); [assessor-role claim](claims/peer-assessment-benefits-assessor.md) [~M] (rater training the strongest moderator; the assessor benefit itself is correlational); [peer assessment in a large college statistics course](claims/peer-assessment-improves-unit-quiz-achievement.md) [+M] (matched randomised crossover, about 300 students, d = .115 on unit quizzes against instructor grading, d = .122 on the [final exam](claims/peer-assessment-gains-persist-to-final-exam.md) [+M]); for two or three reviews per draft, [several peer reviews improved drafts more than one expert's](claims/multiple-peer-reviews-beat-single-expert-reviewer-sword.md) [+W] in one 28-student experiment read second-hand, as the pattern sets out
rows.change: Peers assess each other's drafts against the criteria and each author revises; train raters on the criteria with one anchor example first; expect a small gain, so keep an individual check and do not let peer assessment replace the explaining steps; see the [Structured Peer Review pattern](patterns/structured-peer-review.md)
rows.if: Goal is a written draft or a product judged against criteria

rows.basis: [AI-peer integrated feedback beat conventional peer feedback on all four writing criteria](claims/ai-peer-feedback-writing-gains-differential.md) [+M] (one quasi-experiment in L2 writing classes, d = 1.41 to 1.16 by criterion, smallest gain on coherence and cohesion; read as one study); [AI-assisted peer feedback gave fewer content and argument comments than teacher feedback](claims/feedback-focus-shift-across-tasks.md) [~M] (one quasi-experiment, two classes); [peer groups and ChatGPT-4o did not differ in feedback quality at the first stage](claims/stage1-no-significant-difference-peer-ai-feedback-quality.md) [~M] (13 groups; the AI was rated higher at the second stage; no equivalence test); students read peers as contextual and AI as general but actionable ([complementary-feedback claim](claims/ai-and-peer-feedback-complementary.md) [~W], [perceptions claim](claims/student-perceptions-human-contextual-ai-objective-structured.md) [~W]; reflections, no learning measure)
rows.change: Keep the peer review and add AI as a second source after it, not instead of it: each author reads both, notes where they agree and differ, and decides what to revise; keep a teacher check on content and argument, since AI-assisted peer comments drifted toward technical detail; train peers on the criteria as above
rows.if: AI feedback is available, or the brief wants peer review combined with an AI tool (writing especially)

rows.basis: untested proposal; rater training from the [assessor-role claim](claims/peer-assessment-benefits-assessor.md) [~M]
rows.change: Keep it as given and run the peer exchange on it; change only one thing the evidence says matters: train peers on that rubric once, or add the partner's "restate and ask why" move, or add one individual check
rows.if: The brief names its own routine, rubric, categories or criteria (its own check-in, prompt or template)

rows.basis: [Structured Peer Tutoring Outperforms Unstructured](claims/structured-peer-tutoring-outperforms-unstructured.md) [+M]; sampling is an untested proposal, and contingent help is shown one-to-one only ([contingent scaffolding](claims/contingent-scaffolding-improves-learning.md) [~M]); in an IES study of mathematics curricula, [teachers directing students to help one another, and asking the class whether it agreed with a student's answer, went with higher achievement](claims/class-agreement-and-peer-help-higher-achievement.md) [+W] (correlational, no effect size)
rows.change: Put the structure in the role cards and the check items, not in the facilitator: the facilitator samples two or three pairs per round, corrects the commonest error for everyone, and reads only the individual checks
rows.if: `classroom` with one teacher and a large group, or scarce facilitator time (volunteers, a busy shift, one tutor checking in briefly)

rows.basis: [Collaborative learning opportunities largely disappeared when courses shifted to remote instruction](claims/remote-shift-reduced-collaborative-learning.md) [~W] (case studies of 29 courses; describes what instructors dropped, not learning); the pairing rule is an untested proposal
rows.change: Pair remote with remote and room with room, or give mixed pairs a shared document and an audio channel; schedule the peer exchange explicitly and time it, since it is the activity that tends to be dropped online
rows.if: Mixed modes: some learners remote, some in the room

rows.basis: untested proposal; the [remote-shift claim](claims/remote-shift-reduced-collaborative-learning.md) [~W] shows peer activity disappears unless designed in
rows.change: Asynchronous exchange: each learner records a 1–2 minute voice note or short text explaining one idea; an assigned partner must reply within a set window with a restatement and one question; the explainer answers
rows.if: Online self-paced or phone-only, no live session

rows.basis: [Social engagement in gateway math builds confidence, dependent on faculty fostering a supportive environment](claims/social-engagement-builds-confidence-gateway-math.md) [~W] (interviews and surveys, 76 faculty and 50 students); in interviews with six Thai undergraduates after a genre-based writing course, [some said they had felt uncomfortable working in pairs or groups](claims/gbsri-interview-attributions-and-pair-work-discomfort.md) [~W] even while crediting collaboration for their improvement; the specific moves are untested proposals
rows.change: Pair with a trusted partner; let them rehearse the explanation privately first, explain orally or by showing rather than writing, use sentence starters, and keep the first rounds unassessed; the facilitator models that a wrong explanation is expected and fixable
rows.if: Learners with low confidence, low literacy, or anxious about speaking in front of others

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: The learner controls what is shared and with whom; peers explain the concept on a neutral or invented example, and the learner applies it to their own case privately
rows.if: Material is private or sensitive (personal histories, health, work incidents)

rows.basis: untested proposal; the tested contrast (teaching against studying) does not set a duration
rows.change: One cycle: 3 minutes review, 5 minutes prepare, two 6-minute explain-and-question turns with roles swapped, 5 minutes individual check, 5 minutes teacher correction of the commonest error; report only immediate performance
rows.if: Time is one session only, or a fixed short budget (for example 30 minutes)

rows.basis: the debrief format and the repeat are untested proposals; for presentations, a review of college peer assessment reports [peer review of oral presentation skills improving performance, and peer (not instructor) assessment of four speeches raising self-concept on the last against a control group](claims/peer-oral-presentation-outcomes.md) [+W] (two older studies read second-hand, no effect sizes; the review says such studies are too few to say which feedback works best)
rows.change: Peers watch the whole performance and debrief against the brief's criteria (one strength, one change, one question), rather than splitting it into parts to explain; where it can be repeated, run peer review on an early performance and again on a later one
rows.if: A whole-task performance the brief wants kept whole (a presentation, a clinical encounter, a lesson taught)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use peers as the rehearsal audience: each learner explains or performs to a peer who plays the audience and asks what that audience would ask, before the real event
rows.if: Learners produce for a real audience (a performance, a product for clients)

rows.basis: untested proposal; individual accountability is modelled in [Cooperative Learning](principles/cooperative-learning.md); in one online exam, [peers' marks averaged 0.12 points below the teacher's while authors marked their own papers 0.83 above](claims/peers-undermark-self-assessors-overmark.md) [~W] (descriptive, no test); spot-checks and rewarding review quality are the two kinds of [quality control](claims/peer-assessment-quality-control-proactive-reactive.md) [+W] in one inventory of practice, untested as a comparison; the [Structured Peer Review pattern](patterns/structured-peer-review.md) carries them for drafts
rows.change: Keep peer judgements formative; grade only the individual check or the individual product; record which explanations were corrected; if peer marks are used at all, spot-check a sample against the teacher's (reactive control) and do not use learners' marks of their own work
rows.if: Stakes are high, or grades depend on the work

rows.basis: untested proposal; contingent support evidence is one-to-one ([contingent scaffolding](claims/contingent-scaffolding-improves-learning.md) [~M])
rows.change: Do not start with pair explanations; have every learner answer a diagnostic item first, address the misconception with the whole group, then use pairs to explain the corrected idea
rows.if: A misconception is widespread in the group

rows.basis: [Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows.](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M] (review of cognitive-load studies; gives no crossover point)
rows.change: Novice: more worked steps and closer items, fewer choices. Advanced: skip guided sections after an unaided check and go to harder or transfer items
rows.if: Learners are `novice` on this task, or `advanced` / already succeed on the first item

rows.basis: Adult: [Adult learner groups are more heterogeneous than child groups, calling for individualized instruction and varied learning strategies](claims/adult-learner-groups-more-heterogeneous.md) [+W] (essay, no data). Child: [School level significantly moderates effects: AI-enabled personalized STEM education is more effective in junior and senior high school than in kindergarten](claims/school-level-moderates-ai-stem-effects.md) [~M] (a subgroup comparison across RCTs in one meta-analysis: kindergarten g = 0.118 against 0.42–0.53 from elementary to senior high; between studies, not a test within one); the number of options is untested
rows.change: Child: two options at most, chosen by the teacher from what the child said; personalize contexts more than paths; in kindergarten, expect a small gain from AI-driven personalized practice and do not let it replace the teacher's tailoring. Adult: ask what they already do and want; expect a wider spread of experience, and offer more paths and more choice
rows.if: Learners are young children (`child`), or `adult`

rows.basis: [Individuals with developmental disabilities tend to prefer speech-generating devices over picture exchange and manual signs, with substantial individual differences](claims/sgd-preference-over-pe-and-manual-signs.md) [+M] (overview of reviews; whether preference tracks a child's characteristics or environment is unclear)
rows.change: Run a preference assessment with each child across the candidate systems over several sessions; choose per child, and re-check when the environment's demands change
rows.if: Learners have developmental disabilities and use or are choosing an AAC system

rows.basis: [Prompt style is the largest driver of disability-aware Fit gains, and the Thinking Reward becomes effective only in combination with adaptive prompting](claims/thinking-reward-effective-only-with-adaptive-prompting.md) [+W] (simulated learner personas, LLM tutor ratings, not learners' outcomes); [Outcomes of students with disabilities improve when they receive specially designed instruction responsive to assessment data](claims/specially-designed-instruction-responsive-to-assessment-data-improves-outcomes.md) [+W] (brief citing four studies)
rows.change: Tailor two things separately: how much support (from the learner's baseline accuracy) and what style of support (from the access need, e.g. shorter steps, visuals, read-aloud)
rows.if: Learners have disabilities with different access needs (an AI or human tutor responds)

rows.basis: [Learning Styles Matching Does Not Improve Learning](claims/learning-styles-matching-does-not-improve-learning.md) [-S]
rows.change: Drop the matching; choose format by what the content needs; if learners differ, diagnose prior knowledge instead
rows.if: The brief proposes matching format to learning styles or a preference inventory

rows.basis: [Model gender and observer gender do not affect learning outcomes or near transfer from video modeling examples](claims/no-gender-effects-learning-transfer-video-modeling.md) [-W] (one 2 × 2 experiment; null, equivalence not tested); [Localizing word-problem character names improved MATHia performance only for specific subgroup-majority schools, with no improvement in sense of belonging overall](claims/localized-names-personalization-subgroup-performance.md) [~M]; assigned topics often missed: [topic mismatch](claims/students-report-topic-mismatch-interests.md) [-W]
rows.change: Do not expect the match to raise learning, and do not assign a learner's contexts or "style" from a group label; keep one well-designed model or example for everyone, and where learners want to see themselves in the material, let each learner name or choose the context or model
rows.if: The brief proposes matching models, characters, names or examples to learners' group (gender, ethnicity, culture, background)

rows.basis: [An IES practice-guide presentation recommends personalized problem contexts, asserting without cited studies that students engage more actively and perform better in them](claims/personalized-problem-contexts-boost-engagement-grades-4-8.md) [+W] (practice-guide assertion); [The generative AI relevance intervention did not significantly increase students' interest in the math class](claims/ai-relevance-intervention-no-interest-effect.md) [~W] (high school, a relevance intervention, null on interest)
rows.change: Use learner-named contexts with the structure unchanged; let learners change the context; measure interest directly rather than assuming the context raised it
rows.if: Goal is engagement or interest in a subject (e.g. mathematics word problems)

rows.basis: [In a randomized experiment, personalized paths reduced learning time by 22.0% and improved post-test scores versus a fixed sequence](claims/personalized-paths-experiment-outcomes.md) [+M]; [ITS significantly outperform large-group human instruction, individual computer-based instruction, and textbooks or workbooks, but not small-group or individual human tutoring](claims/its-beats-large-group-cbi-textbooks-not-human-tutoring.md) [+M]; [Students in focus groups were positive about adaptive courseware but reported alignment, access, and reliability concerns](claims/student-focus-group-perceptions-courseware.md) [~W]; [Courseware can bridge gateway math learning gaps through tailored tutorials, study tools, diagnostics, and targeted practice](claims/courseware-bridges-learning-gaps-gateway-math.md) [+W] (faculty and student interviews; perceptions, not outcomes)
rows.change: Use a platform that diagnoses parts of the topic and orders each learner's path; expect time saved and a modest aligned gain; pair it with an instructor learners can reach
rows.if: Setting is `online-self-paced`, with a platform or courseware

rows.basis: Role and insistence: [Participants required GSR self-knowledge of an assertive, conscientious, friendly personality with a customizable role](claims/gsr-self-knowledge-personality-role-requirements.md) [~W] (interviews with university participants about a social robot; what they wanted varied from person to person; preferences, not outcomes). [Real-time detection of SRL processes can personalize scaffold content, with all five scaffolds personalized to some extent but to varying degrees (scaffolds 2 and 5 most, scaffold 3 least).](claims/real-time-srl-detection-personalizes-scaffold-content-varying-degrees.md) [+W] (counts for 18 learners in the personalized condition; shows the content varied, not that it helped); [Personalized scaffolds increased frequencies of high cognition and monitoring relative to control, but learning outcomes did not differ between conditions.](claims/scaffolds-changed-srl-processes-not-outcomes.md) [~W] (same study, a summary of earlier analyses; null on learning, equivalence not tested); [Removing explicit mastery information from learner profiles mainly degrades Adaptivity](claims/mastery-information-needed-for-adaptivity.md) [+W] (model-generated paths, not learners); [One-shot path generation raises Validity but lowers Adaptivity and Efficiency relative to step-by-step interaction](claims/one-shot-generation-lowers-adaptivity.md) [~W] (model paths scored by metrics, not learners); [Emotion features improve tutor performance only when grounded in education-theory-based pedagogical strategies; emotion information alone misguides a smaller model](claims/emotion-plus-theory-prompting-ablation-gain.md) [~W] (a prompt ablation on one model, not learner outcomes); [Emerging evidence indicates generative AI tutors currently struggle to accurately infer student knowledge at the outset of an interaction or as the activity progresses](claims/genai-tutors-struggle-infer-student-knowledge.md) [-W]; [K-12 students and teachers both consider AI imperfect at detecting students' knowledge and assigning appropriate tasks, and therefore prefer more human control over AI decisions](claims/students-teachers-see-ai-imperfect-prefer-human-control.md) [~W]
rows.change: Give it the learner's mastery record for the skill and its prerequisites, and keep a teacher able to override its task choices; have it plan the path step by step from the learner's responses rather than generate the whole path at once; if it reads the learner's emotional state, give it the teaching move to make for each state, not the state alone. If it tailors prompts from detected learning behaviour (what the learner has already planned, monitored or read), log which options each learner was shown to confirm the content really varied, and judge it on the learning measure, since behaviour can change while scores do not. Let each learner set the role it plays (study partner, coach, tutor) and how insistently it prompts them, rather than fixing one manner for all
rows.if: An AI tutor, chatbot or detection system does the tailoring

rows.basis: [Preservice teachers chose the easy video significantly more often for an ethnic minority student than for an ethnic majority student, all other information being equal](claims/ethnic-minority-student-given-easy-video-study1.md) [-M]; [Student achievement level, not ethnic background, predicted preservice teachers' text-versus-video material choice in Study 2](claims/achievement-level-predicts-material-choice-study2.md) [~M] (two vignette experiments with preservice teachers, carried to practising teachers; choices of material, not learning outcomes)
rows.change: Make each choice from the learner's diagnostic and check results and record the basis beside it; in the weekly review, look for easier materials gathering in one group whose results do not differ, and re-place from results
rows.if: A teacher chooses each learner's materials, path or difficulty by judgement

rows.basis: [In mathematics, personalized-learning students in the lowest baseline quintile were the most likely to out-grow their matched comparison students](claims/pl-lowest-baseline-students-greatest-growth.md) [+W] (matched comparison, mathematics, no effect size); [Teachers who made productive adaptations were more likely to consider learning progressions and adapt lessons to below-grade-level content](claims/productive-adapters-consider-progressions-below-grade-level.md) [+W]; who gets reached: [Human-AI tutoring is associated with a 36% rise in IXL skill proficiency, but the gap widened in favor of reactively tutored students (difference-in-differences preprint)](claims/human-ai-tutoring-skill-proficiency-gap-widens.md) [~W] (lower starters approached by tutors fell further behind those who asked)
rows.change: Place them on the continuum where the diagnostic puts them, reaching below grade level if needed, with the same final criterion; track whether they close the gap, not only whether they move; make sure the teacher or tutor goes to them rather than waiting to be asked
rows.if: Some learners start far behind the rest (lowest prior achievement on the diagnostic)

rows.basis: untested proposal; from the folded continuous-progress page ("does not imply a one-to-one teaching ratio")
rows.change: Do not build thirty paths: use the sequenced-sections structure with a short check per section, two or three flexible groups by current section, and a choice board for practice
rows.if: One teacher for a large class, no adaptive software

rows.basis: Pace and check-in target: untested proposal. Who the facilitator reaches: [Human-AI tutoring is associated with a 36% rise in IXL skill proficiency, but the gap widened in favor of reactively tutored students (difference-in-differences preprint)](claims/human-ai-tutoring-skill-proficiency-gap-widens.md) [~W] (a difference-in-differences study; both groups gained, and students tutors approached proactively, who started lower, fell further behind those who asked for help)
rows.change: Tailor one thing only: pace, through self-checking sections; spend the check-in on the learner who has been held longest at one section, and check afterwards whether those learners closed the gap or only moved
rows.if: Facilitator time is scarce (volunteers, a tutor who checks in briefly, a busy shift)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep the diagnostic and section checks short enough for a phone (five items or fewer); post choices as a list both groups see; review remote learners' progress in the same weekly pass
rows.if: Mixed modes (some remote, some in the room) or phone-only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Personalize only the context of problems and a choice of task; keep one path; record what each learner chose and how they did, and do not claim a lasting gain
rows.if: A single session only

rows.basis: untested proposal; the autonomy claim's own discussion warns that premature autonomy can produce anxiety in novices ([Self-determination theory holds that autonomy support raises intrinsic motivation, and a meta-analysis finds expected tangible rewards undermine it](claims/autonomy-supports-intrinsic-motivation.md) [~M], carried to this group)
rows.change: Offer two options, read aloud, with a worked sample of each; let learners name interests orally; avoid open-ended choice early
rows.if: Learners with low confidence or low literacy

rows.basis: [Not all students would benefit from improving the same competencies, suggesting an individualized approach to education may be preferable to a one-size-fits-all approach](claims/heterogeneous-competency-benefits-individualized-education.md) [~W] (an issue brief's analysis of students' competencies and later outcomes; carried to adults in work); contexts: untested
rows.change: Use tasks and cases from each learner's own job as the contexts; let them choose which competencies to work on first after a diagnostic, since not all need the same ones
rows.if: Adults in work settings

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Let the learner choose the topic, medium and audience; keep the criteria for the product common and visible
rows.if: The product or performance is for a real audience

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep it and use its categories; change only what the evidence says matters (diagnose on responses, not styles; ask the learner rather than assign interests; check that the tailoring was enacted)
rows.if: The brief names its own routine, categories, criteria or rubric for tailoring (its own check-in, diagnostic, choice menu)

rows.basis: [Participants required GSR user-knowledge of learning goals, progress, learning type, emotions, and background, with privacy safeguards and informed consent](claims/gsr-user-knowledge-personalization-requirements.md) [~W] (university participants, social-robot design study)
rows.change: Ask only for what the tailoring uses; the learner decides what to share and who sees it; obtain informed consent and say where it is stored
rows.if: Tailoring needs private or sensitive information (interests, emotions, disability, background)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Spend 3 minutes on a two-item check, 2 minutes on a choice of context, 20 on practice at the learner's level, 5 on a common unaided check
rows.if: A fixed short time budget (e.g. 30 minutes)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Personalize the context, topic or means of the whole task, not by splitting it into separately paced parts
rows.if: A whole-task performance the brief wants kept whole

rows.basis: untested proposal; from the earlier page's constraint that adaptive routing can narrow exposure
rows.change: Hold the assessment and criterion identical for every path; check that tailored paths still reach every assessed objective before the test
rows.if: Stakes are high, or a common standard is set externally

rows.basis: [Systematic Phonics Improves Word Reading](claims/phonics-instruction-outperforms-whole-word-for-generalization.md) [+S] (kindergarten to grade 6; largest effects in kindergarten and grades 1–2)
rows.change: Run the full default: daily 20–30 minute lessons through the first school year, with phonemic-awareness work in the first term and decodable text from the first week
rows.if: Learners are `child`, kindergarten or first grade, beginning to read

rows.basis: [Phonemic Awareness Training Improves Reading](claims/phonemic-awareness-training-improves-reading.md) [+M] (preschool to grade 1); [Combined letter name and sound instruction produced greater letter sound gains than number instruction, with a trend over letter sound only instruction](claims/combined-lnls-letter-sound-gains-over-control.md) [+M] (randomised preschool experiment: names-and-sounds beat number teaching on letter-sound production, d = 0.47; over sounds alone, d = 0.51 but p = .051); [Dialogic Reading Improves Expressive Language](claims/dialogic-reading-improves-language-outcomes.md) [+M]
rows.change: Phonemic-awareness games with letters in view, one or two skills (blending, segmenting) at a time, in small groups, 5–18 hours in all; teach letters by name and sound together, a few a week; plus daily interactive read-alouds. Do not start a full decoding programme
rows.if: Learners are pre-readers (preschool)

rows.basis: [Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows.](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M] (a cognitive-load review, carried to reading)
rows.change: Drop phonics lessons; give the screening only, teach the specific gaps it shows, and spend the time on fluency, vocabulary and comprehension
rows.if: Learners already decode accurately (`advanced` for decoding)

rows.basis: [Systematic Phonics Improves Word Reading](claims/phonics-instruction-outperforms-whole-word-for-generalization.md) [~S] (older readers with difficulties: decoding effects remained, comprehension and spelling effects not reliably above zero); [Morphological instruction improves word-level literacy outcomes (decoding, spelling, vocabulary, morphological knowledge) but shows no reliable effect on reading comprehension](claims/morphological-instruction-improves-literacy.md) [+M] (largest gains on decoding, particular benefit for less-able readers, preschool to grade 8)
rows.change: Diagnose the gaps rather than restart the sequence; teach multisyllable decoding and word parts (prefixes, roots, suffixes); pair every phonics lesson with fluency and comprehension work; expect decoding gains before comprehension gains
rows.if: Older struggling readers (grade 2 and above, or `adolescent`)

rows.basis: [Phonics instruction has a small but statistically confirmed effect for children with reading disabilities, while Orton-Gillingham structured-literacy programs show positive but non-significant effects](claims/structured-literacy-interventions-help-struggling-readers.md) [~S] (22 RCTs: phonics the only approach with a confirmed effect, g′ = 0.198; Orton-Gillingham effects positive but not significant). Group size is an untested proposal
rows.change: Keep systematic phonics as the core, delivered one-to-one or in groups of two to four, with more cumulative review and a longer intervention; expect small gains; do not expect a branded multisensory programme to add to them, and do not use coloured overlays
rows.if: Learners have an identified reading disability or dyslexia

rows.basis: untested proposal for adult literacy. An artificial-script experiment with 24 adults found print-to-sound training made new words faster to read than print-to-meaning training, not more accurate ([Systematic phonics outperforms unsystematic or no-phonics instruction on children's reading overall, but its advantage over whole-word teaching on novel words is untested in children and contested](claims/phonics-instruction-outperforms-whole-word-for-generalization.md) [~S]). No claim page here tests phonics teaching with adults learning to read their own language
rows.change: Use adult texts and words from the learner's own life or job for blending and decodable reading; say why the sound work is there; keep checks private; move to the learner's real texts as soon as a correspondence is secure
rows.if: Learners are `adult`, in a literacy programme or at work

rows.basis: untested proposal for beginning readers; the evidence in the next row is from adults who already read their first language
rows.change: Teach the sounds orally before print, with minimal pairs for sounds absent from the first language; use only words whose meaning the learner knows for blending practice; teach meaning alongside
rows.if: Learners are learning to read in a second language, or the language of instruction is not their first

rows.basis: [Automatization of the phonological component through pronunciation practice improves ESP students' reading comprehension more than traditional translation-based instruction](claims/phonological-automatization-improves-esp-reading-comprehension.md) [+M] (60 university ESP students randomised, one semester, pronunciation practice against translation; higher comprehension, no effect size printed); [Lower-level phonological processing efficiency contributes significantly to individual differences in adult ESL reading measures](claims/phonological-orthographic-efficiency-predicts-esl-reading.md) [+W] (correlational, reported second-hand); [Early failure in phonetic recoding and decoding widens the acquisition gap between false beginners and successful learners over time](claims/early-decoding-failure-widens-acquisition-gap.md) [+W] (a conference paper's interpretation, young adult learners; no teaching tested)
rows.change: Do not rely on translation or top-down strategy work alone: give regular class time to pronunciation and letter-to-sound practice on the course's own vocabulary, and screen decoding early so learners who stumble at the start are caught before the gap grows
rows.if: Literate adolescents or adults reading in a foreign language (university language or ESP courses) whose reading is slow or effortful

rows.basis: [Systematic phonics outperforms unsystematic or no-phonics instruction on children's reading overall, but its advantage over whole-word teaching on novel words is untested in children and contested](claims/phonics-instruction-outperforms-whole-word-for-generalization.md) [~S] (whole-language comparison: d = 0.55 decoding, d = 0.19 comprehension); [Automatic word recognition frees resources for comprehension.](claims/automatic-word-recognition-frees-resources-for-comprehension.md) [+W] (a mechanism; no training study)
rows.change: Keep phonics, but do not expect it to carry comprehension: add vocabulary, oral-language and read-aloud discussion time, and measure comprehension separately
rows.if: The goal is reading comprehension, not only word reading

rows.basis: [Phonemic Awareness Training Improves Reading](claims/phonemic-awareness-training-improves-reading.md) [~M] (for phonemic-awareness training, small groups beat whole-class and individual delivery; carried to phonics); [Low reading-group first graders read far fewer words than high-group peers, limiting elaboration](claims/low-group-first-graders-read-few-words.md) [~W] (an observational finding reported second-hand: low-group first graders read 60 words in five days, high groups about ten times as many); the rotation and the equal-time rule are untested
rows.change: Introduce the new correspondence to the whole class in 10 minutes with choral responses and every child showing a written answer at once (whiteboards); then small groups by placement for decodable reading while others practise independently; weekly one-to-one checks rotated across the class; give the lowest-placed group at least as many minutes of connected reading as the others, and regroup as checks are passed
rows.if: One teacher with a whole class of 25–30

rows.basis: untested proposal. Coaching parents in an interactive reading style changed home practice for families of 2- to 3-year-olds but not for families of children at greatest risk ([Dialogic Reading Improves Expressive Language](claims/dialogic-reading-improves-language-outcomes.md) [~M])
rows.change: Record each model on video with the mouth visible; have the learner read the word list aloud into the phone for the teacher to hear; send decodable books home with a one-page guide for the adult on saying sounds without an added "uh" and on correcting by pointing to the letters
rows.if: Mixed modes: some learners at home, some in the room, or practice on a phone

rows.basis: untested proposal; no claim here tests phonics delivered without a teacher
rows.change: Choose or build software that models every sound in audio, has the learner blend before revealing the word, checks reading aloud (speech recognition or a recorded sample a person reviews), and gates new correspondences on the weekly check
rows.if: No teacher present: an app or self-paced programme

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Screen, then teach one correspondence and blend five to ten words with it; give the learner or family the next three correspondences to practise; do not report decoding gains
rows.if: A single session only

rows.basis: untested in reading. Novices given process goals outperformed those given outcome goals in a writing-revision experiment with 84 high-school students, with a shift to outcome goals helping once the skill was mastered ([Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals.](claims/process-goals-outperform-outcome-goals-for-novices.md) [+M]; carried to reading)
rows.change: Begin with a correspondence they will master in the first session; show progress on their own weekly chart, first as the steps they carried out (said each sound, blended, checked the word) and only once a correspondence is secure as accuracy scores; avoid reading aloud in front of peers until the text is fully decodable for them
rows.if: Learners with low confidence after years of failure (older children, adults)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Choose or write a text within the learner's taught code, rehearse it with corrections until accurate, and keep the audience performance after accuracy, not as the practice
rows.if: A performance for a real audience (reading to younger children, a class reading, reading aloud at work)

rows.basis: untested; the claim pages state this on general grounds and record no evidence for it
rows.change: Expect a shorter phonics phase; move to connected text and comprehension sooner, but keep the screening and weekly checks
rows.if: The language has regular spelling (Spanish, Italian, Finnish)

rows.basis: untested proposal; pseudoword decoding is where the phonics effect was largest ([Systematic Phonics Improves Word Reading](claims/phonics-instruction-outperforms-whole-word-for-generalization.md) [+S])
rows.change: Measure decoding with pseudowords as well as taught words, so memorised words do not count as decoding; record which correspondences have been taught
rows.if: Results will be reported or used for placement

rows.basis: [Classroom physical activity…](claims/classroom-physical-activity-improves-attention.md) [+S] (primary-school and 4–17-year-old children; on-task behavior); [Energizers improved on-task behavior…](claims/energizers-improved-on-task-behavior.md) [+M] (10-minute breaks, grades 3–4)
rows.change: Use the default as given: one or two bouts per session, 5 minutes vigorous or more than 10 minutes moderate-to-vigorous, between segments, with a fixed transition
rows.if: Learners are `child` or primary age, in a `classroom`

rows.basis: [The least on-task students show the largest improvement…](claims/energizers-least-on-task-students-largest-gain.md) [+M] (one study, a subgroup of grades 3–4 students; a group chosen for low baseline scores can also improve by regression to the mean). The individual option: untested
rows.change: Keep the whole-class bout short and place it where those learners start to drift, not where the class average does; count their on-task behavior separately before and after; if the rest of the class gains nothing, offer those learners an individual stand-and-move option instead of a whole-class bout. Treat a few learners' state as something they show in that segment, not as a fixed trait
rows.if: Only some learners drift (most stay on task; a few are often off task in long segments)

rows.basis: Dose: [Classroom physical activity…](claims/classroom-physical-activity-improves-attention.md) [+S] (includes ages up to 17). Choice and format: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep the doses; give learners more say in the moves (a menu, rotating leaders), and use walking discussion or an active review game rather than whole-class exercises they may find childish
rows.if: Learners are `adolescent`

rows.basis: untested; the classroom reviews are with children, and the only adult evidence here is about memory timing in labs ([Acute exercise timing…](claims/acute-exercise-timing-memory.md) [~S])
rows.change: Replace exercise routines with a stand-and-move transition: 3 to 5 minutes standing, a walking pair discussion of the next prompt, or a change of station; explain the purpose in one sentence and make it optional
rows.if: Learners are `adult`, or adults in a `workplace-clinical` setting (a long training day, a shift-based course)

rows.basis: [Acute exercise timing…](claims/acute-exercise-timing-memory.md) [~S] (healthy adults, lab episodic memory; carried to classrooms untested)
rows.change: Keep new-material segments still; put recess, PE or a walk after the lesson that introduced it, not before or during
rows.if: The goal is retention of new material a day or more later (`delayed-retention`)

rows.basis: [Physical Experience Enhances Science Learning](claims/physical-experience-enhances-science-learning.md) [~M] (college physics; physical and virtual manipulation equal in one study)
rows.change: Use a short enactment or gesture that maps onto the quantity, then link it explicitly to the diagram or formula; a well-built simulation is an acceptable substitute where movement is not possible
rows.if: The goal is understanding a physical or spatial concept (`concept`)

rows.basis: [Classroom physical activity…](claims/classroom-physical-activity-improves-attention.md) [~S]
rows.change: Keep the break for on-task behavior, and look for the test gain elsewhere in the design (practice, feedback); tell the client the reviews found no consistent achievement gain
rows.if: The goal is test performance or achievement, and the brief expects the break to raise it

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Run the bout as a camera-optional "stand up, follow me" for everyone at once, with the same closing cue; remote and phone learners are invited to stand, stretch or walk away from the screen for the same minutes; do not check who moved
rows.if: Mixed modes: some learners remote, some in the room, or phone-only

rows.basis: untested; the reviews test teacher-led classroom bouts
rows.change: Build a timed prompt into the course after each 20–30 minute block ("stand and move for 3 minutes, then come back to question 4"), with the next task named; let the learner skip it
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use one fixed, scripted routine the group learns once and then leads itself (a student leader, a 5-minute video or audio track), so running it costs the facilitator only the start and the closing cue
rows.if: One teacher with a large group, or scarce facilitator time (a volunteer, a busy shift, one tutor checking in briefly)

rows.basis: Dose: [Classroom physical activity…](claims/classroom-physical-activity-improves-attention.md) [+S] (children). Single-session framing: untested
rows.change: One bout of about 5 minutes vigorous (or a 10-minute active segment) at the point the group first drifts, with the next task named; observe on-task behavior in the 10 minutes after; claim nothing about learning
rows.if: A single session only

rows.basis: untested proposal; the reviews give doses, not time budgets
rows.change: Under 30 minutes: no scheduled bout; at most a 1-minute stand-and-stretch at the change of activity. 30–60 minutes: one bout of up to 5 minutes. Over 60 minutes: one bout per 25–30 minutes of seated work. Count the minutes into the lesson plan so they add up
rows.if: A fixed short time budget (a 30-minute lesson, a 10-minute block)

rows.basis: untested proposal; the timing evidence is about memory for material learned around the bout, not test performance ([Acute exercise timing…](claims/acute-exercise-timing-memory.md) [~S])
rows.change: A short bout of up to 5 minutes 10 to 20 minutes before the start, followed by a calm settling minute; no strenuous activity immediately before, and nothing new to learn during it
rows.if: Stakes are high: right before a test or a performance

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Model every move first, use moves with no wrong way to do them, give a seated version, never single anyone out or rank effort, and use spoken or pictured instructions rather than written ones
rows.if: Learners with low confidence, low literacy, or reluctance to move in front of others

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page (accessibility and safety)
rows.change: Offer seated and upper-body versions, a standing stretch, or a calm alternative ([Mindfulness Activities](principles/mindfulness-activities.md)); keep it optional with no reason needed; do not run vigorous bouts where the space is unsafe
rows.if: Mobility limits, health conditions, a small room, or cultural or dress constraints on movement

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep any personal activity data private to the learner; the learner decides whether to share it, and nothing in the course is graded on it
rows.if: Activity is tracked (step counts, wearables, fitness scores)

rows.basis: Dose: [Classroom physical activity…](claims/classroom-physical-activity-improves-attention.md) [+S]; organised recess: [Playworks…](claims/playworks-better-recess-behavior-and-class-readiness.md) [+M] (one randomized programme evaluation; teacher reports)
rows.change: Keep it; change only what the evidence says matters: place it between segments, keep it to about 5 vigorous or 10+ moderate minutes, and end it with the same transition into a named task
rows.if: The brief names its own break routine, movement programme or recess model (a video series, a school recess scheme, a warm-up)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Record on-task behavior in the brief's own categories; add no new survey, test or rating the brief did not ask for
rows.if: The brief has its own categories, rubric or checklist for behavior or readiness

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Do not break the performance for a bout; place movement before the run-through or after it, and if it runs long, break only at a natural seam the performers choose
rows.if: The brief wants a whole performance kept whole (a rehearsal, a lab, a presentation run-through, a game)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use movement as a warm-up before the performance, led by the performers themselves, out of the audience's sight
rows.if: The product or performance is for a real audience (a concert, a presentation to clients)

rows.basis: [Self Talk Improves Learning And Performance](claims/self-talk-improves-learning-and-performance.md) [+S] (sport; larger on novel tasks); [Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals.](claims/process-goals-outperform-outcome-goals-for-novices.md) [~M] (writing revision, about goals)
rows.change: Write instructional cues that name the steps, as process phrases; model and rehearse them; prompt at the step that fails
rows.if: Learners are `novice` on a new skill with steps (a procedure, a technique)

rows.basis: [Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows.](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M] (cognitive-load studies of instructional formats; carried to self-talk untested)
rows.change: Drop step cues; keep at most one motivational or focusing cue for pressure moments
rows.if: Learners are `advanced`, or the skill is already automatic

rows.basis: [Self Talk Improves Learning And Performance](claims/self-talk-improves-learning-and-performance.md) [+S] (the setting the evidence comes from)
rows.change: Use instructional cue words for fine, precise movements and motivational cues for endurance; train them before use
rows.if: The goal is a motor or performance skill (sport, a lab or clinical technique, an instrument)

rows.basis: [Strategy Instruction Improves Writing Quality](claims/strategy-instruction-improves-writing-quality.md) [+M] (grades 4–10; self-instruction bundled with three other components)
rows.change: Teach self-instructions as part of the strategy (its steps become the cues) with goal setting and self-monitoring, over several sessions
rows.if: The goal is academic writing or problem solving, `child` or `adolescent`

rows.basis: [Thought and language become increasingly interdependent in the first few years, with private speech evolving into inner speech as self-regulation](claims/vygotsky-private-speech-inner-speech.md) [+W] (a theoretical overview; no study)
rows.change: Let them talk aloud while working; the adult models the cue first and the child repeats it, then whispers it; do not treat talking aloud as off-task
rows.if: Learners are young children (`child`, early primary)

rows.basis: [Emotion Labeling Improves Regulation](claims/emotion-labeling-improves-regulation.md) [~M] (adults, spider fear, physiological only); [Brief expressive writing before an exam can raise test-anxious students' scores, but across the wider literature its effect on test performance is negligible](claims/expressive-writing-improves-exam-performance.md) [~S] (a meta-analysis finds a negligible effect of one-session writing)
rows.change: Teach one name-it-then-act routine ("I'm nervous; read question 1 slowly") and rehearse it in a practice test; do not rely on a single pre-exam writing or self-talk exercise on its own
rows.if: Learners are anxious before a test or evaluation

rows.basis: Untested proposal; brief one-off psychological exercises have weak average achievement effects ([Growth-mindset interventions have weak average effects on achievement, including a negligible GPA gain (d = 0.11) for lower-achieving US ninth-graders in one preregistered national trial](claims/growth-mindset-improves-achievement.md) [~M], a different intervention)
rows.change: Give 10–15 minutes: find the moment, model one cue, each learner writes one or two cues and rehearses on two items; report use, not a lasting change
rows.if: Time is one session only

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Spend it as 1 minute recalling the cue, 3 minutes using it on one hard item, 1 minute noting whether it helped; move modeling to the first session only
rows.if: A fixed short time budget per session (for example 5 minutes)

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Show the learner's own cue at the point where errors or long pauses occur (after a wrong answer, after a set idle time), with the next action as a button; let the learner edit their cues
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Model once for the whole class; learners write their own cue cards and rehearse in pairs; the teacher prompts "What's your cue?" only for learners who stall
rows.if: `classroom` with one teacher and many learners

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: One 10-minute teaching session and a pocket card; at each brief check-in the facilitator asks one question: "Where did you get stuck, and what did your cue tell you to do?"
rows.if: Facilitator time is scarce (volunteers, busy shifts, a tutor who drops in)

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Keep the cues in a place every learner sees on their own device (a phone note or lock-screen line); model on a shared screen so remote and in-room learners see the same think-aloud
rows.if: Mixed mode (some remote, some in the room) or phone-only learners

rows.basis: Untested proposal, from the earlier page's credibility constraint
rows.change: Spoken cues in the learner's own words, a picture or symbol beside each; choose plainly true statements over upbeat ones; point out when a cue was followed by success
rows.if: Learners with low confidence or low literacy

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Take cue words from the job's own procedure or checklist (the step names already used on the floor or ward); keep the cards private to the learner
rows.if: Adults in a work setting

rows.basis: Untested proposal, from the earlier page's pre-performance cue cards
rows.change: Prepare a pre-performance cue card with one calming and one first-action cue; rehearse with the card in front of a small audience; the audience sees the performance, not the cards
rows.if: A presentation or performance for a real audience

rows.basis: Untested proposal; training effect from [Self Talk Improves Learning And Performance](claims/self-talk-improves-learning-and-performance.md) [+S] (sport)
rows.change: Keep it word for word as the learner's cue; change only what the evidence says matters: make sure one line names an action, and rehearse it before it is needed
rows.if: The brief names its own routine or script (for example "stop, breathe, plan")

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Write the instructional cues from those terms, not new ones
rows.if: The brief gives its own steps, categories or criteria (a rubric, a procedure, a checklist)

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: The learner keeps their notes on their own talk; no one collects or reads them unless the learner chooses to share; work on cues, not on the content of private thoughts
rows.if: What the learner says to themselves is private or sensitive

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Place cues at the decision points inside full runs of the task rather than splitting it into drills
rows.if: The brief wants a whole task or performance kept whole

rows.basis: [Self Talk Improves Learning And Performance](claims/self-talk-improves-learning-and-performance.md) [~S] (the systematic review found negative self-talk did not impede performance; sport)
rows.change: Do not intervene on tone alone; add an action cue only where performance or persistence falters
rows.if: Learners already talk negatively to themselves but perform well

rows.basis: Untested proposal, from the earlier page's context-blindness constraint

rows.change: Ask what they already do; use items from their own work as soon as the steps are stable; give a job aid laid out in the workplace's own categories and step names, used during practice and kept afterwards; check on a real or realistic task
rows.if: `adult` learners in a work setting, using the procedure on the job

rows.basis: untested proposal; feedback before the next attempt from [contingent scaffolding](claims/contingent-scaffolding-improves-learning.md) [+M] (one-to-one)
rows.change: Keep it and its categories as given; teach and practise with it, and change only what the evidence speaks to: one model of each decision point, feedback before the next attempt, a delayed unaided check
rows.if: The brief names its own checklist, job aid, rubric or routine for the procedure

rows.basis: [Comparing cases side by side…](claims/comparing-contrasting-cases-improves-learning.md) [+M] (raised procedural flexibility, not conceptual knowledge, in one algebra study); [Strategy Instruction Needs Conditional Knowledge](claims/strategy-instruction-needs-conditional-knowledge.md) [~M]
rows.change: After accurate steps, add side-by-side comparison of two methods, items where the procedure does not apply, and "why does this step work?" prompts; check with one changed item per round
rows.if: Goal includes transfer to changed problems, or understanding why, not only accuracy

rows.basis: [Students can apply procedural knowledge to solve integration problems but show limited understanding of basic integration concepts](claims/procedural-strong-conceptual-limited-integral.md) [~W] (calculus, reported second-hand)
rows.change: Do not add more of the same practice; pose items the memorised steps will not solve and ask learners to explain or draw what each step does
rows.if: Learners can already run the procedure but cannot say what it means (e.g. can integrate but cannot explain the integral)

rows.basis: [Interleaving Improves Discrimination](claims/interleaving-improves-discrimination.md) [+M] (mathematics problem types; benefit largest when types are confusable)
rows.change: Once each is accurate alone, practise them shuffled so the learner must choose; warn learners that mixed practice feels harder and is slower
rows.if: Several similar procedures are taught in one unit (e.g. problem types, grammar forms, drug calculations)

rows.basis: [practice included in computer-based lessons](claims/practice-presence-raises-cbi-posttest-achievement.md) [+M] (undergraduates, one lesson; horizon not reported); schedule untested
rows.change: Build the worked example and five to eight practice items with automatic checking and a worked answer after each into the lesson; one step per screen on a phone; an unaided check item before the next procedure; scheduled review prompts two days and one week later
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, no teacher present, or phone-only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Show the model on a shared screen or camera pointed at the hands or the work, not the whole room; have every learner, remote or present, submit each attempt the same way (photo, poll, shared document) so all are seen before feedback
rows.if: Mixed modes: some learners in the room, some joining remotely

rows.basis: untested proposal; contingent-support evidence is one-to-one ([contingent scaffolding](claims/contingent-scaffolding-improves-learning.md) [~M])
rows.change: Every learner shows each attempt at once (mini-whiteboards, cards, a poll); whole-class feedback on the commonest error, then the teacher goes to those still failing; pairs check each other against a worked answer for routine steps
rows.if: `classroom`, one teacher and a large group

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Spend the facilitator's minutes on the first one or two supported attempts and the unaided check; give everything between to self-checking items with worked answers or a job aid; the facilitator looks only at the step the learner flags
rows.if: Scarce facilitator time (volunteers, a busy shift, a tutor checking in briefly)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Model, three or four supported attempts, one unaided item at the end; record what the unaided item shows and do not claim retention or fluency; give learners a job aid and items to practise later
rows.if: Time is one session only

rows.basis: untested proposal; spacing across sessions from [Distributed Practice Improves Retention](claims/spaced-practice-improves-retention.md) [+M] (verbal recall, carried)
rows.change: Per session: 1–2 minutes of unaided items on earlier procedures, 3–5 minutes of model or worked example on the new step only if it is new, the rest supported or mixed practice; one new step per session at most
rows.if: A fixed short time budget per session (e.g. 10 or 15 minutes a day)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Let learners show a step by doing it before explaining it; keep written instructions short with pictures of each step; let early attempts be private (checked by software or one-to-one) before anything is shown to the group
rows.if: Learners have low confidence or low literacy, or work in a second language

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: More supported rounds per step; release only after several consecutive unaided successes on representative tasks; a stage of supervised unaided work before full independence; judge readiness only on unaided performance
rows.if: Errors are costly on the job (safety, compliance, harm to a client) or stakes are high

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Practise the procedure to accuracy first in private, then rehearse the whole performance under the audience's conditions (time, setting, interruptions) at least twice before the real one
rows.if: The procedure is a performance for a real audience (a demonstration, a recital, a service to a client)

rows.basis: [Practice of grammar rules improves only the practiced skill…](claims/skill-specificity-l2-grammar-practice.md) [+W] and [Automatization of L2 skills requires extensive practice in a consistent environment…](claims/automatization-requires-practice-consistent-environment.md) [+W] (both from one review, reported second-hand)
rows.change: Practise the form in the same kind of task the learner will use it in (meaningful communication, comprehension or production), since gains may stay in the skill practised
rows.if: Learners are second-language learners automatizing grammar or speech

rows.basis: [Process Writing Improves Writing Quality](claims/process-writing-improves-writing-quality.md) [~M] (no significant gain for struggling writers); [Strategy Instruction Improves Writing Quality](claims/strategy-instruction-improves-writing-quality.md) [+M] (struggling writers 1.02); transcription supports untested
rows.change: Teach planning and revising strategies explicitly with self-regulation steps (goal setting, self-recording, self-instruction) over several weeks; do not rely on drafting and feedback cycles alone; reduce transcription load (dictation, scribe, keyboard) while strategies are learned
rows.if: Writers are struggling, have a learning disability, or cannot yet write fluently by hand or keyboard

rows.basis: [Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows.](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M] (cognitive-load review, not writing); untested for writing
rows.change: Drop the scripted strategy and prompt cards; let the writer set the revision focus; keep one outside reader's response per piece
rows.if: Writers are `advanced` in the genre (they already plan and revise globally)

rows.basis: [Collaborative Writing Improves Text Quality](claims/collaborative-writing-improves-text-quality.md) [+M] (grades 4–12, and one randomised study of 10–11-year-olds that found larger gains in later individual writing); younger children untested
rows.change: Shorter texts; plan orally or with drawings; co-write with a partner in structured pairs (the more able writer helping the less able); revise one thing per piece
rows.if: Learners are `child` in the early primary grades

rows.basis: untested; neither meta-analysis covers adults (strategy studies stop at grade 10)
rows.change: Use the writer's own work documents as the texts; take the reader from the real setting (the manager, the client, the colleague); keep the strategy modelling but shorten it; respond as that reader first
rows.if: Learners are `adult`, including in work settings (reports, case notes, proposals)

rows.basis: [Review: language proficiency and feedback literacy moderate uptake of written corrective feedback](claims/student-factors-moderate-wcf-engagement.md) [~W] (second-hand); [noticing errors](claims/noticing-errors-decreases-errors-preserves-quality.md) [+W] (second-hand, EFL college writing)
rows.change: Respond to meaning and structure first, in plain language; correct language separately, on two or three error types the writer can recognise, and ask the writer to find further instances; allow planning in the first language
rows.if: Writers are writing in a second language, or have low literacy

rows.basis: [Process Writing Improves Writing Quality](claims/process-writing-improves-writing-quality.md) [~M] (no gain in motivation); [Explicit statement of tasks and standards](claims/explicit-tasks-standards-boost-writing-motivation.md) [+W] (argument only)
rows.change: Do not expect process instruction alone to raise it: add a real reader and purpose, explicit task and standards, and reader-response comments; measure motivation separately
rows.if: The goal includes motivation to write or confidence as a writer

rows.basis: [Feedback Most Effective At Task And Process Levels](claims/feedback-most-effective-at-task-and-process-levels.md) [+M]; [Praise for intelligence, rather than for effort, after success undermines children's motivation and performance after a later failure](claims/feedback-praise-reduces-learning.md) [~M] (person praise; children, not writing)
rows.change: Open every response as a reader (what you understood and found interesting); direct criticism at the text and the next move, never at the writer; give a specific positive comment tied to a criterion, not generic praise
rows.if: Writers have low confidence, or have had harsh feedback before

rows.basis: [Peer Feedback Improves Writing](claims/peer-feedback-improves-writing.md) [+M] (peer vs teacher feedback not reliably different); [Students report teacher feedback on writing is insufficient](claims/insufficient-writing-feedback-scores-over-feedback.md) [~W] (interviews; teachers' load)
rows.change: Peers give the first response with criteria; the teacher reads a sample of peer comments and responds to each writer on two or three priorities only; rotate 5-minute conferences so each writer gets one per composition; do not grade drafts
rows.if: One teacher with a large class or many sections

rows.basis: [peer reviewer accuracy and helpfulness](claims/peer-feedback-accuracy-depends-on-expertise.md) [~M] (secondary writers, correlational); [rubrics and peer reviewers](claims/rubrics-improve-peer-feedback-quality.md) [~M] (online, two quasi-experiments; one found less reflective comments)
rows.change: Train them on example texts with the criteria first; ask them to point to the place in the text and say what a reader would experience; teacher checks a sample
rows.if: Peers are novices as reviewers

rows.basis: [rubrics and peer reviewers](claims/rubrics-improve-peer-feedback-quality.md) [~M] (one MOOC writing course, one online graduate course); [Peer assessment improves academic performance by a small average amount](claims/peer-assessment-improves-performance.md) [+M] (online and offline did not differ)
rows.change: Build in a rubric-guided peer review with practice on rated examples, a reviewer memo with each revision, and a self-check against the criteria before submission
rows.if: `online-self-paced` or asynchronous course, no teacher reading every draft

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Put drafts in one shared document with comment threads so remote and in-room writers review the same way; pair a remote writer with an in-room one for peer review; for phone-only writers keep pieces short, accept voice comments and spoken memos
rows.if: Mixed modes: some writers remote, some in the room, or some on phones only

rows.basis: untested; the strategy studies taught over at least three days ([strategy instruction](claims/strategy-instruction-improves-writing-quality.md) [+M])
rows.change: Plan for 10 minutes against a model text, draft, then one revision against a single criterion with a partner's response; collect the draft and the revision; do not claim a gain in writing ability
rows.if: Only one session is available

rows.basis: untested proposal, from the earlier pages on appropriation and responding as a reader (Shvidko 2020, an essay from practice)
rows.change: Keep the writer as the owner of the decisions: teacher and peers comment as readers and pose options; the writer's memo records what they accepted; add a final edit for conventions before release; keep drafts and comments out of the published version
rows.if: The text goes to a real audience (publication, a client, a public performance), or the audience should see only the final text

rows.basis: [spontaneous sentence production under minimal planning](claims/spontaneous-sentence-production-in-synthetic-planning-increases-understanding.md) [~M] (one experiment, university writers, self-rated understanding; associations within assigned conditions)
rows.change: Plan with one overall goal rather than a detailed outline; let the writer draft spontaneously; then ask for a revision of the global structure (reorder, cut, add sections) and a short note on what they now think; judge the first draft on ideas, not quality
rows.if: The goal is writing to learn: developing the writer's own understanding of a topic, not a polished text

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Practise planning and revising under time limits (for example 5 minutes planning, 5 minutes rereading in a 40-minute task); keep the multi-draft cycle for learning the strategies, and the timed form for applying them
rows.if: Assessment is a timed, unaided essay

rows.basis: [Students report teacher feedback on writing is insufficient, and they value scores over feedback](claims/insufficient-writing-feedback-scores-over-feedback.md) [~W] (one interview study); grade withholding untested
rows.change: Withhold the grade until the final version; require the reviewer memo before revision; give credit for the revision itself
rows.if: Drafts are graded, or writers care only about the score

rows.basis: [Productive failure improves conceptual learning](claims/productive-failure-improves-conceptual-learning.md) [+M] (g = 0.36 over 53 studies)
rows.change: Use the attempt-first design above
rows.if: The goal is conceptual understanding or transfer of a new concept (mathematics, science, statistics)

rows.basis: [PS-I shows no pooled benefit for procedural knowledge](claims/psi-procedural-knowledge-null-pooled-effect.md) [~M] (g = −0.03)
rows.change: Teach first; pooled, a full attempt phase adds time without a procedural gain
rows.if: The goal is fluent execution of a procedure (`procedure`)

rows.basis: [Micro productive failure improved sixth-graders' isomorphic algebraic procedural problem solving](claims/micro-productive-failure-improves-isomorphic-procedural-problems.md) [+M] (η²p = 0.06, held at one week); [Micro productive failure showed no effect on conceptual explanation](claims/micro-pf-no-conceptual-explanation-effect.md) [~M]; one trial, against the pooled null above
rows.change: Teach first remains the default; an alternative is "micro" attempts: a few minutes' attempt before each step is taught, repeated step by step, rather than one long attempt. Do not expect a conceptual gain from it
rows.if: The goal is a multi-step procedure (an algebraic method, a worked calculation), and the teacher wants learners to understand why each step is there

rows.basis: [PS-I effects are negative for 2nd–5th graders and increase with age](claims/psi-effect-increases-with-grade-level.md) [-M]
rows.change: Teach first
rows.if: Learners are in the early primary years (roughly ages 7–11)

rows.basis: [For domain-general skills, one meta-analysis finds a negligible effect (g = −0.17) in favour of I-PS over PS-I](claims/domain-general-skills-favor-ips.md) [-M]; one exception reported secondhand: with a virus-transmission simulation, learners who attempted first did no better at the end of the unit but transferred multivariable causal reasoning better to a new context ([PS-I with a virus transmission simulation showed better transfer of multivariable causality](claims/ps-i-simulation-better-mvc-transfer.md) [+W], an editorial's summary, no effect size)
rows.change: Teach first
rows.if: The target is a domain-general skill (the control-of-variables strategy, a general reasoning heuristic)

rows.basis: [PF students did not outperform DI students when learning social science research methods](claims/pf-effect-not-replicated-non-stem-research-methods.md) [-W] (two quasi-experiments, 364 tenth-graders, even though the pilots showed the attempt phase worked as designed: [the problem met the sweet spot of complexity](claims/pf-problem-sweet-spot-complexity-pilot-tests.md) [+W]); [of eight PF-similar studies in non-STEM or domain-general settings, only one found a positive effect](claims/pf-similar-studies-mostly-null-negative.md) [-W] (narrative overview)
rows.change: Do not assume the advantage carries over; teach first, or run the attempt-first design as a trial against teaching first with a conceptual test
rows.if: The target is outside mathematics and science (a social-science method, a humanities concept)

rows.basis: [PF design fidelity predicts larger PS-I effects](claims/pf-fidelity-predicts-psi-effect-size.md) [+M] (0.56 when instruction built on student solutions, 0.20 when not); [PS-I fosters learning only if contrasting cases or instruction built on student solutions are implemented](claims/ps-i-fosters-learning-only-with-contrasting-cases-or-student-solutions.md) [+W] (review, no pooled effect); [PS-I outperforms I-PS on conceptual knowledge only when instruction builds on student solutions](claims/ps-i-superior-only-with-student-solutions.md) [+W] (Loibl & Rummel 2014, as summarised in a 2025 framework article); [Merely delaying instruction does not improve conceptual understanding](claims/delaying-instruction-alone-no-conceptual-gain.md) [~W] and [contrasting cases without explicit guidance on their use do not improve conceptual understanding](claims/unguided-contrasting-cases-no-learning-effect.md) [~W] (one randomised trial, 181 students; non-significant differences, not shown equivalent)
rows.change: Build it on prepared typical student solutions or contrasting cases instead, and have learners compare the cases explicitly; if the instruction uses neither, expect a much smaller effect or none, and consider teaching first: delaying the instruction is not by itself the active ingredient
rows.if: The teacher cannot or will not build the instruction on the learners' own attempts

rows.basis: [In one meta-regression, the PS-I fidelity benefit tended to shrink for interventions spanning only a few hours](claims/psi-fidelity-time-span-interaction.md) [~M] (marginal, p = .055); [Duration of the initial problem-solving phase reverses the PS-I versus WS-I transfer advantage](claims/ps-phase-duration-reverses-ps-i-ws-i-transfer.md) [~W] (two studies of density and ratio, one problem against two, as summarised in a framework article; the comparison is with a worked solution, not with teaching first)
rows.change: Keep the design simple, or teach first; do not cram every feature into a few hours. A single short problem is the weakest version: if the attempt cannot include two problems in different contexts, explaining a worked solution before instruction may serve transfer better
rows.if: Only a single short session is available

rows.basis: [Collaborative and individual problem solving in traditional PF do not differ in conceptual knowledge after instruction](claims/pf-collaborative-individual-no-conceptual-knowledge-difference.md) [~M] (tenth-graders, a non-significant difference, not shown equivalent); [Learning the CVS with self-generated, vicarious, combined, or no errors during PS-I does not differentially affect posttest performance](claims/cvs-error-type-no-posttest-differences.md) [~W] (others' errors did as well as one's own, on a domain-general skill); [Pre-tests reduced adult learners' persistence in a MOOC](claims/pretesting-can-harm-motivation.md) [-W] (pretests, not PS-I); [Vicarious failure with high solution diversity is as effective as engaging in productive failure oneself](claims/vf-high-as-effective-as-pf.md) [~W] and [outperforms low-diversity vicarious failure and direct instruction](claims/vf-high-outperforms-vf-low-and-di-conceptual.md) [+M] (one randomised trial, 152 secondary students, d ≈ 0.65 over teaching first; equal to attempting, not shown equivalent); [observing the whole problem-solving-and-failing process beat generating one's own attempts](claims/vf-process-outperforms-pf-conceptual-knowledge.md) [+M], more so for learners with more prior knowledge ([prior knowledge moderated the VF-process advantage](claims/prior-knowledge-moderates-vf-process-vs-pf.md) [~M]; one trial, 173 secondary students); both trials were in classrooms, so the self-paced PS-I design as a whole is an untested proposal
rows.change: Individual attempts are acceptable; in the instruction, show learners a set of typical attempts (other learners' or prepared ones) beside the canonical solution. Watch persistence: keep the attempt short, ungraded and visibly expected to fail. Where attempting is impractical, let learners watch a modelled learner work through several different failed methods before the instruction (vicarious failure); the methods shown must be diverse, since a model showing few did no better than teaching first
rows.if: Learners work alone (`online-self-paced`)

rows.basis: [Mixed-ability groups generated a broader range of solution methods than all-low and all-high groups](claims/mixed-ability-groups-broader-rsm-range.md) [+W] (two undergraduate studies, reported in an editorial; method range and uptake of the formula, not a learning test)
rows.change: Mix prior attainment in mathematics or the domain, so each group has at least one member who can drive several methods; avoid all-low and all-high groups
rows.if: The teacher forms the groups for the attempt

rows.basis: [Guidance during initial problem solving does not improve learning from subsequent instruction](claims/initial-guidance-does-not-improve-learning-from-instruction.md) [~M]; [Role-script support during generation led university relearning students to outperform direct instruction in all weeks but the first](claims/tau-role-script-outperformed-di-relearning.md) [+W]
rows.change: Do not steer toward the canonical method during the attempt; guidance raised solution quality but not later learning. Content-general support (a role script that prompts learners to think, ask and explain, without telling the content) is compatible
rows.if: The question is whether to help learners succeed during the attempt (hints, guidance toward the method)

rows.basis: [Role-script support during generation led university relearning students to outperform direct instruction in all weeks but the first](claims/tau-role-script-outperformed-di-relearning.md) [+W] (76 university students, mathematical analysis, four weeks; reported secondhand in an editorial, no effect size)
rows.change: Generation with a content-general script before re-teaching is an option; run it across several sessions, since the first session showed no advantage
rows.if: Learners are relearning material they met before (revision for an exam, a refresher course)

rows.basis: [Invention tasks prepare future learning](claims/invention-tasks-prepare-future-learning.md) [+M]; [PS-I over a year in a university linear algebra course was followed by higher final exam performance than baseline cohorts](claims/ps-i-linear-algebra-higher-exam-performance.md) [+W] (four iterations against earlier cohorts, not randomised; reported in an editorial, no effect size)
rows.change: Use the attempt-first design for the foundational concepts; its benefit shows when learners later learn from new resources. In a university course, repeated attempt-first tasks across the year are a recorded option
rows.if: Learners will meet later material that builds on the concept (a course, not a lesson)

rows.basis: [Minimal guidance is less effective for novices than explicit instruction](claims/minimal-guidance-less-effective-for-novices.md) [-M]; [Expertise reversal](claims/expertise-reversal-effect-compound.md) [~W] (the balance between generating and being told shifts with prior knowledge; a narrative review)
rows.change: Teach first, or give the minimum prior knowledge before the attempt; an attempt with nothing to generate from is minimal guidance, not productive failure
rows.if: Learners are novices with little prior knowledge of the domain, and the problem cannot be attempted without it

rows.basis: [Pre-tests reduced adult learners' persistence in a MOOC](claims/pretesting-can-harm-motivation.md) [-W] shows a cost of failing first on a pretest, not on a PS-I attempt; the framing is an untested proposal
rows.change: State that the attempt is not graded and that not solving it is expected; keep the attempt phase out of the grade
rows.if: Learners are anxious about failure or the setting grades every attempt

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Collect attempts from a sample of groups (or a quick poll of methods) and build the instruction on the three or four most common
rows.if: One teacher for a large class

rows.basis: [Four relational components—positive feedback, rapport, mutual respect, and reciprocal trust—form the relational framework of coaching](claims/four-relational-components-coaching-partnership.md) [+W] (teachers and their coaches, focus groups); otherwise untested
rows.change: Treat the relationship as between colleagues: replace the personal intake with "what do you want to use this for at work, and what do you already do?", let learners bring cases from their work from session 2, and invite them to correct you
rows.if: Learners are `adult` professionals or `advanced` in the field (a workplace course, continuing education)
