rows.basis: [Positive Greetings At The Door Improve Engagement](claims/positive-greetings-at-the-door-improve-engagement.md) [+M] and [A brief online empathic-discipline exercise for teachers halved suspensions in one randomized field experiment, while its preregistered replication found a small, marginal overall effect but narrowed group disparities](claims/brief-intervention-empathic-discipline-cuts-suspensions.md) [~S] (middle school, the population tested)
rows.change: Keep the greeting at the door and the empathic response to misconduct as daily routines; shorten the intake and involve families where appropriate
rows.if: Learners are `adolescent` or `child` (the school studies' population)

rows.basis: [Teachers report that building trust is the first and most important goal with students in foster care, and that trust precedes willingness to work](claims/trust-first-goal-foster-care-students.md) [+W] (teacher discussion groups, children in foster care; carried to adults)
rows.change: Make trust the first goal: more consistency (same time, same greeting, promises kept), private rather than public contact, no personal disclosure required, and no withdrawal of warmth after a setback
rows.if: Learners have reason to mistrust adults or institutions (care-experienced, trauma, earlier exclusion)

rows.basis: [Transgender students report substantially fewer school supports than non-transgender peers, especially caring adult relationships and high expectations](claims/transgender-students-report-fewer-school-supports.md) [~W] (secondary students, descriptive survey; it shows the gap, not what closes it)
rows.change: Use the name and pronouns the learner gives from the first contact, without comment; hold the same high expectations as for everyone; give a private route to raise a problem
rows.if: Learners are from groups that report fewer caring adult relationships (for example transgender learners)

rows.basis: [Schools that mitigated proximity-to-homicide effects had stronger, more positive school climates, including engaging instruction and trusting relationships](claims/positive-school-climate-mitigates-homicide-effects.md) [+W] (Chicago high schools, correlational, cannot say which measure mattered)
rows.change: Pair relationship work with engaging instruction; do not treat warmth as a substitute
rows.if: Learners in a community facing violence or other adversity

rows.basis: untested proposal; the order of steps is from the earlier page's note that adults hold back until comfortable
rows.change: Do the intake by conversation, not a form; stay longer in low-exposure participation (pairs, choosing whether to share); praise effort on the task rather than the person; make the first task one they can do
rows.if: Learners have low confidence, low literacy, or bad memories of school

rows.basis: untested proposal; group-level presence-building is on [Social Presence](principles/social-presence.md)
rows.change: Replace the greeting with a short personal reply to each learner's introduction post in week 1 by name; hold the one-to-ones as 5-minute calls or voice notes; answer by name in forums
rows.if: `online-instructor-led`, asynchronous

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Greet remote learners by name when they join, before the room starts; give them the first turn in each discussion; run the one-to-ones by phone or video for both groups so remote learners are not second
rows.if: Mixed mode: some learners in the room, some remote

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use text or voice messages for the intake and one-to-ones; never require video; keep names visible in the chat
rows.if: Learners on phones only, or low bandwidth

rows.basis: untested proposal; relationships may be weaker in larger groups without lower learning ([Exploratory analyses: students ending the year in larger tutoring groups showed the largest math score increases but reported weaker tutor relationships than peers in smaller groups](claims/blueprint-larger-groups-scores-up-relationships-weaker.md) [~W], tutoring, exploratory)
rows.change: Keep the intake (read a sample, answer the commonest needs in session 2), greet by name those you can, and hold group office hours instead of one-to-ones; delegate one-to-ones to tutors if there are any
rows.if: One instructor for many learners (a lecture of 100+, a large online course)

rows.basis: untested proposal; in tutoring programmes with high attendance and positive effects, many students reported strong tutor relationships ([Strong student–tutor relationships and a sense of belonging characterized tutoring programs with high attendance and positive learning effects](claims/strong-student-tutor-relationships-key-to-tutoring-success.md) [+W], associational)
rows.change: Keep three moves only: the learner's name, one question about their goal at first contact, and one remembered detail at the next; record those in a shared note so the next volunteer can use them
rows.if: Scarce facilitator time (volunteer tutors, a busy shift, a tutor checking in briefly)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Spend about 5 of the first 15 minutes on names, why each person came, and the working terms; take participation in pairs before the whole group; make no promise of follow-up you will not keep
rows.if: A single session only (a workshop, a one-off training)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Greeting during arrival (no class time), working terms in 3 minutes in session 1 only, one-to-ones outside the session; no session gives more than 5 minutes to relational work after the first
rows.if: A fixed short time budget per session (for example 45 minutes)

rows.basis: untested proposal (wave lessons on keeping a brief's routine)
rows.change: Keep it; change only what this page adds: make every item optional, read every answer before the next session, and answer it with one visible change
rows.if: The brief names its own routine (its own intake form, check-in, icebreaker or feedback survey)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use them in the working terms and in feedback; do not substitute your own
rows.if: The brief names its own categories, criteria or rubric

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: The learner controls who sees it: intake answers go only to the instructor, nothing personal is shared with the group without asking, and the course works without anyone disclosing
rows.if: Private or sensitive material (health, immigration status, personal history)

rows.basis: [Trusting teacher-evaluator relationships lessened evaluation anxiety and encouraged teachers to welcome and use REACH feedback](claims/trusting-teacher-evaluator-relationships-reduce-anxiety.md) [+W] (44 teachers, interviews); framing critique is on [Wise Feedback Across Difference](principles/wise-feedback-across-difference.md)
rows.change: Separate the two in time and in words: say when you are coaching and when you are judging, and give critique with the standard and an assurance the learner can reach it
rows.if: Learners are evaluated by the same person who builds the relationship (high stakes, assessors, supervisors)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Stand with the learner as coach before the audience sees it: rehearse privately, give critique there, and say publicly only what supports them
rows.if: Learners produce work or a performance for a real audience

rows.basis: [Belonging Interventions Improve Outcomes](claims/belonging-interventions-improve-outcomes.md) [~S] (college entrants; worked only where the setting gave students' groups opportunities to belong)
rows.change: Add a brief message that early difficulty is common and passes, and make sure the course really gives them chances to take part, or the message does nothing
rows.if: Learners from a group stereotyped in the domain, or at a transition (first term)

rows.basis: [System constraints have minimal effect on already-efficient task-selection strategies while strongly correcting inefficient ones](claims/constraints-selectively-affect-inefficient-strategies.md) [~W] (simulated learners in mastery learning; carried to real learners untested)
rows.change: Keep constraints light: block only the shortcut that skips the target; leave choice of tasks and features open
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` on the task, or already use the tool efficiently

rows.basis: [A closer-to-mastery task-selection constraint sharply reduces overpractice for the risk-averse strategy, with large Cohen's d effect sizes](claims/closer-to-mastery-constraint-reduces-overpractice.md) [+W] (simulated learners; untested with learners)
rows.change: Steer task selection toward skills close to mastery rather than letting them choose freely; show the next skill as the default choice
rows.if: Learners tend to avoid risk (keep practising what they can already do)

rows.basis: Child: [A student began interacting with the sim within 10 seconds and verbalized sense-making without explicit guidance](claims/implicit-scaffolding-supports-immediate-exploration.md) [+W] (one sixth-grade student). Adolescent: [Guardrails in the GPT Tutor largely eliminate the negative exam effect, though no positive exam effect is observed](claims/gpt-tutor-exam-effect-null.md) [~M] (high school mathematics)
rows.change: Children: an opening screen they can act on without reading, controls with visible extremes, and an adult nearby for the first session. Adolescents with an AI tutor: hints only, teacher-written per problem
rows.if: Learners are `child` or `adolescent`

rows.basis: untested proposal; the AI evidence is from students, not workers
rows.change: Bound the assistant to checking and hinting during training tasks, and judge readiness on an unaided task from their own work; tell them why the tool is bounded
rows.if: Learners are `adult` in a work setting (`adult-workplace`), using a tool on the job

rows.basis: [Authors report that flexibility in sim access supports student agency while students tend to explore in a productive sequence](claims/flexibility-supports-agency-productive-sequence.md) [+W] (authors' belief; not tested)
rows.change: Constrain little: make productive actions obvious and leave free movement between parts; add challenges for continued engagement
rows.if: Goal is open exploration of a `concept` or `principle` (a simulation)

rows.basis: [Unfettered GPT-4 access during practice harms subsequent unassisted exam performance in high school mathematics](claims/gpt-base-harms-unassisted-exam-performance.md) [+M]
rows.change: Hints only, after an attempt; an unaided check before moving on
rows.if: Goal is a `procedure` or problem solving where the assistant could produce the answer

rows.basis: [Open AI collaboration yielded the highest supported writing quality, while bounded AI support yielded the highest independent no-AI Week 8 performance](claims/genai-supported-performance-independent-divergence.md) [+M] (one class-clustered quasi-experiment, 168 students)
rows.change: Bound the assistant (feedback on the learner's own draft, not generation) or have learners draft before opening it; assess one piece written without it
rows.if: Goal is writing or a creative product

rows.basis: [Free ChatGPT use boosts originality on the assisted creative task but the advantage disappears when assistance is removed](claims/chatgpt-free-use-originality-gains-vanish-unassisted.md) [~M] (university students; the product gain did not carry over)
rows.change: Open assistance can raise the product's quality; if the learner's own later work also matters, keep a think-first step and one unassisted piece
rows.if: The product goes to a real audience, and the assisted product is what matters

rows.basis: untested proposal; the guardrail trial was in classrooms
rows.change: All steering must be in the tool: a self-explaining opening screen, hints-only assistant, an unaided check item the tool scores; nobody can correct a learner who takes the shortcut
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Let the tool hold the constraint so the teacher is free to circulate; the teacher watches for learners stuck at the same point and gives one spoken pointer to all, then notes it as a screen to redesign
rows.if: `classroom` with one teacher and many learners

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Put the constraint in the tool and the check in a short unaided item the tutor reviews in two minutes; skip designs that rely on the tutor policing tool use
rows.if: Scarce facilitator time (volunteers, one tutor checking in briefly)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Test the opening screen on the phones learners use; give remote learners the same bounded tool rather than whatever assistant they have at home, and the same unaided check
rows.if: Some learners remote and some in the room, or phone-only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: 10 to 15 minutes of exploration with the constrained tool, a 15 to 20 minute challenge, a 5 minute unaided item; claim nothing about retention
rows.if: Single session only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Cut exploration to 8 minutes and the challenge to 15; keep the 5 minute unaided item and the minutes adding to the budget; drop the second challenge before the check
rows.if: Fixed short time budget (for example 30 minutes)

rows.basis: untested proposal; from the earlier page's argument that text directions are a sign of poor design
rows.change: Rely on the screen rather than text: icons and visible results, one action per screen, and spoken help available on request; let learners attempt privately before anyone sees
rows.if: Learners with low literacy or low confidence

rows.basis: [Most introductory physics students preferred a combination chatbot (guidance first, answers when stuck), while few preferred pure guided Q&A](claims/students-prefer-combination-chatbot-over-guided-qa.md) [~W] (anticipated preference, physics students; not a learning outcome)
rows.change: Offer guidance first and an answer only after the learner's own attempt and one hint; record which learners reach the answer step
rows.if: Learners want direct answers, or will rate a hints-only tool poorly

rows.basis: [A guardrailed GPT-4 tutor with teacher-designed hints improves assisted practice performance more than a standard GPT-4 interface](claims/gpt-tutor-improves-practice-more-than-gpt-base.md) [~M] (assisted gain without exam gain)
rows.change: Judge readiness only on unaided work; log assistant use and do not count assisted success
rows.if: Stakes are high or the assessment is unaided

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep it; change only what the evidence says matters: one bound on answer-giving, one unaided check, one think-first step. If its rubric rewards tool use, keep that criterion and add an unaided check beside it
rows.if: The brief names its own routine, rubric or tool configuration

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use them as the list of productive and unproductive uses in the design; do not substitute this page's
rows.if: The brief gives its own categories or criteria for good use

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use a tool whose logs the learner controls; the unaided check is seen only by the learner and whoever the brief names
rows.if: Material is private or sensitive (learners' own writing, health or work data)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Bound the assistant within the whole task (hints on the learner's current step) rather than splitting the task into constrained parts
rows.if: The brief wants a whole-task performance kept whole

rows.basis: untested proposal; the answer-copying pattern is shown in [Students use standard GPT-4 access as a crutch—copying answers rather than engaging with the material—which explains the harm to learning](claims/gpt-base-crutch-mechanism.md) [+M]
rows.change: Use it as the compared case: show the two routes side by side and block or bound that route in the tool
rows.if: The brief reports a shortcut learners actually took (pasting the question into a chatbot)

rows.basis: untested proposal; from the earlier page (motivation and confidence of student writers). The information requirement is [Feedback Most Effective At Task And Process Levels](claims/feedback-most-effective-at-task-and-process-levels.md) [+S], not tested on writing confidence
rows.change: Open with two specific strength comments before any critique; keep critique to one or two priorities with a concrete next step; name the improvement on the next draft first
rows.if: Writers are `novice` in the genre or have low confidence as writers

rows.basis: untested proposal; the earlier page's balance is meant for developing writers
rows.change: One strength comment where it marks something to keep; spend the response on critique at the level they ask for
rows.if: Writers are `advanced` or professional, and ask for critique

rows.basis: [Praise for intelligence, rather than for effort, after success undermines children's motivation and performance after a later failure](claims/feedback-praise-reduces-learning.md) [-S] (fifth graders, reasoning problems); [Praise focused on global intelligence has negative effects on future learning behavior compared with praise about effort](claims/feedback-praise-reduces-learning.md) [-M] (the same experiments, reported by a practice guide)
rows.change: Praise the strategy or effort used ("you added a detail that shows how she felt"), never ability ("you're a great writer"); keep comments spoken or very short
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary age)

rows.basis: untested proposal; the earlier page names language learners among its writers
rows.change: Separate comments on ideas from language comments; praise a language form used correctly when it was the target; limit language critique to one or two error types
rows.if: Writers are second-language learners

rows.basis: [Wise Feedback Across Difference](principles/wise-feedback-across-difference.md) (untested there too); the risk of withholding critique is shown for AI feedback in [LLM feedback for students marked by race, language, disability, gender, or motivation shows positive feedback bias and feedback withholding bias — more praise and less substantive critique than for unmarked counterparts](claims/marked-students-praise-withholding-bias.md) [-M]
rows.change: Keep the full critique; add the statement of the standard and the assurance that the writer can reach it; do not soften critique into praise
rows.if: The writer belongs to a group subject to negative stereotypes about ability, or has reason to doubt the teacher's intent

rows.basis: [LLM feedback sentiment tracks assigned scores: low scores come with more criticism, high scores with more praise](claims/llm-feedback-sentiment-tracks-scores.md) [~M]; [Motivation prompts shift feedback tone: unmotivated students receive enthusiastic, collaborative encouragement while motivated students receive direct, higher-level critique](claims/motivation-prompt-enthusiasm-pedagogy.md) [~M] (both about the comments produced, not their effect on writers)
rows.change: Before using it, read a sample of its comments on weak and strong drafts and on drafts by different students: check that weak drafts still get specific strengths, that strong drafts still get critique, and that comments do not change with the student's described identity or motivation; do not tell the tool a student's group or motivation
rows.if: Comments come from an AI tool (online, `online-self-paced`)

rows.basis: [Non-layered AI feedback produced significantly higher post-test performance than layered AI feedback after controlling for pre-test](claims/non-layered-ai-feedback-beats-layered-post-test.md) [-M] (one online lesson, undergraduates, not writing; layering and encouragement were not separated)
rows.change: Do not assume the encouraging layer helps learning; give the specific critique in the first response and check revised work
rows.if: An AI tool is set to open with encouraging, learner-centred feedback before elaborated feedback

rows.basis: [Students report teacher feedback on writing is insufficient, and they value scores over feedback](claims/insufficient-writing-feedback-scores-over-feedback.md) [~M] (one interview study of Chinese college English students, who reported teachers lacked time and that they cared more about scores); the minutes are an untested proposal
rows.change: Per draft: one specific strength, one priority change, one question, written in under 3 minutes; or a whole-class note on common strengths and one common problem, with individual comments only on the priority. Return comments before the grade
rows.if: One teacher for a large class, or scarce responder time (a busy term, volunteer tutors, one short check-in)

rows.basis: untested proposal; the peer routine is held by [structured peer review](patterns/structured-peer-review.md)
rows.change: Use a structure that requires a specific strength before critique, such as [PQP (Praise-Question-Polish)](strategies/pqp-praise-question-polish.md), and model one strength comment and one weak one ("nice") first
rows.if: Peers give the feedback

rows.basis: untested proposal (wave 5 and 6 review lessons)
rows.change: Keep it. Write strength comments in the rubric's own criteria and words, and add only what the evidence says matters: that each strength names something in the text, and that critique is not dropped
rows.if: The brief names its own routine, rubric or criteria for responding (its own comment template, rubric bands or categories)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Respond only if and as the writer chooses; comment on the writing's craft (what makes a moment vivid), not the experience; no critique of content the writer did not offer for critique
rows.if: The writing is private or sensitive (a journal, a personal narrative)

rows.basis: [School-level constraints prevented two of nine sites from using the four-part written praise strategy](claims/school-constraints-blocked-written-praise-two-sites.md) [~M] (a youth programme evaluation, not writing instruction)
rows.change: Check the setting's rules before using written personal notes; keep strength comments about the work, in the shared document or rubric, or give them aloud
rows.if: Written praise from this responder could be misread (a facilitator of a different sex, a setting with approval rules)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: One product revised once: about 15 minutes drafting, 5 minutes of response (one strength, one priority) from teacher or peer, 15 minutes revising, 5 minutes for the writer to name what changed. Adds no test or survey
rows.if: Single session only, or a fixed short time (for example 40 minutes)

rows.basis: untested proposal; [Students report teacher feedback on writing is insufficient, and they value scores over feedback](claims/insufficient-writing-feedback-scores-over-feedback.md) [~M]
rows.change: Give the grade with a short note of what works and one target for the next piece; do not spend time on extensive critique the writer cannot use
rows.if: High stakes: a graded final text with no revision

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Name strengths in the terms the real reader would use ("a manager can act on this summary"); keep the whole text whole rather than splitting it into exercises; critique against what the audience needs
rows.if: Adults writing for work (reports, case notes), or a product for a real audience

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use comments anchored in the shared document so everyone sees them in place; short audio or text comments for phone-only learners, one strength and one priority each
rows.if: Mixed modes: some learners remote, some in the room, or phone-only

rows.basis: [Interesting but irrelevant details can impair comprehension and transfer, with effects that vary with the material and the learner](claims/seductive-details-effect.md) [~M] (irrelevant material inside lessons, harm larger for lower working memory and lower attentional inhibition; carried from materials to surroundings, untested)
rows.change: Run the full protected block with device rule and a separate talk space; keep the task short enough to finish in the block
rows.if: Learners are `novice` on a demanding text or problem

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep the device rule; drop the timed block and tally, and let them choose their own place and sound
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` on the task, or already work steadily in the current setting

rows.basis: [Classroom Design Affects Learning Progress](claims/classroom-design-affects-learning-progress.md) [+M] (English primary classrooms, observational; noise named in a review)
rows.change: Short blocks (8–10 minutes) with a visible timer; moderate displays; seat focus workers away from group talk; alternate with movement or talk
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary age) in one classroom all day

rows.basis: [Self Monitoring Improves On Task Behavior](claims/self-monitoring-improves-on-task-behavior.md) [+M] (single-case studies, grades 4–12, on-task behaviour not achievement)
rows.change: Add a cued self-recording of on-task behaviour at short intervals, reviewed with the learner; keep the seat away from traffic and talk
rows.if: Learners have attention difficulties, or are students with or at risk for disabilities

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page ("excessively rigid silence can undermine collaboration … or oral language practice")
rows.change: Do not impose quiet; protect only the individual preparation or writing before and after the talk
rows.if: Goal is discussion, oral language practice or collaborative work

rows.basis: [Staying motivated was the most pervasive challenge of learning remotely, and students missed instructor feedback, peer collaboration, and hands-on experiences](claims/motivation-and-lost-interaction-challenges-remote.md) [+M] (undergraduates, survey: finding a quiet place a common problem); the plan is untested
rows.change: Replace room arrangements with a written study-conditions plan (when, where, which notifications off, what to do about the commonest interruption); for phone-only learners, focus mode on and one app open; short blocks that fit the time they have
rows.if: Setting is `online-self-paced`, or learners study at home or on a phone only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Give remote learners the same block start and end and device rule; ask them to mute and move to their quietest available place; in the room, keep the speaker for the remote link off during focus blocks
rows.if: Mixed mode: some learners in the room, some joining remotely

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Schedule focus and talk segments for the whole group at the same time rather than mixing them; mark one quiet zone; offer headphones or ear defenders
rows.if: One teacher for a large group in one room, or a shared or open-plan space

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Make the routine self-running: a printed or on-screen card with the block length, the device rule and the tally; the facilitator only starts the block and reads the tallies afterwards
rows.if: Facilitator time is scarce (volunteers, a busy shift, a tutor who checks in briefly)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: One focus block of 10–15 minutes on one task, the device rule, and an end-of-block tally; do not claim a change in habits
rows.if: Single session only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Give 2 minutes to state the task and set devices aside, 15 minutes of focus work, 3 minutes for the tally and one change; do not add a separate planning activity
rows.if: A fixed short time budget (for example 20 minutes in total)

rows.basis: [Lack of study space and financial issues are associated with higher test anxiety in online exams, and reliable technology with lower](claims/contextual-factors-increase-test-anxiety.md) [+M] (students in online exams, associational: lack of study space linked with higher test anxiety)
rows.change: Help each learner secure a study space and reliable device for the study period and the test; rehearse the test conditions once
rows.if: Learners are preparing for a high-stakes or online proctored test

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page (adult learners with unstable environments)
rows.change: Ask what times and places they actually control; plan short blocks there rather than prescribing long ones; treat a predictable routine as part of the support
rows.if: Adults in work settings, or carrying stress, fatigue or caring duties

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep the block short and the task one they can start alone; keep the tally pictorial or a single mark; do not treat drifting as failure
rows.if: Learners have low confidence or low literacy

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Let the learner decide what to share about where and how they study; the plan is theirs to keep, and the teacher asks only whether it worked
rows.if: Home circumstances are private or sensitive

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep that routine and its name; change only what the evidence here bears on (devices out of attention, talk separated, one end-of-block check)
rows.if: The brief names its own routine for focus time (a focus period, a study hall, a "quiet reading" slot, its own check-in or log)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use them in the tally and the plan in place of this page's categories
rows.if: The brief gives its own categories of distraction or its own criteria

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Do not split it into silent individual pieces; protect only the preparation that is solitary, and run the performance in the conditions of its audience
rows.if: The brief wants a whole-task performance kept whole (a rehearsal, a presentation to a real audience, a group product)

rows.basis: [Learning Space Redesign Alone Insufficient](claims/learning-space-redesign-alone-insufficient.md) [~M] (grade-7 mathematics, three classes; space without changed teaching did not help)
rows.change: Pair it with a change in how the space is used for focus and talk; judge it on the work produced, not on satisfaction
rows.if: The redesign is a room or furniture change only

rows.basis: [Redundancy principle (Mayer 2008)](claims/redundancy-principle-mayer-2008.md) [+M] (5 of 5 experiments, median d = 0.72, transfer); [Redundant on-screen text competing with a visualization](claims/redundancy-principle.md) [~M]
rows.change: Remove the on-screen transcript; keep narration, picture and a few key terms on the picture
rows.if: A narrated animation, screencast or explainer video carries the full narration as on-screen text, for `novice` learners

rows.basis: [Spoken–written beats spoken-only, not written-only](claims/spoken-written-beats-spoken-only-not-written-only.md) [~M] (g = 0.29 against spoken-only); [Verbal redundancy and images](claims/images-animation-eliminate-redundancy-benefit.md) [~M] (g = 0.45 without images)
rows.change: Give the words spoken and written together
rows.if: The words have no picture with them (audio lesson, podcast, read-aloud), learners are low on prior knowledge

rows.basis: [Reader fluency and prior knowledge moderate redundancy](claims/reader-fluency-prior-knowledge-moderate-redundancy.md) [+M] (L2 g = 0.58, nonfluent L1 g = 0.82); [Captioning second-language videos](claims/captioning-second-language-videos-large-benefits.md) [+M] (comprehension g = 0.99)
rows.change: Keep spoken and written words together; for video, captions on by default
rows.if: Learners read in a second language, or are less fluent first-language readers

rows.basis: [Split-attention benefit reverses into redundancy for experienced learners](claims/expertise-reversal-split-attention-redundancy-review.md) [~M]; high prior knowledge g = −0.05 on [reader fluency and prior knowledge](claims/reader-fluency-prior-knowledge-moderate-redundancy.md) [~M]
rows.change: Drop explanatory text that repeats what a diagram already shows; give diagram-only material and text on request
rows.if: Learners are advanced or know this content well

rows.basis: [The redundancy effect did not hold for middle school students](claims/redundancy-effect-not-significant-middle-school.md) [~M] (no detectable difference; equivalence not tested)
rows.change: Do not expect a cost from adding written text to narrated animation; remove it if it crowds the picture, keep it if learners rely on it
rows.if: Learners are children in the middle-school years

rows.basis: untested; no claim here tests redundancy with beginning readers
rows.change: Keep the narration; add short written labels only for words the lesson is teaching
rows.if: Learners are young children still learning to read

rows.basis: [Spoken–written advantage only for system-paced material](claims/system-paced-moderates-verbal-redundancy.md) [~M] (g = 0.12 learner-paced, not detectable)
rows.change: Treat duplication as a low-stakes choice: fluent readers can ignore one channel; give audio on demand
rows.if: Material is self-paced (pages, pausable video)

rows.basis: [Design-principle effects larger in system-paced media](claims/design-principle-effects-moderated-by-pacing-and-complexity.md) [~M] (g = 0.41 against 0.27)
rows.change: Apply the picture rule strictly: this is where design choices matter most
rows.if: Material is system-paced (a live lecture, a video that runs on, a broadcast)

rows.basis: untested in live lectures; carries [Redundancy principle (Mayer 2008)](claims/redundancy-principle-mayer-2008.md) [+M] from narrated animation to slides
rows.change: Cut slides to key terms and pictures; say the sentences
rows.if: Slides with full sentences that the presenter reads aloud

rows.basis: [Redundant text in a diagram made no difference](claims/redundant-text-no-effect-posterior-probability-lesson.md) [~M]; [expertise reversal](claims/expertise-reversal-split-attention-redundancy-review.md) [~M]
rows.change: For novices keep the text, placed next to what it describes; for experienced readers a diagram alone may do
rows.if: Print only, with a diagram and text that restates what the diagram shows

rows.basis: untested; carries the picture rule to a setting no claim here tested
rows.change: Do not float transcript panels in the scene; anchor short labels to objects, captions as a toggle
rows.if: VR, 3D simulation or a game with narration

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Captions as a toggle, not burned in; no duplicated text panels over the picture
rows.if: Phone-only, small screen

rows.basis: [Redundancy principle (Mayer 2008)](claims/redundancy-principle-mayer-2008.md) [+M]; the rest is the default above
rows.change: Apply steps 2–5 of the default; skip the across-session withdrawal of text
rows.if: A single session

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Removing a duplicate costs no time; do not spend minutes building parallel spoken and written versions unless learners are L2 or less fluent readers
rows.if: A fixed short time budget (for example 10 minutes a day)

rows.basis: untested proposal; fluency evidence in the rows above
rows.change: Produce one version with a caption or transcript toggle and let learners choose
rows.if: One teacher for many learners, mixed reading fluency

rows.basis: untested; the redundancy evidence assumes learners hear the narration
rows.change: Captions and transcripts are required access, not redundancy; keep them, and keep the picture uncluttered
rows.if: Learners are deaf or hard of hearing

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Give one audio track: narration plus description of the visual; do not let a screen reader read on-screen text that repeats the narration
rows.if: Learners are blind or have low vision

rows.basis: [Spoken–written advantages larger for retention and multiple-choice](claims/outcome-constructs-test-formats-moderate-redundancy.md) [~M] (retention g = 0.53, transfer g = 0.01)
rows.change: Keep them as given; change only verbatim duplicates over pictures; read a retention or multiple-choice result as favouring duplication more than a transfer result would
rows.if: The brief supplies its own materials, routine, rubric or assessment

rows.basis: [Segmentation moderates verbal redundancy](claims/segmentation-moderates-verbal-redundancy.md) [~M] (g = 0.53 unsegmented, 0.15 segmented)
rows.change: Keep it whole; with no picture, add written key text, which helped more in unsegmented presentations
rows.if: The brief wants a whole demonstration kept whole (no segmenting)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Generate any captions or transcripts in the same protected setting as the recording and do not publish them separately
rows.if: Private material (recorded patients, clients, learners)

rows.basis: [Retention and multiple-choice overstate the spoken–written advantage](claims/outcome-constructs-test-formats-moderate-redundancy.md) [~M]
rows.change: Judge the design on transfer items; do not remove captions or transcripts that access rules require
rows.if: High stakes (certification, safety training)

rows.basis: [Self-assessment accuracy](claims/self-assessment-accuracy-is-low-without-training.md) [~M]; tested with secondary and university students. Process focus: [process goals for novices](claims/process-goals-outperform-outcome-goals-for-novices.md) [~M], goals set before practice by high-school students, not reflection
rows.change: Give a rubric row or an exemplar pair before asking for evaluation; prompts name process steps ("which step?") rather than "how did it go?"; check a sample of self-ratings against a scored result before relying on them.
rows.if: `novice` to the task (first placements, first problem sets)

rows.basis: untested proposal; peer interaction is a moderator in [reflection interventions](claims/reflective-practice-evidence-mixed-in-professional-education.md) [~M], direction not stated on the claim page; reframing: see the teacher-education row
rows.change: Use fewer, more open prompts; add peer discussion of cases; ask for alternatives considered and how the problem was framed, not a recount.
rows.if: `advanced` learners or practitioners

rows.basis: [Elaborated discussion of narrated emotions](claims/elaborated-discussion-of-narrated-emotions-supports-teacher-learning.md) [+W], 66 team meetings in 17 Israeli elementary schools, the learning link rests on one episode; [reframing in a design course](claims/course-emphasis-on-reframing-shifts-teachers-toward-designerly-stances.md) [+W], two cohorts of 43 pre-service teachers, no randomized comparison; [peer reflective groups](claims/peer-reflective-groups-challenge-student-teacher-views.md) [+W] and [coaching methods](claims/teacher-educator-coaching-reflective-practice-methods.md) [+W], both second-hand reports in one ERIC digest
rows.change: Reflect in a small peer group with a coach or teacher educator, using dialogue journals or the teacher's own history as material; when a teacher recounts an episode, including how it felt, colleagues probe its sources and offer other readings ("what triggered you?") rather than only reassure; ask how the problem of practice is framed and who else it involves before asking for a fix.
rows.if: Teacher education or in-service teacher groups (placements, team meetings, coaching)

rows.basis: [Debriefing time underscheduled](claims/reflection-debriefing-time-underscheduled.md) [+W]: the authors' observation across 25 cybersecurity exercises that trainees wanted more debrief time; see also [Debriefing](principles/debriefing.md)
rows.change: Schedule the debrief as a fixed block, long enough for teams to compare their decisions with each other's and hear why the scenario was built as it was; end it with one action per team.
rows.if: After a simulation, tabletop exercise or game

rows.basis: [Constructive conflict vs self-reflection](claims/constructive-conflict-guidance-increases-reconsideration.md) [+W], 45 design students, one self-report item; the action-planning summary is an untested expectation ([feedback synthesizer](claims/synthesizer-expected-support-uptake-action-planning.md) [+W])
rows.change: Have it question or argue against the learner's account, or step them through guided questions, rather than offering an open "reflect here" box; if it summarizes feedback, ask it to turn comments into criterion-linked actions for the next attempt, and check that the learner, not the tool, chooses the action.
rows.if: An AI tool or agent is available to respond to reflections

rows.basis: untested proposal; the school-based meta-analysis in [structured reflection](claims/reflective-practice-improves-outcomes-when-structured.md) [+M] used written tasks and the claim page does not report ages
rows.change: Reflection is oral or drawn, led by the teacher, one specific question at a time, immediately after the task; no written journal.
rows.if: `child` (primary school)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Drop or shorten reflection; spend the time on retrieval practice and feedback, with at most a one-line "which items did I miss?"
rows.if: Goal is `verbal-association` (facts, vocabulary)

rows.basis: [Reflection interventions in higher education](claims/reflective-practice-evidence-mixed-in-professional-education.md) [+M]; tested with `adult` learners in higher education, outcomes pooled
rows.change: Reflect on a recorded or observed performance against named criteria, then reattempt a comparable task; repeat over the course.
rows.if: Goal is a `complex-skill` or professional practice (teaching, clinical, design)

rows.basis: [Formative assessment with reflection](claims/formative-assessment-embedded-explicit-reflective-higher-posttest-nos-sks.md) [~W]; tested with prospective pre-school teachers
rows.change: Pair each reflection with a formative check and feedback on the learner's stated view; do not rely on reflection alone.
rows.if: Goal is `attitude-motivation` or a disposition (beliefs about a discipline)

rows.basis: [Structured reflection](claims/reflective-practice-improves-outcomes-when-structured.md) [+M]; tested in a classroom engineering course, untested self-paced
rows.change: Use task-specific prompts tied to that week's content, require a written next step, and open the next module by showing it back; flag entries that repeat word for word.
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: single session untested, from the earlier page; intervention duration is a moderator in [reflection interventions](claims/reflective-practice-evidence-mixed-in-professional-education.md) [~M], direction not stated on the claim page
rows.change: One session: one reflection of three prompts, about five minutes, at the end, ending in one change to try; no portfolio. A term: reflect after each comparable performance, keep the same criterion, and compare across attempts at least once.
rows.if: Time available: one session (`single-session`) or a `term-plus` course

rows.basis: [Guided vs free reflection](claims/guided-reflection-yields-more-higher-order-paragraphs-than-free.md) [~W], same study as [public vs private reflection](claims/public-vs-private-reflection-mixed.md) [~W]: private journals more analytic; one graduate service-learning course
rows.change: Grade the use of the criterion and whether the planned change was tried, not candour; offer a private channel for analysis of failures.
rows.if: Reflections are graded, or shared publicly

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Allow spoken or recorded reflection, or sentence frames; judge the analysis, not the prose.
rows.if: Learners write in a second language, or writing is a barrier

rows.basis: [Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows.](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M] (cognitive-load studies; carried from guidance formats to teacher responsiveness)
rows.change: Keep the plan; one elicitation point to confirm, then move to harder or transfer items; drop the detour menu
rows.if: Learners are `advanced`, or already on track at the first elicitation point

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page (reasoning may be ahead of expression)
rows.change: Elicit by doing, drawing or pointing as well as speaking; accept home-language explanations; read the idea, not the wording
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary age), or emergent bilinguals

rows.basis: [Erroneous examples improve conceptual understanding](claims/erroneous-examples-build-conceptual-knowledge.md) [+M]; [Instruction that confronts science misconceptions](claims/misconceptions-interfere-with-new-learning.md) [+M]
rows.change: Use the contrast and confrontation moves first; re-observe with an item the misconception gets wrong
rows.if: Goal is a `concept` or `principle` with known misconceptions

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page
rows.change: Keep the planned practice sequence; respond to error rate (more items, worked feedback) rather than to individual ideas
rows.if: Goal is fluency or recall (`verbal-association`, a practised `procedure`)

rows.basis: untested at class scale: teachers using real-time response tools report changing lessons ([Teachers reported that CRS-and-TEFA use gave them more information about student thinking](claims/tefa-formative-information-changed-lessons.md) [+W]; [Teachers use Microsoft Forms for real-time formative assessment](claims/forms-realtime-formative-assessment-uses.md) [+W]); contingent support is shown one-to-one only ([contingent scaffolding](claims/contingent-scaffolding-improves-learning.md) [~M])
rows.change: Elicit from all at once (mini-whiteboards, a poll with a reason box, a quick form); respond to the commonest idea with the whole class; go to the small group still off track while others work
rows.if: `classroom`, one teacher, a large group

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Run every elicitation through one channel all can use (a poll or chat answer with a reason); read remote answers aloud with the room's so both are in the sort; avoid moves that rely on seeing a whiteboard
rows.if: Mixed modes: some learners remote, some in the room, or phone-only

rows.basis: [Generative AI tutors currently struggle to infer student knowledge](claims/genai-tutors-struggle-infer-student-knowledge.md) [-W] (a review citing two studies); intelligent tutors helped whether or not they modelled misconceptions ([ITS effectiveness is not moderated by whether the ITS provides feedback or models student misconceptions](claims/its-effect-not-moderated-by-feedback-or-misconception-modeling.md) [~M], one meta-analysis)
rows.change: Use automatic checks for answers, but add one free-text explanation per lesson reviewed by a person between sessions; do not rely on the system's inference of what the learner knows
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, no teacher present, or an AI tutor does the responding

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: One idea map for the one task; two elicitation points (minute 5 and minute 30 of 45); one move per point; a final unaided item; do not claim retention
rows.if: A single session only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: 3 minutes elicit, 2 sort, 7 move, 3 re-observe, 5 continue the plan; one departure only
rows.if: Fixed short time budget (for example 20 minutes)

rows.basis: [curricular knowledge](claims/curricular-knowledge-enables-responsive-instructional-moves.md) [+M] (undergraduate Learning Assistants with weekly preparation; carried to volunteers untested)
rows.change: Give the facilitator a printed idea map with three likely ideas and one move each; one question at each check-in ("what did you predict, and why?"); a 10-minute weekly debrief on one interaction
rows.if: Scarce facilitator time (volunteer tutors, Learning Assistants, a busy shift, one tutor checking in briefly)

rows.basis: [curricular knowledge](claims/curricular-knowledge-enables-responsive-instructional-moves.md) [~M] (the study calls these small-scale adaptations); teachers report frequent small customizations of a structured curriculum ([Teachers make frequent small customizations to OpenSciEd materials](claims/teacher-customizations-storyline-curriculum.md) [~W])
rows.change: Use only curriculum-embedded moves: hold back when a later section confronts the idea, refer a learner to another section, prioritise the higher-leverage exercises, explain a stuck point by the activity's purpose
rows.if: Scripted pacing, a structured curriculum that must be followed, or a shared exam date

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep it as given; change only what is read from it (sort responses against the idea map) and add one move per common idea
rows.if: The brief names its own routine for eliciting thinking (its own exit ticket, check-in, rubric or prompt)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use them as the idea map's headings and as the feedback's terms; do not substitute this page's menu labels
rows.if: The brief gives its own categories, criteria or rubric

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Collect responses privately (cards, anonymous poll); never put a named learner's error up as the contrast case; let learners show reasoning by doing before explaining
rows.if: Learners with low confidence or low literacy

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: The learner decides what is shared and with whom; respond only to what they choose to share; use invented cases for contrast
rows.if: Private or sensitive material (personal experience, health, identity)

rows.basis: untested; feedback-level evidence is general ([Feedback is most effective at task and process levels.](claims/feedback-most-effective-at-task-and-process-levels.md) [+S])
rows.change: Build the idea map from the errors seen in their work; elicit with a short case from their practice; respond with task and process feedback tied to the job standard
rows.if: Adults in work settings, or professionals

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Elicit at the task's decision points by watching and asking ("what will you do next, and why?") rather than splitting it into items; respond in the rehearsal, not in front of the audience
rows.if: A whole-task performance the brief wants kept whole (a lab, a case, a draft, a performance for a real audience)

rows.basis: untested; the assessment-for-learning claim's own discussion says no recorded study tests grading stakes
rows.change: Keep elicitation ungraded and say so; judge readiness on a separate unaided item
rows.if: Stakes are high, or responses could count toward a grade

rows.basis: [Teachers agreed lesson plans need adjustment when student ability diverges, with STEM subjects more amenable to difficulty scaling](claims/stem-more-amenable-difficulty-scaling.md) [~W] (interviews with teachers)
rows.change: Map ideas as lines of interpretation, not right and wrong; respond by pressing for textual evidence rather than by scaling difficulty
rows.if: Humanities or open-interpretation content rather than STEM

rows.basis: [Retrieval practice improves long-term retention](claims/retrieval-practice-improves-retention.md) [+S]; [Practice testing's meta-analytic benefit](claims/practice-testing-overall-meta-analytic-benefit.md) [+M]
rows.change: Replace some restudy or rereading time with recall: low-stakes quizzes or practice tests on the material just studied
rows.if: The goal is retention of facts, terms or procedures over weeks or a course

rows.basis: [Classroom quizzing improves classroom exam performance in middle school and college](claims/classroom-quizzing-improves-exam-performance-across-grades-and-content.md) [+M], second-hand in one review chapter; [More voluntary practice tests went with higher exam scores](claims/practice-test-frequency-predicts-exam-performance.md) [+W]
rows.change: Run short quizzes in class (clickers, software or paper), daily or at the end of each lecture, on the content the exams will cover. Where quizzes are voluntary, expect uptake to vary and record it: in two undergraduate courses, students who took more of the online practice tests scored higher on the exam with prior knowledge controlled, an association in self-selected use, not a comparison of assigned conditions
rows.if: The setting is a school or college classroom with unit and end-of-term exams

rows.basis: [Retention interval moderates the testing effect](claims/retention-interval-moderates-testing-effect.md) [~M]; [Retrieval practice effects are larger at retention intervals over one day](claims/retrieval-practice-effects-larger-at-retention-intervals-over-one-day.md) [~M] (Rowland's g = 0.69 against 0.41, reported second-hand)
rows.change: Expect a smaller benefit, or none; restudy can match retrieval at very short delays. Judge the design on a test a day or more later
rows.if: The test that matters is the same day or the next morning

rows.basis: [Retrieval practice improves transfer](claims/retrieval-practice-improves-transfer.md) [+S]; [Transfer is weakest to rearranged and untested material](claims/transfer-weakest-rearranged-untested-materials-worked-examples.md) [~M]; [More mathematics test practice gave a small mathematics gain](claims/math-practice-test-improves-math-performance-small-effect.md) [+M]; [Mathematics test practice did not improve domain-general problem solving](claims/math-practice-no-effect-domain-general-problem-solving.md) [-M]
rows.change: Ask practice questions that require inference or application, not only the items to be remembered; expect a smaller effect than for retention. Do not expect practice tests in one subject to raise general problem-solving: in a randomised experiment with about 19,000 15-year-olds in 32 countries, more mathematics on a practice test raised mathematics scores by about 2% of a standard deviation per hour and did not change scores on non-curricular problem-solving tasks
rows.if: The goal is transfer: inference, application, new problems

rows.basis: [Feedback enhances retrieval practice](claims/feedback-enhances-retrieval-practice.md) [+S]; [High-confidence errors are retained better after correction](claims/high-confidence-errors-improve-retention.md) [+M]; [Multiple-choice lures can be learned as false knowledge](claims/multiple-choice-lures-can-be-learned-as-false-knowledge.md) [-M]; [More multiple-choice alternatives help at high initial success and hurt at low](claims/effect-of-more-multiple-choice-alternatives-depends-on-initial-retrieval-success.md) [~M]; [Feedback on a multiple-choice test cut lure intrusions, immediate and delayed alike](claims/feedback-reduces-lure-intrusions.md) [+M]
rows.change: Give corrective feedback after each attempt, and make the correction of a confident error explicit; without feedback, multiple-choice lures can be learned as facts, and more alternatives add to that risk when learners mostly fail the items. Feedback straight after the quiz or later in the session both serve: in one experiment either schedule brought lure intrusions down to the level of learners never shown the lures
rows.if: Practice items can be answered wrongly with confidence, or use multiple choice

rows.basis: [Skipping feedback in fixed time improved delayed recall](claims/skipping-feedback-fixed-time-improves-recall.md) [+M]; [Skipping permits more retrieval attempts](claims/skipping-permits-more-retrieval-attempts.md) [+M]
rows.change: Let learners move past the feedback after a correct answer and spend the saved time on more recall attempts; keep the correction after an error. Undergraduates allowed to skip feedback made about six attempts per item instead of four and recalled more a day or two later. Untested beyond word pairs in a lab
rows.if: Practice time per session is fixed (a timed app session, a flashcard block) and items are often answered correctly

rows.basis: [Targeted short-answer retrieval retained targeted content better](claims/targeted-retrieval-improves-targeted-information-retention.md) [+M]; [Free recall helped untargeted content, on a free-recall test only](claims/holistic-retrieval-improves-non-targeted-information-free-recall-posttest.md) [~M]; [Short-answer versus multiple-choice evidence is mixed](claims/short-answer-versus-multiple-choice-retrieval-practice-evidence-is-mixed.md) [~M]; [Feedback decides whether short answer beats multiple choice](claims/feedback-determines-whether-short-answer-retrieval-outperforms-multiple-choice.md) [~M]; [Practice-test format moderates the effect](claims/practice-test-format-moderates-effect.md) [~M]; [Benefits do not require matching initial and final formats](claims/retrieval-practice-benefits-do-not-require-matching-initial-and-final-test-formats.md) [~M]
rows.change: Either format works; with feedback, short answer can do better, and without feedback multiple choice can do better because more items succeed. Matching the final test's format can help where it is known, but the benefit does not require an exact match. Choose the breadth of the task by what must be kept: short-answer questions on specific points retained those points better than free recall a week later, while free recall of a whole text helped the parts no question targeted, and only on a free-recall test (one within-subject study of 54 university students; overall scores did not differ)
rows.if: The question is which item format to use

rows.basis: [Retrieval failure reduces benefit](claims/retrieval-failure-reduces-benefit.md) [~M]; [Testing without study or feedback can be net harmful](claims/mc-testing-effect-and-net-harm-boundary.md) [~M]; [Effects are more robust when initial retrieval success is high](claims/retrieval-practice-effects-more-robust-when-initial-retrieval-success-exceeds-75-percent.md) [+M]; [Less initial retrieval support produces better retention](claims/less-initial-retrieval-support-produces-better-retention.md) [~M]
rows.change: Give a brief study pass or cues first, so that most attempts succeed; then withdraw cues (free recall rather than recognition, fewer letter cues) as success rises, since less support during practice gave better retention when learners could still retrieve. Never give a multiple-choice quiz on material not yet studied without feedback: in one experiment learners then produced more lures than correct answers later
rows.if: Learners are new to the material and would fail most recall attempts

rows.basis: [Spaced retrieval improves retention](claims/spaced-retrieval-improves-retention.md) [+M]; [Spaced retrieval outperforms massed retrieval despite lower initial recall](claims/spaced-retrieval-outperforms-massed-retrieval-despite-lower-initial-recall.md) [+M]; [Expanding and uniform schedules do not differ](claims/expanding-versus-uniform-retrieval-no-difference.md) [~M]
rows.change: Space the quizzes across sessions rather than massing them; repeated recall in a row right after study adds little, even though spaced attempts succeed less often during practice; an expanding schedule is not better than an even one
rows.if: Practice can recur across the course

rows.basis: [The testing effect generalizes across education levels](claims/testing-effect-generalizes-education-levels.md) [+M]; [Benefits seen in children, older adults and memory-impaired patients](claims/retrieval-practice-benefits-generalize-to-children-older-adults-and-memory-impaired-patients.md) [+M]; [Benefits extend to nonverbal and spatial materials](claims/retrieval-practice-benefits-extend-to-nonverbal-spatial-and-differently-structured-text-materials.md) [+M]; [Practice testing rated high utility across learners and contexts](claims/practice-testing-distributed-practice-high-utility.md) [+W]
rows.change: Use it; the benefit has been found across ages and materials, smaller in elementary school than at university, and clearer at about age 8 than age 6 in a few studies
rows.if: Learners are school children, older adults, or the material is visual or spatial

rows.basis: [Learners underuse effective strategies](claims/learners-underuse-effective-learning-strategies.md) [~M]; [Learners misjudge the benefit of retrieval](claims/learners-misjudge-effective-learning-strategies.md) [~M]; [Adaptive spaced retrieval beat learner-directed AI study at seven weeks](claims/adaptive-retrieval-posttest-retention-advantage.md) [~M]
rows.change: Build the quizzes into the materials and tell learners why; left alone, most reread rather than test themselves. Where a system can schedule review, adapting it to each learner's responses did better than learner-directed study in one study; a fixed schedule did not differ reliably
rows.if: Learners study on their own (`online-self-paced`, revision)

rows.basis: [Higher anxiety is associated with smaller testing effects](claims/higher-anxiety-is-associated-with-smaller-testing-effects.md) [~M]
rows.change: Keep quizzes low-stakes and ungraded; the benefit holds across anxiety levels but is smaller at high anxiety
rows.if: Learners are anxious about tests

rows.basis: [Strategy Instruction Improves Writing Quality](claims/strategy-instruction-improves-writing-quality.md) [+M] (grades 4–10; struggling writers gained more); [Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals.](claims/process-goals-outperform-outcome-goals-for-novices.md) [+M] (high-school students)
rows.change: Teach one move at a time with a modelled demonstration and a process goal, and keep goals as process goals to the end of the course (the next goal is the next move, not the audience's verdict); run strategy teaching over at least three sessions; keep the model text visible during practice
rows.if: Learners are `novice` or struggling writers

rows.basis: [Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals.](claims/process-goals-outperform-outcome-goals-for-novices.md) [~M] (suggests shifting to outcome goals after mastery; does not test advanced learners)
rows.change: Drop scripted move-by-move routines; set outcome goals (the reader's response); give harder audiences, hostile questions and critique of published texts
rows.if: Learners already adapt to readers (`advanced`, experienced professionals)

rows.basis: [Authentic Audiences Improve Student Work](claims/authentic-audiences-improve-student-work.md) [+M] (second graders wrote higher-quality texts for an external audience; within-subjects, abstract only). The oral-first step is untested
rows.change: Write or speak for an outside reader they can picture (a pen-pal class, a local business); keep tasks short and oral first; the teacher models one choice at a time
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary age)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use their own documents and occasions (a proposal to a manager, a client email, a briefing); take the workplace's own categories of document and reader; practise the same message for two levels of seniority
rows.if: Learners are `adult` in work settings

rows.basis: [Congruence of communication varies with situational importance and relationship closeness](claims/congruence-varies-with-situation-importance-and-relationship.md) [~M] (describes variation among college women; does not test teaching)
rows.change: Use paired situations differing in stakes and closeness (step 7); learners decide how direct, warm and formal each reply is, and when saying exactly what they feel fits
rows.if: Goal is interpersonal communication rather than argument

rows.basis: [Argumentation Improves Reasoning](claims/argumentation-improves-reasoning.md) [+M] (online science argumentation; dialogue programme transferred to essays)
rows.change: Make the subject's own standards of evidence the criteria; add structured peer dialogue on a contested question before individual writing
rows.if: Goal is argument quality in a subject (science, history)

rows.basis: [Argumentation Improves Reasoning](claims/argumentation-improves-reasoning.md) [+M] (studies of online and electronically conducted argument; the mixed-mode arrangement is untested)
rows.change: Run argument and peer response as written exchanges in one shared thread, so remote and in-room learners take the same turns; keep each contribution to a few sentences on a phone
rows.if: Learners join remotely, some online and some in the room, or on phones only

rows.basis: [Peer Feedback Improves Writing](claims/peer-feedback-improves-writing.md) [+M] (higher education; carried to school classes untested)
rows.change: Peer response in pairs against the written criteria (one group of three in rotation only if the number is odd); the teacher reads a sample of drafts and gives whole-class feedback on the commonest gap (usually the missing answer to an objection)
rows.if: One teacher with a large group

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: The tutor checks one thing per draft: is the strongest objection answered? Everything else goes to the learner's three-question self-check and to peers
rows.if: Facilitator time is scarce (volunteers, one tutor checking in briefly)

rows.basis: untested; the strategy-instruction studies all ran at least three days ([Strategy Instruction Improves Writing Quality](claims/strategy-instruction-improves-writing-quality.md) [~M])
rows.change: Cut scope to **one product revised once**: one situation and reader, one move, one short script or paragraph. For a 30-minute session: 5 minutes on the reader and the criteria, 5 on one model choice, 8 drafting, 4 writing a one-sentence self-explanation of why the move suits this reader (a partner's comment instead, if there is a partner), 8 revising the same draft = 30. Do not draft or perform a second version for another audience; record what the revision shows and do not claim transfer
rows.if: One session only, including one short online session

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep one product per session and one revision of it; split the time about one third modelling, two thirds drafting, responding and revising, and write minutes that add up (75: 10 reader and criteria, 15 model choice, 20 drafting, 10 partner response, 5 self-explanation of one choice, 15 revising). Drop style analysis before dropping the revision
rows.if: A fixed short time budget per session (for example 45 or 75 minutes)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Work in pairs: an even count makes all pairs; an odd count makes pairs plus one group of three reviewing in rotation; never leave a learner without a reviewer or set triads where pairs fit
rows.if: The brief gives a number of learners

rows.basis: untested; [Some students expanded and generalized class tools and rhetorical concepts into their own activities beyond the course](claims/expansion-generalization-beyond-classroom.md) [+W] shows two second-language learners taking audience awareness into daily life, not a test of these supports
rows.change: Rehearse orally before writing; let learners plan in their first language; first rehearsal with one trusted peer, not the group; gloss the criteria in plain words
rows.if: Learners have low confidence, low literacy or are writing in a second language

rows.basis: [Authentic Audiences Improve Student Work](claims/authentic-audiences-improve-student-work.md) [+M] (immediate product quality); the whole-task rule is untested
rows.change: Keep it whole: draft and rehearse the full speech or document, not separated exercises; rehearse with peers first; judge substance and delivery separately
rows.if: The work is a product or performance for a real audience

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page ("performance pressure can narrow experimentation")
rows.change: Put at least one low-stakes rehearsal with peer response before the graded version; grade evidence and reasoning separately from polish
rows.if: Stakes are high (graded public speech, competition, assessed portfolio)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use them as given; add only an evidence check and an answer-to-objection check if the rubric lacks them, and teach the named categories as choices for a reader
rows.if: The brief names its own rubric, criteria or rhetorical categories

rows.basis: untested proposal; the folded Cyphert and Pace pages use institutional issues, without addressing privacy
rows.change: The learner chooses the issue and who sees the work; positions are not required in public; analyse a public text rather than a classmate's views
rows.if: The topic is personal or sensitive (a learner's own stance, an institutional dispute, their community)

rows.basis: [Teaching style can be reclaimed as an effective tool for socially responsible rhetorical communication](claims/style-teaching-reclaimed-for-critical-pedagogy.md) [+W] (theoretical argument)
rows.change: Teach the convention as one choice with its own audience (the examiner, the journal), alongside a contrasting version for a different reader
rows.if: A convention is mandated (exam essay form, house style)

rows.basis: [Contingent scaffolding improves learning](claims/contingent-scaffolding-improves-learning.md) [+M]
rows.change: Make support contingent: start with the least help that might do, raise it after a failed attempt, lower it after a success
rows.if: One-to-one tutoring or an adaptive system

rows.basis: [A contingent AI tutor keeps metacognitive demand](claims/contingent-tutor-metacognitive-demand-matches-withholding-tutor.md) [+M]; [The contingent tutor surrendered the answer least](claims/contingent-scaffolding-surrenders-full-answer-least.md) [+M]
rows.change: Have it escalate and fade on what the learner does, holding back the full answer; this kept learners doing the thinking
rows.if: An AI tutor will give the support

rows.basis: [AI assistance impairs unassisted performance](claims/ai-assistance-impairs-unassisted-fraction-performance-exp1.md) [-M]; [Supported and independent performance diverge](claims/genai-supported-performance-independent-divergence.md) [~M]
rows.change: Bound it to hints, and schedule regular checks with no AI; answers given in practice lowered later unassisted performance
rows.if: Learners can use an AI assistant that gives answers

rows.basis: [Fading support promotes transfer of responsibility](claims/fading-support-promotes-transfer-of-responsibility.md) [+M]; [Fading worked steps eases the example-to-problem transition](claims/fading-worked-steps-facilitates-example-to-problem-transition.md) [+M]
rows.change: Fade worked steps over a series of problems, from complete example to incomplete to independent, instead of fixed example–problem pairs
rows.if: Learners move from worked examples to problem solving

rows.basis: [Fading support promotes transfer of responsibility](claims/fading-support-promotes-transfer-of-responsibility.md) [+M]; [Faded step position had no effect](claims/faded-step-position-no-learning-outcome-effect.md) [~M]
rows.change: Removing the last steps first is one tested option; in another experiment the position did not matter, so either is defensible
rows.if: The question is which steps to fade first

rows.basis: [Backward fading and principle prompts improve transfer](claims/fading-and-principle-prompts-improve-probability-transfer.md) [+M]
rows.change: Pair backward fading with prompts asking learners to name the principle each step uses
rows.if: Transfer to new problems is the goal

rows.basis: [Uptake of support predicts answer accuracy](claims/student-uptake-of-support-predicts-small-group-answer-accuracy.md) [~W]
rows.change: Before withdrawing support, ask a learner to do or explain the next step; learners who applied support rather than copying it gave more accurate later answers
rows.if: A teacher supports several small groups at once

rows.basis: [Scaffolding improves learning](claims/scaffolding-improves-learning.md) [~M]
rows.change: Fixed scaffolds may serve as well; the meta-analytic effect did not differ by whether scaffolds faded. Check unassisted performance before investing
rows.if: Computer-based STEM scaffolds, and building a fading mechanism is costly

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Hold that level on a changed case and lower it one step at a time; no fading threshold is established
rows.if: A learner succeeds only at the support level last given

rows.basis: [Worked-example guidance becomes less effective with expertise](claims/worked-examples-less-effective-with-expertise.md) [~M]
rows.change: Make the support optional and record whether accuracy changes; guidance can become redundant as expertise grows
rows.if: A learner keeps using support they no longer need

rows.basis: [Scaffolding improves learning](claims/scaffolding-improves-learning.md) [+S]
rows.change: Give support during the attempt (prompts, partial structures, models) rather than leaving them to attempt it unsupported, and judge learning on a later task without the support
rows.if: Learners cannot yet complete the target task alone

rows.basis: [Computer-based scaffolding has a positive effect in STEM](claims/computer-based-scaffolding-positive-cognitive-outcomes-stem.md) [+M]; [Scaffold design features did not moderate the effect](claims/scaffolding-design-features-no-moderation.md) [~M]
rows.change: Build conceptual, strategic or metacognitive scaffolds into the tasks; do not rely on motivational messages alone, which showed no effect on their own
rows.if: `online-self-paced` or computer-based STEM problem solving

rows.basis: [Scaffolding's effect is greater at the principles level](claims/principles-level-assessment-highest-scaffolding-effect.md) [+M]
rows.change: Aim the scaffolds at choosing and applying the principle; the effect was larger at the principles level than the concept level
rows.if: The objective is applying principles, not recalling concepts

rows.basis: [Scaffolding's effect is highest in project-based contexts](claims/project-based-context-highest-scaffolding-effect.md) [~M]
rows.change: Use scaffolds in project-based work; in design-based learning the pooled effect was not distinguishable from zero, so check unsupported performance there
rows.if: The course is project-based, or design-based

rows.basis: [Education population moderates the scaffolding effect](claims/education-population-moderates-scaffolding-effect.md) [~M]; [Scaffolding mitigated the limiting effect of low prior knowledge](claims/scaffolds-mitigate-prior-knowledge-limit.md) [+W]; [Empty-PC dyads built better domain models, concentrated among lower achievers](claims/empty-pc-better-domain-models.md) [-M]
rows.change: Expect a smaller gain from the same scaffolds; check unsupported performance more often and add explicit teaching of the missing knowledge. Scaffolds that structure the domain task can narrow a gap tied to low prior knowledge (one whole-class trial), but heavy regulative scaffolding (goal trees, cues, templates) can crowd out the domain work: in one inquiry-software study lower-achieving pairs built much worse models with the full regulative tool than with an empty one. Aim support at the task the gap is in, keep regulative scaffolds light, and judge them on the domain outcome
rows.if: Learners are underperforming or below grade level

rows.basis: [Scaffolded third-graders outperformed control students on irrelevant-evidence reasoning](claims/scaffolds-improve-irrelevant-evidence-reasoning-third-graders.md) [+M]; [Scaffolding almost fully diminished the disadvantage of lower logical reasoning](claims/scaffolds-diminish-logical-reasoning-disadvantage.md) [+W]; [Inhibition predicted posttest scores only under scaffolding](claims/scaffolds-enable-inhibition-contribution.md) [~W]; [The teacher as adaptive expert in real-time labs](claims/adaptive-expert-teacher-closes-gaps-real-time-labs.md) [+W]
rows.change: Combine a static structuring scaffold on the task with teacher modelling and adaptive verbal prompts that problematise, and give both procedural and conceptual help where learners stall (for example on graphs); in one trial with third graders this raised posttest reasoning over the same inquiry unit without the scaffolds and almost removed the disadvantage of lower prior knowledge and reasoning. Expect the scaffolded version to lean on different capacities: inhibition predicted learning only under scaffolding, so check who is still left behind
rows.if: `classroom`, whole-class inquiry with learners who differ in prior knowledge and reasoning

rows.basis: [Scaffolded tasks elicit more solution-evaluation turns](claims/scaffolds-shift-cps-turn-proportions-p3-p4.md) [+W]; [Scaffolded tasks had process distributions closer to the ideal](claims/scaffolds-lower-gini-cps-process-distribution.md) [+W]; [Final solution scores were higher on the scaffolded task](claims/scaffolds-higher-final-solution-scores.md) [+W]; [No script or reflection effect on later interaction quality](claims/no-script-or-reflection-effect-on-interaction-quality.md) [~W]; [Content support did not moderate script effects](claims/content-support-moderator-not-significant.md) [~W]; [CSCL scripts show positive effects on domain learning and collaboration skills (editorial report)](claims/cscl-scripts-positive-learning-collaboration-skills.md) [+W]; [Only the maximal script outperformed the minimal script on domain-specific argumentation](claims/maximal-cscl-script-outperformed-minimal-domain-specific-mas.md) [+M]; [More choices of the maximal script correlated with lower socio-discursive argumentation](claims/more-maximal-script-choices-correlated-lower-socio-discursive-mas.md) [~W]
rows.change: Build hard scaffolds into the task (prompts for each problem-solving phase) and expect more solution evaluation and better group solutions while they are present; then test the group on a later task without them, because neither a collaboration script nor a reflection scaffold improved interaction in a later unsupported collaboration. In a meta-analysis of collaboration scripts, script effects on collaboration skills did not differ significantly between scripts paired with content information and scripts paired with content scaffolds, at 14% post-hoc power; an editorial reports the same meta-analysis as finding positive script effects on domain learning and collaboration skills. Where scripts differ in how much they prescribe, a fuller script can teach more of the domain-specific skill: in one experiment on mathematical argumentation only the maximal script beat the minimal one. If learners may choose the script level, watch who keeps choosing the maximum: pairs who did so more often scored lower on the social side of argumentation (a correlation, so weaker learners may simply have chosen more help)
rows.if: Groups solve an ill-structured problem together (collaborative problem solving, collaboration scripts)

rows.basis: [Metacognitive scaffolding had no effect on individual domain knowledge](claims/scaffolding-no-domain-knowledge-effect.md) [-M]; [Metacognitive scaffolds increase metacognitive activities, with no difference between scaffold types](claims/scaffolds-increase-metacognitive-activities-equally.md) [~M]; [Problematising scaffolds: small effect on metacognitive knowledge](claims/problematizing-scaffolds-metacognitive-knowledge.md) [~M]; [Problematising scaffolds: small effect on transfer](claims/problematizing-scaffolds-transfer-effect.md) [~M]; [Problematising scaffolds: medium effect on group performance](claims/problematizing-scaffolds-better-group-performance.md) [~M]; [Problematising scaffolds elicit constructive, interaction-embedded metacognitive activity](claims/problematizing-scaffolds-elicit-constructive-interaction.md) [~W]
