rows.change: Prefer problematising prompts, which pose a question the group must resolve, over structuring prompts, which give an example to follow, and judge the prompts on what they target: in one randomised study with collaborating triads, the prompts raised metacognitive activity and metacognitive knowledge but did not change individual domain knowledge (effect sizes near zero), and problematising prompts gave small gains over structuring ones in metacognitive knowledge and transfer and a medium gain in the group's paper. If domain knowledge is the goal, add support aimed at the domain task
rows.if: Software gives small groups metacognitive prompts (planning, monitoring, reflecting), for example from an on-screen avatar

rows.basis: [Multiple kinds of scaffolds are more effective than a single scaffold](claims/multiple-scaffolds-outperform-unique.md) [+M]; [Domain-general scaffolds outperform domain-specific ones](claims/domain-general-scaffolds-outperform-domain-specific.md) [~M]
rows.change: Combine more than one kind of scaffold (for example planning plus monitoring prompts) rather than a single one; in a meta-analysis of 29 studies, multiple scaffolds showed a larger pooled effect than a single scaffold. The same synthesis found domain-general scaffolds ahead of domain-specific ones, but the domain-specific group held three studies and the combined group one, and the STEM meta-analysis above found no difference by context-specificity, so do not choose between them on this basis
rows.if: Software gives individual learners self-regulated-learning scaffolds

rows.basis: [Drawing support did not increase drawing quality; local support decreased it](claims/drawing-support-did-not-increase-quality.md) [-M]; [Local drawing support scored lower than control on recognition](claims/drawing-no-recognition-benefit-local-worse.md) [-M]
rows.change: Do not assume the support helps; start with unsupported drawing and test any support against it. In one randomised study (N = 156), neither global nor local drawing support beat unsupported drawing on drawing quality; local support made drawings much less accurate and lowered recognition below the read-only control, and support raised perceived difficulty
rows.if: Learners draw from a text to learn it (learner-generated drawing) and the plan adds support for the drawing

rows.basis: [Less successful teachers thought prompting was not part of scaffolding](claims/less-successful-teachers-misconception-prompting-not-scaffolding.md) [~W]; [No contingency effect on the knowledge assignment](claims/knowledge-assignment-null-contingency-effects.md) [~M]; [Contingency's effect on achievement depended on independent working time](claims/contingency-by-working-time-interaction-achievement.md) [~M]
rows.change: Treat prompting as part of scaffolding and plan to diagnose a group's understanding before helping. In one classroom intervention, teachers who held that prompting was not scaffolding gave less support, and the trained teachers' more contingent support did not raise scores on the knowledge assignment; on a multiple-choice test its effect depended on how long groups had worked independently. So check student outcomes, not only how contingent the teacher's help became
rows.if: A teacher scaffolds small groups during class work

rows.basis: [Performance trajectories as material scaffolds faded differed by teacher](claims/within-teacher-performance-trajectories-as-scaffolds-faded.md) [~W]; [The two teachers' scaffolding moves differed](claims/teacher-scaffolding-moves-main-effect-differences.md) [~W]
rows.change: Fade them together with teacher moves that take over their work: monitoring the class, prompting peers to share ideas, extending the materials and handing over independence. In one study of two teachers' classes, one teacher's students held their performance as material scaffolds faded while the other's declined across the unit; the teacher whose students held up used those moves more. Teacher and class are confounded in two classes, so treat this as a reason to watch performance as each scaffold is withdrawn
rows.if: Material scaffolds in a class (worksheets, software prompts) will be faded over a unit

rows.basis: [Full-PC dyads wrote better lab reports](claims/full-pc-better-lab-reports.md) [~M]; [Empty-PC dyads built better domain models](claims/empty-pc-better-domain-models.md) [-M]
rows.change: Judge them on the domain outcome, not on the product they template: a full regulative tool gave better-structured, more complete lab reports, while pairs with the empty tool built better domain models
rows.if: Software gives regulative scaffolds (planning, monitoring, report templates) during inquiry

rows.basis: [Failure- and success-driven scaffolding produce similar posttest understanding](claims/failure-and-success-scaffolding-similar-posttest-conceptual-understanding.md) [~M]; [Failure-driven scaffolding gave higher-quality constructive reasoning](claims/failure-driven-scaffolding-higher-quality-constructive-reasoning.md) [+W]
rows.change: Either nudge learners toward suboptimal solutions (failure-driven) or give low-specificity heuristics toward the right one (success-driven); conceptual posttests were similar, and failure-driven support gave higher-quality constructive reasoning, so prefer it when reasoning is the goal
rows.if: Learners attempt problems before instruction (productive failure)

rows.basis: [Tutoring effectiveness comes from scaffolding](claims/tutoring-effectiveness-comes-from-scaffolding-and-feedback.md) [~M]
rows.change: Have tutors prompt the learner to produce the next step before they explain; prompting alone matched ordinary tutoring in one small study
rows.if: One-to-one tutoring is available

rows.basis: [AI assistance impairs unassisted fraction performance](claims/ai-assistance-impairs-unassisted-fraction-performance-exp1.md) [-M]; [Supported and independent writing performance diverge](claims/genai-supported-performance-independent-divergence.md) [~M]; [Structured GenAI training improves problem-solving performance](claims/genai-scaffolding-training-improves-revision-performance.md) [+M]; [Conceptual-map scaffolding and novice LLM performance](claims/conceptual-map-scaffolding-reduces-novice-variance.md) [+W]; [LLM scaffolding level varies, but high-assistance responses dominate](claims/scaffolding-varies-by-request-and-assignment.md) [~W]; [GPT-4 access: more solved in the moment, worse after removal (review attribution)](claims/gpt4-access-worse-after-removal-math.md) [-W]; [AI-assisted performance does not transfer to unassisted performance](claims/ai-assisted-performance-no-unassisted-transfer.md) [-W]
rows.change: Limit it to hints and questions rather than solutions, and test without it; unrestricted help raised assisted work and lowered unassisted results. Consider teaching learners how to use the tool as a partner rather than an answer source: in one trial structured training of this kind beat problem-solving training on a later problem-solving test. For novices, add a short conceptual roadmap of the topic; its benefit in one study was borderline. Do not leave the level of help to the model's defaults: in one corpus of programming-course tutoring chats, high-assistance replies dominated across request types and assignments. Two second-hand reports (high-school maths with GPT-4, and a skill-building task) describe the same pattern of better assisted and no better or worse unassisted performance
rows.if: The support is an AI assistant that can produce the answer

rows.basis: [Differentiated materials exceeded unified ones on comprehension within each proficiency stratum](claims/within-stratum-differentiated-advantage-reading-comprehension.md) [~M]; [No material effect on immediate unsupported application](claims/no-short-term-dependence-cost-unsupported-application.md) [~W]
rows.change: Use them for comprehension of the assigned text, and check reading on a new passage without them: in one randomised EAP study, differentiated materials raised comprehension while present, and on an immediate unsupported passage material condition made no significant difference, so neither a dependence cost nor a carried-over gain was shown (equivalence was not tested)
rows.if: Second-language readers get reading materials adapted to their proficiency (glosses, sentence unpacking, labels), for example generated by AI

rows.basis: [Textual prompts give better near transfer than pictorial](claims/textual-prompts-better-near-transfer-than-pictorial.md) [+M]; [First- and second-attempt accuracy differ by prompt format](claims/prompt-format-first-second-attempt-accuracy.md) [~M]; [Textual prompts yield stronger continuing motivation](claims/textual-prompts-stronger-continuing-motivation.md) [+M]; [Far transfer was at the floor in every condition](claims/far-transfer-floor-effect-and-equal-time.md) [~M]
rows.change: Write the prompts as text rather than diagrams, and do not judge the format by practice accuracy alone: text prompts gave more correct first attempts, pictorial prompts more correct second attempts, and text prompts gave higher near transfer and stronger reported continuing motivation in the same 51-learner experiment. Far transfer was at the floor in every condition, so the study says nothing about far transfer
rows.if: Prompts are delivered in a computer module to novices

rows.basis: [Prompt presentation had no significant performance effect](claims/prompt-presentation-no-performance-effect.md) [~M]; [Learners rated externally regulated prompts more positively](claims/external-prompt-regulation-more-positive-attitudes.md) [+M]
rows.change: Either is defensible on performance: posttest totals did not differ significantly between module-controlled and learner-requested prompts. Novices rated module-controlled prompts more favourably, so default to them and record whether a learner-requested version is used
rows.if: The module could show prompts automatically or let learners call them up

rows.basis: [Fading support promotes the transfer of responsibility](claims/fading-support-promotes-transfer-of-responsibility.md) [+S]
rows.change: Withdraw the support in steps (complete examples, then increasingly incomplete ones, then independent problems), removing the last worked-out steps first; the evidence is for near transfer, not a fading rate or far transfer. See [Scaffolding and Fading](principles/scaffolding-and-fading.md)
rows.if: Learners are moving from studying worked examples to solving problems alone

rows.basis: [Expertise reversal effect](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~S]
rows.change: Make the support optional or remove it; guidance that helps novices can become redundant
rows.if: A learner already does as well without the support

rows.basis: [Journal prompts helped early, became detrimental by term's end; adaptive fading mitigated this](claims/expertise-reversal-writing-journal-prompts-fading.md) [~M]
rows.change: Fade each prompt once the learner applies the prompted strategy satisfactorily, rather than presenting it every week: in two longitudinal field studies, permanent cognitive and metacognitive journal prompts helped early in the term and left lower learning outcomes by its end, while adaptive fading sustained strategy use
rows.if: Prompts will run across a whole term (learning journals, weekly writing)

rows.basis: [Contingent scaffolding improves learning](claims/contingent-scaffolding-improves-learning.md) [~M]
rows.change: Consider explicit strategy instruction first; a dynamic-assessment synthesis ranked it above scaffolding
rows.if: The strategy can be taught explicitly instead

rows.basis: [Repetition and translation as scaffolding can hinder learning](claims/repetition-translation-scaffolding-hinders-learning.md) [-W]
rows.change: Plan support aimed at the step the learner is stuck on; repetition and translation used as unplanned support were reported to hinder learning
rows.if: Language teachers plan to support learners mainly by repeating or translating

rows.basis: [Segmenting improves multimedia learning](claims/segmenting-improves-multimedia-learning.md) [+M]; [segmenting principle](claims/segmenting-principle-mayer-2008.md) [+M] (3 of 3 experiments, median d = 0.98)
rows.change: Cut it at each step into segments with a continue control
rows.if: A narrated animation or explanatory video of a process, for learners new to it (`novice`)

rows.basis: [High prior knowledge learners benefited more on retention](claims/prior-knowledge-moderates-segmenting-retention.md) [~M]
rows.change: Keep the segments; prior knowledge did not remove the retention benefit
rows.if: Learners already know much of the content, and the goal is retention

rows.basis: [Segmentation benefits shrink with expertise](claims/segmentation-benefits-shrink-with-expertise.md) [~M] (efficiency only, one study)
rows.change: Offer longer segments or the continuous version with chapter markers, and check with a changed-condition question
rows.if: Learners already know much of the content and want to move fast; the goal is efficient transfer

rows.basis: [Design principles matter more for complex media](claims/design-principle-effects-moderated-by-pacing-and-complexity.md) [~M] (g = 0.70 vs 0.20, multimedia principles as a family); [easy tasks showed a floor](claims/easy-task-floor-effect-excluded.md) [~M]
rows.change: Do not segment for its own sake; spend the time elsewhere

rows.basis: [Effects confirmed for system-paced segmentation](claims/segmenting-effects-confirmed-system-paced.md) [+M]
rows.change: Build the pauses in: stop at each conceptual break for a few seconds or a short transition
rows.if: System-paced delivery: a live lecture, a video played to the class, a broadcast

rows.basis: [Flow control was rarely used and did not track learning](claims/flow-control-unused-no-learning-correlation.md) [~M]; [learner pacing helped on complex material, learner control in general near zero](claims/learner-paced-beats-system-paced-complex-material.md) [~M]
rows.change: Still cut into designed segments with continue points; do not rely on learners pausing at the right places
rows.if: Self-paced online, learners have pause and replay controls

rows.basis: [Learner pacing helped primary pupils on difficult questions](claims/learner-paced-beats-system-paced-complex-material.md) [~M] (one experiment)
rows.change: Segment the animation and keep the pacing control simple (one continue button)
rows.if: Children (primary school)

rows.basis: [Students said long recorded lectures impeded focus](claims/long-recorded-lectures-impeded-focus.md) [+W]; [engagement declines with video length](claims/mooc-engagement-declines-with-video-length.md) [+W]
rows.change: Re-cut it into several shorter videos at topic breaks, each a coherent step
rows.if: A recorded lecture of 20 minutes or more

rows.basis: untested; the claims here are on transient media, and in one study learners with static pictures navigated far more than with animation ([animations appear to pacify learners](claims/animations-pacify-learners-navigation-imbalance.md) [~M])
rows.change: Segmenting in this sense matters less; use one idea per slide or page and headings, and spend design effort elsewhere
rows.if: Slides or print the learner reads at their own pace

rows.basis: untested proposal; the claims here are on video and animation
rows.change: Break the walkthrough into stages with a stop between them before the learner acts
rows.if: VR, a simulation or an interactive demonstration

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Short segments, each a separate screen or clip with a large continue control

rows.basis: [Segmentation increases learning time](claims/segmenting-increases-learning-time.md) [~M]
rows.change: Segment within the session and budget extra minutes for the segmented version
rows.if: A single session only

rows.basis: untested proposal, from [segmentation increases learning time](claims/segmenting-increases-learning-time.md) [~M]
rows.change: Cut the scope of the session, not the segments: fewer steps per session, each segmented, so the minutes add up
rows.if: A fixed short time budget (e.g. ten minutes a day)

rows.basis: [Effects confirmed for system-paced segmentation](claims/segmenting-effects-confirmed-system-paced.md) [+M]; the prompt is an untested proposal
rows.change: Teacher pauses the shared video at the same breaks for everyone; use the break for a whole-class prompt rather than individual pacing
rows.if: One teacher for many learners

rows.basis: [Segmentation benefit was larger for the ADHD group](claims/segmentation-benefit-larger-for-adhd-group.md) [~M] (interaction not significant); [segmented videos reduced hesitations with ADHD](claims/segmentation-reduces-hesitations-adhd-participants.md) [+M]
rows.change: Segment; expect a benefit at least as large as for other learners

rows.basis: [Spoken–written advantage is smaller for segmented presentations](claims/segmentation-moderates-verbal-redundancy.md) [~M] (g = 0.15 segmented vs 0.53 nonsegmented)
rows.change: Segment, and expect the spoken–written duplication to help less once segmented
rows.if: Low literacy or second-language learners, and the video shows spoken plus written text

rows.basis: [Students said long recorded lectures impeded focus](claims/long-recorded-lectures-impeded-focus.md) [+W] (one student with a hearing disability valued shorter videos for re-watching)
rows.change: Caption each segment; short segments make re-watching one step easier

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Narrate what each segment's animation shows; segment boundaries still fall at the narrated steps

rows.basis: untested (authoring rule)
rows.change: Keep them as given: segment the brief's own material at its breaks, run its assessment as written, and add no test it did not ask for

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Segmenting needs no logging of viewing; do not add pause or view analytics the brief did not ask for

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Segment the demonstration, not the learner's practice: after the segmented walkthrough, the learner performs the whole task

rows.basis: untested; the recorded effects are mostly immediate tests
rows.change: Use segmenting, but do not rely on the recorded effects to carry to a delayed or on-the-job test; check at the horizon that matters

rows.basis: [A brief values-affirmation writing exercise raised African American seventh-graders' grades in two small field experiments, but a large same-district replication found no effect](claims/self-affirmation-improves-outcomes.md) [~S] (European American students showed no effect in either Cohen study)
rows.change: Do not run it; spend the time on instruction or feedback

rows.basis: [self-affirmation claim](claims/self-affirmation-improves-outcomes.md) [~S] (seventh-graders, in class; one positive and one null replication)
rows.change: Teacher hands out the sheet at the start of a lesson early in term; 15 minutes of silent writing; collect nothing, or collect sealed and unread

rows.basis: untested for affirmation with adults in the wiki; the earlier page cites Miyake et al. 2010 (college physics, no claim page). A belonging exercise at college entry is the nearest tested move ([Belonging Interventions Improve Outcomes](claims/belonging-interventions-improve-outcomes.md) [~M], carried from belonging to affirmation)

rows.change: Replace or follow the affirmation with 10 minutes writing about their worries immediately before the exam, for learners who report high test anxiety; claim no general effect

rows.basis: [self-affirmation claim](claims/self-affirmation-improves-outcomes.md) [~S] and [Brief expressive writing before an exam can raise test-anxious students' scores, but across the wider literature its effect on test performance is negligible](claims/expressive-writing-improves-exam-performance.md) [~S]: one-off writing exercises have small and fragile effects on performance
rows.change: Place it immediately before the evaluation in that session (10 minutes), and claim no lasting effect

rows.change: Give everyone the same prompt at the same point: paper in the room, a form online; on a phone, a tap to choose the value and a few typed lines or a voice note
rows.if: Mixed modes: some learners remote, some in the room, or phone-only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use a printed or online sheet that runs itself; the facilitator only reads out the instructions and keeps time; there is nothing to mark
rows.if: One teacher for many learners, or scarce facilitator time (a volunteer, one tutor checking in briefly)

rows.basis: untested proposal, from the earlier page's privacy requirement
rows.change: The learner keeps the sheet or the file; nobody reads it unless the learner chooses to share; if a record is needed, record only "completed"
rows.if: The writing is private or sensitive (values, religion, family)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep that routine; change only the prompt (a value that matters to you, and why) and its timing (before the threatening evaluation)
rows.if: The brief names its own routine (a check-in, a reflective journal, an onboarding "why are you here" prompt)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use that list, with an "other" line, rather than substituting the standard one
rows.if: The brief supplies its own list of values or categories (a school's stated values, a community's own terms)

rows.basis: [The agent's praise was indiscriminate affirmation: validation followed about half of participant turns regardless of what the participant said](claims/indiscriminate-affirmation-reflection-agent.md) [~W] (a reflection agent, not a values exercise; carried as a caution that AI praise is not self-affirmation)
rows.change: Let the learner write; the tool gives the prompt and nothing else, with no praise or evaluation of the answer
rows.if: Delivery is by a chatbot or AI tutor

rows.basis: [Stereotype threat in collaborative contexts can interfere with working memory and reduce meaningful contribution](claims/stereotype-threat-undermines-collaborative-contribution.md) [+W] (a primer's account; the remedy is untested)
rows.change: Run the exercise before groups form, and set roles so each member must contribute
rows.if: The threat arises in group work, where learners from a stereotyped group withdraw

rows.basis: [Belonging Interventions Improve Outcomes](claims/belonging-interventions-improve-outcomes.md) [~M] (a belonging exercise helped only where groups were afforded opportunities to belong; carried to affirmation)
rows.change: Work on the environment first (feedback framing, low-stakes assessment, visible support); run the exercise only alongside it
rows.if: The course or institution keeps sending a threatening message (ranking, deficit talk, no one like the learner succeeding)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Run a short version (5 minutes) shortly before the performance; keep the performance itself whole and unchanged
rows.if: A performance or product for a real audience (a recital, a presentation, a portfolio review)

rows.basis: untested proposal; feedback framing is modelled in [Wise Feedback Across Difference](principles/wise-feedback-across-difference.md)
rows.change: Run the exercise before returning the feedback, and frame the feedback with the standard and an assurance of capacity
rows.if: The learner is about to receive critical feedback on a draft

rows.basis: [Minimal guidance is less effective for novices than explicit instruction](claims/minimal-guidance-less-effective-for-novices.md) [~S] (unassisted discovery against explicit instruction; carried here to learner-directed study, which it did not test as such)
rows.change: Teach the content explicitly with worked examples first; hand over only pace and choice of practice task; start the regulation routine (step 3) on that practice
rows.if: Learners are `novice` on the content

rows.basis: [Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows.](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M] (cognitive-load review; gives no crossover point)
rows.change: Skip the first stage of the arc; let them propose goals and resources from the start, with checkpoints every two weeks and a check of their criteria rather than their plan
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` or experienced in the domain

rows.basis: [Self-regulated learning improves achievement](claims/self-regulated-learning-improves-achievement.md) [~S] (primary and secondary students; training effects larger when researchers delivered it); the narrower hand-over is untested
rows.change: Keep goals and criteria with the teacher; hand over choice among two or three tasks and the order of work within a session; teacher-led planning and review at the start and end of each session
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary age)

rows.basis: [Adult learners expect AI to enhance relevance through real-time goal monitoring, goal breakdown, career companionship, and networking recommendations](claims/ai-enhances-learning-relevance-goal-career.md) [~W] and [Adult learners expect AI to enhance autonomy through choices, flexible learning spaces, metacognitive awareness, and structured self-assessment](claims/ai-enhances-adult-learner-autonomy.md) [+W] (interviews about expectations, not outcomes); the coach from [coaching for low-skilled adults](strategies/coaching-and-support-for-low-skilled-adult-learners.md), untested
rows.change: Start from the learner's own work goal; break it into two-week process goals; offer a progress view and suggested next steps; leave the final judgement of relevance with the learner; for low-skilled adults add a named coach who checks in
rows.if: `adult` learners in work settings, or adults returning to study

rows.basis: [Self-paced mastery programs (PSI) reduce college course completion, though not by enough to explain their examination advantage](claims/self-paced-mastery-programs-reduce-college-course-completion.md) [-M] (college courses, completion); the remedies are untested
rows.change: Fixed checkpoint dates, an automatic content check at each, a reminder when one is missed, and a plan template with self-testing and review slots built in
rows.if: Setting is `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep the log and checkpoint in one shared place that works on a phone (a short form, a message thread); run the weekly checkpoint the same way for everyone, so remote learners' plans are read on the same day as those in the room
rows.if: Mixed modes: some learners remote or phone-only while others are in the room

rows.basis: untested proposal; the risk it guards against is in [Learners misjudge which learning strategies are effective](claims/learners-misjudge-effective-learning-strategies.md) [~M]
rows.change: Read checkpoints by exception: an automatic content check plus a one-line self-assessment from everyone; the facilitator reads only those where the two disagree or a checkpoint was missed, for two to three minutes each; peers review one another's plans against a checklist
rows.if: One teacher for many learners, or scarce facilitator time (volunteers, a busy shift, a tutor who checks in briefly)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Do not hand over goals; give a choice among two or three practice tasks, a two-minute plan at the start, and a two-minute check against the criteria at the end; record what each learner chose and found, and do not claim independence
rows.if: A single session only

rows.basis: untested proposal; [Self-efficacy and motivation positively predict self-directed learning, with motivation the strongest direct predictor](claims/se-mov-positive-predict-sdl.md) [~W] (an associational survey of undergraduates, carried here as a reason to protect early success)
rows.change: Hand over one decision at a time; use a picture- or tick-based log; make the first goals small enough to be met in the session; the teacher states the next choice aloud and checks it in person
rows.if: Learners with low confidence or low literacy

rows.basis: [Students taught with the Self-Determined Learning Model of Instruction gain in self-determination, but not significantly more than a delayed-treatment control group](claims/self-determined-learning-model-of-instruction-improves-self-determination.md) [~M] (cluster-randomised, 312 high-school students with intellectual or learning disabilities; within-group gains, between-group difference small, d = 0.23, and not significant)
rows.change: Use a structured student-directed cycle (set a goal, make an action plan, self-evaluate) in which the student answers each question; train and check that the teacher does not answer for them
rows.if: Students with disabilities, or transition planning

rows.basis: untested; the slot rests on [Instructions increased self-testing and cumulative learning but not study choices or feedback seeking in Experiment 1](claims/instructions-increase-self-testing-cumulative-learning.md) [+M]
rows.change: Keep it; change only what the evidence says matters: one slot for self-testing or review in the plan, one check of the learner's self-assessment against the criteria, a fixed checkpoint date
rows.if: The brief names its own routine (a learning contract, plan template, journal, rubric or check-in)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Learners self-assess against those, in those words; do not add a second rubric
rows.if: The brief gives its own categories, criteria or rubric

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: The learner decides who sees the plan and log; the checkpoint asks only whether the planned step was done and what the learner will do next
rows.if: Goals or journals are private or sensitive (health, career change, personal history)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Allot it: about 3 minutes to plan, 22 minutes of study on the planned task, 5 minutes to check against the criteria and set the next step
rows.if: A fixed short time budget per week (for example 30 minutes)

rows.basis: untested; an extended self-directed project is described in [In one extreme case, two sixth-graders with a choice-rich, ungraded STEAM infrastructure extended a game-design challenge into a year-long self-directed project well beyond its designed scope](claims/choice-rich-infrastructure-supports-productive-deviation-and-learning.md) [+W] (two sixth-graders, an extreme case chosen as such)
rows.change: Keep the project whole; hand over decisions within it (question, sources, form of the product) and put checkpoints at its natural stages (question agreed, draft, rehearsal), not as separate exercises
rows.if: A whole project or performance for a real audience, to be kept whole

rows.basis: [A review of 50 studies reports that AWE tools can improve the organization and overall quality of writing and encourage self-directed learning](claims/awe-enhance-organization-quality-self-directed-learning.md) [+W] (a review's summary statement) and [Thoughtless use of generative AI has a significant negative direct effect on undergraduates' self-directed learning](claims/tuga-negative-direct-effect-sdl.md) [~W] (associational)
rows.change: Allow it inside the log (step 10); ask learners to revise once from tool feedback and once without it, and compare
rows.if: Generative AI or automated writing feedback is available

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep goals, criteria and the final assessment fixed; hand over strategy and pace only, with fixed checkpoints scored on unaided items
rows.if: Stakes are high (certification, a licensing exam)

rows.basis: [Prior Knowledge Needed For Accurate Self Assessment](claims/prior-knowledge-needed-for-accurate-self-assessment.md) [~M] (synthesis of 22 meta-analyses; undergraduates' exam predictions); [Process goals lead to better skill acquisition for novices than outcome goals.](claims/process-goals-outperform-outcome-goals-for-novices.md) [~M] (writing revision, high school)
rows.change: Use a printed process checklist, checks that are tests (answer a question, rework a step) not ratings, every record co-checked in the first two sessions, and more sessions at the shared stage before hand-over
rows.if: Learners are `novice` on the task, or low achievers

rows.basis: Untested; the age and expertise moderators on the self-assessment claims ([Self Assessment Accuracy Is Low Without Training](claims/self-assessment-accuracy-is-low-without-training.md) [~M]: closer agreement in advanced courses) suggest it
rows.change: Start at the low-support stage: learner-chosen checkpoints, no printed checklist, a weekly outside check
rows.if: Learners are `advanced`, or their first checks already match an outside score

rows.basis: [Self Monitoring Improves On Task Behavior](claims/self-monitoring-improves-on-task-behavior.md) [+M] (single-case studies, grades 4–12, on-task behaviour only)
rows.change: Self-recording of on-task behaviour at short cued intervals (an app, a vibrating timer or a tone), after a training session; record the behaviour, not the learning, and check separately whether work completed changes
rows.if: Learners are `child` or `adolescent` with, or at risk for, attention difficulties or disabilities, and the problem is staying on task

rows.basis: [Metacognitive strategy instruction, which includes comprehension monitoring, improves academic performance by a medium amount, and in one non-randomised study comprehension-monitoring training raised low achievers' reading scores](claims/self-monitoring-comprehension-improves-learning.md) [+M] (one non-randomised study, 127 Nigerian senior-secondary students, raw gains 18.92 against 0.93; plus a meta-analysis of metacognitive strategy instruction, g = 0.50 at posttest and 0.63 at follow-up, of which monitoring is one part)
rows.change: Teach a comprehension-monitoring routine (stop, summarise, mark what is unclear, repair) over several weeks, with a stop at every section
rows.if: Goal is reading comprehension, learners are low-achieving secondary students

rows.basis: [Metacognitive prompts improve learning](claims/metacognitive-prompts-improve-learning.md) [+M] (meta-analysis in computer-based environments, g = 0.40 on learning outcomes, larger with feedback, task-specific and adaptive prompts); [diary alone](claims/learning-diary-alone-no-significant-srl-gains-online-math-prep-course.md) [-M]
rows.change: Build the checks into the software as task-specific prompts at natural pauses, each followed by an item with automatic feedback that shows the learner whether their judgement was right; do not rely on a free-text diary
rows.if: Setting is `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: Untested; the behaviour evidence is from individual students in single-case designs
rows.change: Run whole-class checkpoints on a common signal; every learner records on a one-line card; the teacher compares the cards of four or five learners per checkpoint with their work, rotating so each learner is checked at least weekly; whole-class feedback on the commonest mismatch
rows.if: `classroom` with one teacher and many learners

rows.basis: Untested proposal; the partner check stands in for the outside score in step 6, which [self-assessment accuracy is low without training](claims/self-assessment-accuracy-is-low-without-training.md) [~M] says is needed
rows.change: Keep the routine to two fixed pauses per session (one early, one midway) with a three-line card: what I am confident about and the check that shows it, what I am unsure about, my next move. Partners check each other's cards against the posted criteria (the task's own standard, or pictures of it); the group keeps one shared progress board; the facilitator looks at one pair's cards per pause instead of every record, and cards are kept, not graded
rows.if: Facilitator time is scarce: volunteers, busy shifts, a facilitator who drops in

rows.basis: Untested proposal; the check on the "know" line is what [judgments of learning are often inaccurate](claims/fluent-illusions-mislead-self-assessment.md) [-M] calls for
rows.change: Use that routine as the learner's script, word for word, at the checkpoints the brief sets; attach one quick check to the "what I know" line (redo the step, answer one item, compare with the standard) so a confident wrong answer is caught, and let the "unsure" line trigger the next move from the menu in step 4. Do not replace the requested routine with a different one
rows.if: The objective itself names a self-check routine (pause, say what I know, what I am unsure of, my next move)

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Use one shared digital record for everyone (a form or poll with one tick per checkpoint and the check item beside it), so remote and in-room records are checked the same way; on a phone, keep the checklist to three items and the check to one tap or one short answer
rows.if: Mixed mode: some learners remote, some in the room, or learners on phones only

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Teach and run the routine once on two or three items with every record checked; report the match between judgement and score; do not claim a habit or later effect
rows.if: Time is one session only

rows.basis: Untested proposal; underconfidence is described in the [self-assessment accuracy](claims/self-assessment-accuracy-is-low-without-training.md) [~M] claim's Discussion, not its entries
rows.change: Use pictures or a three-point face scale instead of written criteria, let learners show the check by doing (point to the error, redo the step), and point out where their judgement was right as well as where it was wrong; underconfident learners may stop using a strategy that is working
rows.if: Learners have low confidence, or low literacy

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Write the checklist from the job's own standard (a procedure, a safety step, a quality criterion); keep records private to the learner and a supervisor, so the check is not read as surveillance; check against outcomes the work already produces (errors caught, rework)
rows.if: Adults in a work setting

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Monitor drafts privately against the audience's criteria (what the reader or client needs) before anything is shown; the audience sees the product, not the checklist or the learner's ratings
rows.if: A product or performance for a real audience

rows.basis: [Judgments of learning are often inaccurate](claims/fluent-illusions-mislead-self-assessment.md) [-M] (laboratory and video-lecture experiments; carried here to adaptive and graded use)
rows.change: Never route a learner on a self-rating alone; use the check items' scores, and keep the self-ratings as data about calibration
rows.if: Stakes are high, or the self-record will feed a grade or an adaptive system

rows.basis: Untested; the self-assessment claim's Discussion says calibration is weaker on open-ended work, but its entries do not test it
rows.change: Give an annotated exemplar for each criterion and ask the learner to point to the evidence in their own draft for each, rather than score it
rows.if: Task is open-ended (an essay, a design) with no single right answer

rows.basis: [Self-regulated learning improves achievement](claims/self-regulated-learning-improves-achievement.md) [+M]; [Self-regulation strategy instruction improves achievement](claims/self-regulated-learning-improves-achievement.md) [+M]
rows.change: Teach planning, monitoring and evaluation inside the subject lessons, with a worked model on the task; measure subject achievement separately from strategy use and motivation, and expect less than the pooled figures when regular teachers deliver it
rows.if: School learners, and the goal is subject achievement

rows.basis: [Metacognitive prompts improve learning](claims/metacognitive-prompts-improve-learning.md) [+M]; [SRL interventions have a moderate effect online and blended](claims/srl-interventions-moderate-effect-online-blended.md) [+M]
rows.change: Put short, task-specific planning, monitoring and evaluation prompts at natural pauses, paired with feedback on the task
rows.if: Learning happens in a computer-based or `online-self-paced` environment

rows.basis: [A diary alone gave no significant gains](claims/learning-diary-alone-no-significant-srl-gains-online-math-prep-course.md) [~M]; [Training plus a diary raised SRL knowledge and self-efficacy, not mathematics](claims/web-based-srl-training-with-diary-raises-srl-knowledge-and-self-efficacy-not-math.md) [~M]
rows.change: Add brief training in the regulation steps alongside the diary; a diary alone showed no detected gain on any measured outcome
rows.if: The plan is to give learners a learning diary and leave it there

rows.basis: [Peer feedback groups added to SRL training raised self-efficacy and the focus score](claims/peer-feedback-groups-added-to-web-based-srl-training-raise-srl-self-efficacy-and-math-focus-score.md) [+M]
rows.change: Add small peer-feedback groups to the training and diary
rows.if: Learners study as a cohort and can meet in small groups

rows.basis: [Overall mathematics score marginal, focus score significant](claims/srl-interventions-math-overall-score-marginal-focus-score-significant-online-prep-course.md) [~M]; [SRL interventions increased logged time on the platform](claims/srl-interventions-increase-logged-time-investment-online-math-prep-course.md) [+M]
rows.change: Score the chapters or tasks learners chose to work on separately from the overall test, and add a behaviour trace (logged time, plans written); expect regulation measures to move before the broad score does
rows.if: The outcome is a broad test after a few weeks

rows.basis: [Self-assessment accuracy is low without training](claims/self-assessment-accuracy-is-low-without-training.md) [~M]; [Prior knowledge is needed for accurate self-assessment](claims/prior-knowledge-needed-for-accurate-self-assessment.md) [~M]; in AI-assisted writing, a calibration-training condition gave the lowest self-assessment error and overconfidence, and adding a feedback-literacy script did not improve on it: [APCA improved self-assessment accuracy](claims/apca-improves-self-assessment-accuracy-overconfidence.md) [~M]
rows.change: Do not rely on their self-ratings yet: give a short content probe, then model self-assessment on a worked example against the criterion before asking them to rate their own work
rows.if: Learners are new to the content (`novice`)

rows.basis: [Process goals outperform outcome goals for novices](claims/process-goals-outperform-outcome-goals-for-novices.md) [+M]
rows.change: Set goals about carrying out the strategy steps first; shift to outcome goals once the steps are secure
rows.if: Learners are acquiring a new skill or procedure

rows.basis: [A brief reflection prompt reduces acceptance of incorrect AI advice](claims/reflection-reduces-incorrect-ai-advice-acceptance.md) [+M]; [Reflection gave selective, not blanket, rejection of AI advice](claims/reflection-selective-not-blanket-ai-rejection.md) [+M]; [Reflection improved calibration of perceived against actual reliance](claims/reflection-improves-awareness-calibration.md) [+M]; [Metacognitive feedback reduces answer offloading](claims/metacognitive-feedback-reduces-llm-answer-offloading-improves-unaided-performance.md) [+M]
rows.change: Before learners accept an AI answer, ask them to rate their confidence and say how they would check it; give feedback on how they used the assistant
rows.if: Learners have a generative AI assistant in the task

rows.basis: [Unscaffolded GenAI did not change SRL](claims/unscaffolded-genai-no-srl-change.md) [~W]; [Over-reliance on GenAI may harm SRL](claims/genai-overreliance-harms-self-regulated-learning.md) [~M]; a reflective demonstration found the tool became useful only after repeated learner-driven corrections, which themselves demand regulation, and its authors argue unguided use favours learners who already regulate well (argument, not tested): [Reaching useful GenAI output required meta-level interventions](claims/genai-qualitative-shift-requires-meta-level-interventions.md) [~W]; [Unguided GenAI may benefit already advantaged students](claims/unguided-genai-benefits-advantaged-students.md) [~W]
rows.change: Do not count on it; teach and prompt the regulation steps explicitly
rows.if: The brief expects access to an AI tool to build self-regulation by itself

rows.basis: [SRSD potentially positive for writing with SLD](claims/srsd-potentially-positive-writing-achievement-sld.md) [+W]
rows.change: Teach the writing strategy together with self-regulation steps (goal setting, self-monitoring, self-instruction), as in Self-Regulated Strategy Development
rows.if: Students with a specific learning disability, and the task is writing

rows.basis: [Repeated reflective prompts may habituate](claims/reflective-scaffolding-habituation-deskilling.md) [~W]; untested proposal for the fading schedule
rows.change: Plan to remove them one type at a time and check whether planning and checking continue without them; repeated prompts may become routine
rows.if: Prompts will run for a whole term

rows.basis: Undergraduates with higher argumentation quality showed planning and monitoring interleaved with correct reasoning, and spontaneous regulation was rare (associational, 30 students, outcome-defined groups): [Argumentation quality is associated with co-occurring reasoning and self-regulation](claims/argumentation-quality-associated-with-reasoning-self-regulation-co-occurrence.md) [~W]
rows.change: Prompt a plan (hypothesis, which variable to change) before the first experiment and a monitoring check during it (one variable changed at a time, data inspected before concluding), inside the inquiry task rather than in a separate study-skills strand; an untested proposal
rows.if: The task is computer-based scientific inquiry

rows.basis: [The pooled SRL effect does not differ by school level](claims/srl-effect-no-school-level-difference.md) [~M]
rows.change: Keep the same plan, monitor and act structure; adjust the wording and the amount of modelling to the age
rows.if: Primary, secondary or university learners

rows.basis: [Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows.](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M] (a review of cognitive-load studies; gives no point at which to switch)
rows.change: Skip the early stages; start at the first stage they cannot do unaided; drop the primer and the part-task runs; use problem-first and mixed practice from the start
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` on this target, or pass the prerequisite check

rows.basis: [Part-task practice reduces cognitive load for absolute novices during initial skill acquisition.](claims/part-task-practice-reduces-load-for-novices.md) [~M] (one experiment; the joining step is untested)
rows.change: Practise the two or three hardest parts in isolation first, then join them in a whole task within the same week
rows.if: Learners are absolute novices and the task's parts interact heavily (several decisions at once)

rows.basis: [Productive Failure Improves Conceptual Learning](claims/productive-failure-improves-conceptual-learning.md) [~S] (the meta-analysis's advantage reversed for second to fifth graders)
rows.change: Teach first, then practise; do not put problem solving before instruction
rows.if: Learners are children in the early primary grades

rows.basis: [Productive Failure Improves Conceptual Learning](claims/productive-failure-improves-conceptual-learning.md) [~S] (no difference on procedural knowledge; mostly mathematics and physics)
rows.change: Put a short problem-solving attempt before instruction, then teach from learners' attempts; judge it on conceptual and transfer items, not on procedural ones
rows.if: Goal is conceptual understanding or transfer (a `concept` or `principle`), learners older than the early primary grades

rows.basis: [Example–problem sequences reduce cognitive load and improve learning outcomes](claims/worked-example-problem-sequences.md) [+M] (secondary-school novices, circuit troubleshooting, immediate test); the advantage was not detected at the final test with identical pairs ([identical pairs](claims/identical-example-problem-order-advantage-not-detected-at-final-test.md) [~M])
rows.change: Show a worked example before the first problem, then alternate example and problem
rows.if: Goal is a `procedure`, `novice` learners, an immediate test

rows.basis: [Interleaving category examples improves inductive category learning for visual and mathematical materials](claims/interleaving-improves-inductive-learning.md) [~M] (classification tests; reversed for word categories, no benefit for expository texts)
rows.change: Block each new category for a few items, then mix them; test with mixed items at a delay
rows.if: Goal is telling confusable categories or problem types apart

rows.basis: [Pretraining learners on a system's key parts and terms before the main lesson improved knowledge and real-world transfer in one VR experiment](claims/pretraining-improves-transfer.md) [+M] (one VR experiment against no pretraining; carried to other media untested)
rows.change: Give a primer of a few minutes naming the parts and what each does, before the lesson
rows.if: The main lesson is a simulation, demonstration or new tool, and learners do not know its parts

rows.basis: [Refutational text enhanced free recall relative to traditional text](claims/refutational-text-order-enhances-retention.md) [+M] (one experiment with written science text; carried to spoken teaching untested)
rows.change: State the misbelief, then the fact that refutes it, in that order
rows.if: Learners arrive with a known misconception

rows.basis: [Ability moderates the hierarchical-organization advantage](claims/ability-moderates-hierarchical-organization-benefit.md) [~M] (one physics report: low-ability students showed no benefit)
rows.change: Keep the general-ideas-first opening, but add prerequisite checks and corrective rounds at each stage; do not rely on the organisation alone
rows.if: Learners have low prior attainment in the subject

rows.basis: [easy to hard numbers](claims/sld-anticipates-start-but-not-stop-in-mdc-hard-numbers.md) [~W], [prompt-dependent](claims/mdc-stop-anticipation-remains-prompt-dependent.md) [~W] (one case study of one student; carried to other learners untested)
rows.change: Keep the stage, but raise the difficulty of the numbers or items inside it before moving on; count a stage as done only when it goes through unprompted on the harder version
rows.if: Learners have identified learning difficulties in mathematics

rows.basis: [concreteness fading](claims/fading-condition-outperformed-generic-and-concrete.md) [+W] (one experiment with undergraduates on group properties, reported second-hand, no effect size); see [concrete–representational–abstract sequencing](strategies/concrete-representational-abstract-cra.md)
rows.change: Move from a concrete representation to the abstract one across the sequence (concreteness fading), rather than staying concrete or starting abstract
rows.if: Goal is an abstract mathematical idea or notation

rows.basis: [listening first](claims/listening-first-outperforms-intensive-oral-practice.md) [+W] (a review reporting Postovsky's experiments second-hand); [reading cannot exceed listening](claims/sticht-law-reading-cannot-exceed-listening.md) [+W] and [oral language predicts reading](claims/oral-language-predicts-reading-achievement.md) [+W] (both reported second-hand from first-language work, no data printed)
rows.change: Start with listening comprehension and relax demands for speaking at first; bring reading and writing in after learners understand the spoken forms they will read
rows.if: Beginners in a foreign or second language

rows.basis: [free exploration then plan](claims/females-benefit-free-exploration-then-plan.md) [~W], [time-by-group interaction](claims/time-by-group-interaction-problem-solving-plan.md) [~W] (one study of 155 sixth graders, order of test forms; the gain held for girls only, and girls given the plan first scored lower after)
rows.change: Let them attempt the problems freely first, then give the plan; do not judge the plan by a test given before the free attempts
rows.if: Learners are given a step-by-step solving plan for word problems

rows.basis: [vicarious experiences](claims/vicarious-experiences-positive-teaching-efficacy.md) [+W], [mastery experiences not first](claims/mastery-experiences-not-optimal-initially-preservice-efficacy.md) [~W], [mid-point dip](claims/efficacy-dips-midpoint-student-teaching.md) [~W] (one review of correlational agricultural-education studies; outcome is reported efficacy, not teaching performance; no order was tested)
rows.change: Put observing others teach before taking on a full teaching load; add mastery experiences gradually, not by piling on courses; expect confidence to dip mid-practicum and plan support for that point
rows.if: Learners are preservice teachers or new to a practice role

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Put a step they can succeed at first in each session; teach terms in the primer, before they are needed; show a step by doing it before reading about it
rows.if: Learners have low confidence or low literacy

rows.basis: untested proposal; [skill develops through engaging in the target activity](claims/skill-develops-through-engagement-not-drill.md) [~W] (an argument from second-language acquisition, no study)
rows.change: Order by the job's own sequence where it has one, start from a task they already do, and bring forward the steps they need soonest at work
rows.if: Adults in a work setting

rows.basis: untested proposal; [whole-task argument](claims/whole-task-performance-improves-transfer.md) [~W] (a design argument, no study); [4C/ID](patterns/4cid-four-component-instructional-design.md) is the full sequence
rows.change: Keep the whole task as the unit at every stage and simplify the version of the whole, not split it into paper items; isolate a part only where learners stall on it, then put it straight back
rows.if: The target is a whole-task performance the brief wants kept whole (a full procedure, a performance for a real audience, a product)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Build the prerequisite check and the move-on rule into the software or the materials: each stage ends with two unaided items that unlock the next or route back
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep one shared order and one shared check per stage; send the primer and the map as a short item readable on a phone before the session; give remote learners the same stage-end items in a form they can answer by message
rows.if: Mixed modes (some learners remote, some in the room; phone-only learners)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Give the prerequisite check and the stage-end items to everyone at once (cards, a quick poll), keep one main order for the class, and give a short branch (back to a prerequisite, or ahead to mixed practice) to the learners the check sorts out
rows.if: One teacher for many learners

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Put the order in the materials so learners can follow it alone; spend the facilitator's time only at the stage gates, on the learners who did not pass
rows.if: Scarce facilitator time (volunteers, a busy shift, one brief check-in)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Order the session as primer or map (5 minutes), one example, guided items, one unaided check; teach only as many stages as the check can confirm, and do not claim retention
rows.if: A single session only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Fit the order to the minutes: cut stages rather than compress them, keep the move-on check, and put the rest of the map on a list for later sessions
rows.if: A fixed short time budget (for example 20 minutes a day, or two sessions where three were planned)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep its order and categories; change only what the evidence says matters (a prerequisite check before a stage, an example before the first problem, a mixed review once categories are met, an explicit transition)
rows.if: The brief names its own sequence, scope and sequence, syllabus or categories

rows.basis: untested proposal; one emotional-literacy curriculum is described as ordered cognitive to behavioural to affective and external to internal ([PATHS within-lesson order](claims/paths-within-lesson-cognitive-to-affective-sequencing.md) [+W], a document analysis, no outcome), with basic emotions taught before the complex ones built on them ([PATHS basic to complex](claims/paths-basic-to-complex-hierarchical-spiral-sequencing.md) [+W]); see [affective sequencing](principles/sequencing.md)
rows.change: Move from others' or fictional cases to the learner's own experience, from recognising to reflecting; let the learner decide whether and with whom to share their own
rows.if: Content is personal or sensitive (emotions, identity, experience of harm)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Do not move on by the calendar; require unaided success at each stage on representative tasks, and keep a cumulative check of earlier stages in every later one
rows.if: Stakes are high or errors are costly (safety, compliance, a licensing exam)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use the brief's stages as the skeleton and change only what the evidence speaks to inside them: what each stage checks before moving on, where a worked example or partial task goes, and how the trainer samples work when alone with a group; keep time reserved for the brief's own final assessment
rows.if: The brief already names its stages or order ("first the screens, then one field, then a full note")

rows.basis: [Signaling improves learning](claims/signaling-improves-learning.md) [+S] (d = 0.38 over 29 experiments; g = 0.43, k = 209)
rows.change: Use the full default design: overview, headings, one cued element per screen, colour links between words and picture
rows.if: Learners are new to the content (`novice`) and the material is a complex multimedia lesson

rows.basis: [Signaling improves learning](claims/signaling-improves-learning.md) [~M] (signals harmed high-prior-knowledge eighth graders in one field study)
rows.change: Drop the text–picture link cues; keep at most headings; let learners turn highlighting off
rows.if: Learners already know much of the material (`advanced`)

rows.basis: [Revised visuals reduce processing of lesson text for low prior knowledge students but increase it for middle](claims/revised-visuals-processing-text-prior-knowledge-interaction.md) [~M]; [Revisions to visuals had no effect on post-lesson test scores](claims/revised-visuals-no-learning-effect.md) [~M]
rows.change: Give a short prior-knowledge probe and offer the cued version to those who score low; expect no difference on the test for the rest
rows.if: A class with mixed prior knowledge

rows.basis: [The signaling effect holds only for abstract animation](claims/signaling-effect-abstract-only.md) [~M] (one quasi-experiment, d = .35 abstract; not significant concrete)
rows.change: Signal the written text where the animation is abstract (symbols, schematic); a concrete, realistic animation may need less
rows.if: Learners are children in middle school learning from animation

rows.basis: [Narration with finger-tracking animation directs preschoolers' attention to print](claims/enhancing-features-direct-attention-dual-language-e-books.md) [+M]; [Attention drops after the animation ends](claims/animation-phase-dependent-attention-to-print.md) [~M]; [Comprehension benefit only marginal](claims/comprehension-benefit-dual-language-only.md) [~M]
rows.change: Highlight or track each word as the narration reads it, to bring eyes to the print; expect attention to drift once the animation stops, and do not expect a reliable comprehension gain
rows.if: Pre-readers or early readers with a read-aloud e-book

rows.basis: [Signaling improves learning](claims/signaling-improves-learning.md) [+S] (design mattered more for system-paced lessons)
rows.change: Signal heavily: spoken overview, on-screen headings for each segment, a pointer or highlight on the part being described
rows.if: Adults in a short system-paced video

rows.basis: [Clear structure improves learning](claims/clear-structure-improves-learning.md) [~S] (signals shifted what readers recalled more than the amount)
rows.change: Use headings, a preview and a summary; test what is recalled as well as how much
rows.if: A learner-paced text or print reading

rows.basis: [Signaling principle, Mayer 2008](claims/signaling-principle-mayer-2008.md) [+M]; the one-per-slide dose is untested
rows.change: One heading that states the slide's point, one highlighted element per slide, and an agenda slide at the start
rows.if: Slides for a lecture

rows.basis: [Spoken text does not differ from signaled written text](claims/spoken-versus-signaled-written-null.md) [~M] (a null, not a test of equivalence)
rows.change: Signaled written text did as well as spoken text in one middle-school study; if text must stay, signal it
rows.if: The brief chooses between spoken narration and on-screen text for young learners

rows.basis: [The signalled and cued change was most detected](claims/signalled-and-cued-object-change-most-detected.md) [+W]; [Signalling focuses attention and reduces change detection elsewhere](claims/signalling-focuses-attention-reduces-change-detection-elsewhere.md) [~W]; carrying it to VR is untested
rows.change: Pair each highlight with a pointing cue (arrow), keep few objects on screen, and expect learners to miss changes outside the cued area
rows.if: A VR scene, simulation or busy animated display

rows.basis: untested
rows.change: Fewer cues fit: keep the heading and one highlighted element per screen, and put the overview first
rows.if: Phone-only, small screen

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use the early-session design only; there is no later session to fade in
rows.if: A single session

rows.basis: [Signaling (cueing) increases learning and reduces cognitive load](claims/signaling-improves-learning.md) [+M] (reduced load g = 0.25); its time cost is untested
rows.change: Signals add no content, so keep them; spend the minutes on the cued elements, not on extra decoration
rows.if: A fixed short time budget (for example ten minutes a day)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Build the cues into the shared materials once (slides, handouts, video) rather than relying on the teacher to point in the moment
rows.if: One teacher for many learners

rows.basis: [Signaling with labeled illustrations is associated with increased learning (review for emergent bilinguals)](claims/signaling-principle-increased-learning-outcomes.md) [+W]; [Narration with finger-tracking directs attention to the target-language print](claims/enhancing-features-direct-attention-dual-language-e-books.md) [+M]
rows.change: Label illustrations with short text and use colour or arrows to link label and part; pair the written key word with narration for young bilingual readers
rows.if: Low literacy, or learners reading in a second language

rows.basis: untested
rows.change: Carry every cue visually (captions, on-screen headings, highlight, arrow); do not rely on vocal emphasis
rows.if: Learners who are deaf or hard of hearing

rows.basis: untested
rows.change: Carry cues in structure a screen reader announces (real headings, a spoken overview, stressed key words); colour alone signals nothing
rows.if: Learners who are blind or have low vision

rows.basis: [Relevancy of emphasized text directs attention](claims/relevancy-of-emphasis-directs-attention.md) [+M]; keeping the materials is untested
rows.change: Keep them as given; add cues to them (headings, highlight, an overview) and point the cues at what the rubric scores; run the brief's own assessment, and add no test it did not ask for
rows.if: The brief supplies its own materials, routine or rubric

rows.basis: untested
rows.change: No change: signals need no learner data; a prior-knowledge probe, if used, stays with the teacher
rows.if: Private or sensitive material

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep it whole and cue its parts and their order inside it, rather than splitting it
rows.if: The task must be kept whole (a full case, a whole procedure)

rows.basis: [Relevancy of emphasized text directs attention](claims/relevancy-of-emphasis-directs-attention.md) [~M]
rows.change: Cue only what the assessment covers; marking the wrong material raises scores on that material instead
rows.if: High-stakes assessment follows

rows.basis: [Highlighting shows low utility](claims/highlighting-low-utility.md) [-M]; [Students' own underlining did not beat experimenter underlining](claims/experimenter-underlining-effective-as-student-underlining.md) [~M]
rows.change: Supply designer cues; learner highlighting alone has low utility, and in one experiment learners' own underlining did no better than supplied underlining
rows.if: The plan is to have learners highlight their own copies instead

rows.basis: untested; the recorded effects are mostly immediate
rows.change: Keep the cues, but do not count on the immediate-test effects to carry; check at the delay
rows.if: The test that matters is delayed, or is use on a real task

rows.basis: [Pretraining learners on a system's key parts and terms before the main lesson improved knowledge and real-world transfer in one VR experiment](claims/pretraining-improves-transfer.md) [+M]; [Assimilator learners gained significantly more in the VR (guided exploration) mode](claims/assimilators-gain-most-vr-guided-exploration.md) [+M] (one experiment; the learners' ages are not stated on the claim page); concrete framing from [Concrete-task participants achieved higher performance success than intermediate-task participants in simulation-based inquiry](claims/concrete-task-higher-performance-success-than-intermediate.md) [~W] (first-year students, one experiment)
rows.change: Add a 5–10 minute primer on parts and terms; start with a simplified scenario framed in concrete, familiar terms; give a goal and prompts during every run; never begin with free exploration
rows.if: Learners are `novice` on the task or system

rows.basis: untested proposal; the part-task finding is for absolute novices only ([Part-task practice reduces cognitive load for absolute novices](claims/part-task-practice-reduces-load-for-novices.md) [~M])
rows.change: Skip the primer and simplified runs; use unfamiliar or rare scenarios, time pressure and mixed cases; let learners lead the debrief against stated criteria
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` or practising professionals

rows.basis: the format is an untested proposal; the substitution rests on one study of one science skill with fourth- and fifth-graders ([Physical and virtual instructional materials are equally effective for teaching fourth- and fifth-graders to design unconfounded experiments when instructional method is controlled](claims/physical-virtual-materials-equal-cvs-learning.md) [~M], no difference found, equivalence not tested); the guided-VR experiment is the nearest evidence on guidance, and teachers report AI and virtual labs let students "try all materials virtually first, then use real ones" ([Teachers report AI tools enable authentic, contextualized science experiences](claims/ai-enables-authentic-contextualized-science-experiences.md) [+W], teacher interviews only)
rows.change: Use a teacher-led screen simulation with a goal sheet for each run, pairs at a device, and a whole-class debrief that names the real-world phenomenon; keep runs short (10–15 minutes); where physical materials are scarce, a simulation taught with the same instruction can stand in for them
rows.if: Learners are `child` or school-age in a `classroom`

rows.basis: [One RCT found AI-assisted simulation inferior to standardized patient simulation for breast self-examination skills](claims/ai-simulation-inferior-bse-skills.md) [-M] (nursing students)
rows.change: Practise the skill on a mannequin, model, standardized patient or real equipment; use screen or AI simulation only for the decisions and talk around it
rows.if: Goal is a tactile or psychomotor skill

rows.basis: [Controlled GenAI virtual-patient and communication studies reported short-term skill gains, but positive findings were not universal](claims/genai-virtual-patient-short-term-gains-mixed.md) [~M] (medical education)
rows.change: An AI virtual patient or scripted role-play works as rehearsal; add a human check of communication quality, because automated scoring agreed less well for communication than for information gathering, and some learners rated human cases more authentic
rows.if: Goal is communication, history-taking or a decision under uncertainty

rows.basis: [AI-generated and prebuilt simulations produced higher immediate conceptual-assessment scores than physical laboratory work, but the advantage did not persist](claims/simulation-advantage-immediate-not-sustained.md) [~M] (university physics); [Secondary school students learn more complex marine ecology content from interactive computer simulations than from hands-on experiments](claims/simulations-beat-experiments-complex-content-knowledge.md) [+M] (two randomised studies, larger for the complex topic); [Undergraduate students learning nanoscience with agent-based models show greater gains in explanatory knowledge than students learning with visualization videos](claims/abm-greater-explanatory-knowledge-gains-nanoscience.md) [+W] (27 undergraduates)
rows.change: Use the simulation to make the invisible visible, with learners operating the model themselves rather than watching a video of it; then ask them to predict and explain with the simulation off; schedule a delayed check, not only an immediate one
rows.if: Goal is a concept in science (a field, a force, a hidden process)

rows.basis: [Intelligent Extended Reality interventions in VET show consistent positive effects on procedural competence, practical skills, and learner motivation](claims/ixr-vet-positive-effects-procedural-motivation.md) [+M] (review, no pooled effect); adult learners interviewed said they want simulations that closely resemble actual job scenarios ([Adult learners expect AI to support transformative and experiential learning through assumption-challenging simulations, role play, and authentic virtual contexts](claims/ai-supports-transformative-experiential-learning.md) [+W], expectations, not outcomes); one ethnography of forestry-machine simulator training found instruction centred on volume training of routine tasks rather than the risky situations that justify a simulator ([Simulator-based VET instruction in this study centres on volume training of routine tasks rather than rehearsing specific high-stakes, risky situations.](claims/vet-simulator-instruction-volume-training-not-high-stakes.md) [~W]), with the simulator showing errors' consequences ([Simulator feedback responds authentically to student error](claims/simulator-authentic-error-feedback-log-drops.md) [+W]) and teachers using the real machine as the benchmark ([VET teachers use the real machine as the benchmark of legitimacy for simulator instruction](claims/real-machine-benchmark-and-colleague-positioning.md) [+W]); observations of practice, no outcomes; workplace incidents untested
rows.change: Build scenarios from the learners' own workplace incidents, including the rare and risky ones, not only volume practice of routine tasks; make errors produce their real consequences in the simulation; refer settings and moves to the real machine during the run; end with a supervised task at work
rows.if: Adults in work settings (vocational training, safety, customer handling)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use a browser or phone simulation everyone can run, not a headset for some; let remote learners share their screen for the debrief; give everyone the same goal and debrief questions
rows.if: Setting is mixed: some learners remote, some in the room, or phone-only

rows.basis: [Cybersickness remains a persistent practical challenge, affecting approximately 42% of VR users](claims/cybersickness-prevalence-vr-ar-immersive-learning.md) [~M]; a K-12 review also reports dizziness, distraction, cost, infrastructure and a lack of private space for headset use ([VR/AR implementation challenges fall on three fronts](claims/vr-ar-challenges-learners-teachers-schools.md) [~W]); the fidelity point supports a non-immersive version ([Increased perceptual fidelity fails to reliably improve serious game learning outcomes](claims/fidelity-fallacy-serious-games.md) [~M]); high-end equipment can cost over $72,000 a station, and the reported gain for one such system was in engagement, not learning ([In one reviewed study, Anatomage virtual dissection increased medical student engagement by 34% over cadaver-based practice](claims/anatomage-vr-engagement-34-percent.md) [~W])
rows.change: Use a desktop or phone version, or a tabletop or paper scenario with the same decisions; offer a seated, non-immersive option; keep immersive sessions short
rows.if: No headsets, low bandwidth, or learners prone to motion sickness or with disabilities

rows.basis: [The advantage of simulation games shrinks or reverses when the comparison group learns via active instructional methods](claims/active-comparison-instruction-reverses-simulation-game-advantage.md) [~M] (d = −.19 against active methods); [Virtual patients show larger advantages over passive traditional learning than over active learning](claims/vp-passive-versus-active-comparison.md) [~M]; the supplement use is untested here
rows.change: Do not expect the simulation to beat it; use the simulation where it adds what the active method lacks (safety, access, rare cases, unlimited repetition) or as a supplement to it, and compare the two locally on the same aligned check before replacing one with the other
rows.if: The alternative to the simulation is already an active method (hands-on practice, role-play, worked problems with feedback)

rows.basis: untested proposal; contingent-support evidence is mostly one-to-one ([Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support.](claims/contingent-scaffolding-improves-learning.md) [~M], carried to groups it did not test)
rows.change: Build the run's goal and prompts into the simulation; run in pairs or teams of three to four, one observer per team with a checklist; facilitator joins only the debrief, and debriefs the commonest error with the whole group
rows.if: One facilitator for many learners, or scarce facilitator time (volunteers, a busy clinical shift)

rows.basis: [The review reports that insufficient prep time, curriculum-alignment difficulty, and low teacher confidence with new technologies are barriers](claims/teacher-time-confidence-barriers-simulation-implementation.md) [~M]; a K-12 STEM review adds learner distraction, loss of classroom control and difficulty designing activities ([VR/AR implementation challenges fall on three fronts: learner distraction and discomfort, teacher classroom-management and design burdens, and school cost and infrastructure limits](claims/vr-ar-challenges-learners-teachers-schools.md) [~W]) (K-12; the run sheet and room plan are untested)
rows.change: Choose one ready-made simulation aligned to one standard; give the teacher a one-page run sheet (goal, three prompts, debrief questions) and a plan for managing the room while devices are in use (who holds which device, a signal to stop and look up); start with one lesson before a unit
rows.if: Teachers have little preparation time or are new to the technology

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: One primer (5 min), one run (15 min), one debrief (15 min), one second run (10 min), one non-simulated check item (5 min); record the check and claim no retention
rows.if: Time is one session only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Drop the second run before the debrief: primer 3 min, run 8 min, debrief 7 min, one-line plan for next time 2 min
rows.if: A fixed short time budget (for example 20 minutes)

rows.basis: [Learners valued safe, repeatable, nonjudgmental AI practice environments that reduced anxiety](claims/ai-simulation-safe-practice-environments.md) [+W] (nursing, learners' reports); literacy untested
rows.change: Start with a private, repeatable run with no score shown; read prompts aloud or use icons; debrief one-to-one or in a small group first
rows.if: Learners have low confidence, high anxiety or low literacy

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: The learner decides who sees a recording or log; debrief from the learner's own account if they choose; never show an individual's errors to the group without consent
rows.if: Recordings or logs of performance are private or sensitive (errors with a client, personal role-play)

rows.basis: untested proposal; see [Debriefing](principles/debriefing.md)
rows.change: Keep it as given and run it after every run; change only what the evidence says matters (a goal before the run, guidance during it, a second attempt after)
rows.if: The brief names its own debrief routine, rubric or checklist

rows.basis: untested; [A training-design argument … holds that practising whole complex tasks improves transfer](claims/whole-task-performance-improves-transfer.md) [~W]
rows.change: Keep the whole scenario; simplify it by slowing events or removing distractors, not by splitting it into separate drills; debrief at its decision points
rows.if: The brief wants a whole performance kept whole (a full resuscitation, a whole negotiation)

rows.basis: [Simulation Based Education With Deliberate Practice Improves Clinical Outcomes](claims/simulation-based-education-with-deliberate-practice-improves-clinical-outcomes.md) [+M] (procedural clinical skills)
rows.change: Set a mastery criterion for each scenario, require repeated runs until it is met, and confirm on a non-simulated assessment before real practice
rows.if: High stakes (certification, patient or public safety)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use the simulation as rehearsal before the real event; debrief after the rehearsal and again after the real event
rows.if: The product or performance is for a real audience (a briefing to a real client, a demonstration for the public)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Build that error into a scenario as an event the learner must catch, and use it as the compared case in the debrief
rows.if: The brief reports an error learners actually made

rows.basis: [Persistent technical limitations constitute an authenticity gap in AI-powered nursing simulations](claims/ai-simulation-authenticity-gap.md) [~M]; [Students treated the genAI avatar as a sophisticated question base rather than a virtual patient, using predominantly closed-ended, efficiency-focused questioning](claims/genai-avatar-treated-as-question-base.md) [~W] (two medical-school problem-based learning groups, descriptive; the instruction to learners is untested)
rows.change: Brief learners that the agent may respond oddly, lag or lack non-verbal cues; ask them to note such moments, and treat them as a limit of the simulation in the debrief.
