Where the goal is communication, ask learners to talk to the agent as to a person (open questions, plain language) and debrief their questioning, because learners otherwise tend to query it like a database
rows.if: The simulation uses an AI agent or virtual patient

rows.basis: [Physical Experience Enhances Science Learning](claims/physical-experience-enhances-science-learning.md) [~M] (physical = virtual for concepts, one undergraduate study); [Guidance during inquiry learning improves post-inquiry learning outcomes](claims/guidance-improves-inquiry-learning-outcomes.md) [+M]; [Students perceived online lab exercises as more effective when instructors were present online and used scaffolds and probes](claims/online-labs-better-with-instructor-scaffolds.md) [+W]; immediate-only gains ([AI-generated and prebuilt simulations … advantage did not persist](claims/simulation-advantage-immediate-not-sustained.md) [~M]); mentor role from [Mentor Support in Self-Paced Online Learning](patterns/mentor-support-in-self-paced-online-learning.md), untested for labs
rows.change: Use a guided virtual lab in place of the bench: a goal and data table for each run, a required experiment plan before running, prompts during it, an explain-with-the-simulation-off task after; a mentor or instructor reads each write-up and answers within a stated time; schedule a delayed conceptual check
rows.if: Learners study `online-self-paced` with no lab access, and the goal is conceptual knowledge or inquiry skill

rows.basis: [One RCT found AI-assisted simulation inferior to standardized patient simulation for breast self-examination skills](claims/ai-simulation-inferior-bse-skills.md) [-M] (carried from a tactile nursing skill); [Pretraining improves transfer](claims/pretraining-improves-transfer.md) [+M]; no claim in this wiki compares a virtual and a bench science lab on manipulative skill
rows.change: Do not credit the skill from the virtual lab; use the virtual lab to prepare (parts, steps, predictions) and add a hands-on component (a local or campus lab, a residency, a home kit) assessed on real equipment
rows.if: Self-paced online, no lab access, and the competency includes a manipulative or bench skill

rows.basis: [Virtual patients more effectively improve skills than traditional education](claims/vp-traditional-skills-advantage.md) [+M]; [Virtual patients show larger advantages over passive traditional learning than over active learning](claims/vp-passive-versus-active-comparison.md) [~M]; [Higher levels of technology support during simulation are associated with greater effects](claims/technology-support-associated-with-greater-effects.md) [~M]; [Simulation Based Education With Deliberate Practice Improves Clinical Outcomes](claims/simulation-based-education-with-deliberate-practice-improves-clinical-outcomes.md) [+M]; for the conversation see [Practice with Simulated People](patterns/practice-with-simulated-people.md)
rows.change: Use screen-based virtual patients for the reasoning before the skills lab and blended with it, not in place of it; keep the procedure on mannequins, task trainers or standardized patients with a mastery criterion; rehearse the conversation with a simulated person
rows.if: Health-professions skills lab (clinical procedures, examination, resuscitation)

rows.basis: untested for technology sandboxes in this wiki; carried from vocational XR ([Intelligent Extended Reality interventions in VET show consistent positive effects on procedural competence](claims/ixr-vet-positive-effects-procedural-motivation.md) [+M], review, no pooled effect) and from simulation effects being largest on technical performance ([Simulation effects vary by complex skill](claims/simulation-effects-vary-by-complex-skill.md) [~M])
rows.change: Give each lab a fault to diagnose or a configuration goal, a reset button, components opened in stages, and a short written account of what was changed and why that a person reviews; finish on the real or production-like system where the competency requires it
rows.if: Technology labs: a sandbox, virtual machine or simulated network learners configure, break and repair

rows.basis: [Undergraduates learning IoT tasks in VR with ChatGPT-integrated feedback reached significantly higher cognitive levels](claims/gpt-feedback-vr-higher-cognitive-levels.md) [+M] and [GPT feedback in VR … limited impact on creativity](claims/gpt-feedback-hots-problem-solving-critical-thinking-limited-creativity.md) [~M] (one undergraduate RCT, against the VR's ordinary feedback); [SMEs rated ChatGPT's content accuracy acceptable but inconsistent and below human TAs](claims/chatgpt-lab-accuracy-acceptable-inconsistent-below-human-tas.md) [-M]; [Students receiving instructor feedback showed significantly greater improvements in lab assignment scores than students receiving AI-generated feedback](claims/instructor-feedback-greater-lab-score-improvements-than-ai-feedback.md) [-M]; [Personalized ChatGPT-supported feedback in an augmented-reality quantum physics laboratory improved learning outcomes](claims/chatgpt-ar-lab-feedback-improves-outcomes.md) [+M]; see [AI Tutoring](patterns/ai-tutoring.md)
rows.change: Let the AI answer procedure and terminology questions and give feedback during the run in place of the simulation's fixed messages; keep a person reading the write-ups and checking content the AI explains; tell learners the AI can be confidently wrong; do not expect in-run AI feedback to help creative or open design work
rows.if: Learners ask an AI assistant questions during an online lab, or AI gives the lab feedback

rows.basis: [Machine-learned detectors of science inquiry skill made accurate inferences after a student ran a simulation three times](claims/inquiry-detectors-accurate-after-three-runs.md) [+W]; outreach on that signal untested
rows.change: Use the simulation's logs (experiments run, variables changed, plan written or not) as the signal for a mentor to reach out, and check the signal against write-up quality before relying on it
rows.if: A mentor is available on demand but does not watch runs

rows.basis: [Teachers report AI tools enable authentic, contextualized science experiences](claims/ai-enables-authentic-contextualized-science-experiences.md) [+W] (interviews); safety outcomes untested in this wiki
rows.change: Rehearse it virtually first, with the safety decisions as events the learner must handle, then do it supervised on real equipment
rows.if: The procedure is hazardous, or the phenomenon cannot be reached (toxic reagents, high voltage, a rare event)

rows.basis: [Prior knowledge moderates scaffolding effectiveness](claims/prior-knowledge-moderates-scaffolding-effectiveness.md) [~M]; [Presence versus absence of individual scaffolding types did not support the added-value hypothesis, but scaffolding combinations partly did](claims/scaffolding-added-value-partly-supported.md) [~M] (higher education)
rows.change: Give novices worked examples of an experiment or case before they run; give advanced learners reflection phases after the run; do not rely on prompts alone
rows.if: Learners' prior knowledge of the domain differs (`novice` vs `advanced`)

rows.basis: [VR simulation better promoted lab-teaching knowledge development than live classroom simulation, while live simulation better fostered class-teaching knowledge development](claims/vr-vs-live-simulation-domain-specific-teaching-knowledge.md) [~M] (one randomised comparison, 40 teaching assistants, one 4-hour session); [Teachers judged LLM-simulated student ideas realistic and most useful when the ideas sparked sensemaking about student thinking](claims/teachers-perceive-llm-ideas-realistic-sensemaking-useful.md) [+W] (six teachers' judgements, no learning outcome)
rows.change: Choose the medium by the teaching situation: a VR or virtual classroom for situations that are hard to stage live (a lab session, a rare incident), live role-play with peers for whole-class interaction; AI-simulated student ideas can serve as material for practising noticing and planning a response
rows.if: Learners are teachers, student teachers or teaching assistants rehearsing teaching

rows.basis: [Computer-supported collaborative learning with simulation programs fostered conceptual change for students who were cognitively engaged and prepared to reflect on and reconstruct their conceptions](claims/cscl-simulation-conceptual-change-cognitive-engagement.md) [~W] (seven Grade 10 dyads, qualitative); [VR participants lacked mutual engagement in collaborative role-playing during the teaching simulation](claims/vr-participants-lacked-mutual-engagement-role-playing.md) [-W] (teaching assistants); roles and stop points untested
rows.change: Give each person a role (operator, predictor, recorder, or a part in the role-play) and rotate them; stop the run at set points for the pair to say what they expected, what happened and what they now think; in multiuser VR, script who speaks and when, and check that everyone takes part, because shared presence does not produce joint engagement by itself
rows.if: Learners work in pairs or groups at one simulation, or role-play together in a shared VR scene

rows.basis: untested proposal; the case rests on prior knowledge aiding comprehension ([Prior Knowledge Impacts Text Understanding](claims/prior-knowledge-impacts-text-understanding.md) [+W], a practitioner article's synthesis with no new data), not on any test of VR as the source of that knowledge
rows.change: Keep it short (5–10 minutes), name the three or four things learners should notice, and go straight to the text or lesson that uses them; ask learners afterwards what they saw that the text mentions
rows.if: A simulation or VR "field trip" is used to build background knowledge before reading or a lesson

rows.basis: [Minimal guidance is less effective for novices than explicit instruction](claims/minimal-guidance-less-effective-for-novices.md) [-S]; [Part-task practice reduces cognitive load for absolute novices during initial skill acquisition.](claims/part-task-practice-reduces-load-for-novices.md) [~M]; both carried to sprints from other tasks
rows.change: Do not start with the sprint. Teach the components with worked examples or part-task practice first; run the first sprint on a smaller deliverable, with process criteria and a coach at every checkpoint
rows.if: Learners are `novice` on the component skills

rows.basis: untested proposal; the late-sprint stage of the arc above
rows.change: Let them scope the deliverable and write the criteria; checkpoints become peer reviews; spend coach time on the debrief and on stretching the criteria
rows.if: Learners are `advanced`, or experienced staff

rows.basis: untested proposal; the goal and feedback evidence above is from adults, older students and work tasks
rows.change: Shorter blocks (20–30 minutes), a deliverable finished within one or two lessons, criteria given as a short checklist with pictures or examples, teacher at every checkpoint, explicit roles
rows.if: Learners are `child` or `adolescent`

rows.basis: untested proposal, from the earlier page's sources on workplace sprints (Longmuss & Hohne 2017), which have no claim page here
rows.change: Let them bring the problem and the deliverable (a changed procedure, a tool, a brief to a manager); keep criteria in the workplace's own terms; schedule blocks around shifts; end with the change tried at work and reported at the next sprint
rows.if: Adults in a work setting, on a problem from their own job

rows.basis: [Minimal guidance is less effective for novices than explicit instruction](claims/minimal-guidance-less-effective-for-novices.md) [-S]; see [Problem-based Learning](principles/problem-based-learning.md) for problem-first designs
rows.change: Teach it before the sprint, or use the sprint only as the application after instruction; check understanding unaided after the debrief, not only by the product
rows.if: The goal is a `concept` or `principle` learners have not met yet

rows.basis: untested proposal; the debrief's place rests on [Reflective Practice Improves Outcomes When Structured](claims/reflective-practice-improves-outcomes-when-structured.md) [+M]
rows.change: One deliverable, revised once: kickoff and criteria 10 min, build 30 min, checkpoint 10 min, revise 20 min, test 5 min, debrief 15 min (90 in all); shrink the deliverable before cutting the checkpoint or debrief
rows.if: Only one session, with a fixed short time budget (e.g. 90 minutes)

rows.basis: untested proposal; contingent support evidence is mostly one-to-one ([Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support.](claims/contingent-scaffolding-improves-learning.md) [~M])
rows.change: Stagger checkpoints so the coach sees each team for 5 minutes per checkpoint; between visits, teams score their work against a written criteria checklist and swap with one peer team; the coach leads one whole-group debrief
rows.if: One coach or teacher for many teams, or scarce facilitator time (volunteers, a busy shift)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Put the deliverable, criteria and checkpoint notes in one shared document everyone can edit or comment on from a phone; give remote members a named part; at checkpoints the remote member presents first; keep camera-off options for the debrief
rows.if: Mixed modes: some learners remote, some in the room, or some on phones only

rows.basis: untested proposal; the written reflection step rests on [Reflective Practice Improves Outcomes When Structured](claims/reflective-practice-improves-outcomes-when-structured.md) [+M]
rows.change: Split the sprint over days with a fixed deadline per block; checkpoints are a self-check against the criteria plus one asynchronous peer review; the debrief is a structured written reflection (what happened, one decision and why, one change)
rows.if: Online and self-paced, no live coach

rows.basis: untested proposal; the last point draws on [Feedback Most Effective At Task And Process Levels](claims/feedback-most-effective-at-task-and-process-levels.md) [+S]
rows.change: Smaller deliverable, criteria shown with examples rather than text, roles chosen so each learner starts with a part they can do, debrief spoken rather than written, feedback on the work and method only
rows.if: Learners have low confidence or low literacy

rows.basis: untested proposal; see [Authentic Audiences and Purposes](principles/authentic-audiences-purposes.md)
rows.change: Keep a test with that user at the end; separate the version the audience sees from the learners' notes and reasoning, which stay in the debrief; criteria come from what the user needs
rows.if: The product goes to a real audience or user (a client, a manager, the public)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Learners decide what goes into the shared deliverable and who sees it; use anonymised or invented cases at checkpoints if a team prefers; the debrief discusses decisions, not the private content
rows.if: The work uses private or sensitive material (client records, staff problems, learners' own situations)

rows.basis: untested proposal; the three changes rest on the claims in steps 2, 4 and 6
rows.change: Keep it. Run it as given, and change only what the evidence above bears on: criteria written before work starts, one review-and-revise checkpoint, and an unhurried debrief that ends with a named change
rows.if: The brief names its own routine (a stand-up, a retrospective template, a rubric, a design-sprint schedule)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use them as the sprint's criteria; do not substitute these. If the rubric rewards use of a tool, keep that criterion and add one unaided check beside it
rows.if: The brief gives its own categories, criteria or rubric

rows.basis: [A training-design argument, not tested by any study recorded here, holds that practising whole complex tasks improves transfer of complex skills](claims/whole-task-performance-improves-transfer.md) [~M] (argument only)
rows.change: Keep it whole in the sprint; put any practice of a weak part in a short side-block and return to the whole
rows.if: The brief wants a whole-task performance kept whole (a full presentation, a full repair, a whole product)

rows.basis: [Forced pacing eliminates positive transfer from computer aiding and leads subjects to use strategies requiring many more tests than necessary](claims/forced-pacing-eliminates-aiding-transfer.md) [-M] (twelve subjects, fault diagnosis); [Letting learners pace instruction helped on complex material in one experiment, while learner control in general showed almost no effect across 18 studies](claims/learner-paced-beats-system-paced-complex-material.md) [~M]
rows.change: Keep the forced pace in later sprints only, once the task is learned unhurried, and always follow a paced run with an unpaced debrief
rows.if: Time pressure itself is part of the target (incident response, live service)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Judge each learner on an individual unaided task after the sprint, not on the team's deliverable; keep the sprint for practice
rows.if: Stakes are high, or the assessment is individual and unaided

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use it at the first kickoff as a compared case: show a past deliverable with that error beside one without it, and turn the difference into a criterion
rows.if: The brief reports an error learners actually made (shipped without testing, one member did everything)

rows.basis: [Group rewards combined with individual accountability](claims/cooperative-learning-group-rewards-and-individual-accountability.md) [+M] (64 at-risk 4th and 5th graders, maths computation; reward plus structure best; effect figures second-hand)
rows.change: Use pairs with scripted tutor and tutee roles, switching each session; team score = sum of both members' daily individual quiz scores
rows.if: Learners are `child` (upper primary), or at risk of failure

rows.basis: [Cooperative learning improves achievement](claims/cooperative-learning-improves-achievement.md) [+S] (meta-analysis of 148 studies of early adolescents, direction only; Learning Together method d = 0.70–0.91 from an unpublished report)
rows.change: Use cooperative goal structures as the default arrangement for multi-week units, with individual checks feeding a team score
rows.if: Learners are `adolescent` (early secondary)

rows.basis: [Small group learning improves STEM achievement](claims/small-group-learning-improves-stem-achievement.md) [+M] (39 undergraduate STEM studies, d = 0.51; compared groups with non-group instruction and does not isolate interdependence)
rows.change: Use small structured groups for problem sets, labs and design tasks, with individual assessment kept separate from the group product
rows.if: Learners are `adult` / `postsecondary`, in a live course

rows.basis: [Interdependence type did not affect posttest achievement](claims/interdependence-type-no-achievement-effect-asynchronous.md) [~M] (280 undergraduate business majors, triads; non-significant, no effect size); [more interactions went with higher posttest scores](claims/interaction-quantity-correlates-posttest-online-groups.md) [+W] (same study, correlational)
rows.change: Do not rely on assigned roles or a group reward to raise achievement; require each member to post a stated number of contributions that respond to others', and assess individually
rows.if: Setting is `online-self-paced` or asynchronous online groups

rows.basis: [Structured interdependence and obligation to contribute](claims/structured-interdependence-contribution-obligation-attitude.md) [+M]; [reward interdependence and benefit attitudes](claims/reward-interdependence-benefit-attitudes.md) [+M] (self-report, same online study; not achievement)
rows.change: Assign roles or a group reward: members in any structured condition agreed more that teammates' duty to contribute helped them learn; reward groups agreed more that they gained from others
rows.if: The aim includes participation, sense of obligation or attitudes to group work

rows.basis: untested proposal; improvement-based scoring from the Discussion of [group rewards combined with individual accountability](claims/cooperative-learning-group-rewards-and-individual-accountability.md) [~M], not from its entries
rows.change: Teach and model the content first; use interdependence for practice and explanation, not first acquisition; set improvement-based team scores so low starters can contribute
rows.if: Learners are `novice` on the content, or members differ widely in what they know

rows.basis: untested; the reward evidence comes from programmes of four weeks or more ([free-riding without accountability](claims/cooperative-learning-group-rewards-and-individual-accountability.md) [~M])
rows.change: Use pairs, one short shared task, and an individual check at the end; do not claim an achievement effect
rows.if: Time is one session only

rows.basis: [Pairs worked better than triads in one inquiry](claims/pairs-better-than-triads-in-stellar-inquiry.md) [~W] (authors' teaching experience, one astronomy activity, no measured outcome)
rows.change: Prefer pairs for tightly coupled tasks and three or four for tasks needing several skills; watch for a member drifting out in larger groups
rows.if: Group size is open

rows.basis: [Secondary-school review: STAD most and Jigsaw least successful](claims/secondary-cooperative-learning-newmann-thompson.md) [~M] (review of 27 secondary studies; the link to missing reward and accountability is the authors' speculation)
rows.change: Add an individual quiz on all segments and a team score from it, so experts are rewarded for teaching, not only for presenting
rows.if: The structure is Jigsaw or another resource-only design

rows.basis: [Free-riding without individual accountability](claims/cooperative-learning-group-rewards-and-individual-accountability.md) [~M] (school studies; carried to high-stakes settings untested)
rows.change: Never give every member the same grade for one product; grade the group from individual results, or grade individually and report the group product separately
rows.if: Stakes are high (the group grade counts toward a qualification)

rows.basis: [Social interdependence, not role interdependence, correlated with performance](claims/social-interdependence-predicts-performance.md) [~W] (40 brokerage offices, correlational; "social interdependence" there means team belonging, not goal structure)
rows.change: Build belonging and shared goals (harmony, a sense of one team) rather than formal role dependence alone; measure what each member can do
rows.if: Learners are `adult-workplace` teams

rows.basis: [High affiliation motive and attitudes to group work](claims/high-affiliation-motive-favorable-group-attitudes.md) [~M] (attitudes differed, achievement did not; online undergraduates); culture untested, from the earlier page
rows.change: Explain how the team score works and why, before the first cycle; let them see that their own score is counted in it; expect less favourable attitudes at first, not lower achievement
rows.if: Some learners expect individual, competitive evaluation, or are low in affiliation motive

rows.basis: [Online community required deliberate, planned effort](claims/online-community-requires-conscious-effort.md) [+W] (interviews with web-based high-school teachers; carried to adult courses); the steps are untested
rows.change: Run the full default: course-tied introductions with two named replies, weekly named announcements, small stable groups, a reply frame, one optional live meeting a fortnight at a time outside working hours, recorded
rows.if: `online-instructor-led`, asynchronous, text-only, `adult` learners who work or care for others

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Put remote and in-room learners in the same small groups, with a shared text chat for each group; in plenary, take a remote contribution after each in-room one; ask in-room learners to introduce themselves in the same shared space as remote ones, so the remote learners see who is in the room
rows.if: Mixed mode: some learners in the room, some joining remotely

rows.basis: [Microblogging and mobile blogging promote target-language interaction and a sense of community](claims/microblogging-promotes-interaction-community-language-learners.md) [+W] (a review's second-hand reports of three small language-learning studies, no comparisons; carried to other subjects); the rest untested
rows.change: Make every presence activity possible by text or a short voice note; never require video or a photo; keep live meetings to audio with chat; a short-post channel the group already uses on phones (a group blog or microblog) can carry introductions and replies
rows.if: Learners work on phones only, or have poor bandwidth

rows.basis: untested proposal; the earlier page says benefits shrink at large enrolment. Structuring roles or rewards in online triads did not change achievement in one experiment ([Structuring positive interdependence did not affect posttest achievement](claims/interdependence-type-no-achievement-effect-asynchronous.md) [~M]; undergraduates, a non-significant difference, not equivalence)
rows.change: Do not promise personal replies to all; make presence a property of small groups (4–6, kept for several weeks, with rotating roles) and of a weekly whole-course message that quotes or names a few contributions; let peers answer peers first
rows.if: One instructor for many learners (a large online course, a MOOC)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Spend it on three things only: a templated but personal welcome, one weekly message naming a few contributions, and one private message to anyone silent after week 2 (about 30–45 minutes a week for 20 learners); hand reply-giving to peer roles; skip live meetings rather than run them badly
rows.if: Scarce facilitator time (a volunteer tutor, a teacher on a busy shift, one brief check-in a week)

rows.basis: untested proposal; the earlier page says benefits shrink in short settings
rows.change: Replace profiles with a 3–5-minute paired introduction that asks each person what they want from the session and one related experience, then use those answers in the session's first task
rows.if: A single session only (a workshop, a one-off training)

rows.basis: [Positive teacher–student relationships are associated with greater student engagement and, more weakly, with achievement](claims/teacher-student-relationships-improve-engagement.md) [+M] (correlational meta-analyses, preschool to high school, plus a learner-centred synthesis; not a test of any routine)
rows.change: Presence cues are already there; spend effort on names, on the teacher's warmth and expectations, and on routines that let quiet pupils be heard (pairs before plenary), not on profiles
rows.if: Face-to-face `classroom`

rows.basis: [Teacher–student relationships](claims/teacher-student-relationships-improve-engagement.md) [+M] (associations; negative relationships mattered more in primary school); the routines are untested
rows.change: No public photos or personal profiles; introductions through a class activity the teacher runs (what I like, what I am good at); presence comes mainly from the teacher's relationship with each pupil, built in short regular contacts
rows.if: Learners are `child` or `adolescent`

rows.basis: [Belonging Interventions Improve Outcomes](claims/belonging-interventions-improve-outcomes.md) [~M] (college entrants, randomised; worked only where the setting afforded opportunities to belong); [peer contact judged needed against isolation in online supervision](claims/virtual-communities-counter-supervision-isolation.md) [+W] (one design case); [SPICE learners report that the virtual Center reduced their rural isolation](claims/spice-learners-report-reduced-isolation.md) [+W] (adult family-literacy learners' testimonials in one case study, no comparison)
rows.change: Offer a private, low-risk first contact (small group only, audio, a short call); say early that difficulty and doubt are common and pass; follow up by name after a quiet week; make sure there are real chances to be part of the group, not only a message; for learners studying alone at home far from others (rural adult education), give them a shared online space where they meet the same peers regularly
rows.if: Learners with low confidence or literacy, first in family, or at risk of isolation or dropping out

rows.basis: [Peer monitoring among MBA learners goes beyond CoI social presence by involving professionally relevant evaluation of peers' contributions](claims/peer-monitoring-exceeds-social-presence.md) [~W] (interviews with six MBA students)
rows.change: Make introductions professional: role, expertise, a problem from their work they want help with; group learners so their expertise complements; let them judge peers by what they offer, and build peer review of work on that
rows.if: Adults in work settings or professional programmes (an MBA, clinical or workplace training)

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page's constraint that forced self-disclosure can reduce trust across cultural contexts
rows.change: The learner controls what is shared and who sees it: disclosure optional at every step, a professional-only introduction always acceptable, small-group rather than whole-course spaces for anything personal, and no grade for personal disclosure
rows.if: Private or sensitive material, or norms that discourage self-disclosure (cultural, professional, a history of harm)

rows.basis: [Discussion boards produced no corrective feedback](claims/discussion-board-no-negative-feedback-synchrony-required.md) [-W] (one study of second-language learners); [Audio discussions produced no significant change in willingness to communicate](claims/audio-discussions-no-significant-wtc-change.md) [~W] (36 language students, self-report; non-significant, not equivalence)
rows.change: Use a synchronous channel (text chat or video) where correction and negotiation are wanted, and the forum for prepared posts; offer voice notes as an introduction mode
rows.if: Learners study in a second language, or the goal includes spoken interaction

rows.basis: [Anonymous real-time sharing of student responses mitigates evaluation apprehension (authors' account)](claims/anonymity-mitigates-evaluation-apprehension.md) [~W] (an undergraduate physics course; the authors' argument, not tested; anonymity trades against being seen as a person, so it is a way in, not the end state); the rest untested
rows.change: Have them post first in their small group or as a draft that peers comment on before the whole class sees it; the instructor replies to the attempt, not only to the correct posts; in live sessions, collect answers anonymously to the group while the instructor can still see who wrote each, then move to named discussion once errors have been seen to be safe
rows.if: `novice` learners on the content, afraid of being wrong in public

rows.basis: [Peer monitoring](claims/peer-monitoring-exceeds-social-presence.md) [~W] (MBA interviews); otherwise untested
rows.change: Shorten the social opening; move quickly to peer critique of each other's work and decisions; presence comes from the value of what peers offer
rows.if: `advanced` learners or experienced professionals

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep it; change only what the evidence points to: make disclosure optional, add one step that asks for a named reply to a peer, and tie its output to the next task
rows.if: The brief names its own routine for presence (its introduction activity, a weekly check-in, a discussion template or rubric)

rows.basis: untested; interaction counts are associated with posttest scores ([interaction quantity](claims/interaction-quantity-correlates-posttest-online-groups.md) [+W]), which is not a reason to reward volume
rows.change: Use those criteria to judge and give feedback on posts; do not add a separate score for social presence, and do not grade posts by count
rows.if: The brief sets its own criteria or rubric for discussion quality

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Fit it: week 1, 10 minutes for introductions and two replies; later weeks, 5 minutes for one named reply in the small group and 5 for reading the instructor's weekly message; one live meeting a month only if time allows
rows.if: A fixed short time budget for community work (say 10 minutes a week)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Build presence inside the project: a kickoff meeting where members introduce what they bring, agreed roles, and regular short live check-ins; do not split the project into individual posting quotas
rows.if: The course ends in a group product or performance for a real audience, or a whole-task project the brief wants kept whole

rows.basis: [Human embodiment in video](claims/human-embodiment-video-presence-effects.md) [~M] (second-hand review; perceived learning higher with the instructor's face, performance not different); [Guo et al. found engagement depends on video production style](claims/guo-video-style-engagement-findings.md) [~W] (a review's report of one large study of edX science and engineering videos; engagement and preference, not learning)
rows.change: Put effort into replies, weekly named messages and live contact rather than into the instructor's face in every content video; where a face is cheap, a small talking head beside slides in short videos is enough
rows.if: The course is pre-recorded video and the budget goes on production

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Grade the substance of contributions against stated criteria, never personal disclosure or post counts; keep social spaces ungraded
rows.if: High stakes for the learner, or participation is graded

rows.basis: [Spaced practice improves retention](claims/spaced-practice-improves-retention.md) [+S]; [Spaced repetition improves retention](claims/spaced-practice-improves-retention.md) [+M]; [Spaced sessions improve final-test performance](claims/spacing-improves-final-test-performance.md) [+M]; [Relearning-to-criterion designs confound spacing with practice amount](claims/relearning-confound-distributed-practice-designs.md) [~W]
rows.change: Split the same total study time into several sessions on different days instead of one block; when comparing schedules, hold total practice constant (a fixed number of review trials, not relearning to a criterion)
rows.if: The goal is retention of facts, terms, vocabulary or procedures over weeks or a course

rows.basis: [Preschoolers showed no spacing effect in free recall](claims/preschoolers-no-spacing-effect-free-recall.md) [~M]; [First-graders showed the spacing effect](claims/first-graders-spacing-effect-free-recall.md) [+M]; [Grade and spacing interacted in children's recall](claims/grade-by-spacing-interaction-free-recall.md) [~M]
rows.change: Rely on repetition itself and do not expect spreading the repetitions within a session to add to it; from about age six (first grade) the spacing benefit appeared under the same procedure. Untested at day-scale gaps for this age in the wiki, so if a programme for young children spaces sessions across days, check recall at a delay before claiming a spacing gain
rows.if: The learners are preschool children (about age 4)

rows.basis: [The optimal gap grows with the retention interval](claims/optimal-isi-increases-with-retention-interval.md) [+M]; [Eight-day review beat one-day review](claims/eight-day-review-improves-five-week-science-test-versus-one-day-review.md) [+M]; [Short spacing won at a short test, long spacing at a long one](claims/proportionality-rule-long-spacing-weeks.md) [~M]
rows.change: Lengthen the gap between study and review as the delay grows; in one classroom simulation a review eight days after the lecture beat one after a day on a test five weeks later. Do not treat any single gap as universal
rows.if: The test or use that matters is weeks or months away

rows.basis: [The spacing benefit holds at very short retention intervals](claims/spacing-benefit-short-retention-no-peterson-paradox.md) [+M]; [Short spacing won at a short test, long spacing at a long one](claims/proportionality-rule-long-spacing-weeks.md) [~M]
rows.change: Short within-day gaps still beat massing, but expect a smaller gain; do not use week-long gaps for a test that close, since in one word-list experiment they lost to same-day repetition on an immediate test while winning a week later. Add a later check if retention beyond the test matters
rows.if: The test is the same day or the next morning

rows.basis: [One review argues spreading over years can be worse than over months](claims/distributed-practice-limits-l2.md) [~W]; [Spaced listening outperformed comparison ESL students](claims/svas-spaced-listening-outperforms-comparison-end-of-experiment.md) [+W]
rows.change: Revisit each item on a schedule matched to when it will next be used; do not stretch gaps to many months just because the calendar allows it. Monthly repetition of target vocabulary through short audio lessons is one tested arrangement, in a small quasi-experiment
rows.if: The programme runs a year or more (a language course, a certificate)

rows.basis: [Spaced retrieval improves retention](claims/spaced-retrieval-improves-retention.md) [+M]; [Spaced beat massed retrieval and no practice on financial knowledge](claims/spaced-beats-massed-and-control-financial-knowledge.md) [+M]; [Retrieval practice improves long-term retention](claims/retrieval-practice-improves-retention.md) [+S]
rows.change: Make the spaced sessions retrieval with feedback, not rereading. The first two links compare spaced with massed retrieval, so they show spacing matters within retrieval; recall over rereading rests on the testing-effect evidence
rows.if: Each return to the material can be a quiz or recall prompt

rows.basis: [Total spacing mattered, relative schedule did not](claims/total-retrieval-spacing-beats-massed-but-relative-schedule-not-distinguished.md) [~M]; [Expanding and uniform schedules do not differ](claims/expanding-versus-uniform-retrieval-no-difference.md) [~M]; [Spacing out retrieval practice beats massing it](claims/spaced-retrieval-outperforms-restudy.md) [~M]; [Expanding gaps led in an earlier synthesis, tentatively](claims/expanding-isis-better-than-fixed-tentative.md) [~W]; [Expanding was no better than fixed in one experiment](claims/expanding-not-better-than-fixed-interval.md) [~W]
rows.change: Use equal gaps if they are simpler to run; at matched total spacing, expanding schedules have not reliably beaten equal ones. Spend the design effort on total spacing. An earlier synthesis found expanding gaps ahead overall but called it tentative given wide variation between studies; the later meta-analysis and a 1-5-9 against 5-5-5 experiment found no advantage. The [pattern's expanding-intervals row](patterns/spaced-learning.md#fitting-the-design-to-a-situation) says when expanding might still be worth trying
rows.if: The brief asks for expanding intervals (1, 3, 7 days…)

rows.basis: [Spaced retrieval after a financial workshop improved retention at five months](claims/spaced-beats-massed-and-control-financial-knowledge.md) [+M]; [Spaced beat massed retrieval and no practice](claims/spaced-beats-massed-and-control-financial-knowledge.md) [+M]
rows.change: Add at least one later review: short spaced quizzes after the session, spread over days and weeks rather than given together. A credit workshop followed by spaced quizzes retained more at about five months than massed quizzes or none, and massed quizzes did not differ detectably from none
rows.if: A single workshop or one-off session

rows.basis: [Weekly spaced recall quizzes improved six-month retention](claims/spaced-recall-quizzes-improve-long-term-retention-fundamental-math-concepts.md) [+M]; [Spaced recall raised the post-test without harming new learning](claims/spaced-recall-improves-posttest-without-harming-new-learning.md) [+M]; [Spaced recall quizzes helped without immediate feedback](claims/testing-effect-persists-without-immediate-feedback.md) [+W]; [The benefit held across instructor experience](claims/spaced-recall-effective-regardless-instructor-experience.md) [+W]; [The benefit held across class hours](claims/spaced-recall-effective-regardless-class-hour.md) [+W]
rows.change: Replace part of the quizzing on current material with a short weekly recall quiz cycling through earlier fundamental concepts; feedback released later the same day was enough. The [pattern's taught-course row](patterns/spaced-learning.md#fitting-the-design-to-a-situation) gives the cycle and the trial's numbers. The current-material exam did not differ detectably and the benefit did not vary detectably with instructor experience or class hour (non-significant tests, not shown sameness)
rows.if: A taught course that keeps moving to new topics (mathematics, a cumulative curriculum) with no spare class time

rows.basis: [Learners misjudge spacing benefits](claims/learners-misjudge-spacing-benefits.md) [~M]; [Learners judged massed items more memorable though recall was worse](claims/judgments-overconfidence-massed-items.md) [~M]; [Learners underuse spacing and retrieval practice](claims/learners-underuse-effective-learning-strategies.md) [+W]
rows.change: Schedule the review sessions in the course (dated releases, reminders); left alone, learners mass their study and judge massing to work better. In one flashcard study spacing beat massing for 90% of participants, yet 72% judged massing more effective after their first session; in a free-recall experiment learners rated massed items as more memorable while recalling them worse
rows.if: Learners study on their own (`online-self-paced`, revision before exams)

rows.basis: [Retention diverged by centre](claims/podcast-retention-divergence-massed-vs-distributed.md) [~W]
rows.change: Encourage listening spread over the weeks before the assessment rather than in a burst, and check recall at a delay, not only right after. Untested as a manipulation: the one study is a centre comparison of naturally occurring use
rows.if: Learners revise from audio or other material they consume when they choose (podcasts, recorded lectures)

rows.basis: [Structured CAI with spaced practice and review beat unstructured CAI](claims/structured-cai-spacing-improves-recall-and-retention.md) [+W]; [Structured CAI learners held their recall to the retention test](claims/structured-cai-maintains-memory-recall-to-retention.md) [+W]
rows.change: Build spaced practice and spaced review into the programme's structure rather than leaving the sequence open; the tested version changed structure and spacing together; within groups, the structured version showed no significant drop from recall to retention while the unstructured one did (equivalence not tested, no effect size printed, a dissertation)
rows.if: The course is delivered by software that can schedule practice (computer-assisted instruction, an app)

rows.basis: [Too many new items left items stuck in the first deck](claims/excess-new-item-rate-leaves-items-stuck-in-first-leitner-deck.md) [~M]; [New-item rate beyond a threshold causes a phase transition in learning rate](claims/leitner-queue-network-phase-transition-in-learning-rate.md) [~M]; [The optimal schedule reviews lower decks more often](claims/optimal-leitner-schedule-reviews-lower-decks-more-often.md) [+W]; [Learning rate shows increasing returns to review budget, in the model](claims/leitner-learning-rate-shows-increasing-returns-to-review-budget.md) [~W]
rows.change: Cap how fast new items enter: past an optimum rate, fewer items were mastered and more stayed stuck in the first deck. Give the lower decks (new and recently missed items) more of the review time than the higher ones. Both the rate's threshold and the deck allocation come from one queueing model and one crowd-worker vocabulary experiment; the allocation and the budget result are model output only, so tune the rate locally by watching how many items pile up in the first deck
rows.if: The software runs a flashcard or review queue (Leitner boxes, a spaced-repetition app)

rows.basis: [Spaced retrieval wins at the final test despite lower initial recall](claims/spaced-retrieval-outperforms-massed-retrieval-despite-lower-initial-recall.md) [+M]
rows.change: Keep the gaps; judge the schedule on a delayed test, not on practice accuracy
rows.if: Practice scores drop when sessions are spread out

rows.basis: [Eight-day review beat one-day review](claims/eight-day-review-improves-five-week-science-test-versus-one-day-review.md) [+M]; [The spaced benefit reflects transfer, not item memorisation](claims/spaced-practice-benefit-reflects-transfer-not-item-memorization.md) [+W]
rows.change: Use new or rephrased questions on the same concepts in the reviews; the classroom spacing gain extended to rephrased application questions, less firmly than to facts
rows.if: The goal is application or understanding, not only recall of the items

rows.basis: [Spaced repetition improves retention](claims/spaced-practice-improves-retention.md) [~M]
rows.change: Still space practice, but expect a smaller benefit than for verbal material
rows.if: The skill is a complex task or a motor skill rather than verbal recall

rows.basis: [SAT underpredicts girls' performance](claims/sat-underpredicts-girls-performance.md) [~W]; [National Merit awards skew male](claims/psat-national-merit-awards-skew-male.md) [~W] (both 1987 testimony, second-hand); the directions by group are the earlier page's (Young 2004)
rows.change: Add a second piece of evidence (grades, a work sample) for every applicant within a band of the cut; run a differential-prediction check once first-year outcomes are in, and do not assume which direction any gap runs
rows.if: The score gates admission or a scholarship with a single cut-off

rows.basis: [Culturally and linguistically diverse students under-identified nationwide](claims/gifted-underrepresentation-diverse-students.md) [~W] and [teachers under-refer them](claims/teacher-underreferral-diverse-gifted.md) [~W] (one issue brief); [a narrative review attributes under-representation to biased measures](claims/culturally-diverse-underrepresentation-biased-measures.md) [~W] (second-hand, Ford 2003); [traditional identification tests omit classroom-learning components](claims/traditional-identification-tests-fail-learning-potential.md) [~W] (argument). None tests universal screening or multiple measures
rows.change: Screen every learner rather than relying on teacher referral; use more than one measure, including a performance or classroom-learning measure; compare each group's identification rate with its share of enrolment every year
rows.if: The decision is gifted or enrichment identification

rows.basis: Untested in the wiki (stereotype threat has no claim page); affirmation: [raised grades in two small trials, null in a large replication](claims/self-affirmation-improves-outcomes.md) [~M] (seventh graders, term grades, not test scores)
rows.change: Move demographic questions to after the test; describe the test by its use, not as a measure of ability; consider a values-affirmation exercise only as a measured trial
rows.if: Learners belong to a group negatively stereotyped in the tested domain (women in mathematics; Black or Latino students in academic tests) and the sitting is high-stakes

rows.basis: [Math anxiety degrades performance](claims/math-anxiety-degrades-performance.md) [~M] (meta-analysis of correlations; does not test these moves); [higher anxiety goes with smaller testing effects](claims/higher-anxiety-is-associated-with-smaller-testing-effects.md) [~M] (retrieval practice, review chapter)
rows.change: Two or three untimed, then timed, practice sittings in the real format with feedback; ask the test owner whether extended time is allowed; read a single timed high-stakes score with caution
rows.if: Learners are anxious about tests, or the test is timed and speed is not the construct

rows.basis: [Verbal tests may underestimate subject knowledge](claims/verbal-achievement-tests-may-underestimate-via-symbolic-mismatch.md) [~W] (argument); [minority-testing research has rarely examined alternative symbolic forms](claims/minority-testing-research-neglects-alternative-symbolic-forms.md) [~W] (a 1986 review noting the gap)
rows.change: Use the accommodations the test allows (glossaries, read-aloud for non-reading tests, extra time); do not read a low score as low subject knowledge without a second, low-language measure; for items you write, keep reading load below the construct
rows.if: Learners are taking the test in a second language, or have low literacy

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Do not use one sitting for a placement; observe over several occasions; use pictures and spoken instructions; re-screen within the year
rows.if: Learners are young children (`child`) taking a screening or readiness test

rows.basis: [ICC and LDF methods flag different items](claims/icc-and-ldf-methods-identify-different-dif-items.md) [~M]; [item purification flags more items](claims/item-purification-increases-dif-detection-sensitivity.md) [~M]; [NC-DIF chi-square over-sensitive at large n](claims/nc-dif-chi-square-overly-sensitive-large-samples.md) [~M] (simulation, attributed to Fleer 1993); [male-oriented item content](claims/male-oriented-item-content-biases-test-scores.md) [~W]
rows.change: Content review by reviewers from varied backgrounds, then DIF with at least two methods on large samples; every flagged item gets a content review before it is dropped; record which method flagged it
rows.if: You write or own the items (a district, an awarding body, an assessment product)

rows.basis: untested proposal; DIF Type I error rates rose with more and larger DIF items in simulation ([DIF Type I error increases with DIF items and magnitude](claims/dif-type-i-error-increases-with-dif-items-and-magnitude.md) [~M]), so small or contaminated samples give unstable flags
rows.change: Skip DIF and regression statistics for now; rely on content review and on second evidence near the cut; pool several years before running them
rows.if: Groups are small (a single school or programme, under about 100 per group)

rows.basis: [Later-positioned item more difficult](claims/later-position-item-more-difficult-fatigue-effect.md) [~M]; [DIF items differently positioned across booklets](claims/dif-items-differently-positioned-across-booklets.md) [~M] (one national examination)
rows.change: Keep item positions fixed across forms, or check each item's difficulty by position before comparing groups who took different forms
rows.if: Several forms or booklets are used

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Give the same items, time and aids, or record the difference beside each score; avoid long passages and wide tables on phones; compare score distributions by mode before pooling, and check that mode is not standing in for a group (rural, low-income)
rows.if: The test is taken in mixed modes: some in a centre, some remote, some on phones only

rows.basis: untested proposal; the prediction check (step 3) applied to a job criterion
rows.change: Check that the items sample the job's tasks, not general reading or cultural knowledge; validate the score against observed job performance by group; add a work-sample task for candidates near the cut
rows.if: Adults in work settings: a licensing, promotion or job-entry test

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use one full practice sitting under real conditions, self-marked against an answer key with worked reasons, and spend the scarce contact time only on the three items most learners missed; move demographic forms after the test, which needs no time
rows.if: One teacher or tutor prepares many learners, or facilitator time is scarce (volunteers, a short weekly session)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use it for one timed practice in the real format with immediate feedback and a walk-through of the instructions; do not add new content
rows.if: Only a single session is available before the real test

rows.basis: untested; the three changes follow the three mechanisms above
rows.change: Keep it; change only what the evidence here says matters: no single-score cut without a second look near it, demographics after the test, and a by-group check of who is selected and how they later do
rows.if: The brief names its own routine (its own admissions rubric, test-prep programme, identification checklist)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Report by group with the number of test-takers and the uncertainty; do not compare groups on a score whose prediction has not been checked for them; link the use to [High-Stakes Testing and Accountability Effects](principles/summative-assessment.md)
rows.if: Results are reported publicly or drive accountability (school league tables, programme funding)

rows.basis: [Teacher expectation bias predicted Dutch secondary students' performance up to five years later, after controls for prior achievement, IQ and motivation, in one large correlational cohort study](claims/teacher-expectation-effects-on-achievement.md) [+M] (correlational, Dutch secondary cohort; not a test of intervening on expectations); [Teachers underrefer culturally and linguistically diverse students for gifted identification](claims/teacher-underreferral-diverse-gifted.md) [+W] (a brief summarising referral research)
rows.change: Collect strengths from a new low-stakes task in several response modes before reading the file; write barriers and supports beside them; set at least one task above the level the label implies
rows.if: Learners have been labeled (disability, special educational needs, "low ability" set) or have a record of failure

rows.basis: [Assessment tasks built on family-identified funds of knowledge elicited computational thinking from K-2 children in a small design-based study that made no comparison with standard assessment](claims/funds-of-knowledge-tasks-reveal-computational-thinking.md) [+M] (K-2, 13 children, no comparison); [Praise for intelligence, rather than for effort, after success undermines children's motivation and performance after a later failure](claims/feedback-praise-reduces-learning.md) [-S] (fifth graders, intelligence praise)
rows.change: Collect strengths through families and play-based tasks built from home practices; name strengths aloud as what the child did, never as "smart"; keep the self-record oral or pictorial
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary age)

rows.basis: Adults: untested proposal. Feedback channel: [The effect of social persuasion on student teacher efficacy depends on its form](claims/social-persuasion-form-moderates-efficacy-effect.md) [~M] (student teachers, reported in a review: verbal feedback from the cooperating teacher related to efficacy; a structured rating tool was detrimental against a control)
rows.change: Ask what they already do at work that the course builds on, and use those tasks as entry points; feedback comes from the supervisor or mentor in person, naming a specific performance, rather than through a rating form
rows.if: Learners are `adult` in work settings (trainees, career changers, professionals)

rows.basis: [Proximal goals and ability attributional feedback for early learning raise self-efficacy more than distant goals and effort feedback, by a review's report of earlier studies](claims/proximal-goals-feedback-peer-models-build-learning-efficacy.md) [+M] (review of experiments, second-hand); [Learners' task-specific self-efficacy beliefs predict…](claims/self-efficacy-predicts-academic-persistence.md) [+M] (narrative reviews)
rows.change: Shorten the first tasks so success comes early and is genuine; credit early success to the learner's own skill and strategy; set close-at-hand goals; never give praise that the learner can see is unearned
rows.if: Learners have low confidence after repeated failure in this subject

rows.basis: untested proposal; from the earlier page (multilingual learners, interrupted education)
rows.change: Let learners show a strength in their home language, by demonstration or drawing; record it; teach the academic register explicitly as the next target, not as the measure of the strength
rows.if: Learners are multilingual or have low literacy in the language of instruction

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Replace individual conferences with a written two-line strengths-and-next-target comment on one piece of work per learner per fortnight, and a learner self-record checked at the same time; use the low-stakes task in step 1 for everyone in the first week
rows.if: `classroom` with one teacher and a large group

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Build the strengths record into the platform: a short self-report on what has worked, and feedback that names the specific item the learner got right and the next item it unlocks; keep each entry to a few lines
rows.if: Setting is `online-self-paced`, or learners work on phones only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Collect strengths from submitted work and the chat as well as from talk in the room, so remote learners are not judged only by what the teacher hears; hold the strengths conference one-to-one by call
rows.if: Some learners join remotely while others are in the room

rows.basis: [Growth-mindset interventions have weak average effects on achievement, including a negligible GPA gain (d = 0.11) for lower-achieving US ninth-graders in one preregistered national trial](claims/growth-mindset-improves-achievement.md) [~S] (a brief online intervention moved ninth graders' GPA by a negligible amount; meta-analyses weak overall); carried from mindset messages to strengths framing
rows.change: Give one low-stakes task, then one piece of specific feedback naming what worked and a next target; do not run a mindset or encouragement talk in place of it, and claim nothing about lasting change
rows.if: Time is one session only

rows.basis: untested proposal; [Teachers underrefer culturally and linguistically diverse students for gifted identification](claims/teacher-underreferral-diverse-gifted.md) [+W] for the referral check
rows.change: Judge readiness on the standard task, not on the familiar-form task; record both; for referral or placement, use step 1's evidence to check that learners are not left out because of how they show competence
rows.if: Stakes are high (certification, placement, gifted referral)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Assign production roles from recorded strengths for the first product, rotate them for the next; name to each learner which part of the finished product shows their strength
rows.if: Learners produce work for a real audience (a performance, a product, a client)

rows.basis: [A brief values-affirmation writing exercise raised African American seventh-graders' grades in two small field experiments, but a large same-district replication found no effect](claims/self-affirmation-improves-outcomes.md) [~S]; [Growth-mindset interventions have weak average effects on achievement, including a negligible GPA gain (d = 0.11) for lower-achieving US ninth-graders in one preregistered national trial](claims/growth-mindset-improves-achievement.md) [~S]
rows.change: Keep it, if at all, as a small complement placed before a high-stakes moment; put the design effort into feedback, task entry points and support
rows.if: A brief belief exercise (values affirmation, mindset lesson) is proposed as the strengths component

rows.basis: [Specific, difficult goals lead to higher performance than easy or vague "do your best" goals.](claims/specific-difficult-goals-lead-to-higher-performance.md) [~M] (one narrative review, adult task performance; carried to classrooms)
rows.change: Little framing is needed: name strengths briefly and spend the time on harder, specific goals
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` on the task, or already confident

rows.basis: [Classroom quizzing delivered by clickers, computer software, or paper improves student performance on classroom exams in middle school and college courses](claims/classroom-quizzing-improves-exam-performance-across-grades-and-content.md) [+M] for quizzing during the course; the practice run itself is untested
rows.change: Add a full practice run in the end-point's format a week before, with worked answers; keep the first summative of the course lower in weight
rows.if: Learners are `novice` on the format (first exam of this kind, first-year students, a new kind of task)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Judge over several short occasions and observed work rather than one long test; read questions aloud where reading is not the outcome
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary age)

rows.basis: untested proposal; threshold decisions are held by [Competency-Based Assessment](principles/competency-based-assessment.md)
rows.change: Make the end-point a task from their work, observed or produced on the job, judged against a stated competency threshold; ask what they already do and test only what is new
rows.if: Learners are `adult` professionals, or in `adult-workplace` training

rows.basis: [A training-design argument, not tested by any study recorded here, holds that practising whole complex tasks improves transfer of complex skills](claims/whole-task-performance-improves-transfer.md) [~W] (an argument about training, carried here to assessment)
rows.change: Include a whole-task performance, scored with a rubric, plus short component items so a failure can be traced to a part
rows.if: Goal is a `complex-skill` (a design, a case, a clinical or practical performance)

rows.basis: [University examination questions concentrate at the lower cognitive levels of Bloom's Taxonomy, dominated by comprehension and knowledge](claims/exam-questions-concentrate-lower-bloom-levels.md) [~M]; [Students perform better overall on LOCS exam questions than on HOCS exam questions](claims/locs-exam-questions-outperform-hocs.md) [~M]; [HOCS clicker questions during learning improve performance on LOCS exam questions more than LOCS clicker questions do](claims/hocs-clickers-improve-locs-exam-performance.md) [+M] (one nonmajors biology course)
rows.change: Blueprint the paper so those levels carry marks; expect lower scores on them and practise them in class beforehand
rows.if: Outcomes ask for analysis, evaluation or creation, not only recall

rows.basis: [In one community-college lab class, six scorers rating six teams with an engineering rubric differed by a mean of 1.2 of 9 points, which the authors read as a sign the rubric may not be reliable](claims/engineering-rubric-low-scoring-reliability.md) [-W]; [Grade cutoffs are arbitrary because adjacent scores receiving different grades are not significantly different, per the author's statistical argument](claims/grade-cutoffs-arbitrary-adjacent-scores.md) [~W] (an argument)
rows.change: Several tasks or occasions; criteria and cut set in advance; two calibrated scorers on every judged task; review all scripts within a few marks of the cut; a reassessment route
rows.if: Stakes are high (certification, progression, licensing)

rows.basis: [Math anxiety has a small-to-moderate negative correlation with math achievement (r = −.28) in a meta-analysis of correlations from 223 studies](claims/math-anxiety-degrades-performance.md) [~M] (correlational); [Brief expressive writing before an exam can raise test-anxious students' scores, but across the wider literature its effect on test performance is negligible](claims/expressive-writing-improves-exam-performance.md) [~M] (helped highly anxious ninth-graders in one study; a meta-analysis found a negligible effect); [Retrieval practice benefits learners regardless of trait anxiety level, but higher trait or induced anxiety is associated with smaller testing effects](claims/higher-anxiety-is-associated-with-smaller-testing-effects.md) [~M]
rows.change: Low-stakes quizzing through the course; untimed or generously timed papers where speed is not the outcome; weight spread over several occasions. A brief writing exercise about worries just before the exam is optional: evidence for it is mixed
rows.if: Learners have test anxiety, low confidence, or a history of failing exams

rows.basis: untested proposal for the item language; for language learners measured on a rising grade-level cut, also report growth on the measure, since learners who start low can gain every year and never cross it ([ELs who did not reach proficiency by eighth grade showed continued growth but started first grade with much lower ACCESS scores, and rising grade-level thresholds meant they never met the proficiency cut](claims/non-proficient-els-low-first-grade-access-growth.md) [~W], one district's records); the measurement case is in [Validity, Reliability and Bias in Classroom Assessment](principles/validity-reliability-and-bias-in-classroom-assessment.md)
rows.change: Keep the language of items below the level being assessed; offer an oral or demonstrated response where the outcome is not reading or writing; gloss terms that are not the target
rows.if: Learners have low literacy, or are assessed in a second language

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Give remote and in-room learners the same tasks, time and permitted aids; prefer open-book items that ask for application to a new case over recall that can be looked up; follow a sample of submissions with a short oral check of the learner's own work; make tasks readable on a phone screen
rows.if: Setting is `online-self-paced`, phone-only, or some learners remote while others sit in the room

rows.basis: [An adaptive mastery testing strategy reduces test length by 30% to 81% while reaching the same mastery decision as the conventional test for 96% of trainees](claims/adaptive-mastery-testing-reduces-length-preserves-decisions.md) [+W] (a military-training simulation); the marking plan is untested
rows.change: Machine-score the knowledge items; judge a smaller set of performance tasks with a short rubric; double-mark a sample of about one in ten, not all; return results by outcome with one comment each. A computerised adaptive test can shorten a mastery test while reaching nearly the same decision
rows.if: One teacher marks for a large group, or marking time is scarce (volunteers, a busy shift, one tutor)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Do not report a summative judgment of the capability; give an end-of-session check, report it as immediate performance, and say what it cannot show
rows.if: Time is a single session only (a one-day workshop)

rows.basis: untested proposal; the task design is in [Authentic Assessment](patterns/authentic-assessment.md)
rows.change: Judge against the published criteria by trained assessors; record audience response as separate information, not as the grade; keep a component check for each criterion
rows.if: The end-point is a product or performance for a real audience (an exhibition, a client report, a recital)

rows.basis: [Dental students in a revised low-stress TBL format scored higher on the individual summative assessment (iSAT) than medical students in the original high-stakes format, in a non-randomised comparison of two cohorts](claims/low-stress-tbl-higher-isat-scores.md) [+W] (two cohorts, confounded); [Competitive (norm-referenced) grading pits students against one another and discourages cooperation, according to the author's argument](claims/competitive-grading-pits-students-against-each-other.md) [-W] (an argument)
rows.change: Keep an individual component in the summative grade; avoid grading on a curve, which sets team members against one another; consider lowering the stakes of in-module team tests
rows.if: Learners work in teams (team-based learning, group projects)

rows.basis: [Approximately 40 percent of educators reported spending less time on social studies and science as a result of the promotion policy](claims/policy-reduced-time-social-studies-science.md) [-W]; [Some CHSRI small schools struggle to align their themes with CPS graduation standards and PSAE content, and accountability pressure is reshaping instruction](claims/chsri-theme-standards-psae-alignment-difficulty.md) [~W] (teachers began modelling their own finals on the state test); [Incorporating the ACT into high-stakes accountability has not, by itself, produced instructional practices teaching more high-level skills](claims/act-accountability-alone-insufficient-for-rigor.md) [~W]; [High-stakes testing without investment did not improve achievement and narrowed instruction](claims/high-stakes-testing-without-investment-failed.md) [-W]; [Standardized tests measure only part of what teachers expect students to learn and are not taken in all subjects](claims/standardized-tests-partial-information-learning.md) [~W]; [Districts' most frequently stated testing weaknesses are lack of alignment with standards and curriculum and time taken from instruction, each cited by 24 percent](claims/district-testing-weaknesses-alignment-time.md) [~W]. All are school- or district-level surveys, interviews and trend reports; none tests the moves in this row
rows.change: Teach and run coursework against the full outcomes, not only the part the test samples; keep time for subjects and outcomes the test does not cover; limit format preparation to one practice run in the test's format, not weeks of test practice; give the course its own end-point on the untested outcomes and read the external score as one sample of what learners can do
rows.if: The end-point is an external test the teacher does not set (a state accountability test, an exam-board paper), with stakes for the school or programme

rows.basis: untested proposal; the three changes rest on the claims cited in the rows above
rows.change: Keep it. Change only what the evidence here speaks to: check its items against the outcomes and levels (one blueprint pass), add low-stakes retrieval before it, and calibrate scorers on a sample
rows.if: The brief names its own end-point (its own exam, rubric, grading scheme or portfolio)

rows.basis: the [whole-task claim](claims/whole-task-performance-improves-transfer.md) [~W] is a design argument; the rest is untested
rows.change: Keep a single whole-task scenario as the judgment; do not split it into paper items. Put recall and recognition checks into the low-stakes practice before it; inside the scenario, prompt the learner to say decisions aloud from the start and tell them the assessor will not confirm answers, so "is that what you wanted?" gets no reply and is not marked down
rows.if: The capability is one integrated performance (a clinical scenario, a full repair, a live service) and the brief asks for an authentic assessment

rows.basis: untested proposal; the associational turn-count finding ([conversational turns](claims/conversational-turns-predict-language-development.md) [+M]) and the [child-directed speech](elements/child-directed-speech.md) element. The dialogic-reading trials did not include infants
rows.change: Respond to gestures, sounds and pointing as turns; name what the child attends to; use books as things to point at and talk about rather than to read through; keep exchanges to a few turns at a time across care routines
rows.if: Infants, or children not yet using words

rows.basis: [Dialogic reading improves expressive language](claims/dialogic-reading-improves-language-outcomes.md) [+S] (moderate effect against typical shared reading; larger for younger children)
rows.change: Make daily dialogic reading the core routine (completion and recall prompts, expansion, repeated books), one-to-one or in small groups, and coach the parents or staff who do it
rows.if: Typically developing children of about 2 to 3

rows.basis: [Dialogic reading improves language outcomes](claims/dialogic-reading-improves-language-outcomes.md) [~S] (effect substantially smaller at 4–5); [Explicit Vocabulary Instruction](principles/explicit-instruction-vocabulary.md)
rows.change: Shift to open-ended and "your own life" prompts and retelling by the child; add short, explicit teaching of a few selected words from each book; do not expect the same gain from reading alone
rows.if: Children of about 4 to 5

rows.basis: [Potentially positive effects for children with disabilities](claims/dialogic-reading-potentially-positive-communication-language-disabilities.md) [+M] (two trials, 52 children with language delays); [Dale et al. 1996](claims/dale-1996-significant-lexical-diversity-play-total-utterances-book-reading.md) [+M] (gains on 2 of 6 measures); [parent-led dialogic reading showed no significant differences](claims/crain-thoreson-dale-1999-parent-led-null-effects.md) [-M] (19 children); the hub's smaller effect for children at risk [~S]
rows.change: Use one-to-one or very small groups, more sessions, simpler prompts, and work with a speech-language professional; do not rely on a parent-led reading routine alone, and judge progress on the child's own talk (utterances, variety of words)
rows.if: Children with language delays or disabilities

rows.basis: untested here; from the earlier page (early sign-language exposure is time-sensitive). No claim in the wiki was read for it
rows.change: Give early, full access to a language the child can perceive (including a sign language), with the same responsive turn-taking in that language; involve specialists early
rows.if: Children who are deaf or hard of hearing

rows.basis: untested here; [Preserve Heritage Language While Acquiring an Additional Language](principles/heritage-language-maintenance.md); the turn-count claim's note that some of the original "word gap" reflected different, not deficient, home practices ([conversational turns](claims/conversational-turns-predict-language-development.md) [~M])
rows.change: Ask caregivers to talk and read in the language they speak most fully; do not advise dropping the home language; in the setting, support both where staff can
rows.if: The home language differs from the setting's language, or families speak several

rows.basis: [Parent coaching outperforms information only](claims/parent-coaching-outperforms-information-only.md) [+M] (carried from parenting and child behaviour outcomes, not language); [parent-implemented interventions improve outcomes](claims/parent-implemented-intervention-improves-outcomes.md) [+M] (carried from children with autism); the hub's finding that families at greatest risk did not change home reading [~S]
rows.change: Coach rather than inform: show the routine, have each parent practise it with their own child while someone gives feedback, follow up once or twice; expect the families most at risk to need the most support to change routines
rows.if: Delivered through parents or caregivers at home

rows.basis: [READY4K! text messages](claims/ready4k-texts-improve-preschool-literacy.md) [+M] (over 1,000 preschool families; small effect on an early-literacy screen, not on oral language). Remote coaching of the dialogic routine is untested
rows.change: Send one short, concrete prompt a week (one thing to say or ask during a routine the family already has, such as bath time or a bus ride), and, where possible, one short video of the routine; do not rely on texts alone for a child with a delay
rows.if: Phone-only contact with families, or no in-person sessions

rows.basis: [the teacher-delivered replication failure in the hub](claims/dialogic-reading-improves-language-outcomes.md) [~S]; [frequency of implementation moderates effects](claims/implementation-level-moderates-dialogic-reading-effects.md) [~M]; group sizes are untested proposals
rows.change: Rotate small groups of 4–5 for 10-minute dialogic sessions while others play; train assistants or volunteers to run some groups; check once a week that sessions happen and children talk on most pages
rows.if: `classroom` with one teacher for 15–20 children

rows.basis: untested proposal; [frequency of implementation moderates effects](claims/implementation-level-moderates-dialogic-reading-effects.md) [~M]
rows.change: Teach one move, not the sequence: one prompt per page plus expanding the child's answer, on a pocket card; spend coaching time on watching one session and giving one piece of feedback; protect frequency over length
rows.if: Scarce facilitator time (volunteers, a busy shift, a home visitor with an hour a month)

rows.basis: untested proposal; the hub claim's three ingredients ([dialogic reading](claims/dialogic-reading-improves-language-outcomes.md) [+S])
rows.change: Keep it; change only what the evidence says matters: the child talks on most pages or turns, the adult expands what the child said, and it happens most days. Use the brief's own checklist and categories to record this; add no new test
rows.if: The brief names its own routine (a curriculum's story time, a home-visiting script, its own observation checklist)

rows.basis: untested proposal; coaching evidence is from multi-session programmes ([parent coaching](claims/parent-coaching-outperforms-information-only.md) [~M])
rows.change: Spend it on one modelled reading, each adult practising once with their own child with feedback, and a take-home card with two prompts; do not claim a change in children's language from it
rows.if: Single session only (one parent workshop, one library story time)

rows.basis: untested proposal; the dialogic routine is built from prompts and responses, not decoding
rows.change: Use wordless picture books, photo books or the family's own stories; the prompts and expansion do not need the adult to read the text; praise what the caregiver already does
rows.if: Caregivers with low literacy or low confidence reading aloud

rows.basis: [experiential training of early childhood workers](claims/experiential-training-ecd-workers-better-child-outcomes.md) [+W] (an argument, untested); [parent coaching](claims/parent-coaching-outperforms-information-only.md) [+M] carried
rows.change: Train through practice with the children they work with and feedback, not lectures; give time in the rota for small-group reading
rows.if: Adults in work settings (childcare staff, health visitors)

rows.basis: [no discernible effects on phonological processing](claims/dialogic-reading-no-phonological-processing-effects.md) [-M]; [Phonics](principles/phonics.md)
rows.change: Add explicit code-focused activities; dialogic reading alone will not produce them
rows.if: Goal includes phonological awareness or letter knowledge

rows.basis: untested proposal; the turn-count claim's caution about word-count framing ([conversational turns](claims/conversational-turns-predict-language-development.md) [~M])
rows.change: The family decides whether to record and who hears it; use any count only as feedback to the family on turns, never as a judgement of the family or a ranking of homes
rows.if: Recording home talk (audio recorders, turn counters) or other private material

rows.basis: [Vocabulary-focused programmes are probably insufficient to close the vocabulary gap](claims/vocabulary-programs-insufficient-to-close-vocabulary-gap.md) [~M] (school-age linguistic comprehension programmes, carried to early years)
rows.change: State a smaller, measurable goal (the children's own talk and the words taught), and do not promise to close a gap with a vocabulary programme alone
rows.if: A gap-closing target (a programme expected to close a vocabulary gap)

rows.basis: untested proposal; the earlier page's example of the advanced kindergarten reader who stops progressing
