rows.change: Compact by pre-check within the class; give harder texts or problems in the same topic for the freed time; keep the student in class routines; review the arrangement every unit
rows.if: The student is a `child` in primary school, well ahead in reading or number

rows.basis: untested proposal; the earlier page's constraint that repeated grade-skipping opens large maturity gaps
rows.change: Subject acceleration in that subject (the next course, online or with an older class), with the student staying with their year group for other subjects
rows.if: The student is an `adolescent` in secondary school, ahead in one subject

rows.basis: untested proposal; the earlier page records that acceleration works but not indefinitely, citing a chapter not held as a claim
rows.change: Decide with the student, family and next teacher, on the student's work across subjects and their social readiness, for one grade at a time; set a review after the first term
rows.if: Whole-grade acceleration (grade-skipping) is being considered

rows.basis: [Intelligent tutoring systems improve achievement over non-individualised instruction](claims/adaptive-learning-improves-outcomes.md) [+M] (general populations, not gifted students); [expertise reversal](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [+M] carried from training studies
rows.change: Prefer acceleration: move to the next unit's content once the pre-check is passed, through adaptive or self-paced material with a teacher check each week
rows.if: The target is cumulative (`procedure`, `principle`, as in mathematics or a language's grammar)

rows.basis: untested proposal; long expert development is described in [Even the most talented performers need around 10 years of intense involvement](claims/ten-year-rule-expert-performance.md) [~W] (a review, chess, music, sport)
rows.change: Prefer enrichment: an open task with a professional's standard and a real audience, with a mentor in the field where one can be found
rows.if: The target opens outwards (`complex-skill`, writing, art, music, a research project)

rows.basis: [Accumulated deliberate practice distinguishes more from less accomplished musicians](claims/deliberate-practice-hours-differentiate-musicians.md) [~W] (a review reporting one retrospective study); [relative-age effects bias selection into elite youth sports](claims/relative-age-effect-talent-selection-bias.md) [~W] and [early training produces adaptations misread as talent](claims/early-training-adaptations-misread-as-talent.md) [~W] (the same review, reporting other studies); untested as a school design
rows.change: Count it: give access to training, a teacher or coach in the field, and practice time, and judge it by performance, not by an IQ score; when selecting for a squad, ensemble or programme, compare a student's performance with others of the same age within the year group and with the same amount of training so far, and re-select each year rather than once
rows.if: The talent is in music, art, sport or another field outside the academic subjects

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use one pre-check and two or three tiers of replacement work the teacher can run at once; check in with the ahead group together for 5 minutes twice a week rather than individually
rows.if: One teacher, a full mixed class, several students ahead at different points

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Give the visiting adult one job each visit: read the latest draft, ask one question that raises the standard, and agree the next step and date; the contract carries the rest between visits
rows.if: Scarce teacher time (a busy class, a gifted coordinator who visits weekly, volunteer mentors)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Put the compacted student's replacement work and contract online; hold the weekly check-in as a short call; keep the student's role in the class's shared discussion when present
rows.if: Some students join remotely, or work from a phone or tablet at home

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Give one hard, open task with a model of the standard, time to attempt it, and feedback naming what the student did; do not claim it as provision
rows.if: Only a single session is available (a one-off enrichment day, a visiting class)

rows.basis: [Extracurricular involvement and adult mentorship are associated with reversal of gifted underachievement](claims/extracurriculars-mentoring-reverse-underachievement.md) [+W] (one issue brief, associational)
rows.change: Check the work's level first (a pre-check on the next unit); if it is below the student's level, change the work before treating the behaviour; offer a mentor or an extracurricular in the area of talent
rows.if: The student is bored, handing in little or behaving badly

rows.basis: [Praise for intelligence rather than effort](claims/feedback-praise-reduces-learning.md) [+M] (fifth graders, general population; not gifted students)
rows.change: Set work hard enough that mistakes happen; name the student's strategy and effort, never "you're so smart"; show the student the improvement over drafts
rows.if: The student has low confidence, avoids hard work, or fears being wrong

rows.basis: [Underrepresentation of culturally and linguistically diverse students](claims/gifted-underrepresentation-diverse-students.md) [~W], [teacher under-referral](claims/teacher-underreferral-diverse-gifted.md) [~W] (one issue brief); [underrepresentation attributed to biased measures](claims/culturally-diverse-underrepresentation-biased-measures.md) [~W] (a narrative review's position, no data); [a talent search admitting by SAT score invited over 2,500 boys and 1,081 girls in one summer](claims/test-scores-gate-gifted-program-entry.md) [~W] (one witness's testimony); see [Standardized Test Fairness and Bias](principles/standardized-test-fairness-and-bias.md)
rows.change: Screen every student, use the unit pre-check as a second route in, and compare provision with enrolment by group each year
rows.if: Identification is by a test score cut-off, or by teacher referral

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep it. Change only what the evidence and the earlier page say matters: a pre-check on the unit's own work before deciding, replacement work that is harder rather than more, feedback that names what the student did, and the student's own interests in choosing the task
rows.if: The brief names its own routine (a school's gifted programme model, an extension menu, a published enrichment curriculum, its own rubric for advanced work)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use them, and raise the level by the task, not by substituting another rubric
rows.if: The brief's own rubric or criteria for the advanced work

rows.basis: [expertise reversal](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [+M] (electrical trainees, among others); untested as a test-out design
rows.change: Let them test out of modules by doing the module's task to its standard; give them the hardest cases or a role reviewing others' work for the freed time
rows.if: Adults in a work setting who are far ahead of a training course (an experienced hire in onboarding)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Plan the extension work towards it from the start, with the audience's standard as the criterion and at least one rehearsal or review by someone from that field
rows.if: The product is for a real audience (a competition, an exhibition, a published piece, a presentation to experts)

rows.basis: [Standardized Test Fairness and Bias](principles/standardized-test-fairness-and-bias.md) for score-based decisions; [Traditional gifted identification tests cannot fully determine learning potential](claims/traditional-identification-tests-fail-learning-potential.md) [~W] (an argument in one review)
rows.change: Decide on more than one source of evidence (the student's work across units, a pre-check on the next level, the student's own view), never a single score; record the decision and review it after one term
rows.if: Stakes are high (programme entry, a grade-skip, an accelerated exam entry)

rows.basis: [Praise for intelligence rather than effort](claims/feedback-praise-reduces-learning.md) [+M] (fifth graders, general population) for the feedback; the rest untested
rows.change: Keep steps short (5–10 minutes of focused practice), practise daily inside routines, name what the student did after each success, and use pictures or objects for each step
rows.if: The student is a `child` in primary school

rows.basis: [Self-determination instruction](claims/self-determination-instruction-improves-outcomes.md) [+M] and [student-led IEP meetings](claims/self-directed-iep-increases-student-participation.md) [+M] (high-school students with intellectual or learning disabilities); post-school outcomes not measured
rows.change: Move practice into community and workplace tasks; teach the student to set and review their own goals weekly and to lead their own planning meeting, rehearsed beforehand
rows.if: The student is an `adolescent` or young `adult` near transition (work, independent living)

rows.basis: [Mnemonic instruction](claims/mnemonic-instruction-improves-recall-for-students-with-disabilities.md) [+M] (includes mild developmental disabilities; recall outcomes, abstracts)
rows.change: Add a keyword or acrostic cue the student can decode, practise retrieving through it, and review it at spaced intervals
rows.if: The target is facts or vocabulary (`verbal-association`)

rows.basis: untested; the mnemonic claim's own page says benefits shrink for conceptual content
rows.change: Do not rely on mnemonics; teach with concrete objects and the real setting, and check with a changed task the memorised steps would not solve
rows.if: The target is understanding a `principle` or using a skill in a new setting

rows.basis: untested proposal; mastery pacing ([Mastery learning improves outcomes](claims/mastery-learning-improves-outcomes.md) [+M]) carried from general classes
rows.change: Teach it as a task analysis of 4–8 steps in its real setting, practise until three consecutive unaided successes on two days, then fade to weekly review
rows.if: The target is a daily-life `procedure` (money, time, travel)

rows.basis: [Peer tutoring improves achievement](claims/peer-tutoring-improves-achievement.md) [+M] (tutee ability level not a moderator, mathematics); the rest untested
rows.change: Build the student's steps into the class task (same activity, smaller step, picture checklist), seat a trained peer partner, and check the student's attempt first when circulating
rows.if: One teacher, a full general class, the student needs intermittent support

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Give the visiting adult one job: watch one attempt at the current step, record which step was reached, and set the next step; leave a picture checklist so the student and a peer can practise in between
rows.if: Scarce adult time (a shared aide, a specialist who visits weekly, volunteers)

rows.basis: untested proposal; [parent-delivered intervention](claims/parent-implemented-intervention-improves-outcomes.md) [+M] is evidence for children with autism only
rows.change: Send the same step and checklist home with a short video model of the step; have the student or a family member show one attempt on video or in a call each week; keep the in-class group role when the student is present
rows.if: Some learners join remotely, or the student works from a phone or tablet at home

rows.basis: [Aided AAC systems over manual signs](claims/aided-systems-advantage-over-manual-signs.md) [+W] (a review's report, children with autism, a tendency); for the planning move see [Universal Design for Learning](principles/universal-design-for-learning.md)
rows.change: Give a way to respond that does not depend on speech or print (pointing, a picture or symbol board, a speech-generating device), and keep the same academic target
rows.if: The student has limited speech or does not read yet

rows.basis: [Praise for intelligence rather than effort](claims/feedback-praise-reduces-learning.md) [+M] (children after failure, general population); choice untested here
rows.change: Restart one step below where they failed so that the first attempts succeed, name each success specifically, and let the student choose which of two practice tasks to do first
rows.if: The student has low confidence after repeated failure, or avoids tasks

rows.basis: [Self-monitoring improves on-task behavior](claims/self-monitoring-improves-on-task-behavior.md) [+M] (single-case studies, students with or at risk for disabilities; on-task behaviour, not achievement)
rows.change: Teach the student to check and record at intervals whether they are working (a cue every few minutes, a tally card or app), alongside the step checklist
rows.if: The student has trouble staying with a task during independent practice

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Teach one step of one functional task, practise it three or four times with feedback naming what the student did, and end with one unaided attempt; record what it shows and do not claim retention
rows.if: Only a single session is available (a one-off workshop, a visiting class)

rows.basis: untested proposal; from the earlier page's inclusion guidance
rows.change: Give the student a defined, rehearsed part with a visual script; rehearse in the real space at least twice; agree beforehand how they can ask for help during it
rows.if: The product is shown to a real audience (a class presentation, a school event, a job trial)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep it. Change only what the evidence says matters: one observable step per goal, feedback that names what the student did rather than the student, a practice dose the timetable actually holds, and the student stating the goal themselves
rows.if: The brief names its own routine (an IEP goal format, a school's praise or reward system, a published curriculum, a specialist's prompt hierarchy)

rows.basis: [Teacher expectation effects](claims/teacher-expectation-effects-on-achievement.md) [~M] (associational, general cohort); the rest untested
rows.change: Judge readiness on unaided attempts in the real setting, never on assisted success; record every prompt given; check the target is still the age-appropriate one, not one lowered to fit the label
rows.if: Stakes are high (a placement decision, an accountability test, a work trial)

rows.basis: [The Self-Determined Learning Model of Instruction improves self-determination](claims/self-determined-learning-model-of-instruction-improves-self-determination.md) [~M] (312 high-school students; within-group gains, small non-significant difference from controls)
rows.change: Keep the student answering the model's questions and train the adult to facilitate, not answer for them; do not expect a gain over usual instruction to be shown
rows.if: The plan is the student's choice of goals (self-determined learning model)

rows.basis: [Educator involvement in choosing a pilot tool is associated with higher engagement and fidelity](claims/educator-buy-in-engagement-fidelity-edtech-pilots.md) [~M] (shows the cost of no voice in district pilots; untested for mandates generally)
rows.change: Skip the selection step. Map the system and plan the bundle around the mandate. Put early effort into what adopters can still shape (how, when, with what support) and into how the innovation is perceived
rows.if: The innovation is already chosen and mandated from above

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep the map to one page: the assessment, the time and the one or two people around the user. Do not run the full process
rows.if: The change is a single tool or course for one teacher or one class, touching nothing else

rows.basis: [Later-implementing PBIS schools showed the greatest organizational health improvements, while fast adopters started higher](claims/pbis-later-implementers-greatest-gains.md) [~M] (a group-randomised trial of one school-wide programme in 37 schools; hedged "tended")
rows.change: Map each site as well as the whole. Expect sites with healthier organisations to adopt fastest, and do not leave the others out: plan more support and longer for them
rows.if: A district-, college- or organisation-wide change across many sites

rows.basis: [Follow-up contact related most strongly to adoption success](claims/follow-up-contact-strongest-adoption-success-factor.md) [+M] (school dissemination; carried to workplaces untested)
rows.change: Map roles, workload, incentives and supervision as the subsystems. Use the adopters' own work tasks as the trial material. Put follow-up contact into the working week
rows.if: Adopters are `adult` professionals in `adult-workplace` settings (staff, clinicians, trainers)

rows.basis: [Teachers' ability to deliver strong instruction depends on school context, family resources and the larger community](claims/instruction-delivery-depends-on-school-context.md) [+W] (a book chapter's framing)
rows.change: Include families and community organisations in the map, and plan a part of the bundle for them
rows.if: The change concerns `pre-k-12` schools where families and community shape what teachers can do

rows.basis: [Technical implementation falls short when adaptive components have not shifted](claims/adaptive-shift-precedes-technical-restorative-success.md) [+W]; [restorative outcomes follow a slow trajectory](claims/restorative-practices-three-to-five-year-timeline.md) [~W] (one practitioner guide)
rows.change: Before formal training, give a ramp-up period to the reasons and to trust between the people involved. Judge early progress on relationships and practice, not outcomes
rows.if: The change is a technical routine resting on values or relationships (restorative practices, inclusion, a feedback culture)

rows.basis: [Inquiry environments are hard to scale because they require changes in roles, participation and system coherence](claims/inquiry-environments-ambitious-systems-hard-to-scale.md) [+W] (a handbook chapter's conjecture)
rows.change: Plan role changes, participation and coherence across the system as part of the bundle. Do not plan to scale by distributing materials
rows.if: An ambitious, inquiry-type innovation that changes teacher and learner roles

rows.basis: [A tool's effectiveness results from the whole configuration in which it is used](claims/tool-effectiveness-depends-on-context-configuration.md) [+W]; [digital education innovations are an interplay of technological, pedagogical, organisational and governance dimensions](claims/digital-education-innovation-four-dimension-interplay.md) [+W] (a book introduction's conceptual argument)
rows.change: Map who supports it, the devices, the data, and what users do with what it produces, as well as the tool itself. Plan its use inside the lesson or workflow, not only its installation
rows.if: The innovation is technology

rows.basis: [Without attention, educational innovations tend to exacerbate learning gaps](claims/educational-innovations-exacerbate-learning-gaps-without-attention.md) [~W] (an article citing Reich 2020)
rows.change: Put access and the conditions of lower-resourced learners in the map. Check use and effects separately for them at each review point
rows.if: The innovation is meant to narrow gaps between better-off and lower-resourced learners

rows.basis: [Compact collaboration did not yield systemic change within the grant period](claims/compact-activities-small-scale-improvements-not-systemic-change.md) [~M] (interviews and site visits; perceived small gains)
rows.change: Name the small, nearer gains the period can show (use, practice, relationships), and do not promise systemic change within it. Plan who carries the work on after the grant
rows.if: Short funding or a fixed grant period (one year or less)

rows.basis: [Follow-up contact related most strongly to adoption success](claims/follow-up-contact-strongest-adoption-success-factor.md) [+M] for keeping contact; the short format is an untested proposal
rows.change: Keep the map and the bundle plan but make contact short: a 10–15 minute call per site every two to four weeks. Train one local lead per site to carry the rest
rows.if: Scarce facilitator time (one coordinator for many sites, a busy shift, volunteers)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use the time for the problem statement (about a quarter), the map of who must change what (about half), and named owners for the two or three parts most likely to block (the rest). For example, in 90 minutes: about 20, 45 and 25 minutes
rows.if: A single planning meeting only, of a fixed length

rows.basis: untested proposal; the risk of a routine done as compliance: [continuous improvement can fall short as a checklist](claims/ci-compliance-activity-undermines-equity.md) [~M]
rows.change: Keep it. Add only what it lacks: a list of the other parts of the system that must change, and a review of that list with the people in it at each cycle
rows.if: The brief names its own planning routine or framework (its own improvement cycle, logic model template or implementation checklist)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Map in those categories, not Ellsworth's. Check only that adopters, environment and the innovation's own attributes are covered somewhere
rows.if: The brief gives its own categories for the system (its own stakeholder groups, its own framework components)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Record roles and conditions, not named individuals' failings. Let people choose what they say in a group and what they tell the change team privately
rows.if: Some of what the map would record is sensitive (staff performance, conflicts, a family's circumstances)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Map and review in a shared document everyone can edit. Hold follow-up by call or video at the same interval. Ask remote sites separately what their own conditions are, since they differ from the main site's
rows.if: Some adopters join remotely, or across sites, and others are in the room

rows.basis: untested proposal; from the framework (resistance cause: low confidence in the system)
rows.change: Treat low confidence as a cause of resistance to diagnose. Ask what has failed before. Start with a small, visible early success and keep promises about support
rows.if: Adopters have low confidence in the change, or in the system that is making it

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Include the audience in the map and the trial. Judge the trial on whether the audience can use what is produced, as well as on adopters' use
rows.if: The change ends in a product or service for a real audience (a new course launching to students, a public programme)

rows.basis: [Discussion promotes more active thinking than lecture, though lecture is no worse for transmitting information](claims/discussion-promotes-more-active-thought-than-lecture.md) [~M] (college classes)
rows.change: Keep a clear, short teacher explanation as the main move; add one 3–5 minute pair talk or written summary per 10–15 minutes of explanation to check what landed
rows.if: Goal is information learners lack (facts, a procedure to follow), not understanding

rows.basis: [Some classroom discussion approaches improve text comprehension, but gains are not uniform across approaches and more student talk alone does not produce them](claims/structured-discussion-methods-improve-comprehension.md) [~M]
rows.change: Use text-based questions that require evidence and follow-up; teach one discussion move per mini-lesson; judge the discussion by reasons given, not by minutes of talk
rows.if: Goal is comprehension of a text or a concept, or reasoning

rows.basis: untested proposal; the claims recorded here are not on beginners or low-literacy learners
rows.change: Let them plan in their first language or by drawing; give sentence frames; talk before writing; accept short answers at first and build length across sessions; gloss content words
rows.if: Learners are `novice` in the target language, or have low literacy

rows.basis: [Students view games as relaxing and fun, building confidence for speaking](claims/games-relaxing-fun-confidence.md) [+W] (undergraduate EFL learners' reports); [Fear of making mistakes is the most significant cause of foreign language speaking anxiety among Iranian EFL learners (81%)](claims/fear-of-mistakes-top-speaking-anxiety-iranian-efl.md) [~W] (survey, associational); [AI reduces foreign language anxiety and strengthens self-efficacy and self-confidence, supporting the Affective Foundation Pathway](claims/ai-reduces-fl-anxiety-private-practice.md) [+W] (a systematic review's thematic synthesis of EFL studies on private AI practice; no pooled effect); [Anxiety in foreign language classroom learning experiences is linked with oral performance among Japanese EFL learners](claims/flca-linked-with-oral-performance-japanese-efl.md) [~W] (two-learner case study: why anxiety matters for oral grades, not what reduces it)
rows.change: Start with pairs and private writing, not whole-class turns; never correct a speaker's form mid-idea; use games and role-play for the first speaking turns; let a learner pass once and come back; where learners have it, offer private rehearsal (a voice recorder, a speaking app or an AI conversation partner) of the turn they will take in class
rows.if: Learners are anxious or low in confidence about speaking

rows.basis: [Deeper-learning inquiry strategies in low-income mathematics classes reduced linguistic, ethnic, and class outcome disparities](claims/deeper-learning-math-inquiry-reduces-disparities.md) [+W] (a policy report's one-sentence account of one study, no design details or effect size; collaborative discussion was one ingredient with relevant problems and inquiry); the home-language move is an untested proposal
rows.change: Use problems drawn from the learners' lives, and have learners explain and discuss their thinking with each other on them; allow the home language for that talk; track whether the gaps between groups of learners narrow, as well as the class average. A gap between groups reflects circumstances and treatment, not the groups themselves
rows.if: Learners are from a linguistic-minority or low-income community, studying a subject other than language (for example mathematics)

rows.basis: untested proposal; the writing evidence includes elementary grades ([Writing-to-learn activities improve content learning in Grades 1–12, with effects in mathematics indistinguishable from those in science and social studies, in one meta-analysis](claims/writing-improves-mathematical-understanding.md) [+M]), the talk evidence here is from grade 4, grade 9 and college
rows.change: Keep turns short; model each move first; use talk partners who stay the same for several weeks; write with frames and drawings
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary age)

rows.basis: untested proposal; carried from school and college evidence
rows.change: Take the content to be discussed from their own work (a case, a document, a decision); let them explain to a colleague who was not there; keep writing to short notes they can reuse at work
rows.if: Learners are `adult`, or in a work setting

rows.basis: [WTC decreases as class size increases on both talk-time and turns of talk](claims/wtc-decreases-as-class-size-increases.md) [~W] (three EFL classes, associational); the moves are untested proposals
rows.change: Every learner talks to a partner before anyone speaks to the class; call on pairs in a known order; collect one written sentence from everyone at the end, and read a sample, not all
rows.if: One teacher, a large class (30 or more)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Give each group a printed question card and roles so the talk runs without the teacher; the facilitator visits each group for one follow-up question ("why?" or "where does it say that?") and reads one written sentence per learner
rows.if: Scarce facilitator time (one tutor checking in briefly, volunteers, a busy shift)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Pair remote learners with each other in breakout rooms, not with the room; take written contributions in a chat or shared document as full turns; for phone-only learners, use short voice messages or texts in place of long typing
rows.if: Mixed mode: some learners remote, some in the room, or phone-only

rows.basis: [Off-the-shelf LLM tutors are more verbose than human tutors, leaving students only 5-15% of talk time versus close to 30% in human tutoring](claims/off-the-shelf-llms-verbose-low-student-talk-time.md) [~W] (benchmark simulations); [Students who teach a ChatGPT teachable agent in natural language achieve greater knowledge gains than students who learn the same material from online videos](claims/chatgpt-teachable-agent-knowledge-gains.md) [+W]; [Interactive dialogue with the AI tool, available only in some sites, promoted deeper engagement and student agency during revision](claims/interactive-genai-dialogue-promotes-engagement.md) [+W] (multiple-case study of school writers; engagement observed, learning not measured); [AI reduces foreign language anxiety and strengthens self-efficacy and self-confidence, supporting the Affective Foundation Pathway](claims/ai-reduces-fl-anxiety-private-practice.md) [+W] (anxiety and confidence, not understanding); the follow-up-question rule is an untested proposal
rows.change: Set it up so the learner does most of the talking: tell it to ask questions and keep its turns short, or have the learner teach it; for writing feedback, turn on a conversational mode so the learner can ask follow-up questions about the feedback, and require each question to name the sentence it is about; check what the learner can explain or write without it
rows.if: Learners use an AI chat tutor or chatbot for practice

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Spend about 10 minutes explaining, 5 thinking or writing alone, 10 in pairs, 10 in a whole-class discussion on one evidence question, and 5 writing a short explanation; record what the writing shows and claim no change in confidence
rows.if: A single session only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Cut the whole-class discussion, not the individual turns: 5 minutes of explanation, 2 of jotting, 6 of pair talk on one question, 7 of writing a two- or three-sentence answer; the minutes add up to the budget
rows.if: A fixed short time budget (for example 20 minutes)

rows.basis: untested proposal; see the [Debate pattern](patterns/debate.md) for one format
rows.change: Rehearse the talk in pairs first; use the audience's questions as the discussion's evidence questions; keep the performance whole, and do the talk and writing-to-learn before it, not by splitting it into exercises
rows.if: Learners will produce or perform for a real audience (a presentation, a published piece, a debate)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep it; change only what the evidence here says matters: that each turn must do something with the content, that every learner gets a turn, and that writing is short, frequent and ungraded for language. Use the brief's criteria to judge the talk, not this page's
rows.if: The brief names its own routine, rubric or categories (its own discussion protocol, question set or writing template)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Let learners choose what they share and with whom; keep personal writing private to the writer unless they offer it; discuss the content, not the learner's own case, in the whole group
rows.if: The material is private or sensitive (personal experience, migration, identity, health)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep the talk and writing, but add the exam's own task, unaided, near the end of the arc; judge readiness on that, not on fluency in discussion
rows.if: High stakes: an unaided test or a language exam follows

rows.basis: untested; the one study ([core senses with diagrams](claims/cl-core-sense-preposition-instruction-improves-use.md) [~M]) taught `advanced` learners only
rows.change: Teach two or three high-frequency uses as phrases first, in meaningful use; bring in the core-sense diagram only once learners have several uses to connect, and keep it short
rows.if: Learners are `novice` in the L2, or do not yet produce the form

rows.basis: [core senses with diagrams](claims/cl-core-sense-preposition-instruction-improves-use.md) [+M] (advanced learners); [L1-induced errors persist in advanced learners and risk fossilization if learners rely on compensatory communication strategies](claims/l1-interference-errors-fossilization-risk.md) [+W] (one learner's diary)
rows.change: This is the main case: spend the time on the diagnostic sample and the L1 contrast, take examples from learners' own work, and ask learners to notice their own uses rather than relying on paraphrase to avoid the form
rows.if: Learners are `advanced`, with long-standing errors on a form

rows.basis: untested; no claim here concerns children
rows.change: Fewer verbal explanations: act out the core scene (stand *at* the door, walk *to* it), use pictures, and keep explanations in the language the children understand best; short choice games rather than written reasons
rows.if: Learners are `child`

rows.basis: [Thai students overuse the causal connective because](claims/thai-overuse-because-l1-influence.md) [+W] (Thai learners overused *because* while Hong Kong and Singaporean learners underused it); the grouping is untested
rows.change: Do the contrast step in L1 groups with a prepared table per L1, or contrast the form with its L2 neighbours instead; expect different groups to deviate in different directions
rows.if: Learners share no single L1

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page's scope ("structures with complex distributional patterns")
rows.change: Teach it as a rule with practice, or as a fixed phrase; do not invent a core sense
rows.if: The form's uses have no meaning motivation (an arbitrary agreement, a fixed idiom)

rows.basis: [Practice of grammar rules improves only the practiced skill](claims/skill-specificity-l2-grammar-practice.md) [~M] (a review reporting one longitudinal study; carried from rule practice to concept teaching)
rows.change: Make the choice practice comprehension tasks: interpret what the form signals in a sentence, choose between two readings
rows.if: The target is comprehension (reading, listening), not production

rows.basis: [Monitoring lowers accuracy for unlearnable rules](claims/monitoring-lowers-preposition-accuracy.md) [~W] (one Korean student was less accurate with prepositions in edited writing); untested as a design rule
rows.change: After the explanation, move quickly to timed and oral choice practice; do not ask learners to check each form consciously while speaking, and judge progress on unedited speech
rows.if: The target is fluent speech under time pressure

rows.basis: untested
rows.change: Give the diagram as an image card the learner can reopen; make choice items automatically checked, with each explanation pointing to the core sense; replace partner explanation with a typed or recorded one-sentence reason
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, or phone-only

rows.basis: untested
rows.change: Put the diagram on the shared screen and in a file everyone holds; pair remote learners with each other for the explanation step (breakout or chat); collect choice answers through one poll so both groups are seen
rows.if: Some learners remote, some in the room

rows.basis: [conceptual deviations guide where to focus](claims/conceptual-deviation-awareness-guides-teacher-attention.md) [+W]; the class-scale tally is untested
rows.change: Take the diagnostic sample as one shared short writing task, tally the commonest deviation for the class, and teach that first; use mini-whiteboards or a poll for the choice items
rows.if: One teacher with a large class

rows.basis: untested
rows.change: Learners tally their own uses with a checklist built from the diagram; the tutor checks three of each learner's explanations per visit and the one form the tally flags
rows.if: Scarce facilitator time (a volunteer, a tutor checking in briefly)

rows.basis: untested; [Explicit teaching is more effective for EFL copular be learning but its effect is not durable](claims/explicit-teaching-effective-but-not-durable.md) [~M] is why no lasting change should be claimed
rows.change: 5 minutes: diagnose from five sentences; 15: the core sense and two or three uses; 10: partner explanations; 10: choice items; 5: one short paragraph using the form. Record what the paragraph shows and claim no retention
rows.if: A single session only (about 45 minutes)

rows.basis: untested
rows.change: Keep it. Use the brief's categories as the uses to derive from the core sense, keep its rubric and task as given, and add only the diagram, one explanation prompt and one choice check
rows.if: The brief names its own routine (its own error codes, rubric, textbook list of uses, writing task)

rows.basis: untested
rows.change: The learner chooses which samples are used and who sees them; they tally their own uses privately and share only examples they choose, with names removed
rows.if: Learners' own writing or work documents are private or sensitive

rows.basis: untested
rows.change: Do the concept work before drafting, and give feedback on the form inside the finished product; do not split the performance into gap-fill items
rows.if: The brief wants a whole performance kept whole (an essay, a presentation, a report for a real audience)

rows.basis: untested
rows.change: Draw examples and the diagnostic sample from their own genre (emails, reports, client calls); state the form's use in terms of what it does for the reader in that genre
rows.if: Adults in work settings

rows.basis: untested
rows.change: Lean on the picture and on gesture; keep grammatical terms out; let a learner show a choice by pointing or acting before explaining it
rows.if: Learners with low confidence or low literacy

rows.basis: untested
rows.change: Practise in the assessment's format, as the brief gives it, and add one sample from the learner's own writing beside it so that test success is not read as use
rows.if: High stakes, or an assessment with its own item format

rows.basis: [Minimal guidance is less effective for novices than explicit instruction](claims/minimal-guidance-less-effective-for-novices.md) [~S] (its table counts 13 distinct studies)
rows.change: Keep a short explanation and one worked example before the task; give prompts and feedback during it; do not leave the key idea to be found
rows.if: Learners are `novice` on the target and cannot begin a representative task

rows.basis: [Minimal guidance is less effective for novices than explicit instruction](claims/minimal-guidance-less-effective-for-novices.md) [~S] (a review in it says the advantage of guidance recedes once learners have enough prior knowledge; no crossover point is given)
rows.change: Drop the opening explanation; start at the late-session division of labour, with the teacher as consultant and questioner
rows.if: Learners already succeed on the first task unaided

rows.basis: untested; from the Piaget handbook folded into this page. Mead's argument ([method of thought cannot be transferred](claims/method-of-thought-cannot-be-transferred.md) [+W]) is theoretical, as are the Vygotskian claims that [children can imitate actions beyond their independent capabilities and profit from instruction](claims/children-imitate-beyond-independent-capability.md) [+W] and that [in pretend play the child behaves beyond her average age and daily behaviour](claims/pretend-play-child-head-taller.md) [+W] (one review paper restating Vygotsky, no data)
rows.change: Use concrete materials they can act on, introduce one variable at a time with ample repetition, and question rather than tell; keep the routine and the choice of activity with the teacher; model an action a step beyond what the child does alone and let them imitate it; use pretend and role play as a context where children attempt more than they do in routine tasks
rows.if: Learners are `child` in preschool to grade 3

rows.basis: [Active learning improves exam performance](claims/active-learning-improves-exam-performance.md) [+S] (STEM undergraduates, end-of-course exams); [most active-learning conditions kept a substantial lecture component](claims/active-learning-courses-retain-lecture-component.md) [~M]
rows.change: Replace a large share of lecture time with tasks learners do in class with feedback on what they produce; a short lecture can stay
rows.if: An undergraduate STEM course taught mainly by lecture

rows.basis: [Teacher-guided inquiry outperforms student-led](claims/teacher-guided-inquiry-outperforms-student-led.md) [+S] (a between-study moderator, not a head-to-head trial; its table counts 5 distinct studies)
rows.change: Keep the inquiry, but teacher-led: the teacher structures the question, prompts, monitors and leads the synthesis of findings
rows.if: School science, and the brief asks for inquiry or discovery

rows.basis: Drill: [A 1982 bilingual-education teacher-training packet asserts, citing Krashen, that repetitive drill and grammar-focused instruction are ineffective for second language acquisition](claims/drill-and-grammar-focus-ineffective-for-l2-acquisition.md) [+W] (an assertion, no data). Explicit rule: [Explicit L2 grammar instruction leads to larger learning effects than implicit instruction](claims/explicit-l2-grammar-instruction-superior-to-implicit.md) [~S] (meta-analyses; its table counts 7 distinct studies). Input alone leaves grammar weak: [Comprehensible input alone is insufficient for acquisition of high levels of grammatical proficiency](claims/comprehensible-input-insufficient-grammar-acquisition.md) [~M] (a review of immersion and communicative programmes: good listening and reading, low grammatical accuracy; its table counts 12 distinct studies); [informal evidence that adults do not automatically process input to develop competence](claims/input-processing-insufficient-for-adult-competence-terrell.md) [~W] (an annotated bibliography, citing Terrell). Input over drill, as theory and narrative review: [structured input alone, without explicit information, is sufficient to cause changes in learner knowledge](claims/structured-input-alone-sufficient-for-acquisition.md) [+W] (a review of processing-instruction studies, no effect size printed); [skill develops through engaging in the target activity, not drill of isolated components](claims/skill-develops-through-engagement-not-drill.md) [+W] (theoretical). Whether explicit-rule gains reach competence is disputed: see Evidence and qualifications
rows.change: Spend most time on meaningful input and communicative tasks rather than repetitive drill; where accuracy on a grammar form counts, teach the rule explicitly and then have learners use it in tasks
rows.if: The goal is communicative use of a second language

rows.basis: [Lecturing on values does not transact values effectively to children](claims/lecturing-on-values-does-not-transact-values-effectively.md) [+W] (reported second-hand, no study design given)
rows.change: Build the value into subject activities learners discuss and act on, not into separate lecture classes
rows.if: The goal is a value or attitude (value education, citizenship, ethics)

rows.basis: [Collaborative learning is an extension of social constructionism into composition](claims/collaborative-learning-is-an-extension-of-social-constructionism-into-composition.md) [+W] (theoretical argument)
rows.change: Make drafts the object of peer conversation (response groups, peer criticism); the teacher acts as co-worker, resource and referee, not as lecturer on writing
rows.if: College writing or composition

rows.basis: untested; from the studio-course page folded in here (students rated the instructor as "a mentor and a consultant more than a typical teacher" at 4.17 of 5, a survey, not a comparison)
rows.change: Teacher as mentor and consultant: guide the design process (brainstorm, prototype, test), meet each group at fixed check-ins, push on ideas and user needs, help obtain resources, and let groups try and sometimes fail before stepping in
rows.if: A project- or studio-based course in higher education

rows.basis: [Teacher mediation, institutional support and responsible use were what successful AI use depended on](claims/teacher-mediation-institutional-support-ai-integration.md) [+M] (review of 11 studies, Arab university English classes); [AI-mediating orchestration](claims/ai-mediating-orchestration-type.md) [+W] (one teacher, 46 episodes); [instructor roles shift from exclusive information source toward orchestrating and regulating AI-mediated activities](claims/instructor-role-shift-orchestrating-genai.md) [+W] (conceptual synthesis, higher education; instructors keep task design and validation of AI output); [teachers as ethical supervisors of AI use](claims/teacher-role-shift-facilitator-ethical-supervisor.md) [+M]; [AI integration increased staff workload](claims/ai-integration-shifted-staff-roles-facilitation.md) [~M]
rows.change: Keep the teacher between the tool and the learner: check AI output, restate correct AI feedback in curriculum terms learners understand, model and require marked, verifiable AI use; budget extra teacher time
rows.if: Learners will use generative AI tools in the task

rows.basis: [E-teachers reported shifting toward a facilitator role online](claims/e-teachers-widen-object-toward-independent-learning.md) [+M] (one teacher's interview; describes the shift, does not test its effect); [both teachers remained peripherally active and concentrated their contributions on tutoring](claims/peripheral-teacher-tutoring-contributions.md) [+W] (one networked learning community, content and network analysis, no comparison)
rows.change: Provide the task, tools and criteria up front; mediate through written questions on submitted work and scheduled feedback rather than live circulation; in a discussion forum, post as a participant and tutor at the edges rather than answer every thread, and post less as groups begin to run the discussion themselves
rows.if: `online-self-paced` or web-based course, teacher not present in real time

rows.basis: [Interactionist mediation in synchronous chat revealed learners' movement toward responding to less explicit help](claims/scmc-da-mediation-reveals-microgenetic-development.md) [+W] (two adult EFL learners, with backsliding; the form was not fully internalized); [learners at the same CEFR level differ in their ZPDs](claims/dialang-cefr-levels-miss-zpd-differences.md) [+W]
rows.change: Mediate an error with graded prompts, from implicit (highlight the place, "look again") to explicit (name the error, give the form); record the level each learner needed and start the next session one level less explicit; place learners by that record rather than by a static test level
rows.if: Online synchronous mediation (text chat, video call) with one learner or a pair

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Same task for both groups; every learner posts their answer or product to one shared space the teacher can see; alternate the teacher's questioning between remote and room learners; phone-only learners get a task completable in short text or voice replies
rows.if: Mixed mode: some learners remote, some in the room, or phone-only

rows.basis: untested; contingent-help evidence is one-to-one ([Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support.](claims/contingent-scaffolding-improves-learning.md) [~S], cited for its limit)
rows.change: Have every learner show an answer at once (cards, mini-whiteboards, a poll), mediate the commonest misunderstanding for the whole class, then go to those still stuck; peers check each other against stated criteria
rows.if: One teacher with a large class

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Put the mediation in the materials: a printed question card for each stage, a self-check against a worked answer, and one fixed question the facilitator always asks at a check-in ("show me how you got this")
rows.if: Scarce facilitator time (volunteers, a busy shift, one tutor checking in briefly)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Run the six steps in one session (goal 5, explanation 10, task 20, expression 10, transfer 5 minutes); record what learners could explain at the end and do not claim retention
rows.if: Single session only

rows.basis: [MLE mediation is reported as beneficial despite barriers](claims/mle-beneficial-despite-barriers-or-late-mediation.md) [+W] (authors' assertion, no test); [the SES gap in elaborated talk appeared only in the low-mediating classroom](claims/mediation-ses-interaction-elaborated-utterances.md) [~M] (early childhood classrooms, association only); in the same three classrooms [high teacher mediation went with more children talking, in both elaborated and restricted talk](claims/high-mediation-more-child-talk-both-codes.md) [+W] (observation, association only, no effect size), and [more children who could shift between elaborated and restricted talk were in the highest-mediating teacher's classroom](claims/code-shifting-highest-mediating-teacher.md) [+W] (same study)
rows.change: Mediate more, not less: more explicit goals, more frequent short questions and success on early items; let learners express understanding orally or by doing before writing
rows.if: Learners with low confidence, low literacy, special educational needs or disadvantaged backgrounds

rows.basis: [Teacher guidance distribution tracked perceived willingness to collaborate, not group outcome level or prior science competence](claims/guidance-follows-willingness-not-outcome.md) [~W] (four school science classrooms, computer-supported inquiry, network analysis, not found for every teacher; shows where help went, not what reallocating it would do)
rows.change: Plan the round: visit every group on a fixed rotation, keep a tally of visits, and give extra time and socio-emotional support to quiet or low-confidence groups rather than to the groups that call the teacher over
rows.if: Learners work in small groups while the teacher circulates (collaborative inquiry, lab or project groups)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Ask what they already do on the job; set tasks from their own work; the teacher acts as resource and consultant, explaining only what the work shows they lack
rows.if: `adult` learners in a work setting

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep the product whole and real; the teacher consults on drafts at check-ins; the audience sees the product, not the learners' working or the teacher's comments
rows.if: A product or performance for a real audience

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep it; change only what this model says matters: add one moment where learners explain in their own words, and hold back answers during the task
rows.if: The brief names its own routine (a rubric, check-in, prompt or template)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use them as the criteria for peer checking and for the teacher's questions; do not substitute new ones
rows.if: The brief supplies its own categories, criteria or rubric

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Learners decide who sees what they write; the teacher mediates through questions to the whole group and private, opt-in conversation, not by reading entries
rows.if: The material is private or sensitive (personal experience, values, health)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep the goal (2), task (12), and one learner explanation (6 minutes); drop the separate transfer step and set it as a later prompt
rows.if: A fixed short time budget (for example 20 minutes)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Do not split it into exercises; mediate inside it at decision points, with questions and check-ins
rows.if: A whole-task performance the brief wants kept whole (a project, a conversation, a full essay)

rows.basis: [Taiwan's constructivist mathematics reform was stopped in 2003 after its students underperformed](claims/taiwan-constructivist-math-reform-stopped-2003.md) [-M] (a historical account, no statistics)
rows.change: Keep explicit explanation for content the exam requires and use mediation for practice and application; check exam-like performance before widening the change
rows.if: Stakes are high on content coverage (a national exam, a mandated syllabus), or a large-scale reform

rows.basis: untested; from the constructivist-classroom and studio-course pages (teachers who believed in constructivism "often did not know how to use it in practice")
rows.change: Script three or four questions per stage in advance, decide when to step in (after the learner's second unsuccessful attempt), and review one session with a colleague
rows.if: The teacher is new to facilitating

rows.basis: [A home visit before the school year reduced the likelihood of a disciplinary incident (effect size = +0.10)](claims/pthv-home-visit-reduces-disciplinary-incidents.md) [+M] (grades 1–5, matched comparison); [A replication trial with 267 preschoolers found greater gains in social skills and stronger teacher-child and parent-teacher relationships than controls](claims/getting-ready-replication-relationships.md) [+M] (Nebraska preschools, randomised)
rows.change: Lead with a home or chosen-place visit before the year and a partnership programme for any child with behaviour difficulties; keep messages about one concrete home routine
rows.if: Children are young (`child`, pre-K to grade 3)

rows.basis: [Ninth-grade teachers report less communication with and academic support for parents than eighth-grade teachers](claims/ninth-grade-teachers-less-parent-communication.md) [+W] (Chicago teacher surveys); [Parents want more academic interaction with high schools, but schools focus communication on rules and problems](claims/parents-want-academic-interaction-schools-focus-rules.md) [+M]
rows.change: Plan the contact deliberately at the transition, because it tends to fall away there: an early positive call per family in grade 9, and academic content (what the student needs to do well) rather than rules
rows.if: Students are in high school (`adolescent`), especially the first year

rows.basis: [Translation features in mobile apps enabled direct communication between educators and parents who speak languages other than English](claims/app-translation-features-direct-communication.md) [+W] (focus groups, Spanish-speaking parents)
rows.change: Write in the family's language (app translation, an interpreter, a bilingual liaison co-hosting meetings); do not route every contact through one bilingual staff member
rows.if: Families speak a language other than the school's

rows.basis: [Mobile apps increased timely, direct communication between parents and educators during remote schooling](claims/mobile-apps-timely-parent-teacher-communication.md) [~W] (focus groups; perception, no outcome)
rows.change: Make the phone the default channel for everyone (short texts, a call for the first meeting) and treat in-person events as extras, so phone-only families are not second tier
rows.if: Some families meet in person, others only by phone; or contact is phone-only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Rotate: a first message to every family in the first month, then a fortnightly class-level message, and individual calls to five or six families a week, starting with those not yet heard from
rows.if: One teacher, many families (a secondary teacher with 150+ students)

rows.basis: untested proposal; the guidance gap is shown in [Teachers and caregivers called for additional guidance and support in their communication and collaboration](claims/educators-insufficient-guidance-family-communication.md) [+M]
rows.change: Keep two moves only: a positive first contact before any problem, and the rule of calling the family before escalating. Drop regular individual messages before dropping those
rows.if: Teacher time is scarce (volunteers, a busy shift, a few minutes a week)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Make it a listening contact (what the family wants for the child, how to reach them) and end with one agreed next step; do not claim a relationship has been built
rows.if: Only one contact is possible

rows.basis: untested proposal (Mead's two roads, old page)
rows.change: Meet before writing; describe, ask, agree one action each and a date to talk again; explain the teaching method and its reason if that is the complaint; escalate only after two meetings or where policy requires
rows.if: A problem has already happened (behaviour, absence, a complaint about a teaching method)

rows.basis: untested; a limit on this principle
rows.change: Follow the statutory procedure at once; this page does not override it. Keep the relationship by telling the family what will happen where the procedure allows
rows.if: A safeguarding or legally mandated concern

rows.basis: untested proposal; academic content from [Parents want more academic interaction with high schools, but schools focus communication on rules and problems](claims/parents-want-academic-interaction-schools-focus-rules.md) [+M]
rows.change: Keep it; change only what the evidence says matters: the first contact comes before any problem, messages carry academic content, and parents rehearse a home routine rather than receive a handout
rows.if: The school names its own routine (a conference template, a communication app, a home–school agreement)

rows.basis: [Parent Coaching Outperforms Information Only](claims/parent-coaching-outperforms-information-only.md) [+M] (carried from parent-training programmes); the rest untested
rows.change: Speak or meet rather than send long text; show the home routine rather than describe it; ask what they already do with the child and build on it; keep early contacts free of requests
rows.if: Families have low confidence or low literacy, or bad memories of school

rows.basis: untested proposal; group sessions deterring sensitive matters is noted on [Zoom Family Hours](strategies/zoom_family_hours.md)
rows.change: The family decides what is recorded and who sees it; never discuss it in a group session; ask before writing anything down
rows.if: The family's circumstances are private or sensitive (health, immigration status, custody)

rows.basis: [Home visits are rarely offered and rated lowest of any engagement resource, with Black, Latino, and multilingual parents rating them less favorably](claims/home-visits-rare-and-lowest-rated.md) [~M] (parent and teacher surveys)
rows.change: Ask families whether they want a visit and where; offer a school, community or virtual alternative; check afterwards whether they felt it was done well
rows.if: Home visits are proposed for Black, Latino or multilingual families

rows.basis: [Home visits improved standardized math scores (ES = +0.11) but showed no difference in ELA scores](claims/pthv-home-visit-math-gain-no-ela-difference.md) [~M]; [Parent involvement is associated with higher academic achievement in meta-analyses of mostly correlational studies](claims/parent-involvement-improves-achievement.md) [~M] (correlational)
rows.change: Do not promise it: plan the relationship work for trust, behaviour and attendance, and measure achievement as a secondary, longer-run outcome
rows.if: The goal is a gain in test scores this year

rows.basis: untested; carried by analogy from the school setting
rows.change: Read "parents" as the community the learner answers to (an employer, a sponsoring agency, family who shape study time); the move is the same: explain the course to them before relying on attendance rules or sanctions
rows.if: Adult learners (`adult`, `adult-workplace`), with no parents in the picture

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Let the child lead and explain the work; the teacher interprets the standards behind it; ask families one question about what they noticed
rows.if: Learners produce work for families to see (a showcase, a portfolio conference)

rows.basis: [Descriptive user-study patterns suggest GPT output may scaffold lower-prior-knowledge IVDA students but reduce performance when prior knowledge is higher (CV)](claims/gpt-output-effect-depends-on-prior-knowledge-and-domain.md) [~M] (computer science students, descriptive, multiple-choice)
rows.change: Allow tool explanations after an attempt, but keep the unaided check; watch for dependence
rows.if: Learners are `novice` on this task

rows.basis: Same claim [~M]; [Active engagement with AI outputs (cross-verifying, refining prompts, revising) supports productive learning and depends on learners' prior knowledge](claims/active-ai-engagement-depends-on-prior-knowledge.md) [~W] (reported second-hand: more experienced writers revised AI text more thoroughly)
rows.change: Restrict the tool to critique of the learner's own finished work; where AI text is used, require the learner to verify and revise it
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` or already competent on the task

rows.basis: [Digital tools complemented hands-on investigations by providing opportunities not possible in the classroom and letting children easily practice what they learned in hands-on activities.](claims/nico-nor-digital-tools-complement-hands-on.md) [+W] (pilot report, early science); [The impact of AI on learning, motivation, and meaning differs by life stage: AI functions as a supplement for those with established skills but risks bypassing foundational experiences for younger learners](claims/ai-benefits-differ-by-developmental-stage.md) [~W] (theoretical)
rows.change: Keep hands-on exploration first; use digital tools for practice and for what the classroom cannot provide; do not give open generative AI for the core task
rows.if: Learners are `child` (early years or primary)

rows.basis: [Unguarded answer-giving AI harmed unaided exam performance while a guarded version of the same model erased the harm (Bastani et al., 2025, as reported)](claims/gpt4-access-harms-learning-after-withdrawal.md) [+M] (high-school mathematics, reported second-hand)
rows.change: Use a guarded tutor (hints, no answers) for practice and an unaided exam; never an open chatbot for graded practice
rows.if: Learners are `adolescent` (secondary school)

rows.basis: [AI support during drafting lowers ownership substantially more than support during planning or revision, and planning support preserves more ownership than revision support.](claims/drafting-support-largest-ownership-decrease.md) [~M] (adults; ownership ratings, not learning)
rows.change: Keep drafting with the learner; allow AI for planning ideas or for questions on a finished draft
rows.if: Goal is writing, and the learner's ownership of the text matters

rows.basis: [VR-based training with radiation field visualization received significantly higher ratings for radiation understanding and visualization than conventional training (r=0.878)](claims/vr-radiation-visualization-higher-understanding-ratings.md) [+M]; [Conventional training received significantly higher ratings for perceived realism and immersion than VR-based training (r=0.774)](claims/conventional-training-higher-realism-immersion.md) [~M] (20 students with prior procedural training, self-ratings)
rows.change: Teach the procedure hands-on first; add VR for what cannot be seen (radiation, hazards); assess on the real procedure
rows.if: Goal is a clinical or practical procedure (`skill-performance`) in `workplace-clinical` training

rows.basis: [AI-generated and prebuilt simulations produced higher immediate conceptual-assessment scores than physical laboratory work, but the advantage did not persist in later examinations](claims/simulation-advantage-immediate-not-sustained.md) [~M] (one quasi-experiment, reported in a review)
rows.change: Keep at least one physical run of each key experiment; check understanding at a later exam, not only right after
rows.if: Goal is `conceptual-understanding` in a science lab, and simulation is proposed in place of the lab

rows.basis: [Student-defined boundary locations agree internally but often differ from the simulation's calculated values, through how students define the boundary](claims/magnetopause-lab-student-fits-agree-internally-but-differ-from-simulation-values.md) [~W]; [students find crossings well in field data, struggle with particle data, and are unsettled by data sets with no crossing](claims/magnetopause-lab-crossing-search-field-versus-particle-data.md) [~W] (one undergraduate physics lab, instructor observations over eleven years, no comparison; carried to other sciences untested)
rows.change: Run simulation and real data in parallel; learners define their own criterion for the feature and apply it to both; compare their value with the simulation's calculated one and discuss the gap; include at least one real data set without the feature
rows.if: A science lab where real observational or measured data can sit beside a simulation (research data, a field data set)

rows.basis: [AI facilitation of ISLE inquiry is fragile: under student pressure the Gem crossed from scaffolding reasoning to inventing data](claims/ai-facilitation-fragile-invents-data.md) [-M]; [In a small case study, students given ChatGPT feedback valued its immediacy and alternative analytical perspectives, but one distrusted its answers as 'often made up' for complex data analysis](claims/chatgpt-feedback-hallucination-undermines-trust.md) [~W]; in a study reported by a scoping review, [only 6 of 23 students learned a set of criteria correctly from ChatGPT self-study, against all 23 from internet search, and the model had fabricated a similarly named syndrome](claims/genai-self-study-fabrication-curated-resources.md) [~W] (medical students, second-hand)
rows.change: Learners record their own measurements; require a source or a check for every AI-supplied value
rows.if: The tool reports facts or data the learner cannot check (a chatbot in a lab, AI feedback on data analysis)

rows.basis: [In one preregistered experiment, metacognitive feedback on learners' own LLM use lowered the odds of answer offloading and raised the odds of a correct unaided answer on one-sided tests, with 95% intervals reaching no effect](claims/metacognitive-feedback-reduces-llm-answer-offloading-improves-unaided-performance.md) [+M] (online experiment); [A brief metacognitive reflection prompt reduces acceptance of incorrect AI advice compared with open ChatGPT support alone](claims/reflection-reduces-incorrect-ai-advice-acceptance.md) [+M]
rows.change: Build in the reflection prompt before accepting AI answers and an automated report of each learner's own offloading; end each module with an unaided item
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: [Real-time AI alerts can expand teachers' situational awareness but in some cases overload teachers' attention or draw focus away from their own observation flow](claims/ai-alerts-can-overload-teacher-attention.md) [~W] (K-12 review, reported second-hand); [Teachers who positioned AI as a partner remained instructional leaders, weaving the tool into rich instruction and using score data to decide what to re-teach](claims/partner-positioning-instructional-leadership.md) [+M] (qualitative)
rows.change: Limit alerts to a few the teacher acts on; the teacher keeps their own observation round; the teacher decides re-teaching from the data
rows.if: `classroom` with one teacher and many learners, teacher-facing AI alerts or dashboards

rows.basis: [Teachers reported that rubric-aligned AI feedback saved time on repetitive comments, enabling focus on higher-order instruction](claims/teachers-report-time-savings-higher-order-instruction.md) [+W] (five teachers' self-reports); [Reflective and hybrid feedback outperform direct GenAI feedback on delayed AI-free transfer](claims/agentic-designs-delayed-ai-free-transfer.md) [+M]
rows.change: Use rubric-aligned AI comments for routine points and spend the teacher's minutes on one higher-order comment per learner; keep the learner revising
rows.if: Scarce facilitator time (one tutor for many drafts, volunteers, a busy shift)

rows.basis: [In unguided GenAI collaboration, ethnic minority preparatory students' strategy talk co-occurred with passive sharing and uncritical acceptance, forming a plan-and-paste loop](claims/unguided-strategy-talk-plan-and-paste-loop.md) [+W]; [After scaffolding, strategy talk reconfigured around summarizing, critical evaluation, and co-construction, indicating repurposing toward critical scrutiny of AI outputs](claims/scaffolded-strategy-talk-repurposed-critical-evaluation.md) [+W] (one design study, groups of preparatory students over two weeks; carried to low literacy untested)
rows.change: Teach how to question and summarise AI output in a scaffolded group task; do not rely on technical training or unguided use
rows.if: Learners are under-resourced, have low confidence with the tool or low literacy

rows.basis: [Nearly all postgraduate research students in the study used GenAI across multiple research stages, positioning it as a supportive assistant with human oversight retained](claims/pgr-genai-supportive-assistant-human-oversight.md) [+W] (focus groups, 27 of 28 students; reported use, not outcomes); in the same study, [students rejected AI generation of research ideas, original arguments or whole papers while accepting surface-level support](claims/genai-authorship-boundary-rejected-substitution.md) [+W] and [found AI ideation acceptable only while they kept decision-making authority](claims/conditional-ideation-dialogic-aid-vs-outsourcing.md) [+W] (one qualitative study, stated norms); the unaided task is an untested proposal
rows.change: Teach the tool as part of the work, with explicit human checks at each stage; agree with the learners which parts the tool may do (language polishing, searching, summarising) and which stay theirs (the idea, the argument, the judgement), starting from the line they already draw; still keep one unaided task for the core judgement
rows.if: Adults in work settings or postgraduate researchers who will use the tool in their job

rows.basis: [After a lesson on LLM use, the share of physics students using LLMs for solutions more often than they believed ideal rose from 53% to 75%](claims/usage-exceeds-ideal-for-solution-generation.md) [+W] (one course, pre/post self-report, no comparison group); [most participants given an AI assistant reported using it mainly to get answers, matching their chat logs](claims/majority-use-ai-for-direct-answers.md) [+W] (online adults)
rows.change: Keep the lesson or policy, but do not count on it: also configure the tool for hints (step 3), show each learner their own use pattern (step 6) and keep the unaided check
rows.if: The brief relies on telling learners about AI risks (a lesson, a policy, an honour statement) to keep them doing the work

rows.basis: Untested proposal as a plan; the single-session effect of AI use on an unaided test is in [the fraction-problem experiment](claims/ai-assistance-impairs-unassisted-fraction-performance-exp1.md) [+M]
rows.change: Independent attempt (10 minutes), tool in hint mode (20 minutes), unaided check (5 to 10 minutes); report only the unaided check, and claim no retention
rows.if: Time is one session only

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Spend it on the independent attempt and the unaided check; let the tool be used outside it, and do not cut the check to make room for tool use
rows.if: A fixed short time budget (for example 30 minutes a week)

rows.basis: Untested proposal; [Greater answer offloading during learning is associated with lower subsequent unaided performance (exploratory)](claims/answer-offloading-associated-lower-unaided-performance-exploratory.md) [+M]
rows.change: Make sure the unaided form is practised before the assessment (unaided checks in each session); keep any assisted work the brief grades, and record tool use on it
rows.if: Stakes are high, or the final assessment is unaided

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Keep the task whole; place the tool after the learner's full attempt, as critique, rather than splitting the task into AI-assisted parts
rows.if: A whole-task performance the brief wants kept whole (a full essay, a full procedure, a full investigation)

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Give everyone the same independent attempt and unaided check in a form that works on a phone (short typed answer, photo of handwritten work); keep tool settings the same for all
rows.if: Mixed modes: some learners remote, some in the room, or phone-only

rows.basis: Untested proposal; ownership evidence as in the writing row ([drafting support](claims/drafting-support-largest-ownership-decrease.md) [~M])
rows.change: Make the authorship rule public (which parts the tool may do) and have learners state how they used it; keep drafting with the learner
rows.if: A product or performance for a real audience

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Keep it; change only what the evidence says matters: whether the tool gives solutions or hints, and whether there is an unaided check
rows.if: The brief names its own routine (its AI-use policy, rubric, prompt template or check-in)

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Use them as the tool's feedback criteria and as the unaided check's criteria; do not substitute this page's
rows.if: The brief gives its own categories, criteria or rubric

rows.basis: Untested proposal as an assessment design; the reason for the added unaided check is [Greater answer offloading during learning is associated with lower subsequent unaided performance (exploratory)](claims/answer-offloading-associated-lower-unaided-performance-exploratory.md) [+M], which says nothing against assessing tool use
rows.change: Keep those criteria as given and grade them; add a short unaided check beside them, reported separately; ask for a brief note with each assisted submission of what the tool did and why the learner accepted or changed it
rows.if: The brief's rubric scores tool use itself (appropriate use, the learner's justification of it, the assisted product)

rows.basis: Untested proposal; the hint-not-solution reasoning is carried from [How genAI is used, not who uses it, predicts whether independent performance declines or improves](claims/persistence-costs-concentrated-among-direct-solution-users.md) [+M] (online settings, not offline)
rows.change: Do not plan around a live tool. Use offline materials: worked examples and hint cards the learner opens only after an attempt (paper, or files preloaded on the device), answer keys with explanations to check their own work, a printed self-check card for any pre-generated tool output; keep the independent attempt and the unaided check exactly as in the default; if a tool is available only at set times (a supervised session, a sync point), use it then for critique of work already done offline
rows.if: Offline or no connection (a prison, a remote site, a phone with no data), so no live AI or simulation

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Make each session self-contained: one independent attempt, hints after, one unaided check, a few minutes each; open each return with a short unaided item on the last topic before new work; let a learner move to freer tool use only after two unaided checks in a row are close to their assisted work, however far apart the sessions
rows.if: Intermittent attendance (learners miss sessions, shift work, release dates, irregular study on a mobile device)

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: The learner decides what goes into the tool; use local or institution-approved tools; never require uploading private work
rows.if: Private or sensitive material (personal writing, patient data, learner records)

rows.basis: Untested proposal; from the folded collision-carts page
rows.change: Say what the simulation omits; add recorded real-world video to analyse; schedule hands-on practice before any assessment of the procedure
rows.if: No physical equipment or hands-on practice is available

rows.basis: [Discussion board interactions generated no negative feedback at all, suggesting synchrony is required to foster corrective feedback](claims/discussion-board-no-negative-feedback-synchrony-required.md) [+M] (12 groups of French biology students, descriptive mode comparison; carried to other languages untested)
rows.change: Use small-group chat on closed tasks with content prepared beforehand; keep the chat synchronous rather than a board where correction is wanted; review logs for self-correction afterwards
rows.if: Learners are second-language learners and the goal is negotiating meaning or accuracy

rows.basis: [Videoconferencing was conducive to more negotiation of meaning than text chat and discussion board, measured as proportion of negotiated turns](claims/videoconferencing-more-negotiated-turns-than-chat-and-board.md) [~M] (one study, proportions of turns, no learning outcome)
rows.change: Use chat as a rehearsal stage only: run the task in chat first, then the same task by audio or video, where turns are longer and more of them are negotiated
rows.if: The goal is spoken interaction or oral proficiency

rows.basis: [Content-related problems trigger most negotiation routines, and syntactic triggers are absent from text chat where turns are short](claims/content-triggers-dominate-syntactic-triggers-absent-text-chat.md) [~M] (chat turns about 9 words against 55 and 130; one study)
rows.change: Do not rely on chat; use a board, shared document or spoken discussion, and bring only short questions to the chat
rows.if: The goal is extended argument, explanation or syntax practice

rows.basis: [Closed meaning-focused tasks foster more negotiation of meaning and negative feedback than open tasks in CMC](claims/closed-tasks-foster-more-negotiation-than-open-tasks.md) [+M]; [subtitled videos before chat tasks](claims/subtitled-videos-increase-negotiation-of-meaning-online-tbll.md) [+M]; [Unfocused tasks elicit significantly more confirmation checks and clarification requests than focused tasks](claims/unfocused-tasks-more-confirmation-and-clarification-strategies.md) [~M] (36 learners, mode not stated on the claim page: a qualification on "closed is always better")
rows.change: Give a closed task with one outcome and 5–10 minutes of prepared content first; supply sentence starters for the first session
rows.if: Learners are `novice` in the language or the topic, or the task is open

rows.basis: untested proposal; contingency at class scale is not shown ([Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support.](claims/contingent-scaffolding-improves-learning.md) [~M])
rows.change: Use one class chat as a question and example channel with a named monitor and planned pauses every 10–15 minutes; for task conversations, split into groups of two to four with their own chats
rows.if: One teacher with a large class, or a lecture or presentation

rows.basis: untested proposal; see also [Social Presence](principles/social-presence.md) for mixed groups
rows.change: Run one shared chat for everyone, in-room learners included, so remote learners' questions sit beside the room's; the monitor reads remote posts first at each pause; keep messages short enough to type on a phone and allow voice notes
rows.if: Mixed mode: some learners in the room, some remote; or some on phones only
