rows.basis: [Iterative redesign of a peer-feedback task increased class engagement across three rounds](claims/iterative-task-redesign-increased-engagement.md) [+M] (one teacher's blended language classes; no comparison group)
rows.change: Open with anonymous or ungraded posts of a specific kind (what you heard, one question), then named posts in small groups once the norms hold
rows.if: Learners have low confidence speaking aloud, or are new to the group

rows.basis: untested proposal; from the earlier page's access and typing constraint
rows.change: Allow dictation ([Speech-to-text](elements/speech-to-text.md)) or voice notes in the chat; give more time per turn, a dyad rather than a group of four, and pre-written phrases they can paste
rows.if: Learners have low literacy or slow typing, or a disability affecting typing

rows.basis: untested proposal; the chat studies here are with university students or adult learners
rows.change: Keep chats teacher-visible and within a class platform; dyads or groups of three; 10 minutes per segment; one closed task
rows.if: `child` learners, or `adolescent` learners in school

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use the team's own chat tool and a real decision from their work as the closed task; agree what is kept from the log
rows.if: `adult` learners in a work setting

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Do not run it in a group chat; use a one-to-one channel the learner controls, or an anonymous question box; say who can read the log and how long it is kept
rows.if: Material is private or sensitive (health, personal history, workplace conflict)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Give each group a closed task with a written outcome to post, a learner monitor, and one check-in per segment by the tutor reading only the posted outcomes
rows.if: Facilitator time is scarce (a volunteer, a busy shift, one tutor checking in briefly)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: 5 minutes norms and task, 5–10 minutes preparation, 10–15 minutes chat in groups of two to four, 5 minutes for each group to post its outcome; do not add a quiz or review the brief did not ask for
rows.if: Single session only, or a fixed short time budget (for example 30 minutes)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep it; change only what the evidence here says matters: make the task closed, prepare the content, or name a monitor
rows.if: The brief names its own routine for chat (its protocol, prompts, rubric or categories)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Run the whole task in chat or by voice as one piece; use the log afterwards for review, not to split the task into separate chat items
rows.if: The brief wants a whole-task performance kept whole (a negotiation, a case conference, a client conversation)

rows.basis: [In-class chat engagement significantly predicts higher test scores in MAIC courses](claims/chat-engagement-predicts-test-scores.md) [~M] (correlational, controlling for earlier module scores; does not show chat caused the scores)
rows.change: Treat chat activity as a signal of engagement, not of learning; check learning with an unaided task
rows.if: The chat partners include AI agents or an AI tutor

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Grade the posted outcome or summary, not message count or speed; never judge proficiency from chat alone, where turns are short and self-corrected
rows.if: Stakes are high, or chat posts will be graded

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page ("some learners comprehend better through print")
rows.change: Do not build the lesson around speech; offer it as an optional control for fatigue or proofreading only, and keep it off during reading practice and any check of reading
rows.if: Learners are fluent readers of this text (`advanced` for its print), or the goal includes reading the words unaided

rows.basis: [Repeated listening improves oral reading fluency in second-grade students, with Listening Only outgaining Reading While Listening and Reading Only](claims/repeated-listening-improves-oral-reading-fluency.md) [~M] (one seven-week study of 75 second graders, reported second-hand in a review; reading while listening had the smallest fluency gain and an average comprehension loss; no statistical test printed)
rows.change: Use speech or read-along for access to stories and content above their reading level, not as the main fluency practice; keep the child reading the words aloud themselves in separate practice, and check comprehension after read-along rather than assuming it
rows.if: Learners are `child` early readers building fluency

rows.basis: [Audio narration with finger-tracking animation directs bilingual preschoolers' attention to the target-language print in dual-language e-books, including the nondominant language](claims/enhancing-features-direct-attention-dual-language-e-books.md) [+M]; [Multimedia features improved story comprehension in dual-language e-books (marginal trend) but not in single-language e-books](claims/comprehension-benefit-dual-language-only.md) [~M] (one eye-tracking study, bilingual preschoolers)
rows.change: Choose narration with a highlight that tracks the words, in the language whose print the child should look at; ask two or three story questions after, since attention to print did not reliably become comprehension
rows.if: Young children with an e-book or app, possibly in two languages

rows.basis: [Phonics instruction has a small but statistically confirmed effect for children with reading disabilities, while Orton-Gillingham structured-literacy programs show positive but non-significant effects](claims/structured-literacy-interventions-help-struggling-readers.md) [~M] (speech itself untested here)
rows.change: Give speech for content reading and tests of content in every subject; keep explicit decoding instruction in its own time; record that the content scores were earned with speech
rows.if: Learners have a reading disability or dyslexia

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page (vision loss); [Universal Design for Learning](principles/universal-design-for-learning.md) holds the alternative-route rule
rows.change: The learner will not follow print, so make the text navigable by ear: real headings, alternative text on images, tables that read in order, equations in a speakable form; let the learner use their own screen reader and settings rather than an in-app voice
rows.if: Learners have low vision or are blind and use a screen reader

rows.basis: [Reading and listening yield similar proportions of incidental vocabulary learning, with reading ahead only on some immediate posttests](claims/reading-versus-listening-incidental-vocabulary-gains.md) [~S] (second-language vocabulary only; says nothing about synthetic voices)
rows.change: Use speech to hear the pronunciation of new words while reading them and to read along with texts at their listening level; expect vocabulary from listening or read-along to be learned at proportions similar to reading, with reading ahead on immediate tests only
rows.if: Second-language learners

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Let workers listen to the document on their own device, in sections, and act on each section (find the step, fill the field) rather than only listen; fix the voice's pronunciation of product names and codes first
rows.if: Adults in work settings (manuals, procedures, compliance documents, forms)

rows.basis: [Presenting words as spoken narration rather than on-screen text alongside graphics improves learning](claims/modality-effect-narration-over-text.md) [~S]; [Redundant on-screen text impairs learning when it competes with a visualization, though written text duplicating narration alone can help](claims/redundancy-principle.md) [~M] (multimedia lessons with recorded narration, carried to synthetic speech)
rows.change: Speak the explanation and show only labels and key terms on the visual; if the learner controls pace, full text can stay available on demand
rows.if: The text explains a diagram, animation or chart

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page (synthetic voices distort domain vocabulary)
rows.change: Do not rely on default speech; provide a version written for listening or a human recording, or limit speech to the prose around the notation
rows.if: Text is dense with notation (equations, code, tables, citations)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Build the speech control into every page and question, put a question or summary prompt at each section break with automatic checking where possible, and add the periodic with/without check from the default arc
rows.if: Setting is `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Give everyone the same digital text so each can use their own device's speech with headphones; for phone-only learners, keep sections short enough for one screen and avoid layouts that read out of order
rows.if: Mixed modes: some learners remote, some in the room, or phone-only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Make speech available to all rather than assigned to a few; at each section break use a whole-class check (a quick poll or one written line) so the teacher sees who is lost, and go to those learners
rows.if: One teacher for a large class

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Spend the facilitator's time once, on showing the controls and the section-break routine; after that, the learner works alone with the supplied questions, and the facilitator looks only at the answers to one or two questions per text
rows.if: Scarce facilitator time (volunteers, a busy shift, a brief check-in)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Ten minutes on the controls with a short text, then one section-by-section reading of the real text with supplied questions; record the answers and do not claim lasting benefit
rows.if: A single session only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Offer speech privately (headphones, own device), as a normal option for everyone rather than a label; let the learner choose rate and voice; start on short texts that matter to them
rows.if: Learners with low confidence or low literacy, adult or child

rows.basis: untested; follows from step 1
rows.change: If the test measures content, allow speech as an accommodation and say so in the record; if it measures reading, do not, and give the learner a fair version of the test that does not depend on speech for its instructions
rows.if: Stakes are high, or the test is meant to measure reading

rows.basis: untested proposal (a lesson from page testing, not from a claim)
rows.change: Keep that routine and its categories as given; add only speech for the text and a break at each section where the routine's own question or code is applied
rows.if: The brief names its own routine (its reading log, question set, rubric, annotation code or listening guide)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: The learner decides who hears it: headphones, their own device, and an on-device voice rather than a cloud service where the text would leave the device; nobody else listens unless the learner asks
rows.if: The material is private or sensitive (a learner's own writing, a health or HR document, a personal letter)

rows.basis: untested proposal (speech runs at roughly the voice's set rate, so time the actual audio first)
rows.change: Fit the text to it: one text of about 600–900 words in three or four sections, 3–4 minutes of listening per section plus one minute at each break, the last five minutes for the brief's own task
rows.if: A fixed short time budget (for example, 20 minutes)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep the real document and the real decision; use speech and section breaks inside it, and do not split it into separate comprehension items
rows.if: The brief wants a whole task kept whole (read a real policy and decide; follow a real procedure)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: For proofreading, have the learner listen to their draft at a slow rate and mark every place it sounds wrong. For audio a real audience will hear, check every name and term by ear and have a person approve it before release
rows.if: Learners use speech on their own writing, or produce audio for a real audience (an announcement, a podcast, a museum guide)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use short texts (about 100–250 words, one procedure) read sentence by sentence; teach playback control as a skill (slow the voice, replay a sentence, replay a single word for pronunciation) and let learners practise privately with headphones; give teacher feedback in a form TTS can read aloud; each lesson end with one unaided reread of a step. If the brief names its own assessment (accuracy, control of playback, a reflection comparing listening and unaided reading), assess exactly those, and keep checks to one or two items so the class is not mostly testing
rows.if: Adult second-language learners in short evening classes, reading workplace instructions

rows.basis: [Part-task practice reduces cognitive load for absolute novices during initial skill acquisition.](claims/part-task-practice-reduces-load-for-novices.md) [~M] (load, not transfer); [interleaving](claims/interleaving-improves-inductive-learning.md) [~M] (claim page notes novel material can reverse the benefit)
rows.change: Secure the taught case first with worked examples and guided practice; start with two cases, not four; practise parts briefly before integrating; delay mixing until each type has been introduced
rows.if: Learners are `novice` on this task, or the task is high in element interactivity

rows.basis: [Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows.](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M] (review of cognitive-load studies; not about transfer designs)
rows.change: Skip the early stage; give unprompted varied and far cases with selective feedback, and ask learners to generate their own cases
rows.if: Learners are `advanced`, or already solve the taught case unaided

rows.basis: untested; the case-comparison and retrieval-transfer evidence here is mostly with undergraduates
rows.change: Use concrete, familiar surface forms; give the comparison prompt every time and state the principle yourself; keep to two cases per session
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary age)

rows.basis: [The closer training content is to authentic clinical scenarios, the smoother its translation into practice](claims/contextualized-teaching-facilitates-transfer.md) [+W] (interviews with neurosurgical nurses; perceived, not measured)
rows.change: Take the late-stage cases from their own work; ask them to bring one; check that their workplace offers the cases and equipment to use the skill
rows.if: Learners are `adult` or professionals

rows.basis: [Analogical Reasoning Improves Transfer](claims/comparing-contrasting-cases-improves-learning.md) [+S] (undergraduates, negotiation; meta-analysis across domains)
rows.change: Pair cases and prompt comparison before stating the principle; test on new cases rather than definitions
rows.if: Goal is a `principle` or `concept` to be used in new cases

rows.basis: [Interleaving category examples improves inductive category learning for visual and mathematical materials, but not for expository texts or word categories](claims/interleaving-improves-inductive-learning.md) [~M] (classification of new examples; smaller for mathematics, reversed for word categories)
rows.change: Mix problem types in practice once each is introduced, so the learner must decide which applies; expect slower, error-prone practice
rows.if: Goal is choosing among several `procedure`s (which method fits which problem)

rows.basis: [Task rehearsal improves fluency and complexity on the repeated task but does not transfer to a new task of the same type](claims/task-repetition-fluency-complexity-same-task-only.md) [~M] (second-hand report of one language-learning study)
rows.change: Vary the task within the type rather than repeating one task; repeat a task only to build fluency on that task
rows.if: Goal is spoken or performed fluency on a type of task (e.g. a language task)

rows.basis: [Retrieval Practice Improves Transfer](claims/retrieval-practice-improves-transfer.md) [~S] (lab and prose-passage studies; carried to self-paced courses untested)
rows.change: Build the comparison prompt and the principle statement into the materials; use automatically checked retrieval questions in changed formats; add an unprompted transfer item before the next unit
rows.if: Setting is `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: [Analogical Reasoning Improves Transfer](claims/comparing-contrasting-cases-improves-learning.md) [+S] (immediate tests favoured in the meta-analysis)
rows.change: Teach two cases side by side, prompt the comparison, state the principle, and end with one near-transfer item; do not claim far or delayed transfer
rows.if: Time is one session only

rows.basis: untested; the comparison evidence includes classroom experiments in the meta-analysis but no class-size result
rows.change: Pairs compare the two cases on one sheet and write what is the same; the teacher collects answers and states the principle from them; every learner does one unaided transfer item on paper
rows.if: `classroom` with one teacher and a large group

rows.basis: [All learners … showed a floor effect on far-transfer problems](claims/far-transfer-floor-effect-and-equal-time.md) [~M]; [no increases for far-transfer problems](claims/germane-load-gains-limited-to-identical-and-near-transfer-problems.md) [~W] (one study each, engineering and a game task)
rows.change: Add cases from the target domain itself rather than relying on transfer from another; assess on representative target tasks after a delay
rows.if: Stakes are high, or the objective is far transfer to another domain

rows.basis: [Transfer of advanced competencies is limited by institutional case exposure, technical platforms, and multidisciplinary maturity rather than training deficiencies](claims/advanced-competency-transfer-limited-by-institutional-resources.md) [~W] (interviews, one programme in China)
rows.change: Agree with the workplace when the learner will meet the cases; plan refresher cases or simulation if they will not; report use separately from knowledge
rows.if: `workplace-clinical`, and the course teaches advanced competencies the setting rarely uses

rows.basis: [Explicit instruction produces greater learning than unassisted discovery learning under most conditions](claims/minimal-guidance-less-effective-for-novices.md) [-M] (meta-analysis across domains; not studio-specific)
rows.change: Demonstrate and explain the procedure first; keep clue-led exploration for the principle the procedure serves
rows.if: Learners are `novice` on a procedure or technique they have never seen (a drawing convention, software steps)

rows.basis: [The advantage of guidance begins to recede only when learners have sufficiently high prior knowledge to provide internal guidance](claims/guidance-advantage-recedes-with-high-prior-knowledge.md) [~M] (a review's statement; gives no crossover point)
rows.change: Fewer, looser clues; learners set their own problems and lead the critique; the teacher only asks
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` on the target, or already name and use the principle

rows.basis: [Productive Failure Improves Conceptual Learning](claims/productive-failure-improves-conceptual-learning.md) [~S] (problem-first reversed for second to fifth graders); [Age moderates discovery-learning effects: the explicit-instruction advantage over unassisted discovery is larger for adolescents than adults, and the enhanced-discovery benefit larger for adults than children](claims/age-moderates-discovery-effects.md) [~M]
rows.change: Name and show the idea first, then a short guided exploration with the teacher at the table; keep critique to two or three works
rows.if: Learners are `child` (about 7 to 11)

rows.basis: [Age moderates discovery-learning effects: the explicit-instruction advantage over unassisted discovery is larger for adolescents than adults, and the enhanced-discovery benefit larger for adults than children](claims/age-moderates-discovery-effects.md) [~M]
rows.change: Keep exploration guided throughout (prepared questions, a teacher check-in per group); never leave a group to discover alone
rows.if: Learners are `adolescent`

rows.basis: Untested for adults at work; carried from a high-school English unit ([Positioning personal experience as an epistemic resource supports expansion from inward to outward critical orientations](claims/positioning-personal-experience-as-epistemic-resource-supports-critical-orientation-expansion.md) [+W])
rows.change: Start from a case from their own work as the problem; use their experience as material the analysis is built on, not a warm-up; name the principle with their cases
rows.if: Learners are `adult` in a work setting (`adult-workplace`)

rows.basis: [Discussion promotes more active thinking than lecture, though lecture is no worse for transmitting information](claims/discussion-promotes-more-active-thought-than-lecture.md) [~M] (college teaching, older reviews)
rows.change: Tell it, clearly and briefly; keep exploration for the parts that need understanding
rows.if: Goal is information to remember (facts, terms, rules to recall)

rows.basis: [For domain-general skills, one meta-analysis finds a negligible effect (g = −0.17) in favour of I-PS over PS-I](claims/domain-general-skills-favor-ips.md) [-M]
rows.change: Teach the strategy first, then practise it on varied problems
rows.if: Goal is a domain-general skill (designing a fair test, a general reasoning strategy)

rows.basis: Untested at scale; the recorded episodes show the unprepared teacher interjecting explanation was the more frequent pattern ([Subtle teacher guidance, not imposition, enables interdisciplinary integration in small-group deliberation](claims/subtle-teacher-guidance-not-imposition-enables-interdisciplinary-integration.md) [~W])
rows.change: Groups explore; the teacher circulates with three or four prepared guiding questions per week, joins each group once, and critiques a sample of six to eight works with the whole room
rows.if: One teacher with a large group or many groups

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Put the guiding questions on a card the group works through; the tutor's one visit asks a single question on the group's own partial idea and checks the closing naming of the principle
rows.if: Facilitator time is scarce (one tutor dropping in, volunteers)

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: 5 minutes clue and problem; 15 minutes making; 15 minutes critique of four or five works; 10 minutes naming the principle from those works; 5 minutes on one new case. Do not claim lasting understanding
rows.if: Single session only, or a fixed short time (for example 50 minutes)

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Learners photograph or upload each version to one shared board; critique on the shared screen with remote learners speaking first; questions in the chat when voice is not possible
rows.if: Some learners remote, others in the room; or learners on phones only

rows.basis: Untested here; carried from mathematics: [Erroneous examples improve conceptual understanding by forcing comparison with correct models.](claims/erroneous-examples-build-conceptual-knowledge.md) [+M]; [PS-I fosters learning only if specific design features (contrasting cases or building instruction on student solutions) are implemented](claims/ps-i-fosters-learning-only-with-contrasting-cases-or-student-solutions.md) [~M]
rows.change: Build the questions into the task as prompts after each attempt; then show contrasting example works (one that shows the principle, one that breaks it) and a short explanation that refers back to the learner's attempt
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: Untested proposal; see [impersonal critique](principles/understanding-cultivated-not-described.md)
rows.change: Critique the work, not the maker; let works be shown without names; allow a learner to explain by pointing and sketching; open each critique with what works
rows.if: Learners have low confidence, low literacy, or find public critique hard

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: The learner decides what is shown to the group and what stays with them; critique only what is shared
rows.if: The material is private or personal (own experiences, own life as the problem)

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Keep the routine and its categories as given; change only the teacher's move during making (a question instead of an explanation) and add the closing naming of the principle
rows.if: The brief names its own critique routine, rubric or criteria (a jury format, a programme rubric, its own categories)

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Do not split it into exercises; put the clue inside the project brief and run question-led check-ins at its stages
rows.if: The brief wants a whole project kept whole (a full design, a performance)

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: State the constraints directly at the start; explore within them; check the final work against them explicitly
rows.if: The work goes to a real audience or client, or has non-negotiable constraints (safety, codes, accessibility)

rows.basis: [Erroneous examples improve conceptual understanding by forcing comparison with correct models.](claims/erroneous-examples-build-conceptual-knowledge.md) [+M] (children, decimals; carried to design critique)
rows.change: Put a work showing that error beside one that does not and ask what differs, before naming the principle
rows.if: The brief reports an error learners actually made (for example, symmetry everywhere read as balance)

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: The check is the learner's own explanation of their work and of one new case during the critique; add nothing graded
rows.if: The brief asks for no test or quiz

rows.basis: [Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows.](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M] and [Multiple representations improve learning](claims/multiple-representations-improve-learning.md) [~M] (benefit depends on skill at connecting representations); bounding the number of options is untested
rows.change: Curate options to two or three; integrate representations rather than offering many in parallel; model each choice before asking for it
rows.if: Learners are `novice` on this content

rows.basis: [Instructional guidance that helps novices can become redundant or counterproductive as expertise grows.](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M] (cognitive-load studies; no crossover point given)
rows.change: Drop the extra representations and step-by-step supports by default and leave them available on request; widen choice of task and format
rows.if: Learners are `advanced`, or succeed on the first task unaided

rows.basis: untested proposal; the learning-styles experiment with fifth graders shows only that matching to a reported style did not help ([Learning Styles Matching Does Not Improve Learning](claims/learning-styles-matching-does-not-improve-learning.md) [~S])
rows.change: Fewer, concrete choices (pick one of two); the teacher demonstrates each support; read-aloud and picture supports by default
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary age)

rows.basis: [modifications may be necessary for older beginners and learners with disabilities](claims/modifications-essential-for-vulnerable-learners.md) [~W] (one practitioner's judgment, adult ESL)
rows.change: Ask learners which barriers they meet; keep individual accommodations; offer formats drawn from their own work
rows.if: Learners are `adult` or professionals, including older beginners or learners with disabilities

rows.basis: [Learning Styles Matching Does Not Improve Learning](claims/learning-styles-matching-does-not-improve-learning.md) [~S] (systematic review and a randomized experiment with fifth graders)
rows.change: Do not; offer the routes to everyone and let content decide the primary mode (a diagram for spatial structure, speech for pronunciation)
rows.if: A colleague proposes assigning materials by each learner's "learning style"

rows.basis: [Multiple representations improve learning](claims/multiple-representations-improve-learning.md) [+M] (undergraduate physics, one field study) and [Adding relevant pictures or graphics to text improves learning from it, with a small pooled effect on reading comprehension, though whether dual coding explains the benefit is disputed](claims/dual-coding-improves-learning.md) [+S] (comprehension from text with graphics)
rows.change: Pair a visual and a verbal representation of the same relation and ask learners to translate between them; feedback on the process, not only the answer
rows.if: Goal is a `concept` or `principle`

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page (options in how learners engage and access, not in what they are expected to learn)
rows.change: Keep the expression format fixed; vary only the routes into the content and the practice supports
rows.if: Goal is a `procedure` or `complex-skill` whose format *is* the goal (handwriting, oral fluency, a clinical technique)

rows.basis: [Letting learners pace instruction helped on complex material in one experiment](claims/learner-paced-beats-system-paced-complex-material.md) [~M] (primary-school animation and a meta-analysis of learner control; achievement gain not general); the rest untested
rows.change: Build the access layers into the media (editable text, captions and transcripts, pause and replay, glossary links); give automatic, criterion-referenced feedback on each product format
rows.if: Setting is `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: [Redundant on-screen text impairs learning when it competes with a visualization](claims/redundancy-principle.md) [~M] (lab multimedia lessons; captions remain a necessary accommodation for deaf and hard-of-hearing learners)
rows.change: Captions on request rather than always on; put essential words in the narration; give a transcript separately
rows.if: Narrated video or animation is the main medium

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Offer choice at the level of the whole task (two versions of one activity) rather than per learner; one shared rubric displayed for all formats; check-ins on who is stuck

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Do only steps 1, 3 and 4 (goal, two routes into the content, segmenting and pause); skip format choice
rows.if: Time is a single session

rows.basis: untested proposal; the concern that a single verbal format underestimates some learners is [an argument](claims/verbal-achievement-tests-may-underestimate-via-symbolic-mismatch.md) [+W]
rows.change: Validate that each expression format measures the same capability before allowing it; mark anchor samples in every format; record accommodations given
rows.if: Stakes are high (certification, grading)

rows.basis: [Autonomy support increases intrinsic motivation, engagement, and persistence](claims/autonomy-supports-intrinsic-motivation.md) [+M] (motivation outcomes; learning outcomes weaker, see [Autonomy](principles/autonomy.md))

rows.if: Learners have stopped engaging, or work only for marks

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page (largest payoff for novices to the interface's conventions)
rows.change: Add the first-session walk-through (step 9) and test with first-time users; use plain labels from their own words, not system terms
rows.if: Users are `novice` with this kind of interface, or new to digital learning

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep the platform's conventions rather than inventing new ones; test only the new or changed tasks; skip the orientation
rows.if: Users are experienced with this platform's conventions

rows.basis: untested proposal for the session design; adults rating a tool for children: [Adults rated the LLM-powered iCub storytelling system as usable, with a total SUS score of 76.70 indicating good product usability](claims/icub-storytelling-sus-76-good-usability.md) [~W] (25 adults rated a storytelling robot that most of them judged suited to children under 10; no children were tested, so the rating says nothing about whether children can use it)
rows.change: Test with children of the age, in the setting, with a teacher or parent present and consent from both; watch rather than ask (ratings questionnaires are written for adults); keep sessions to 15–20 minutes; adults' ratings on a child's behalf do not replace a test with children
rows.if: Learners are `child`

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Test in their workflow, on their work device, in 20–30 minute sessions; put the tasks they do most on the first screen
rows.if: Learners are `adult` or `adult-workplace` users with little time

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page (accessibility-dependent learners named as a main beneficiary)
rows.change: Recruit them for every test round, not a final check; test each core task with their own assistive technology; include them in the card sort
rows.if: Learners depend on accessibility features (screen readers, captions, keyboard only; learners with autism or attention differences)

rows.basis: [Students encountered usability obstacles: text-recognition errors, feedback-generation delays, and overly complex vocabulary](claims/ai-helper-usability-obstacles.md) [~W] (one think-aloud case study of an AI feedback tool; carried to interfaces generally)
rows.change: Use short labels, icons with text, and feedback vocabulary they use; test whether they can say back what a message means
rows.if: Learners have low literacy or are working in a second language

rows.basis: [Participants who accessed the report card site with mobile devices had more difficulty using it](claims/mobile-access-increases-report-card-difficulty.md) [~M] (report card site, not a course; the mixed-mode part is an untested proposal)
rows.change: Design the phone layout first and test on phones in every round; run remote test sessions by screen share and in-room ones by observation, on the same tasks
rows.if: Many users are on phones, or some join remotely while others are in the room

rows.basis: [Technical issues (login scanning, internet connectivity, projector setup, and glitches) frustrated students and created a significant barrier to playlist implementation](claims/technical-issues-barrier-playlist-implementation.md) [-M]; [Digital game loading time caused issues but students had no significant navigation problems once the game loaded.](claims/hero-elementary-game-loading-time-navigation-issues.md) [~W]
rows.change: Fix and test login, loading and offline behaviour in the real setting before any design test; allow work to be saved and resumed
rows.if: Unreliable connections, shared devices or school-managed logins

rows.basis: [Students encountered usability obstacles: text-recognition errors, feedback-generation delays, and overly complex vocabulary](claims/ai-helper-usability-obstacles.md) [~W] (one think-aloud case study); [System usability was rated low in both conditions, with no significant difference between them](claims/low-usability-both-conditions.md) [~M] (42 seventh graders; adding an LLM emotional-support chat to a mathematics tutor left both versions rated low, D and F grades; a non-significant difference, not shown equivalent)
rows.change: Test the operation of the AI separately from the quality of what it says: whether it accepts the learner's input (text recognition, uploads), how long a response takes and what the learner does while waiting, and whether learners can read the vocabulary of its generated messages; do not expect better content or a friendlier support layer to lift a low usability rating on its own
rows.if: The interface wraps an AI tutor, chatbot or AI feedback tool

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: One round only: a 30-minute heuristic walk-through of the three core tasks, then three users doing them while thinking aloud (10 minutes each); fix the worst stall
rows.if: One designer, no budget, a fixed short time (one day, or one 60-minute slot)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Replace sessions with five-minute "hallway" tests of one task each, and ask for one screenshot of where they got stuck
rows.if: Scarce facilitator or user time (volunteers, a busy shift, a tutor who checks in briefly)

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page (UCD's evidence comes from data about real users, not designer assumptions)
rows.change: Treat personas and heuristics as assumptions; make the first cohort's first two weeks the test round (step 10) and say so
rows.if: No access to real users before launch

rows.basis: [Making year-over-year change salient helped users identify which schools improved most but lowered usability and satisfaction ratings](claims/year-over-year-salience-mixed-effects.md) [~M]; [The system receives a good average usability rating (SUS 69.7, grade B) but with wide individual variation attributed to UI consistency issues](claims/photon-fusion-sus-good-but-variable-usability.md) [~W]
rows.change: Keep it and run it as given; add only what the evidence says matters: a task-success check beside the rating, and the spread of individual scores
rows.if: The brief names its own routine (its own usability questionnaire, rubric, review checklist, or template)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use them as the starting navigation; card sorting checks them with users rather than replacing them
rows.if: The brief gives its own categories, labels or course structure

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Learners control who sees their records; in tests use invented data, never real learners' records; ask consent before recording screens
rows.if: The interface shows private or sensitive data (grades, analytics, reflections, health)

rows.basis: [Reporting the number of points possible for each metric led to better understanding of how the STAR score is calculated](claims/points-possible-improves-score-understanding.md) [+M] (public report card study)
rows.change: Test with that audience, not with staff who know the system; check they can read the key number correctly, not only that they find it
rows.if: A real audience reads the product (parents reading a school report, the public, an employer)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Test with practice items and a mock submission, never during a live assessment; give every user one practice run before the real one
rows.if: High stakes (an exam platform, a certification submission)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Test whole task flows end to end, not isolated screens
rows.if: The learning task is a whole performance (a simulation, a project tool) the brief wants kept whole

rows.basis: untested; brief convention
rows.change: Add no learning test or survey of your own; use task success on the brief's own tasks as the check
rows.if: The brief does not ask for a test of learning

rows.basis: [Raters differed in severity](claims/raters-differed-severity-mfrm.md) [~M] (open-ended items, three raters); [rubric guidance improved peer raters' placement of writing on complex criteria](claims/rubrics-improve-peer-feedback-quality.md) [+M] (MOOC and graduate peers, carried to teachers); one class's rubric scores varied by a mean of 1.2 of 9 points across six scorers ([engineering rubric low scoring reliability](claims/engineering-rubric-low-scoring-reliability.md) [~W])
rows.change: Use a performance task scored by a rubric with level descriptors and anchors; calibrate markers before marking and double-mark a sample; report the score with the number of tasks it rests on
rows.if: The goal is a `complex-skill` or extended performance (a lab, an essay, a presentation, a clinical task)

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page (item-count arithmetic, selected-response trade-off)
rows.change: Use many short selected-response or short-answer items for breadth and reliability; keep the language plain; add a few items that ask for the procedure on a changed case if transfer matters
rows.if: The goal is `verbal-association` or a `procedure` recalled or carried out quickly

rows.basis: State-test word problems with heavier linguistic demands were disproportionately hard for ELLs of the same overall mathematics score ([DIF for ELLs](claims/mcas-math-word-problems-dif-for-ells.md) [+M]; [linguistic features of the flagged items](claims/linguistic-features-of-dif-mcas-word-problems.md) [+M]; one large-scale study, fourth grade); [Verbal tests may underestimate subject knowledge](claims/verbal-achievement-tests-may-underestimate-via-symbolic-mismatch.md) [~W] (argument); Spanish–English bilingual kindergarteners did better on mathematics assessments given in Spanish ([bilinguals better tested in Spanish](claims/bilinguals-better-math-tested-in-spanish.md) [+W], a brief citing one study, no effect size); the fractions example is from the earlier page (Linn & Miller)
rows.change: Keep reading load below the target; gloss non-target words; read items aloud or allow a spoken, drawn or demonstrated answer where reading is not the construct; where it can be done, assess content knowledge in the learner's stronger language as well; do not read a low score as low content knowledge without a second, low-language check; for word problems, have a colleague mark the items whose wording (long or embedded clauses, unfamiliar vocabulary, cultural references) goes beyond the mathematics, and simplify those first
rows.if: Learners are learning in a second language, or have low literacy

rows.basis: Achievement moves untested; a short behavioural self-regulation task (Head-Toes-Knees-Shoulders), video-scored with inter-rater reliability of .95–.98, related to teachers' ratings of first graders' social skills and problem behaviour ([HTKS validity for first graders](claims/htks-validity-first-graders.md) [+W]); a preschool number-sense task correlated only .46 with itself three months later, which its authors read as too unstable for young children ([moderate test-retest reliability in preschoolers](claims/ans-task-moderate-test-retest-reliability-preschoolers.md) [~W]); both research tasks, carried to classroom observation; a review argues questionnaires are hard to use validly with young children, who have limited reading and cannot yet self-assess abstract states ([questionnaires poor fit for young children](claims/questionnaire-measures-poor-fit-young-children.md) [+W], about curiosity measures); an argument that on-demand standardised tests alone are problematic for young children ([standardised tests problematic for young children](claims/standardized-tests-problematic-young-children-outcomes.md) [+W], argument)
rows.change: Use pictures, objects and spoken instructions; short sessions; observe the performance rather than relying on written answers; more occasions, fewer items per occasion; for dispositions such as curiosity, interest or self-regulation, use an observed behavioural task, not a questionnaire the child completes; expect a single sitting to be unstable, and repeat a measure before acting on one result
rows.if: Learners are young children (`child`)

rows.basis: [Male-oriented item content biases scores](claims/male-oriented-item-content-biases-test-scores.md) [~W] (second-hand); a Korean translation of a psychosocial measure kept acceptable reliability but its inter-scale correlations were not as expected in 79 immigrant adults ([cross-cultural measurement bias in translated instruments](claims/cross-cultural-measurement-bias-in-translated-psychosocial-instruments.md) [~W]; adults, research instrument, carried to classroom questionnaires); where a Likert questionnaire is repeated to track growth, response styles (such as always agreeing) can shift the estimated slope, differently by construct and scoring model ([response styles affect growth estimates](claims/response-style-growth-effects-vary-by-construct-and-model.md) [~M]; [effects vary by construct and model](claims/response-style-growth-effects-vary-by-construct-and-model.md) [~M]; one study of social-emotional surveys)
rows.change: Review every context for taught or shared knowledge; balance people in items; for a translated self-report scale, check its internal consistency and whether its scales relate to each other as expected in your own group before interpreting scores
rows.if: Learners come from varied cultural or national backgrounds, or a questionnaire has been translated

rows.basis: [Math anxiety degrades performance](claims/math-anxiety-degrades-performance.md) [~M] (meta-analysis of correlations; does not test these moves)
rows.change: Drop time limits unless speed is the target; give low-stakes practice in the same format first; allow scratch work; interpret a score from a timed, high-pressure sitting with caution
rows.if: Learners are anxious about tests, or mathematics anxiety is common in the group

rows.basis: [Decision consistency lowest at the distribution peak](claims/dc-lowest-at-score-distribution-peak.md) [~M] (simulation); [Cohen's kappa paradox](claims/cohens-kappa-paradox-decision-consistency.md) [~W] (worked example); [grade cutoffs arbitrary](claims/grade-cutoffs-arbitrary-adjacent-scores.md) [~W] (argument)
rows.change: Put more items or tasks behind the decision; seek a second piece of evidence for learners near the cut; report decision consistency rather than kappa; allow a re-take or appeal on a comparable task
rows.if: Stakes are high: a grade boundary, pass mark, placement or certification

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page (a single item's weight in a short test)
rows.change: Use it to steer the next lesson, not to grade an individual; aim the few items at the one decision you need; combine with other evidence before any grade
rows.if: Time is one session only, or the assessment is a single short quiz

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use selected-response or short-answer items for breadth; reserve judgement-scored tasks for the objectives that need them; mark one question across all scripts at a time rather than one script at a time; re-mark the first ten scripts at the end to check for drift
rows.if: One teacher marks for a large group

rows.basis: The comparability moves are untested proposals; a systematic review of automated proctoring reports that several studies acknowledged its accuracy varies with learners' demographics, lighting and hardware, which could disadvantage some students ([proctoring accuracy varies across demographics](claims/proctoring-accuracy-demographic-bias.md) [-W], acknowledged limitations, no figures on the page)
rows.change: Give every learner the same items, aids and time, or record the difference beside the score; avoid long passages, drag-and-drop and wide tables for phone users; compare remote and in-room score distributions before treating them as one set; for a performance, use the same observer checklist live and on video; if remote sittings use automated camera-based proctoring, treat its flags as prompts for a person to review, never as evidence on their own
rows.if: Learners take the assessment in mixed modes: some in the room, some remote, some on phones only

rows.basis: An interview rating of teachers' use of an innovation correlated .65 with readers' ratings of written ethnographic protocols, which its authors read as support for its validity ([LoU interview validated against observation](claims/lou-interview-validated-against-ethnography.md) [+W]; teachers, research instrument; the way validity was checked is carried, not a result about learners)
rows.change: Assess the task as it is done at work, with an observer checklist; use two observers on a sample; check validity by comparing the assessment's ratings with independent observation of practice
rows.if: Adults in work settings, or the capability is a job task

rows.basis: In one online course, peer marks on two exact-science exams did not differ significantly from the teacher's and correlated .88–.91 with them ([peer assessment equivalent for exact-science exams](claims/peer-assessment-valid-exact-science-exams.md) [~M]; one course, a clear marking scheme, `r1`; non-significance is not equivalence); rubric training helped peer raters most on complex criteria ([rubric guidance for peer raters](claims/rubrics-improve-peer-feedback-quality.md) [+M]); in a MOOC experiment, telling students about their own grading bias was followed by more accurate peer grading ([feedback on grading bias increased accuracy](claims/grading-bias-feedback-increases-accuracy.md) [+W], no statistic printed); in MOOC peer-grading data, higher-scoring students were generally more reliable graders, and students were least biased grading work near their own level, the strongest marking the weakest work down and the weakest marking the strongest up ([grader level and grading reliability](claims/grader-grade-relates-to-grading-reliability.md) [~W]); a review reports adequately reliable peer assessment of 187 medical interns' professional performance ([peer assessment of professional skills](claims/peer-professional-skills-reliability-outcomes.md) [~W], second-hand)
rows.change: Count peer marks only where the marking scheme leaves little to judgement (exact answers, stated point allocations) and each script has several peer markers; have the teacher mark a sample and compare before using the marks; for subjective or complex criteria, train peers on a rubric with anchors first, or use peer marks as feedback rather than a grade; after a calibration round, show each peer marker how their marks compared with the teacher's (too generous, too harsh) before they mark for real; expect markers to be least accurate on work far above or below their own, so mix the levels of each script's markers
rows.if: Peers mark each other's work and the marks count toward a score

rows.basis: Across published online self-regulation questionnaires, alphas of relevant scales ranged from .52 to .95 and all but two instruments had at least one scale outside .70–.90 ([existing online SRL scales show reliability problems](claims/existing-online-srl-scales-reliability-issues.md) [~W], the authors' review); in the new questionnaire's own validation, nine of ten subscales exceeded .70 and the three-item one fell to omega .665 ([SRL-O internal consistency](claims/srl-o-internal-consistency.md) [~W]); a scenario-based test of strategy knowledge correlated moderately with a strategy questionnaire but low and mostly non-significantly with a microanalytic measure taken during a learning task ([convergent with the questionnaire](claims/skt-srl-convergent-validity-questionnaire.md) [~W]; [weakly related to the online measure](claims/skt-srl-microanalysis-low-correlation.md) [~W]; one instrument, college students). Arguments, no data on the pages: off-line self-reports rest on reconstructing earlier processes from memory, with more distortion the longer the delay ([off-line self-reports and memory reconstruction](claims/off-line-self-reports-memory-reconstruction-problem.md) [~W]); the questions themselves can prompt reports of strategies never used, unequally across learners ([prompting distorts retrospective self-reports](claims/prompting-effect-distorts-retrospective-self-reports.md) [~W]); questionnaires may capture perception rather than performed strategies ([questionnaires measure perception](claims/questionnaires-measure-perception-not-performed-strategies.md) [~W]); a review reports internal consistency of .62–.94 for self-efficacy measures, which tracked domain measures and not general ones ([self-efficacy measures reliable and domain-specific](claims/self-efficacy-measures-reliable-domain-specific.md) [+W]), so a well-built, domain-specific scale can be consistent
rows.change: Read its scores as learners' perceptions, not as what they did; ask about a specific task straight after it rather than about general habits; check a sample against a trace of what learners actually did (their work, a think-aloud, logs) before acting on it; check reliability in your own group, subscale by subscale rather than for the total, and treat short (two- or three-item) subscales as the likeliest to fall short; do not read a test of what learners know about strategies as a record of what they do; do not use it for an individual high-stakes decision
rows.if: A self-report questionnaire (strategies, study habits, self-efficacy, attitudes) is used alongside achievement measures

rows.basis: In one problem-solving game, the stealth assessment's facets reached alpha .76 with middle-school students while the established reference test (MicroDYN) reached only .67 and .43, which the authors put down to the tasks being hard for that age ([stealth facets reliable, reference test not](claims/internal-consistency-stealth-versus-microdyn.md) [~W]); a review reports deep-learning stealth assessment predicting middle-schoolers' science knowledge from gameplay, with a demographic bias audit and debiasing without loss of accuracy, and AUCs of .85–.91 across studies ([stealth assessment accuracy and bias audits](claims/stealth-assessment-accuracy-and-bias-audits.md) [~W], second-hand). In one profiling game, questionnaire-like in-game items (diary ordering, ranking, narrative questionnaires) matched a reference interest inventory best, diary ordering 78 per cent of the time, while other item types managed 10–22 per cent ([item types differed in correlation with the questionnaire](claims/jeu-serai-item-type-correlation-quality-ranking.md) [~W]), and most items for one interest type did not work ([enterprising items failed](claims/jeu-serai-enterprising-items-failed.md) [~W]); vocational interests, not achievement, carried here as a validation procedure
rows.change: Treat each kind of in-game item as an untested instrument: before using the scores, compare each item type with an established measure of the same thing in a pilot group, keep the item types that agree and drop or rework the rest; check every target dimension separately, since one can fail while others work; check the reference measure's own reliability in your age group before treating disagreement as the game's fault; where the game's model predicts learner states, compare its accuracy across groups before using it
rows.if: The assessment is embedded in a game or simulation (stealth or in-game assessment)

rows.basis: untested proposal; the audience relationship is owned by [Authentic Audiences and Purposes](principles/authentic-audiences-purposes.md)
rows.change: Score it against the criteria by markers who have calibrated, separately from the audience's reaction; record audience response as its own observation, not as the grade
rows.if: The work is a product or performance for a real audience

rows.basis: [Ignoring local dependence overestimates reliability](claims/ignored-local-dependence-overestimates-reliability-simulation.md) [~M] (simulation of a large-scale reading test)
rows.change: Count passages, not items, when judging whether there is enough evidence; estimate consistency at the passage level
rows.if: The test uses several items on one passage, case or data set

rows.basis: [Later-positioned item more difficult](claims/later-position-item-more-difficult-fatigue-effect.md) [~M] (national examination; one item)
rows.change: Keep item order fixed across versions, or compare an item's difficulty across positions before treating versions as equal
rows.if: Several versions of the test exist (shuffled order, A/B forms)

rows.basis: Among Chicago graduates, a standard deviation of high school GPA was associated with a 15 percentage point rise in four-year college graduation against 7 for test scores ([GPA predicts graduation more than tests](claims/hsgpa-predicts-college-graduation-more-than-tests.md) [+M]); in another Chicago analysis GPA's link to graduation held across high schools while ACT added nothing once GPA was in the model ([HSGPA strongly predicts graduation](claims/hsgpa-strongly-predicts-college-graduation.md) [+M]; [HSGPA slope consistent across schools](claims/hsgpa-slope-consistent-across-schools.md) [+M]; [ACT a weak predictor](claims/act-weak-predictor-noise-exceeds-signal.md) [~M]; [ACT adds little beyond HSGPA](claims/act-adds-little-beyond-hsgpa.md) [~M]); ninth-grade GPA was the most predictive single indicator for every English Learner group ([GPA most predictive for English Learners](claims/gpa-most-predictive-attainment-english-learners.md) [+M]); diagnostic topic scores predicted algebra proficiency beyond a prior state test ([MDTP topic scores predict proficiency](claims/mdtp-topic-scores-predict-algebra-proficiency.md) [+M]); a placement test's multiple-choice part predicted passing as GPA did while its writing part predicted nothing ([placement components differ in prediction](claims/cmi-gpa-and-multiple-choice-similarly-predict-ela-passing.md) [~M]); a practice guide cites 24–33 per cent of college entrants misplaced by single tests ([misplacement rates](claims/misplacement-rates-24-33-percent.md) [~W], second-hand); a narrative review attributes under-identification of diverse students for gifted programmes to the measures ([biased identification measures](claims/culturally-diverse-underrepresentation-biased-measures.md) [~W], argued, not tested). Second-hand reports of the same Chicago work: freshman-year GPA alone identified 80 per cent of on-time graduates against 65 per cent for eighth-grade tests and risk measures together ([freshman GPA predicts on-time graduation](claims/freshman-gpa-predicts-80-percent-ontime-graduation.md) [+W]), and among students with the same ACT score college graduation was 77 per cent at a GPA of 3.5 or more against 40 per cent at 2.0–2.4 ([GPA outpredicts ACT at equal scores](claims/gpa-outpredicts-act-college-graduation.md) [+W]); studies finding grades less predictive are said to rest on restricted samples or self-reported or weighted GPAs ([restricted samples explain divergent findings](claims/restricted-samples-explain-divergent-grade-predictions.md) [~W], an interview, no data). By group: in Arkansas records almost all middle and high school indicators predicted later outcomes about equally well across student groups, with exceptions for science and English language arts proficiency in middle school and science proficiency in high school ([predictive strength similar across groups, with exceptions](claims/academic-indicator-predictive-strength-similar.md) [~W]); a practice guide reports that SAT mathematics scores underpredict women's performance in college mathematics and that girls scored lower than boys on timed NAEP tests at the same course level ([timed-test gap and underprediction](claims/timed-test-gender-gap-underpredicts-college-performance.md) [~W], second-hand, no effect size), so a test can mispredict for a group whose later performance it is used to forecast; in advanced university STEM courses, school-leaving grades clustered near the maximum (means about 93 of 100) did not account for later differences between groups, which the authors read as a ceiling effect ([school grades show a ceiling](claims/high-school-grades-ceiling-effect-gap.md) [~W], an interpretation). A logistic-regression approach estimates, for each English-proficiency score, the probability of reaching proficiency on the content test, as a way to set an English-proficient cut ([half-probability criterion](claims/logistic-regression-half-probability-criterion.md) [~W], a method described in a federal evaluation, no result on the page). All associational, mostly US secondary and college records, carried to classroom placement
rows.change: Do not place on one test alone: combine it with course grades or a second measure; use the full scale score rather than a pass or proficiency label; check locally which components actually predict the later outcome and drop or down-weight those that do not; where a cut on one measure (a screener, an English-proficiency score) is meant to signal readiness for another, set it from local records of the share of learners at each score who went on to succeed, not by convention; review placement and identification rates by group, and check that the measure predicts as well for each group; a measure on which most learners sit near the top cannot separate them, so do not place on it
rows.if: The score will be used to place learners or to predict who will need help later

rows.basis: Grades differed by race, ethnicity and gender among Chicago students with the same test scores, attendance, courses and teachers ([grade differences by group net of test scores](claims/race-gender-grade-differences-persist.md) [~M]), while a practice guide reports girls scoring lower than boys on timed NAEP tests at the same course level and SAT mathematics underpredicting women's college mathematics ([timed-test gap and underprediction](claims/timed-test-gender-gap-underpredicts-college-performance.md) [~W], second-hand): grades and tests disagreed, in different directions for different groups, which is why neither is read alone; language load produced item-level gaps for English-language learners ([DIF for ELLs](claims/mcas-math-word-problems-dif-for-ells.md) [+M]); most indicators predicted equally well across groups in one state, but not all ([predictive strength similar across groups, with exceptions](claims/academic-indicator-predictive-strength-similar.md) [~W]). All associational records; none tests the classroom moves
rows.change: Treat the gap as a question about the measures, the marking and the teaching, never as a property of the group; compare the group's test results with its grades, since the two can disagree; blind-mark a sample of work with names removed and compare with the marks given; check the items for language load, untaught background and time pressure (steps 5, 6, 8, 10); where a score is used to predict or place, check that it predicts as well for each group; with small groups, wait for a second administration before concluding anything
rows.if: Results will be compared across groups (gender, race or ethnicity, language background, family income), or a gap between groups has been noticed

rows.basis: Agreement fell sharply on mid-range short answers while the extremes were scored well ([mid-range degradation](claims/ai-mid-range-scoring-degradation-u-shape.md) [~M]); lower linguistic quality raised the odds that every one of eleven AI approaches underestimated Grade 9 physics understanding ([AI scoring underestimates linguistically weak explanations](claims/ai-scoring-underestimates-linguistically-weak-physics-explanations.md) [-M]); repeated ChatGPT sessions on the same essays reached Krippendorff's alpha 0.625 ([limited reproducibility](claims/llm-grading-session-variability-limited-reproducibility.md) [~M]) while its best single-pass agreement with examiners was weighted kappa 0.718 ([strongest examiner agreement](claims/chatgpt-thinking-mode-strongest-human-grading-agreement.md) [~M]); the best of many models reached ICC 0.470 with programming teachers, and models split into lenient, strict and middling graders ([moderate agreement at best](claims/llm-grading-moderate-human-agreement-icc.md) [~M]; [grading styles differ](claims/llms-differ-liberal-restrictive-balanced-grading-styles.md) [~M]); repeat-run reliability ranged widely by model ([reliability stratified by model](claims/llm-essay-scoring-reliability-stratification.md) [~M]); prompting strategy changed agreement and direction of bias, and agreement differed by rubric dimension ([Fs+CoT strongest agreement](claims/fscot-strongest-teacher-agreement-run1.md) [~M]; [RAG systematic leniency](claims/rag-systematic-leniency-overscoring.md) [-M]; [strategy-specific bias](claims/strategy-specific-bias-profiles.md) [~M]; [dimension-specific agreement](claims/dimension-specific-scoring-reasoning-strongest-terminology-weakest.md) [~M]); a revised workflow raised exact agreement on physics question parts from about 63 to about 70 per cent, with partial credit hardest ([question-part agreement](claims/question-part-agreement-partial-credit-limits.md) [~M]); revising a rubric to state its constructs raised human–machine agreement ([rubric revision improves alignment](claims/rubric-revision-improves-machine-alignment.md) [+M]); a review argues AI analyses may perform unevenly across student groups ([uneven performance across populations](claims/ai-uneven-performance-across-student-populations.md) [~W]). On one computer-science exam double-marked by human pairs, whose totals differed by a mean of 2.61 of 35 points, six closed-model configurations came within that human-to-human difference, the best at 1.64 ([LLM graders within the human floor](claims/closed-llm-graders-below-human-floor.md) [~M], preprint), which is the comparison this row asks for; five LLMs scoring IELTS essays mostly marked lower than human raters, some also compressing scores into a narrow range ([systematic underestimation](claims/llm-essay-scoring-systematic-underestimation.md) [~W]); four LLMs grading 32 public-health exam essays agreed poorly with human grades in fast mode (weighted kappa 0.07–0.29) and better in thinking mode ([fast mode limited, thinking mode better](claims/llm-fast-mode-limited-thinking-mode-better-agreement.md) [~W]); models grading the same open-ended answers differed significantly in leniency ([grades differ across models](claims/genai-grade-differences-wilcoxon.md) [~W]); a single model judge re-run three times gave nearly identical scores, so consistency with itself says nothing about agreement with teachers ([within-judge stability](claims/within-judge-stability-llm-rubric.md) [~W], scoring generated videos, not learner work); an older automated essay scorer agreed with human raters 94.6–98.2 per cent but needed many pre-scored essays to calibrate, which a review judged impractical for most small classes ([AES agreement and calibration constraint](claims/aes-high-agreement-calibration-constraint.md) [~W], second-hand); LLM-run assessment conversations were observed to give away more than intended and to be harder to score than scripted ones ([LLM conversations leak information](claims/llm-cba-information-leakage-scoring-challenge.md) [~W], one case study). Mostly single studies of 2025–2026 models, many preprints
rows.change: Use it as a second reader under a teacher's control, not as the grader of record; before relying on it, compare its marks with teachers' on a sample of your own scripts, dimension by dimension, and check for systematic leniency or severity; send mid-range responses and those from learners with weaker written language to a teacher; where repeat runs differ, score more than once and take the median; write the rubric so it names what counts as evidence; judge the scorer's disagreement with teachers against how far two teachers disagree on the same scripts, not against perfect agreement; check that it uses the whole scale rather than marking low or bunching marks in the middle; if it runs reasoning and fast modes, use the reasoning mode; if an LLM conducts a conversational assessment, read sample transcripts for turns that give the answer away before scoring them
rows.if: AI or an LLM will score constructed responses

rows.basis: An evidence-centred argument that AI contribution breaks the link from a product to the learner's proficiency, almost completely for recall and routine tasks ([GenAI disrupts evidence rules](claims/genai-disrupts-evidence-rules-asymmetrically.md) [~W], argument); an argument for assessment twins ([assessment twins](claims/assessment-twins-triangulate-evidence-mitigate-threats.md) [+W], argument); an LLM detector was poor on short answers though better on programs and longer reflections ([self-detection task-dependent](claims/llm-self-detection-task-dependent.md) [-M]); a review cites a discontinued classifier's false positives and detector bias against non-native writers ([AI detection unreliable and biased](claims/ai-detection-unreliable-biased-high-stakes.md) [-W], second-hand); another review reports a benchmark in which seven detectors flagged authentic TOEFL essays by non-native writers as AI-generated at a mean false-positive rate of 61.3 per cent, far more than native writers' essays ([61.3 per cent false positives for non-native writers](claims/detector-61-3-percent-false-positives-non-native-toefl.md) [-W], second-hand); in a large sample of Reddit education discussions, students described detectors as linguistically biased, unreliable and distressing ([detectors reported unreliable and biased](claims/ai-detectors-reported-unreliable-biased.md) [-W], reports, not a test of detectors); undifferentiated rules are argued to turn language disadvantage into integrity risk ([undifferentiated GenAI rules](claims/undifferentiated-genai-rules-convert-language-disadvantage-into-integrity-risk.md) [-W], argument)
rows.change: Name the construct the task targets; for recall or routine procedures, assess under supervision; pair a take-home product with a supervised twin (a short oral explanation or an in-class task on the same capability) and read the two together; do not treat AI-detector output as evidence for an integrity decision, least of all for second-language writers; separate permitted language support from substitution in the rules
rows.if: Learners may use generative AI on work done outside supervision

rows.basis: [Expert teachers interpret complex classroom phenomena more accurately and fluidly than novices and postulants](claims/expert-teachers-interpret-classroom-phenomena-better.md) [~M]; [Authentic video outperformed virtual simulation on the higher-order analysis and support dimensions of observation assignments](claims/av-advantage-analysis-support-dimensions.md) [+M] (preschool teacher candidates watching others' video, not their own)
rows.change: Run sessions 1–2 on others' clips with a coach-set focus of one or two items; time-stamp and describe before interpreting; the coach picks the moments in early own-clip sessions
rows.if: Learners are `novice` (teacher candidates, first-year trainees)

rows.basis: untested proposal; the coaching reports below are from in-service teachers ([Video-based self-observation of teaching was among the most powerful parts of the coaching process for teachers](claims/video-self-observation-powerful-coaching-component.md) [+W])
rows.change: Skip others' clips; let the practitioner choose the focus and clip from the first session; the coach asks and adds only what was missed
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` (experienced practitioners)

rows.basis: [Young children's video interpretation of their own mathematical play reveals both mathematical and social-affective sensemaking](claims/childrens-video-interpretation-of-play-reveals-mathematical-and-social-sensemaking.md) [+W] (four children, no comparison; shows what they notice, not a learning gain)
rows.change: Use very short clips (under two minutes) of the children's own work or play; ask what they notice in their own words before any focus; an adult runs the device and keeps the recording
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary age)

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page (self-video "can feel exposing"); teachers reported getting past initial self-consciousness ([Video-based self-observation of teaching was among the most powerful parts of the coaching process for teachers](claims/video-self-observation-powerful-coaching-component.md) [+W])
rows.change: Start with others' clips; review the learner's own clip privately first, then with one trusted person; open with a moment that went well; allow spoken or pointed-to analysis instead of written notes
rows.if: Learners have low confidence, performance anxiety or low literacy

rows.basis: untested proposal; medical students valued recorded review of simulated consultations but asked for clear feedback criteria ([Learners valued repeatable practice and recorded review in MedEasy while questioning missing actions and feedback criteria](claims/learners-value-repeatable-practice-question-gaps.md) [+W], 12 students, interviews)
rows.change: Record a real or simulated work task (a consultation, a call, a handover); take the focus from the workplace's own standard; keep reviews in protected time, 20–30 minutes, and give the recording's owner the right to delete it
rows.if: Adults in work settings (clinical, customer-facing, trainers)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Record and keep the whole performance; choose clips only for analysis, and end each cycle by reviewing one clip in its place in the whole (what came before and after it)
rows.if: The goal is a `complex-skill` performance the brief wants kept whole (a full lesson, a whole consultation, a complete routine)

rows.basis: [Prompting learners to self-explain improves understanding and problem solving on immediate tests by a moderate average amount, with little evidence yet on delayed or classroom gains.](claims/self-explanation-improves-conceptual-understanding.md) [~S] (carried from texts and examples); see [Observation and Shadowing](principles/observationshadowing.md)
rows.change: Use others' or shared clips only; pause and ask for explanations of each moment; no own recording is needed
rows.if: The goal is understanding or noticing (`conceptual-understanding`), not changing one's own performance

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Share clips by a link with time-stamped comments; each learner reviews on their own device before a short joint debrief; on a phone, keep clips under two minutes and the focus to one item
rows.if: Mixed modes: some learners remote, some in the room, or phone-only

rows.basis: untested proposal; the contingent-support evidence is one-to-one ([Contingent scaffolding improves learning more than fixed or absent support.](claims/contingent-scaffolding-improves-learning.md) [~M])
rows.change: Learners review their own clip alone or in pairs with a prompt card (focus, time-stamps, three questions, one change); the coach reads only the one-change line and the chosen moment, for 5 minutes per learner, and sees one clip a cycle
rows.if: One coach or teacher for many learners, or scarce facilitator time (volunteers, a busy shift, one check-in)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Record and review in the same session: one 2–3 minute performance, one focus, 5 minutes of paused review, one change, a second short attempt recorded and compared; do not claim lasting change
rows.if: A single session only

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: 2 minutes focus, 4 minutes performance, 6 minutes paused review, 4 minutes second attempt, 4 minutes comparison and one change
rows.if: A fixed short time budget (e.g. 20 minutes)

rows.basis: untested; coded data from a named tool did reveal patterns the teacher had not seen ([EQUIP data reports surfaced participation inequities that teachers were unaware of and motivated instructional change](claims/equip-data-surfaces-unseen-participation-inequities.md) [+W])
rows.change: Keep it as the focus and the debrief; change only what this page's evidence says matters: pause at moments, ask the learner to explain each one before telling, end with one change and a recorded next attempt
rows.if: The brief names its own observation tool, rubric, checklist or debrief routine

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page (privacy and storage)
rows.change: The learner controls who sees the recording and the notes; review one-to-one or alone; crop or blur others, record only with consent, store locally and delete at the end of the cycle; no clip is shown to a group without the owner's agreement
rows.if: Private or sensitive material (a teacher's own lesson, patients or minors on screen, a learner's struggling attempt)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Record a rehearsal, not the event, for detailed review; after the event, review only with the performer's agreement and focus on one moment for next time
rows.if: The performance is for a real audience (a public talk, a client, a performance)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Keep formative replay apart from the assessed recording; the learner chooses what the assessor sees; judge readiness on an unreviewed performance
rows.if: High stakes (a licensing assessment, a graded placement)

rows.basis: [Pairing coaching with group trainings is associated with larger effects on instruction and achievement; instructional materials with larger, and video libraries with smaller, effects on instruction](claims/coaching-complementary-elements-moderators.md) [~M] (between-study association in a coaching meta-analysis, not a causal contrast)
rows.change: Use the library only for sessions 1–2; tie each library clip to the learner's own focus and move to the learner's own recordings with a debrief
rows.if: The programme supplies a library of model videos and little else

rows.basis: untested; the video findings above do not transfer to notes
rows.change: Use an observer's time-stamped notes of what was said and done, or an audio recording, with the same focus, explanation and one change
rows.if: Recording cannot be made (policy, no device, no consent)

rows.basis: untested; the strategy page's view that the framing is redundant for confident learners with established trust
rows.change: Keep the critique and the named standard; shorten the assurance to one clause; do not drop the critique to protect the relationship
rows.if: The learner already trusts the giver, or has a long record of success with them

rows.basis: [Praise for intelligence, rather than for effort, after success undermines children's motivation and performance after a later failure](claims/feedback-praise-reduces-learning.md) [-M] (fifth graders; tests the praise, not the framing)
rows.change: Give the three parts spoken, short and about the work; praise the strategy or effort, never "smart"; the assurance in plain words ("I know you can get this part right; let's try it again now") and an immediate second attempt
rows.if: Learners are `child` (primary age)

rows.basis: untested here; the earlier page and the strategy page's account of field experiments with seventh graders, which have no claim page
rows.change: Put the standard-and-assurance sentence at the top of the written comments, before the critique, and require a revision
rows.if: Learners are `adolescent`, with written feedback on graded work

rows.basis: untested; [Feedback improves learning by a medium amount on average, but its effect varies widely with the information it carries, and more than a third of feedback interventions reduce performance](claims/feedback-improves-learning.md) [~S] covers field and work settings and warns that feedback turning attention to the self can lower performance
rows.change: Name the job's own standard (the competency, the protocol, the client outcome) as the standard; say what in the learner's practice shows they can meet it; agree one change to try on the next shift or case
rows.if: `adult` learners in `workplace-clinical` settings (a supervisor, mentor or clinical educator across a difference)

rows.basis: [Belonging Interventions Improve Outcomes](claims/belonging-interventions-improve-outcomes.md) [~M], carried: brief belonging messages helped stereotyped groups at college entry, and only where the institution gave them opportunities to belong; it does not test feedback
