rows.basis: [Explicit group regulation infrequent and challenge-driven](claims/explicit-regulation-infrequent-challenge-responsive.md) [~W]; [Challenging situations drive plan–perform switching](claims/challenging-situations-drive-plan-perform-switching.md) [~W]; [Only the adaptable script improved monitoring](claims/adaptable-script-monitoring-self-regulation-effects.md) [~W]
rows.change: Expect explicit group regulation mainly when the group meets a challenge; put planning and monitoring prompts at those points (a stuck problem, a disagreement), and prefer a collaboration script the group can adapt
rows.if: Learners regulate as a group on a long project, online or face to face

rows.basis: [Process goals outperform outcome goals for novices](claims/process-goals-outperform-outcome-goals-for-novices.md) [+M]
rows.change: In step 1, have learners plan around process goals (the strategy steps), and move to outcome goals once the steps are secure
rows.if: Learners are acquiring a new procedure

rows.basis: [Fluent illusions mislead self-assessment](claims/fluent-illusions-mislead-self-assessment.md) [~M]
rows.change: Ask for the self-rating after a retrieval attempt or after scoring an exemplar, not straight after study; fluent presentation raises confidence without raising learning
rows.if: Learners rate their work after rereading or after a fluent explanation

rows.basis: [Overall mathematics score marginal, focus score significant](claims/srl-interventions-math-overall-score-marginal-focus-score-significant-online-prep-course.md) [~M]
rows.change: In step 5, score the learner's chosen focus areas and the broad test separately, and keep a behaviour trace beside any questionnaire
rows.if: The outcome is a broad end-of-course test over a few weeks

rows.basis: [Reflection reduces acceptance of incorrect AI advice](claims/reflection-reduces-incorrect-ai-advice-acceptance.md) [+M]; [Metacognitive feedback reduces answer offloading](claims/metacognitive-feedback-reduces-llm-answer-offloading-improves-unaided-performance.md) [+M]; [Advice feedback reduced reminder bias, ranking feedback changed beliefs only](claims/feedback-effects-on-offloading-mixed.md) [~W] (review); [As reliance on AI rises, error detection falls and confidence does not](claims/verification-bottleneck-confidence-dissociation.md) [~W] (second-hand)
rows.change: Add a step-3 prompt before learners accept AI output (confidence, how would you check it), and feedback on their own AI use
rows.if: Learners use a generative AI assistant during the task

rows.basis: [No trace format supported calibrated self-evaluation](claims/no-trace-format-supported-calibrated-self-evaluation.md) [~W]; [Delegating the terminal evaluation is self-defeating](claims/delegating-evaluation-self-defeating.md) [+W] (argument, no data)
rows.change: Do not treat reading the traces as self-evaluation; keep a scored check against which learners compare their own rating, and do not hand that check back to the AI: the learner still has to accept or reject what it returns
rows.if: The AI tool shows its reasoning traces to learners

rows.basis: [Repeated reflective prompts may habituate](claims/reflective-scaffolding-habituation-deskilling.md) [~W]; untested proposal for the order of removal
rows.change: In step 5, remove one prompt type at a time and reobserve; repeated prompts may become routine rather than build a habit
rows.if: The unit is long and prompts would run throughout

rows.basis: untested proposal; [Within-session SRL change not associated with post-test](claims/srl-change-no-posttest-association.md) [~W]
rows.change: Keep steps 1 and 3 only (a plan, a prediction, feedback on the gap); skip fading, which needs repeated observation, and do not read a change in regulation within the session as learning
rows.if: A single session, not a unit

rows.basis: [Students wanted advance notice and clarity on scheduling and roles](claims/inclusive-innovation-implementation-barriers.md) [~M]; [youth advisors on inadequate involvement and unclear follow-through](claims/youth-advisors-report-inadequate-involvement-in-decisions.md) [~W]; both interview accounts, not tests
rows.change: Give students seats with a stated decision, advance notice of every meeting and a written description of each role; hold meetings in school time; report back to the wider student body in a form they use.
rows.if: The group is `adolescent` students (student voice on climate, safety, a programme)

rows.basis: Untested; from the folded principle *Co-create learning environments with and for students from identity groups that most frequently experience inequities*, which cited no claim
rows.change: Co-create a small number of class norms or one routine with the children (15–20 minutes, revisited every few weeks); the teacher states in advance which decisions are the children's.
rows.if: The group is `child` learners (under 12) and the target is the classroom environment

rows.basis: [Participatory budgeting case](claims/resolving-participation-double-bind-requires-redesigned-activity-structures.md) [+M] (one Chicago ward, `adult` immigrants); [many districts employ family liaisons](claims/sv-leas-family-liaisons-bridge-multilingual-families.md) [~W] (a survey count of staffing, not of effect)
rows.change: A body that deliberates in that language with its own decision standing; bilingual staff or a family liaison convenes it; bring its decisions to the joint body translated, not re-argued.
rows.if: Families or community members speak a language other than the meeting's

rows.basis: [Framing instructors as part of the solution shifted a design toward supporting instructor judgment](claims/instructors-part-of-the-solution-frameshift.md) [+W] (one project's dialogue)
rows.change: Frame them as part of the solution: design so the tool or policy supports their judgment, and give them a co-design role from the first session.
rows.if: The excluded group is staff or instructors (`adult-workplace`), e.g. in a technology or evaluation design

rows.basis: Untested proposal; no claim here compares meeting modes
rows.change: Run every deciding session so remote members have the same turn and vote (an agenda sent by text two days before, a phone dial-in, a round where remote members speak first, votes by text). Do not hold the deciding phase in a mode part of the group cannot use.
rows.if: Some members join remotely while others are in the room, or members have only a phone

rows.basis: [Calibrated support](claims/calibrated-support-co-leadership.md) [~M], carried to settings with less staff time than its projects had
rows.change: Hand tasks over earlier: by the second meeting a member co-chairs; the facilitator's time goes to preparing data in a usable form and to the report-back, not to running discussion.
rows.if: One facilitator for a large group, or scarce facilitator time (volunteers, a busy principal)

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Use it to document where the group drops out (step 1) and to agree with the group what decision it will hold and when it will meet again; do not call one session co-creation.
rows.if: A single session only

rows.basis: Own-language deliberation from the [case](claims/resolving-participation-double-bind-requires-redesigned-activity-structures.md) [+M]; the rest untested
rows.change: Oral deliberation in their language; visual budgets or options; decisions recorded by a scribe and read back; pairs before plenary.
rows.if: Participants have low confidence or low literacy in the meeting's language

rows.basis: [Each school designed its own alumni survey, with researcher support](claims/codesign-culturally-responsive-alumni-surveys.md) [+W] (a descriptive brief)
rows.change: Keep it; change only what this policy says matters: who holds the decision, the language and agenda control, and the report-back.
rows.if: The brief names its own routine (its survey, its check-in, its meeting format or rubric)

rows.basis: [Core Teams judged solutions against outcomes they had defined](claims/inclusive-innovation-solutions-perceived-met-outcomes.md) [~M]; [districts piloting ed-tech defined success differently, which made a common standard hard to set](claims/varied-success-definitions-hinder-evaluation.md) [~W]: keep the group's definitions and add the shared observations alongside
rows.change: Use the group's own outcome definitions to judge the work and report against them; add attendance and decisions changed as observations, not as replacement criteria.
rows.if: The brief has its own categories, outcomes or success criteria

rows.basis: [Youth designers' ground rules](claims/youth-designed-norm-setting-and-flexibility-tech-talk.md) [+W]; [CBO leaders described working through institutional hurt as part of the process](claims/wss-codesign-restorative-healing-process.md) [~W]
rows.change: Members decide what is recorded and who sees it; consent before any quotation; ground rules on confidentiality set by the group before the first working session; a separate channel for what members will not say in front of officials.
rows.if: The material is private or sensitive (experiences of policing, discrimination, immigration status)

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Per meeting: 5 minutes check-in, 10 report-back on the last decisions, 30 deliberation in small groups, 10 decision, 5 reflection on roles.
rows.if: A fixed short time budget (e.g. 60-minute meetings)

rows.basis: [Leaders filtered community voices and retained security personnel](claims/leaders-filter-community-voices-security-retained.md) [-M]
rows.change: Write the decision rule before deliberation (what is binding, what is advisory, who can overrule and how they must explain it); publish each recommendation with the response.
rows.if: High stakes or contested policy (school safety, discipline, budget cuts)

rows.basis: [WSS co-designers described the process as novel and replicable](claims/wss-codesign-seen-novel-replicable-policymaking.md) [+W] (perception; the source notes the novelty is contestable)
rows.change: Members co-author and present it; credit the group by name where members agree; say in the document which parts the group decided.
rows.if: The product is a public framework, policy or plan with a real audience

rows.basis: Flexible agenda norms in the [case](claims/resolving-participation-double-bind-requires-redesigned-activity-structures.md) [+M]; untested apart from the full redesign
rows.change: Give the body the whole decision to deliberate and let it set its own agenda within it, rather than pre-cutting items for it to rate.
rows.if: The brief wants the whole decision kept whole (the whole budget, the whole framework)

rows.basis: [Sustainability factors](claims/inclusive-innovation-sustainability-factors.md) [+M]; [turnover](claims/turnover-threatens-sustainability-inclusive-innovation.md) [~M]; [a standing committee structure keeps change going through turnover](claims/committee-structure-sustains-change-despite-turnover.md) [~W] (consultants' experience)
rows.change: Embed the body in an existing structure before the change; get support at several levels; brief the successor.
rows.if: Leadership turnover is likely (new principal, new superintendent)

rows.basis: [Early-childhood SEL synthesis](claims/sel-programs-improve-social-emotional-skills.md) [+S]: 63 studies of universal curricula in centres; [SEL moderators](claims/sel-effects-moderators-implementation-delivery.md) [~M]: in a preschool meta-analysis of 33 studies (as summarised in a review), family-and-school programmes did better than a classroom teacher alone; the play-based format and lesson length are untested proposals
rows.change: Teach through play, picture emotion cards and puppets; lessons of 10–15 minutes; adults name emotions as they happen; add a family component (the week's skill and one way to practise it at home); measure social and emotional competence by observation and more than one informant.
rows.if: Learners are aged 2–6, in an early-childhood centre

rows.basis: [Taking Part training](claims/taking-part-training-increases-sharing-behaviors.md) [+W]: one small randomized comparison in six preschool classrooms; sharing rose well above reinforcement alone, time in a group not significantly
rows.change: Teach the target social behaviour explicitly (name it, model it, practise it with prompts) alongside reinforcing it, rather than only reinforcing it when it happens; measure the specific behaviour by direct observation; expect one behaviour to move before broader participation does.
rows.if: Young learners with developmental delays or disabilities

rows.basis: [Autonomy support](claims/autonomy-supports-intrinsic-motivation.md) [~M], carried from intrinsic motivation to SEL; [mindfulness programmes](claims/mindfulness-programs-benefit-adolescent-regulation.md) [+W] and [self-regulation interventions with high schoolers and young adults](claims/sr-interventions-improve-cognitive-regulation-young-adults.md) [+W], one practice brief's review, no effect sizes; [SEL moderators](claims/sel-effects-moderators-implementation-delivery.md) [+M]: longer secondary programmes with in-session practice, insight building, problem-solving and whole-staff involvement were the more effective, in a 104-study meta-analysis as summarised in a review
rows.change: Frame skills around fairness, identity, friendship and real stakes; let learners choose scenarios and lead discussion; avoid scripts that feel young; offer mindfulness or breathing practice as one strategy among several; plan a longer programme with practice inside every session, and involve the whole staff team that teaches them.
rows.if: Learners are `adolescent`

rows.basis: Untested: no claim here tests SEL with adults; the examples are the earlier page's
rows.change: Present the skills as professional competence; use cases and structured reflective discussion of real encounters (Balint-style groups) instead of scripted lessons; assess on observed practice.
rows.if: `adult` learners in work settings (health care, teaching, management, customer service)

rows.basis: [SEL and achievement](claims/sel-programs-improve-behavior-and-achievement.md) [~S]: small at post-test in the older synthesis (significant only with school-staff delivery), negligible in randomised trials of a recent one, larger for GPA
rows.change: Keep SEL, but embed the skills in academic lessons, delivered by the subject teacher, and promise only a small achievement effect; measure achievement on an independent test, not the programme's own.
rows.if: The goal is academic achievement

rows.basis: [SEL and achievement](claims/sel-programs-improve-behavior-and-achievement.md) [~S] and [SEL skills](claims/sel-programs-improve-social-emotional-skills.md) [~S]: delivery by non-school personnel and multicomponent programmes showed weaker or non-significant effects; [SEL moderators](claims/sel-effects-moderators-implementation-delivery.md) [~M]: higher implementation quality went with stronger outcomes
rows.change: Train and involve the class teacher, who cues the skill daily; or, failing that, expect smaller effects and measure them.
rows.if: An outside provider or a pull-out session will deliver it

rows.basis: [SEL needs an educative, inclusive environment](claims/sel-requires-educative-inclusive-environments.md) [~W]: a policy report's own assertion, no study; [belonging interventions](claims/belonging-interventions-improve-outcomes.md) [~M]: at college entry, a brief belonging intervention raised first-year completion only where the institution afforded students' groups opportunities to belong, carried from college to school; [empathic discipline](claims/brief-intervention-empathic-discipline-cuts-suspensions.md) [+M]
rows.change: Change the adults' side alongside the lessons: an empathic-discipline exercise for teachers, restorative rather than exclusionary responses to incidents, and staff cueing the taught skill instead of only sanctioning its absence; do not expect skill lessons alone to hold. Track exclusions and belonging by group, reading any gap as a difference in circumstances and treatment, not in the learners.
rows.if: The school's discipline is punitive or exclusionary, or the climate tells some learners they do not belong

rows.basis: [Empathy-building claim](claims/building-empathy-improves-intergroup-attitudes.md) [~M]: most prejudice-reduction studies test light-touch interventions with unclear long-term effects; [empathic discipline](claims/brief-intervention-empathic-discipline-cuts-suspensions.md) [+M]: a brief teacher exercise reduced suspensions for high-risk groups, with a marginal overall effect in the preregistered replication
rows.change: Do not promise durable change. Teach one skill and leave a routine (a check-in card, a breathing step) the teacher will run daily; or spend the session on the adults' discipline mindset instead.
rows.if: A single session, assembly or workshop only

rows.basis: [Empathic discipline](claims/brief-intervention-empathic-discipline-cuts-suspensions.md) [+M] (middle-school mathematics teachers); [positive greetings](claims/positive-greetings-at-the-door-improve-engagement.md) [+M] (middle school, engagement and disruption)
rows.change: Add a short empathic-discipline exercise for teachers and a daily greeting routine before or alongside the student programme; track exclusions by group.
rows.if: Exclusions, suspensions or disruption are the presenting problem

rows.basis: [Follow-up evidence](claims/sel-benefits-persist-follow-up.md) [+S]: a preschool SEL and language programme for low-income children showed young-adult advantages 17 years later and buffered adverse childhood experiences; the privacy rule is untested
rows.change: Start with regulation and predictability before social sharing; keep emotional disclosure private and optional; plan for multiple years.
rows.if: Many learners live with adversity, poverty or chronic stress

rows.basis: [Emotion labelling](claims/emotion-labeling-improves-regulation.md) [~M], carried from fearful adults in a clinical laboratory; [direct SEL instruction with deaf students](claims/intentional-sel-instruction-deaf-students.md) [+W]: one school leader's account of adopting a curriculum for direct instruction, no outcome measured; the visual supports are untested
rows.change: Use visual emotion scales and choice cards; teach the emotion words directly, in the learners' own language (a signed language for deaf learners); allow pointing or drawing in check-ins; extend practice cycles. Where learners have had little deep communication at home (many deaf children have hearing parents who do not sign fluently), teach the skills more directly and explicitly rather than expecting them to be picked up.
rows.if: Learners use a language other than the language of instruction, have low literacy, or are deaf or hard of hearing

rows.basis: [Follow-up synthesis](claims/sel-benefits-persist-follow-up.md) [~S]: benefits similar across race, socioeconomic status and school location (abstract); adaptation itself is untested
rows.change: Adapt scenarios, emotion vocabulary and norms for expression with families and learners; keep the explicit, active, sequenced structure.
rows.if: The programme was designed in another country or culture

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Run the skill lesson whole-class with paired rehearsal and cue cards; use a 2-minute written check-in instead of a sharing circle; coach a few learners each day in rotation.
rows.if: One teacher with a large class (30+) and little time

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Run check-ins as a private poll or chat message so remote learners are seen equally; pair each remote learner with one in the room for rehearsal (breakout or phone call); send the week's skill as a short text with one practice task.
rows.if: Mixed modes: some learners remote, some in the room, or phone-only

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Use short video models and private reflection prompts; ask learners to log one real use of the skill a week; add a human contact (tutor message, peer partner) where possible, since coaching and modelling in the moment cannot happen.
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, no adult present

rows.basis: [Group rewards on individual learning](claims/cooperative-learning-group-rewards-and-individual-accountability.md) [~M], carried from achievement in cooperative methods; the audience format is untested
rows.change: Rehearse the exact interaction first with role-play and feedback; give each learner an individual role they are accountable for; debrief privately after.
rows.if: Learners will run something for a real audience (peer mediation, a family evening, mentoring younger pupils)

rows.basis: [Early-childhood synthesis](claims/sel-programs-improve-social-emotional-skills.md) [~S]: effects varied by informant and assessment type; [emotion labelling](claims/emotion-labeling-improves-regulation.md) [~M]: the physiological measure moved when self-report did not
rows.change: Add an observed or teacher-rated measure and a conduct record; report each separately.
rows.if: The evaluation relies on student self-report

rows.basis: [Spaced practice improves retention](claims/spaced-practice-improves-retention.md) [+S]
rows.change: Plan each topic's first study and at least one later review in a different week; keep the total practice time the same rather than adding sessions
rows.if: A course of several weeks with a final exam

rows.basis: [Spaced practice improves retention](claims/spaced-practice-improves-retention.md) [+S];  [The optimal gap grows with the retention interval](claims/optimal-isi-increases-with-retention-interval.md) [+M]; [The gap's effect depends on the retention interval](claims/isi-effect-nonmonotonic-joint-retention-interval.md) [~M]; [Short spacing won at a short test, long spacing at a long one](claims/proportionality-rule-long-spacing-weeks.md) [~M]
rows.change: Set longer gaps between first study and review for material needed later; review again closer to the date. Do not fix one gap for every course. In one experiment the best gap grew with the delay but shrank as a share of it (about 20–40% of a week, 5–10% of a year), and past the best gap recall declined slowly. The gap that suits a distant test can hurt a near one: in a lab experiment with word lists, repeating words a week apart rather than on the same day lowered recall on an immediate test (.24 against .42) but raised it on a test a week later (.14 against .06), so a course with both an early quiz and a late exam needs both short and long gaps
rows.if: The exam or use is months away

rows.basis: [Spaced retrieval improves retention](claims/spaced-retrieval-improves-retention.md) [+M]; [Spacing out retrieval practice beats massing it](claims/spaced-retrieval-outperforms-restudy.md) [+M]; [Retrieval practice improves long-term retention](claims/retrieval-practice-improves-retention.md) [+S]
rows.change: Make each review a recall attempt with corrective feedback rather than a reread, and space the quizzes rather than giving them together. The meta-analysis behind the first two links (29 studies, g = 0.74) compared spaced with massed retrieval, so it shows spacing matters within retrieval; recall over rereading rests on the testing-effect evidence
rows.if: Reviews can be short quizzes in an app or LMS

rows.basis: [Expanding and uniform schedules do not differ](claims/expanding-versus-uniform-retrieval-no-difference.md) [~M]; [More exposures favour the expanding schedule](claims/exposures-moderate-expanding-schedule-benefit.md) [~M]; [Expanding gaps led in an earlier synthesis, tentatively](claims/expanding-isis-better-than-fixed-tentative.md) [~W]; [Expanding was no better than fixed in one experiment](claims/expanding-not-better-than-fixed-interval.md) [~W]
rows.change: Default to equal intervals for simplicity; consider expanding only if each item will be retrieved many times. Across 54 effect sizes the two did not differ (g = 0.034); studies giving more retrievals per item tended to favour expanding, a between-study moderator with no printed size, not a within-study test. An earlier synthesis of mostly paired-associate studies found expanding gaps ahead overall but called the result tentative because the studies varied widely, and a word-pair experiment found a 1-5-9 expanding schedule no better than 5-5-5
rows.if: The brief asks for a choice between expanding and fixed intervals

rows.basis: [Too high a new-item rate causes a phase transition in learning rate](claims/leitner-queue-network-phase-transition-in-learning-rate.md) [~M]; [The optimal schedule reviews lower decks more often](claims/optimal-leitner-schedule-reviews-lower-decks-more-often.md) [+W]
rows.change: Cap the number of new items introduced per session; above a threshold, items pile up in the first deck and learning stalls. Give the lower decks (new and recently missed items) more review time than the higher ones. The threshold comes from a queueing model and one crowd-worker vocabulary experiment; the deck allocation is model output only, so tune the rate locally by watching how many items pile up in the first deck
rows.if: A flashcard or Leitner-box system with a steady flow of new items

rows.basis: [Long-gap dropout matched conventional schedules in fewer trials](claims/dropout-long-isi-similar-performance-fewer-trials.md) [+W]; [Dropout helped initially missed items most](claims/dropout-benefits-initially-incorrect-items.md) [+W]; [Dropout depends on the interval](claims/dropout-effectiveness-depends-on-interval.md) [~W]; [Short-gap dropout lowered final recall](claims/short-isi-dropout-lower-performance.md) [-W]
rows.change: Drop an item from the session's practice once it is recalled, but only where other items separate its repetitions by a long gap; spend the saved trials on missed items. With short gaps, keep the item in practice. The saved trials pay off mainly on the items missed at first. One lab study of undergraduates with foreign-word pairs; untested in classrooms or apps in the wiki
rows.if: Session time is short and the item list is long

rows.basis: [Spaced retrieval after a financial workshop improved retention at five months](claims/spaced-beats-massed-and-control-financial-knowledge.md) [+M]
rows.change: Add spaced follow-up quizzes in the weeks after the workshop
rows.if: A one-day workshop with no follow-up sessions

rows.basis: [Weekly spaced recall quizzes improved six-month retention](claims/spaced-recall-quizzes-improve-long-term-retention-fundamental-math-concepts.md) [+M]; [Spaced recall raised the post-test without harming new learning](claims/spaced-recall-improves-posttest-without-harming-new-learning.md) [+M]; [Spaced recall quizzes helped without immediate feedback](claims/testing-effect-persists-without-immediate-feedback.md) [+W]; [The benefit held across instructor experience](claims/spaced-recall-effective-regardless-instructor-experience.md) [+W]; [The benefit held across class hours](claims/spaced-recall-effective-regardless-class-hour.md) [+W]
rows.change: Give a short weekly recall quiz on a fixed set of earlier fundamental concepts, cycling so each returns about every four weeks, in place of part of the quizzing on current material. If feedback cannot be immediate, release scores and worked solutions later the same day. In one randomised trial in 17 precalculus sections (128 students), this raised a retention index on those concepts six months later (81.6% against 77.3%) and the whole post-test (72.4% against 68.5%), while the final exam on current material did not differ detectably (74.9% against 76.4%; equivalence not tested; no effect size printed). The benefit did not vary detectably with instructor experience or class hour, which is a non-significant test, not shown sameness
rows.if: A taught course that keeps moving to new topics (mathematics, a cumulative curriculum) with no spare class time

rows.basis: [Learners misjudge spacing benefits](claims/learners-misjudge-spacing-benefits.md) [~M]; [Learners underuse spacing and retrieval practice](claims/learners-underuse-effective-learning-strategies.md) [+W]
rows.change: Release review sessions on a schedule and send reminders; do not leave the timing to learners, who prefer massing and, by a review's account, underuse spacing generally
rows.if: `online-self-paced` with learners choosing when to study

rows.basis: [Learners rarely opened immediate transfer cards and asked for delayed review](claims/transfer-practice-timing-mismatch-delayed-review.md) [~W]
rows.change: Offer a later, collected review of saved or missed problems (a weekly "wrong-book") rather than an immediate follow-up card
rows.if: Learners want saved problems back later rather than straight after solving

rows.basis: [Distributed practice benefits L2 learning, with limits on very long spreads](claims/distributed-practice-limits-l2.md) [~W]
rows.change: Space vocabulary reviews across the term; do not stretch the gaps across years
rows.if: Second-language vocabulary in a course of a semester or longer

rows.basis: [Spaced retrieval wins at the final test despite lower initial recall](claims/spaced-retrieval-outperforms-massed-retrieval-despite-lower-initial-recall.md) [+M]
rows.change: Report a delayed test as well; spaced reviews lower practice accuracy while raising delayed recall
rows.if: The schedule is judged by practice accuracy

rows.basis: [Spaced practice improves retention](claims/spaced-practice-improves-retention.md) [~M]
rows.change: Still space practice, but expect a smaller benefit than for verbal material, and do not lengthen gaps as far as for facts: in a meta-analysis across task types the effect (d = 0.46 overall) was smaller for complex tasks, and longer gaps helped verbal tasks but reduced the benefit for skills such as typing
rows.if: The skill is a complex task or a motor skill rather than recall of items

rows.basis: [Preschoolers showed no spacing effect in free recall](claims/preschoolers-no-spacing-effect-free-recall.md) [~M]; [Grade and spacing interacted in children's recall](claims/grade-by-spacing-interaction-free-recall.md) [~M]
rows.change: Rely on repetition itself and check recall at a delay before claiming a spacing gain; the preschool row under *Fitting the design to a situation* on the [principle](principles/spaced-learning.md) gives the evidence and its limits (lag within one list, no day-scale test at this age in the wiki)
rows.if: The learners are preschool children

rows.basis: untested proposal; [argumentation improves reasoning](claims/argumentation-improves-reasoning.md) [~M] names prior knowledge as an open question on its claim page, not a tested moderator
rows.change: Lengthen preparation (a prior reading, or 20+ minutes with a structured source pack per side) and give an argument frame. Shorten open discussion. Defer SAC until a short explicit input on the evidence has been given.
rows.if: Expertise `novice` on the topic (cannot name evidence on either side)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Cut preparation and the source pack. Spend the time on the reversal and synthesis. Raise the synthesis bar: name the evidence that would settle the disagreement.
rows.if: Expertise `advanced` (graduate students, professionals who know the debate)

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page ("topics can be chosen to match learner maturity", "sentence stems"); [argumentation](claims/argumentation-improves-reasoning.md) [~M] reports larger effects in K-12 than higher education for online science argumentation, untested for SAC with children
rows.change: Use concrete, local questions (a class or school rule), pairs of two not four, sentence starters for restating ("You think… because…"), an oral synthesis recorded by the teacher, and shorter turns (about 2 minutes).
rows.if: Age `child` (upper primary)

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page (target learners); untested proposal for the adult change
rows.change: Use the default sequence. For adults, ask for the learner-valued goal explicitly, since adults often arrive with a held view; collect the starting position privately.
rows.if: Age `adolescent` or `adult` in civics, ethics, history or policy

rows.basis: [structured discussion methods](claims/structured-discussion-methods-improve-comprehension.md) [~M]: only a minority of discussion approaches improved comprehension or critical thinking (general discussion, not SAC)
rows.change: Put the content check in the source pack and in step 8 (an individual item on the evidence itself). Do not assume discussion delivered the content.
rows.if: Goal is `concept` or `principle` knowledge of the topic, not argument

rows.basis: untested proposal; perspective-taking and attitudes are not tested for SAC in this wiki
rows.change: Measure it separately, with a self-report or behaviour, at a `delayed` horizon. Do not infer it from a fair restatement in the session. Expect the effect of a single session to be small or short-lived.
rows.if: Goal is `attitude-motivation` (tolerance, openness to the other side)

rows.basis: untested proposal; [argumentation](claims/argumentation-improves-reasoning.md) [~M] includes online science argumentation, not SAC
rows.change: Use breakout rooms of four with a shared document whose columns are position / restatement / reversal / joint conclusion. Visit each room at the reversal. Give the timing in the document.
rows.if: Setting `online-instructor-led` (synchronous video)

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Run it asynchronously over `days-weeks`: positions posted, restatements as replies that the original author must accept, reversal posts, then a joint document. Grade the restatement and the individual position, not post counts. A shared misconception and a caricatured reversal will go unseen, so add a facilitator check before the synthesis.
rows.if: Setting `online-self-paced`, or no teacher present

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page ("strongest when the synthesis stage is treated as the instructional endpoint")
rows.change: Keep restate, reverse, synthesise and the individual check. Cut open discussion and do preparation from a one-page source sheet. Do not cut the synthesis or the individual check: they are what distinguish SAC from debate.
rows.if: `single-session` only (under 45 minutes)

rows.basis: [individual accountability](claims/cooperative-learning-group-rewards-and-individual-accountability.md) [~M], school studies of four weeks or more; untested for SAC
rows.change: Grade each learner's own position and restatement. If the joint report counts, make it a small share, or score it on each member's ability to defend a part chosen at random.
rows.if: High stakes: individual grades, or a joint report graded for the group

rows.basis: untested; from the earlier page ("emotional intensity", "performance pressure"); untested proposal for the language change
rows.change: Choose a question about a policy or interpretation, not a group of people. Let learners pick which position they prepare first. For learners working in a second language, give bilingual or simplified sources and allow written restatement.
rows.if: The topic is charged for someone present, or learners argue in a second language

rows.basis: [Rater training](claims/peer-assessment-benefits-assessor.md) [+M] (moderator across 58 studies, roles pooled); [rubric guidance](claims/rubrics-improve-peer-feedback-quality.md) [+M] (MOOC writers; graduate students)
rows.change: Run collaborative evaluation on two anchors first; give three criteria with described levels and sentence frames; one draft per reviewer; the teacher reads and returns a sample of comments each cycle; keep the teacher's own comments on content accuracy.
rows.if: Reviewers are `novice` in the genre or domain

rows.basis: [Rubric guidance](claims/rubrics-improve-peer-feedback-quality.md) [~M]: in a graduate course a rubric changed comment content and restrained reflective and divergent commentary
rows.change: Let the author name the criteria and the questions to answer; drop frames and anchors; ask for one substantial alternative rather than a list of fixes; use the rubric as shared vocabulary, not a score sheet.
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` or practising professionals

rows.basis: [Collaborative writing](claims/collaborative-writing-improves-text-quality.md) [+S]: in one small randomised study, 10–11-year-olds writing in structured pairs gained more in their individual writing; that was co-writing, not peer review. [Peer assessment](claims/peer-assessment-improves-performance.md) [+M] found no difference by education level
rows.change: Two criteria phrased as questions, with a picture or worked anchor; review in structured pairs, spoken first and then one written suggestion; the teacher models with a class draft each time; revise in the same or the next lesson.
rows.if: Learners are `child` (under 12)

rows.basis: [Peer accuracy](claims/peer-feedback-accuracy-depends-on-expertise.md) [~M]: AP English students' averaged rubric ratings correlated with expert scores about as well as teachers' did, in lower- as in higher-performing schools; correlational. [Web-SPA](claims/web-spa-peer-review-consistency-and-improvement.md) [+W]: 76 high-school computing students' peer marks were broadly consistent with the instructor's and work improved after review (a before-and-after report with no comparison group, read second-hand)
rows.change: Anonymous drafts, four or five reviewers per essay with a well-specified rubric, and the average of their ratings shown to the author beside the comments; teacher reads flagged disagreements.
rows.if: Learners are `adolescent` secondary-school writers

rows.basis: Untested proposal. [Process writing](claims/process-writing-improves-writing-quality.md) [~M] did not improve struggling writers' compositions (grades 1–12), which is a reason not to rely on the cycle alone for them; in one online peer-assessment study, [the cognitive feedback students received did not predict their project scores](claims/cognitive-feedback-benefits-assessors-not-assessees.md) [-W] and the authors conclude weak students did not gain from receiving more of it (correlational), so let these learners review as well as be reviewed
rows.change: Short drafts or one section; a "what works and should stay" field first; spoken comments recorded or scribed; one criterion per cycle; the teacher adds one direct comment so the author is not relying on peers alone.
rows.if: Learners have low confidence or low literacy, or are struggling writers

rows.basis: [Peer accuracy](claims/peer-feedback-accuracy-depends-on-expertise.md) [~M]: secondary-school writing only; [peer ratings of programming assignments](claims/sitthiworachart-peer-ratings-objective-judgements.md) [+W] correlated with instructors' and were more accurate on objective than subjective judgements (one tool evaluation, read second-hand); [students new to statistics](claims/peer-feedback-soft-evaluative-judgement-statistics.md) [~M] valued peers' alternative explanations but did not trust peer feedback for final application, because their peers were beginners too (one qualitative case study); the split of roles is untested
rows.change: Peers comment on clarity, structure and whether claims are supported; the teacher or an expert checks correctness unless there is an objective check reviewers can run (does the code pass the tests, does the answer match a worked one), in which case give them that check and let them judge against it.
rows.if: Quality turns on correctness (a calculation, code, a clinical or technical claim)

rows.basis: [Rubric guidance](claims/rubrics-improve-peer-feedback-quality.md) [+M]: MOOC writing raters, benefit concentrated on subjective, complex criteria and negligible on simple ones; in programming, [peers judged objective qualities more accurately than subjective ones](claims/sitthiworachart-peer-ratings-objective-judgements.md) [+W] without training, which is where calibration has least to add
rows.change: Spend calibration on those criteria; do not train or prompt for simple ones, which a checklist can cover.
rows.if: Criteria are subjective or complex (argument quality, audience fit), not simple and objective

rows.basis: [Assessor meta-analysis](claims/peer-assessment-benefits-assessor.md) [+M]: computer-mediated peer assessment did better than paper; [peer assessment](claims/peer-assessment-improves-performance.md) [+M] found no online/offline difference; [rating received reviews](claims/peerscholar-accountability-improves-expert-peer-correlation.md) [+W] raised peer–expert agreement in one tool's evaluation. The other tool rules are untested
rows.change: Use a tool that assigns drafts at random, hides authors' names, locks a review once submitted, shows the author all reviews together and lets the author rate each review's usefulness; a calibration anchor before the first review; a deadline for the revision plan.
rows.if: `online-instructor-led` or `online-self-paced`, asynchronous

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Run review asynchronously for everyone in one shared document or form, so no one reviews by ear; keep drafts short enough to read on a phone (one to two pages, or one section); in-room learners write comments in the same place rather than talking them across the table.
rows.if: Mixed modes: some learners in the room, some remote, or phone-only

rows.basis: [Peer feedback on writing](claims/peer-feedback-improves-writing.md) [+M]: number of peers did not moderate the effect; [several peer reviews beat one expert's](claims/multiple-peer-reviews-beat-single-expert-reviewer-sword.md) [+W] on draft-to-final improvement in one 28-student experiment; [peer accuracy](claims/peer-feedback-accuracy-depends-on-expertise.md) [~M]: averaged ratings, one subject, correlational; [MOOC grader bias](claims/grader-grade-relates-to-grading-reliability.md) [~W] varied with the gap between grader's and author's attainment, observational
rows.change: Two to three reviewers per draft at random, mixing reviewers' attainment; the teacher reads comments only where an author flags a disagreement, spot-checks a small sample of drafts against the peer scores, and gives one class-wide note on the commonest problem; use averaged ratings rather than single reviews.
rows.if: One teacher for a large class, or no teacher reaches each pair

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: One short draft brought to the session; 10 minutes on one anchor; one review of one draft; 10 minutes to plan and start revising in the room; the author leaves with the plan.
rows.if: `single-session` only

rows.basis: [Grading the quality of reviews rather than peer-assessed marks](claims/grading-review-quality-reduces-tensions-improves-correlations.md) [+W] reduced tensions and raised student–instructor mark agreement over three semesters of one undergraduate course (reported second-hand, no effect size); tying part of the reviewer's mark to review quality is a [proactive quality control](claims/peer-assessment-quality-control-proactive-reactive.md) [+W] in one inventory of practice; [rubric use](claims/rubrics-improve-student-work.md) [~M] came with more stress and a performance-avoidance orientation in pre-service teachers' self-assessment, carried to peer review
rows.change: Keep review formative; mark the final version (teacher) and, if anything, the quality of comments given against the teacher's reading; never the peer rating of a peer's work.
rows.if: High stakes: peer ratings would count towards marks

rows.basis: [Probing feedback with revise-and-resubmit](claims/probing-feedback-revise-resubmit-evidence.md) [+W]: a case study of teacher candidates in clinical placements, instructor feedback not peer; progress was not linear
rows.change: Review the real work product against the workplace's own standards; the author states what decision the draft must support; a senior colleague reviews alongside peers and requires a revise-and-resubmit where evidence is missing.
rows.if: Adults in a work setting (design teams, clinical or teaching placements)

rows.basis: [Authentic audiences](claims/authentic-audiences-improve-student-work.md) [+S]: seventh-graders' compositions to distant peers were rated higher than to the teacher; a small study, not of review
rows.change: Reviewers read as that audience: one criterion is "what would this reader do or misunderstand"; where possible include one reviewer from outside the class; the final version goes to the audience after revision, not the draft.
rows.if: The product will go to a real audience (a client, a publication, a public showing, a hiring panel)

rows.basis: [Anonymous sharing](claims/anonymity-mitigates-evaluation-apprehension.md) [~W], authors' account of one undergraduate physics course, no test; in one MOOC, [graders rated work from their own country 3.6% higher](claims/in-group-favoritism-peer-grading-country.md) [~W] than work from elsewhere, a bias of graders and not a difference in the work, observational
rows.change: Anonymous to authors and with authors' names and origins hidden from reviewers (named to the teacher); "what works and should stay" first; random assignment of reviewers, across sites where there are several; no marks on reviews.
rows.if: Status or friendship differences, reviewers and authors from distinct sites or countries (a MOOC, a cross-site course), or reviews have hurt before

rows.basis: See the AI-feedback evidence on the [Peer Learning principle](principles/peer-learning.md), which this page does not repeat: there, [adding AI feedback to peer feedback](claims/ai-peer-feedback-writing-gains-differential.md) [+M] raised rated writing over peer feedback alone in one university L2 quasi-experiment. Here, [AI-supported diagnostic review](claims/revision-architecture-meaning-change-versus-surface.md) [+W] went with more meaning-level revision in one two-class study. The division of labour is untested
rows.change: Keep the peer step and its revision plan; let the AI comment on surface and technical points and ask peers for audience, argument and context; have authors say in the plan which source each change came from.
rows.if: Peer comments are combined with AI feedback on the same draft

rows.basis: [IRAT is more strongly associated with the final exam than TRAT](claims/irat-stronger-final-exam-association-than-trat.md) [+W]; [TRAT correlates weakly with lecture assessments](claims/trat-weak-correlation-lecture-assessments.md) [+W]
rows.change: Use the individual readiness test, not the team test, as the signal of individual preparation; in one pharmacy course it tracked the final exam more closely
rows.if: The instructor needs to know who prepared the reading

rows.basis: [Team RAT scores are higher than individual RAT](claims/team-rat-scores-higher-than-individual-rat.md) [~W]
rows.change: Expect this; do not read the team score as each member's learning, and recheck individuals on the missed items later
rows.if: Team test scores are much higher than individual ones

rows.basis: [Low-stress format had higher iSAT scores](claims/low-stress-tbl-higher-isat-scores.md) [+W]; [Low-stress format lowered stress and frustration](claims/low-stress-tbl-lower-stress-frustration.md) [+W]
rows.change: Lower the grade weight of the readiness tests; in one non-randomised comparison a low-stress format gave similar readiness scores, less stress and higher individual summative scores
rows.if: The cohort is in a high-stakes professional programme (medicine, dentistry)

rows.basis: [Feedback enhances retrieval practice](claims/feedback-enhances-retrieval-practice.md) [+M]; [Multiple-choice lures can be learned as false knowledge](claims/multiple-choice-lures-can-be-learned-as-false-knowledge.md) [-M]
rows.change: Give immediate feedback on every team item (scratch cards or digital), and on individual items if the team test is dropped
rows.if: Readiness tests are multiple choice

rows.basis: [Group rewards with individual accountability](claims/cooperative-learning-group-rewards-and-individual-accountability.md) [+W]
rows.change: Tie team credit to each member's individual performance, with peer evaluation, rather than to a single team product
rows.if: Team work counts towards grades

rows.basis: [Half of ND students report discomfort with semester-long teams](claims/nd-semester-long-team-discomfort.md) [~W]; [ND students prefer defined team roles](claims/nd-prefer-defined-team-roles.md) [~W]
rows.change: Give teams defined roles, let students have a say in forming them, allow teams of three to five, and check in on team comfort during the term
rows.if: Some learners are neurodivergent, or teams last a whole semester

rows.basis: [Peer discussion improves conceptual understanding](claims/peer-discussion-improves-conceptual-understanding.md) [+W]
rows.change: Give a short instructor explanation of that concept only, after the teams have discussed it
rows.if: The team test shows a concept most teams missed

rows.basis: [Active learning is strongest in small classes](claims/active-learning-strongest-small-classes.md) [~M]
rows.change: Keep the application exercises, which replace lecture time, but expect smaller gains than in classes of 50 or fewer
rows.if: The course is a large lecture section

rows.basis: [TBL module prepared students for independent projects](claims/tbl-module-prepares-independent-projects.md) [+W]
rows.change: Use a TBL module on the core concepts before learners design their own projects
rows.if: The course is a laboratory with independent projects later

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Run a single readiness cycle (individual test, team test with feedback, clarification, one application problem) with ad hoc teams; drop peer evaluation and appeals
rows.if: The brief is a one-off workshop, not a course

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Run the individual test in the platform, the team test in breakout rooms with a shared answer form that gives immediate feedback, and simultaneous reporting by posting answers at once
rows.if: The course runs live online

rows.basis: [Peer discussion improves conceptual understanding](claims/peer-discussion-improves-conceptual-understanding.md) [+M]
rows.change: Use the Peer Instruction configuration: a committed individual answer, pair discussion, a revote and a new question answered alone
rows.if: The prompt is a conceptual question with one defensible answer and a known misconception

rows.basis: [Longer wait time goes with higher-level responses](claims/increasing-wait-time-improves-response-quality.md) [+W]
rows.change: Lengthen the think phase and ask for a written note before talking
rows.if: Many learners rarely speak, or are working in a second language

rows.basis: [Minimal guidance is less effective for novices](claims/minimal-guidance-less-effective-for-novices.md) [~M]
rows.change: Give a short explanation or example before the prompt; the think phase needs something to think with
rows.if: Learners have not yet been taught the needed concept (`novice`)

rows.basis: [Interactive engagement requires constructive turn taking](claims/interactive-requires-constructive-turn-taking.md) [~W]
rows.change: Assign turns: one explains, the other questions, then swap; ask both to say where they disagree
rows.if: One partner tends to do all the talking

rows.basis: [Pairs worked better than triads in one inquiry](claims/pairs-better-than-triads-in-stellar-inquiry.md) [+W]; [ND students prefer teams of 3–5](claims/nd-prefer-teams-of-3-to-5-nt-prefer-pairs.md) [~W]
rows.change: Default to pairs, and offer trios where some learners prefer them; neurodivergent students in one survey were more comfortable in teams of three to five, neurotypical students in pairs
rows.if: The brief asks whether to use pairs or larger groups

rows.basis: [ND students avoid courses requiring public presentations](claims/nd-coping-failure-avoidance-public-presentations.md) [~W]
rows.change: Let the share be written or reported by the pair, not a forced individual public answer
rows.if: Some learners find speaking to the whole class hard

rows.basis: [Group rewards with individual accountability](claims/cooperative-learning-group-rewards-and-individual-accountability.md) [~M]
rows.change: Base any group credit on each learner's individual answer
rows.if: The routine will be used weekly as graded group work

rows.basis: [Some discussion approaches improve comprehension](claims/structured-discussion-methods-improve-comprehension.md) [~M]
rows.change: Teach a few discussion moves (asking for evidence, building on a partner's point) before using the routine; talk volume alone did not raise comprehension
rows.if: The prompt asks for interpretation of a text

rows.basis: [Discussion promotes more active thinking; lecture is no worse for information](claims/discussion-promotes-more-active-thought-than-lecture.md) [~W]
rows.change: Explain directly; use the routine where learners must do something with the information
rows.if: The aim is only to deliver information

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Call on randomly chosen pairs, or collect the share through a poll or written slips
rows.if: The class is large and a whole-class share would take too long

rows.basis: untested proposal
rows.change: Use breakout pairs with a timed think phase in the chat or a shared document, and collect the share in writing
rows.if: The class runs live online

rows.basis: [Lecture no worse for information](claims/discussion-promotes-more-active-thought-than-lecture.md) [~M]: reviews of college teaching-method comparisons
rows.change: Lecture is a defensible vehicle: keep segments and checks (step 3) and put the effort into assigned study and quizzes rather than replacing the lecture.
rows.if: The objectives are mostly terms, facts and descriptions to recall (acquiring information)

rows.basis: [Discussion promotes more active thought](claims/discussion-promotes-more-active-thought-than-lecture.md) [-M]; [Active Learning Improves Exam Performance](claims/active-learning-improves-exam-performance.md) [-S] (undergraduate STEM)
rows.change: Move those objectives out of lecture: in each session give at least one segment's worth of time (15–20 minutes, proposal) to problems or discussion with feedback, and assess application, not recall.
rows.if: The objectives include problem-solving, application or synthesis (promoting thought)

rows.basis: [Discussion claim](claims/discussion-promotes-more-active-thought-than-lecture.md) [~M] (Bligh's synthesis only); [Lecturing on values does not transact them to children](claims/lecturing-on-values-does-not-transact-values-effectively.md) [-W] (an article's report of value-education research in India, no designs printed)
rows.change: Do not rely on lecture; plan group discussion that works towards a shared conclusion, with the lecture limited to the information the discussion needs.
rows.if: The objective is a change of attitude, belief or values

rows.basis: [Lecture and 4C/ID matched on knowledge](claims/no-knowledge-difference-lecture-vs-4cid-consent-training.md) [~M]; [4C/ID scored higher on OSCEs, not significantly](claims/osce-advantage-4cid-not-significant.md) [~M]: one quasi-experiment with 21 emergency-care professionals; too small to settle either outcome
rows.change: Lecture only the knowledge the task needs, in one short segment; spend the rest on practicing the whole task with feedback, and assess the performance, not a written test.
rows.if: The objective is a practical or clinical skill, and the brief wants the whole task kept whole

rows.basis: [Lecture and 4C/ID matched on knowledge](claims/no-knowledge-difference-lecture-vs-4cid-consent-training.md) [~M], carried from emergency-care consent training to other work settings; untested beyond it
rows.change: Same as the skill row: a 10–15 minute explanation, then practice on the job task; do not expect the lecture to change performance by itself.
rows.if: Adults in work settings with a short training slot

rows.basis: Untested here; the [Active Learning principle](principles/active-learning.md)'s novice row carries the guidance evidence
rows.change: Keep lecture at the higher early share, with worked demonstrations, and checks after every segment; do not leave learners to discover the content in the activity time.
rows.if: Learners are `novice`, in the first weeks of an introductory course

rows.basis: [Active learning: largest effects in classes of 50 or fewer](claims/active-learning-improves-exam-performance.md) [~S]; [wireless keypads](claims/wireless-keypads-convert-passive-audience-to-active-learners.md) [+W] (one lecturer's account)
rows.change: Keep segments and checks, using formats that scale: one multiple-choice question per segment answered on phones or clickers, a projected answer distribution, and pair discussion when answers split; expect a smaller gain than in small classes.
rows.if: A large lecture hall with one lecturer for hundreds of learners

rows.basis: [Only high-intensity active learning narrowed gaps](claims/active-learning-improves-exam-performance.md) [~S]: 15 STEM studies; results varied widely between studies
rows.change: Make activity a large share of each session from the start (the late-session shares above), not an occasional break in lecture; track the gap per section.
rows.if: Narrowing gaps in exam scores or pass rates between student groups is a goal

rows.basis: [Lecture students 1.5 times more likely to fail](claims/lecturing-increases-stem-failure-rates.md) [-M]: 67 undergraduate STEM comparisons
rows.change: Treat lecture-only teaching as a known risk: add in-class activity and weekly checks, and monitor failure rates by section.
rows.if: Pass rates matter (gateway course, high failure)

rows.basis: [Long recorded lectures impeded focus; shorter segments appreciated](claims/long-recorded-lectures-impeded-focus.md) [~W]: student interviews in spring 2020 STEM courses; the segment length is untested
rows.change: Cut recordings into short pieces (proposal: under 10 minutes each) with one question after each; give a written summary of each piece's key point.
rows.if: Recorded lectures in a self-paced online course

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Use one response tool that works on a phone browser for everyone; read remote learners' questions aloud; caption the stream and post the slides with the key points written.
rows.if: Some learners join remotely while others are in the room, or learners have only a phone

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Plan three segments of about 12 minutes, one check question after each, and a 3-minute written summary at the end; give one short reading to take away instead of assigned study before.
rows.if: One session only (a guest lecture or a one-off talk)

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Two segments of 7–8 minutes, one check question each, and a 2-minute written summary; lecture only the information objectives and leave the others for another occasion.
rows.if: A fixed short time budget (for example 20 minutes)

rows.basis: [Students missed key points of a lectured proof](claims/students-did-not-recognize-lecture-proof-key-points.md) [~M] (one university mathematics lecture, as reviewed), carried to these learners; otherwise untested
rows.change: Give guided notes with the key points already written and gaps to fill; state each key point aloud and in writing; make check answers anonymous.
rows.if: Learners have low confidence, low literacy or are studying in a second language

rows.basis: [Observations: most teachers relied on passive lecture; students felt unchallenged](claims/ousd-passive-lecture-unchallenged-students.md) [-W] (one district's classroom observations; describes practice, does not test an alternative)
rows.change: Keep teacher talk to short segments and give most of the period to tasks that engage learners with the content.
rows.if: Secondary-school learners (`adolescent`)

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: One check question per segment with an answer key shown afterwards; read a sample of ten end-of-session summaries rather than all; let learners mark weekly quizzes automatically.
rows.if: Scarce facilitator time (no teaching assistants, one lecturer)

rows.basis: Untested
rows.change: Keep it; change only what this page's evidence says matters: put the brief's questions after lecture segments rather than at the end, and keep one check per segment.
rows.if: The brief names its own routine (its own clicker questions, quiz, rubric or study guide)

rows.basis: Untested
rows.change: Use them as given to sort objectives into information, thought, attitude and skill; do not substitute this page's examples.
rows.if: The brief gives its own categories, criteria or objectives

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Make in-session responses anonymous, show only the distribution, and let learners keep their written summaries.
rows.if: Sensitive topics, or answers learners would not want seen

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Keep the audience's experience whole: one or two questions put to the audience, no quiz; any assessment of a learner presenter is of the talk as given.
rows.if: The lecture is itself a performance for a real audience (a public lecture, a learner giving a talk)

rows.basis: [Learners in active classes felt they learned less](claims/active-learning-felt-learning-paradox.md) [~W] (a paper's report of one study)
rows.change: Tell learners that sessions with activity can feel less productive than a smooth lecture; judge learning with checks and quizzes, not ratings.
rows.if: Learners will rate the sessions, or the course will be judged by evaluations

rows.basis: [Active conditions more often had quizzes and homework](claims/active-learning-conditions-more-other-pedagogical-features.md) [~M]; [most active conditions kept a lecture component](claims/active-learning-courses-retain-lecture-component.md) [~M]
rows.change: Record every feature that changed besides class activity (quizzes, homework, exam preparation, lecture minutes) and hold what you can constant.
rows.if: The redesign will be compared with the old lecture course

rows.basis: [Example-based sequences outperform problem-only practice for novices](claims/worked-examples-with-practice-improve-transfer.md) [+M]; [Example–problem sequences reduce cognitive load](claims/worked-example-problem-sequences.md) [+M]
rows.change: Open with a fully worked example with the reasoning for each step visible, then a comparable problem
rows.if: A first lesson on a structured procedure for learners who have not met it

rows.basis: [Example-first beat problem-first on an immediate test](claims/worked-example-problem-sequences.md) [+M]
rows.change: Sequence example → problem in each pair, never problem → example
rows.if: One lesson with room for about four pairs

rows.basis: [Order advantage not detected at the final test](claims/identical-example-problem-order-advantage-not-detected-at-final-test.md) [~M]
rows.change: Vary the paired problem's surface or numbers, and do not expect an order effect to last to a final test
rows.if: The paired problem is identical to the example

rows.basis: [Fading worked steps eases the move to problem solving](claims/fading-worked-steps-facilitates-example-to-problem-transition.md) [+M]
rows.change: Move from full examples to examples with the last step left out, then two steps, then bare problems
rows.if: A unit of several lessons

rows.basis: [Learners learned most about the faded principles](claims/learners-learn-most-about-faded-principles.md) [+M]; [Backward fading and principle prompts supported transfer](claims/fading-and-principle-prompts-improve-probability-transfer.md) [+M]
rows.change: Fade the steps that apply the principles to be learned, and prompt learners to name the principle at each step
rows.if: Learners will be tested on the principles, not only the procedure

rows.basis: [Worked examples become less effective as expertise grows](claims/worked-examples-less-effective-with-expertise.md) [~M]
rows.change: Skip to completion or independent problems for those learners, and check again on a changed problem
rows.if: The first attempt shows learners can already solve and explain the problem

rows.basis: [Lower-prior-knowledge learners did better with full than completion examples](claims/lower-prior-knowledge-learners-score-higher-with-full-than-completion-worked-examples.md) [+M]
rows.change: Give full, not completion, examples to these learners
rows.if: The first attempt shows little task knowledge

rows.basis: [Split-attention examples lose their advantage](claims/split-attention-effect-in-worked-examples.md) [~M]; [Dual-mode presentation helps, except under high visual search without cues](claims/dual-mode-worked-example-presentation.md) [~W]
rows.change: Integrate the text into the diagram; if narration is used, add cues that direct attention when the visual search is heavy
rows.if: Examples come as a diagram plus separate text, or as narrated slides

rows.basis: [High variability aids learning from examples but harms learning from problems](claims/variability-effect-format-interaction.md) [~W]
rows.change: Pair varied problems with worked examples rather than with conventional problem solving
rows.if: The practice set uses widely varied problems

rows.basis: [Worked examples appeared in only about 42% of responses](claims/algorag-worked-example-retrieval-42-percent.md) [-W]
rows.change: Check that examples are actually delivered; one system included them in about 42% of responses despite a large problem bank
rows.if: An AI tutor or retrieval system is meant to supply worked examples

rows.basis: [Minimal guidance is less effective for novices](claims/minimal-guidance-less-effective-for-novices.md) [~S]: discovery and explicit-instruction comparisons, not workshops; 13 distinct studies in its table
rows.change: Lengthen the mini-lesson to 15–20 minutes with a guided "we do" before release; pull the novices into a small group for the first 10 minutes of the work block; use worked or partly completed models; shorten the independent block at first and lengthen it as they keep going unprompted.
rows.if: Learners are `novice` in the practice (cannot start or sustain a piece alone)

rows.basis: [Guidance can become redundant as expertise grows](claims/expertise-reversal-effect.md) [~M]: circuit-diagram trainees and cognitive-load reviews (14 distinct studies in its table), carried to classroom workshops
rows.change: Cut the mini-lesson to a teaching point and one model (3–5 minutes) or let learners choose a clinic; give the time to work; use conferences to extend rather than repair.
rows.if: Learners are `advanced` or already fluent in the practice

rows.basis: [Process writing](claims/process-writing-improves-writing-quality.md) [~M] gave a modest gain and none for struggling writers; [strategy instruction](claims/strategy-instruction-improves-writing-quality.md) [+M] was large, larger with self-regulation procedures and for struggling writers (grades 4–10)
rows.change: Teach each planning or revising strategy explicitly over at least three days, with goal-setting and self-monitoring (a checklist the writer ticks), and do not rely on drafting and conferring cycles alone.
rows.if: The goal is writing quality, or the class includes struggling writers

rows.basis: [Active learning](claims/active-learning-improves-exam-performance.md) [+S]: undergraduate STEM, active learning against lecture, largest in classes of 50 or fewer; carried to the workshop arc
rows.change: Run the work block as problem-solving in pairs or small groups; the teacher circulates, selects two or three solutions, and the share compares them; keep the block at least half the period.
rows.if: Undergraduates, or mathematics or science classes

rows.basis: Untested; from the earlier page's guidance on processing time
rows.change: Mini-lesson 5–10 minutes on the carpet; work block starting at 10–15 minutes and building stamina across weeks; oral rehearsal (tell a partner) before writing; shares in pairs.
rows.if: Young children (about 5–7)

rows.basis: [Contingent support](claims/contingent-scaffolding-improves-learning.md) [~M]: evidence mostly one-to-one tutoring (20 distinct studies in its table), and the review reports contingency across 30 students is hard
rows.change: Keep conferences to about 3 minutes, use small-group conferences for shared needs, keep a conference record so each learner is seen once a week, and teach a peer-conference protocol so partners give each other a first response.
rows.if: One teacher with 30 or more learners

rows.basis: [Task- and process-level feedback](claims/feedback-most-effective-at-task-and-process-levels.md) [~S]: meta-analyses of feedback content, not of brief checks; the one-check routine is untested
rows.change: Make each check one question and one written next step: "What are you working on? Here is one thing to try next." Put the stuck-menu and criteria on the wall or the page so the work goes on between checks.
rows.if: Scarce facilitator time (volunteers, a busy shift, a tutor who checks in briefly)

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Give the mini-lesson to everyone on the same screen; remote learners work in a shared document; the teacher rotates conferences in one queue across both groups (video or chat for remote learners) and takes one remote sharer each day. Phone-only learners get the model as a photo or short text and reply with a photo or voice note.
rows.if: Some learners in the room, some joining remotely, or phone-only

rows.basis: Untested proposal; [task- and process-level feedback](claims/feedback-most-effective-at-task-and-process-levels.md) [~S] carried to asynchronous feedback
rows.change: Mini-lesson as a 3–5 minute video with one model; the work block is the learner's own piece with the criteria checklist; replace conferring with written feedback on a submitted draft before the final version, and a forum share of one strategy tried.
rows.if: `online-self-paced`, no teacher present

rows.basis: Untested proposal; [high-intensity active learning](claims/active-learning-improves-exam-performance.md) [~S] narrowed gaps where lower intensity did not
rows.change: 5-minute mini-lesson, 23-minute work block with 4 conferences, 5-minute share, 2 minutes to set tomorrow's goal; or alternate days of mini-lesson-plus-work and work-plus-share. Do not let the mini-lesson take the work time.
rows.if: A fixed short time budget (for example a 35-minute period)

rows.basis: [A shareback of newly made work](claims/shareback-inflection-point-engagement.md) [+W] (adult workshops, one practitioner's observation); the timings are untested
rows.change: One product, revised once: 10-minute model, 20-minute draft, 10-minute partner or group share, 10-minute revision against one criterion, 5-minute whole-group share.
rows.if: A single session only (a one-off workshop)

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: The work block is the learner's own work product (a report, a care plan, a code change), the mini-lesson one technique from the job, and the share a peer showing how they used it; conferences are with a supervisor or experienced colleague.
rows.if: Adults in work settings

rows.basis: Untested; from the earlier page
rows.change: Post a "what to do when stuck" menu; partner the work so it is not solitary; confer early and briefly with these learners; allow oral rehearsal and dictation; keep anchor charts up during the work block.
rows.if: Learners with low confidence, or low reading or writing fluency

rows.basis: [Peer response groups](claims/peer-response-groups-writing-idea-units.md) [~M]: 46 fourth-grade English learners, more idea units, no significant gain in composition quality
rows.change: Use peer response to generate and add ideas, and teacher or criteria-based feedback for quality; do not expect peer groups alone to raise quality.
rows.if: English learners, or peer response in the work block

rows.basis: [Classroom discussion](claims/structured-discussion-methods-improve-comprehension.md) [~M]: gains in some approaches only, more talk alone did not produce them
rows.change: Structure the share or book-club talk with taught discourse moves (asking an authentic question, giving a reason from the text), taught in a mini-lesson first.
rows.if: Reading workshop, comprehension the goal

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Name the audience at launch; derive the criteria from what that audience needs; make the last share a publication or presentation to them; if the audience should not see drafts or the reasoning behind them, keep drafting and conferring private and show only the finished product.
rows.if: Products or performances for a real audience

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: The learner decides what is shared and with whom; conferences discuss craft, not content, unless the learner raises it; sharing is opt-in and a learner may share a strategy without showing the text.
rows.if: Private or sensitive material (personal writing, reflective journals)

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Keep the work block on the whole piece every day; teach each strategy as a move applied inside it; do not break the product into separate exercises.
rows.if: A whole-task performance the brief wants kept whole (a full essay, a complete investigation, a patient handover)

rows.basis: Untested proposal; [task- and process-level feedback](claims/feedback-most-effective-at-task-and-process-levels.md) [~S] for the one change
rows.change: Keep it and run it as given; change only what the evidence says matters (feedback that names the task or process and one next step, one strategy per mini-lesson). If the rubric rewards tool use, keep that criterion and add an unaided check beside it. Add no test or survey the brief did not ask for.
rows.if: The brief names its own routine, categories or rubric (a conference form, a check-in, a rubric, its own criteria)

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Use it as a worked contrast in a mini-lesson: show the error beside a corrected version and ask what changed.
rows.if: The brief reports an error the learners actually made

rows.basis: Untested proposal
rows.change: Map mini-lessons to the assessed outcomes; track coverage in conference records; keep the unaided end-of-unit piece as the measure rather than the conferred drafts.
rows.if: High stakes, or assessment and pacing systems built around uniform coverage

attitude-motivation.meaning: interest, beliefs, self-efficacy as the target

classroom.meaning: school or university class with a teacher

complex-skill.meaning: whole-task performance integrating several of the above

days-weeks.meaning: several sessions over up to about two months

novice.meaning: little or no prior knowledge of the target

online-instructor-led.meaning: digital with a live instructor or cohort

principle.meaning: rules, causal models, explanations to be understood to be applied

procedure.meaning: a step sequence to carry out
